Rethinking Humanitarianism | The rise of privatised aid: A conversation with Fogbow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:02:36 UTC
19:02:36 KST

Share & more
When private companies employ former military personnel and work with controversial political actors in the name of humanitarian aid, should they still follow humanitarian principles? And who holds them accountable?
These were some of the questions that animated an impassioned conversation between Fogbow CEO Brook Jerue and host Tammam Aloudat. The latest collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network tackles the rise of privatised, militarised, and politicised players in the humanitarian landscape.
“We are abiding by the same principles that everybody else is abiding by,” says Jerue, who argues that traditional humanitarian agencies also have ex-military in their fold, and that being a corporation allows them to deliver life-saving aid where others can’t.
Fogbow is an American firm that says it specialises in logistics – enabling access in tough environments. It counts former World Food Programme boss David Beasley as an adviser. So far, its work in humanitarian emergencies has mostly consisted of small air drops and truck deliveries in highly complex conflict zones in South Sudan, Sudan, and Gaza.
Critics say companies like Fogbow could be part of a new wave of private actors willing to take on projects that instrumentalise aid and serve the interests of particular governments – and that bypass traditional aid agencies that insist on following humanitarian principles.
Some say Fogbow’s operations could compromise humanitarian principles, have aided a party to the conflict in South Sudan, and could put aid recipients at risk.
Jerue disputes these claims, distinguishing Fogbow from players like the controversial Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, and instead painting a picture of a company using its military know-how to do what UN agencies can’t, and whose shareholders are willing to break even “because they just want to be a part of something that is bigger than themselves”.
“The reason why we can operate where we operate is because we're a private entity, because we're small and agile… if you turn into another WFP, you're just going to run into the same bureaucracy and problems they have,” says Jerue.

Harry and Meghan surprised by King Charles' letter on their status
LONDON, Sept 8 - Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are surprised by a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that they were no longer working members of the royal family and that they would remain private citizens, their spokesperson said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children returned to live in Britain last month, six years after stepping down from royal duties and moving to the U.S. during a period of estrangement and awkward relations with the royal family.
The return was a surprise even to close family with Harry's father, the king, only being told days before the news became public.
In a letter, authorised by Charles and sent to senior British officials on Monday, it was made clear that Harry and Meghan were no longer working members of the royal family.
A spokesperson for the couple said they had only been informed shortly before it was sent out and they were surprised by what had occurred.
The letter said their status, which was originally agreed with the late Queen Elizabeth in 2020, gave the couple personal latitude "in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish".
"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. ... The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it said.
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."
Since leaving for the U.S., the couple have continued to make the headlines as Harry accused the royals of neglect, the tabloid press of ruining his life and the government of failing to provide automatic police protection which would allow him to return home.
A committee which decides on what level of security he should be afforded at public expense is due to meet this week to decide what protection he should have now his family have returned to Britain.
They have also struck a number of commercial deals, most notably with streaming giant Netflix, while Meghan has launched a lifestyle brand As Ever. REUTERS

How South Korea finds itself trapped in the US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

How South Korea finds itself trapped in the US-Iran war
Washington is pressuring a reluctant Seoul to support its naval blockade of Iran; Tehran is threatening consequences.
Tehran has threatened “serious consequences” for South Korea if it interferes in the US-Israel war on Iran.
The warning comes amid reports that Seoul is mulling contributing to the US naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz passage, which has hampered Iran’s oil exports.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Philippines warns China may reassert itself amid US-South Korea drill cuts
- list 2 of 4Iraq faces sovereignty test as US-led military coalition exit nears
- list 3 of 4Oil prices surge as US-Iran strikes intensify in Strait of Hormuz
- list 4 of 4As fuel prices rise again, Iran’s government urges citizens to cut back
In a statement posted on X on Monday, Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran and South Korea had more than 64 years of diplomatic relations based on mutual respect and that Tehran values that friendship.
However, if South Korea joins the United States in its military actions against Iran at a time when the country is defending itself from what he called US aggression and “war crimes against women and children”, then there will be consequences, he warned.
Baghaei threatened that Iran would regard any military presence or participation in operations by another country in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz “would inevitably be regarded as direct support for the aggressor and would have serious consequences”.
“No sovereign and responsible country should succumb to US pressure and intimidation and become complicit in acts of aggression and horrific crimes against the great Iranian nation,” he added.
Seoul did not respond directly, but a Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement on Monday said it is communicating with the international community over the situation in the passageway.
Here’s what we know about how South Korea is getting roped in:
Why is South Korea involved?
Seoul, a close ally of Washington, has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump.
The issues began in mid-August, when Trump revealed in an interview, and later online, that he had spoken to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and asked that Seoul give “a little hand” in the war on Iran.
According to media reports, the two leaders had spoken over the phone on May 17.
Seoul said, “No, thanks!”, according to Trump’s message on social media.
However, as South Korea now knows, saying no to Trump has repercussions.
On August 16, Trump announced that the US would significantly scale back joint military drills it holds annually with South Korea – the evening before they were scheduled to begin.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercises are meant to sharpen Seoul’s readiness in case of a North Korean attack. They usually last for more than 11 days but were reduced to five.
In a post on his Truth Social site, Trump claimed the drills were “costly” and that they send a “hostile” signal to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with whom he is trying to build a relationship. South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said in parliament there was no warning from the US.
Trump also questioned why South Korea would refuse his request when thousands of US soldiers are stationed on the Korean Peninsula.
The US also cancelled another military exercise scheduled for September, although South Korea’s military revealed it received a notification much earlier in June, with Washington citing constraints due to the war on Iran.
How has South Korea responded?
President Lee, a liberal who pushes for a dialled-down defence posture, has opted to negotiate. His office earlier released statements saying it hopes for “meaningful dialogue” with Trump.
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported on Monday that Washington has, however, “ratcheted up pressure” on Seoul.
On Friday, a South Korean presidential official told Yonhap that Seoul could consider a military contribution to international measures seeking to free up navigation in the passageway as long as it does not affect the country’s defence readiness.
South Korea is looking at various options, the official said, including possible cooperation with France, the United Kingdom and other allies on sending noncombat and search-and-rescue forces.
The South Korean military has also started reviewing assets and troops that could be deployed, including maritime patrol aircraft, explosive ordnance disposal teams and unmanned mine detection and clearing systems, he added.
Such a move would be unpopular. The opposition has spoken out against a possible deployment, as have some within Lee’s ruling Democratic Party. Many South Koreans have also protested against the US-Israel war on Iran.
What is the history of US-South Korea relations?
South Korea became one of the US’s closest allies after Washington backed Seoul against Pyongyang in the Korean War of 1950.
The US supported Seoul’s economic and military growth in the years after. Under a treaty, some 29,000 US soldiers have been stationed permanently on the Korean Peninsula since the end of the war. Seoul has also relied on US defence might to deter nuclear-armed North Korea.
In return, South Korea supported several US wars, including the Iraq War, and is designated an important non-NATO ally.
In 2025, however, Washington imposed a 25 percent tariff on the country, testing relations. Seoul opted to negotiate rather than retaliate, leading the US to lower tariffs to 15 percent.
Many South Koreans were also alarmed after hundreds of South Koreans were arrested in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids on a Hyundai plant in Georgia in September 2025.
Last October, Trump travelled to Seoul in a historic state visit, and earlier this year, President Lee visited the US. Lee is also trying to resume dialogue between Washington and Pyongyang.
How is South Korea being affected by the US-Israel war on Iran?
South Korea is facing an economic crisis. The country relies on the Gulf supplies via the Strait of Hormuz for 60 to 70 percent of crude imports, meaning supply is being severely hit. The war has led to soaring inflation, causing the Korean won to fall to a 17-year low.
Seoul therefore has an interest in freeing up the strait. However, under Korean law, the government will require parliament’s approval before a military deployment, although some governing party members could oppose it.

A moderate dose of beer reduces your willingness to help others in pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

A moderate dose of beer might not impair your ability to read someone’s emotions, but it could make you less willing to help them if they are in pain, a new study suggests. Research published in Human Psychopharmacology: Clinical and Experimental indicates that social drinkers who consume a moderate amount of alcoholic beer show a reduced willingness to assist people in distressing situations. However, the study did not find evidence that drinking beer altered people’s ability to accurately perceive the feelings of others.
Empathy is a complex social skill that involves both recognizing how someone else feels and responding to that feeling. Scientists often divide this into different components, such as empathic accuracy and behavioral empathy. Empathic accuracy refers to the ability to correctly interpret another person’s emotional state, like realizing a friend is secretly sad even when they are smiling. Behavioral empathy describes the willingness to take action to help someone experiencing physical or emotional pain.
Alcohol is frequently consumed in social settings, prompting scientists to explore how it might alter these empathic abilities. Prior research has yielded mixed results, leading researchers to wonder if the type of beverage matters. For example, a 2018 study found that a moderate dose of vodka impaired the ability of men to accurately read positive emotions in others.
Lead author Isabelle Cristina Baltariu, a clinical psychologist and psychotherapist based in Romania, designed the new study with colleagues at the University of Groningen to build on this research progression. They wanted to test whether the same impairment holds true when people drink beer, which is widely consumed in everyday social situations, and whether alcohol dampens the actual willingness to help people in pain.
“This study was part of my doctoral research investigating the link between alcohol dependence, aggression, and empathy,” Baltariu told PsyPost. “Beyond the clinical curiosity shared with my advisors, this research addresses a critical societal issue in Romania, where alcohol-related violence and femicide remain widespread.”
“I wanted to look deeper into human psychological traits—specifically empathy—to help explain the mechanisms behind this aggression and find potential avenues for clinical intervention,” she said.
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 66 individuals, 62% of whom were men, with an average age of 25. Participants first completed baseline questionnaires, including a measure of their typical drinking habits to identify any hazardous patterns. The researchers then randomly assigned participants to drink either a moderate dose of alcoholic beer or an equivalent amount of non-alcoholic placebo beer.
The alcoholic beverage contained 6.6% alcohol, and each participant received a dose scaled to their body weight. On average, the blood alcohol concentration in the alcohol group peaked at 0.56 milligrams per liter about ten minutes after finishing the drink. Participants completed two tasks measuring empathy both before and after drinking.
Empathic accuracy was measured by having participants watch short video clips of people recounting positive or negative autobiographical events. Participants continuously rated how the person in the video was feeling, and these ratings were compared to how the individuals in the videos had actually rated their own feelings. To measure behavioral empathy, participants read hypothetical scenarios involving people in high levels of physical or emotional pain, or low-pain situations.
After reading the scenarios, participants used a slider scale from 0 to 100 to indicate how willing they would be to help the person in distress. When analyzing the results, the researchers did not replicate the findings of the 2018 study. They found no reliable evidence that drinking beer worsened participants’ ability to accurately read either positive or negative emotions in the video clips.
The ability to recognize emotions remained largely intact regardless of whether participants drank alcoholic or non-alcoholic beer. “The most remarkable aspect was observing the sheer degree of variability in how alcohol influences empathy across different measures—both within our study and across past literature,” Baltariu noted.
“Running a precise pharmacological experiment like this is a rare opportunity, and actually capturing these controlled behavioral and emotional shifts in real time reinforced just how complex human social cognition really is,” she added.
However, the alcoholic beer did alter participants’ willingness to help others, and this effect depended on their typical drinking habits. Among individuals who reported low, non-hazardous drinking habits on the initial questionnaire, behavioral empathy scores decreased after consuming alcohol.
This means they became less willing to help people in painful scenarios after a few drinks. Interestingly, this reduction in helpfulness did not appear among participants who regularly engaged in heavier, more hazardous drinking. The alcohol also did not reliably affect general helping behavior in low-pain scenarios for any group.
“I want to be careful to avoid oversimplification: alcohol does not instantly erase empathy,” Baltariu explained. “How significant that impairment is depends on the individual, their drinking habits, and the social context. It is about a loss of accuracy and sensitivity, not a total shutdown of human caring.”
The finding that alcohol reduces the willingness to help people in distress is generally consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2020. That earlier study indicated that sober young binge drinkers show impaired neural processing when viewing others in pain, requiring compensatory brain effort. The new study adds to this by showing an immediate drop in behavioral willingness to help after acute alcohol consumption.
On the other hand, the lack of an effect on emotion recognition stands in tension with a 2025 study covered by PsyPost. That research found that an intoxicating dose of alcohol impaired people’s ability to recognize angry expressions while increasing self-reported emotional connection with peers. It is worth noting that these studies measured distinct facets of empathy across different alcohol types and drinking populations, which might explain the differing results.
The 2025 study used live group interactions and measured anger recognition, while the new study used video-based empathic accuracy and hypothetical willingness to help.
“The main message is that alcohol can create a deceptive gap between how connected we feel and how accurately we actually read others,” Baltariu said. “In everyday life, knowing that alcohol quietly degrades our emotional radar helps explain why mild misunderstandings can easily turn into real friction over a couple of drinks.”
“It is important to view these findings as a foundational baseline,” she continued. “A moderate dose shows us that alcohol can measurably alter our capacity to empathize with others, even if the effect size appears modest under controlled laboratory conditions.”
“In real-life scenarios—or with higher alcohol intake—those subtle shifts in emotional accuracy can be the difference between de-escalating a disagreement and escalating it,” Baltariu pointed out.
There are a few other things to keep in mind when interpreting these new results. First, the researchers had a smaller number of female participants than they originally planned.
This was partly because they excluded women using hormonal contraceptives, as previous research suggests these medications can independently alter emotion recognition. Because of this smaller sample, it is difficult to say for sure whether men and women experience these alcohol-induced changes in empathy differently. Additionally, the study used a moderate dose of beer, which might act differently on the body and brain than a moderate dose of hard liquor.
Beer is carbonated, which can change how quickly alcohol is absorbed into the bloodstream. The researchers noted that different types of alcohol, consumed at varying doses, might produce different effects on social skills.
Future research could explore how alcohol alters empathy during live, unstructured social interactions rather than relying on computer-based video tasks and written scenarios.
“My immediate next step is concluding a clinical study that explores the alcohol-aggression link in individuals diagnosed with Alcohol Use Disorder,” Baltariu said. “Using a case-control design, we assessed both cognitive and affective empathy alongside proactive and reactive aggression.”
“Long-term, my goal is to pinpoint how specific empathy impairments drive different types of aggression, providing the necessary insights for clinical practice to develop targeted psychological interventions and treatments for alcohol-related violence,” she concluded.
The study, “Empathic Accuracy and Behavioral Empathy After a Moderate Dose of Beer,” was authored by Isabelle Cristina Baltariu, Violeta Enea, Teresa B. Prucker, and Marije aan het Rot.

‘Time waits for no man’: Chinese man’s 33-year, US$1.5 million world trip inspires many
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:00:18 KST

‘Time waits for no man’: Chinese man’s 33-year, US$1.5 million world trip inspires many
Chen draws a parallel between running a business and exploring the world – both require perseverance through challenges
A Chinese man has recently achieved his ambitious goal of travelling to 233 countries and regions around the world, sharing the life wisdom that “time waits for no man.”
Chen Jinwei, 53, returned to his hometown in Zhuji, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, after a remarkable 33-year global tour that ended when he returned from Peru after visiting various corners of the world.
Reports indicate that only about 70 individuals in China have previously travelled to 233 countries, territories, and regions.
As the owner of a machinery company, Chen invested a total of 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) into his journeys.
His international adventures began in 1993 with a trip to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.
At that time, the internet was still not widespread, and Chen felt a strong desire to learn “what the other side of the world looks like” – not through books or hearsay, but through his own firsthand experiences.

Spanish archaeologists find 4,400-year-old tomb in Egypt with original colours intact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:10 UTC
19:00:10 KST

A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological team has found in Saqqara an outstanding late Fifth Dynasty tomb with two chapels and colourful reliefs of farming and offering processions.
A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological mission, led by Spanish Egyptologist Josep Cervelló, has uncovered a "striking and beautiful" tomb dating from the late Fifth Dynasty of Egypt's Old Kingdom (2494-2345 BC) in the Saqqara necropolis, southwest of Cairo.
The find was made during this summer's excavations, led by the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities. It is an exceptional mastaba with two funerary chapels, commissioned by Yunmen, a senior official under Pharaoh Djedkare Isesi, who also ordered that his father, Iti, a lower-ranking official, be buried there.
Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities confirmed that the tomb dates from the end of the Fifth Dynasty, during the reign of Djedkare Isesi, and is located in the Mariette necropolis, north of Saqqara. According to the statement, it contains "two funerary chapels belonging to two high-ranking officials, Younmin and his father, Ity".
According to the UAB, the tomb has made it possible to identify figures of great historical, social and cultural interest. For the archaeological team, the discovery has also been a surprise because of the richness and beauty of the monument.
Among the most notable features are a high-quality architrave and funerary texts adapted to the figure and offices of their owner. The Egyptian ministry also highlights the exceptional state of preservation of the scenes and reliefs, which show "agricultural activities and processions with offerings", and notes that many of them "have retained their original colours".
The decoration also includes depictions of donkeys and other animals. According to the Egyptian authorities, the discovery "provides new and valuable data on the architecture, art and administrative life of ancient Egypt at the end of the Fifth Dynasty".
The excavation reveals daily life in the Saqqara necropolis
As well as its historical and scientific value, the mastaba stands out for its beauty. Archaeologists believe that the double tomb may reflect the social ascent of Yunmen, the son of a provincial official who rose to a senior position in the central administration and wanted to share his funerary destiny with his father.
The area has been known since the excavations carried out by Auguste Mariette in the 19th century, but it had never been studied and documented in depth. The research aimed to reconstruct the topography of Saqqara and to understand the necropolis as a living space, where ancient Egyptians brought offerings and worked continuously on the construction of funerary monuments.
The aim is to understand how the necropolis was organised and operated, from its streets and squares to the movement of people and the cult rituals. The analysis of maps and the reconstruction of the layout led the team to a previously unknown mastaba and to indications of two more nearby, which they hope to excavate in future seasons.

The Leaders AI Innovation Needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

For over 25 years, I have studied exceptional leaders of innovation, individuals from a range of companies and countries, from the Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi to Pixar. For hundreds of hours, I have observed leaders who have figured out how to get their colleagues to adopt emerging technologies to innovate and change the game for their customers.
What I have learned from doing this work is this: leading AI innovation is not about having a vision and getting others to follow you to the future; rather, it is about inviting others to co-create the future with you.
This is also true of the AI age. While virtually every company is scrambling to adopt new AI practices, the leaders who have made the most progress are those who believe the value of AI will come from using the technology to do work people could never do themselves, and the least value will come from simply swapping machines for people. Their goal is to pursue solutions that augment human ingenuity. And they appreciate that their toughest challenge is about people, not technology. These leaders know that we all need help navigating uncertainty, and they encourage others to try out new ways of working despite real intellectual and emotional demands.
Innovation is rarely the feat of a solo genius but rather the fruit of co-creation, which requires collaboration, experimentation, and learning from people with differing expertise and perspectives. Collaboration entails weaving together diversity of thought through constructive conflict to create a marketplace of ideas. Experimentation involves actively testing, pivoting, and refining. And learning happens when individuals and collectives reflect on what they have gleaned from those experiments—and then adapt their course of action.
To generate and scale innovative AI solutions, leaders rely on a repertoire of interrelated roles, what we refer to as the “ABCs” of leadership: architects, bridgers, and catalysts.
Architects know they cannot mandate innovation; they foster the culture and capabilities that enable co-creation. These leaders start by raising their organization’s collective aspirations through a shared sense of purpose and values. By re-shaping the social environment of their organizations, these leaders encourage their colleagues to work through the inevitable conflicts of collaborating with others and the fear of failure. They reward thoughtful risk-taking, treat intelligent failures as learning opportunities, and provide people the tools, data, and perhaps most importantly, the permission to try.
Bridgers work at the boundaries of their enterprises, building trust-based partnerships with those outside their walls. No company, no matter how well-resourced, has all the talent and tools they need for innovation given the unprecedented pace at which technology is advancing. With AI, I hear that there is a shortage of individuals who know how to translate and work across technology and business. Technical experts who are developing AI solutions typically do not have the contextual intelligence about the realities of business and what customers want, while the businesspeople do not appreciate the opportunities and risks of implementing the technology.
Catalysts have to mobilize stakeholders across whole industries, sectors, or nations to address the most audacious innovation challenges. Catalysts are also essential if we are to establish the global norms and guardrails that keep AI aligned with human interests. They can bring in overlooked voices, surface second-order effects, and help mitigate AI risks and share the benefits of AI more equitably.
Many leaders must be prepared to reinvent themselves if they hope not only to generate AI innovative solutions but actually turn them into reality—launch or commercialize them so they have the desired impact. They must give up being the smartest person in the room and get comfortable collaborating, experimenting, and learning with “unusual suspects.”
Even AI-first executives admit we do not know where AI will take us nor how we are going to get there. The winners of the AI race will be the companies whose leaders accept that their task is wayfinding. Leaders must enable their colleagues to have the courage and curiosity of explorers who once crossed the uncharted oceans without clarity about their destination. Fortunately, we have access to more sophisticated tools than the ancient seafarers. For AI to make a positive difference for customers and society, it will take individuals at all levels of our organizations to be willing and able to join the journey.

first single-family home in greece achieves LEED platinum certification for sustainable living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

19:00:02 KST

HOME UNIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL ENGINEERING AND SMART SYSTEMS
Greek studio ECLÉDE designs a 425-square-meter residence located between Lycabettus Hill and Kolonaki. Named Boomerang Athens, this is the first single-family home in Greece to achieve LEED Platinum certification under LEED v4.1 BD+C, the world’s most widely recognized green building rating system, providing a global framework for healthy, efficient, and cost-effective architecture. Designed as a climate-responsive urban home, the project unifies architecture, engineering, smart automation, and material restraint into a cohesive concept. Central to its environmental design, a rhythmic vertical screen controls solar exposure and privacy while filtering shifting shadow patterns indoors. Integrated planting zones weave greenery across this exterior shell, complementing ground-level solar panels that supply clean electricity.
Boomerang Athens by ECLÉDE | all images courtesy of ECLÉDE
ECLÉDE INTEGRATED ARCHITECTURAL ETHOS
Directed by founder Vassilis Siafaricas, Athens-based practice ECLÉDE bridges architecture, engineering, and construction into a single discipline. Drawing on his multidisciplinary background, Siafaricas establishes a framework where spatial concepts are continuously evaluated against structural logic, energy performance, and construction quality. The firm’s project has earned global recognition, receiving the German Design Award 2026 for Excellent Architecture alongside honors from the A’ Design Awards and the Architecture & Design Community Award, while Siafaricas was named to Architizer’s Visionary 100 list.
designed to reduce energy demand while preserving privacy, natural light, and material warmth
AN INVISIBLE INFRASTRUCTURE OF COMFORT
Designed to reduce energy demand while preserving privacy, light, and material warmth, the four-level residence functions as a continuous vertical landscape, drawing the eye upward from street level to the open sky. The layout comprises four en-suite bedrooms, open-plan living areas, a private elevator, panoramic terraces, and a rooftop pool overlooking Athens. Inside, the atmosphere relies on a tactile material discipline, where smooth marble, raw stone, warm natural timber, and bespoke joinery blend with expansive triple-glazed openings that flood the rooms with soft daylight and frame sweeping urban views.
Behind these architectural surfaces lies a technical infrastructure engineered for maximum efficiency. An advanced thermal envelope works alongside heat pumps, underfloor heating, smart ventilation, and a KNX automation system that centrally manages lighting, solar shading, and microclimate. Low-emission materials and acoustic dampening further protect indoor air quality and comfort. Through this synthesis of engineering and craft, Boomerang Athens presents a contemporary vision of Greek residential architecture grounded in durability, environmental accountability, and functional precision.

US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

In January, the New York Police Department’s counterterrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media.
“The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read.
The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism.
One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions.
“Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate, or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded.
Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording.
The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counterterrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read.
US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people.
Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge.
Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement wants the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them.
“These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.”
“The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies.
“Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued.
Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counterterrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York.
Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Times obtained. The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read.
Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”.
“Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said Meta spokesperson Dina El-Kassaby.
Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people.
The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states.
Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they’re not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm.
“Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys. ”
The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone.
The concern over Meta’s smart glasses are part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use.
In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing.
The memo was a response to “AI 2027”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech.
Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest.

‘In parks you only see dogs, never children’: can Bogotá adapt to its ageing population?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

From his wheelchair, Alberto Delgado Londoño can see over the wall of the sunlit courtyard towards the mountains east of Bogotá, Colombia’s capital. The 74-year-old lives in a care home for destitute elderly people, which opened at the end of last year.
Social workers found him in hospital, where he was being treated for throat cancer and a head injury that left him partly paralysed. “I had nowhere to go,” he says. “My daughter couldn’t take me in because she’s a single mother, she already has two children.”
Delgado Londoño is one of a growing number of Bogotanos with nowhere to turn in old age – an estimated 1,100 elderly people in the city are homeless, without families to care for them. To reach this vulnerable group, Bogotá unveiled a plan last year to integrate its social care and health systems.
“We have to be a society that knows how to care for its adults,” says Gerson Bermont Galavis, Bogotá’s health secretary. This means overhauling healthcare, social care and employment, requiring “a totally different city”, he says.
The capital’s population peaked this year at about 7.9 million; it is forecast to start shrinking from 2027. Nearly 16% of its residents are aged over 60, with the number projected to reach nearly 20% by 2035, according to Bogotá’s Health Observatory.
Meanwhile, the old-age dependency ratio across Colombia is projected to double from 20.6% in 2025 to 42% by 2070, according to modelling by the country’s central bank. That means fewer taxpayers to foot the bill for public pensions and support a healthcare system already under strain from a national funding crisis.
As people live longer and birthrates fall, the UN’s Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (Eclac) notes that “the ageing process in the region is occurring faster than in other regions of the world”. By 2050, the UN projects that nearly one in five people will be over the age of 65, up from one in 11 in 2020. Bogotá is not yet the oldest city in the region, but the sudden slump in its birthrate suggests it could soon match other South American capitals, such as Buenos Aires, Santiago and Montevideo.
Bogotá’s total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is likely to have over her lifetime – is lower than Tokyo’s, at 0.82 in 2025. Nationally, the rate has also fallen sharply – down to 1.6 children for every woman in 2024, from 6.7 in 1960. It is far below the replacement rate of 2.1 required to maintain a stable population.
“In the parks you only see dogs, you never see children,” says Juliana Jaramillo, an economist who studies demography at Colombia’s central bank.
“But it’s really difficult for a government to reduce the cost of having a child,” she adds. “Instead of trying to reverse the trend, you have to adapt to a new scenario.”
The city is already adjusting to the demographic change. Nursery enrolment in Bogotá fell by 13% between 2019 and 2023, the steepest drop in the country, and 287 schools, mostly private, closed in the capital between 2019 and 2024.
“We have a city that is ageing very rapidly, and we’re not responding quickly enough,” says Dr Manuel González, who designs Bogotá’s health policy. Increased longevity means more people enduring unhealthy and lonely lives, he says. “We are spending 10 years of our lives in ill health.”
While increasing the birthrate is hard, the city is focusing on boosting “healthy life” expectancy and changing how the capital thinks about growing old.
At the heart of this attempt to rethink ageing is San Juan de Dios, a 100-year-old hospital complex in Bogotá’s historic centre, close to Colombia’s leading institutes for oncology, dermatology and neonatal care. It closed in 2001 amid a funding crisis, but the constitutional court subsequently declared it a site of national heritage and ordered that its 24 buildings be restored. Eleven are now being renovated.
The 16-hectare (40-acre) hospital campus that is being created will encompass centres for youth and mental health but also residential care for older people, health and research facilities, rewilded gardens and a cultural centre, costing about 4tn pesos (£940m) to restore.
“It’s being conceived of as a miniature city,” says González. “But the way it operated 100 years ago is no longer what we need.”
He thinks San Juan de Dios should work as an intergenerational model of healthcare, spanning birth to old age. In March, the Centre for Thought and Innovation on Ageing opened in the hospital’s old laundry. It will advise Bogotá and the surrounding region on preventive care, chronic diseases and disability management. At a new training centre, caregivers can learn practical skills, from managing catheters to transferring patients into wheelchairs.
“In Latin American countries like Colombia, caregiving has always fallen on households … and mainly on women,” says Paola Camelo Urrego, of the University of the Andes. In Bogotá, women devote nearly five hours a day to unpaid care and multigenerational homes are becoming less common, meaning fewer family members to help with dependents.
In 2020, Bogotá’s former mayor Claudia López opened “care blocks”, where caregivers can drop off a toddler or an elderly parent for a few hours. This network of 20 community centres also teaches people to live healthier, more independent lives. Inside one, a boisterous group of over-65s learn to use WhatsApp. Afterwards, they may learn English or how to repair a motorbike.
These centres have given caregivers greater recognition, says Camelo Urrego, but they have not redistributed who does the grandparent duties. “Women get home to find nothing has changed.”
“Loneliness really gets to me,” says Don Jorge, a 76-year-old who has recently recovered from a bout of tuberculosis. He rarely receives visitors in the nursing home and he misses having someone to confide in.
To reduce social isolation, the city has begun prescribing culture and nature-based activities. Instead of getting pills to cure their ills, patients can take part in activities such as visits to the botanic gardens, traditional marketplaces or community-run gardening. Last December, a gran baile mayor (seniors’ grand ball) drew about 4,500 older people who danced to live salsa at the city’s Movistar Arena.
Equally vital is changing how people think about ageing. “We can’t think of people over 50 as grandparents,” says María del Pilar López Uribe, Bogotá’s economic development secretary. “The problem isn’t finding people over 50 who want to work, it’s finding companies willing to take a chance on them.”
The city offers short courses to retrain older workers. Companies hiring workers over 50 receive a bonus, with an additional payout if the worker is retained. In time, other measures such as raising the retirement age may be needed. Colombian men now generally retire at 62 and women at 57, while average life expectancy is about 78.
As it is, the city can scarcely afford to pay for more pensioners. Bogotá’s GDP per capita was less than £10,500 in 2024, about a fifth of Tokyo’s. Colombia’s high inequality compounds the problem. About a third of workers in the capital operate informally, meaning a financially precarious old age is likely. Just 17% of retired women in Bogotá have a pension, and 29% of men.
Yet Jaramillo says Bogotá’s demographic trajectory is not set in stone. Most Colombian women have their babies aged between 20 and 29 – 10 years earlier than in developed countries, making the issue of fertility less pressing.
“That puts us in a very different position to Japan and the US, where policymakers might be worrying about how women can have children,” she says.
Meanwhile, Delgado Londoño remains upbeat about the future, despite his problems. “I’m working on a collection of poems,” he says, pulling out his phone to reveal a 100-verse poem about an arriero (muleteer) plodding through Colombia’s coffee region. “I keep writing.”

Press review: Iran expands its naval war with US and EU blocks US ambitions in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. Iran is pursuing a new approach to counter the US-imposed naval blockade of its ports; NATO’s European allies are trying to counter US ambitions in Greenland; and the EU is entering the heating season with the lowest level of gas storage in 15 years. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Iran expanding scope of its naval war with US
Tehran is fundamentally changing its approach to countering the US-imposed naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Islamic Republic will soon unilaterally establish a restricted-access zone in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Under this new initiative, any vessel attempting to head toward the Strait of Hormuz from either side without Iran’s approval will be added to a sanctions list. In other words, Tehran intends to oversee the entire maritime area, from the line of the US-imposed naval blockade to the loading ports deep within the Persian Gulf. This appears to be an attempt to prevent the operation of the alternative Strait of Hormuz corridor established by the US.
Yury Lyamin, a senior researcher at the Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that Iran’s "no-go zone" idea has clear objectives. "Most shipowners do not risk passing through the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian permission. However, the US has found companies willing to transport cargo, primarily oil, through the strait under Iranian fire with American air cover," the expert noted. "These include, first and foremost, the shipping division of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the Saudi Bahri national shipping company, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company (KOTC), and South Korea’s Sinokor company," he listed.
If these companies’ tankers transported oil directly to the buyer countries, it would not have a significant impact on supplies, Lamin pointed out. "That is why these companies’ tankers are now effectively moving back and forth between the Persian Gulf, where they load oil, and the Gulf of Oman, where they transfer that oil at sea to tankers belonging to other companies that do not want to take the risk of being targeted by Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz," the expert stressed.
"If Iran extends the no-go zone to the Gulf of Oman - and not just extends it, but begins to strike tankers there just as it does in the Strait of Hormuz - this will sharply increase the risks. This is especially true during the process of transferring oil from one tanker to another. This is a fairly lengthy operation, during which two tankers moored side by side are particularly exposed to any type of attack," the expert emphasized.
Izvestia: How European allies blocking US ambitions in Greenland
The Arctic Shield military drills have begun in Greenland, involving nearly 400 servicemen from ten NATO countries. Several other countries are represented by observers and logistics specialists. The exercises are officially intended to test allied coordination in challenging Arctic conditions and bolster NATO’s capabilities in the region. However, the drills are taking place amid US President Donald Trump’s ongoing claims to Greenland and discussions about whether European allies can independently ensure the island’s security. Experts believe the exercises also aim to show Washington that European countries are willing to strengthen Greenland’s defenses independently.
"Statements about containing China are nothing more than a media myth," military expert Vasily Dandykin told Izvestia. "NATO’s main focus in the Arctic has always been anti-Russian. At the same time, against the backdrop of Trump’s rhetoric, Denmark is trying to show its readiness to defend its territories and demonstrate the concept of ‘a Europe capable of acting without the US’," he noted.
According to the expert, the Europeans are unable to fully deploy a large military force in the region due to a lack of necessary infrastructure, and the military buildup itself only intensifies separatist sentiments among the local population.
The tensions around Greenland highlight a deeper crisis in relations between the US and European NATO members, Colonel Andrey Koshkin, head of the Political Analysis and Socio-Psychological Processes Department under the Plekhanov Russian University of Economics, emphasized. "From a defense standpoint, Washington has no problems in this region: the necessary military infrastructure was established there back during the Cold War. The attempt to reclaim ownership of the island is perceived by Europeans as a demonstration of harsh political domination," the expert pointed out. "Against this backdrop, European members of the alliance are forced to consider their own strategic autonomy. The growing uncertainty will inevitably lead to a transformation of NATO’s structure," he stressed.
At the same time, both experts agree that the real reason for the increased attention on Greenland is the competition over resources and the transport routes of the future.
Izvestia: Europe approaching winter with record gas shortage
Amid an abnormal heat wave and risks to LNG supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, the European fuel market is becoming increasingly unstable. Having turned away from Russian pipeline gas, the EU now depends on the US and Norway for nearly 60% of its gas supply. Experts say that the main threat this winter may not be a shortage of hydrocarbons but rather another surge in prices. The EU is entering the heating season with gas storage facilities at their lowest level in 15 years: 65.6%. Germany, Europe’s traditional industrial powerhouse, is among the most vulnerable EU countries. The Bundestag emphasizes that the current gas pricing model in Europe undermines the international competitiveness of German industry.
Over the past four years, Europe has almost completely reshaped the structure of its fuel imports. Currently, Norway accounts for 30-33% of supplies, and the US accounts for 25%. Together, these two countries cover nearly 60% of the EU’s needs. However, unlike pipeline gas, LNG is sold on the global market, with tankers heading to wherever the price is highest. Therefore, during the winter months, the EU will have to compete for available volumes with not only its neighbors, but also Asia’s largest importers: China, Japan, and South Korea.
Matthias Moosdorf, a German lawmaker representing the Alternative for Germany party, told Izvestia that relying on American LNG and Norwegian gas does not compensate for the advantages of previous long-term contracts with Russia. "That was a big mistake. We turned our backs on Russian pipeline gas, but we continue to buy that same gas through intermediaries at much higher prices," he emphasized. "Today, German industry and businesses pay some of the highest energy rates, and companies are losing their international competitiveness. This is not in Germany’s best interests," the politician noted.
Europe’s energy dependence has not disappeared; it has merely taken on a different form. Rather than relying on a single major pipeline supplier, the EU now depends on the global market, where gas prices are determined by demand at the largest LNG export terminals: Rotterdam, Doha, Houston, Tokyo, and Beijing, Alexander Frolov, deputy director of the Institute of International Economic Relations at MGIMO, told Izvestia. That is precisely why the main threat to Europe will be not so much a physical fuel shortage as a new round of rising gas prices, he explained.
The current situation differs significantly from the 2022 crisis. Back then, Europe faced a sharp decline in pipeline supplies. Today, Europe is dependent on the global LNG market, where tankers go wherever they can secure the highest price.
Vedomosti: Reasons behind North Korea, Russia quickly building road bridge across Tumen River
The bridge across the Tumen River on the border between Russia and North Korea opened to traffic on September 7. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song participated in the event via video conference, after which the first convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge. For the first time in history, the new bridge has linked these two neighboring countries with regular road traffic.
The idea of building a road bridge between North Korea and Russia had been on the negotiating agenda for several decades, but a final decision was not made until the 2024 summit between the leaders of these two countries, and this project was urgently needed, Alexander Vorontsov, head of the Korea and Mongolia Department at the Oriental Studies Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. The expert noted that North Korea (and, in the long term, the entire Korean Peninsula) is now essentially connected by road to the entire Eurasian continent. Although freight traffic between the countries will not immediately increase after the new bridge opens, it will obviously grow due to the diversification of transport routes, Vorontsov pointed out. In addition, it is now much more convenient for tourists from Russia’s Primorsky Region to travel, for example, to the border town of Rason on the Sea of Japan coast, which is part of North Korea’s first trade and economic zone or a little further, to the border with China, where ski tourism is developing on Mount Paektu.
At the same time, Russia and North Korea will take advantage of new opportunities "across the full spectrum of the two countries’ foreign policy and foreign economic interests," Vorontsov emphasized. As for the height of the bridge, it is indeed "not the tallest" - just like the railway bridge - but the two parties made the decision on its technical specifications, possibly even before 2024. The Tumen is a shallow river that carries a great deal of sediment. However, if a political decision is reached, further work could be carried out, such as deepening its bed. The Chinese have alternative ideas as well, such as digging a parallel navigable canal, the expert recalled.
The very fact that this project is underway is significant because it is the first road bridge between the two countries despite their long history of relations dating back to 1948, Alexander Zhebin, a leading research fellow at the Korean Studies Center of the China and Modern Asia Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, stated. Given the authorities’ serious plans to develop trade, the road bridge in particular could become an important means of transporting goods and also help boost tourist traffic, he noted.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Who can regulate global oil market right now?
The actions of OPEC+ have all but ceased to influence the global oil market, becoming little more than background noise. Although the alliance’s decisions affect buyer and seller sentiment, they are powerless to change the situation radically. China and the US are now vying for the role of oil market regulators. As the largest oil importer, China was expected to import up to 11.6 million barrels per day by 2025, accounting for 11% of global demand. The country possesses enormous oil reserves in storage, estimated at between 1.2 and 1.4 billion barrels. The US is also competing for this role. It produces more oil than any other country: 13.8 million barrels per day. Like China, the US has large oil reserves, but they have been depleted following significant market interventions this year. In addition, the US effectively controls production in Guyana, Canada, and Venezuela.
OPEC+ reached its peak influence on the global market has already passed, driven by several fundamental factors, energy expert Kirill Rodionov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. First, oil production is growing in North and South America. Second is the slowdown in global demand growth, partly due to the electrification of transportation in China, where electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids already account for more than half of new passenger car sales. The "supply race" for oil was expected to begin this year, with OPEC+ countries participating, but the Hormuz crisis prevented this from happening, the expert emphasized.
Without a recovery in production and export volumes from the Persian Gulf countries, even taking into account production growth in non-OPEC+ countries, it will take more than a year for the market to reach a balance between supply and demand. Iran and the US are currently responsible for ensuring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. They are effectively regulating the oil market, but since they are adversaries who cannot reach an agreement, chaos results instead. Even if the strait opens, a surplus will be a long way off. According to DA Consulting CEO Daniil Tyun, a significant portion of production will recover within one to two months, reaching about 70% of the previous level within three months and about 90% within six months. The remaining volumes will take longer to recover. Exports will take even longer to recover, he pointed out.
In the current situation, Russia has the opportunity to increase oil production and exports. However, according to Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov, Russia is falling short of its OPEC+ quotas by nearly one million barrels per day. Moreover, due to shipping issues in the Black Sea, Russian maritime oil exports have declined slightly over the past month, which could lead to a further decrease in production.

Gen AI Tools Are Now Being Used to Push ‘Slop Jihad’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video that depicted its members lowering men locked in a cage into a swimming pool and drowning them. Today, that video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon depicting fish in orange jumpsuits inside the cage, as SpongeBob lowers the cage into the water while Squidward films the scene.
The video, shared on TikTok, is part of what a new report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD) calls “Slop Jihad,” a trend where young supporters of Islamic terror groups like ISIS and al-Qaida appear to use generative AI tools to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes designed radicalize a new generation of online backing.
This shift “signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online,” concludes the report, which was shared exclusively with WIRED.
“The principal concern is the growing volume and diversity of material,” says Adam Hadley, executive director of Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed counter terrorism organization that has also written a report about the Slop Jihad trend. “Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences while reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently through fan edits, cartoons, memes, and other entertainment-oriented formats, after which engagement can drive algorithmic recommendations of related, more overt propaganda.”
Islamic terror groups have long demonstrated their capacity to adapt to new media environments to get their messages to a wide audience online, leveraging new and emerging technologies to aid recruitment and create a decentralized network of propaganda. This was seen in the early 2020s Alt Jihad movement, which sought to co-opt the aesthetics of the alt-right in the Islamic terrorism content.
These groups have also been making use of generative AI technology for a number of years. In 2024, the Islamic State-affiliated news program News Harvest began using AI-generated anchors to help disseminate propaganda videos quickly and cheaply.
But today, the look and feel of the content produced with generative AI is markedly different.
“This is new and it's still growing, it has not peaked by any means,” says Moustafa Ayad, the research chair in global Islamism and counter terrorism at ISD. “There's always been really shoddy content that's been produced in the support ecosystem, but it wasn't SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.”
Generative AI tools have also been utilized to quickly and cheaply turn official content from terror groups into animated videos. In one example, one TikTok account was turning the weekly al-Naba newsletter from ISIS into anime.
The Slop Jihad trend has seen some pushback from more traditional supporters who don’t like the new aesthetic. “There seems to be some animosity towards it, because they don't believe the producers of Slop Jihad are true believers,” Ayad says, referring to some reactions to the SpongeBob video. “But again, some accounts that have shared traditional official propaganda are sharing the newer videos. So there seems to be a love-hate relationship with the Slop Jihad content.”
For years now, TikTok has been central to Islamic terror groups online messaging campaign, taking advantage of the platform’s powerful algorithmic recommendations to spread their message. A report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2024 found that TikTok was among the top 10 platforms used to spread terrorist and extremist content.
While Ayad did find a limited number of Slop Jihad videos on other platforms like Instagram and Facebook, the vast majority of the videos were found on TikTok. In total, he found 150 Slop Jihad videos from 71 accounts with more than 5.4 million total views on the platform. Ayad believes the prevalence of this content on TikTok is down to the platform’s For You Page algorithm “that is hyper-targeted to user interests.” He also credits the high level of general AI slop on the platform and “an existing entrenched ecosystem of jihadist support on the platform.”
TikTok contested the findings of the report. "This report's vague methodology reaches poorly evidenced conclusions and doesn't reflect how people use our platform,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED. “We prohibit the presence of violent and hateful organisations, and we use a combination of advanced moderation technology, safety teams, and partnerships to proactively detect and remove violative content, as we keep TikTok a safe space for our community. All the content referenced in this report has been removed from TikTok."
Dozens of the videos identified by ISD for their report were deleted after WIRED shared them with TikTok.
WIRED shared the ISD report with several outside experts on Islamic terror groups' use of social media to radicalize followers, and all broadly agreed with ISD’s findings. “What is notable here is the ease with which generative AI allows a much broader and more decentralized set of users to remix jihadi figures and imagery and the extent to which that material can circulate across communities whose interest may be driven as much by violence, trolling, or notoriety as by actual commitment to jihadi ideology,” Aaron Zelin, a researcher who specializes in Jihadi extremism at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, tells WIRED.
While Ayad admits that some of the wilder Slop Jihad content may be difficult to identify as terror-related, much of it is very clearly supportive of terror groups and ideologies. TikTok has taken down some of the accounts Ayad was monitoring, but many of them have backup accounts in place and have signaled to their followers where they can find them in the case of a takedown.
“Some of the content is surviving for months at a time and continues to evade moderation efforts, whether it's their AI system that's meant to detect terrorist material or not,” Ayad says.

Insta360 X6 Review (2026): A Great 360 and Action Camera Hybrid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Larger sensors provide clearer, sharper video. Low-light performance improvements. 8K/50 fps 360 video. Shoot both 4K linear files and 8K 360 video simultaneously. Smaller body. Built-in storage and microSD card slot.
TIRED
Unresponsive haptic buttons. Mediocre pro recording features.
The combination of good video quality and user-friendly software has kept Insta360 at the forefront of the 360 camera world even as competitors like DJI and GoPro have carved out their own niche. With its latest camera, the Insta360 X6, the company is hoping to leap ahead of the pack again.
The Insta360 X6 brings a slightly larger sensor, faster video frame rates, better low-light performance, and tools to help you spend less time editing and more time filming. While it’s not a huge leap over its predecessor, the X6 is a solid improvement with several new features that might make upgrading worth it for some users.
What’s New
The X6 looks a little bit like if the X5 and the GoPro Max 2 had a baby. It’s shorter, squatter, and a tad bit wider than the X5, but not as small as the Max 2. That might sound like I’m setting it up to say it’s the Goldilocks size, but that’s not really the case. I actually like the individual sizes of the X5 and Max 2 better, the first for its narrower profile and the second for its much smaller overall size.
Along with the smaller size come two other major changes from the X5: the screen is smaller, and the physical buttons at the bottom are gone. Though there is noticeably less coverage, I didn’t find the smaller screen to make much difference. I could still see what I wanted to shoot, but the point of a 360 camera is you don’t need to frame shots. The main thing I use the screen for is making sure that the stitch line isn’t on my main subject.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
I do miss the X5’s physical buttons on the front, one to record and the other for the menu. There is still a record button, now on the side of the X6, but the onscreen buttons just aren’t as good. They provide haptic feedback (the buttons vibrate when you press them), but they don’t respond 100 percent of the time. I found them noticeably harder to activate compared to the X5’s physical buttons, and I prefer the X5’s front button to start recording.
Another change to the outside is one of the better things about the X6: There are now power contact points on the bottom, which means you can attach a powered selfie stick and charge your camera while you use it. This is a great new feature that I hope other manufacturers copy. And don’t worry, the standard 1/4-inch tripod mount is still there.
Insta360 also says the X6’s new replaceable lens covers are harder than those on previous models. I have never scratched the lenses on my X5, nor did I acquire any scratches during the couple of months I tested the X6. The camera has an IP68 rating, and it’s dustproof and waterproof down to 66 feet.
Speaking of batteries, perhaps my favorite thing about the redesigned X6 is that the battery is now … just a battery. In older X-series cameras, the battery door was part of the battery, which always seemed unnecessary and meant there was no chance of ever using the same battery in another Insta360 camera, like the Ace Pro 2. Now that is potentially possible. If you’re listening, Insta360, give us the same battery for the Ace Pro 3 that’s in the X6. Battery size has also increased from 2,400 mAh to 2,600 mAh compared to the X5.
New Innards
The X6 uses a larger 1/1.1-inch sensor, the same size as the one in the DJI Osmo 360. That’s up from the 1/1.28-inch sensor in the X5 (and note that 360 cameras have two sensors since they have two lenses), and it gives you marginally sharper, clearer video. I did not notice a huge difference when recording in 360 mode. Of the Insta360, GoPro, and DJI cameras I’ve tested, I still find the GoPro Max 2 footage to be the best quality overall, and to GoPro’s point when it launched the Max 2, the X6 only records 7.2K video versus the Max 2’s 8K video.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
At night, though, the X6 wins. It’s much brighter than the X5 or the GoPro for starters, and while sometimes it does render colors a little wonky, with blues tending toward green and yellows going more orange than they are in real life, it still produces the best 360-degree low-light footage I’ve shot. The Osmo 360 is a close second, but at times I find it has quite a bit of weird blur-like artifacts in low light.
One of the more exciting new features is single-lens mode, which, at least on the spec sheet, goes a long way to making the X6 a viable action camera replacement. I dream of one camera that can do it all, and the X6 is definitely closer than other 360 cameras in fulfilling that wish.
The X6 can now record up to 5K video in single-lens mode (up from 4K in the X5), but even better is the new InstaFrame 2.0 feature, which is Insta360’s name for the ability to record both 360 video and a single-lens shot at the same time. This greatly simplifies editing since you have a flat file to work from, and if you miss the shot in that one, you have the 360 footage to fall back on. This was always a great feature, but in the X5 the non-360 file was capped at 1080p, which made it less than useful. The X6 bumps that footage to 4K for the single-lens recording and up to 8K at 30 frames per second for the 360 footage recorded simultaneously, which makes this very usable and is, in fact, how I shot most of the time.
As I have said many times, no one wants to see raw 360 footage (yeah, yeah, I know VR is going to catch on one day, but I am not holding my breath), and while InstaFrame makes editing it down to a traditional linear video file about as easy as is possible, it is still kind of a pain. Advanced users will also find it annoying that you cannot use Insta360’s I-Log format (video log modes are to video what a RAW file is to still images, and capture a much wider dynamic range) with InstaFrame 2.0, but there are some pretty good preset color modes, and I recommend using them for everyday shots.
With I-Log, the X6 supports 10-bit recording when recording in 360 mode. In single-lens mode, you can only shoot in 8-bit I-Log. The higher the bit rate, the more color information is available (1,024 shades in 10-bit versus 256 in 8-bit). That’s a shame because, at least for my needs, this stops the X6 from replacing an action camera in my kit. Perhaps we’ll get this in the X7. For non-pro users, this is likely a moot point.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
Other new features in the X6 include 47 GB of internal storage. There’s still a microSD card slot, which is what I used in almost all my testing, but it’s nice to have the internal storage for those times that you forget an SD card, as I do from time to time. Even though I don’t use the internal storage, I love that it’s there as a backup.
The photo tools also got a bump, with 120-megapixel images (up from 72 MP in the X5) and a new AI reframing feature. In this mode, just press the shutter button and the camera will take three photos, one facing you, one facing out at (presumably) your subject, and one of those tiny world images. (I find the first two photo styles useful, but the latter is lame.) You also get the original 360 photo.
To my mind, useful software-driven features, like the triple-photo feature and InstaFrame 2.0, are what have always separated Insta360 from GoPro and DJI. They make it easier to get usable images and video out of the camera.
Finally, I’d like to point out something I haven’t seen mentioned much, but I love how fast the X6 starts up. You press power, and it’s up and running in about 200 milliseconds, which is the fastest start-up time of any action or 360 camera I’ve tested.
360 for Newbies
If you already own the X5, this is very much an incremental update. The new features are nice to have, but the basic video quality is comparable to the X5. If you’ve been thinking of getting a 360 camera but haven’t pulled the trigger yet, the X6 is worth considering. While I prefer the GoPro Max 2 in many shooting scenarios, the X6 wins in low light. I also love the ability to use it as a 5K action camera when you don’t need the 360 footage, as well as the option to shoot 4K and 360 video at the same time, neither of which is possible with the GoPro Max 2. Throw in the very nice editing software Insta360 offers, and you’ve got a great option for 360 camera newcomers.
Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More
