British officials have also considered personal sanctions against individual Israelis and restrictions involving goods originating in east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, although it remains unclear which measures will be included in the final package. Israel does not currently expect a major expansion of Britain’s restrictions on arms sales.
London has described the emerging policy as part of a broader “reset” toward Israeli settlements. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said his government is examining measures aimed at preventing trade with settlements.
Israeli officials are waiting to see whether Britain confines the measures to economic activity connected to settlements or also imposes sanctions on specific individuals. Officials assess that the European Union is less enthusiastic about taking such steps immediately before Israel’s election, partly out of concern that they could strengthen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu politically.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar warned last week that Israel would retaliate if London moved ahead.
“If Britain acts against the State of Israel, the State of Israel will act against Britain,” Sa’ar told ynet last week, referring to possible British measures linked to Israel’s advancement of construction plans in the E1 area.
Herzog, however, framed his appeal more broadly, urging foreign governments to abandon sanctions and boycotts altogether in favor of engagement.
“Stop,” he said. “Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts.”

- The drill is part of Super Garuda Shield 2026, a 21-nation exercise running through September 11 involving roughly 4,700 personnel across Indonesia.
U.S. and Indonesian forces fired rocket artillery and flew combat aircraft together during a live-fire exercise at Baturaja Combat Training Center on September 4 and 7, part of the ongoing Super Garuda Shield exercise in Indonesia.
The ground-fire portion combined U.S. Army M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems with Indonesian Army ASTROS II Mk6 launchers and Indonesian Marine Corps RM-70 Vampire launchers. In the air, Indonesian F-16 fighters flew alongside U.S. Army and Indonesian AH-64 Apache attack helicopters.
“Today was a great example of working together to conduct safe and responsible training,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Ed Matthaidess, Army Forces commander for Super Garuda Shield, after the September 4 event. “It’s a huge coalition effort, a lot of synchronization goes into that.”
“The combined joint land strike demonstrated what the United States and Indonesia can achieve when we train together,” said U.S. Marine Corps Maj. Jonathan Bowman, fires and effects coordinator for Marine Rotational Force-Darwin. “We are grateful to our Indonesian counterparts and hosts for their support and for the opportunity to learn from one another. Exercises like Super Garuda Shield strengthen the cooperation we need to operate together effectively.”
Getting different rocket systems and aircraft from two militaries firing on the same range required participants to reconcile differences in equipment and procedure well before anyone pulled a trigger.
“Executing joint and multinational fires coordination is among the most demanding tasks in modern combined arms warfare,” said U.S. Army Capt. Eric Brown, a fires planner with the 4th Infantry Division.
Brown said aligning Army, Marine Corps and Indonesian capabilities meant working through differing technical requirements and doctrine, and credited the Army’s Next Generation Command and Control technology with helping units share targeting data and synchronize fires in real time.
For the crews on the ground, that coordination came down to repetition.
“Lots of practicing, lots of run-throughs,” said U.S. Army Sgt. Madeleine Rocha, a HIMARS crew member with the Iowa Army National Guard. “We made sure that everything runs seamlessly.”
Rocha said training alongside Indonesian and other partner forces gave crews a chance to see how other militaries approach the same problems and adjust their own procedures as the exercise progressed.
The live-fire event is one piece of a much larger exercise. Super Garuda Shield 2026, running from August 31 to September 11 across sites including Bandung, Jakarta, Lampung, Baturaja and North Kalimantan, involves roughly 4,700 personnel from 21 countries this year, according to Indonesia’s military. Originally a bilateral drill between the U.S. and Indonesia dating back to 2007, the exercise expanded into its current multinational format in 2022 as regional security concerns in the Indo-Pacific grew, and this year’s iteration also included a coordinated multinational parachute jump into Baturaja involving Indonesian, American, Indian, Japanese and French troops.
Indonesia has continued to describe its participation as consistent with a foreign policy of strategic non-alignment, having also conducted separate military exercises with China this year, even as it deepens training ties with the United States and other Western partners.

China's Tianyu Telescope to be commissioned for scientific observations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:27:59 CST
18:27:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Tianyu Telescope, located in Lenghu, northwest China's Qinghai Province, has successfully captured an image of the North America Nebula and the Pelican Nebula in the constellation Cygnus, along with more than one million surrounding stars in the Milky Way in a single exposure.
This feat signals the telescope's transition to the scientific observation stage, according to People's Daily on Tuesday.
Initiated in 2022 and led by the Tsung-Dao Lee Institute (TDLI) of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, with the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences responsible for its development, the telescope is expected to begin formal scientific survey operations in October 2026.
The Tianyu Telescope covers a sky area of nearly nine square degrees in a single exposure, equivalent to more than 40 full moons.
Many violent events in the universe, such as stellar explosions and gravitational-wave flashes from neutron star mergers, often fade away within seconds to minutes. When space telescopes or gravitational-wave detectors send out alerts, the Tianyu Telescope can rapidly slew toward the target and "rewind" the sky area under its real-time monitoring, restoring the celestial view from seconds before the burst, said the report.
The Tianyu Telescope will carry out sustained photometric monitoring of hundreds of millions of celestial objects, capturing subtle variations in their brightness to discover exoplanets, various types of variable stars, supernovae and small bodies within the solar system, Feng Fabo, an associate professor at the TDLI and project director of the Tianyu Telescope, was quoted as saying by the newspaper.
The Tianyu project has already attracted research teams from Britain, Belgium and Chile, and its data will be coordinated with multiple survey projects both at home and abroad.
Moving forward, the Tianyu Telescope will undergo a phased transition from commissioning observations to stable operations, and from remote-controlled to fully-automated observing modes. ■

Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:27:44 UTC
18:27:44 KST

Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, brought Kyiv some "pretty good, decent" ideas on how to end Russia's war against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Sept. 8.
Zelensky said it remains unclear whether the proposals can actually work.
"We need to understand whether we can implement them and make them effective," the Ukrainian president said. "I don't know yet if it will work out."
His comments came days after Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv with revised peace proposals in an apparent attempt to restart negotiations that have been deadlocked for months.
Zelensky stopped short of disclosing the details of the U.S. proposals but pointed to two issues that could play an important role in any potential agreement: grain and energy.
"Grain and energy are sensitive issues for Ukraine and Russia," he said.
Grain, energy
One new proposal discussed during the talks involved a potential truce in the air, either focused on energy infrastructure or halting aerial strikes altogether, one person familiar with the negotiations previously told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia has not agreed to the proposal so far.
Both Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war. While Ukraine has targeted Russia's energy exports to cut off a key source of funding for the war, Moscow has focused on destroying Ukrainian power plants and substations in an effort to trigger blackouts across the country.
The issue has become particularly urgent for Kyiv ahead of another winter, when Ukrainian officials expect Russia to intensify attacks on the country's energy grid.
Last winter, Kyiv faced a major Russian campaign against its energy infrastructure, causing mass blackouts amid freezing temperatures.
Grain has also emerged as another sensitive issue.
Russia has intensified attacks on shipping corridors in the Black Sea, including deadly strikes on civilian grain ships. The campaign has contributed to declining exports, rising costs, and a shrinking number of vessels willing to dock at Ukrainian ports.
Zelensky said the consequences extend far beyond Ukraine and Russia.
"These are pressing issues for the entire world," he said. "And these are pressing issues for India today, for the Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Asia, and many other countries. We are ready to find a compromise here."
read also
Meeting with Trump
Zelensky said he hopes to meet Trump around Sept. 20 and plans to raise Ukraine's need for additional anti-ballistic missiles.
"We need a package of anti-ballistic missiles from the U.S. They heard in detail what we need," Zelensky said. "I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic."
Ukraine faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has increasingly used against Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky did not disclose the details of the proposed support package.
"I cannot disclose all the details here," he said. "We have agreed with the American side that we will prepare everything and then communicate with the Europeans."
Moscow's demands remain
Despite the renewed U.S. push, the central obstacles to a peace deal remain unchanged.
The negotiations have been effectively deadlocked since earlier this year as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire along the current front lines and demands that Ukraine cede Donbas — the strategically important, partially occupied region in eastern Ukraine — and abandon its NATO membership aspirations.
The Kremlin has not signaled that it is prepared to compromise on its territorial demands.
At the same time, Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing to escalate attacks on Ukrainian cities and the country's energy infrastructure over the winter.
"Putin still hopes to break us this winter and isn't willing to agree to anything," one Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent.

SINGAPORE, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's workplace safety and health performance remained broadly stable in the first half of 2026, with the annualized major injury rate falling to an all-time low, although the fatal injury rate rose, the Ministry of Manpower said on Tuesday.
The annualized major injury rate, excluding platform workers, improved to 14.6 per 100,000 workers in the first half from 15.8 a year earlier, the ministry said in a statement.
However, the overall fatal injury rate increased to 1.1 per 100,000 workers from 0.97 in the first half of 2025 and 0.96 in the second half of 2025, with 21 workplace fatalities recorded. Vehicular incidents were the leading cause, accounting for nine deaths.
The increase prompted the ministry and the Multi-Agency Workplace Safety and Health Taskforce to step up safety measures after seven workers died over four weeks in late May and June. These included tougher penalties and a two-week nationwide voluntary Safety Time-Out.
The ministry is also reviewing further measures to strengthen workplace safety ownership and accountability, including tougher enforcement, it said.
Minister of State for Manpower Dinesh Vasu Dash said the rise in fatal injuries, particularly those involving vehicles, remained a serious concern and urged employers and workers to stay vigilant. ■

WELLINGTON, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's student performance in science and mathematics has improved or stabilized after more than 20 years of decline, while reading fell to a new low, according to the 2025 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA).
New Zealand students remained above the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average in all three subjects, ranking ninth in reading, 10th in science and 16th in mathematics, broadly similar to 2022 results, a government statement said on Tuesday.
New Zealand's average science score rose from 504 to 509 points, while mathematics increased by one point to 480. Reading fell four points to 497, driven by a decline in boys' scores. The changes were statistically insignificant, Radio New Zealand reported.
Positively, New Zealand students were amongst the highest performers in computational problem-solving, the statement said.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said in the statement that the results indicated achievement was stabilizing after years of decline, but more needed to be done to raise performance.
However, New Zealand did not meet the OECD participation requirements for PISA 2025, with only 52 percent of selected schools and 76 percent of students participating. The results may therefore be more positive than those from a fully representative sample and should be treated with caution, the statement said.
Nearly a quarter of New Zealand students were low performers in reading, while 29 percent were low performers in mathematics, according to the PISA 2025 results. ■

Taiwan flu epidemic begins as severe cases, deaths climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:26:48 UTC
18:26:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday that the country has entered a flu epidemic period, with 105 severe cases and 19 deaths reported in one week.
CNA reported that health authorities recorded 115,136 flu-related outpatient and emergency visits from Aug. 30 to Sept. 5, up 11% from the previous week. Flu-related visits accounted for 11.2% of all outpatient and emergency visits, exceeding the 11% epidemic threshold.
Taiwan reported 105 new severe flu cases from Sept. 1-7, including 97 linked to H1N1, four to H3N2, and four to untyped influenza A. Authorities also reported 19 deaths, including 18 linked to H1N1 and one to untyped influenza A.
Laboratory monitoring shows influenza A remains the main type circulating in Taiwan. H1N1 accounted for 79.4% of detected flu viruses.
Taiwan has recorded 1,329 severe flu cases and 253 deaths so far this flu season. Most severe cases involved people aged 65 or older and those with chronic health conditions, while 68.6% of severe patients had not received this season’s flu vaccine.
COVID-19 infections continued to decline but remained at epidemic levels, health authorities said. Taiwan recorded 20,199 COVID-19-related outpatient and emergency visits from Aug. 30 to Sept. 5, down 9.7% from the previous week.
Authorities also reported 73 new severe local COVID-19 cases and 15 deaths from Sept. 1-7. Since October last year, Taiwan has recorded 622 severe local cases and 106 deaths.
Most severe COVID-19 cases involved people aged 65 or older and those with chronic health conditions. Among severe patients, 84.9% had not received this season’s COVID-19 vaccine.
Health authorities advised people with symptoms including a sore throat, cough, stuffy or runny nose, fever, fatigue, headache, or muscle pain to seek medical care. They said anyone experiencing difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, low blood pressure, or a high fever lasting more than 72 hours should seek treatment immediately.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ability Enterprise Co. posted its highest monthly revenue in a decade in August as it shifts from traditional camera manufacturing toward AI and smart imaging products.
The company reported August revenue of NT$1.3 billion (US$41 million), up 34.7% year-on-year. Consolidated revenue for the first eight months of the year totaled NT$8.3 billion, an increase of 50.06% from the same period last year, according to CTEE.
Ability is expanding beyond conventional camera products into areas such as edge AI, machine vision, and smart sensing, building on its experience in optics and imaging. The shift comes as AI applications expand from cloud-based systems to physical devices and machines.
Ability said 2026 marks an important stage in its transformation, with three new product lines — robot vision, drones, and AI smart lenses — moving from development and certification into mass production and shipments. With existing projects expanding and new customers and models being added, the company remains positive about its future operations.
Ability expects robot vision to become a major growth driver. The company has developed next-generation sensing and vision modules with Japanese and US customers for use in humanoid robots, service robots, and automated guided vehicles.
As AI-powered robots move from the concept stage toward commercialization, machine vision is becoming an important technology for helping them perceive their surroundings and identify objects.
For drones, Ability has developed high-end camera lenses and optical modules for environmental monitoring, infrastructure inspections, and public safety. The products have completed customer certification and are now entering delivery.
For the European market, Ability's AI smart lenses combine AI processing and image sensing for smart cities and traffic management. Ability expects orders to increase in the second half of the year.

U.S. and Russian warplanes to appear together at Egypt’s airshow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:24:47 UTC
18:24:47 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is sending F-16s, F-15Es, A-10s and C-130s to Egypt's El Alamein International Airshow, opening September 8 alongside more than 80 countries.
- Russia is separately showcasing its Su-57E stealth fighter at the same airshow, putting American and Russian military aircraft on display together.
American and Russian military aircraft will appear at the same airshow this week, as the U.S. Air Force sends fighters and cargo planes to Egypt’s El Alamein International Airshow alongside a Russian delegation set to showcase its Su-57E stealth fighter.
The 2026 Egypt International Airshow officially opens September 8 at El Alamein International Airport, drawing participants from more than 80 countries and more than 50 aircraft on display, according to a statement from U.S. Central Command. The event marks its second iteration and is intended to highlight Egypt’s aerospace capabilities while reinforcing the decades-long U.S.-Egypt defense relationship.
The U.S. Air Force and the Texas Air National Guard are sending personnel and aircraft to the show, including C-130J Super Hercules and C-130H Hercules cargo planes, A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, F-16 Fighting Falcon fighters, and F-15E Strike Eagle strike fighters. The U.S. delegation is also opening a pavilion featuring more than 25 American aerospace and defense companies.
“The United States is proud to participate in the El Alamein International Air Show 2026 and to open the U.S. Pavilion, featuring more than 25 American companies from among the world’s leading aerospace and defense innovators,” said Eric Gaudiosi, Charge d’Affaires ad interim at the U.S. Embassy in Cairo. “Our strong presence reflects the depth of the U.S.-Egypt partnership and our longstanding cooperation across the aviation, aerospace, defense, space, and commercial sectors. We look forward to building new partnerships and expanding opportunities that benefit both our countries.”
Russia is also attending the show with its own aircraft. Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, has said it will fly its Su-57E stealth fighter in a demonstration and display it on the ground, alongside the public debut of two new weapons built for the jet, according to Russian state media reports covered separately by The Defence Blog. Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheev has said the company has signed new Su-57E export contracts ahead of the show, though he has not named the buying countries or disclosed contract values, and Russia’s claims about the jet’s proven combat record have not matched independently documented losses of the aircraft during its war in Ukraine.
Egypt has maintained defense ties with both Washington and Moscow for decades, operating American-made F-16s alongside Russian-made air defense systems and other Soviet-legacy equipment, a balancing act reflected in this week’s airshow drawing military hardware from both countries onto the same tarmac. The U.S.-Egypt defense relationship dates back to the 1978 Camp David Accords, and Egypt remains one of the largest recipients of U.S. military aid in the world.

How the US war is driving up the cost of survival in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:22:20 UTC
18:22:20 KST

Breadcrumb
The things Iranians can no longer afford: Surviving the US war, sanctions and soaring inflation
"If you sit in my car right now, you would think it sounds like an old tractor," says Mohsen, a 40-year-old father of a three-year-old girl in Tehran. He knows his car is breaking down, but taking it to a mechanic is a luxury he can no longer afford.
"When I prioritise my family's expenses, repair costs never make the cut."
Mohsen earns a fixed monthly salary of 50 million tomans as an office employee. At the start of the Iranian calendar year, that amount was worth roughly $300.
Today, as Iran's currency continues its freefall amid tightening US sanctions and regional geopolitical turmoil, his wages translate to less than $200.
His predicament has become the new normal for Iran's middle and working classes.
While sanctions, and US sanctions in particular, are said to target the government, the reality on the ground tells a different story.
The intersection of international isolation, recent escalations, and domestic economic vulnerability has placed an unprecedented squeeze on ordinary citizens, reshaping their dietary habits, access to healthcare, and basic social lives.
According to the Statistical Centre of Iran, annual inflation reached 69 percent in August. The macroeconomic horizon offers little optimism: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects a stark reality for 2026, forecasting a 5.4 percent contraction in real GDP alongside consumer price inflation hovering at 68.9 percent.
For salaried employees like Mohsen, the gap between a fixed income and skyrocketing prices means constantly recalibrating how to survive.
"Being an employee in Iran means you agree on a fixed salary at the start of the year, and no matter what happens in the country, whether there is a war, intensified sanctions, or a blockade, your income stays the same," he explains.
He used to buy meat for his family every week; now it's a once-a-month purchase. Fresh fruit has seen a similar reduction.
Hoping to supplement his income, Mohsen recently registered with a ride-hailing app to work evening shifts, but the embarrassing mechanical noises of his deteriorating car forced him to stop.
Still, he considers himself one of the lucky ones. Because of an inherited property, he doesn't pay rent. "Looking at the terrifying housing market right now, almost all my colleagues are tenants who give up a massive chunk of their salaries just to keep a roof over their heads."
His primary anxiety is no longer his own comfort, but whether he can secure a baseline of welfare for his young daughter.
The rising cost of survival
The Iranian government is acutely aware of this mounting pressure. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh recently acknowledged the severe impact of inflation on daily life during a televised interview, announcing plans to increase the value of electronic coupons (Kala-barg) for lower-income brackets.
Currently, the state allocates a one-million-toman monthly credit to each citizen, restricted to basic goods such as meat, chicken, and milk. But the sheer speed of price hikes is rapidly eroding the effectiveness of this safety net.
The crisis extends far beyond the dinner table, altering family dynamics and fraying the social fabric.
Nasrin, a 39-year-old single mother and teacher in southern Tehran, can no longer afford private kindergarten for her five-year-old daughter, and public options in her area are virtually nonexistent.
When schools reopen for in-person classes this autumn, she will have no choice but to bring her child to the girls' elementary school where she works.
"Instead of playing with kids her age, she will have to sit in my classroom or the school office from early morning until noon," Nasrin says.
She admits that without her own parents' help providing basic groceries, surviving on a teacher's salary would be nearly impossible.
Beyond food and childcare, the cost of basic healthcare has surged, turning routine illnesses into financial emergencies.
Despite theoretical humanitarian exemptions in US sanctions, the medical supply chain has been choked by a combination of factors: pervasive "de-risking" and over-compliance by international banks, the Iranian government's severe shortage of foreign currency, and an ongoing maritime blockade.
A recent market analysis by Ham-Mihan highlighted staggering year-on-year price hikes for domestically produced and imported essential medications between September 2025 and September 2026.
The price of a standard package of Amoxicillin jumped from 320,000 to 1.23 million tomans. Acetaminophen with codeine surged from 137,000 to 650,000 tomans, and Clarithromycin more than tripled to 1.58 million tomans. Gabapentin, used for nerve pain, rose from 300,000 to 960,000 tomans.
These figures represent just a fraction of a broader, systemic pharmaceutical crisis that leaves patients with chronic or rare conditions highly vulnerable.
Feeling the squeeze
The physical and technological infrastructure ordinary Iranians rely on is also buckling under the weight of the geopolitical standoff.
Recent US strikes targeting Iran's petrochemical facilities have disrupted gasoline supplies, sparking widespread anxiety over potential fuel price hikes.
The economic daily Donya-e-Eqtesad recently warned that given Iran's structural dependence on energy subsidies, any sharp increase in petrol prices could trigger catastrophic disruptions across production chains and urban life.
At the same time, digital connectivity, a lifeline for education, business, and youth culture, is becoming prohibitively expensive.
Following the recent 40-day war, basic technological goods have seen massive markups. The Samsung Galaxy A07, considered an entry-level economy smartphone, now costs at least 50 million tomans on the local market, more than double a standard worker's monthly wage, up from under 20 million tomans just weeks earlier.
For the younger generation, this economic siege means the systematic stripping away of small, daily joys and personal milestones.
Fatima, a 27-year-old social media expert in the private sector, recently had to take out a new bank loan just to pay off the overdue instalments on previous debts.
"Every day, it gets harder to make my money last until the end of the month," she says. Her daily cafe routine was replaced by home-brewed coffee, which has now disappeared entirely, too. She's downgraded to the cheapest available brand of cigarettes. Cosmetics, like sunscreen, are being phased out of her budget, and dining out with friends is a relic of the past.
Yet Fatima's frustration is directed as much at the international actors shaping her reality as at the domestic situation.
Walking through Tehran in a short-sleeved T-shirt and jeans, without a headscarf, a direct defiance of the country's mandatory hijab laws that carries heavy risks of arrest, the severing of mobile networks, and loss of basic state services, she reflects on the geopolitical messaging directed at Iranians.
"The US President tweets asking why the Iranian people don't pour into the streets," Fatima says. "It's ridiculous. They torture us, so we protest? We are in a daily struggle. Just the way we look when we step outside is a struggle in itself."
Ariya Farahmand is an Iranian journalist
The writer has used a pseudonym for security reasons

Ministers hold to Swiftsure dismantling deadline this year

The Ministry of Defence remains committed to dismantling the former submarine Swiftsure by the end of 2026 despite the challenges recorded against the Submarine Dismantling Project in the latest major projects report, according to a written answer published on Monday.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked about the nature of the unforeseen challenges associated with the project as recorded in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority Major Projects Annual Report for 2025 to 2026.
Mr Pollard said: “The matters identified in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) Major Projects Annual Report relate to the complexities inherent in delivering a first-of-class submarine recycling project including the technical, planning, regulatory and commercial challenges.”
He said: “The Department continues to work constructively with its prime supplier and wider delivery partners to address these issues, improve programme planning and controls, strengthen delivery assurance and explore Fingleton Nuclear Regulatory Review opportunities where possible.”
On the timetable, he said: “Progress continues to be made, and the Department remains committed to dismantling Swiftsure by the end of 2026 safely, effectively and in accordance with regulatory requirements.”
Addressing the figures in the report, he said: “The increase in the project’s Whole Life Cost is primarily due to the maturation of infrastructure (alongside other costs), while the end date extended to October 2028 represents the formal closure of the project and is separate from the milestone to complete the recycling of Swiftsure by 2026.”
Swiftsure is the demonstrator for a programme that has to deal with a substantial number of boats. Decommissioned submarines are held afloat at Devonport and at Rosyth, where seven laid-up vessels are stored and where work under the Submarine Dismantling Project began in 2016.
Defuelling of decommissioned submarines at Devonport stopped in 2004, and the recommissioning of 14 Dock there is intended to allow legacy defuelling operations to resume, work Mr Pollard confirmed last week forms part of the £7.1 billion being invested in the naval base and dockyard over the next decade under Project Royal Oak. He said the department is exploring opportunities to accelerate work on 10 and 14 Dock following the nuclear regulatory review.
Graeme Downie, the Member of Parliament whose constituency covers Rosyth, has been pressing the department for news on submarine recycling at the yard alongside other work, saying last month that he hoped to hear good news soon.

As sanctions, isolation and strained alliances mount, who will be Israel’s next foreign minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:19:36 UTC
18:19:36 KST

Sanctions pressure is growing, relations with key Western governments are deteriorating and Israel’s international standing is emerging as one of the biggest challenges awaiting the next government. 
After years of war, repeated confrontations with European governments and mounting criticism of Israeli policy in the West Bank, ties with several countries have fallen to some of their lowest points in decades. In a growing number of capitals, officials are no longer limiting themselves to condemnations and are considering concrete measures against Israel.
European governments have in recent months discussed a range of possible steps, including in response to plans to advance construction in the E1 area. Diplomatic officials say one of the main questions is timing: some European capitals fear sanctions imposed shortly before Israel’s election could strengthen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and right-wing parties by allowing them to portray the measures as foreign interference. Britain, however, is moving toward restrictions on trade in goods, and in some cases services, originating in Israeli settlements, while considering additional measures as part of a broader shift in policy toward Israel.
The deterioration is increasingly visible beyond official diplomacy as well. Israelis have reported cases across Europe in which they were refused accommodation or services because of their nationality or origin. In Germany, authorities opened an investigation after an Israeli family seeking to book a room at a Bavarian hotel received a message saying Jews were not welcome.
Against that backdrop, the identity of Israel’s next foreign minister could become far more consequential than an ordinary coalition bargaining question. Whoever takes the job will have to manage relations with Washington and Israel’s regional partners while trying to prevent further sanctions, repair strained alliances and reverse a broader trend of diplomatic isolation.
Right-wing government: Sa’ar wants to stay, Katz could return
If Netanyahu forms another government, the natural candidate to remain foreign minister is Gideon Sa’ar. He wants to stay in the post and continue a strategy centered on expanding Israel’s circle of friendly governments, with particular emphasis on Latin America. Sa’ar designated 2026 the Foreign Ministry’s “Year of Latin America,” seeking to capitalize on political shifts across the region.
During his tenure, Israel restored diplomatic relations with Bolivia after years of rupture, while a change of government in Colombia led to the full restoration of ties and a decision to move its embassy to Jerusalem. Israel and the United States also established a joint strategic dialogue focused on Latin America. Jerusalem has meanwhile begun a cautious rapprochement with Venezuela, where consular services were restored in August, 17 years after relations were severed. The next major target is Brazil, where Israeli officials hope future political change could create an opening to repair badly strained relations.
Even if Sa’ar wants to stay, however, the Foreign Ministry could become a focus of internal coalition bargaining. Defense Minister Israel Katz has already served twice as foreign minister. His preference would likely be to remain at the Defense Ministry, but if that portfolio goes elsewhere during coalition negotiations, Katz could seek a return to the Foreign Ministry, forcing Netanyahu to choose between Sa’ar and one of Likud’s most senior figures.
Centrist government: Lapid leads, Bennett and Lieberman in the picture
If parties opposed to Netanyahu form the next government, Yair Lapid would begin as the leading candidate for foreign minister. Lapid held the post from 2021 to 2022 and built direct relationships with governments in Europe and the United States. Within B’Yachad, he would also be a natural candidate for a senior portfolio if Naftali Bennett becomes prime minister.
A Lapid-led Foreign Ministry would likely put repairing relations with Europe near the top of its agenda. While the current government has relied partly on friendly states to block measures against Israel inside European institutions, a centrist government could try to rebuild direct dialogue with Brussels, Paris, Berlin and London and prevent punitive measures from gaining momentum in the first place.
Lapid would not necessarily be the only option. Bennett himself could seek the Foreign Ministry if he does not receive the defense portfolio, or if a rotation agreement leaves him outside the Prime Minister’s Office for part of the government’s term. Avigdor Lieberman could also enter the picture. The Yisrael Beytenu leader served twice as foreign minister, from 2009 to 2012 and again from 2013 to 2015, and his candidacy would depend largely on which portfolio he prioritizes in coalition negotiations.
The first mission: stop the snowball
Whoever gets the job will inherit a diplomatic crisis that is already moving. The European Union has imposed additional sanctions this year on settlers and Israeli organizations while continuing to debate broader measures, including restrictions involving trade with settlements. More sweeping steps have so far encountered opposition from individual EU governments, including Czechia and Slovenia, preventing the formation of the majority required for some measures.
The challenge for the next foreign minister will therefore be twofold: preserve the governments still willing to help Israel block punitive action, while expanding that group before it shrinks further. As criticism of Israel spreads, relying on a small number of friendly capitals becomes increasingly precarious.
Whether the job goes to Sa’ar, Katz, Lapid, Bennett, Lieberman or another candidate, the task will be the same: stop the diplomatic snowball before sanctions, isolation and strained alliances become much harder to reverse.

Sweden to buy Lockheed Martin's HIMARS rocket artillery in €630 million deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:18:16 UTC
18:18:16 KST

Sweden's government has authorised its armed forces to buy the US-made HIMARS rocket artillery system from Lockheed Martin for around 7 billion Swedish crowns, almost €630 million, and has signed a parallel agreement with Finland to operate the two countries' rocket artillery together.
Stockholm is adding long-range firepower to its arsenal.
The Swedish Ministry of Defence confirmed on Monday that the armed forces will procure the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) from Lockheed Martin in a deal valued at almost €630 million, with first deliveries expected in 2027, funded through the military's regular investment plan.
Specifically, the agreement is for ten HIMARS systems and ammunition, as it fills a gap in Sweden's military, with the ministry describing the deal as an "opportune purchase".
Rocket artillery reaches considerably further than conventional guns and is designed for precision strikes at distance, complementing Sweden's existing Archer artillery and grenade launchers rather than replacing them.
It also allows Swedish forces to cover far larger areas than current equipment permits, and is compatible with systems used by NATO allies.
The purchase forms part of Sweden's total defence bill for 2025 to 2030, the spending framework adopted as the country integrates into the alliance it recently joined, and at a time when European countries across the board are increasing investments in defence.
A shared system with Finland
Alongside the procurement, Swedish Defence Minister Pål Jonson and his Finnish counterpart Antti Häkkänen signed a joint declaration covering cooperation and coordination on rocket artillery.
The arrangement spans training, education, capability development, maintenance, security of supply and joint production, as the logic is technical as much as political.
Finland already operates the Multiple Launch Rocket System, which uses the same munitions and components as HIMARS, meaning the two neighbours can pool stockpiles and maintenance rather than duplicating them.
"The introduction of rocket artillery clearly demonstrates that Sweden is taking responsibility for security in Europe," Jonson said, adding that "together, we [Sweden and Finland] are developing important capabilities for NATO's collective defence."
Something for Swedish-owned Saab too
The deal has an industrial dimension that keeps some value in Sweden.
Lockheed Martin and Swedish defence group Saab are signing their own declaration covering the possible integration of Saab's Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb with HIMARS, and the production of munitions for both HIMARS and other systems including the Patriot air defence platform.
That matters beyond this contract.
European governments have been buying American weapons while facing domestic pressure to build up their own industrial base, and munitions production in particular has become a bottleneck across the continent since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Philippines wants to be a global semiconductor giant by 2030. Can it get there?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:18:12 UTC
18:18:12 KST

Philippines wants to be a global semiconductor giant by 2030. Can it get there?
An ‘ambitious’ road map aims to more than double annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030
The Philippine Semiconductor and Electronics Industry road map, launched by the Philippines’ Semiconductor and Electronics Industry Advisory Council (SEIAC) on September 2, aims to grow annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030, and move beyond manufacturing and assembly into higher-end operations.
SEIAC chief and executive secretary Ralph Recto said the goal was to transition to chip design, engineering, research and innovation to boost regional competitiveness.
One target is raising the Philippines’ share of global assembly, testing and packaging – already the country’s top semiconductor activities – from 4 per cent to 7 per cent by 2030.
Other goals include growing the country’s share of the global electronics manufacturing services market from less than 1 per cent to 4 per cent and building an integrated circuit design sector that generates US$2 billion to US$3 billion in annual exports.

Mike Huckabee addresses the press during his visit to the Israeli-occupied West Bank town of Turmus Ayya on Sept. 5, 2026. | John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee suggested Tuesday the U.S. could retaliate against the U.K. over new trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements, a further escalation between London and Washington hours ahead of an expected policy rollout.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will make a statement in the House of Commons Tuesday afternoon, and is expected to impose a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements, having last month condemned Israel's plans for 1,200 new homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
But Huckabee, who over the weekend condemned the government's “Jew hate” despite Miliband being Jewish, told the BBC that the decision would be a “discrimination against the Jewish people.” He also suggested that individual U.S. states — specifically Florida — might take trade action against the U.K.
Advertisement
Huckabee’s comments came after Florida Congressman Randy Fine warned on X that sanctions would effectively “ban any British company forced to comply from doing business with any state or local government in Florida” under state law.
The diplomat’s comments will unnerve British exporters, who are already navigating an increasingly fragile trading relationship with the U.S.
Speaking at an awards ceremony in Jerusalem on Tuesday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said the imposition of trade sanctions on Israeli settlements would prove to be a "grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history,” according to a readout of the comments provided by Herzog's office.
In a post on X written in Spanish, Israel’s Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, said Israel should recognize the Falkland Islands as Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently stole from the Argentine people.
The U.K. retained its control of the Falklands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, after a 74-day war following Argentina's invasion of the territory in 1982.
'Comprehensive reset'
Miliband's expected announcement, and promise of “comprehensive reset” of policy on Israel, marks a sharp shift in Britain's stance on Israeli settlements under new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
It comes just two weeks before Burnham's expected trip to New York for the U.N. General Assembly — and a potential first in-person meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Advertisement
Burnham and Trump spoke Monday about the “U.K.'s commitment to working towards peace and security” in the Middle East and stressed the “importance of the two state solution,” according to a readout from the British side.
While Trump has yet to respond to the sanctions, political differences have previously influenced his decisions on trade.
In January, the president threatened to impose 10 percent tariffs on eight countries, including the U.K., for opposing his demands to use military force to take control of Greenland. More recently, he has threatened to slap European countries imposing digital services taxes on American tech firms with 100 percent tariffs.
Other Labour politicians fell in behind Miliband, withWork and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden defending the reset on the BBC, insisting that the U.K.'s strong security relationship with Israel would continue: “There is a difference between that ongoing relationship and the approval of specific policies by this Israeli government at this time.”
The move will be welcomed by many Labour MPs, who have called for tougher action against the Israeli government after its actions in Gaza.
But backbench Labour MP Peter Prinsley warned that opponents of Israel would not distinguish between Israeli government policy and British Jews, who have faced an uptick in violent antisemitic attacks. “As far as they're concerned, the whole thing's the same and I think it carries a real risk of increased chances of attacks on the British Jewish community,” he told the BBC.

We have tools,” Sa'ar told a podcast by media outlet Ynet. Britain, he said, “will be making a big mistake."

At least two Palestinians, including an elderly man, were killed and two others wounded by Israeli fire in Gaza, marking another violation of an ongoing ceasefire agreement, medical sources said.
A medical source said on Tuesday that a 69-year-old man died of injuries he sustained from Israeli gunfire targeting tents of displaced people southwest of Khan Younis in southern Gaza. Another Palestinian was wounded in the attack.
Another Palestinian succumbed to wounds sustained in an Israeli drone strike west of Khan Younis on Friday, the source said.
In northern Gaza, a Palestinian was moderately wounded in Israeli artillery shelling that targeted a home in the Al Faluja neighbourhood west of Jabalia refugee camp, another medical source said.
In central Gaza, eyewitnesses and local sources said that several Israeli military vehicles made a limited advance in the Abu al Ajin area east of Deir al-Balah, amid heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.
The sources said Israeli vehicles, including a bulldozer, advanced dozens of metres west of the so-called Yellow Line in the area and carried out bulldozing operations on residents’ land.
‘A decisive lifeline’
In a related development, Gaza’s health ministry said on Tuesday that Israel’s genocide has caused 5,000 amputations, 300 neurological and spinal injuries, and left 10,000 patients in need of intensive and long-term rehabilitation.
In a statement marking World Physiotherapy Day, the ministry said physical therapy and medical rehabilitation services in Gaza have become “a decisive lifeline” and “the first line of defence” against permanent disabilities among thousands of wounded Palestinians.
“The direct targeting of health facilities has forced most specialised rehabilitation centres out of service, while thousands of patients face the risk of severe health complications due to shortages of medical supplies, prosthetics and assistive devices, as well as restrictions on travel for treatment outside Gaza,” the ministry said.
It called on international organisations and UN bodies to urgently coordinate and intervene to bring in rehabilitation supplies, equipment and prosthetics, and to open crossings for critical cases requiring advanced rehabilitation and high-tech prosthetic limbs.
Despite the ceasefire deal that took effect on October 10 2025, Israeli forces have killed 1,352 Palestinians and wounded 4,511 others since, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
Since October 2023, Israeli forces have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 in Israel’s genocidal war that has destroyed or damaged much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi oil facilities and wound more than 70

Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi oil facilities and wound more than 70
Attacks on Saudi Arabia Tuesday claimed by Yemen's Houthis wounded more than 70 people and ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in the kingdom's southern region, authorities said, in a major escalation in the renewed conflict between an important US ally and the Iranian-backed rebels.
A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia Tuesday wounded more than 70 people and ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in the kingdom's southern region, authorities said, a major escalation in the renewed conflict between an important US ally and the Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen.
The attacks come after weeks of escalating clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, which shattered a four-year truce in the country’s civil war.
The flare-up delivered a new jolt to a region already destabilised by nearly three years of wars and brings more uncertainty for the global economy. The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis threatens to squeeze shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical route of the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global trade. It also comes at a time when the Iran war has nearly halted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway that moved about one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Fighting has raged on multiple fronts including Yemen’s west coast, with government forces saying they have made territorial gains in the provinces of Hodeida, Taiz and Baydah. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The attacks early Tuesday hit “civilian and economic facilities” in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, said Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen.
Al-Malki said the attacks wounded 73 people, including women and children. He didn’t provide further details.
The attacks ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in Saudi Arabia’s southern region, the kingdom’s energy ministry said in a statement. Operations at the oil facilities and utilities were temporarily suspended, it said.
The southern region houses major oil facilities, including a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in Jazan, which is one of Saudi Arabia’s largest. The Houthis had previously attacked the Abha airport.
The ministry said firefighters were battling the fires Tuesday morning.
Al-Malki called the attacks a “serious escalation” and a “flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty, and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents".
He vowed retaliation, saying that the Saudi-led coalition “will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve".

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they were in response to recent Saudi attacks on the rebels across Yemen.
In a prerecorded video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the rebels’ military spokesman, said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at oil and economic facilities, as well as an air base in southern Saudi Arabia.
He said they attacked Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, a major industrial and logistics hub on Saudi Arabia’s southwestern Red Sea coast. The rebels also attacked Aramco facilities in Najran and Abha, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.
Saree blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation, warning that “every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response".
Nasruddin Amer, deputy head of the Houthi media office overseeing the Saba news agency run by the rebels, took to social media to laud the attacks.
“The Saudi enemy has to understand that the time for committing crimes and massacres against the Yemeni people without response, deterrence or paying a price has ended,” he said.
The attacks came hours after the rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for an air strike that hit a prison in Yemen’s northern province of Jawf. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others were wounded in the strike in the Yemeni city of Hazem, the Houthis said.
The latest escalation stemmed from a Houthi attempt to fly a plane from Tehran to Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, challenging a decade-long air and naval blockade by the Saudi-led coalition. A coalition air strike struck the runway of the Sanaa airport, preventing the landing of the flight.
Read moreIran-backed Houthis strike Red Sea port of Mocha, threatening shipping routes
The Houthis responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, and a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, ending a 2022 truce that had largely halted fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
The rebels also launched attacks on Saudi-allied forces inside Yemen, prompting government forces to respond with attacks on the Houthis across Yemen’s west coast and elsewhere in the country.
Government forces reclaimed territory from the Houthis in the provinces of Hodeida and Taiz, and attacked the rebels in the northern province of Jawf as well as the central provinces of Marib and Bayda.
The flare-up displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organisation for Migration.
“Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it’s safe to go back,” said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen’s Chief of Mission. “Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before.”
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power.
The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine.

Kenya: Crackdown on foreign traders prompts xenophobia fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:14:00 UTC
18:14:00 KST

Kenya: Xenophobia fears amid crackdown on foreign traders
September 8, 2026
Kenyan authorities are moving in on some foreign nationals working in the country's informal economy after President William Ruto called for small-scale businesses focused on hawking and petty retail to be primarily reserved for Kenyan citizens.
"We have a bill in parliament [requiring] that there are some trading activities that foreigners can't do in Kenya," he explained, adding that foreign nationals should not come to Kenya to compete with citizens in business settings which need little capital.
The government had announced that the enforcement of this law would begin on Monday, September 7 — and appears to have made good on its pledge.
Ruto framed the latest move as a protection measure for Kenya's economy, highlighting that the focus in the country's economic development should shift to foreign investors who bring capital, create jobs and contribute to local production.
"The investor confidence we have built is for investors, not traders and hawkers. From next week, all traders doing those small businesses should close them," Ruto emphasized, highlighting also that there has been a step increase in informal traders from China in the country.
Mixed reactions to a complex situation
Reactions among Kenyans to these developments have been mixed; some welcomed the crackdown, arguing that foreign traders have been taking away job opportunities in a struggling economy.
"We have been suffering for long. Our jobs are taken," said Nairobi resident James Mwaurah, adding that many Kenyans are unemployed, competing with foreign workers who often are willing to work for lower wages.
"We say thanks to the president for what he has done," Mwaurah added.
Others meanwhile have expressed support for the government's initiative to enforce immigration laws and business regulations, but reject the idea of simply sending foreigners home.
"We accept to have foreigners in our country. Legally, we live with them very peacefully," another local resident, Babu Claudius, told DW on the streets of Nairobi.
In his view, Kenya continues to need foreign workers as well as international business, warning that "chasing them away might scare investors."
Many Kenyans — including Claudius — however seem to agree on one thing: Foreign nationals "have to be here legally."
There are some 17.4 million people who work in Kenya's informal sector, according to official numbers published in 2024; eight in ten of those workers engage in registered business dealings.
For many people, hawking or running a small shop in the informal economy — with or without papers — remains one of the few accessible ways to make a living — including foreigners in the country.
Kenya's mood ahead of elections
Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang says that there is little evidence suggesting "that if you were to kick out the traders, that would immediately result in Kenyan nationals having more opportunities."
According to Olang, there may be other motivations at play, as the new policy appears to come at a "convenient" moment ahead of elections.
In her view, "a lot of it is also just populist," describing the current crackdown on foreign traders as a "feel good policy" ahead of the polls; she highlights that the policy could also serve as a message to external players at this moment: "Foreign investors coil back or they freeze or they wait until the election is finished."
Olang argues that since Kenya wants to keep making itself more attractive to serious foreign investment, it should rather concentrate on tackling broader structural problems instead of focusing on smalltime foreign traders.
"We need to work on corruption. We need to work on our Ease of Doing Business Index so that it's easy to invest within Kenya," she told DW.
The East African country meanwhile attracted a record $3.2 billion (€2.75 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025 — an increase of almost 38% compared the previous year, according to UNCTAD.
Ruto remains keen to expand on this success story.
A wider push for local opportunities
One approach in Ruto's arsenal is the proposed Local Content Bill 2025, which is currently before parliament. The draft law would require foreign companies covered by the legislation to source at least 60% of certain goods and services locally.
Among other things, it would require at least 80% of their workforce to be Kenyan citizens.
But according to Olang, the measure would not address the roots of Kenya's unemployment crisis, in particular among the country's discontent youth:
The World Bank estimates the unemployment rate among Kenyans aged between 15 and 24 to stand at 15.25%, though local and regional organizations like the Federation of Kenya Employers often cite a much higher figure of roughly two-thirds of all young Kenyans being affected by unemployed and underemployment.
Who is actually affected by the policy?
The government has not published a comprehensive list of businesses that will be affected by the crackdown, as it remains unclear how many foreign nationals could be impacted by the move.
Meanwhile, Kenya's Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Abraham Korir Sing'oei emphasized that foreign nationals who meet all existing legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, will remain legally protected to operate their businesses in the country.
He said that Ruto's current initiative was direcly linked to the introduction of the Local Content Bill, and should not be regarded as a push to get rid of foreigners in the country.
Questions remain over the broader legality of the developments: Under the East African Community's Common Market rules, citizens of member states have the right to move and provide services across the region — though they have to comply with national licensing and other legal requirements.
The debate has also resulted in comparisons being drawn to recent developments in South Africa, where widespread frustration over a sluggish economy has led to foreign-owned businesses and migrants repeatedly being targeted by anti-immigration campaigns this year.
Kenya has not experienced anti-migrant violence on the scale seen in South Africa — yet.
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

U.S. Air Force to buy 60 DroneBuster counter-drone systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:13:31 UTC
18:13:31 KST

- The Air Force's Pacific Air Forces command is seeking 60 DroneBuster 5 counter-drone jammers to boost its drone-defeat capabilities across the Indo-Pacific.
- The solicitation notes that funding is not yet available and the government has no obligation to pay until money is formally allocated.
The U.S. Air Force wants to buy 60 handheld counter-drone jammers for its Pacific forces, according to a solicitation Pacific Air Forces published September 8, though the purchase can’t move forward until funding becomes available.
The notice, posted by PACAF’s 18th Contracting Squadron, calls for 60 DroneBuster 5 units equipped with a GPS-focused add-on kit, intended to boost the command’s ability to detect and defeat small drones across its area of responsibility in the Indo-Pacific. Companies have until September 11 to submit responses. The Air Force said in the notice that funds for the contract are not currently available, and that it has no legal obligation to pay for the purchase until money is formally allocated and the contracting officer confirms it in writing.
The DroneBuster is a handheld radio-frequency jammer originally developed by Portland, Oregon-based Flex Force Enterprises. Roughly the size and shape of a rifle, it disrupts the radio link between a small drone and its operator, and can also jam GPS signals the drone relies on for navigation. Flex Force is now part of DZYNE Technologies, a defense technology company that absorbed Flex Force through a series of private equity acquisitions completed in 2024, after which DZYNE itself was acquired by Ondas Inc. for roughly $875.8 million in July 2026 and folded into Ondas’s Sentinel autonomous defense business.
The Pentagon’s Joint Counter-UAS Office has designated the DroneBuster the only handheld electronic attack system it has approved for defeating drones, and the company has said it has delivered more than 1,700 units worldwide to the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps and a range of international militaries and police agencies, including a 2025 contract to supply Australia’s defense force under its LAND 156 counter-drone program.
The version PACAF is requesting, the DroneBuster 5, adds a capability earlier models lacked. According to Flex Force, newer DroneBuster variants can take over a drone’s onboard flight computer rather than simply jamming its signal, letting the operator interrupt a GPS-guided drone that’s flying a pre-programmed route without a live operator to jam in the first place. Flex Force has said that capability works at distances of roughly 800 to 1,400 meters (2,600 to 4,600 feet). Standard DroneBuster units run on rechargeable batteries, weigh under 5 pounds (2.3 kilograms), and offer about three hours of continuous jamming or ten hours of drone detection on a single charge, with the company saying new users can learn basic operation in under five minutes.
The solicitation includes two corrections issued after its initial posting. One notes that the document had mistakenly referenced an older model, the DroneBuster IV, on one page, when the actual requirement is for DroneBuster 5 units. The other clarifies that the part number should specify the U.S. 433 MHz frequency variant of the system rather than the European 868 MHz version.

Ex head of Swiss Bankers Association convicted of corruption
On Tuesday the Swiss Federal Criminal Court found Pierre Mirabaud guilty of bribing foreign public officials and money laundering. The former president of the Swiss Bankers Association has been given a two-year suspended prison sentence.
The Federal Criminal Court, which was trying the now-retired Geneva banker under summary proceedings, upheld the facts set out in the indictment by the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland (OAG). After questioning Mirabaud, the Court read out the operative part of its judgement on Tuesday morning.
According to the indictment, Pierre Mirabaud granted benefits totalling CHF82 million ($100 million) at the request of a senior Kuwaiti official so that the latter would invest public funds in the bank of the same name.
In return, the Kuwaiti national, who was chairman of the Public Social Security Institution (PIFSS) of that Gulf state, invested part of the institution’s funds – amounting to more than $500 million (CHF405 million) – with the Geneva-based private bank.

Ukrainian AI company after NATO competition: effectiveness of strikes on Russian airfields could increase tenfold
In a comment to Ukrinform, the company’s head, who uses the call sign Wild Cat, said the solution presented at the NATO competition would make strikes on enemy airfields many times more effective, as it represents an entirely new technological level.
“In short, our development is artificial intelligence for making the destruction of enemy airfields ten times more effective. It involves precision targeting of airfields, and the solution can be used both on UAVs and missiles,” the company head said.
He explained that Russia should not be underestimated, as it has one of the world’s best air defense systems, combined with one of the world’s best electronic warfare systems, which makes it considerably more difficult for Ukrainian forces to strike its airfields.
“Essentially, we are dealing with the protection of military airfields at a level that may not exist anywhere else in the world. Despite this, Ukraine is managing to effectively ‘reach’ Russian aircraft and helicopters at their airfields, both in Crimea and deep inside their territory,” Wild Cat said. At the same time, he believes that introducing the new development “will fundamentally change this situation.”
Read also: Ukrainian Forces Test New Robotic Turrets with Machine Guns on the Front Line
“This will help Ukraine significantly improve the effectiveness of strikes on enemy airfields,” the head of the Ukrainian company emphasized.
He noted that he had expected to win NATO’s Innovation Competition because he benchmarks his company against its main competitors in Ukraine and around the world, including the U.S. company Palantir Technologies, which develops artificial intelligence, including for Hornet “middle-strike” drones, “with which the Ukrainian side is currently wreaking havoc on the enemy’s logistics.”
According to him, Palantir remains stronger in the logistics sector, but the Ukrainian development has an advantage in airspace protection and operations against enemy airfields.
The company head said that winning the NATO competition represents recognition of the Ukrainian company’s solutions at the Alliance level.
“We are the only Ukrainian company to have won this competition. This means that our solution has been recognized as the best in this field across the Alliance. We are being invited to take part in further testing and trials, with the prospect of implementing our solutions at the NATO level. This is a huge boost for the company’s development and integration into the Alliance’s defense system,” he emphasized.
The head added that the company had been developing its technology since 2022 and had since collected, in his assessment, globally unique databases for training its artificial intelligence.
“No one else in the Western world has anything like this. And training data accounts for more than half of success,” the head of the Ukrainian AI company said.
Read also: Ukraine and Britain Sign Historic Artificial Intelligence Agreement
Wild Cat said that during the event, the company had also reached cooperation agreements with several other partners, including an agreement on joint production with a foreign company, as well as cooperation with a Ukrainian manufacturer. He added that since the company develops exclusively software modules, practical implementation of the solution requires cooperation with manufacturers of drones or missile systems.
The company head also said that a presentation of the solution at a training range was scheduled to take place within several weeks as part of an exercise. The next steps will include flight and combat trials, followed by the production of a small batch to identify shortcomings under real operating conditions, and only later full-scale production. According to the company head’s preliminary estimates, it should take between six and eighteen months for the development to enter combat use.
Regarding the financial prize in NATO’s Innovation Competition—the three winning companies will receive a total of €250,000—Wild Cat said it amounts to approximately 5–7% of the project’s current costs. However, he said the main value of the victory was not financial but reputational, providing an argument for potential investors and partners.
Assessing the development’s potential impact on the course of hostilities, the company head described it as “an ongoing confrontation between means and countermeasures.”
“We are now considering what the war will look like in two or three years. To some extent, we are already anticipating how the Russians will protect their airfields in the future—for example, they are already actively building bunkers for aircraft. We are developing the solution so that even these bunkers will not help them,” he emphasized.
The head of the AI company added that it had been working on strikes against enemy airfields since 2022, and that the current development takes into account its previous experience and the countermeasures Russia has attempted to use to reduce the effectiveness of Ukrainian attacks.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, NATO’s 19th Innovation Competition, organized by NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC), focused on persistent airfield denial . The Persistent Airfield Denial competition sought innovative technologies capable not only of damaging a military airfield but also of making it difficult for the enemy to restore its operations for an extended period.
The Ukrainian company took third place with an artificial intelligence-based solution for autonomous control of unmanned aerial vehicles. The technology enables operation without a constant connection to an operator, as well as the use of autonomous navigation and target recognition.
First place in the competition went to Czech company LPP Holding, which presented an autonomous long-range unmanned system capable of operating in conditions of active electronic warfare and without GPS navigation.
Second place went to Polish company Supercluster with its StratoAIM concept. The development involves using high-altitude balloons to launch autonomous gliding systems.

Secondhand smoke linked to nearly 1.7M deaths worldwide in 2023: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:11:42 UTC
18:11:42 KST

Beril Canakci
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Nearly 1.7 million people globally died from exposure to secondhand smoke in 2023, according to a study published Tuesday.
Secondhand smoke is smoke inhaled by people who are near someone using tobacco products.
More than 2.7 billion people worldwide, including about 767 million children, were exposed to secondhand smoke in 2023, according to the study published in The Lancet Public Health.
Researchers examined data from 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023 and found that exposure to secondhand smoke was linked to 1.66 million deaths and 44.8 million years of healthy life lost in 2023.
Ischemic heart disease was the leading cause of death associated with secondhand smoke exposure among adults, while exposure was also linked to 5.2 million lower respiratory infections among children in 2023, the study found.
Although the proportion of people exposed to secondhand smoke has declined since 1990, the overall number has remained broadly stable as a result of population growth, with exposure particularly increasing in parts of Africa and the Middle East.
The researchers said second-hand smoke remains a major global health risk and called for stronger tobacco-control measures to protect people, particularly women and children.
