Two convicted for injury to skater at Lausanne Youth Olympics
The Lausanne Police Court on Monday convicted two people in connection with a serious accident involving a Russian skater during a practice session at the 2020 Youth Olympic Games in Lausanne.
The defendants, technicians at an events organisation company in German-speaking Switzerland, were sentenced to a fine of CHF9,000 ($11,100), suspended for two years. They were found guilty of causing serious bodily harm through negligence, the presiding judge stated.
According to the judge, they had failed in their duty of care. The husband of the figure skater, Olga Sevastianova, who acted as her assistant during her performances, and two other technicians from the Swiss German company were acquitted.
The lawyer for one of the two convicted men has already announced his intention to appeal, while the other is waiting to analyse the full text of the judgement. According to her lawyer, Elza Reymond, Sevastianova “will be satisfied with the judgement, having waited six years for justice to be done”. Her husband’s lawyer described the court’s legal reasoning as “convincing”.
More
Hobby ice-skaters urged to wear helmets
The incident took place on January 7, 2020. The acrobat was performing aerial manoeuvres above the ice, suspended from a rope at the Malley ice rink, when she fell from a height of five metres. Sevastianova, who was 35 at the time of the incident, was admitted to Lausanne University Hospital (CHUV), where she was placed in an induced coma, initially in a life-threatening condition.
Her injuries included severe liver damage, the removal of part of her skull, four broken ribs, fractures to the bones of one hand and several facial bones, as well as damage to the optic nerves. As a result of these injuries, she was unable to return to work.
The investigation had established the technical cause of the accident, namely the incorrect installation of the winch that was holding Sevastianova suspended in the air.

From the airport to a new life: ynet Global Aliyah Summit answers biggest questions facing new olim | Live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:45:28 KST

The decision to make aliyah can take years. But once the ticket is booked and the suitcases are packed, questions about identity and belonging quickly give way to much more practical ones.
What do you do when you land? Which documents do you need? How do you choose a health fund, open a bank account, transfer money, find work or rent a home? And if something happens in the middle of the night, who do you call?
Today, September 8, ynet Global is holding its Global Aliyah Live Summit, a day of broadcasts devoted to answering those questions and helping prospective and newly arrived immigrants understand what life in Israel actually looks like after the plane lands.
Follow the live broadcasts and continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
The summit brings together senior public officials, Aliyah and absorption organizations, specialists in healthcare, banking, employment and housing, and new immigrants who are experiencing the process firsthand.
Broadcasts will be held in Russian, English and French, with coverage also appearing across ynet and ynet Global.
Today’s broadcast schedule, Israel time
13:00-14:00 — Live broadcast in Russian, in cooperation with Vesti
14:00-17:00 — Live broadcast in English on ynet Global and ynet
17:00-18:00 — Live broadcast in French on ynet Global
You landed in Israel. What happens next?
One of the summit’s central discussions focuses on the first 24 hours after aliyah, when months or years of planning suddenly become reality.
After the flight, the welcome and the first photo in Israel comes a new challenge: navigating a bureaucracy and public-service system that can be unfamiliar even to people who prepared extensively before arriving.
Which documents do new immigrants receive? What must be done immediately and what can wait? When should they register with a health fund, open a bank account or begin dealing with government offices? What benefits are available and how are they accessed?
Today’s summit brings those steps together, giving new immigrants a practical guide to the first days of building a life in Israel.
What should be done before the flight?
Some of the most important preparations begin before an oleh ever reaches Ben Gurion Airport.
The summit will address which documents should be brought to Israel, what arrangements should be made with banks overseas, what to do with savings and other assets abroad and when to begin looking for work.
New immigrants will also discuss the less technical side of leaving: saying goodbye to family and friends, leaving a job, packing a home and confronting the uncertainty of having to build a new routine in another country.
Money, banking and buying a home
Opening an Israeli bank account can raise questions that go far beyond simply choosing a branch.
A financial panel featuring experts and representatives including Bank Leumi and mortgage advisers will examine how newcomers should navigate the Israeli financial system.
Among the issues: transferring money from abroad, handling overseas income and assets, understanding Israel’s credit system, foreign currency and international transfer fees.
The summit will also look ahead to one of the largest financial decisions many olim eventually face: buying a home in Israel.
Mortgage advisers will discuss what new immigrants should know before entering the Israeli property market and what needs to be checked before taking out a mortgage.
Bringing your career to Israel
For many new immigrants, moving countries also means confronting the possibility of starting again professionally.
A doctor, engineer, teacher, executive, entrepreneur or tech professional may arrive with a decade or more of experience only to discover that the Israeli job market does not automatically recognize the career they built overseas.
Employment specialists taking part in the summit will discuss when to start searching for work, how to adapt a résumé for Israel, how to build a local professional network and which professions require Israeli licensing.
The sessions will also address entrepreneurship, retraining and starting a business.
The goal is not simply to help olim find their first Israeli job, but to help them preserve and use the skills and experience they already have.
Healthcare and the number every newcomer should know
Israel’s healthcare system can also require an adjustment for immigrants arriving from countries with very different models of medical care.
Representatives from Clalit Health Services will explain how to join a health fund, choose a doctor, make appointments and begin using the services available to new immigrants.
The summit will also cover medical emergencies.
A dedicated segment will explain what happens when someone calls Magen David Adom at **101**, what information dispatchers need and what newcomers should expect from Israel’s emergency medical system.
Among the many new numbers an oleh needs to learn, 101 is one worth knowing from the first day.
Hearing from olim themselves
The summit is not only about officials and experts.
New immigrants at different stages of the aliyah process will discuss what surprised them after arriving, what proved more difficult than expected, where bureaucracy caused problems and what they wish they had known before boarding the plane.
They will also talk about finding jobs and apartments, building communities and adjusting to everyday Israeli life.
That firsthand perspective is central to today’s event. Sometimes the most useful advice for someone preparing to make aliyah comes from someone who made the same move only weeks or months earlier.
The organizations behind aliyah
The Global Aliyah Live Summit features representatives from many of the major organizations involved in bringing immigrants to Israel and helping them integrate, including the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Hayesod, Ofek Israeli, Nefesh B’Nefesh, Clalit Health Services, Bank Leumi, the Jerusalem Municipality, Masa Israel Journey and Magen David Adom.
Participants also include the minister of Aliyah and Integration and the chairman of the Jewish Agency, who will address the broader questions surrounding immigration to Israel: Who is making Aliyah today? What has changed in recent waves? What barriers remain? And what does Israel need to do not only to bring new immigrants to the country, but to help them build successful lives once they arrive?
Aliyah does not end at the airport
ynet Global’s Global Aliyah project has followed prospective and new immigrants throughout the year with guides, personal stories and practical information about life in Israel.
Today, that conversation goes live.
The summit is designed for those who have already booked their flights, those planning Aliyah in the coming months and those still sitting in Paris, London, New York, Toronto, Moscow or elsewhere wondering whether the time has come.
Throughout the day, the broadcasts will address the large and small questions behind starting a new life: work, money, healthcare, housing, bureaucracy, community and belonging.
Watch the Global Aliyah Live Summit and follow continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
Because aliyah does not end when you land at Ben Gurion Airport.
That is where it really begins.

The European commute: Which EU country spends the most time getting to work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:44:56 UTC
17:44:56 KST

Just how long do Europeans spend getting to work? Across the continent, the daily average commute sits at 48 minutes, but that hides a massive divide.
For millions of workers across the continent, the daily journey to the office is an unavoidable ritual. But just how long do Europeans actually spend getting to work?
According to new research from talent management company SD Worx, the daily average commute across Europe sits at 48 minutes. However, that continental average masks how differently nations experience geography, traffic, and worker mindsets.
While the European average hovers around three-quarters of an hour, individual countries experience vastly different realities on their roads and rail lines.
Countries such as Italy and Slovenia manage to keep daily travel times relatively brief, hovering around 35 minutes.
At the opposite end, countries push much closer to the hour mark. Sweden and Ireland report hefty averages of 57 and 56 minutes, respectively.
Taking the top spot overall, Belgium officially crosses the one-hour mark at 61 minutes a day. This is driven by the fact that 13% of its workforce are "super-commuters", according to SD Worx, spending two hours or more on the road—the highest rate in Europe—with 14% travelling over 120 kilometres daily.
Distance vs. congestion: The Netherlands and Romania
The data also reveals fascinating differences in why commutes take as long as they do. For instance, the Netherlands and Romania both average 53 minutes for a daily commute, but the underlying dynamics are entirely polar opposite:
Workers in the Netherlands cover 63 kilometres on average, leaning on efficient infrastructure to handle long-distance travel.
In Romania, workers spend that same 53-minute window covering much shorter geographic distances, where heavy traffic and urban congestion eat away at the clock.
The commuting paradox
Perhaps the most intriguing takeaway from the research is how workers psychologically handle their travel times.
Even in Belgium—where the average commute surpasses the 57-minute limit that people generally consider "acceptable"—only 34% of workers view that time as wasted.
Despite enduring some of the longest transit times on the continent, demand for more remote work among Belgian employees sits at just 32%, staying right below the international average.
Across Europe, the daily commute remains a patchwork of infrastructure challenges and personal routines, proving that the time we spend getting to work is about much more than just kilometres on a map.

MSF response not needed in Nepal following flash floods

As communities in Nepal turn to recovery, immediate needs do not require MSF response
Share
Project Update8 September 2026
The human cost of the flash floods in Nepal of 26 August is devastating. Thousands of people have been killed, with many still missing, and many thousands more have lost their homes and livelihoods.
After arriving in Nepal on 27 August, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams have carried out assessments in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, the parts of Nepal worst affected by the flash floods. Our teams spoke with people affected, visited health facilities and relief centres, and spoke with municipal, district and disaster management authorities coordinating the response to this tragedy.
People have repeatedly told us that their biggest needs now are for recovery – for roads and markets to reopen, for schools, homes and infrastructure to be rebuilt. It is clear that continued, significant, relief efforts and funding for people in affected communities is required now and in the weeks and months to come.
As an emergency humanitarian medical organisation, MSF’s expertise is in providing humanitarian assistance in the most acute phases of emergencies. Our teams have assessed that the humanitarian response is well mobilised and managed. The government-led response, in coordination with local communities, United Nations agencies, and other humanitarian organisations, has succeeded in meeting people’s immediate humanitarian needs.
MSF has therefore decided not to launch a humanitarian response, as our expertise does not lie in the recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction activities that people in Nepal now need. We extend our admiration and respect to local communities, the Nepali authorities and all those responding tirelessly under difficult conditions, helping people recover from this disaster.
We send our heartfelt sympathies to the people of Nepal and all those who have lost loved ones in this tragedy.

United Russia’s ratings are falling, so why is the Kremlin demanding better election results? Putin joined the campaign.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:42:51 UTC
17:42:51 KST

United Russia’s ratings are falling, so why is the Kremlin demanding better election results? Putin joined the campaign.
Warning: this text contains profanity. If that is unacceptable to you, please do not read it.
Russia’s Presidential Administration has raised the KPI targets set for regional officials based on how the ruling party, United Russia, performs. In regions that are neither prone to protest nor overly loyal — where the party’s ratings run average — the new target is 47%.
Back in July, Meduza reported that the Kremlin’s political bloc had lowered the targets for these regions from 50% to 45%. The Russian business daily Vedomosti wrote in June that United Russia’s nationwide KPI had been cut from 55% to 50%. Sources told Meduza the reduction reflected falling ratings for the party and the president, driven by a gasoline shortage, rising prices, and public fatigue with the war.
Two deputy governors overseeing domestic policy, a political strategist who works with regional authorities, and a source close to the Presidential Administration told Meduza about the sudden increase in the targets.
In regions with average support for the authorities, the KPI rose from 45% to 47%, while in regions with a “higher degree of mobilization,” it rose from 50% to 52-53%. Nationwide, United Russia is now expected to score “more than 50%.”
“Things are heating up,” the political strategist who works with regional authorities complained to Meduza. He had welcomed the earlier cut in his region’s KPI with relief, since United Russia’s ratings were falling and the targets no longer matched reality, but the increase now worries him.
The deputy governors Meduza spoke with share this concern.
“When the KPI depends on reality at least to some extent, that’s reasonable. It’s clear that the results [of the election] and real ratings are different things. But when the rating is falling, and your KPI gets raised, the situation isn’t normal. Normally there’s a direct correlation, not an inverse one,” one of the deputy governors said.
The official said he’ll need to step up “administrative-industrial mobilization” to hit the new targets. Efforts by state-funded organizations and state corporations to get Russians to vote — often through coercion — are typically known as “corporate mobilization.” But in private directives, officials have recently begun calling this tool something new.
“We’re already squeezing out [what we can]. Many people are used to it: they’re understanding about it, so to speak. Those who really don’t want to vote usually weren’t pressured much. Well, now we’ll have to,” the same source suggested.
Meduza has previously reported that authorities tightened corporate mobilization efforts. At large workplaces, employees have been designated “mobilization foremen,” responsible for tracking turnout among a group of colleagues ranging from 10 to several dozen people.
A deputy governor and a political strategist who works with regional authorities say the higher KPI means factoring in a larger share of outright fraud, which Meduza’s sources modestly call “correction.”
“It’s mockery! When they announced the increase, they also talked about legitimacy, about making the results look believable. But those are mutually exclusive things!” the regional official said. “When you’re meeting the targets, you demand that your subordinates bring more people out to vote. If there’s room for correction at some polling station, you give it a higher percentage.”
According to him, officials often exceed the Kremlin’s KPI out of excess caution, but “no one has ever been punished for that.”
He and other sources — another deputy governor and a political strategist working in the regions — say officials have started facing pressure at conference calls with presidential envoy offices to deliver strong election results. “Otherwise, we’re fucked,” one regional official summed up.
At one presidential envoy’s office, officials tied the high target directly to Vladimir Putin’s involvement in the party’s campaign: “the president has put his shoulder to the wheel, we’re working for him.” A source close to the Presidential Administration also links the higher KPI to Putin’s active role in the campaign.
Putin has been actively touring regions beyond the reach of Ukrainian drones and has already met with the top five candidates on United Russia’s list. During his remarks at the second stage of the United Russia congress on August 22, he spoke of “the unity of the front and the rear,” and said he was confident the election results “will confirm the stability of the state, the maturity of the political system, and its ability to withstand any external threats, blackmail, and aggression.”
“He’s lending his personal rating, plus he personally spoke about voting at the [party] congress. There’s no turning back now,” says the source close to the Presidential Administration.
Even so, he calls raising the KPI under current conditions “illogical and wrong.” A political strategist close to the Presidential Administration had earlier not ruled out a further cut in the KPI, but that forecast came before Putin became actively involved in the campaign.
“From a political-technology standpoint, lowering the targets is still the right move,” the political strategist said. “But now the work is aimed at making sure the president is satisfied: he supported the party, it got impressive numbers, and we’ve once again proven something to the West.”

Argentina sues Israeli oil firm as Ben Gvir urges Netanyahu to back its Falklands claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:41:47 UTC
17:41:47 KST

Argentina is to file criminal charges against several companies linked to Israeli oil firm Navitas for operating without authorisation in the Falklands, as Milei steps up his offensive against the Sea Lion project with new sanctions and measures to bolster territorial defence.
The Argentine government announced on Monday that it will file a criminal complaint against several subsidiaries of the Israeli oil company Navitas for operating without authorisation in the Malvinas (Falkland Islands), which are administered by the United Kingdom but whose sovereignty is claimed by Argentina.
The decision triggered an immediate reaction in Israel. The Minister for National Security, Itamar Ben Gvir, called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to recognise Argentine sovereignty over the Malvinas and to impose sanctions on the United Kingdom "for as long as the occupation continues", accusing London of seizing Argentine territory and oil resources.
According to the Argentine presidency, the complaint will target Navitas Petroleum Development & Production Ltd, Navitas Petroleum Atlantic United, Navitas Petroleum LP, JHI Associates Inc and Eco Atlantic Oil & Gas Ltd, as well as their executives and representatives.
Argentina maintains that these companies "allegedly hold licences granted by the illegitimate government of the United Kingdom" to explore and exploit hydrocarbons in the North Malvinas Basin, in violation of Argentine law. The case also targets directors, managers, statutory auditors and any representatives who have taken part in the project.
This is not the first time Buenos Aires has taken action over oil activity in the area. Argentina had already declared these operations illegal in 2012 and filed a similar complaint in 2015. In 2022 it sanctioned Navitas directly and, in December 2025, Javier Milei's government formally rejected investors' announcement they will pour €1.808 billion into the project to start production.
Sea Lion, the oilfield at the heart of the dispute
Navitas operates and controls 65% of the Sea Lion project, located around 220 kilometres north of the Falkland Islands, in waters disputed by Argentina and the United Kingdom. Its partner is the British company Rockhopper, which owns the remaining 35%. The project is in the development phase and is expected to start pumping crude oil in March 2028.
The two companies had already responded to the measures announced by Argentina before the criminal complaint was submitted. Following Milei's speech last Thursday, they issued a joint statement insisting that they operate under licences "legally granted" by the islands' government and with "the full and ongoing support" of the United Kingdom.
The companies stressed that they do not expect the Argentine measures to delay the Sea Lion project timeline. Rockhopper's shares fell by more than 6% on the London Stock Exchange after the announcement.
Ben Gvir urges Netanyahu to recognise Argentine sovereignty
The complaint against the subsidiaries of an Israeli oil company comes amid rising diplomatic tension between Israel and the United Kingdom. Ben Gvir called on Netanyahu to recognise Argentine sovereignty over the territory and to adopt sanctions against London "for as long as the occupation continues".
The Israeli minister accused the United Kingdom of seizing territory and oil resources that, he argued, belong to the Argentine people. Hours earlier, Israel's Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, had called for the expulsion of the British ambassador to Israel.
The remarks come amid widening rifts between London and Tel Aviv over British policy towards Palestine. For the moment, Ben Gvir's words do not amount to a change in Israel's official position on the islands' sovereignty.
Milei steps up his offensive
President Javier Milei announced on Thursday that he intends to toughen sanctions on oil companies operating in the Falkland Islands under licences issued by the British territory. He also said he would send a bill to Congress that would extend sanctions to the suppliers of these companies and bar offenders from contracting with the Argentine state.
That same day he confirmed that he will revive plans to build a naval base in Ushuaia, around 700 kilometres from the islands. On Monday, Milei instructed Economy Minister Luis Caputo to give the project priority in the 2027 budget, which the government will send to Congress this month.
"These measures are part of a comprehensive policy aimed at strengthening the Argentine state's ability to defend its territory, protect its natural resources and safeguard its strategic interests," the government said in a statement.

Estonia ranks among top countries in latest PISA results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:41:00 UTC
17:41:00 KST

Estonia ranks among top countries in latest PISA results
Only Japan and South Korea surpassed Estonia in 2025 overall PISA test scores among OECD countries. At the same time, education experts are concerned about the continued decline in functional reading literacy.
"This is undoubtedly a festive day, because compared with others we are in a very good place, but at the same time it also sets off an alarm bell. Over a ten‑year view, PISA results have fallen everywhere. Our situation is better and the picture is not as steep, but Estonia's best results were actually in 2018," said Gunda Tire, head of international studies at the Education and Youth Board (Harno).
The OECD organizes PISA tests every three years to assess the knowledge and skills of 15‑year‑old young people. In Estonia, the tests are mostly taken by ninth‑grade students.
Unlike classical exams, PISA does not measure how well students have mastered the national curriculum, but gives an indication of whether a young person can apply the knowledge acquired in mathematics, science and functional reading in real life.
To keep pace with the world, OECD experts assessed computational problem‑solving ability for the first time this time.
Estonian 15‑year‑old students have been taking PISA tests since 2006. The country stands out globally as an example. For instance, in 2022, only young people from Singapore, Japan and South Korea scored higher overall than Estonian students, with certain special administrative regions of China added. The same happened this time.
Among OECD member countries, only Japan (538) surpassed Estonia (average 527 points) in science. In mathematics, young people from Japan (525 points) and South Korea (522 points) performed better than Estonian students (508 points).
In the functional reading literacy test, only young people from Japan (503 points), South Korea (501 points) and Ireland (500 points) achieved better results than Estonian youth (499 points).
In the newly added field of computational problem‑solving, only young people from Japan (557 points) surpassed Estonian students (541 points).
If non‑OECD countries, such as Singapore, are included in the ranking, and China's special administrative regions are treated separately, Estonian young people place 6th in science, 8th in mathematics and functional reading literacy, and 7th in computational problem‑solving.

Robot revolt? Polish company stages protest demanding stricter AI rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:40:20 UTC
17:40:20 KST

In Warsaw, marching robots waved flags and chanted slogans outside the digital affairs ministry, calling on Poland's government to regulate AI before it costs people their jobs.
Waving flags, "chanting" slogans and marching in circles, around 30 robots took to the streets of Warsaw on Monday to campaign for AI regulation in front of Poland's digital affairs ministry.
The protest was organised by Democratism, an initiative that, according to its website, aims to launch debate on how AI and robotisation affect the labour market.
In a scene that blurred the line between protest and product demonstration, one of the machines fielded questions directly from journalists.
"The robots present here are meant to show that this technology is already a reality," Agibot A3, one of the AI-powered humanoid robots, said — a statement that proved its own point rather neatly.
Chants of "Defend workplaces," "Time for rules" and "Don't wait, regulate" played on loudspeakers as the robots — which ranged from bipedal humanoids to dog-like quadrupeds — demonstrated.
"We particularly want to address the issue of the potential replacement of people both by humanoid robots and by artificial intelligence in cognitive work," said (human) organiser Grzegorz Kuliś.
"If we don't react now, we may soon have a problem," he added, emphasising the need for "rules and regulations that would serve as a shield protecting workers".
Aside from attracting the attention of several passers-by, Kuliś said the use of robots was meant to demonstrate their existing capabilities and, by extension, the urgency of the issue.
"These robots can already move around freely, they're already 'protesting,'" he said — leaving unaddressed the question of whether a machine reading out a pre-loaded chant counts as protesting at all.
Minister comes out to meet organisers
The marching robots were met with a visit from Poland's Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, who spoke to Kuliś on site.
"Uncontrolled (AI) models, implemented into humanoids that will also keep evolving as robotisation moves forward, are a major problem," he said.
Kuliś, who is now the chief information officer of a robotics company and chief executive of an employment agency, served two terms on the Labour Market Council at the Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy.
"We feel responsible for starting to inform society about the rapid and dynamic technological changes which personally frighten us," he said.
Who's behind the machines
Local Polish outlet Opolska360 reported that the robots used in Monday's protest were built by Delta Robots, a company that has been producing both humanoid and quadruped machines for more than a decade.
Kuliś is also president of Weegree, a recruitment firm that has operated for more than 20 years — both companies are based in Opole, in southern Poland.
That detail sharpens the irony at the heart of Monday's demonstration, as the robots warning of job losses were built by the very industry sounding the alarm about them.
Opolska360 also quoted Kuliś describing Democratism as a movement he hopes will go international, saying the goal is "not to fight change, robotics or technological development," but to launch a debate on its consequences and how to counter the negative effects.
According to the outlet, Gawkowski told the gathered protesters that Poland is the first EU country to introduce oversight of the AI market and announced plans to set up a Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence, along with regulatory sandboxes that would let companies test AI solutions before wider rollout.
In July, Poland's conservative-nationalist President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill put forward by the ministry to implement the EU's AI Act.
It created a national authority capable of enforcing existing EU regulations, which had already formally come into force.

Mistral AI raises record €3 billion in Samsung-led funding round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:39:02 UTC
17:39:02 KST

French artificial intelligence company Mistral AI has raised €3 billion in a round led by Samsung Electronics, nearly doubling its valuation to more than €21 billion in what the company says is the largest equity fundraising ever completed by a European technology firm.
Europe's answer to OpenAI has just become considerably better funded.
The Paris-based company Mistral AI announced its Series D on Tuesday, three years after being seeded, with the memory chip giant Samsung leading alongside the EU-backed Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, and existing investor PSG Equity.
The step up is steep.
Mistral was valued at €11.7 billion in 2025 after a €1.7 billion Series C led by Dutch chipmaker ASML, meaning the company has almost doubled its valuation in a year.
Much of the money is going into concrete rather than code. CEO Arthur Mensch announced the funding would build out data centres and computing capacity that Mistral can rent to others but that will also ensure autonomy.
"Long term, the plan is to fully rely on capacity that we are building ourselves, and so that means that the amount of compute that we own is going to grow around 100% in the next five years," Mensch said, adding that the company would train "bigger and faster models."
Mistral is already spending €4 billion on data centres across France and Europe, with one facility running outside Paris and another under construction in Sweden.
It raised further debt financing in March for the same purpose, and Microsoft has agreed to fund capacity from its European network, built around thousands of Nvidia chips.
Both Microsoft and Nvidia are also investors in Mistral, with the latter also adding exposure in this funding round.
The company says more than 125 enterprises across 20 countries use its technology, and Mistral projects it will pass a billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026.
Europe lags behind in the AI race
Despite the news, Europe continues to critically lag behind in the global AI race.
Mistral's valuation sits far below OpenAI and Anthropic, and Europe's wider AI sector remains a fraction of the American one, with enterprise adoption across the bloc running at around 13.5%.
Other European contenders exist but are smaller.
Germany's Aleph Alpha focuses on government and regulated industries rather than competing at the frontier, while Helsing has grown quickly in defence applications, and Switzerland's Apertus offers fully open models and training data.
Brussels is trying to close the gap.
The InvestAI initiative carries a €200 billion headline commitment, and in July the Commission opened tenders for up to seven AI gigafactories, aiming to unlock more than €30 billion in investment, though those sites are not expected to operate until next year or 2028.
Thirteen smaller AI factories are already being built across seven EU countries.
The AI Act became applicable in August, but its toughest obligations were pushed back by the digital omnibus agreed in May, with high-risk rules now landing in December 2027 and August 2028, a delay Brussels framed as making the policy more innovation-friendly.

Sea ice helps transport young Antarctic krill: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:38:57 CST
17:38:57 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Larval Antarctic krill could be carried far from their birthplace by drifting sea ice, linking distant ecosystems in ways conventional ocean-current models may miss, new research finds.
The study, published in Global Change Biology Communications, modeled how ocean circulation, sea ice drift and vertical migration influence the overwinter transport of Antarctic krill in the southwest Atlantic sector of the Southern Ocean, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Australian Antarctic Program Partnership (AAPP).
Antarctic krill are a key part of the Southern Ocean food web and are also the target of its largest fishery, the statement said.
"Krill are spending time sheltering in sea ice and use the ice as an extra transport system that moves and connects populations more widely than ocean currents alone," said lead author Aditya Sharma, a PhD student with the AAPP at Australia's University of Tasmania.
Using 32 years of high-resolution ocean current and sea ice simulations, researchers found that greater exposure to sea ice drift reduced krill retention near the Antarctic Peninsula while increasing northward transport toward the Scotia Sea and South Georgia.
Using a particle-tracking model, researchers released virtual "krill" and tracked their movements from April to October. The model indicates a strong tendency for krill to move eastwards away from the Antarctic Peninsula, largely due to the prevailing Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
With ocean currents alone, 17 percent of simulated krill moved east into the open ocean, but when particles spent all available time associated with sea ice, 48 percent moved east away from the peninsula.
The researchers said declining Antarctic sea ice could change the pathways transporting young krill across the Southern Ocean, potentially reshaping connectivity between krill populations and fishing regions. ■

According to Wong, ministers and other political officeholders will initially receive an adjustment of up to 9 percent, depending on factors including individual performance and when their salaries were last revised. ■

The €15 million Sicily villa that never existed: How a fake scandal targeted Édouard Philippe

2026-09-08

17:37:49 KST

It's not the first time that the leader of the Horizons party or other French presidential candidates have been targeted in this run-up to the 2027 election.
A fake story on X has claimed that former French prime minister and current Le Havre Mayor Édouard Philippe bought a luxury villa in Sicily, and linked it to a real but unrelated investigation into his alleged misuse of public funds.
A video shared online said Philippe acquired the estate from Le Havre local councillor Stéphanie de Bazelaire, and raised questions about how the alleged purchase was financed.
It was initially shared by a mock-up Italian online newspaper called "Repupplica.com", which has now been taken down.
The domain, however, sounded very similar to the genuine news outlet Repubblica.it. In other words, a fake website designed to be easily mistaken for the real one.
The video also cites an article by news outlet Affari Italiani, which says that Philippe is indeed being investigated. The article, however, has been taken out of context, as the investigation doesn't mention a house in Sicily.
Repubblica did not publish the story, no credible source confirms that Philippe bought a €15-million Sicilian villa, and there is no evidence connecting that case to a villa in Sicily.
But, as often happens with fake stories, the names involved were not picked at random.
Philippe and de Bazelaire are involved in a real, but completely separate, investigation in France concerning the management of a multi-million-euro digital-development project in Le Havre.
The investigation includes allegations of favouritism and misuse of public funds.
However, Philippe has denied any wrongdoing, and the investigation is still ongoing.
Philippe had already been targeted with fake online stories ahead of France’s presidential election. One of them falsely claimed he had dementia.
Other presidential candidates like Raphaël Glucksmann and Gabriel Attal were also targeted.
French authorities have linked some of these operations to pro-Russian networks, and prosecutors are examining suspected foreign interference targeting the potential candidates.
The first round of the next presidential election will be held on 18 April 2027.

Defence Intelligence reveals 155 Russian companies producing components for Russian weapons
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 155 companies belonging to the Russian Ruselectronics holding company that manufacture components for Russian weapons, including ballistic missiles, aircraft, UAVs and electronic warfare systems. Some of these companies are not subject to any sanctions imposed by Ukraine's partner countries.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Quote: "DIU has released data on 155 companies that are part of or managed by the Ruselectronics holding company, fully owned by Russia's state-owned corporation Rostec, in the Aggressor's Military-Industrial Complex section of the War&Sanctions portal."
Details: DIU noted that the holding company brings together companies and research organisations specialising in the development and production of radio and electronic components and technologies, communications equipment and systems, automated control systems, robotic systems, microwave electronics, computing equipment and telecommunications equipment.
Ruselectronics products are used in almost all types of Russian weapons, including ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, electronic warfare systems, military equipment and radar and communications systems for tactical, operational and strategic aviation, among others.
The holding company includes, in particular, companies involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M tactical missile system and 3M22 Zircon missiles:
- Girikond Research Institute JSC, a manufacturer of precision potentiometers for Zircon missiles
- NICEVT JSC, which supplies flight data processing units for Iskander missiles
- NPP Integral-V JSC, a manufacturer of pulse and heating transformers used in Iskander missiles.
The latter company is currently not subject to sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition, as is the case with almost half of all the holding company's businesses identified by DIU.
"However, the inclusion of Girikond and NICEVT on the sanctions lists of most partner countries has had little impact on the overall production volumes of these missiles. This does not mean that sanctions are ineffective, but rather demonstrates the need to improve mechanisms for monitoring compliance with them and strengthen accountability for violations," DIU noted.
DIU also stressed that components, equipment, software and critical raw materials must not fall into the hands of intermediaries and buyers who cannot confirm that the end recipient is a company with no links to Russia's military-industrial complex.

The Foundation for Science, Innovation and Development (FSID) at IISc has adopted a new governance and leadership model.
Bengaluru: The Foundation for Science, Innovation and Development (FSID) at IISc has adopted a new governance and leadership model, appointing Omprakash Subbarao as its CEO and bringing an industry professional to the helm for the first time.The change marks a new phase for FSID, which said it is seeking to build a self-sustaining Section 8 company anchored around two pillars: innovation and incubation. Historically, the organisation has been led by faculty members of IISc.Under the new structure, Subbarao will be a full-time CEO reporting to the FSID Board, with full operational autonomy and responsibility for the organisation’s day-to-day management, external engagement and execution of activities. Prof Suryasarthy Bose will serve as Professor-in-Charge, providing institutional oversight and acting as the principal interface between FSID and IISc.Subbarao, an IISc alumnus, brings experience across technology, industry, public digital infrastructure and innovation. Before his appointment, he was CEO of CORE Labs at FSID, where he led research and innovation collaborations with large corporations.
“As the world of research, innovation and technology translation evolves rapidly, so too are the expectations of industry, govt and other external stakeholders,” Subbarao said. To respond to these changing requirements “with greater agility, professionalism and scale”, he said, FSID was strengthening its governance and leadership structure.“For the first time, we’re having an industry leader as the CEO to drive this transformation,” he added. FSID has set a target of undertaking 1,000 industry projects and building a portfolio of 300 deep-tech startups by 2030.“With a vision of ‘Built on Science, Scaled for the World’, we are building FSID around two strong pillars: Innovation and Incubation,” Subbarao said. The organisation wants to deepen engagement with multinational corporations, Indian corporates and MSMEs while creating stronger pathways for science and research to translate into real-world impact, he said.
Over the past year, FSID has expanded industry engagement through Innovation Hub, or iHUB, its innovation and research facility that brings corporates and startups closer to IISc’s scientific ecosystem.The facility provides R&D laboratories for corporate partners and infrastructure for incubated startups. BEML, Toyo Ink and Schaeffler are among companies that have established research labs and workspaces there. FSID serves as IISc’s single-window interface for its deep science and deep-tech capabilities, supporting collaborative research, incubation, product development, consulting and industry-funded research.

Nothing else stopped, and Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites while the delegation was in Moscow.
Russia launched another massive attack on Kyiv the moment the envoys left, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
"[Russian President Putin's] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy. Strike after strike on residential buildings brings him no closer to winning this war—it is nothing but senseless terror," the minister wrote.
Russian forces resumed strikes on the capital after a three-day break tied to the American visit, RFE/RL's Belarus service reported.
What Russia launched
The attack ran from 18:00 on 7 September through the night, the Ukrainian Air Force reported, without giving the total number of launched ballistics.
Russia fired Oniks anti-ship missiles, ballistic Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 missiles, and 32 Kh-101 cruise missiles from four of its regions and occupied Crimea, along with 166 Shahed-type drones, more than half of them jet-powered, and decoys launched from two Russian regions and occupied territory. Air defense downed or suppressed 175 targets by 08:30: two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones. Kyiv Oblast and Odesa Oblast were the main axes.
"It was a hard attack, which the Russians deliberately tried to calculate for the greatest possible harm to life," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine put its own peace proposals on the table as two US envoys reached Kyiv for the first time
Results against cruise missiles were very good, he said, while ballistics remain especially hard, and Ukraine proves that need for interceptors to its partners every day. He said he had already discussed it with the Americans and Europeans and would meet states and companies the same day about supplies and about Ukraine's FREYJA anti-ballistic system.
Ukraine has 67 companies working on interceptors, three to five with real results.
Two dead and 13 rescued in the capital
First explosions in Kyiv came at 03:30. Fires and damage reached at least 16 locations in five districts, the Kyiv Military Administration reported. Warehouses, garages, and cars burned, fire spread from a garage to a business center, and a strike on a 26-story non-residential building wrecked structures at the 23rd floor, the State Emergency Service said. Ten people were freed from a blocked five-story block, the service said, and rescuers saved 13 in all, according to Zelenskyy. Morning drone attacks added a warehouse fire, the city said, and the night's damage forced it to reroute a series of bus, tram, and trolleybus lines.
Beyond Kyiv
Two Russian drones hit the locomotive of the Kyiv–Sumy train in the morning, which a monitoring team had stopped in time to evacuate passengers and crew without casualties, Ukrainian Railways board chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said.
Outside Odesa the strike damaged pavilions at the 7th Kilometer market, the country's largest wholesale market for non-food goods, and hospitalized its 58-year-old guard, oblast head Oleh Kiper said.
In Kharkiv two people were injured, one of them a 17-year-old, and Russian forces most often target energy sites, according to oblast head Oleh Syniehubov, who said they struck settlements across the oblast almost 800 times last week alone.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv Oblast's critical infrastructure, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were also hit.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s semiconductor industry has been recruiting about 47,000 workers per month this year, up more than 20% from a year earlier, according to 104 Job Bank.
The company’s 2026 semiconductor talent report found that the three biggest hiring areas were manufacturing and quality control, technical and maintenance work, and research, per Anue. Sixty percent of operations, technical, and maintenance job openings were open to applicants from any academic major.
AI-driven capacity expansion is shifting hiring needs from existing production-line operations toward workers who can support factory construction, equipment installation, mass production, and yield improvement, according to the report. Skills in technology transfer, knowledge replication, and system integration are also becoming more important as companies bring new capacity online.
The industry is also seeking more interdisciplinary talent. Companies are placing greater emphasis on knowledge spanning electronics, optics, and materials, as well as collaboration across disciplines.
AI-related semiconductor jobs have averaged more than 10,000 openings per month this year, up 67% from five years ago, with about one in four openings now related to AI. 104 Job Bank Chief Talent Sustainability Officer Chung Wen-hsiung (鍾文雄) said faster growth since last year shows companies are moving from evaluating AI to using it in production and research, per CNA.
Overseas hiring is also expanding, with US and Canadian job openings reaching a recent-year high. Asia excluding China, Hong Kong, and Macau remains the largest market for overseas assignments, per Tai Sounds.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian independent outlet Astra, citing an analysis of eyewitness footage, reported that the apparent target was the Saratov oil refinery, one of Russia’s oldest, operated by state-owned oil giant Rosneft.
The refinery processed 5.8 million metric tons of crude in 2024, accounting for about 2.2% of Russia’s total oil refining. It produced 1.2 million tons of gasoline, 1.9 million tons of diesel and 1 million tons of fuel oil.
The Saratov refinery has been targeted by Ukrainian drones four times this year, on March 21, May 31, July 8 and Aug. 2. Previous strikes forced the facility to halt oil processing. After the Aug. 2 attack, a Reuters source said repairs could take two to three weeks.
Ukrainian strikes cripple Russian refining
The latest strike comes as Ukraine intensifies its campaign against Russia’s oil infrastructure, seeking to disrupt a key source of revenue and fuel for Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian drones have struck Russian oil refineries at least 70 times since the beginning of 2026, pushing Russia’s refining output to its lowest level in two decades.
Ukrainian Drones Set Major Russian Refinery Ablaze for 8th Time This Year
By the end of August, gasoline production covered only around 70% of domestic demand, leaving a shortfall of roughly 30,000 tons per day.
At least 17 Russian regions have introduced restrictions on fuel sales, including limits of 30-40 liters per vehicle and “odd-even” systems based on license-plate numbers.
At least seven Russian refineries fully or partially halted production in August following drone attacks.
On Sept. 2, the KINEF refinery in Leningrad Oblast – Russia’s second-largest refinery by capacity – completely stopped processing.
Moscow turns to foreign fuel
The worsening shortage has forced Russia to take an unprecedented step: importing gasoline by sea.
Russian authorities have begun bringing in fuel from India, Morocco and Turkey, while also increasing gasoline purchases from Belarus to record levels.

To match China’s economy, India must accept its investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:30:12 UTC
17:30:12 KST

Advertisement
The View
To match China’s economy, India must accept its investment
Border rivalries shouldn’t block Chinese capital, just as wartime history never stopped Japanese investment from powering East Asia
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Winston Mok, a private investor, was previously a private equity investor. 
Although President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared a brief exchange last week at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the real action will unfold later this week at the Brics summit when Xi arrives in New Delhi with an expected delegation of 400 officials.
China is one of India’s top trading partners, yet it remains unclear whether Chinese companies are welcome as investors in India. The two countries’ trade and investment relationship has diverged starkly. Between 2016 and 2025-26, bilateral trade between China and India more than doubled from US$71.5 billion to US$151.1 billion. However, China’s investments in India have fallen from a height of US$705 million in 2015 to a mere trickle of US$6.5 million last year.
The two trends are related. Fuelled by its growing economy, India buys more from China, particularly capital goods. These expanding imports are driven by a lack of domestic alternatives which could have been established by Chinese investments. Restricting Chinese investments has only exacerbated the growing trade deficit with China.
The pathway towards greater economic sovereignty for India lies not with restricting but expanding foreign direct investment from China. After all, FDI is how China became the manufacturing powerhouse it is today.
The subdued level of Chinese FDI into India is a result of India’s choices. In the wake of their border dispute, India curtailed the level of investment from China, a chill that has only recently begun to thaw. However, even lifting all of India’s investment restrictions will not suddenly turn the country into an attractive destination for manufacturing. While software and services are the dominant targets for FDI into India, the pharmaceuticals sector – one of India’s most competitive exports – receives only about 4 per cent of inbound investment.
Potential investment in India’s manufacturing sector is hampered by a range of structural shortcomings, from regulations to infrastructure. China offers useful lessons.

Israel sees sharp decline in mathematics, reading, and science scores for students according to new PISA results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:29:43 UTC
17:29:43 KST

Israel sees sharp decline in math, reading, and science scores for students, according to new PISA results
The Ministry of Education claims that Israel maintained its ranking in reading and science, but in practice, Israel's average score is the lowest since the study began
The scores of Israeli students have dropped in mathematics, reading, and science, among the sharpest declines recorded in OECD countries since the PISA study began in 2000. This is according to alarming data published Tuesday by the National Authority for Measurement and Evaluation in Education (RAMA) and the Ministry of Education.
According to the findings, alongside a moderate decline in average achievement scores of OECD countries in reading and mathematics, Israel’s decline was sharper in all areas tested: in reading, Israel dropped by 38 points (to 436 points), in mathematics by 25 points (to 433 points), and in science by 23 points (to 442 points).
On average, OECD countries dropped by 14 points in reading and 9 points in mathematics (the change in science is not significant).
The Ministry of Education claims that “Israel maintained its ranking in reading and science compared to 2018 and dropped by one place in mathematics.” However, Israel's average score is the lowest since the study began, and is similar to the score it reached in 2006 in mathematics and reading, and in 2009 in science.
The Ministry of Education attributes the decline in students' achievements to the war and its effects, although according to the research findings, based on principals' reports, the reasons for the impairment in students' abilities lie in the fundamental problems of the Israeli education system. About half of the principals reported a shortage of teachers and a mismatch or insufficiently trained teachers as the main reasons for the decline, alongside a lack of infrastructure and digital equipment to support the learning environment.
According to the study, as mentioned, the declines in Israel are among the sharpest recorded in OECD countries since the PISA survey began in 2000, especially in reading. There have been four cases recorded to date, including Israel, in which the achievements of an OECD country dropped by 35 points or more in a single cycle in this area.
Israel's average score in the three domains is the lowest since it began participating in PISA, and is not significantly different from the score it reached in 2006 in mathematics and reading and in 2009 in science.
Meanwhile, the proportion of students classified as struggling has risen to its highest level since 2006, while the proportion of outstanding students is plummeting. According to the findings, 46% of 15-year-olds in Israel struggle with mathematics, 41% with reading, and 40% with science.
In reading, the proportion of outstanding students dropped from 11% to 5%. About two-thirds or more of Arabic-speaking students were classified as struggling in all subject areas.
Additionally, the gaps between Israeli students, which stood out in previous PISA studies, narrowed this time, but not due to an improvement among the weaker students, rather because of a decline among the stronger students.
Within Israel, the sharpest decline in achievement was among Hebrew-speaking students in the state education system, where drops of 52 points in reading, 29 points in mathematics, and 28 points in science were recorded. In light of the decrease in the achievements of Hebrew-speaking girls in the state education system, there is currently no group of girls whose average achievements are significantly higher than those of girls in ultra-Orthodox educational institutions.
Suggested articles
In the PISA 2025 study, more than 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries and economic entities participated. In Israel, the study was conducted among 7,330 students from 215 schools, constituting a nationally representative sample.
Minister of Education Yoav Kisch refused to take responsibility for the PISA data: "The education system did the best it could under the circumstances. We are doing everything to provide significant solutions. PISA reflects the changes that have taken place over the past three years, and especially the impact of the situation here, of the war, on the education system." After being asked about responsibility for the data, Kisch cut the press conference and the promised questions short.

Russia’s Defense Ministry proposes clawing back part of contract bonuses from convicted soldiers ‘to motivate compliance with the law’
Russia’s Defense Ministry has proposed clawing back part of the federal signing bonus paid to military personnel who are convicted of crimes but are not sentenced to prison. The draft resolution was published on the government portal for draft legal acts. Verstka, an independent Russian news outlet, was among the first to notice it.
The measure would apply to Defense Ministry and Russian National Guard personnel who received a sentence not involving imprisonment and remained in service. They would have to repay part of the bonus, with the amount calculated in proportion to the number of months left until the end of their service. The lump-sum payments themselves total either 195,000 or 400,000 rubles.
The resolution’s stated goal is to “increase service members’ motivation to comply with Russian law,” according to its explanatory memo. The decision to draft it followed an April 24 meeting of Russia’s Security Council. That meeting addressed measures to prevent crimes in the military “in light of the experience of the special military operation.”
Alexey Tabalov, founder of the human rights project “School for Conscripts,” told Verstka he suspects the authorities are simply trying to save money on payments to service members.

SZ-HK-Guangzhou cluster tops innovation index again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:27:15 UTC
17:27:15 KST

For the second straight year, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster retained its top spot in 2026 in the latest Global Innovation Index (GII) of the world's top 100 innovation clusters which was published by the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) on Tuesday.
“We warmly welcome the innovation cluster ranking published by WIPO, which reaffirms the outstanding innovative capacity and the innovation and technology (I&T)-supporting financing ecosystem of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area,” a government spokesman said.
It noted that expediting I&T development has been the administration's priority and its work had begun to show results.
For instance, the number of start-ups in the SAR has surged by more than threefold to over 5,200 last year compared with a decade ago.
The two local flagship tech hubs – Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport – have nurtured about 20 unicorns so far, the spokesman said.
More than 100 technology enterprises and institutions have already signed leases with the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Co-operation Zone even though it only opened in December last year.
Along with the Hetao zone, the spokesman said the San Tin Technopole would "form a crucial node for the integrated development of upstream, midstream and downstream industries".
It also noted that Hong Kong ranks second in Asia after the mainland for private equity assets under management of nearly US$250 billion, adding that the government had been stepping up the development of venture financing as a crucial element for the city's I&T and commercialisation ecosystem.
Looking ahead, the government spokesman said the SAR would actively align with the nation’s 15th Five-Year Plan to step up the city’s strategic positioning as an international I&T hub.
The spokesman added that Hong Kong would further step up collaboration with GBA cities and contribute to the nation’s development.
The GII Cluster ranking identifies local concentrations of world-class innovation activity through three key metrics, including the number of international patent filings via WIPO's Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), the number of scientific publications produced, and the number of venture capital deals completed. 
The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster filed more than 2,200 PCT applications, published more than 4,000 scientific articles, and had roughly 140 venture capital deals – all per one million inhabitants over the last five years.

Business conditions took a tumble in August, with profitability falling 10 points to the lowest level since the pandemic, NAB's monthly business survey showed on Tuesday.
How much businesses are able to pass through those costs to consumers will help determine how sticky inflation will remain going forward.
And it will depend on how willing households are to keep spending.
Confidence drops among mortgage borrowers
Expectations of more rate rises caused sentiment among home owners to collapse in September, the Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index showed.
Confidence plummeted 14 per cent among mortgage holders in the month, compared to a 0.9 per cent fall among renters.
''Interest rate concerns had a clear negative impact on consumers with a mortgage," Westpac's head of Australian macro-forecasting Matthew Hassan said.
Overall, the consumer sentiment index declined 5.2 per cent to 84.4, as interest rate expectations climbed 7.3 per cent.
Despite economists forecasting the housing downturn to deepen as high interest rates combine with federal budget tax changes, only 32 per cent of consumers expected prices to decline over the next 12 months, with 42 per cent expecting a rise.
HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham expects nationwide house prices to fall 13 per cent peak to trough, which would be "the largest housing price correction in modern history".
Already, $34.1 billion has been wiped off Australian property values in the three months ended June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
The 0.3 per cent decline pales in comparison to the 12.3 per cent increase since the start of 2025.

Intelligence publishes data on 155 Ruselectronics enterprises producing components for ballistic missiles, aircraft, drones, and EW systems
Ukrinform reports this, citing the Main Intelligence Directorate’s post on Facebook .
Data on 155 enterprises that are part of or managed by Ruselectronics, a holding company of Russia’s state-owned Rostec corporation, have been published in the “Aggressor’s Military-Industrial Complex” section of the War&Sanctions portal.
The holding company brings together enterprises and research organizations specializing in the development and production of electronic components and technologies, communications equipment and systems, automated control systems, robotic systems, microwave electronics, computer technology, and telecommunications equipment.
Their products are used in nearly the entire range of Russian weapons, including ballistic and cruise missiles , UAVs, electronic warfare systems, military equipment, and radar and communications systems for tactical, frontline, and strategic aviation.
Ruselectronics includes, among others, enterprises involved in the production of 9M723 missiles for the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system and 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles:
JSC NII Girikond — a manufacturer of precision potentiometers for Zircon missiles;
JSC NITSEVT — a supplier of flight-data processing units for Iskander ballistic missiles;
JSC NPP Integral-V — a manufacturer of pulse and heating transformers used in 9M723 missiles.
The last of these enterprises is still not subject to sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition, as is almost half of all the holding company’s enterprises currently listed.
However, the inclusion of Girikond and NITSEVT on the sanctions lists of most partner countries has had little impact on the overall production volumes of these missiles. This does not mean that sanctions are ineffective; rather, it primarily demonstrates the need to improve mechanisms for monitoring compliance with sanctions and strengthen liability for violations, the intelligence service noted.
Components, equipment, software, and critical raw materials must not reach intermediaries and buyers who cannot confirm that the final recipient of the products is an enterprise unrelated to Russia’s military-industrial sector.
The HUR calls for tighter control over supply chains to prevent sanctions evasion and the transfer of critical technologies and materials to Russia.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the Main Intelligence Directorate published data on 17 scientists and developers from Russian institutes and organizations involved in military and dual-use R&D.

- This display highlighted ongoing military cooperation between China and Pakistan, and revisited disputed military claims from the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.
AI generated
ISLAMABAD – Pakistan’s military showcased an air defence system that resembles a Chinese platform in a promotional video, potentially signalling another layer to the defence cooperation that has deepened since the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.
Pakistan did not identify the six-wheeled military vehicle with a large rectangular radar array in a promotional video of its weapons released on Sept 7 on its official X account.
Features of the vehicle, shown about 28 seconds into the video, resemble China’s HQ-17A short-range surface-to-air missile system, which was developed based on Russia’s Tor system, said Tianran Xu, senior analyst for Open Nuclear Network.
If Pakistan has acquired the system, it would mark China’s first sale of the HQ-17A to the South Asian nation. The Pakistan military and air force, as well as China’s Defence Ministry, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The official press account of China’s armed forces confirmed the model in a post on X on Sept 7. It is common for footage of foreign purchases of Chinese weapons to emerge before a public announcement.
Xu said the HQ-17A should have good defensive capabilities against cruise missiles, manned aircraft and other low-altitude targets, adding that it could be integrated with Chinese command-and-control systems provided to Pakistan.
“However, the effectiveness of the HQ-17 or similar systems against emerging and fast-evolving drone threats remains to be tested on a real battlefield,” he said.
The HQ-17A is manufactured by the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corp and was first publicly displayed at the National Day military parade in 2019. The People’s Liberation Army has an estimated 200 HQ-17 and 50 HQ-17A systems, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In the past few years, Serbia and Tajikistan have also acquired the HQ-17AE, an export variant based on the HQ-17A, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Military cooperation between Pakistan and China drew global attention when Pakistan used Chinese-made J-10C fighter jets in the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.
Pakistan said the jets downed multiple Indian aircraft, including French-made Rafales. India has disputed those claims, and the J-10C’s performance has drawn intense scrutiny since the conflict.
India’s air force said it destroyed about a dozen Pakistani aircraft during the confrontation, including at least five advanced fighters, such as US-made F-16 or Chinese-made JF-17 jets.
The exact number of aircraft destroyed remains disputed, and analysts have questioned claims of military success by both sides in previous conflicts. BLOOMBERG

Sahin Demir

Yemen’s Houthi group on Tuesday confirmed carrying out large-scale missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and vowed to continue operations deep inside the kingdom amid a sharp escalation between the two sides.
In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group carried out a “large-scale” military operation using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
He said the attacks targeted Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as Khamis Mushait Air Base.
Saree claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and caused extensive damage to the targeted facilities.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was in response to Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, claiming that Saudi Arabia had carried out 121 strikes over the past three days in Marib, Al-Bayda, Al-Hudaydah, Taiz and Al-Jawf provinces.
He also accused Saudi Arabia of striking the Central Prison in Al-Hazm, Al-Jawf, causing casualties among inmates and visitors, including women and children.
“We will continue our operations deep inside Saudi territory, target its military buildups, and consolidate the equation of ‘blockade for blockade’ until the aggression stops and the blockade on our dear country is lifted,” Saree said.
The statement came after Saudi authorities said earlier Tuesday that Houthi attacks on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran injured at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi Energy Ministry also reported fires at energy facilities in the kingdom’s southern region and said some operations at the targeted sites were temporarily halted.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and said the coalition would take all necessary operational measures to deter the Houthis and neutralize sources of threats.
The latest escalation comes as Yemeni government forces have reported battlefield gains against the Houthis on several fronts, including in Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda, Taiz and Al-Hudaydah.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Tartu drops plan to subsidize new early Riga bus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

Tartu drops plan to subsidize new early Riga bus
Tartu has dropped plans to subsidize an early-morning bus service to Riga, while passenger train operator Elron plans to introduce a morning rail connection in the first half of next year.
The first bus from Tartu toward Riga currently leaves the university city at 11:10 a.m. Late last year, the City of Tartu said it was prepared to temporarily use taxpayer money to subsidize an early-morning bus service from Tartu toward Riga. The subsidy was estimated at around €30,000 a year.
The plan was to hold an open tender to find an operator under de minimis state aid rules. However, a decision has now been made not to introduce such a measure, Tartu City Secretary Jüri Mölder said.
"This has been prompted by changes in the economic environment around us, which force us to look at the situation more broadly. It has also been prompted by lower-than-expected city budget revenues, meaning we need to assess more carefully what we use the city's money for," Mölder said.
As of December, two companies had expressed interest in operating such a subsidized service: A-buss and Lux Express. The latter has previously offered an early-morning departure from Tartu toward Riga on a commercial basis.
Lux Express currently runs between Tartu and Riga twice a day. CEO Ingmar Roos said Lux Express will not introduce an early-morning commercial service from Tartu to Latvia this season either because there are too few passengers traveling between Tartu and Riga.
"On the existing services between Tartu and Riga, from January through May the better-performing departures carried an average of 20 passengers, while the weaker ones carried fewer than 10. It is true that from June through August, during the tourist season, the number of passengers approached 30 a day, but with the start of September, it has fallen again," Roos said.
"Twenty passengers between Tartu and Riga is still around 30 percent below the threshold at which a bus company operating solely on ticket revenue could provide the service."
Roos added that the existing departures from Tartu toward Riga are made more viable by the fact that the services have been extended to Narva.
"The key is the additional passengers from Narva and Tartu who are traveling to Riga. In that combination, the service is viable. As for the question of how to create a morning connection from Tartu, naturally it would not be feasible to structure the Narva and Riga legs around departures in the middle of the night in order to have a bus leave Tartu at 8 a.m.," the bus company executive explained.
Elron, however, plans to add a morning train in the first half of next year alongside its current evening Tartu-Riga departure. Elron will be able to introduce a morning Tallinn-Tartu-Riga train once its new Škoda electric trains begin operating between Tallinn and Tartu, the company's communications manager Kristo Mäe said.
"We currently have information from infrastructure owner Estonian Railways that we will be able to start serving the Tallinn-Tartu route with Škoda electric trains in January. After that, we will be able to provide the exact dates. It certainly won't happen on January 1," Mäe said.
Elron currently runs one train a day from Tartu to Riga in the evening, with the return service in the morning. Statistics for the first eight months show that more than 29,000 train journeys have been made with Elron to Latvia or Lithuania or from those countries to Estonia, including nearly 12,000 passenger journeys on the direct train.
