Aid cuts force mass clinic closures across Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:19:17 UTC
17:19:17 KST

- As war is driving people's health needs in Sudan, humanitarian aid funding cuts are leaving people without lifesaving care.
- As more clinics close, people are forced to take longer, more dangerous journeys to reach care.
- Governments and institutional donors must protect funding for essential health services, and provide flexible transitional financing where facilities are at risk of closure.
Amidst a brutal ongoing war and a catastrophic humanitarian crisis, people in Sudan face reduced access to healthcare as facilities across the country close their doors. The impact of broad and historic international aid funding cuts by governments has begun to take hold. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that this withdrawal of support from an already chronically underfunded crisis is cutting off lifesaving care and pushing the few remaining hospitals to breaking point.
As world leaders gather at the UN General Assembly, governments and institutional donors must protect funding for essential health services in Sudan and provide flexible transitional financing where facilities are at risk of closure.
With aid organisations pulling out, local clinics are left without the funds or medicines needed to function. For patients, this means enduring long, dangerous journeys just to receive treatment. As they seek help wherever they can, the few hospitals still operational are absorbing the overflow: between January and April 2026, admissions in MSF supported facilities in Zalingei and Rokero, in Central Darfur state, jumped by 22.5 per cent compared to the same time last year. The situation has deteriorated even further as in May alone 45 general healthcare centres in Central Darfur stopped receiving support as the organisation that had been providing resources lacked funding.
“War is driving Sudan’s needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response,” says Muhammad Ibrahim, MSF head of mission in Sudan. “MSF’s work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours.”
But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours.
“Donors must protect essential health services and provide sustained, flexible funding to organisations that depend on it,” says Ibrahim.
In Tanedba camp, in Gedaref state, home to 18,400 refugees, the sudden departure of a humanitarian organisation in June resulted in the camp’s maternity and surgical wards closing. Pregnant women who need caesarean sections now face three-hour journeys to the nearest city. MSF has stepped in to run the emergency room there through the end of 2026.
In 2021, around 35 aid organisations were working in and around Um Rakuba camp in Al-Gedaref state. Today, fewer than 10 remain. The camp now hosts around 17,000 refugees, mostly women and children.
“Our hospital in Um Rakuba is now the only lifeline left for both refugees and the local Sudanese community,” says Fabrizio Locuratolo, MSF humanitarian affairs manager. “But the cuts here go well beyond healthcare. Food rations are shrinking and protection programmes are being dismantled, pulling away the last safety nets and leaving refugees completely exposed.”
After the United States (US) government announced the closure of USAID1 in 2025, the grants to many organisations funded to work in Sudan ended in June this year. Although the US government continues to be the largest donor to Sudan, providing funding to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and other organisations, many of the existing healthcare providers have been unable to find alternative funding to continue providing services, with health facilities closing in Sudan as a result.
Just as health providers faced the impending removal of US support, many European governments also reduced their assistance to people in Sudan. European and multilateral aid budgets are also shrinking globally. OECD2 preliminary data show that aid from EU institutions fell by 13.8 per cent in 2025, while several major European donors also reduced their overall aid spending.
Globally, humanitarian aid fell by 35.8 per cent. These figures do not represent equivalent cuts to Sudan, where some European donors have maintained or increased their support. But they point to a sharply contracting international funding environment. In Sudan, that wider squeeze is compounding an already severe health crisis, as specific funding withdrawals and programme closures reduce access to healthcare.
“Closing a clinic does not remove a single patient. It just sends them to the next facility,” says Sebastián Traficante, MSF emergency coordinator in Darfur. “After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full. MSF can reinforce some services, but we cannot absorb every closure.”
In Central Darfur’s Hamidiya displacement camp, a health centre that previously provided maternity, paediatric, and mental health care is now operating at sharply reduced capacity after an international aid organisation ended its support. Daily patient visits have dropped from 200 to barely 40, and vaccinations have stopped. The fall was not a sign that people had become healthier. They had stopped making the journey to a centre that could no longer treat them. A labourer in Darfur earns roughly US$13, a day. The US$2 transport fare to reach a working clinic therefore costs about two days’ wages, leaving residents to choose between healthcare and food. 
“That money could buy food instead,” a patient told MSF. “If there is no food, there can be no health.”
That money could buy food instead. If there is no food, there can be no health.
Despite the presence of around 50 NGOs in Tawila, critical gaps persist for up to 600,000 displaced people. MSF runs the only 200-bed hospital in the area and is the only organisation capable of mounting a large-scale epidemic response. Malaria and malnutrition cases are already rising despite limited rainfall, ahead of the peak of the rainy season — and we expect numbers to increase as the rain intensifies. In August, our teams admitted 191 children under five with severe malnutrition to our inpatient feeding centre, and nearly 22 per cent also tested positive for malaria.
These closures are happening during a large-scale, severely underfunded humanitarian crisis. The UN reports that 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition and 19.5 million people faced crisis-level hunger earlier this year, meaning families either do not have enough food to eat or can only meet basic food needs by resorting to measures such as selling the assets they depend on to survive. Yet the UN’s $2.87 billion response plan is barely 41 per cent funded, and 37 per cent of Sudan’s health facilities are estimated to be completely out of service.4

Bengaluru-based space technology startup GalaxEye has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system.
BENGALURU: Bengaluru-based space technology startup GalaxEye has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, with the company claiming that it is the first Indian startup to receive a US patent for satellite imaging technology.The patent covers the architecture and system developed by GalaxEye to align and synchronise optical and microwave sensors for simultaneous acquisition of spatially and temporally matched data. The same foundational technology has already been patented in India.“The development strengthens GalaxEye’s intellectual-property position as it prepares to build a planned constellation of 30 satellites over the next five years. The company expects the network to support defence, govt and commercial applications across national security, agriculture, infrastructure, insurance, maritime intelligence and disaster management,” a statement issued Monday, read.At the heart of the technology is a challenge in Earth observation. Optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors operate on different physical principles and have traditionally been deployed independently or combined through post-processing.
Even when both types of imagery are available for the same location, they can be captured at different times, from different viewing geometries and by different platforms, creating temporal gaps and spatial misalignment.GalaxEye said its patented system addresses this challenge at the sensing architecture level. The technology forms the basis of the company’s OptoSAR approach, combining the visual and spectral information of optical imaging with SAR’s ability to operate in all weather conditions, day and night.
Former Isro chairman S Somanath described the patent as an example of innovation emerging from India’s private space ecosystem. He said the technology’s “uniqueness lies in synchronising optical and SAR sensors at the system level” to deliver spatially and temporally matched Earth observation data, adding that it had commercial potential across applications requiring more actionable intelligence.GalaxEye founder and CEO Suyash Singh said: “This is not just a patent for us. This is an invention, an invention that came out of India,” he said, adding that the US protection was validation of what Indian deep-tech companies could create.The company took the technology to orbit through Mission Drishti, its first satellite, launched on May 3, 2026. However, the satellite was later declared as a failure.

PISA report: one in three Flemish 15-year-olds fails to reach the basic level in reading, fewer high achievers in Flanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:18:53 UTC
17:18:53 KST

Three in ten Flemish 15-year-olds fail to reach the basic level in reading. In vocational education, this figure rises to as many as three-quarters of the pupils. The figures are contained in a new international PISA study involving nearly 4,000 Flemish pupils. Flanders still scores above the European average in reading, maths and science, but has fewer and fewer high achievers and an increasing number of pupils who perform poorly.
PISA report: one in three Flemish 15-year-olds fails to reach the basic level in reading, fewer high achievers in Flanders
Many Flemish pupils are at a complete loss when it comes to basic skills. In science, one-fifth (22.6 per cent) fail to reach the basic level; in maths, one-quarter (25.6 per cent); and in reading, 29.4 per cent fail to reach the basic level.
At the same time, the group of top performers in the classroom is getting smaller and smaller. Whereas in 2003 one in three Flemish pupils could call themselves a maths top performer, that figure is now just one in nine.
For science and reading, this group is even smaller: 8.2 per cent and 5.6 per cent of Flemish pupils, respectively, are in the top group. Flanders continues to score above the EU average in all three subjects, the scores are continuing to fall systematically over the years.
Political initiative
Flemish Education Minister Zuhal Demir (Flemish nationalist N-VA) intends to get in touch with the relevant European Commissioner and her European colleagues: “You cannot build a strong society without people with sufficient knowledge. We used to be among the best in the world and must now take the lead to get back to that level.”
Another striking finding when compared with the OECD average is that, when Flemish pupils are surveyed, they appear to be less curious and show less perseverance.
They are also less likely than average to say they receive support from their families when it comes to schoolwork. It is striking that, whilst the teacher shortage does cause problems, these problems are perceived as more serious in other countries than they are in Flanders.

Low turnout threatens Commons vote on assisted dying, say MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:16:30 UTC
17:16:30 KST

MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about turnout affecting the vote on Friday, when the bill returns to the Commons for its second attempt to become law.
Those who back the change in the law in England and Wales have been emphasising the “undemocratic” nature of the bill’s rejection by the House of Lords after it was talked out by a handful of peers after passing the House of Commons. The bill fell despite multiple days of debate from peers because of the number of amendments tabled in the Lords.
Several former cabinet ministers and ministers say they intend to speak out on the bill now they are freer to express their views, especially on the conduct of the Lords.
The private member’s bill – originally sponsored by Kim Leadbeater – has been revived by the Labour MP Lauren Edwards. It had passed last year by a majority of 23 in the Commons.
In an article for the Guardian, Edwards said the bill was “the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by former Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper”. She said the Lords should not be “allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time”.
Edwards said she rejected some accusations from Labour MPs that she was reopening divisions in the party at a moment when there was a chance to reunite it now that Andy Burnham had replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister.
“Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions,” Edwards said.
“Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial.
“It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.”
Backers of the bill have stressed that MPs should see the vote as a moment to assert the Commons’ decision-making power, rather than rerun the arguments.
Two former cabinet ministers told the Guardian they now wanted to speak out on their reasons for supporting the bill.
The former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn said he was motivated by the death of his first wife to want to relieve suffering of a loved one. “All of us who have experienced the loss of a loved one to a terminal illness – 47 years ago my first wife, Rosalind, died of adrenal cancer – know how hard it is.
“If someone who has only months to live is facing the prospect of unbearable pain – despite the best efforts of palliative care – how can we look them in the eye and say that we will not help them to bring their lives to an end in a way of their choosing surrounded by those they love and who love them?” he said.
He said that the House of Lords would have “huge responsibility to listen and to vote on the bill rather than repeat the procedural obstruction we saw last time. Those suffering at the end of their lives deserve nothing less.”
Jo Stevens, a former Welsh secretary, said: “I’ve always supported the principle of assisted dying. I have constituents and friends who desperately wanted one and a constituent who I helped after they were arrested for escorting someone who chose an assisted death at Dignitas.
“I and many other MPs, including MPs who didn’t support the bill, are furious at the outrageous behaviour of a small number of unelected peers who went against the will of the Commons. Many of these are former MPs who should know better, especially former ministers who were rejected by the electorate.”
However, several MPs said they believed it was the pro-side that was finding it hardest to convince MPs to stay and vote on Friday. “No one has changed sides, but the numbers are going to be tighter because people are absent,” one MP said.
Two MPs who voted in favour of the bill are no longer in parliament: Starmer, who quit as an MP last week and is yet to be replaced; and the former Makerfield MP Josh Simons, who was replaced by Burnham, who has said he will abstain.
Other high-profile supporters of the bill, including the cabinet minister Louise Haigh, minister Ian Murray and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, have written to constituents previously saying they were uneasy about using the Parliament Act to pass the law. The act would come into force, within certain conditions, if the Lordswere to reject the bill a second time.

Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:15:19 UTC
17:15:19 KST

Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch flying car maker PAL-V has been given the go-ahead to start building something that could be in the skies in 2028.
The European aviation safety agency EASA gave the company, based in Noord-Brabant, a production licence, meaning it now has every permit it needs to begin building. It first began designing flying cars 20 years ago.
“Now that EASA approval is in, we will really start producing the first cars soon,” chief executive Robert Dingemanse told broadcaster NOS. “We then have to test them again to show once more that we meet all the guidelines. That takes about a year and a half.”
PAL-V’s models have faced repeated promises and delays in the past – its first car was cleared in 2020 and it said its first commercial model would follow in 2021, which was then postponed to 2025 and then 2026.
The Liberty, which folds its rotor blades away to drive on the road, costs between €299,000 and €499,000. The first 250 are already sold, NOS reported, and the company has stopped taking orders because it can only build 100 per year.
Around half the buyers are fire brigades, police forces and the military, Dingemanse said. The rest are specialists who need to get somewhere fast, plus a handful of wealthy private owners. Apart from the Dutch fire brigade, almost all of them are foreign.
Don’t expect one over your street
 The bad news for anyone dreaming of skipping national traffic jams is that the flying car is likely going nowhere in the Netherlands for regular people, no matter how rich you are.
It has to follow the same rules as any aircraft, and can only take off and land at around 20 small airstrips nationwide. “You can’t just fly anywhere,” Delft University aviation professor Jacco Hoekstra told NOS. “And Dutch airspace is pretty full.”
Aviation expert Joris Melkert said the Netherlands has a perfectly good road network, and that unlike a country like Norway, where getting across a fjord in a hurry can be impossible, “a flying car is not crucial here.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Estonian firm buys Lithuanian agricultural group Litagra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

Estonian firm buys Lithuanian agricultural group Litagra
Infortar's subsidiary Infortar Agro is expanding into Lithuania by buying agricultural group UAB Litagra, which operates in milk and crop production, poultry farming, feed manufacturing and other farming activities.
Litagra is a Lithuanian agricultural group that began operations in 1991. The Litagra group includes UAB Joniškio Grūdai, UAB Litagros Žemės Ūkio Centras and Agrohold Estonia OÜ, whose shares belong 100 percent to UAB Litagra. In total, in addition to the parent company, the Litagra group includes 34 companies.
The transaction expands Infortar's agricultural operations into Lithuania and complements Infortar's existing investments in this field in Estonia. Once the transaction is completed, the farms owned by the group will have a total of 16,600 animals, annual milk production will reach 93,000 tonnes and the total area of farmland will increase to 23,000 hectares. Poultry farming, including turkey and broiler farms, will become a new area of activity.
"Estonia and Lithuania have historically been agricultural countries. Our latitude and climate are well suited to milk production, our cows are among the highest-yielding in Europe, and our farms are among the most modern. Milk is one of our most important natural resources. By increasing production, it could become an important export product and strengthen our position in international markets," said Ain Hanschmidt, CEO of Infortar.
Infortar's managing director Martti Talgre added that they have operated in Lithuania for eight years, experienced an investor‑friendly environment and taken part in economic growth.
"Agriculture is highly valued in Lithuania, and both performance and productivity are strong. This is why we decided to make one of Estonia's largest foreign investments in Lithuanian agriculture and acquire a well-established company with a long history," said Talgre.
According to Invalda INVL, which has been a Litagra shareholder since 2011, the transaction confirms the value created in the company and marks the end of a successful investment cycle.
"Fifteen years ago, we invested in Litagra with the ambition of building a competitive company operating in high-value, profitable segments of the food and agriculture industry. Over the years, we consistently invested in dairy and poultry production, expanded into new businesses and exited activities that no longer fit our strategy," said Invalda INVL's CEO Darius Šulnis.
Litagra's current management will continue to run the company's daily operations, and Infortar does not plan significant changes to the company's existing activities as a result of the transaction. To complete the transaction, permits and approvals from authorities must be obtained and other additional conditions fulfilled.
The Litagra Group employs almost 400 people. As of the end of last year, the group's consolidated turnover was €69 million and EBITDA €14.5 million. The group has a total of 10,500 hectares of arable land.
Litagra's subsidiary UAB Sūduvos Ūkis, which is wholly owned by UAB Joniškio Grūdai, is the largest turkey farming company in the Baltic States. The company operates six production sites comprising a total of 29 modern barns with a total of 160,000 turkeys.
In addition, the group operates broiler production facilities with capacity for approximately 360,000 broilers per production cycle. The poultry operations are supported by the group company UAB Joniškio Grūdai, which produced 69,000 tonnes of compound feed and related products in 2025, including protein, vitamin and mineral supplements, premixes, baits and pet food. The company also supplies compound feed to Litagra Group's poultry farming companies.
Litagra's subsidiary UAB Litagros Žemės Ūkio Centras (LŽŪC) is the third-largest dairy farming company in Lithuania by herd size. The company operates eight farms and focuses on dairy production and crop farming. The company's dairy herd comprises approximately 8,300 cows and young cattle, and it produces an average of 35,000 tonnes of raw milk per year.
Infortar operates in seven countries; the company's main fields of activity are maritime transport, energy and real estate. The group includes 107 companies, and excluding associated companies, Infortar employs 6 890 people.

International Pisa education ratings show disadvantaged students in England outperforming European peers
Richard Adams
Richard Adams is the Guardian’s education editor.
The OECD’s triennial programme for international student assessment (Pisa) comes as a controversial intervention in England’s policy debate about schools and what they should teach.
The Pisa 2025 rankings published today show England’s teenagers doing as well as ever in traditional subjects, and well above average, at a time when international test results in reading and maths have declined. But the policy mood within England’s government is that schools are too academic for those who struggle in exams such as GCSEs.
Lucy Powell, education secretary for England, said in an interview with the Observer that while she applauded the Pisa results, she wanted to “replace the exam factory with the talent factory” and argued that “the gap between the classroom and that new world of work is just too big”.
But the Pisa results - based on tests and surveys of 15-year-olds - showed that disadvantaged students in England outperform students in other European countries.
Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education and skills, said:
Today we can see that the most disadvantaged students in the UK are doing better than their counterparts in Germany, for example.
Today’s Pisa scores tell a positive story about our school system and the hard work of teachers and school leaders. While the global decline in reading scores is deeply concerning, the UK is bucking the international trend, with England performing particularly strongly.
England is the only UK nation where performance across all three subjects has held up since 2015. That suggests there are important things our education system is getting right.

Two children were killed and 15 people injured in Houthi shelling targeting a gathering of displaced people in Yemen’s central Marib province, local authorities said Tuesday.
The government-run local authority said in a statement that the Houthis fired several projectiles at a gathering of displaced people in the Raghwan district in northern Marib on Monday evening.

Several fronts in Yemen have witnessed renewed military escalation in recent days between government forces and the Houthis, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda provinces, alongside airstrikes on Houthi positions.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Three paintings with an estimated value of €9 million ($10.5 million) were stolen from the Auguste Renoir Museum in southern France during an overnight burglary, local media reported Tuesday.
Two thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, overnight from Monday to Tuesday, French broadcaster BFM Nice Cote d’Azur reported, citing a police source.
Surveillance footage showed two people entering the former residence of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir and taking four works, according to Mayor Bryan Masson.
“They fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings during their escape. The perpetrators are currently being actively sought,” Masson said.
Surveillance footage reportedly showed the suspects cutting paintings from their frames before a security alarm was triggered at 5.48 am local time (0348GMT).
Initial reports said the thieves entered the building by smashing a glass door and cut paintings from their frames. Investigators also found two zippered bags in the museum garden that may have belonged to the suspects.
The judicial police have taken over the investigation, while the museum has been closed to the public until further notice.
The Sub-Directorate for Combating Organized Crime and Specialized Delinquency is leading the investigation.
Housed at Les Collettes, the final residence of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, the museum holds around 10 original paintings by the artist and approximately 40 sculptures, as well as his furniture, personal belongings, photographs, and archives.

Malaysian woman who stabbed boyfriend to death over sex demand gets 12 years
An appeal court nearly doubled the woman’s jail term, calling the initial sentence ‘over-sympathetic’
A Malaysian court has nearly doubled jail time for a woman who stabbed her boyfriend to death for demanding sex after ruling that the sentencing court had been “over-sympathetic” towards the accused.
The Court of Appeal increased the prison sentence for the woman, identified only as Shy to protect her identity, from the six and a half years imposed by the Johor Bahru High Court to 12 years, Free Malaysia Today news portal reported on Tuesday.
Evrol Mariette Peters, one of the three judges in the panel, said in the grounds for judgment that the state court had placed too much emphasis on Shy’s age while failing to give sufficient weight to the seriousness of her actions.
Shy was 19 at the time of the incident.
According to court papers, she and her then boyfriend, 29, checked into a hotel near Jalan Austin Heights in Johor Bahru on September 20, 2022. The couple had been going out for about a year.
In the room, Shy’s boyfriend asked for sex but she refused, saying she was menstruating. The boyfriend pulled out a knife and threatened her with it.
She fought to take the weapon away from him and, in the struggle, stabbed him multiple times in the chest. An autopsy later found 28 stab wounds on his body.

The Eiffel Tower reopened on Tuesday after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologised.
The operating company that runs the Paris landmark, SETE, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit on Saturday be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
The Eiffel Tower, which says it receives nearly seven million people a year, reopened on Tuesday morning, with visitors making their way through security checkpoints at the base.
The monument was closed on Monday, when SETE said it held a meeting between staff and management.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologised for "any pain or inconvenience caused" by the incident.
"To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower," the organisation wrote on X.
"Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others."
Eiffel Tower staff condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the visit by the delegation.
"Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation," the staff said in a statement, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.
"Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present."
New temple outside Paris

BAPS spiritual leader Mahant Swami Maharaj, 93, consecrated it himself. The BAPS organisation claims a worldwide network of more than 1,300 temples, some of which have been inaugurated by Modi himself.

Candidates in next year's presidential election also weighed in.
Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen also criticised the incident, saying France would "never accept that women's presence be 'limited'".
Gabriel Attal, a centrist rival to become head of state, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no religion, nothing and no one can come and dictate to women what their place should be."

A year on, Nepal remembers 76 lives lost in protests that ousted government
The commemoration came as the country continues to mourn the vast loss of life from devastating floods two weeks ago
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Dozens of young people congregated at Nepal’s burnt-out parliament building on Tuesday to mark the anniversary of deadly anti-corruption protests that toppled the former government.
The gathering in memory of those who died in the demonstrations came as the Himalayan nation continues to mourn the vast loss of life from devastating floods two weeks ago.
The rallies on September 8-9, 2025, were initially sparked by anger over a brief government ban on social media but were driven by deeper frustration over economic hardship, corruption and entrenched political practices.
The unrest caused the deaths of 76 people and the torching of the parliament building in the capital, Kathmandu, as well as the prime minister’s office and other government buildings.
It also led to the downfall of the administration of KP Sharma Oli, setting in motion a series of events that culminated with the election of youthful Prime Minister Balendra Shah in March.
“The loss of life was of course terrible. But the impact on politics was worth it, we have seen changes,” said former protester Aastha Shrestha, 23, on the grounds of the ruined building.

Smash and grab: Thieves steal works worth €10m from Renoir Museum in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:04:38 UTC
17:04:38 KST

Police in southern France are searching for two thieves who stole "four works of art" worth an estimated €9 million from the Renoir Museum dedicated to French impressionist, dropping one as they fled.
A major manhunt is underway around the southern French Mediterreanean resort of Cagnes-sur-Mer after thieves broke into the Renoir Museum and stole four artworks but abandoned two while they escaped.
A group of “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves entered the building via the garden, the town’s mayor, Bryan Masson, told reporters at the scene.
They sliced through a fence with an electric knife or saw, entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Masson said in remarks carried by local broadcaster Ici Azur.
According to Masson, the pair were "spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras.
Initial reports estimated the stolen haul to be worth up to €9 million euros.
In a written statement obtained by the AP news agency, two of the stolen works were found in the museum garden, but the two others - “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well” - are still missing.
Authorities in the French Riveira town say the alarm at the museum went off at 5h48 on Tuesday morning and police were on the scene five minutes later.
The Renoir Museum, located between Cannes and Nice, is the Mediterranean coastal town most famous attraction.
Open since 1960, it was the painter's last home before his death in 1919 from pulmonary congestion when he was 78-years old.
Its collection includes portraits, landscapes and nudes painted by Renoir as well as objects and furniture which belonged to artist.
Renaissance robberies
The heist comes just under a month since Italian police recovered Renoir paintings among several other Renaissance artists works stolen in less than three minutes from a villa near Parma in northern Italy in March.
Video footage released by police showed two thieves wearing headlamps and with their faces covered entering the Magnani-Rocca Foundation by breaking through a window.
They headed straight into a room where the three paintings hung and took them off the wall, before heading back to the window and passing them through to an accomplice waiting outside.
Security at museums and galleries in France has been under general scrutiny since October last year when eight items worth around €100 million were snatched during a daring daylight robbery from the Louvre.
The four suspected robbers have been arrested but the stolen items are yet to be recovered despite an international hunt.
Art crime experts say works that are instantly recognisable are often stolen to order as they can not be sold through reputable channels. Instead, it's thought the goods often pass between criminals as collateral for other illegal activity.
Art theft consultant James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register told AP that thieves are increasingly targeting valuable artifacts, including traditional art.
“Sadly, without further funding to improve museum security, we are likely to see an increase in the number of museum thefts we see. Each time thefts occur, it draws yet more attention to the perception of these museums as relatively easy targets

The disruption affected more than 340,000 travellers and approximately 2,900 flights.

Anak Krakatau, which had a major eruption on Saturday, sits in a strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.

“The impact is not as big as the previous eruptions, but we’ll continue to monitor,” the head of the Geology Agency, Lana Saria, told the Reuters news agency.
Anak Krakatau is one of about 130 active volcanoes in Indonesia, which straddles the “Pacific Ring of Fire”, a highly seismically active zone where different plates on the Earth’s crust meet to create a large number of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
An outburst in 2018 partly collapsed the volcano’s crater, which triggered a tsunami along the coasts of Java and Sumatra, killing more than 400 people.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis struck four cities in southern Saudi Arabia Tuesday, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil facilities ablaze in a major escalation of the regional war.
The Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas including the capital, said they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory. They used drones and missiles to strike a Saudi airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia's state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border and Jazan, a major Red Sea port city that houses a large refinery and power plant.
Saudi authorities described blazes at the sites and said women and children were among the 73 people hurt. The reports of such large numbers of wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.
Confirmed images of the aftermath of the Houthi attacks in Saudi cities were not immediately available and witnesses could not be reached in a country where media is tightly controlled.
The Houthis released pictures showing thick smoke and explosions of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia that they had hit in separate strikes at the border in another area further east Monday.
Houthi-controlled media reported later Tuesday that Saudi warplanes had carried out four airstrikes in Yemen's Jubah district east of the capital Sanaa.
After a month of calm in August, fighting in the Gulf has resumed, with Iran and the U.S. exchanging fire, sending global oil prices back up to levels unseen since July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2% Tuesday, above $99 a barrel.
Houthi attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war's global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a cease-fire there has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.
The International Organization for Migration said more than 18,500 people had fled their homes because of fighting along Yemen's west coast over the past three days.
"The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confronts its hostile approach," Col. Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a statement on X.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.
The wider war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills between the U.S. and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield.
Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran's exports with a blockade just beyond it.
Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a "maritime exclusion zone" that will extend from the perimeter of the U.S. blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.
Washington fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at U.S. warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack American ships.
"In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran's new missiles," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on X.
"Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward U.S. warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated," he added.
Despite U.S. barrages that have degraded Iran's conventional forces and punished its already ailing economy, Iran still possesses missiles and drones that can threaten oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and have been used to attack U.S. military bases scattered throughout the region.
About a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the strait before the war.
The fighting has caused global shortages of crude oil and, even more acutely, the fuels that are produced by refining it. Diesel fuel in the United States is now at a record average retail price of more than $5.90 a gallon, harming the political prospects of President Donald Trump's Republicans.
"Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran. Three Dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below Two Dollars a gallon. It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon," Trump said on social media.

Latvian authorities plan to ban regular bus service to Russia and Belarus, including routes that transit through the country. The Transport Ministry has drafted the amendments and submitted them for the government’s consideration, the Latvian news outlet Delfi reported.
Currently, one regular bus route runs between Latvia and Russia, operated daily by the company Norma-A under the Ecolines brand. The permit for that route is valid until January 9, 2027, and there are no plans to extend it.
Latvian authorities banned irregular bus passenger transport to Russia and Belarus starting November 1, 2025. That ban runs through October 31, 2026, and officials plan to extend it for another year.
The Transport Ministry acknowledged that restricting regular routes from Latvia would have limited practical effect, since passengers can still travel via connecting routes through Estonia and Lithuania, or use minibus services that fall outside the rules governing bus transport.
The ministry stated that it “will continue assessing security aspects and economic and international obligations, in order to reach a coordinated decision at the level of the Baltic states and the European Union.”
Latvian authorities have repeatedly urged residents to refrain from traveling to Russia and Belarus, and the State Security Service has warned of recruitment risks.
In May 2026, when reports emerged of plans to ban regular bus service from Latvia to Russia, the carrier Ecolines estimated the direct damage from such a move at roughly four million euros a year, with additional losses from an idle bus fleet adding another roughly two million euros a year.
Regular bus routes are one of the cheapest ways to travel to Russia and Belarus from European countries. However, passengers on such buses often have to spend many hours at the border, including because of checks by Russian security services.

Yemen frontlines heat up as Saudi-backed forces challenge Houthis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:01:58 UTC
17:01:58 KST

The last 48 hours in Yemen have seen movement and clashes on numerous frontlines as the Yemen government seeks to push the Houthis back and weaken the Iranian-backed group. Meanwhile, the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has backed the Yemen government for more than a decade in its struggle against the Houthis. After years of fighting, there has been a kind of ceasefire since 2022. However, tensions have recently flared up again.
According to the Major General Turki Al-Maliki, the official spokesman for the "Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen" forces, the Houthis have escalated their attacks. They made a number of attempts to “target Saudi Arabia, its national assets, its citizens, and residents on its territory is a dangerous escalation,” reports said.
The Saudi Press Agency noted that Maliki had said that “the reckless terrorist attacks by the Houthi militias, the latest of which targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of (Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran), resulted in the injury of (73) civilians, including women and children.”
It is clear that Riyadh will respond. This "constitutes a blatant violation of the Kingdom's sovereignty and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents on its territory,” Maliki said.
Yemeni forces advance backed by Saudi Arabia
Over the last day, there have been numerous reports about advances in Yemen by government forces. Backed by Saudi Arabia, they want to try to liberate areas from the Houthis. The Houthis are dug in throughout the hill country of Yemen, essentially dominating the middle of the country’s western region.
The coalition general noted that "these heinous and unjustified attacks committed by the terrorist Houthi militias deliberately harm Saudi Arabia's national assets, facilities, and civilian objects, and confirm their extremist criminal behavior that rejects achieving peace and stability in Yemen and its Arab and Islamic neighbors."
He affirmed that "the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter these terrorist militias and confront their hostile approach with all firmness, in defense of the Kingdom's sovereignty, preservation of its national capabilities, and protection of the safety of its citizens and residents on its territory."
The Houthi attacks were widely reported in Arabic media in the Gulf. Media in Saudi Arabia also reported on the casualties from the attacks. “Houthi attacks have left more than 70 people injured, including women and children, in various towns and cities across Saudi Arabia, a military spokesman said on Tuesday, adding that the Kingdom would take measures to counter the group,” Arab News noted.
The next moves will be up to Saudi Arabia and the Yemen government. Riyadh has been the major leader of the coalition against the Houthis since it intervened in Yemen in 2015. Over the years, some other members of the coalition have sought to shift their policies. The UAE, for instance, had some tensions with Riyadh last year over the UAE’s backing of the Aden-based Southern Transitional Council.
The challenge in Yemen is that the various forces fighting the Houthis are divided geographically. Some forces are near Saudi Arabia in Jawf. There are others fighting near Taiz. Because the Houthis control a huge central, mountainous area, the coalition members are divided along various frontlines. With internal lines, the Houthis can easily shift forces from one sector to another. This creates a complex military challenge. It remains to be seen if Riyadh can accomplish today what it has been unable to do since 2015.

INTERVIEW – UN Security Council to decide future of Lebanon peacekeeping mission: Spokesperson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:01:57 UTC
17:01:57 KST

- Israeli army presence north of Blue Line ‘constitutes a violation’ of Resolution 1701, says UNIFIL spokesperson
The UN Security Council will decide the future of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) after the end of the peacekeeping mission’s mandate, the force’s spokesperson said.
In an interview with Anadolu, Dany Ghafri said the council has several options regarding how to continue implementing Resolution 1701, including monitoring, observation and assistance to the Lebanese army.
UNIFIL’s mandate expires at the end of 2026 amid international discussions over its future, while Lebanon insists on maintaining the mission’s presence as a key element of stability in the south.
UNIFIL has been deployed since 1978 under Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and help maintain security and stability in the area.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the previous war between 2023 and 2024, while it advanced more than 10 kilometers during its current assault.
Mission operations
Ghafri said Security Council Resolution 2790, issued in August 2025, extended UNIFIL’s mandate for a final time until Dec. 31, 2026.
UNIFIL continues, under current circumstances and capabilities, to carry out all tasks required of it under Resolution 1701, he said.
“But by the end of Dec. 31, 2026, the mission’s operations will stop, and UNIFIL will begin a gradual and safe withdrawal during 2027,” he added.
“UNIFIL is preparing plans for the withdrawal in coordination with troop-contributing countries and with the Lebanese government and army,” Ghafri said.
“The mission is expected to hand over its tasks to Lebanese authorities,” he added.
Since March 2, Israel has been carrying out an assault on Lebanon that has killed at least 4,362 people, injured 12,378 others and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
Lebanon’s government and lawmakers have called for reconsidering Resolution 2790, warning of a vacuum in southern Lebanon after UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
On Thursday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun stressed Lebanon’s commitment to UNIFIL remaining in the country given the “important role” it plays.
If an extension of UNIFIL’s mandate is not possible, Lebanon would welcome any “brotherly or friendly” country willing to continue aspects of the mission’s work, Aoun said.
The president added that contacts are underway “to find the legal formula for such an international presence” to support the Lebanese army and residents of the south in humanitarian, social, health and educational fields.
Major challenges
Ghafri said UNIFIL currently consists of around 7,500 peacekeepers from nearly 50 countries.
Asked about the Lebanese army’s ability to assume the security tasks carried out by UNIFIL, he said the situation in the mission’s area of operations has “changed radically” since Resolution 2790 was issued.
“The Israeli army is present in a large part of UNIFIL’s area of operations,” he added.
Ghafri noted that Israeli airstrikes and shelling continue, although at a lower pace than what southern Lebanon witnessed in March and April.
“We are still living in an area facing major security challenges,” he said.
He added that since the cessation of hostilities understanding in November 2024, the Lebanese army has carried out a major redeployment in UNIFIL’s area of operations, with the mission helping facilitate the deployment.
Resolution 1701
On the future of implementing Resolution 1701 after UNIFIL’s mandate ends, Ghafri said: “Resolution 1701 remains valid, and its principles remain in place.”
“The resolution addresses the extension of state authority, strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese army, the withdrawal of the Israeli army, the return of residents to their areas, and the exclusivity of arms or disarmament of armed groups,” he continued.
The Lebanese government is implementing a plan to place all weapons, including Hezbollah’s arms, under state authority, while Hezbollah insists on keeping its weapons and says it is a resistance movement against Israeli occupation.
“Any sustainable agreements or solutions reached in the area would be based on the principles of Resolution 1701,” Ghafri said.
He called on all parties to commit to implementing the resolution and to stop violence and hostilities in southern Lebanon to provide a safe life for residents on both sides of the Blue Line.
Asked about UNIFIL’s role in implementing a US-mediated framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel, Ghafri said the agreement “does not include a role for UNIFIL and does not mention Resolution 1701.”
“But the principles of Resolution 1701 remain in place, and the framework agreement and the cessation of hostilities understanding can be included within those principles,” he said.
UNIFIL, Ghafri added, is “ready to assist if asked to do so.”
Under US sponsorship, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed the framework agreement on June 26. It provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the Lebanese army’s deployment there and the disarmament of armed groups.
UN options
On the future of the UN presence in southern Lebanon after UNIFIL’s withdrawal, Ghafri said the Security Council asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to present options by June on how to continue implementing Resolution 1701 after the mission leaves.
“Guterres sent a letter to the council on June 1 outlining options for how the UN presence in southern Lebanon could continue for the purpose of monitoring, observation and assisting the Lebanese army,” he said.
The letter is now with the council, which can meet to discuss the options, adopt one of them, amend them, or take no decision, he continued.
“If the council does not take any decision by the end of 2026, UNIFIL will continue implementing Resolution 2790,” which provides for ending its operations by the end of this year and beginning withdrawal in 2027, he said.
Israeli assault
On security developments in southern Lebanon, Ghafri said the first days of the ceasefire saw a decrease in the intensity of airstrikes inside UNIFIL’s area of operations.
“Unfortunately, this trend has risen again, and we began seeing large numbers of projectiles from the Israeli side, while we have not monitored projectiles from the Lebanese side since June,” he said.
“The UNIFIL monitors the presence of the Israeli army inside Lebanese territory north of the Blue Line, which constitutes a violation of Resolution 1701,” he added.
Ghafri said the mission has repeatedly asked the Israeli army to withdraw from areas it occupies in southern Lebanon.
“UNIFIL has monitored demolitions and explosions in those areas, as well as major damage to civilian infrastructure,” he continued.
He warned that this is “very dangerous,” not only because of the physical impact of explosions and bulldozing, but also because of its psychological impact on the return of residents to UNIFIL’s area of operations in the coming period.
“The mission’s goal is to restore stability to its area of operations before the end of its mandate, and this must be accompanied by the safe return of residents to their villages,” he stressed.
Pilot zones
Regarding the “pilot zones” included in the framework agreement, Ghafri said two out of three are located within UNIFIL’s area of operations.
“The mission cooperates with the Lebanese army within its area of operations, and UNIFIL can respond to any request submitted by the Lebanese army,” he said.
“UNIFIL, within its capabilities, also assists residents who have returned to their areas as well as displaced people in other areas, including Sidon and the capital Beirut,” he added. “The assistance includes food, clothes and medical aid.”
In addition to occupying Lebanese territory, Israel occupies Palestine and territories in Syria and refuses to withdraw or allow the establishment of an independent Palestinian state as stipulated in UN resolutions.

Talik Gvili, mother of fallen soldier and slain Gaza hostage Ran Gvili, was given a reserved place on the Likud list, the party announced on Tuesday, as an internal battle continued over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's remaining reserved slots and the process for approving them.
She was given the ninth slot on the list.
Gvili was killed by a Hamas terrorist on October 7, and his remains were taken into Gaza. He was the final hostage remaining in Gaza before his remains were retrieved to Israel for burial in January.
Later in the day, Likud also added Channel 14 commentator and Netanyahu's confidant, Yaakov Bardugo, who received the 11th slot.
Likud also announced it would reserve a slot for Elisha Medan, an IDF reservist who was seriously wounded in the Gaza Strip and lost both legs, in the 15th slot.
Israel's ruling party later on Tuesday announced that attorney David Peter, who represented the government and some of its ministers, will join the Likud slate ahead of the upcoming elections. Peter represented Justice Minister Yariv Levin and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, as well as representing the government in its battle with the High Court of Justice over the closure of Army Radio. He was given the16th slot.
Former Labor MK Eli Goldschmidt, who served in the Knesset from 1992 to 2001, was also added to the Likud list and given the 26th slot.
Likud later announced it had also reserved a slot for Brig.-Gen. (res.) Amir Avivi, founder of the Bithonistim (Israel Defense and Security Forum). Avivi, who is also a frequent panelist on Channel 14's Patriots, was given the 35th slot.
The Likud court was set to convene at 11 a.m. on Tuesday to determine whether the party secretariat's vote on the reserved slots Netanyahu is seeking will be secret or open. The dispute centers on the approval process and the ability of secretariat members to influence the final list Netanyahu will bring before them just hours before the deadline for submitting candidate lists.
Likud officials estimate that an in-person discussion by the secretariat could change the dynamic that has prevailed in recent years and lead to a compromise.
Netanyahu could secure approval for some of the reserved slots he wants, while a solution may also be found that would allow several MKs who were elected in the primaries but pushed into problematic positions to move higher on the list.
"The assumption is that once there is an in-person discussion in the secretariat, they will reach a compromise that will allow Netanyahu to reserve several places for worthy names, while also allowing several members who were elected to the national list to move higher on the list," Likud officials estimated.
Likud officials say 'flawed procedure has taken root' within party
Likud officials say that in recent years "a flawed procedure has taken root," under which secretariat decisions were sometimes approved by telephone.
According to them, this effectively prevented substantive discussion: Secretariat members did not convene together, did not hear the arguments for and against, and were not given an opportunity to persuade one another.
Following the court's intervention, an in-person discussion is now expected over the names Netanyahu seeks to place in reserved slots.
Under telephone approval, each secretariat member gives their position separately, sometimes in a conversation with a person who contacts them seeking their support for a particular proposal. In a joint meeting, members can raise objections, consult one another, and try to influence Netanyahu as well.
If candidates are presented whose appointments some members oppose, they will have time and space to try to organize opposition and change the proposal before it is brought to a vote.
For several MKs elected in the primaries but not positioned in what is considered a safe spot, the struggle has immediate personal significance.
Reserved slots in realistic positions could push candidates chosen by Likud members lower down the list, depending on their placement and the final structure of the slate.
Tuesday's hearing follows a confrontation that developed on Monday between Netanyahu and the party court after a petition by MK David Bitan. The court ordered the Likud chairman to publish his proposal for the reserved slots by 9 p.m. and warned that revealing the names close to the vote could be seen as an "improper fait accompli." Netanyahu did not publish the list by the deadline set by the court.
In previous rulings, the court has already recognized Netanyahu's authority to make reserved appointments and approved the placements of Gideon Sa'ar, Israel Katz and Haim Katz. This time, the hearing concerns the way the proposal will be brought before the secretariat for approval and the amount of time members will be given to review the names, consult and decide how to vote.
"The court creates the mechanisms. It does not determine who will be given a reserved slot and who will not," Likud officials said. "The secretariat decides that, but in a proper manner."
The court will also be required to decide how the vote will be conducted. If the names are published sufficiently in advance of the secretariat meeting, secretariat members will be able to decide whether the vote will be open or secret. Support from just 10% of all secretariat members is required to demand a secret ballot.
Open voting or secret ballots could affect outcome
The manner of the vote could affect the outcome. In an open vote, the party chairman and his associates will know how each secretariat member voted. In a secret ballot, those who object to a particular reserved appointment can vote against it without immediately confronting the party leadership.
Likud officials believe the joint meeting itself could resolve some of the disputes even before the vote.
Meanwhile, Netanyahu's effort to complete his roster of reserved candidates is continuing. He entered the final day for submitting party lists with some of the places available to him still not finally filled.
Oren Dobronsky, whom Netanyahu had already announced he intended to place in a reserved slot, said he was giving up the place on the list and would prefer, if a government led by Netanyahu is formed, to be appointed as a professional minister responsible for artificial intelligence. Following his decision, Netanyahu was left with six reserved slots in realistic positions.
At the same time, several figures Netanyahu approached rejected his offer to join the list. The reasons vary, and in not every case is it known what ultimately drove the decision. In Dobronsky's case, one of the considerations involved in entering the Knesset was the need to relinquish his US citizenship.
He chose to give up the reserved slot and leave open the possibility of being appointed in the future to a professional government role if Netanyahu forms the next government.
The refusals make it harder for Netanyahu to achieve the effect he had sought through the reserved slots. A realistic position on the Likud list has long been a highly sought-after political asset, especially when the offer comes directly from Netanyahu.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

AfD surge in Germany exposes deep divisions on the Italian right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:58:31 UTC
16:58:31 KST

A landslide win for Germany's AfD has forced Italy's right-wing leaders into the open, revealing sharply different views on Russia, Ukraine and how far the political mainstream should go in engaging with Europe's rising far right.
As the far right made significant gains in local elections in Germany, divisions have opened up within Italy's political right.
The AfD (Alternative for Germany) took 43.8 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, a historic result that has shaken the federal government in Berlin. The shockwave reached Rome, where reaction from Italy's governing parties was sharply divided.
Sunday's election result in Saxony-Anhalt is "a worrying signal", said Forza Italia leader and foreign minister Antonio Tajani. "A negative signal," he added, although there is no need to "overdramatise" it, he told Il Messaggero.
"It was widely expected — it was known that the AfD could score a clear victory. After all, most of their success comes in eastern Germany," said the deputy prime minister. "That region is the poorest part of Germany, and extremism always takes root where there are the greatest economic difficulties."
Transport and infrastructure minister Matteo Salvini took a very different view. "An extraordinary success, which highlights the strong demand for change, security and jobs," the League leader said in a post on X.
"Fear? Terror? Danger? No, it's called DEMOCRACY. Another Europe is possible," he concluded.
Italy's two deputy prime ministers remain split over support for the AfD who is opposed to arming Ukraine and keen to end sanctions on Moscow in return for cheaper energy supplies. Meloni herself chose not to comment directly, leaving Galeazzo Bignami, Brothers of Italy's leader in the Chamber of Deputies, to speak on her behalf.
"This is neither a positive nor a negative assessment," he said. "When the electorate speaks, the outcome of the vote must always be accepted, whatever it is."
"Handing out certificates of democracy or otherwise to a force that has taken part in the democratic game and been democratically elected seems to us a prejudiced judgement," Bignami added.
The Vannacci question and the rise of the pro-Russian right
The election result in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany's poorest state, has made the question of how to handle the rise of former general Roberto Vannacci even more complex for Rome.
The former Folgore Brigade commander — now an MEP and leader of Futuro Nazionale — celebrated the AfD's victory on social media. "Europe is changing," he wrote on Facebook. "Nessun dorma."
Vannacci's platform overlaps closely with the AfD's: both attack the EU, call for forced "remigration", and push for cuts to aid for Ukraine. According to the latest YouTrend polling, his party stands at 7.9 per cent, ahead of Forza Italia (7.1 per cent) and the League (4.4 per cent) — putting Meloni's next election at risk without his support.
Vannacci has repeatedly criticised the governing coalition's approach to migration and aid for Kyiv, earning him the Financial Times label "Russia's Trojan horse". Russia remains one of the sharpest fault lines on the right: the AfD opposes aid to Ukraine, and leader Alice Weidel has proposed scrapping sanctions on Moscow and resuming Russian gas and oil imports.
The result was welcomed in the Kremlin. "The historic AfD victory humiliates the arrogance, narrow-mindedness, warmongering, ineptitude and hypocrisy of the discredited German governing coalition," wrote Kirill Dmitriev, the Kremlin's special envoy and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, in a post on X.
This pro-Russian wave — echoed in Italy by Vannacci — creates headaches for Meloni, who has pledged support for Ukraine, underscored by defence minister Guido Crosetto's appointment of former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as an adviser on military innovation.
Divisions on the right are visible in Europe
Italy's right is split on how to treat the AfD, and the divide is sharpest on foreign policy — particularly Russia.
Forza Italia takes the toughest line. As Italy's member of the European People's Party (EPP), the centre-right group that dominates the European Parliament, it firmly backs NATO unity and supports a "cordon sanitaire" — a deliberate political isolation — to keep the AfD shut out of mainstream EU politics.
Meloni's own party, Brothers of Italy, sits in a different group, the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), but takes a broadly similar view.
Salvini's The League's relationship with the AfD has followed a different path. The two parties were once allies in the European Parliament, first in a group called Europe of Nations and Freedom, then in its successor, Identity and Democracy. That alliance collapsed in May 2024, when the League voted to expel the AfD after its lead candidate, Maximilian Krah, made controversial remarks about the Nazi SS.
Since then, the two parties have gone their separate ways. The League now sits with the Patriots for Europe group, while the AfD leads its own bloc, Europe of Sovereign Nations although Salvini's overtures could pave the way for closer cooperation once again.

Russia's deadline to capture Donbas slips again as military asks for more time, Ukraine says
Russia has again postponed its deadline to fully capture Ukraine's Donbas, now setting March 31, 2027, as the target date, Deputy Presidential Office head Pavlo Palisa said on Sept. 7.
The new deadline comes as Moscow continues to demand that Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas, which includes the partially occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, as part of the U.S.-led peace process, rejecting a ceasefire without such concessions.
Russia's political leadership wants to capture the Donbas by the end of 2026, while the military is seeking to extend the deadline to March 31, 2027, Palisa wrote on social media following a military briefing for U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
"Russians have failed to achieve any operational success in Donetsk Oblast," Palisa said. "They have already postponed the deadlines for reaching the oblast's administrative borders 15 times."
Ukraine still controls 21% to 22% of Donetsk Oblast, meaning slightly more than one-fifth of the region remains outside Russian control.
Moscow is effectively demanding that Kyiv surrender territory in a peace deal that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Kyiv privately told the Trump administration that Russia may be unable to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of Donetsk Oblast even in 2027, according to a document previously seen by the Kyiv Independent.
Russia's territorial advances have slowed to less than 100 square kilometers (around 40 square miles) per month. At that pace, the document says, Moscow's stated objectives in Donetsk Oblast could be pushed "potentially" beyond 2027.
The Kremlin has already missed several of its own deadlines for capturing the region. Moscow previously aimed to seize Donetsk Oblast and the rest of the Donbas by the end of 2025 and reportedly communicated those intentions to Trump. Despite sustained offensives, Russian forces have failed to achieve a breakthrough.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had also ordered his troops to seize the entirety of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by March 2023.

Donald Trump as Green Lantern? Why the Trump administration needs to stop (mis)using pop culture references
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:57:47 UTC
16:57:47 KST

If you reference a pop culture touchstone in an AI-generated clip, it's probably best you understand even the most basic tenet of the source material.
Another day, another AI slop rampage from Donald Trump, whose latest Truth Social posting spree has left the internet saying one thing in unison: Enough.
Trump is no stranger to bulk posting AI-generated imagery as part of what has been referred to as “memetic warfare” - a tactic which sees him and his administration flood the zone when it comes to AI-generated imagery in order to appeal to his base and beyond. But the increasing frequency and quantity of the posts (as well as the very bizarre content) is leading people to seriously wonder about the mental health of the president, the security of the modern world, and the Trump administration's loose grasp on pop culture references.
One social media user argued: “Something is very wrong with the president. And yet, still has the codes to our nuclear arsenal and is the single person who can order their use.” Another pointed out: “The man with the nuclear codes. You'd be concerned if these were being posted by an elderly relative.”
In his latest posting spree, Trump renamed New Mexico as “New America”, shared an image of his silhouette over Iran, proposed new uniforms for the United States Space Force (which gave off Starship Troopers fascist chic), and even declared the Moon as US territory...
Yes, really. He declared the celestial body “is ours”.
It goes without saying that the Moon is in fact not owned by anyone, as stated by Article II of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. Still, the internet was quick to point out that Trump should have more pressing priorities...
“Maybe get control of the Strait of Hormuz before you start on the moon,” one social media user wrote, while another posted: “Reporter: What do you say to Americans who want affordable food, gas, healthcare, and no war? Trump: The Moon is Ours.”
“WTF? Honestly this dude is losing his mind,” another commented.
One AI-generated image has angered comic book and film fans – and not for the first time.
Trump has previously appropriated several pop culture touchstones, including Superman, Hannibal Lecter, Jedis and Spider-Man, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks display a lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.
The latest is an image of Trump as a DC Universe superhero. He could be seen wearing a Green Lantern Ring and appearing to build a green border wall with the ring’s power. Then, there’s a holographic “American manufacturing” cityscape that appears, before green military aircrafts fly over his head.
You couldn’t make this up.
The clip was posted by the official White House account, which captioned the clip by reappropriating the oath spoken by heroes in the Green Lantern Corps: “In brightest day, in blackest night, no evil shall escape my sight. Let those who worship evil's might beware my power... Green Lantern's light!”
Beyond the fact that “America is actually being run by a 12 year old on iPad privileges,” as one person shrewdly commented on X, as well as the very serious real-world issues Americans are facing (“Day 190 of the Iran War,” someone pointed out online, while another argued: “Anything to distract from gas prices”), Trump’s White House shows once again that it has misused the cultural reference and that the ironic implications clearly escape them.
Much like the backfiring Jedi image (red lightsabers are for the baddies, Donald), the glaring irony of Trump portraying himself as Superman (technically an illegal immigrant on Planet Earth) and how Spider-Man would actually be fighting ICE, not supporting them, the Green Lantern reference misfires.
You see, the Green Lantern Corps are an intergalactic peacekeeping force that protects the entire universe without borders. Hijacking this character to symbolize an "America First" agenda and using the ring to build physical border walls is contradictory to the core principles of the fictional character.
Plus, all card-carrying nerds will rush to correct this clip, as Trump would not be a Green Lantern, which imbues hope. A more accurate colour would be Yellow, for the love of chaos, or Orange - chiefly due to his greed and hunger for power.
In addition to the thesis that the Trump administration might be culturally illiterate is the fact that using artificial intelligence to display supreme strength and dominance only highlights imaginary power. Not true might that would decry from real-world policy.
Understand your references, or they risk rebounding and making you look like cosmic embarrassments.
“In brightest day, in blackest night, no backfiring AI shall escape from my device during outrunning iPad privileges.”
Granted, it doesn’t have the same ring to it, but lessons need to be learned.

Von der Leyen and Costa called Ratko Mladić's Belgrade funeral 'shocking,' after senior Serbian officials attended with military honours, clouding Serbia's EU bid for the foreseeable future.
The heads of the EU's two main institutions have condemned the presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral of the convicted war criminal, in a joint statement published simultaneously on X on Tuesday morning.
"The images from Ratko Mladić's funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking. Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa wrote on X.
Ratko Mladić, known as the Butcher of Bosnia, died in late August aged 84 in a UN detention facility in The Hague. The Bosnian Serb had served in the Army of Republika Srpska with the rank of colonel-general during the Yugoslav Wars.
Following his death, his body was flown to Belgrade on a state plane, given an honour guard by the Serbian military and various security forces, and commemorated by the public broadcaster and the Serbian Orthodox Church. His coffin was wrapped in a Serbian flag.
On Friday, the glorification of the war criminal attracted the ire of senior EU officials, national ministers and diplomats, while Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos warned the funeral would be an "important test" for Serbia's accession bid.
"He died while serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide and other crimes. The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," the post continues.
On Monday, the Commission's chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, caused a public backlash after telling the daily press conference that "we had heard that there was a funeral foreseen with state honours, and that has not been the case."
"Five ministers from the Serbian Government were seated in the front row at the funeral, a convicted war criminal was given military honours, and his body was flown in on a Serbian Government aircraft," the official X account of the Foreign Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina wrote, calling Pinho's statement "a disgrace to the entire European Union."
Von der Leyen and Costa's joint statement appears to cement the EU's institutional condemnation of Mladić's glorification, stressing that Serbia's failure to confront a dark chapter of European history contradicts the values underpinning EU membership. It also marks a sharp escalation from warning to institutional condemnation.
In July, the Commission tried to revive Serbia's accession bid by putting the opening of Cluster 3 back on the table. Eight member states blocked the move, citing rule-of-law concerns and Belgrade's failure to align with EU sanctions against Russia.
"Everyone can see that, following this heinous glorification of Mladić, the opening of Cluster 3 is completely out of the question for now," an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to Serbia, while a Commission spokesperson denied that von der Leyen had ever had a visit to Serbia planned at all.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić called for snap parliamentary elections to take place in late October.
