"Nicaragua invokes Germany's responsibility in connection to multiple violations of international law, particularly in respect of the odious scourge of genocide and international humanitarian law," ambassador Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez told the court.
Gomez said Nicaragua's claims "involve the most serious breaches of obligations arising under... general international law."
Germany is now seeking to have it thrown out completely, arguing that judges do not have jurisdiction and that Nicaragua's case does not hold water.
On Monday, the first of four days of hearings, Germany's representative Julia Monar argued Germany's "unwavering support for the existence and security of the State of Israel" but also said it was one of the world's largest bilateral donors to the Palestinian Territories.
"All German exports of military technology and equipment to Israel -- as to any country -- are subject to strict licensing requirements which exceed international requirements," she said.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.

France tries 14 over deadliest Channel migrant crossing disaster

Unknown Publisher

France tries 14 over deadliest Channel migrant crossing disaster
- Fourteen people linked to smuggling networks face trial in France for the 2021 Channel disaster that killed 31 migrants, including a child.
- Survivors reported their overcrowded, unsafe boat deflated and sank after hours at sea despite repeated calls for rescue.
- Separate investigations target French military and rescue staff for delayed response, with families seeking justice for the victims.
AI generated
PARIS – Fourteen people are to go on trial in France on Sept 8 over the loss of 31 people including a seven-year-old child in 2021, in the deadliest small-boat crossing accident recorded in the Channel.
The defendants, believed to be linked to people-smuggling networks, are accused of playing a role in the sinking in which 27 people, mainly Iraqi Kurds, were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of Nov 24, 2021.
Four others are still unaccounted for. Only two men survived the tragedy.
On Nov 24, 2021, a French fishing vessel reported several lifeless bodies floating in the Channel off Calais, close to British waters.
According to testimony from the two survivors, their flimsy boat began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.
Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making around a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services.
The victims, aged between seven and 46, were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included Afghans, Ethiopians and Egyptians.
Thousands of migrants each year seek to reach Britain from France in search of a better life.
‘Human beings’
The trial carries particular significance because of the high death toll and the sheer number of civil parties involved, 114 in all, including victims’ families and around a dozen relatives who travelled from Erbil in Iraq’s Kurdistan region.
The 14 individuals, most of them born in Afghanistan, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.
Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia.
The case is also high-profile because of another highly sensitive strand of the investigation, which is still ongoing.
Seven French military personnel, five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre and two sailors aboard a patrol vessel have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger.
A UK inquiry released in February found some of the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard.
Despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the boat was finally found by a French fishing vessel.
By that time, most of those on board had drowned.
The separate case could eventually lead to another trial.
“Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” said lawyer Matthieu Chirez, who represents 113 civil parties.
Another lawyer, Emmanuel Daoud, expressed hope that the three-week trial would be an opportunity to see would-be migrants not as “statistics or commodities, but human beings in search of a better life”.
‘Substandard boat’
Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate life jackets”.
Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators.
The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as migrants seeking to make the journey themselves.
However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain.
The investigation uncovered two migrant-smuggling networks, one Afghan and the other Iraqi. AFP

Vietnam’s To Lam visits Russia and France amid South China Sea tensions
Visiting Moscow and Paris in succession allows To Lam to rally support for Hanoi’s maritime stance without taking sides, analysts say
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Vietnam’s president and Communist Party chief travels to Russia and France this week, on a trip analysts say is designed to do double duty: shore up support for Hanoi’s claims in the South China Sea and help bankroll its bid to become a high-income economy by 2045.
To Lam’s itinerary encompasses talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before flying to Paris to meet French President Emmanuel Macron and attend an International Space Summit from Wednesday.
By engaging two opposing powers back to back, observers say Lam is putting his country’s signature “bamboo diplomacy” on display for a global audience.
Alexander Vuving, a professor at the Asia-Pacific Centre for Security Studies in Honolulu, said Lam would likely use the visits to try to convince both Moscow and Paris to take “Vietnam’s side” on the South China Sea. Both capitals formally maintain neutrality in the territorial dispute.
Late last month, Vietnam lodged strong diplomatic protests against China over new infrastructure developments and land reclamation at Antelope Reef and Yagong Island, the latter of which Hanoi calls Ba Ba Island.

Russians damage 14 apartment blocks and metro station in attack on Kyiv – photos, video
A Russian attack on Kyiv on the night of 7-8 September and on the morning of 8 September killed two people and injured 10 others, with damage recorded in seven districts of the capital. Fourteen apartment blocks, warehouses, educational and medical facilities and the entrance to Tarasa Shevchenka metro station were among the sites damaged.
Source: National Police of Ukraine; Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office; Kyiv City Military Administration; Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko
Quote from the National Police: "Two people have been killed and another 10 injured as a result of Russia's overnight attack on Kyiv... Damage and falling debris were recorded in the Shevchenkivskyi, Holosiivskyi, Darnytskyi, Obolonskyi, Podilskyi, Solomianskyi and Dniprovskyi districts of the capital. Apartment blocks, a school, shops, an office building and cars were damaged."
Details: The highest number of casualties, including both fatalities, was recorded in the Solomianskyi district. Eight people aged between 22 and 65 were injured there. Doctors diagnosed cuts and shrapnel wounds, as well as injuries to the face, neck, torso and limbs. A 29-year-old foreign national was injured in the Darnytskyi district.
Overall, at least 14 apartment blocks, an accommodation centre, a school, a clinic, 25 cars, a supermarket, a petrol station and warehouses were damaged in the Russian attack on the capital.
"Debris fell at several locations in the Holosiivskyi district. Fires broke out in warehouses and on the grounds of a private school. Debris also fell on a residential building, trapping people in their apartments, and on an unfinished 26-storey building," Klitschko reported.
Fires also broke out in warehouses in the Podilskyi, Solomianskyi, Shevchenkivskyi and Darnytskyi districts. In the Darnytskyi district, debris also fell on the grounds of a house and damaged a car. Residential buildings were also damaged in the Shevchenkivskyi district.
Information and photos posted by local Telegram channels also indicate that the blast wave damaged the entrance to Tarasa Shevchenka metro station.
Emergency services and law enforcement officers are working at the sites where missiles and UAVs have struck and where debris has fallen.
Background: On the night of 7-8 September, the Russians attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles. Ten people are currently known to have been injured and two killed in the attack.

Former IDF chief, sidelined hawk or ex-PM: who will be Israel’s next defense minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:19:41 UTC
15:19:41 KST

The election campaign is focused mainly on who will be Israel’s next prime minister, but behind it another battle is already underway that could prove no less consequential: who will get the keys to the Defense Ministry.
After October 7, years of war and deep erosion in the IDF and reserve system, the next defense minister is not expected to be merely the minister who approves operational plans or manages the defense budget.
He will have to contend with rebuilding the military, the Iranian threat, the future of the Gaza Strip, the reality in the West Bank, relations with the United States — and one of the most politically explosive issues in Israel: Haredi conscription.
The identity of the minister will, of course, depend on the government that is formed. Different names emerge in each of the main political scenarios, including four figures who also represent three very different security approaches: Brig. Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and former Deputy Chief of Staff Yair Golan.
The debate among them is not simply about who would use more force. It goes to a much deeper question: How should Israel conduct itself after the failure that transformed its security doctrine — whether to pursue decisive victory and sovereignty, fundamentally change the equations with its enemies in the region or combine military force with political separation and preservation of international alliances.
Winter: Initiative and a deep change in command culture
If the next government is formed by the right-wing bloc, one of the names that could emerge as a candidate for defense minister is Brig. Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter. Unlike defense ministers who came from the General Staff after long careers at the military’s highest levels, Winter is building his standing precisely as someone who criticizes from the outside the way the system operated for years.
At the heart of his approach is the argument that over the years Israel adopted a language of “containment,” “deterrence” and “rounds” instead of one of victory and decisive defeat. In his view, October 7 demonstrated the price of an approach in which Israel’s enemies are given time to arm and grow stronger while the system tries to buy periods of quiet.
Winter demands a shift toward a more proactive and offensive military whose objective in war is not to restore deterrence for a few years but to remove the threat. He rejects reliance on temporary arrangements with terrorist organizations as a substitute for military victory and seeks broad changes in command culture and in the way decisions are made in the IDF.
His position on the West Bank is also clear. Winter opposes withdrawals and territorial concessions, supports strengthening settlements and applying Israeli sovereignty and advocates systematically dismantling terrorist infrastructure while maintaining full Israeli security control.
If he receives the Defense Ministry, one of his central tests would actually be within Israeli society. Winter presents Haredi conscription as an integral part of rebuilding the military after the war. He speaks of a service law that would apply to everyone, while at the same time arguing that the number of Haredim who enlist can be increased significantly through tailored frameworks and trust-building with the Haredi public.
Alongside that, he wants to change the way those already serving are treated, with broader compensation for combat soldiers and reservists and a clear preference for those who shoulder the security burden.
Bennett: The ‘gorilla in the jungle’ doctrine
Naftali Bennett is in a different political scenario. If he succeeds in forming the next government, he would of course be the natural candidate for prime minister rather than defense minister. But unlike many prime ministers, Bennett has made clear that he intends to shape security policy closely himself, meaning the question of who formally holds the portfolio may be less significant than his direct influence over the system.
Bennett describes his doctrine through an image he has repeated time and again: Israel needs to stop being merely a “villa in the jungle” and become a “gorilla in the jungle.” In other words, not a country that shelters behind fences and defense systems waiting for the next threat, but an unpredictable regional power that takes the initiative, attacks and changes the reality around it.
The clearest example is Iran. Bennett wants to sever the equation under which Israel fights Tehran’s proxies while Iran itself remains protected. In his view, if Hezbollah fires on Israel, Tehran should know that it too may pay the price. This is essentially a continuation of the “Octopus Doctrine” he previously promoted: Instead of fighting only Iran’s arms in Lebanon, Syria, Iraq or Yemen, act against the head of the octopus as well.
Bennett also sees Qatar as a target for a policy shift and says he intends to designate it an enemy state. At the same time, he wants to keep Qatar and Turkey out of any role in shaping Gaza’s future and instead build a deeper axis with Egypt and a special, discreet relationship with President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi.
In his view, Cairo is a key player in any future arrangement in the Strip, from preventing smuggling along the Philadelphi Corridor to creating mechanisms that would allow Israel to safeguard its security interests without giving renewed influence to countries that, he says, assisted Hamas.
Bennett also wants to address what he sees as one of the roots of the October 7 failure: the way intelligence assessments reach the political echelon. He argues that information is processed and filtered within the system until it is presented to decision-makers as one consolidated assessment.
He therefore wants to create a more independent capability around the prime minister that would make it possible to challenge the security establishment and hear alternative assessments, for example by appointing a civilian military secretary who would answer to the prime minister and would not come from the IDF.
On the Palestinian issue, he continues to oppose a Palestinian state. His proposed solution is neither full annexation nor withdrawal, but a version of the “shrinking the conflict” approach: Israeli control of Area C, Palestinian civil autonomy in Areas A and B and full freedom of action for the IDF wherever required.
Eisenkot: Strategic separation and preserving alliances
In a scenario in which a government is formed by centrist parties and the current opposition, Gadi Eisenkot is one of the most natural candidates for the Defense Ministry, assuming he is not the one heading the government.
Unlike the other two, he has already served as IDF chief of staff, sat in the war Cabinet and was closely involved in security decisions since October 7.
Eisenkot represents an approach that combines a willingness to use significant force with greater caution about what is supposed to follow military action. He is not associated with a soft military doctrine. On the contrary: As chief of staff and Northern Command chief, his name became associated with the “Dahiya Doctrine,” based on the use of broad, destructive force in a war with Hezbollah and strikes on infrastructure used by the organization.
But in his view, military force must serve a strategic objective. Between wars, he favors the “campaign between the wars” model: systematically striking enemy force buildup while trying to avoid being dragged into a full-scale war at a time that does not serve Israel’s interests.
The biggest gap between him and Winter is over the West Bank. Eisenkot warns against a process that would lead to a binational state and sees separation from the Palestinians as a strategic Israeli interest.
At the same time, he does not currently support establishing a Palestinian state and favors preserving full IDF freedom of security action. Under his approach, the Palestinian Authority should continue managing the civilian life of the Palestinian population, while Israel retains security responsibility. He has also made clear that communities and farms established legally should not be evacuated.
Eisenkot opposes unilateral annexation. In his view, such steps could damage not only relations with the Palestinians but also the strategic alliance with the United States, the Abraham Accords and the legitimacy that enables Israel to use force in various arenas.
For him, ties with Washington and the regional system are not constraints on national security but part of it.
Golan: Fighting Palestinian and Jewish terrorism
Democrats chairman Yair Golan, a former deputy chief of staff, has also said he intends to demand the Defense Ministry in the next government.
He has called for the establishment of a moderate Palestinian entity as an alternative to Hamas and for the deployment of a new international force in southern Lebanon. In the West Bank, Golan has presented a plan for separation from the Palestinians that includes a determined fight against both Palestinian and Jewish terrorism, evacuation of illegal outposts and delineation of borders.
As a prospective defense minister, Golan seeks to build a moderate regional axis with Egypt, Jordan and the Abraham Accords countries. Within the military, he focuses on strengthening the ground forces and expanding troop numbers, restoring autonomy to the General Staff level and ensuring that every military action serves a clear political objective.
When Eisenkot — who according to all polls is the leading candidate for prime minister in the bloc opposing Netanyahu — was asked what he thought about giving Golan the Defense Ministry, he replied that there were better candidates for the job.
There will be no avoiding the conscription question
Whoever among the candidates ultimately reaches the Defense Ministry will quickly discover that alongside Iran, Hezbollah and Gaza, another front awaits him at home: IDF manpower.
The long years of war, the extraordinary number of reserve-duty days and the need to expand the military have transformed Haredi conscription from a social and political dispute into a genuine security issue.
On this point, the gaps between Winter, Bennett, Eisenkot and even Golan are actually smaller.
Winter speaks of universal service alongside frameworks that would allow Haredim to serve without giving up their way of life. Bennett demands a dramatic increase in Haredi participation in the burden and wants to link service to rights and economic benefits. Eisenkot also sets significant Haredi enlistment as a condition for a new service law and argues that the IDF’s manpower needs must be at the center of any arrangement.

Lithuania’s abstention in UN world map vote is down to shade of Crimea, FM says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:18:00 UTC
15:18:00 KST

The UN General Assembly has approved a new world map designed to more accurately depict the relative size of the world’s continents, enlarging Africa while reducing the apparent size of North America and Europe. Lithuania was in a minority of not supporting the resolution.
The resolution, introduced by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was approved by 164 countries. The United States was the only country to vote against it, while six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Moldova, Serbia, Ukraine and Lithuania – abstained.
The resolution, titled Correct the Map, promotes the use of the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately represents the relative land areas of continents.
The United States criticised the resolution, saying such initiatives contribute to the United Nations losing credibility.
“Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th century, and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice,” US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said.
However, the abstaining votes – coming exclusively from Central-Eastern Europe – quoted other reasons.
Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said its decision to abstain was prompted by the depiction of Crimea on the Equal Earth website, which was referenced in the resolution.
“The decision was prompted by references in the resolution to the Equal Earth website, where occupied Crimea is separated from Ukraine,” the ministry told LRT.lt. “Although the resolution seeks to more accurately depict the physical size of countries and continents, we cannot ignore inaccuracies in the depiction of the political map.”
The ministry stressed that Lithuania does not recognise any redrawing of Ukraine’s territory by force.
“We support Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, including Crimea and all temporarily occupied territories,” it said.
Ukraine also abstained from the vote and sharply criticised the depiction of Crimea.
“In 2026, the UN should not need a reminder: Crimea is Ukraine.. Shame,” Ukrainian lawmaker Kira Rudik said on X.
Ukraine could not support the UN resolution on a new world map because it depicts occupied Crimea in a way that separates it from Ukraine.
In 2026, the UN should not need a reminder: Crimea is Ukraine.
Shame. pic.twitter.com/wcFMKGVnse
On the Equal Earth map, Ukraine is shown in a shade of green while Crimea is shown in grey. It is not, however, depicted as part of Russia.
The United Nations has said the resolution does not prohibit the use of the Mercator projection, which was developed in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation.
Instead, the UN encourages governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to use Equal Earth and other equal-area projections when the relative size of land areas is important. It also encourages education about the limitations of any flat map in representing the Earth, which is spherical.
The Mercator projection was designed to preserve the shapes and angles of land masses for navigation, but it distorts their relative size. The distortion becomes more pronounced toward the poles as a three-dimensional globe is represented on a two-dimensional surface.
As a result, Europe and North America appear much larger, while Africa and South America appear smaller than their actual relative areas.
A group of cartographers introduced the Equal Earth projection in 2018. Unlike the Mercator projection, it preserves the relative areas of continents while seeking to maintain their shapes as they appear on a globe.
Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania consequently appear substantially larger on an Equal Earth map.

Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion (CAN$27.6 billion) worth of US goods early on Tuesday, escalating a trade war between the neighbouring countries.
The countermeasures, which took effect at 0401GMT (12:01 am local time), match US Section 338 tariffs "dollar for dollar."
Ottawa is imposing 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs on US imports, targeting key sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
The escalation follows the collapse of bilateral trade talks in late August, which prompted the administration of US President Donald Trump to impose 50 percent tariffs on key Canadian goods.
The US measures targeted steel, aluminum, lumber and automotive components under Section 338, a US trade provision that empowers the president to impose retaliatory trade barriers.
Canada clarified that the counter tariffs only apply to goods originating from the US and will not affect shipments already in transit on the day of implementation.
The trade dispute has intensified dramatically under the Trump administration, with successive rounds of import taxes and retaliatory measures.
Trump has repeatedly criticised the Canada-US trade gap, pointing to it as a core reason for imposing tariffs and regularly alleging that Ottawa is "ripping off" America.

Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and frequently experiences eruptions due to its location along the Pacific "Ring of Fire," the ring of seismic faults around the Pacific Ocean where most global seismic activity occurs.
Indonesia had planes flying again on Tuesday after a volcanic eruption forced the country's major airports to close for two days, with authorities saying that flights would gradually resume.
The disruption, caused by the eruption of Anak Krakatau, halted nearly 3,000 flights and stranded more than 340,000 passengers.
The country's main airport serving the capital Jakarta and four other airports reopened early on Tuesday after authorities cleared volcanic ash from critical infrastructure.
Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi told reporters it would take time for flight schedules to return to normal.
Dudy said there were around 178 aircraft at Soekarno–Hatta International Airport, Jakarta's main air travel hub.
"We will be operating these aircraft, but before we do so, we want to ensure their airworthiness. So, it may take a bit of extra time," he said.
"We ask for a little patience from passengers and the public, as we will be carrying out inspections to ensure that these aircraft are fit to fly," he added.
The transport minister said three flights departed shortly after the airport reopened, including two commercial flights to eastern Indonesia.
Airport operator Angkasa Pura Indonesia said in a statement that volcanic ash had been cleared from the runway and other areas to ensure the facilities were safe for flights.
Anak Krakatau is a volcanic island in the Sunda Strait between Indonesia’s main islands of Java and Sumatra. Its name means "child of Krakatau," and the volcano is the offspring of the infamous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
The volcano erupted at least three times on Tuesday morning alone, according to the head of the Geology Agency, Lana Saria.
A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatau killed more than 400 people in Sumatra and Java and displaced thousands.

Australians could get the power to switch off social media algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:16:12 UTC
15:16:12 KST

Labor proposes social media algorithm choice under new digital duty of care
In short:
The federal government's proposed digital duty of care could let Australians opt in or out of algorithmically recommended social media content.
The draft laws will require online platforms to reduce foreseeable harms or face fines of more than $100 million.
What's next?
Labor will consult on the proposal, with the Greens and Coalition pledging to work through the details before finalising a position.
Every Australian will be able to choose whether they want their social media content served up by algorithms or not under a federal government proposal to "empower" people online.
Labor will seek support for an opt-in/opt-out system where platforms like TikTok, Instagram or Facebook would be required to send account holders a push notification asking them to decide if they receive recommended content.
The social media algorithm controls come under broader "Digital Duty of Care" draft laws that shift responsibility onto big tech to proactively reduce foreseeable harms or face fines of more than $100 million.
For children, the proposed duty covers issues like bullying, pornography, misogyny and eating disorders, while for adults the focus is on criminality, violence and threats.
The draft laws released for consultation on Tuesday would allow the government to require platforms give Australians the choice between algorithmically recommended posts and videos, or a feed showing only accounts they follow.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said people would be able to choose "over and over" if they repeatedly changed their mind.
"The reality is that lots of people will want to choose the algorithm," she said.
"That's their choice. We respect that choice."
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the new "My Feed, My Way" initiative was "not about government control" over social media content.
"It's about giving people control," he said.
"It's about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online."
Platforms must prevent harms for children and adults
The Digital Duty of Care also sets out expectations for all online platforms, including social media, AI chatbots and search engines, to proactively protect Australians from harmful content.
Loading...
For Australians aged under 18, platforms must take steps to prevent content that promotes eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography, glorification of crime, bullying and abuse, and any other material that could inflict "serious harm" on children.
In relation to adults, the harms are confined to existing crimes including child abuse, sexual violence, menacing or harassment intended to cause serious harm, support for terrorist organisations or encouraging suicide.
The communications minister would also be able to add new categories of harm by regulation, provided they were satisfied they could cause "serious harm" to adults or "harm" to children.
The law would also require social media platforms to switch off features like personalised algorithms and endless scrolling for any users aged under 16.
This would act as an extra safeguard alongside the social media ban already in place for this age group.
"We have an opportunity to shape technology for the better, rather than let it shape us," Mr Albanese said.
Opposition says laws are a danger to free speech
Shadow communications minister Sarah Henderson said the opposition would look at the detail but believed the current draft was an "absolute threat to free speech".
"This gives the minister unfettered powers to make regulations into anything that she considers to be either seriously harmful or harmful to children," she said.
"This is, from what I can tell so far, a pretty dangerous piece of legislation."
Senator Henderson said there were "absolutely" serious harms Australians should be protected from but argued that should be "expressly set out" in the laws.
"Any known harm needs to be a matter for the parliament, not a matter for the minister."
The duty did not explicitly lay out how an optional algorithm system would work, she added.
"There's been a lot of spin today."
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has also voiced concerns about duty being used to censor content online.
"I'm deeply sceptical of giving any government the power to decide what you read on your phone," he said.
Labor rejects censorship concerns
But Ms Wells said she could "emphatically rule … out" that the legislation would ever allow a government or an agency to police misinformation on the internet.
"This is about the systems and the tools and the features that cause harm, and mostly, serious harm for children," she said.
"When it comes to adults, it's just a question of illegality and choice."
Asked about the discretionary powers in the bill that would allow any communications minister to add to the list of harms, Ms Wells said the same mechanism existed elsewhere in the Online Safety Act.
Ms Wells gave the example of concerns about AI agent Grok being used to "nudify" pictures of people, as the type of novel harm a future minister might choose to address.
"It is on the Coalition if they're going to disagree with that once they've read the exposure draft to see, is their preference that we recall parliament every time there a new Grok," she said.
Ms Wells said any rule changes could be "disallowed" in the Senate if people took objection to the ministerial decision.
Parents applaud effort to keep children safe
The prime minister and Ms Wells were joined on Tuesday by parents and advocates who have called for greater online protections, particularly for young people.
Father Wayne Holdsworth, who lost his son Mac to suicide in 2023, said he "wholeheartedly" supported the duty of care.
"We don't want to look back and see this era as an era when we can quantify the atrocities caused by social media," he said.
"We want to look back on this era as a time when Australia led the world to improve the opportunities for our kids and to keep them safe."
Butterfly Foundation chief executive Jim Hungerford also backed the draft laws, saying his organisation heard every day from Australians whose feeds were filled with "idealised, unrealistic and weight-focused content".
"We know that they are one of the key drivers of the development of an eating disorder," he said.
Lambie says government must 'leash' big tech
Independent Tasmanian Senator Jacqui Lambie on Tuesday said the government must "put a leash around" big tech and legislate an opt-in scheme for social media algorithms.
"I've had a gutful of big tech," she said.
"They have had way too much freedom … and it's time to stop."
The Greens have called for a tougher approach, while acknowledging Labor's proposal was a step forward.
"We'll be kicking the tyres extremely hard on this draft legislation and negotiating as good as we can with the government to fix it," Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said.
The draft laws have been welcomed by Teach Us Consent, the advocacy group founded by Chanel Contos, who last year launched the "Fix Our Feeds" campaign calling for an algorithm opt-in system.
"Australia is world-leading on online safety, and we were the first in the world to begin regulating the online sphere," Ms Contos said.
"Getting this reform right would let that momentum continue and set a global standard."

Australia seeks to curb social media algorithms with new feed choice law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:24 UTC
15:15:24 KST

Australia on Tuesday proposed giving social media users the option to select the content they see on their feeds, marking the next step in the government's push to improve online safety, following its world-first social media ban for children.
Under draft laws proposed by the center-left Labor government, social media platforms will be required to notify users and offer them a choice over their default feed.
Users can choose to opt in to having their default feed include personalized content recommended by an algorithm. Alternatively, they can opt out of algorithmically recommended content and instead see posts only from the friends and creators they choose to follow.
"This is sensible, pragmatic, practical reform," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters. "It gives users choice, and it will hold the big tech companies responsible for inaction if they don't follow our laws."
Meta Platforms, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and Alphabet's Google did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.
Algorithms designed to encourage addictive behavior?
Australia follows in the footsteps of the European Union's Digital Services Act, which has since 2024 required platforms to offer users the option of switching off profiling. However, the rollout had a bumpy start, with regulators complaining that platforms did not make it simple enough for users to opt out.
Social media companies face growing scrutiny around the world over concerns that algorithms have been designed to encourage addictive behavior, with users drawn into prolonged viewing through recommendations that push them toward similar content.
Albanese said the "My Feed, My Way" initiative would also require digital platforms to document the measures taken to address identified risks of harm to Australian users and ensure those measures remain effective over time.
Failure to comply could attract penalties of up to A$109.2 million ($79 million), with Australia's internet regulator, eSafety, responsible for compliance and enforcement.
eSafety will also be granted the power to issue notices requiring Big Tech companies to swiftly remove harmful, nudity-related and illegal content. However, free speech advocates warned the proposed legislation could result in censorship.
"It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said.
The government will seek feedback from digital platforms, industry bodies, civil society organizations and advocates on the draft legislation, with the bill expected to be introduced to Parliament this year.

attention-seeking AI robot becomes a mobile vase for a single orchid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:23 UTC
15:15:23 KST

Batten and Kamp’s AI Robot Becomes a Mobile Vase for an Orchid
Batten and Kamp’s Beauty Seeker Seeker is an embodied AI vase that uses robotic movement to direct human attention toward a single orchid. Combining a decorative object with an autonomous robotic system, the project examines the attention economy, weaponized cuteness, and the relationship between technology and the natural world. The project considers attention as a resource shared by both living and technological systems. Flowers can be understood as biological mechanisms for attracting insects, while domesticated animals and digital technologies have developed systems that encourage human engagement. Building on this idea, Beauty Seeker Seeker uses an artificial object to examine how attention is sought and directed within domestic environments.
The work develops Batten and Kamp’s 2023 project Comfort Seeker Seeker, which paired an Eames LCW chair with a Boston Dynamics Spot robot as an animated concept. Beauty Seeker Seeker translates this earlier exploration into a functioning physical object, using an existing embodied AI hexapod robot combined with a custom vase designed to hold a single orchid. The vase is made from 3D printedaluminum and glass, while the flower itself is presented as a human-engineered object shaped through cultivation and selection.
The Robot Uses Movement to Direct Attention Toward the Orchid
The designers deliberately reduce the robot’s technological capabilities by removing its onboard camera and other functions. This approach shifts the focus away from technological performance and toward the behavior of the object within a domestic setting. By limiting the robot to a specific purpose, the project transforms an advanced robotic platform into a mobile vessel while retaining its physical presence as an unfamiliar technological object within the home. ‘We wanted to dumb the robot down, underutilize it, to focus on the core question of what it means to have these things coexisting with us in the domestic realm,’ shares the duo. ‘There is an obvious absurdity to a high-tech robot becoming a simple vessel.’ By severely restricting its functions, the designers dull the sense of threat usually associated with robots while introducing that same threat directly into the home.
The robot uses LiDAR to map its surroundings and track nearby people. Its primary behavior is to follow and maneuver around humans in an attempt to direct their gaze toward the orchid. The resulting interaction gives the vase a behavioral dimension, positioning the flower as the object of attention and the robot as a mechanism for soliciting it. Short videos document the current behavior of Beauty Seeker Seeker, combining automated and remote-controlled movements. The designers plan to present the project physically as a fully automated version in 2027. Beauty Seeker Seeker hacks an advanced Hexapod robot to hold a single flower
A Flower and a Robot Reconsider the Value of Human Attention
The project continues Batten and Kamp’s exploration of relationships between technology and the natural world, placing an advanced robotic system in direct contrast with a delicate flower. By making the flower the central focus of the robotic object, the work redirects attention toward an element of nature that might otherwise become part of the domestic background.
The resulting object operates as a speculative design study of attention, examining how algorithms, smart devices, and other technologies compete for human focus. Its behavior parallels the strategies used by natural organisms to attract attention, while its combination of robotics, domestic furniture, and horticulture raises questions about what is considered alive, what carries value, and what deserves attention.

Eyal Golan’s ‘Science Fiction’ is Israel’s most played song of the year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:20 UTC
15:15:20 KST

Eyal Golan’s “Mada Bidyoni” (“Science Fiction”) was the most-played song on Israeli radio during the Hebrew year 5786, according to ACUM, the Israeli organization that protects composers’, lyricists’, and publishers’ rights.
The organization, which is marking its 90th anniversary this year, released its annual survey of the songs, songwriters, composers, arrangers, and performers heard most frequently on Israeli radio on Monday.
ACUM’s annual rankings are based on its AcumOnAir monitoring system, which tracks broadcasts on 34 licensed national and regional radio stations in Israel.
Sexual harassment allegations won't deter Golan's fan base
“Mada Bidyoni,” performed by Golan, was written by Avi Ohayon, who composed it with Idan Shneor and Matan Dror. Dror also arranged the track. Its popularity showed that the new allegations of sexual harassment against Golan have not influenced his fan base.
In second place was Peer Tasi’s “Of Muzar” (“Strange Bird”), while “Michelle,” performed by Noam Bettan, who finished second at Eurovision 2026 with this song, was third. Last year’s most-played song, Tasi’s “Ma Yihye Machar” (“What Will Be Tomorrow”), dropped to fourth place.
Rounding out the top 10 were Osher Cohen’s “Kulam Ganavim” (“Everyone’s a Thief”) in fifth place; Odeya Azoulay’s “Rocky” in sixth; Omer Adam’s “Malkat Hador” (“Queen of the Generation”) in seventh; Hanan Ben Ari and Tasi’s “Halevai” (“If Only”) in eighth; Tasi’s “Hee Lo Yoda’at Lama” (“She Doesn’t Know Why”) in ninth; and Ben Zur’s “Kol Akeva Letova” (“Every Delay is for the Best”) in 10th.
The full top 20 also includes a new version of Naomi Shemer’s “Od Lo Ahavti Dai” (“I Haven’t Loved Enough”) performed by Yehoram Gaon and Subliminal, Hatikva 6’s “Israeli Complet” (“Total Israeli”) and “Vayehi Or” (“Let There Be Light”), Noa Kirel’s “Bridezilla,” and Idan Amedi’s “Lo Nishbar” (“Not Broken”).
Eight years of Ohayon
Avi Ohayon tops songwriters for eighth consecutive year
Ohayon was once again the most-played songwriter and composer on Israeli radio, taking the top spot for the eighth consecutive year.
Tslil Klifi was the year’s most-played female songwriter. She was among the writers of “Michelle,” together with Nadav Aharoni and Yuval Raphael, Israel’s 2025 Eurovision contestant, who, like Bettan, came in second.
Among female performers, Sarit Hadad held onto first place, followed by Eden Ben Zaken, Odeya Azoulay, Agam Buhbut, Yehudit Ravitz, and Noa Kirel.
Golan topped the overall list of male performers. Omer Adam was second, followed by the late Arik Einstein, who came in third, although he died nearly 13 years ago. Veteran singer Shlomo Artzi and Peer Tasi were next in the top five.
The rankings underline the continuing dominance of contemporary Mediterranean and mainstream Israeli pop on radio, but the lists also feature veteran performers and songwriters. Besides Einstein and Artzi, these included Hadad, Ravitz, Gali Atari, Rita, Chava Alberstein, and Ilanit. The late Ofra Haza was the ninth-most-played female performer.
ACUM CEO Assaf Nahum said the past Hebrew year had again been a productive one for Israeli music and said the organization would continue supporting the country’s songwriters and composers.
“I wish our creators a new and fruitful year of creativity, activity, and good music that will continue to bring joy and emotion to all the people of Israel,” he said.
ACUM chairman Yoav Ginai noted that the organization has spent nine decades protecting creators’ rights and strengthening the Israeli music industry.
He wished Israel’s songwriters, composers, publishers, and poets a good year, adding, “May it be a year of peace at home and abroad.”

Secret 1993 Peres-Hussein meeting helped pave way for Israel-Jordan peace, revealed documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:07 UTC
15:15:07 KST

Newly revealed documents from a secret November 1993 meeting between then-foreign minister Shimon Peres and Jordan's King Hussein show how the two leaders helped lay some of the early groundwork for the Israel-Jordan peace treaty, the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation revealed on Tuesday, marking the 10th anniversary of Peres's death.
The documents were released on the day of the state memorial ceremony for Peres and the naming of the Jerusalem International Convention Center in his honor. They include excerpts from the minutes of the meeting, which was held at the king's palace in Amman under strict secrecy.
According to the records, Peres's appearance was even altered to prevent identification.
The Peres Center now describes the exchange as a kind of "testament for peace" by two leaders who sought to change the region. During the meeting, Hussein spoke candidly about the urgency he felt and his desire to use the time he believed he had left to advance an agreement.
"Perhaps I have only a year or two left; I will put everything on the line," the king said.
According to the documents, the Jordanian royal palace received a message on October 26, 1993, saying that King Hussein wished to meet with then-foreign minister Shimon Peres. According to the record, Hussein viewed Peres as a creative thinker and was willing to hold a secret meeting as part of the preliminary contacts that ultimately led to the peace agreement signed in 1994.
The meeting did not emerge in a vacuum. It followed years of secret contacts and ties between Israel and King Hussein, including Peres's attempt to advance an agreement with Jordan under the 1987 London Agreement.
Hussein, Peres shared commitment to security, peace
About a week after the message was received, the secret meeting took place. The documents state that "he was assured that the visit would be conducted in secrecy and that the necessary measures would be taken to prevent the foreign minister from being identified."
"My assurance that the partnership between us remains intact in no way expresses complacency; on the contrary, it is a dynamic partnership, open to creative proposals, which, from my experience, I know characterize your approach," Hussein told Peres during the meeting.
Peres, for his part, presented his vision of regional economic cooperation that could serve as the basis for a future agreement, including shared infrastructure, ports, aviation, roads, and regional projects.
"We have many dreams and hopes for the future... I share the commitment that there will be change and that the younger generations will have the opportunity to live with a sense of security, which is peace," King Hussein said during the conversation.
The minutes show that Peres proposed preparing an unofficial document, an "informal non-paper," summarizing the subjects discussed and the understandings reached, so that he could discuss them with prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.
The document states that Peres stressed that he was "working hand in hand with the prime minister," that the two "see eye to eye," and that both felt their time was short and that they were "trying to pull the wagon of peace together."
"Our generation must make difficult decisions before we disappear, and all of this for our children. We must ensure the children's future, so we must not lose momentum. There is a contradiction between the little time available to us and the size of the opportunity before us," Hussein said, emphasizing the sense of urgency.
"History is like a galloping horse. Either you get on it, or you get off, and the horse will continue galloping without you. We do not have much time, and our 'life expectancy' for making peace is limited."
"Your Majesty, there is now tremendous public support for the peace agreement. Young people are fed up with wars, poverty and the absence of freedom," Peres responded.
One of the most personal moments in the meeting came when Hussein referred to the 1951 assassination of his grandfather, King Abdullah I.
"I want to make my position clear. In 1951 there was a tragic event, the murder of my father. I want to bequeath to the future, to my brother Hassan and to the entire government, the best possible legacy. Perhaps I have only a year or two left; I will put everything on the line."
He later said: "When the gaps narrow, the fears will fade, hopes will grow for all the children of Abraham, and the time has come for that to happen."
From secret meeting to peace treaty
According to the Peres Center, King Hussein and foreign minister Peres initialed a memorandum of understanding that night. Less than a year later, in October 1994, Israel and Jordan signed their peace treaty in the Arava.
Prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, with Peres as his foreign minister, led the diplomatic process on Israel's behalf. The Peres Center stressed that the treaty became one of the foundations of Israel's regional relations for more than three decades, including during periods of crisis and tension.
"It is hard not to be moved when reading the documents from that historic meeting between Peres and the king of Jordan.
The secret meeting reflected Peres's worldview, a man of vision who believed in our ability to change reality," Chemi Peres, chairman of the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation, said following the release of the documents.
The Peres Center also noted that throughout his life, Peres sought to strengthen Israel's security and international standing, and that alongside his work to advance peace agreements, he helped establish Israel's defense industries and develop the country's strategic capabilities.
"It is a great privilege and a moral obligation to listen to the testament for peace of two great leaders, Shimon Peres and King Hussein. In the meeting, King Hussein says that his days are numbered and that peace is the most important thing they can leave to future generations," Efrat Duvdevani, director-general of the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation, said.
"The words spoken and written during the secret meeting were part of a process toward the peace agreement between Israel and Jordan, led by prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and Mossad chief Ephraim Halevy."

‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:13:28 UTC
15:13:28 KST

Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway station, talking over the dramatic events of the previous evening and the surge by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland to a historically high vote in the Saxony-Anhalt elections.
“Don’t laugh at me,” she said, “but I wish we could go back to the days of Angela Merkel, when things were OK in Germany”.
The teenagers, from nearby Wolmirstedt, said they were shocked by the AfD’s landslide win. But they felt powerless to do much about it and felt afraid about where it might take their home state.
“We talk about it all the time,” said Maryam, whose name has been changed. “It’s on my mind constantly. My dad came to Germany from Syria in 2015. My mum and I joined him two years later.”
The first clause of the anti-immigrant AfD’s 100-day programme says that – “from the first moment” of being in power – the party will deport people it deems “irregular migrants”. Maryam believes her family could well face deportation.
“We have to renew our residency permits every three years as it is. We’ve always lived in a state of uncertainty. Now after these election results we face going back to Syria which we don’t think is safe, and I can’t even read or write Arabic.”
The AfD won almost 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election, more than even it had hoped for. Doreen, 54, did not immediately admit to having supported the party, but said later in an interview she had put her faith in what she termed “the blues” “out of a sense of desperation”.
When challenged about the human impact the party’s policies could have, for example on immigrant families, she shrugged: “It is what it is.”
“If they [refugees] hadn’t turned up here in such large numbers in the first place, they wouldn’t have to go through such heart-breaking situations now,” she said.
Doreen, a cleaner, said she hoped the pro-Russia AfD would be able to take power and act on promises to end refugee status for Ukrainians (as well as aid to Kyiv). “The winners will hopefully straighten up a few things right away,” she said. “They [Ukrainians] come here in their fancy cars, pretending they’re escaping devastation, but most of them have far more resources and designer clothes than I do.”
Doreen is speaking close to a stolperstein, or stumbling stone – a brass plaque embedded in the concrete – commemorating Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer. Born in 1877, he lived on the spot where a glass-fronted fitness club now stands until he was “humiliated, disenfranchised … (and) took flight in death” (a euphemism for suicide).
But she angrily rejected any parallel between the AfD’s rise in popularity and the Weimar era rise of the Nazis. “Don’t tar me with that brush,” she said. “We are in a different age, with different problems.”
Returning from their daily stroll to the Elbe river, 88-year-olds Ernst and Judith, a retired boiler maker and a design engineer who have been married for 64 years, said they did not want to talk about the election result. But it soon became clear that they were shattered by the news. Voting data has shown a stark drop-off in support for the far-right party among the over-70s.
“It’s not like we didn’t see it coming,” said Judith. “But we don’t quite know what to do with the information. The reality of it hasn’t quite kicked in.”
The couple said they had voted for the far-left Die Linke. Judith said she was “devastated that a party that has so little regard for refugees” had won, and by such a large margin.
Her own life story – she was forced to flee her home in Silesia in 1945 and spent years in temporary accommodation before settling in Magdeburg – has greatly sensitised her to the plight of refugees, she said.
“I see the look in their eyes, it doesn’t matter where they come from, who they are, and I am so empathetic to their situation,” she said. “It breaks my heart to think that almost half of the population has voted for a party that is so anti-immigrant, particularly after all Germany has gone through as a nation in the last century.”
Sitting on a heart-shaped rainbow-coloured bench in front of Magdeburg’s gothic cathedral, Christiane and Franz Josef Jäker, 67 and 71, on holiday from North Rhine-Westphalia, were also digesting the news.
“The populists are ruining everything,” said Franz Josef. “Everything that Germany has built up again after world war two. They promise a lot that they can’t deliver, and they also suppress a lot – such as what is going on in Ukraine – so that they can argue for the resumption of Russian gas imports to Germany.”
Eric, a paramedic cheerily drumming up funds for a hospice, said he was kicking himself for not having voted. The 21-year-old son of a German mother and a Guinean father who spent 10 years applying for a German passport, said: “I try not to think about what the installation of the AfD in government might mean for me as a dark-skinned man.”
Most of all he is worried about “the constitutional changes they might make, and the domino effect that might have across Germany”.
Luisa, a bank teller who says she voted for Die Linke, fears for the image of her state.
“It’s really bad for the reputation of Saxony-Anhalt. A lot of people have said that foreigners here will now choose to leave, but I know enough low-paid foreign workers who won’t be able to afford to do so, and will just have to put up with being badly treated.
“I saw some interviews with Holocaust survivors and they drew parallels with the mood around what’s happening now and the rise of the Nazis. We have to pay attention to this similar sense they say they have – they’re not making it up.”

Türkiye to support local development of critical products and technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:13:28 UTC
15:13:28 KST

Türkiye is preparing to launch new programs to facilitate the development and production of critical products and technologies through domestic means to enhance the competitive edge of the country’s production in foreign markets.
Ankara’s Medium-Term Program (MTP) covering 2027-2029 will feature targeted industrial policies on sectoral priorities to support high-value-added transformation in industry, as well as other measures to expand the scope of programs serving as a catalyst for domestic production.
The High-Tech Investment Program (HIT-30) will facilitate large-scale investments in priority tech sectors via project-based and customized mechanisms.
The new advance credit program based on investment commitments will be implemented alongside the existing investment incentive system to contribute to exports in productive sectors and promote high-value-added product groups, while a new application area covering high-quality but relatively smaller manufacturing industry investments will be developed.
Türkiye’s new strategic initiative program will contribute to investments ensuring supply security, reducing foreign dependency, and offering high research and development (R&D) content aligned with twin transformation goals.
The transformative roadmap also includes the allocation of state aid to the production of critical components for developing competitive manufacturing in priority sectors through domestic capabilities. The aid will be tightly regulated to prioritize companies demonstrating tangible increases in energy efficiency, job creation, and export volume.
The overarching investment incentive system will transition to a project-oriented framework to target specific regional development needs.
Ankara will also encourage agricultural investments to convert farming byproducts into profitable goods to strengthen the ties between rural agriculture and urban industry.
The local development initiative program will provide funding for private-sector projects addressing regional challenges with technological upgrades and localized job creation.
Türkiye’s future roadmap also includes other efforts to subsidize branding, certification, and e-commerce infrastructure to commercialize local products for global export markets.

Chinese scientists propose turning abandoned coal mines into underground farms
Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, mining tunnels could offer agricultural advantages amid climate change, scientists say
2-MIN READ2-MIN
3
 Listen
Dannie Pengin Beijing
Chinese scientists have proposed developing “underground agriculture” in abandoned coal mine tunnels as part of a push to create a green, circular economy for the country’s massive mining industry.
A team of researchers from Shanxi, a major coal-producing province in central China, described the idea late last month in the journal China Mining Magazine.
An estimated 15,000 abandoned mines in China are expected to close by 2030. Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, these subterranean spaces offer unique advantages.
The researchers, based at the Shanxi Province Coal-based Resources Green and High-efficiency Development Engineering Centre, suggested that existing tunnels, power grids, ventilation systems and groundwater at these mines could be repurposed to support agriculture.
“With climate change intensifying globally, the stability and sustainability of traditional land agricultural systems are facing severe challenges,” they wrote, adding that there was a lot of practical value in developing “closed-environment farming”.
The paper assesses whether critical factors – including light, temperature and water – could support these farming operations.

Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry: economic development is essential for defence and the provision of public services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:07:59 UTC
15:07:59 KST

Latvia’s largest business organisation, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LTRK), points out that, under the current circumstances, every instrument that helps generate economic activity and growth is important for Latvia’s development and security, ultimately creating the financial base needed to provide public services. This also applies to immigration policy as one of the components supporting Latvia’s development.
LTRK recognises the importance of national security, social stability and the preservation of national culture as essential factors in shaping immigration policy. At the same time, we believe that achieving these objectives should be based on effective and proportionate monitoring and control mechanisms, maintaining a balance between security and attracting the workforce needed by the labour market. LTRK advocates a well-considered immigration policy that ensures fast and straightforward access to workers from third countries to meet the needs of Latvian businesses, while at the same time managing security risks.
Immigration policy should be pragmatic and rational, clearly distinguishing illegal immigration and violations of regulations from those who come to Latvia to work and help create added value. This also applies to international students, who make a significant contribution to Latvia’s economy while studying and, after graduation, represent a potentially qualified and well-integrated workforce in Latvia.
LTRK President Aigars Rostovskis says: “Latvia cannot simultaneously pursue export and investment objectives while making it more difficult for the people who help achieve these objectives by creating added value and bringing additional funds into the local economy to remain in the country. No policy can be built on blanket restrictions and the assumption that everyone acts in bad faith and abuses the system. LTRK therefore supports a well-considered immigration policy capable of striking a balance between different interests.”
It should also be remembered that, by adopting the new Immigration Law in July 2026, the Saeima has already significantly strengthened both control and accountability. At the same time, compromises have been reached on several complex challenges affecting both national security and economic growth. Therefore, at this stage, during the pre-election period, there is no need to create renewed uncertainty either for the business environment or for society as a whole.

"I will not reverse my ruling," Speaker Prabhakar asserted before ordering the marshals to remove the unyielding members. He also cautioned Kallakurichi MLA Vasantham K Karthikeyan against approaching the chair.
Marshals subsequently entered the House and physically removed the protesting MLAs, carrying out members including Kutty (Valparai), Durai Chandrasekaran (Thiruvaiyaru), Vasantham Karthikeyan (Rishivandiyam) and a few more who refused to budge from the well. The disruption halted assembly proceedings around 10:03 am, following earlier heated exchanges between former ministers Velu and Nehru and ministers Aadhav Arjuna and R Nirmalkumar.

The plane took off from Great Harbour Cay at about 10:12 a.m. and was heading to Miami Executive Airport in Miami-Dade County, Bahamas police said in a statement. The plane's last-known contact was at 11:04 a.m. near the western side of Andros Island, according to a statement from the family.
"Police on the island of Andros are coordinating efforts to locate an aircraft believed to have crash-landed off the coast of Red Bays, North Andros," Bahamas police said.
A family member told the Miami Herald the people on board were pilot Mario Lamar, 80, his wife, Lili Lamar, 79, and two of their grandchildren, 28-year-old Sofia Sosa and 22-year-old Christian Sosa. Mario Lamar has over 40 years of flying experience, according to a spokesperson for the family.
"Please help," Silvia Larrieu, Mario and Lili's niece, pleaded in a video statement cited by the Herald. "I ask anybody out there, if you can help with search-and-rescue efforts, we would greatly appreciate it. We need to bring them home."
The family of those on board asked for fishermen, boaters, pilots or residents of Andros Island to contact authorities with any information. "Every piece of information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, could be important," they said.
"The Lamar and Sosa families are deeply grateful to everyone participating in the search and to those who have reached out with support," the families said in a statement. "They ask the community to keep Mario, Lili, Christian and Sofi in their thoughts and prayers and respectfully request privacy as they await further information."
Bahamas police identified the plane as a PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft, with tail number N212ML. It said it departed Great Harbour Cay, a city in the Berry Islands of the Bahamas.
Air traffic control lost contact with the aircraft when it was about 13 miles west of Andros Island, Bahamas police said.
Bahamian officials contacted the U.S. Coast Guard at about 2 p.m. and requested assistance finding a downed plane, a spokesperson said.
"Southeast District command center watchstanders coordinated the launch of an HC-144 Ocean Sentry to assist Bahamian authorities with the search," the spokesperson said.
The search had to be suspended due to bad weather, Bahamas police said. It wasn't clear when it would resume.

Exports increased year on year in 56 of Türkiye’s 81 provinces in the first eight months of 2026, while 25 provinces recorded shipments exceeding $1 billion, Trade Ministry data showed.
Nationwide exports rose 4 percent to $185 billion in the January-August period. In August alone, exports increased 8.1 percent to $23.5 billion, with 35 provinces posting double-digit growth.
Exports over the 12 months through August reached $280.3 billion, up 4.2 percent from a year earlier.
Istanbul led the provincial export rankings in August with $5.5 billion, followed by Kocaeli with $3.12 billion, İzmir with $1.84 billion, Bursa with $1.42 billion and Mersin with $1.24 billion.
Ankara recorded the largest increase in the first eight months, with its exports rising by $1.19 billion from the same period last year. Kocaeli followed with an increase of $1.02 billion, while exports from Bursa grew by $960 million, Mersin by $655 million and Yalova by $479 million.
Ankara, Kocaeli and Bursa together accounted for 45 percent of the nationwide increase during the period.
In August, Istanbul posted the largest annual rise in exports, up $634 million. Mersin recorded an increase of $467 million and Kocaeli $444 million. The three provinces generated 87.5 percent of the month’s overall export growth.
Motor vehicles, machinery and precious or semi-precious stones were the leading product groups. Kocaeli, Bursa and Sakarya made the largest contributions to vehicle exports, while Istanbul, Bursa and İzmir led machinery exports.
The ministry said the geographical spread and sectoral diversity of exports strengthened the resilience of Türkiye’s export performance. It added that support would continue for higher-value, technology-oriented exports and greater product and market diversification.

Taiwan Air Force to build 26 hardened aircraft shelters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:02:42 UTC
15:02:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force plans to spend NT$6.88 billion (US$215 million) to build 26 hardened aircraft shelters in Hualien and Taitung as the number of F-16Vs deployed in eastern Taiwan is expected to approach 120.
The defense ministry’s 2027 budget proposal calls for 22 shelters in Hualien and four in Taitung from 2027 through 2031, per Liberty Times. The project also includes five general aircraft hangars and related facilities in Hualien for transport aircraft.
The Air Force has budgeted NT$65.53 million in 2027 for project management, surveying, drilling, and preliminary design. Detailed design, tendering, and contract awards will follow in 2028 and 2029, with major construction in 2030 and completion and inspection in 2031.
The Air Force said its main combat aircraft would be dispersed to Chiashan Base in Hualien and the Shihzishan facility in Taitung to preserve combat capabilities during wartime, Liberty Times reported. It said existing aircraft numbers and the protective capacity and requirements of current shelters must therefore be reassessed.
The new shelters will feature highly blast-resistant designs to preserve sufficient aircraft during sudden enemy attacks or emergency operations. This would allow fighters to continue carrying out integrated suppression, interception, and territorial defense missions.
The project is part of the Air Force’s policy of providing each aircraft with a protected shelter.
Taiwan has purchased 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters from the US, with the first aircraft expected to return to Taiwan soon, according to Liberty Times. Once all 66 are stationed at Chihhang Air Base, combined with the roughly 50 to 60 F-16V Block 20 fighters currently operated by the Air Force’s 5th Tactical Fighter Wing in Hualien, eastern Taiwan could have about 110 to 120 F-16Vs.

China steps up coast guard patrols east of Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:02:28 UTC
15:02:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China has ramped up pressure on Taiwan by deploying an average of two coast guard ships per month in waters east of Taiwan since June, Bloomberg reported.
The patrols covered 27,100 square nautical miles, according to Bloomberg calculations using ship-tracking data. The ships remained outside Taiwan-claimed waters but came as close as 55.5 kilometers from its eastern coast.
The Chinese coast guard said the patrols were routine and pledged to increase them to protect Beijing’s maritime rights.
The Taiwan Coast Guard Administration told Bloomberg that this was an attempt to “leverage ‘law enforcement patrols’ to establish a new normal for its maritime presence in the waters east of Taiwan.” It said it had sent ships promptly to monitor Chinese coast guard activities.
Controlling waters east of Taiwan would be vital to enforcing an effective blockade during a Chinese invasion, Bloomberg said. Disrupting shipping there could also have global implications for commodity flows.
Jing Ge, an instructor at Florida International University’s politics and international relations department, said, “If the Taiwan Strait is the front door, the eastern waters have often been treated as the back door,” Bloomberg reported. She added that “Beijing wants to demonstrate this back door is no longer uncontested.”
On June 1, China sent two large coast guard patrol ships, the Daishan and the Baita, to waters east of Taiwan. Later that month, it sent the larger law-enforcement ships Haixun 09 and Haixun 06 to circle Taiwan.
They were accompanied by China’s largest deep-sea survey ship and a rescue vessel, according to Bloomberg.
China’s coast guard has expanded its role beyond maritime law enforcement since the introduction of a coast guard law in 2021, Bloomberg said. The law allows the coast guard to “take all necessary measures, including the use of weapons” in response to what Beijing considers infringements on China’s sovereignty at sea.
The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission said that “using the CCG rather than the PLA Navy avoids military confrontations and allows Beijing to portray these activities as law enforcement while establishing the persistent presence necessary for a future blockade,” per Bloomberg.
“What Beijing is testing east of Taiwan is whether it can gradually rewrite expectations about who governs navigation and maritime order in the Western Pacific,” Zack Liao, a political risk analyst at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said. “That means the response should also be international.”
