Meanwhile, for smaller travel parties, NG Sign’s one-bedroom suites can accommodate two people and will feature ceramic flooring and wall tiles, as well as terraces for an ideal spot for viewing Bodrum’s horizon.
The hotel is set to have fitness, yoga and meditation areas alongside the Aliva Spa, where guests will be able to take full advantage of open-air massages alongside sea views, hammam treatments.
There will also be no shortage of dining spots, either. Guests will be able to have breakfast, brunch and lunch dishes at Egio Restaurant, seafood dinners at Ilios Restoran, pan-Asian cuisine at Signio, and sweet treats at Rosetta Patisserie.
Gist Istanbul, Tapestry Collection by Hilton
Slated to open in 2027, Hilton will be bringing 46 new keys to bustling Istanbul.
According to the hotelier, the Gist Istanbul, Tapestry Collection will be a stone’s throw away from the Bosphorus Strait, a 32-kilometre-long waterway connecting Europe and Asia, as well as Galataport, where visitors can enjoy waterfront dining, shopping and explore cultural hubs.
The hotel will also feature a restaurant and rooftop bar, and a fitness space for guests to use throughout their stay.
Also set to open next year is the brand’s Hilton Garden Inn Kocaeli Dilovasi in the country’s north west. It will feature 104 contemporary guest rooms, an in-house restaurant as well as wellness facilities, including an indoor pool, gym and Turkish hammam.
Les Temps Istanbul Karakoy, Curio Collection by Hilton
If 2027 and 2028 are too long of a wait, Les Temps Istanbul Karakoy, Curio Collection by Hilton opened its doors to guests this summer. On offer are a selection of 93 guestrooms and suites within the 1909-built Generali Han – a historic building on what was once Istanbul’s most important commercial hub, Bankalar Street.
Now restored and close by to destinations such as Taksim City Centre and the Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque, the property pays homage to its heritage with the Generali Han Suite accommodating up to three guests.
For rest and relaxation, the hotel’s La Calme Wellness area offers an array of treatments and therapies, including a steam room, sauna and cold plunge area. Meanwhile, the state-of-the-art gym is open 24 hours a day.
After working up an appetite, guests can either order room service or head to the Levantin Restaurant where breakfast, lunch and dinner is served. For lighter options, opt for Café du Temps, where Turkish sherbet, coffees and artisanal pastries can be enjoyed beneath the same ceiling that once hosted Istanbul’s bankers and merchants of old.
Fortuna of Cappadocia, Autograph Collection by Marriott Bonvoy
Nestled in the hillside village of Uçhisar, Marriott Bonvoy's Fortuna of Cappadocia, Autograph Collection hotel also opened in 2026.
Overlooking Cappadocia's extraordinary landscapes, the property includes 125 guest rooms and suites. It also features 28 private villas, with all stays designed to blend seamlessly with the surroundings, including its fairy chimneys.
The hotel’s Fortuna Table offers all-day dining inspired by the flavours of Cappadocia, while the Fortuna Terrace welcomes guests from the afternoon through to the evening, with Mediterranean offerings against a rooftop view.

On the food front, guests can try a mix of Cappadocian and Anatolian cuisine at Colastre.

The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

You might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?
For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.
This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.
A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.
Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.
Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.
Leaflets saying only the Greens, or only Labour, can win here are arriving through letterboxes – and it’s true, no one else is likely to. That Polanski is seeking the nomination boosts the Greens. Tot up issues where they challenge Labour, and many resonate with the student population. They oppose nuclear weapons and seem divided over increased defence spending. They back rent controls that Burnham has rejected. They oppose Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea oil and gas drilling, which may both be approved any day now. They want rapid nationalisation of utilities, where Labour hesitates. Locally they campaign on crime, mobile phone thefts and housing.
But it’s Gaza that may shift votes from Labour to Green: in the 2024 election, Starmer’s vote share was slashed and a pro-Palestinian, independent candidate came second with 18.9% of the vote. Arresting thousands for terrorism for silently holding placards supporting Palestine Action is another gift to the Greens. Labour instead points to impossible promises in the party’s £160bn tax, spend and borrowing pledges.
The Green campaign asks: “Why elect just another Labour MP, when a Green MP in parliament will challenge the government?” But this week Labour looks set to select not just “another Labour MP” but Sagal Abdi-Wali, Camden council’s leader and community organiser, popular with her party and a well-known dynamic force locally. Green criticism of Labour over Gaza comes up against a hijab-wearing Muslim woman who has spent years calming racial and religions tensions, and building relationships with many Jewish voters here, too. “If Greens stir up community antagonisms over Gaza,” she says to me, “that would be disgraceful”.
Reform has no foothold here but its attacks on her from afar may galvanise Labour people to come out and vote. Its poisonous home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spits out Reform’s usual ethno-nativist bile, pointing out on X that Abdi-Wali “was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” Georgia Gould MP, former Camden council leader, ripostes on X that she “has dedicated her life to public service” and is “the elected leader of Camden council, a community where she grew up and has lived for 35 years” who “embodies the best of our values … an outstanding example of British success”. Telegraph headlines similarly define her primarily as a “Somali refugee”. All this will remind Labour voters that fighting off the racist right is Labour’s great cause.
On the doorstep with Abdi-Wali, in a social housing estate, I saw how she is known and liked for her community work. She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism. But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will “never vote Labour again”. Not for Abdi-Wali? It’s all about Palestine.
Nonetheless, Polanski takes a big risk here after sliding in the polls. For Labour, the challenge is to show how Burnham’s raft of positive policies can ward off hopeless wishes and still reach the left with his hopefulness.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

One of my favourite summer memories is making collares de moras as a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces. We’d always eat some too, of course, as well as wearing them, and we’d always come home with stained hands and big smiles. At the time, I never imagined that one day I’d be cooking sardines and pairing them with those same wild berries, but that’s the magic of food. The ingredients that filled my childhood with such simple joy have become part of the dishes I love creating today. Every time I make this recipe, it takes me straight back to those carefree summer days.
Grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
Prep 10 min
Cook 25 min
Marinate 1 hr+
 Serves 4
3 tbsp olive oil
  2 banana shallots, peeled and finely sliced
1 red or orange bell pepper, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely sliced
4-5 fresh thyme sprigs 
  2 tsp coriander seeds
  1 tsp black peppercorns
  1 small pinch chilli flakes (optional)
200ml white-wine vinegar, or cider vinegar
200ml white wine
  150g blackberries, washed
  Sea salt and black pepper
  8 good-sized fresh sardines, butterflied (ask the fishmonger to do this for you, if need be)
Heat a tablespoon of the oil, then gently fry the shallots and bell pepper for six or seven minutes, until lovely and tender. Add the thyme and spices, fry for a minute more, then add the vinegar, wine and 100ml water, bring to a simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced by about half. Stir in the blackberries, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.
Meanwhile, put the rest of the oil in a large nonstick frying pan on a high heat. Season the butterflied sardines inside and out, then fry them skin-side down for three or four minutes, until golden and crisp. Flip over and fry for just a minute longer on the flesh side.
Arrange the cooked sardines skin-side up and side by side in a suitable deep-sided dish, pour the warm escabeche all over the top, then leave to marinate and cool down for at least an hour. Serve at once, or cover and chill in the fridge until you’re ready to eat.

UK retailers to create 100,000 placements for young people out of work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

UK retailers plan to create up to 100,000 short-term placements for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years to give them a first step on the ladder to paid work.
In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home, Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The move comes after the former health secretary Alan Milburn warned in a recent report that the 1 million Neets in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervened.
Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, welcomed the retailers’ initiative, saying too many young people were stuck in a vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities.
He said: “Six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. Unless we can increase work opportunities, Britain’s Neet crisis will get worse not better.”
Other employers signed up to the scheme include Tesco, New Look, Wickes, Currys and Greggs.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.”
The scheme, known as Opening Shift, follows the appointment earlier this year of the former M&S chief executive, Marc Bolland, to head a taskforce to tackle the growing youth unemployment crisis.
Bolland, who led the retail chain from 2010 to 2016, has secured the support of retailers for the work placement scheme amid warnings that the country risks a “lost generation” without urgent intervention.
Participants will continue to receive universal credit throughout their placement, mainly because of the logistical barriers claimants face when accepting short-term jobs that mean quitting and then rejoining the welfare programme.
The programme was developed with retailers through the British Retail Consortium and the DWP and has 11,305 placements already pledged.
Bolland, who is also a senior non-executive director at the DWP, is understood to have been chosen for the role thanks to his involvement with the charity Movement to Work, which had already helped more than 200,000 unemployed young people find jobs.
He said: “My work as founder and chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what’s possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people.
“Today’s announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain’s biggest industries and I’d encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.”
Each participant will be guaranteed an interview at the end of their placement, which will vary from 16 to 35 hours each week. Retailers will offer each recruit a “buddy” to help them navigate the new role, with the aim of moving as many recruits as possible into a job should one be available, Bolland added.
The DWP said it would use jobcentres to allow Neets to access the scheme.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the Neets crisis, given the industry’s scale and reach touching every corner of the country.
“Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the Neet crisis.”

One billion euros: Lithuania’s debt bill approaches a crucial threshold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania’s cost of managing its government debt is set to top 1 billion euros for the first time next year, an increasingly visible burden for a country whose debt remains relatively low by European standards but is moving steadily higher.
The figure alone does not signal a debt crisis, says Živilė Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė, an economist at the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists. But the trajectory is becoming more important, she said, as Lithuania moves closer to the 60% of gross domestic product threshold that constrains its room for additional spending.
Lithuania’s general government debt stood at 33.3 billion euros at the end of 2025, or 39.5% of GDP, according to the State Data Agency.
That remains among the lowest debt ratios in the European Union. Greece had the highest at 146.1% of GDP, followed by Italy at 137.1%, France at 115.6%, Belgium at 107.9% and Spain at 100.7%. Estonia, Luxembourg, Denmark and Bulgaria had the lowest ratios, at 24.1%, 26.5%, 27.9% and 29.9%, respectively.
The contrast is even sharper with the United States, the world’s largest economy, where government debt this year reached 122.7% of GDP. In 1980, the US ratio was 34.7%, close to Lithuania’s current level.
That does not mean Lithuania is destined to follow the path of the United States or heavily indebted European economies, Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė notes.
The European Commission forecasts Lithuania’s debt will rise to 48.4% of GDP in 2027, while the International Monetary Fund estimates that, without additional fiscal measures, it could reach about 60% around 2033.
“The more important issue than the 100% threshold itself is the direction and speed of debt growth,” Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė says. “Over a relatively short period, we are moving from around 40% toward 50%, and over the longer term potentially toward 60% of GDP.”
Higher debt leaves the government with less fiscal room to respond to an economic, financial or geopolitical crisis and forces it to devote a growing share of its budget to interest payments, she explains.
“The main question today is not whether Lithuania will ever reach the symbolic 100% threshold, but at what debt level it will be stabilised and how to ensure that its current growth does not become a permanent trend.”
The Finance Ministry also pointed to the 60% threshold. Assuming fiscal rules are followed, the government’s debt-to-GDP ratio should stabilise over the long term and remain below 60%, ministry officials told LRT.lt.
Once that level is reached, spending growth limits are set so that the debt ratio either reliably declines over the medium term or remains at a prudent level below the threshold.
A growing burden
The cost of servicing Lithuania’s debt has risen sharply in recent years.
The state budget allocated 554.3 million euros for debt management costs in 2025. That figure is to rise to 753.8 million euros this year and 1.03 billion euros in 2027.
Under the current plan, debt management costs will reach 1.15 billion euros in 2028, including 1.14 billion euros in interest payments.
The IMF estimates that government interest expenses will rise from about 0.9% of GDP in 2025 to 1.3% in 2027 and could reach 1.7% by 2030, Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė says.
The concern is not simply the size of the annual bill. It is what those payments mean for other government priorities.
“Every additional 100 million euros spent servicing debt is 100 million euros that can no longer be spent on education, health care, defence, investment or reducing the tax burden,” she said.
Rather than focusing on the symbolic 1 billion euro mark, Lithuania should address the structural growth in debt, she argues, by ensuring sustainable revenues for recurring spending, using public money more efficiently and directing borrowing toward investments that strengthen national security, productivity and the economy’s long-term potential.
Borrowing is getting more expensive
At the same time, Lithuania’s borrowing costs have been rising.
According to the Finance Ministry, the weighted yield on a government bond maturing in August 2028 was 2.684% in January. By August, it had risen to 3.098%.
Borrowing costs have also been climbing in the United States, major European economies and Japan.
SEB Bank said last week that the yield on US 10-year Treasury bonds had risen to 4.75%, while the 30-year yield reached 5.27%. Ten-year yields on French and German bonds rose to 3.32% and 4.18%, respectively. The French yield was at its highest level since 2008, while the German yield was the highest since 2011. Japan’s 10-year yield approached 3%, a level last seen in 1996.
Expectations for future European Central Bank interest-rate increases are one factor behind higher borrowing costs. But for Lithuania, economists at the Bank of Lithuania say other factors affecting the country’s risk premium may be even more important.
Expectations of tighter ECB monetary policy tend to push up risk-free eurozone interest rates, which in turn increases government bond yields. But yields on many government bonds have risen by more than eurozone risk-free rates as investors have priced in additional risks, according to Bank of Lithuania economists Vaidotas Tuzikas, Rokas Kaminskas and Linas Jurkšas.
For Lithuania, those risks include the size and expected trajectory of government debt and the budget deficit, economic growth prospects, credit ratings, the size and liquidity of the bond market, investor perceptions of risk and the geopolitical environment, they say.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sharply increased geopolitical uncertainty across the region. At the same time, soaring energy and commodity prices hurt inflation and economic prospects.
Those pressures were particularly significant for the Baltic states and Poland because of their geographic position and greater exposure to the economic shock caused by the war. At one point, Lithuanian government bond yields rose to levels comparable with Italy’s, the Bank of Lithuania economists say.
Trust remains intact – for now
Despite the rising costs, there are currently no signs that Lithuania is struggling to maintain investor confidence or access to international borrowing markets, according to Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė.
Lithuania borrowed 2 billion euros on international markets in January 2026. The yield was about 3% on five-year bonds and 4.24% on 15-year bonds, while investor demand was several times higher than the amount offered.
But even relatively small differences in borrowing costs can become expensive over time.
A 1 percentage-point increase in the cost of financing 10 billion euros of debt would add roughly 100 million euros to annual interest expenses, she says.
Lithuania cannot control the broader interest-rate environment across the eurozone, but it can influence the premium investors demand to hold its debt, according to Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė. That means maintaining credible fiscal policy, controlling the debt trajectory, preserving strong credit ratings and managing refinancing risks.
It also means making greater use of cheaper EU financing instruments where possible, including the SAFE defence financing mechanism, she adds.
“In other words, Lithuania cannot change how much money costs across the eurozone, but it can seek to ensure that its own fiscal decisions do not make borrowing unnecessarily more expensive.”
Geopolitics could also prove more important than small changes in Lithuania’s budget deficit.
A credible and lasting peace in Ukraine could, in the short term, reduce Lithuania’s risk premium more than a modest reduction in the budget deficit, Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė believes.
The war has raised perceptions of geopolitical risk across the Baltic region, pushing Lithuanian bond yields close to Italian levels at times in 2022. But the rise in borrowing costs cannot be attributed to the war alone, she says: Across the eurozone, interest rates were also rising rapidly as inflation surged and the ECB tightened monetary policy.

U.S. embargo causes Cuba record economic losses of over 8 bln USD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:58:59 CST
13:58:59 KST

HAVANA, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Washington's stepped-up trade embargo against Cuba caused the island a record economic loss of 8.083 billion U.S. dollars from March 2025 to February 2026, 7 percent higher than the previous year's figure, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Monday, denouncing the embargo's devastating impact on all aspects of Cuban life.
Cuba has been under a U.S. trade embargo for more than six decades. The government said the cumulative economic damage has exceeded 178.7 billion dollars at current prices, up 4.7 percent from the previous period.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has stepped up the embargo by effectively banning fuel supplies to Cuba through executive orders that threaten sanctions against companies operating tankers or shipping lines, leading to an acute energy crisis.
"The embargo does not punish a government; it punishes the daily lives of a people in every aspect," Rodriguez said. "It is an act of collective punishment that manifests itself in the long months of living with only two or three hours of electricity a day, or less. It has damaged the entire fabric of family life."
A ship carrying 100,000 metric tons of crude oil could drastically reduce power outages for about two weeks, he said, noting that sanctions also blocked parts for thermoelectric power plants, as well as the solar panels and batteries needed for photovoltaic parks that could be installed in 45 days.
The energy crisis is also affecting water supplies, as power outages disrupted water sources, pumping stations and pipeline pumps, while fuel shortages due to the U.S. sanctions made it difficult to run generators, Rodriguez said.
The power shortages have also affected hospitals and other health care facilities, including those providing essential care for newborns, he noted, adding that surgeons have at times been forced to operate by the light of rechargeable lamps or cellphones, while fuel shortages have also hindered ambulances and access to medications.
According to government data, Cuba's infant mortality rate rose from four per 1,000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 in 2025, a trend Rodriguez attributed to a lack of resources in the public health system and difficulties providing medical care and services.
Transportation and education have not been spared, he added, as fuel shortages have made it difficult for workers, students and teachers to commute.
Sanctions are eroding quality of life, Rodriguez said. "This is not a matter of 'collateral damage,' a phrase that is also unacceptable in the context of the U.S. criminal war against Cuba."
"These are the victims of an aggressive strategy, of a coldly calculated plan. It is the objective of the measures being implemented. It is collective punishment against Cubans to achieve political goals," he said.
Cuba's government will continue to prioritize meeting the needs of the people, and will move forward with the economic and social reforms approved by the National Assembly of People's Power, he said. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched all-out search and rescue operations. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest progress in China:
-- Forty-three people had been confirmed dead and 519 others remained missing as of 6 p.m. Saturday. A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as being among those missing.
-- The identities of some of the victims have been confirmed. So far, none of the bodies retrieved are foreign nationals.

A 24-hour hotline for families of missing foreign nationals has received 509 calls, with feedback provided promptly, Yang added.
-- A dedicated identification team has been set up. More than 60 forensic specialists have been dispatched to the site, with three dedicated laboratories equipped with advanced instruments now in operation.
For identification, each body is numbered, photographed and sampled for DNA and dental records at the scene.
-- Green channels for foreign personnel entry and exit have been opened. A total of 3,388 foreign nationals originally planning to leave via Gyirong Port have been diverted, and authorities have helped 365 Nepalese border residents cross the border to return home.
-- Preventing secondary disasters remains a priority. More than 170 experts and technicians are now monitoring the area with over 150 sets of equipment, including slope radar and drones.
Along the main rescue route, 58 geological hazard spots have been identified, seven of them high-risk. ■

Officials from Prosecutor General Office may have received US$7,000 a month from each scam call centre – sources
Representatives of the Prosecutor General's Office may have received approximately US$7,000 a month from each scam call centre they protected.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda article
Quote: "According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in law enforcement agencies, approximately US$7,000 could have been passed to representatives of the Prosecutor General's Office every month from each call centre. If at least 100 call centres were operating under such 'protection', that would amount to US$700,000 in 'financial proceeds' every month."
Details: Ukrainska Pravda's sources said that, at the peak of activity in 2026, the representatives may have controlled up to 500 scam call centres, potentially generating up to US$3.5 million a month.
Previously: According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Kravchenko and Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, on 7 September.
The decision on whether Kravchenko can continue as prosecutor general was expected to be made following the meeting.
Speaking to journalists on 7 September, Kravchenko said that he had no plans to resign amid the scandal which has arisen following the publication of materials from Operation Carthage, an investigation being conducted by NABU.
On the evening of the same day, Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation as prosecutor general amid the NABU and SAPO investigation into the "protection" of scam call centres.
Background:
- On 4 September, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) were conducting searches at the premises of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his deputy Mariia Vdovychenko and Oleh Kiper, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration.
- On 5 September, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that NABU detectives had conducted searches in official premises "used by Kravchenko".
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in business circles, NABU and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) had detained Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the International Legal Cooperation Department of the Prosecutor General's Office.
- On 5 September, NABU and SAPO announced that they had uncovered a criminal organisation which investigators said is headed by the head of a department at the Prosecutor General's Office. Members of the organisation are suspected of regularly taking bribes from scam call centres and money laundering. Sources told Ukrainska Pravda that the department head in question is Serhii Kropyva.
- On 6 September, Kropyva was remanded in custody with bail set at UAH 120 million (US$2.7 million).
- On 7 September, the High Anti-Corruption Court imposed a pre-trial restriction on 24-year-old Yelyzaveta Ivakhnenko, a suspect in NABU's Operation Carthage investigation into the alleged protection of scam call centres, ordering 60 days' detention with bail set at UAH 20 million (US$450,000).
- Serhii Kropyva's driver, Serhii Kutsyi, has also been remanded in custody with bail set at UAH 3 million (US$67,500).

6 killed in Satya Niketan building collapse; FIR against owner
NEW DELHI: A Supreme Court-appointed amicus curiae on Wednesday filed a report before the top court on the building collapse in Satya Niketan and requested the apex court to direct its appointed committee to carry out inspections and safety audits of all PG accommodations, private hostels and similar student-accommodation establishments situated in and around colleges and universities across Delhi.Senior advocate Ajit Kumar Sinha, in his report, said that the Satya Niketan incident assumes significance as the locality had witnessed another building collapse in April 2022, in which two people were killed and four injured.
“The present incident is also required to be viewed in the context of an earlier building collapse in Satya Niketan in April 2022, in which two persons lost their lives, and four others were injured. The recurrence of such an incident in the same locality raises serious concerns regarding the effectiveness of the existing mechanism for inspection, identification of dangerous structures, and enforcement of building bye-laws”, the amicus report said.He also noted that construction-related work was being undertaken in or around the basement and that there were reports of waterlogging in the basement immediately before the latest collapse.
The amicus has sought a time-bound inspection and safety audit of PGs, private hostels and similar student-accommodation establishments around colleges and universities across Delhi, including checks on sanctioned building plans, actual construction and number of floors, basement construction and alterations, land use, structural and fire safety, ingress and egress, and dangerous or ruinous conditions.
This comes after seven people were killed when a building collapsed in Satya Niketan on Sunday.Meanwhile, Municipal Corporation of Delhi also directed its executive engineers (building) across all zones to inspect structures under their jurisdiction and submit comprehensive reports by September 10, following the deadly building collapse in south Delhi's Satya Niketan, which killed seven people, officials said.Officials said the information collected during the inspections would be incorporated into an affidavit to be filed before the Delhi High Court within 10 days.The inspections and submission of reports will be personally monitored and supervised by the additional commissioners concerned in each zone, according to the order, they added.

Mladic’s funeral: Were no lessons learned?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:47:56 UTC
13:47:56 KST

Mladic’s funeral: Were no lessons learned?
Thirty years of international justice has taught political leaders little.
Today, thousands gathered in the Serbian capital Belgrade to pay their respects to Ratko Mladic, the head of the Bosnian Serb army, who was convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY).
Anyone glorifying Mladic is approving mass murder of thousands of innocent people. What should we then make of the Serbian state that organised a funeral with state honours for him? Or of the Serbs from Serbia proper and the Bosnian Serbs who attended it?
Does the glorification, I have been asked, reflect the limits of international justice by showing that international law has failed to stop wars and whatever else can stick with the criminality of war?
First, the highly restricted ability of international justice to teach us anything has been proven by the wars started by the likes of Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, to name but two.
With about three decades of international humanitarian law in action at international courts and tribunals from which to learn, they picked up nothing, it seems. Not even that their citizens mostly abhor wars and have no desire to be in them.
Putin’s war was never justified, but he has no qualms about feeding hundreds of thousands of his own people into killing machines to kill blameless Ukrainians. Trump’s wars are no different.
In comparison, the 1990s wars in the Western Balkans were comparatively less significant and historic, as Balkan conflicts usually are.
Lessons may yet come from the Russian, US, Israeli, Iranian and other major conflicts and wars.
Second, Mladic will, in all probability, be swiftly forgotten everywhere except in Serbia and Bosnia’s Republika Srpska. There are already university students from other parts of former Yugoslavia who do not recognise his name.
Were there legitimate war aims justifying in any way what he did? No. Was starving and shooting the people of Sarajevo justified? Never. Was killing 8,000 plus men and boys from Srebrenica justified? Of course not.
Is the lesson to be learnt from Mladic’s death and funeral how potentially good people can be made bad by bad political leaders and by experience in wars?
Their glorification of Mladic, however wicked, has to provide a universal lesson or no lesson at all. Perhaps it is important to remember from where Mladic emerged.
I first visited Yugoslavia as a schoolboy on a student exchange in 1963 and stayed – without knowing at the time – with a Serb family where the father worked for Aleksandar Rankovic, a famous Serb and communist politician considered to be the third most powerful man in Yugoslavia after President Josip Broz Tito.
The exchange family hosted me on the Croatian coast, in Plitvice near the famous lakes and in Belgrade where, with my schoolboy host, we waived flags for Tito and Soviet leader Nikita Khruschev, as they passed in a motorcade.
In 1971, I worked as a UK tour representative in Cavtat, Croatia and was an occasional bus guide for English-speaking tourists from Dubrovnik to Cetinje, the former royal capital of Montenegro.
At all times in all places and with all people, there was plenty of “brotherhood and unity” – the Yugoslav state slogan – to be seen and felt, regardless of whatever was bubbling under the surface.
In 1998, I found myself, as a UN employee, prosecuting Bosnian Croats and a Bosnian Serb for dreadful crimes against Bosnian Muslims and from 2002, prosecuting Slobodan Milosevic for all he did in the wars against Croats, Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and Kosovars.
“Brotherhood and unity” was no more. Political manoeuvring had removed it. Hating the others was now OK.
The lesson – always the same from wars – was that people can be turned by political and military leaders into killers. Sometimes it may seem justified – Ukrainians fighting Russians now, for example; other times not.
Was Mladic justified? A definite not. There was no justification for what he did in Sarajevo, Bosnia generally or Srebrenica in particular. He was a war criminal and should be recorded in history as one, in the way the UN ICTY judgments do.
As the former Yugoslavia started to break up, some Serbs and Bosnian Serbs were encouraged to believe that Serbia’s entitlement to hegemony of the Western Balkans could justify what Mladic was doing.
Hegemonic desire of leaders – Putin for Ukraine and the rest of the former USSR, Trump for resource-rich lands – justifies and excuses nothing. For Mladic’s mourners to justify his actions with the desire to control the Western Balkans or even simply to have all Serbs in a single state achieved by murderous ethnic cleansing of areas that had no Serb majority is as bad as killing someone in the street for a packet of sweets.
Mladic was extraordinarily bad. Are those who mourn him in public show today like him? They will in time, we can hope, realise that today’s event has no place in civilised society and that those taking part lose a claim to being civilised.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

From crowns to pirates: Israel’s fringe parties turn election filing day into a spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:42:59 UTC
13:42:59 KST

Every Israeli election brings them back: the tiny parties with little expectation of entering parliament but every intention of making their appearance at the Central Elections Committee memorable. They were back Monday as candidate slates were formally submitted for the upcoming Knesset election, alongside the larger parties fighting to cross the electoral threshold and, in some cases, lead the next government.
This year’s breakout character was “Sharshar,” the stage name of Eitan Shvili, who arrived at the Knesset wearing a blue cape and crown to submit the slate of his party, “Sharshar for Love and Unity of the People.” 
The party requested the Hebrew ballot letters “Tzedek” (צדק), meaning “justice.” Even Central Elections Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg joined in, asking him: “Where is the queen?” Shvili said his slate included 12 candidates and described his mission as giving a voice to hundreds of thousands of Israelis suffering from post-traumatic stress and combat trauma. “I go everywhere and donate to soldiers. I want to unite the people. I will be Israel’s next prime minister,” he said.
The “queen,” he explained, is Tami, a travel agent who holds the No. 2 spot on the slate. “With God’s help, I’ll make sure she gets a position,” he promised. Shvili said Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana had already assured him he could walk through parliament wearing his cape and crown. “It’s a unique treatment method for post-trauma,” he said. Speaking to ynet later, this time without the cape but holding a large number of U.S. dollar bills, he added: “Netanyahu will be foreign minister in my government. The people are hungry for money, and I’m coming to put things in order. I’m 100% post-traumatic, and proudly post-traumatic.”
Immediately after Sharshar came the Pirates. Israel’s Pirate Party, which requested the Hebrew ballot letters “Tzaf” (צף), has contested elections since 2013 but has never crossed the threshold. This time, however, it arrived with a high-profile recruit: behavioral economist Prof. Dan Ariely, author of Predictably Irrational, who was placed third on the slate. Wearing a pirate hat, Ariely also found himself in an unusual exchange with Sohlberg, who jokingly asked whether the number he had received was “rational.”
“The party was founded at a time when there was internet piracy, in order to rethink intellectual property,” Ariely said. “After that, we added questions about what democracy is. People come once every four years and give up responsibility, and we think modern democracy needs more transparency.” He added: “We want to appeal to people who feel they don’t have a place. Those who haven’t found a political home should join us.”
Another slate registered Monday was “Gan Eden,” or “Garden of Eden,” which requested the Hebrew ballot letters ה or יה, both associated with the name of God. Its chairman, Yeshua Ben David, is described on the party’s website as its candidate for both prime minister and finance minister. Wearing a breastplate-style badge evoking the biblical High Priest, he said he would like to serve as a priest in the future Temple. “If I can’t, we’ll start with the Knesset. It’s a Sanhedrin,” he said.
The party platform calls for a partially religious-law-based state, sweeping debt forgiveness including the cancellation of mortgages, changes to the judicial system and the closure of the Welfare Ministry. Asked why he was running despite the party’s remote chances of crossing the electoral threshold, Ben David said: “I think that if we break through in the media, it will allow the people of Israel, who are getting a lot of judgments imposed on them here, to choose new parties.”
Who pays?
According to a report in the Israeli financial newspaper Calcalist, new parties competing in the election, including Naftali Bennett’s Beyachad and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, receive election financing according to the number of lawmakers they eventually bring into the Knesset, plus one financing unit worth 1.835 million shekels. Because Bennett is running on a joint slate with Yesh Atid, an existing parliamentary party, the two parties will receive public campaign funding separately and under different formulas.
When candidate lists are filed with the Central Elections Committee, parties are eligible for campaign-finance advances based on their existing number of Knesset members. New parties can obtain an advance of about 10 million shekels by providing a bank guarantee, protecting the state if they fail to cross the electoral threshold. A new party that wins at least 1% of valid ballots but does not enter the Knesset is entitled to one financing unit worth 1.835 million shekels; if it is left with unpaid debt, the guarantee can be collected.
After the new Knesset is inaugurated, parliamentary factions can also take out 54-month loans to cover campaign expenses and debts. Repayment is deducted from part of the monthly public funding each faction receives, currently about 98,000 shekels per lawmaker, while each faction also receives a fixed monthly payment of the same amount regardless of its size. Parties running together on joint slates receive that fixed payment separately even when they contest the election under one combined list.

In Brief
- Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi and independent senator Lidia Thorpe were among the attendees.

Dozens of activists have demanded Israel's ambassador in Canberra be expelled following the decision not to pursue criminal charges against officers who ordered strikes that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom in Gaza.
The group converged in front of the Israeli embassy in Canberra on Tuesday displaying dozens of pictures of Palestinians killed by Israel since October 7 across the road from the embassy, with protesters chanting in unison: "Kick out the Israeli ambassador".
Israel's ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman last month declined to apologise to Zomi Frankcom’s family following the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) investigation which determined those responsible for the April 2024 strike that killed Frankcom and six of her colleagues would not be prosecuted.
Newman had said at the time he felt for the family but that the outcomes of Israel's investigation must be respected.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
A group called the Red Rebels staged a demonstration walking slowly to the embassy and pointing to its highly guarded gates, carrying a symbolic fake baby to represent the children killed by Israeli strikes in Gaza.
Activists blocked the entry to the embassy, leading police to physically move them from the driveway across the road. There was a tense standoff as protesters chanted "free Palestine" in front of a line of police officers.
Zomi's friend Karuna Bajracharya was among the protest group, saying he found remarks by one of the Israeli officers involved in the strike that he did not regret the attack as "disgusting".
Former IDF reserve colonel Nochi Mendel has told the ABC and the Guardian in separate interviews he would do "exactly the same thing" again and that he believed the World Central Kitchen workers killed were "not innocent".
"It's infuriating. It's maddening," Bajracharya told SBS News.
"Like, disgusting the fact that he said, 'I'm not sorry', and the fact that he said he'd do it again.
"The people that we vote for and we put into power and that our taxes pay is supposed to represent us, the Australian people, and we are begging them: send this guy (the ambassador) home, send a clear message, cut the two-way arms trade. But it's obvious that our government is hamstrung."
Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi described the federal government as "cowards" for not declaring how it will proceed with its next steps to seek accountability over Frankcom’s death.
"They have power. They have responsibility, and we will hold them to account. They should have sanctioned Israel a long time ago," Faruqi told protesters.
"When Israel abrogated themselves of this crime, senator Wong told us how angry the Australian government was. Instead, they were considering what action to take next, and here we are, almost three weeks later, with nothing. Nothing, not a peep out of the government," Faruqi said.
In a 2024 report, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found the incident was caused by failures to follow IDF procedures, mistaken identification and decision-making errors exacerbated by confirmation bias.
Binskin's report into the 1 April 2024 incident called for an apology and compensation for Frankcom's family but backed the IDF assessment of the incident as a "grave mistake" that "should not have occurred".
In Australia's strongest condemnation of Israel's actions, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said last month she was "outraged" following Israel's decision not to pursue criminal charges over the strike that killed the aid workers.
Wong said questions remained about why the drone strike occurred in a humanitarian fire control zone, and came after the brigade commander had been told not to engage the convoy of vehicles.
Last month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Israel had fallen short of the accountability required and the federal government would continue to press for justice for Frankcom and her colleagues.
Independent senator Lidia Thorpe was also among the protest attendees, carrying a box with individual shreds of paper with the names of the 20,000 Palestinian children killed by Israel, reading some of them to protesters.
Thorpe says she witnessed Newman in the Parliament House members' lounge on Monday, accusing him of having "free rein" in parliament.
SBS News has contacted the Israeli embassy and Wong's office for comment on the protest.
Hamas militants killed around 1,200 people in the October 7 2023 attack and 251 people were taken hostage, including children, according to Israeli tallies and Amnesty. All but one have since been released, most of them as part of ceasefire deals and some in Israeli military operations.
The attack precipitated Israel's war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians according to Gaza authorities, left swathes of the enclave in ruins and much of its population homeless.

Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:38:29 UTC
13:38:29 KST

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.
Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.
Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.
Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.
New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.
They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.
The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.
“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.
Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.
The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.
“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.
“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”
The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.
“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”
The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.
The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.
“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.
“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.
“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”
A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.
“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.
“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”
Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.
“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”
Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.
“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”
Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.

Relatives arrive carrying photographs of loved ones, looking for a wall to post fliers, hoping someone might recognise a face.

Country diary: This moorland needed rainfall – it got something even better | Ed Douglas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:30:26 UTC
13:30:26 KST

Can a landscape sigh with relief? It felt that way, pushing through bilberry and cowberry hung with pearls of overnight rain that soaked my lower legs.
On the path, dry, dusty soil had reverted to reassuring gloop. I was thrilled, at one point, to step cautiously round a puddle. Overhead, a buzzard wheeled and a small gang of swallows skimmed across heather whose purple intensity was already fading, too soon it seemed to me. To the west, a kestrel was quartering the slopes of Wet Withens.
The downward curve of the moor steepens here, as it drops towards Highlow Brook, but before it does, there’s a bench, a flat space, which in the bronze age was used for a barrow. Next to it is a henge, with its circle of small stones, the most prominent of which was long ago dubbed “the chair”.
I noticed that a raptor, perhaps the kestrel nearby, had recently been dismantling something small and furry on top of the chair, so I moved quickly on to the barrow.
The view from here is among the best I know – evidence that our distant forebears had a grand feeling for landscape. I could see in the distance the spire of St Michael’s in Hathersage, its location no less harmonious, nestling in the crook of the hills opposite, ridgelines intersecting like arms round shoulders.
The barrow itself is a jumble of stones, torn apart in the mid-18th century when the nearby turnpike was built and workmen came looking for material. This was decades before the commons were snaffled by acts of enclosure, in this case for the Duke of Devonshire. Later in the 19th century he turned it into a grouse moor.
These twisting strands of deep history show how varied our uplands have been, from sacred space, to sheepwalk, to elite playground. Now this place has a new story. An anonymous benefactor has presented Eyam Moor to the Derbyshire Wildlife Trust to be a haven for biodiversity, a gleam of light in a troubled sky.

WASHINGTON, September 8. /TASS/. November’s US midterm elections will most likely strengthen the Democrats’ position in Congress but are unlikely to improve the legislature’s attitude toward Russia, former US Congressman Dennis Kucinich told TASS.
"I think the Democrats will take back the House of Representatives," remarked Kucinich, who represented Ohio in the lower chamber of Congress from 1997 to 2013. He suggested that the opposition Democratic Party could win "10-20 seats" more than the ruling Republican Party, while allowing for a wider margin. "The question is, if that happens, will the policies change in any dramatic way? I’m not so sure of that yet," he stressed. "As far as the Senate, I think the Senate could be close. At this point, it appears the Democrats might have a slight edge in the Senate, maybe 51 to 49," added the former lawmaker, who ran for president in 2004 and 2008 and served as mayor of Cleveland, Ohio.
Asked whether Congress’s overall attitude toward Russia might become any less hostile after the midterms, Kucinich replied: "I wish I could give you a yes answer, but here’s the concern that I have: if the Democrats resume control of the House of Representatives, there are still many Democrats in office who are working under the misunderstanding of the nature of the conflict <...> regarding Russia." "People have to get informed and understand how the war in Ukraine started," Kucinich said. Earlier, he noted that US actions were the main cause of the conflict. In his view, Democrats should also acknowledge that claims of Russian interference in US elections are unfounded. Kucinich co-founded a working group in the House of Representatives to promote friendship, mutual understanding and cooperation with Russia.
The US midterm elections will take place on November 3, with a third of the Senate and all seats in the House of Representatives up for election. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress.

China exports accelerate on strong demand for autos and high-tech goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:27:18 UTC
13:27:18 KST

China’s export growth accelerated in August, rising 25% from a year earlier, buoyed by autos and high-tech goods.
China’s exports accelerated in August, jumping 25% from a year earlier on strong demand for autos and high-tech goods, its customs agency said on Tuesday.
The data came ahead of US President Donald Trump’s planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, set for late September, though Beijing has not yet confirmed the exact date for the visit.
Exports grew 23.9% year-on-year in July.
Imports climbed 28.2% in August from a year earlier, up from July’s 27.5% rise. That led to a $119.1 billion (€102.4bn) trade surplus for China, widening from $112.5 billion (€96.8bn) in July.
“China is very competitive in its tech goods exports,” Chi Lo, a senior market strategist for Asia Pacific at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said.
In recent years, rising exports of electric vehicles, industrial machinery and semiconductors have helped fuel China’s robust shipments globally.
“China has moved aggressively up the value chain and has become a major player in AI infrastructure and industrial automation,” he added.
China has also largely been weathering disruptions from the Iran war better than many countries, while it has also been exporting more to Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, shielding it from impacts on its overall exports following elevated US tariffs.
Policymakers in the US and Europe have raised concerns over China’s ballooning trade surplus, which surged to a record $1.2 trillion (€1.0trn) last year.
Trade is expected to be among the key topics of discussion between Trump and Xi when the two leaders meet. The strategic stalemate between China and the US will however likely remain, said Lo.
“Both sides hold each other hostage in some strategic products, with the US withholding high-end tech goods from being sold to China and China withholding rare-earth exports to the US,” he said.
China and the EU are also set to meet for ministerial level trade talks in the fall, as the EU grapples to reduce its around 1 billion euros a day of trade deficit with China.
The EU has already implemented measures in July to protect its steel industry and has limited tax-exempt imports of Chinese e-commerce small parcels. At home, China is still struggling to boost its economy as consumption and investment remained sluggish following a yearslong real estate sector downturn.
On Sunday, China said it was injecting around $54 billion (€46bn) into state banks and insurers to help lift its economy.

Al-Maliki described the attacks as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, warning that they posed a direct threat to the kingdom’s citizens and residents.
He said the coalition would take “all necessary operational measures” to confront the attacks and act against the sources of the threat.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy said in a separate statement that several “energy sector facilities and installations” in southern areas of the kingdom were hit early on Tuesday.
The attacks wounded a “number of citizens and residents” and sparked “fires at several locations”, forcing a “temporary halt in some operations”, the statement said.

Riyadh has not commented on the allegation.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year.
Fighting between the two sides largely halted after a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022, but resumed following the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran in February.
Hostilities restarted in July when the Houthis launched missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia’s Abha international airport, following an attack on Sanaa airport. Later that month, the Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and began attacking Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea.
On Thursday, the Houthis launched a major offensive, attempting to advance through western Taiz and southern Hodeidah towards the port city of al-Makha (Mocha) along the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.
Fighting was initially concentrated west of Taiz and south of Hodeidah, but has now spread to the provinces of al-Dhalea, Marib, al-Jawf and al-Bayda, as the government seeks to stretch Houthi forces and increase pressure on the group.
The World Health Organization said some 1,078 people have been killed or wounded since August 24, while more than 21,000 people have been displaced since Thursday.

Indonesia Reopens Airports After Suspension Due to Volcanic Eruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:26:00 UTC
13:26:00 KST

Indonesia reopened five airports early this morning, after a volcanic eruption over the weekend forced them to suspend operations for two days.
Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began erupting late on Friday and remained active for around 25 hours.
The eruption threw up black plumes of volcanic ash that were carried by the wind over the skies of the capital, Jakarta, which lies around 150 kilometers to the east, and across Lampung province in the southern part of Sumatra.
This forced the closure of eight airports, including two servicing Jakarta. As the BBC reported, “snaking queues had formed at the departure halls in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.” Indonesian officials said yesterday that 2,961 flights were disrupted, leaving around 341,000 people stranded.
In a statement today, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said that Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the capital’s primary airport, resumed operations this morning after wind blew the ash away from the vicinity, Reuters reported. Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighboring city of Bandung, also reopened today. Two airports remain closed, while one resumed operations yesterday.
Dudy told reporters that authorities would now need to confirm the airworthiness of the 178 aircraft that were at Soekarno-Hatta during the closure. “Perhaps it’ll take some little extra time to prepare the planes,” he said.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatoa,” emerged from the sea in the 1920s in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa, which destroyed the island of Krakatau and unleashed a tsunami that killed more than 36,000 people. It has been sporadically active for much of the last decade, and an eruption in 2018 caused a devastating tsunami that killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.
On Sunday, the Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said that although the volcanic eruption has come to an apparent end, Anak Krakatau remained on alert, and further eruptions were possible.
Also yesterday, Malaysian authorities lifted a declaration of emergency in Serian, a district in the southwest of Sarawak state, that was imposed due to toxic haze from wildfires across the border in Indonesia. Sarawak, which runs along the north of the island of Borneo, is one of the areas most affected by the resulting air pollution, which has forced the closure of 647 schools across the state.
Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim, gave his consent to end the state of emergency following reports from government agencies showing that air quality readings in Serian were no longer at a hazardous level, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement.
“The Federal government and the Sarawak state government will continue to closely monitor the situation, and residents in affected areas are advised to limit outdoor activities and to always comply with instructions from the authorities,” it added.

Netanyahu's pick Oren Dobronsky drops Likud Knesset bid rather than give up US citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:25:47 UTC
13:25:47 KST

Tech entrepreneur Oren Dobronsky has dropped out of Likud’s Knesset slate rather than give up his U.S. citizenship, abandoning a top-10 spot offered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opting instead for a potential role as a professional minister responsible for artificial intelligence.
Under Israeli law, Dobronsky would have been required to take steps to relinquish his U.S. citizenship before being sworn in as a member of Knesset. The decision could also have carried a significant financial cost because renouncing U.S. citizenship can trigger an “exit tax” for wealthy Americans with substantial assets. The citizenship issue had emerged in recent weeks as a major obstacle to his candidacy.
Dobronsky announced overnight that he had decided not to run for parliament, saying he and Netanyahu had agreed that he would instead join the Likud team as a professional, non-Knesset minister for AI if Netanyahu forms the next government.
“The prime minister asked me two months ago to join the Likud team in the coming elections, and that is what will happen,” Dobronsky wrote on Facebook.
“The prime minister offered me the position of minister for AI affairs and a reserved spot in the top 10 of the list,” he said. “Nevertheless, I preferred to serve only as a professional minister, where I can contribute the most from my experience, and not to be on the list itself as a member of Knesset, and that is what we agreed.”
“I intend to work hand in hand with Prime Minister Netanyahu, as part of the Likud team, to make sure that the State of Israel becomes an AI superpower,” he added.
Dobronsky’s withdrawal came as Netanyahu continued to hold back the names of his remaining reserved candidates, even after a deadline imposed by Likud’s internal tribunal expired.
The tribunal had warned that the delay could open the way for a secret ballot among members of the Likud Secretariat. Likud officials nevertheless told ynet that Netanyahu “has no intention of allowing such a vote.”
Netanyahu appears determined to leave his remaining decisions until the final hours. A meeting of the Likud Secretariat, which is supposed to approve the reserved slots and was originally scheduled for 11 a.m. Tuesday, was first postponed until 2 p.m. Even that time was not considered final.
The national deadline for political parties to submit their candidate lists to Israel’s Central Elections Committee is 10 p.m. Tuesday.
Netanyahu, through attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud’s legal adviser, criticized the tribunal’s ruling. Bombach said Netanyahu intended to provide the list of reserved candidates Tuesday morning, giving Secretariat members what he described as “several hours of sufficient time” to review it.
“Only 115 minutes were allocated to study a petition consisting of dozens of pages and appendices, receive instructions, establish the facts, formulate a position and submit a legal response,” Bombach wrote. “This was despite the fact that, as far as the respondent knows, the petition itself had already been submitted at around 12 p.m.”
He said the timetable was “unreasonable and disproportionate” and materially impaired the party’s ability to present its case.
“The situation is particularly serious because the decision was issued ex parte, without first requesting the respondent’s position, and even created a new operative outcome regarding the voting mechanism in the Secretariat,” Bombach wrote. “This response is therefore being submitted under protest, solely out of caution, and without exhausting the respondent’s arguments or waiving any procedural or substantive claim.”
The dispute stems from a ruling Monday by the Likud tribunal, signed by attorney Yitzhak Bam. Bombach had informed the tribunal that political circumstances made it impossible to comply fully with an earlier requirement to notify Secretariat members of Netanyahu’s proposed reserved slots 48 hours before the vote.
“Extreme political constraints may justify a deviation from this timetable,” Bam wrote. “But it appears that after some of the parties that created those constraints have already submitted their lists to the Central Elections Committee, the proposal regarding reserved slots, if the movement chairman intends to use them, should be published promptly.”
Bam said the 48-hour notice period was designed to give Secretariat members time to consider the proposed candidates and, if they believed it necessary, demand a secret ballot.
“Publishing a proposed decision shortly before the vote could be interpreted as an improper fait accompli,” he wrote.
The tribunal said that if no formal proposal was delivered to Secretariat members by 9 p.m. Monday, Likud’s legal adviser would have to explain why the failure should not be regarded as implicit consent to a secret ballot without the usual requirement to collect signatures from 10% of Secretariat members.
Netanyahu has nevertheless continued to hold his cards close until the final hours.
He has already spoken with prospective candidates. One has even filmed campaign material, but the video has not been released because Netanyahu has yet to make a final decision.
Senior ministers and members of Netanyahu’s close circle, including his wife, Sara Netanyahu, and son Yair Netanyahu, have also been pressing him to select candidates firmly identified with the political right.
One argument repeatedly raised in the discussions concerns the possibility of a deadlock between Israel’s political blocs. Netanyahu’s allies want to avoid a scenario in which a lawmaker elected with his bloc later crosses sides and provides the rival camp with the 61 seats required for a Knesset majority.
Behind the delay is not only Netanyahu’s tendency to postpone major political decisions until the last moment. He has also so far failed to secure a candidate regarded within Likud as an electoral “game changer.”
Netanyahu has already announced several candidates for reserved positions, including Gideon Sa’ar, Haim Katz and Israel Katz. Likud lawmaker Michel Buskila, a close ally of Sa’ar, is also expected to receive a reserved slot under the agreement with Sa’ar’s New Hope party.
According to senior Likud officials, attorney David Peter is considered one of the most certain candidates for another reserved position. Peter, a lawyer and researcher at the conservative Kohelet Policy Forum, is identified with the political right and has represented the government in several High Court petitions, as well as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Anthony Albanese says he's not trying to stop you from doomscrolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:22:59 UTC
13:22:59 KST

In brief
- Digital duty of care laws will compel social media companies to protect users from harmful content.
- It will also offer Australians the option to opt out of seeing personally recommended content from social media algorithms.
Australian internet users will be given the choice to opt out of algorithmic recommendations under proposed social media reforms.
Draft laws setting up a digital duty of care were introduced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday.
As part of the measures, social media companies will need to provide tools for people to choose what they see in their online feeds, under a government initiative called My Feed, My Way.
Social media companies have been accused of creating addictive algorithms that keep people endlessly scrolling through recommended content. Advocates have called for a reversion to chronological feeds that show posts from friends and other accounts a user follows.
"This is not about giving government control. It's about giving people control. It's about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online," Albanese told reporters in Canberra.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"If people want to doom scroll, as you call it, that's fine, that's up to them," he said.
"But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them with the opportunity."
He pointed to global discussion over harms linked to social media, including at the United Nations.
"It's a debate that's taking place in countries all around the world, because of the sort of impact that we're seeing," he added, citing a rise in mental health issues and eating disorders as examples.
The reforms had drawn backlash from both the Coalition and Greens before being formally announced, with Opposition leader Angus Taylor suggesting it could be akin to censorship.
Meanwhile, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for the opt-out algorithm to be made the default setting.
'A global reckoning coming for big tech'
Under the draft laws, social media companies will also be required to protect people from harmful content online.
Harmful content will include the promotion of eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography or content that glorifies crime.
Albanese said the legislation would empower the government to issue removal notices for 'nudify' apps and websites, which typically use artificial intelligence to create fake nude images of people without their consent.
Sharing that type of content — nonconsensual deepfake sexualised images — is already illegal in much of Australia, but developing the tools to do so isn't.
Companies could face fines of $100 million if they don't enact the duty of care.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said the duty of care would build on the world-leading ban on social media for under-16s Australia introduced last year.
"The digital duty of care is not about controlling adults online. It is about giving adults a choice," she said.
"Tech companies can still move fast, but they will no longer be allowed to break things because online harms have real-world consequences.
"There is a global reckoning coming for big tech."
It follows the government looking to pursue stronger penalties for social media companies as part of measures to bolster the under-16s ban.

Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on CAN$27.6 billion ($20 billion) worth of US goods early Tuesday, escalating a trade war between the neighboring countries.
The countermeasures, which took effect at 12.01 a.m. local time (0401GMT), match US Section 338 tariffs "dollar for dollar."
Ottawa is imposing 15%, 25% and 50% tariffs on US imports, targeting key sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
The escalation follows the collapse of bilateral trade talks in late August, which prompted the administration of US President Donald Trump to impose 50% tariffs on key Canadian goods. The US measures targeted steel, aluminum, lumber and automotive components under Section 338, a US trade provision that empowers the president to impose retaliatory trade barriers.
Canada clarified that the counter tariffs only apply to goods originating from the US and will not affect shipments already in transit on the day of implementation.
The trade dispute has intensified dramatically under the Trump administration, with successive rounds of import taxes and retaliatory measures.
Trump has repeatedly criticized the Canada-US trade gap, pointing to it as a core reason for imposing tariffs and regularly alleging that Ottawa is "ripping off" America.
