IAEA warns over Iran nuclear access as Western powers push UN referral
Baghaei warns that Iran will take ‘necessary measures’ if the Western powers pursue the resolution.
France, Germany, the UK and the US are pressing the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to report Iran to the UN Security Council, as the nuclear watchdog warns that it remains unable to verify Tehran’s nuclear material more than a year after losing access to key facilities.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the agency’s Board of Governors on Monday that Tehran had provided no information during the latest reporting period on the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities, and inspectors had been unable to conduct on-site verification.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
- list 2 of 4After six months of war, what have US, Iran gained and lost?
- list 3 of 4Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
- list 4 of 4Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
“It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge” over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent at facilities hit in US and Israeli attacks in June 2025, Grossi said.
He described the lack of information and access as a proliferation concern that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency”, calling on Iran to restore effective cooperation with the IAEA.
The nuclear watchdog’s warning comes as the four Western powers seek support for a draft resolution at the 35-member board that would send the Iran issue back to the UN Security Council (UNSC) for the first time in two decades, according to Reuters.
The proposed text asks Grossi to transmit the resolution, previous board decisions and his latest report to the UNSC and General Assembly. It also calls on Iran to provide the information and access required by inspectors.
Iran has rejected the move and maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Western governments were again turning to the IAEA after failing to achieve their objectives elsewhere.
“Whenever they run out of options, they turn to the agency and Grossi,” Baghaei said at his weekly news conference on Monday.
He argued that restrictions facing inspectors were a consequence of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and that it was unreasonable for those governments to blame Tehran for the resulting loss of access.
Baghaei warned that Iran would take “necessary measures” if the Western powers pursued the resolution.
The draft has not yet been formally submitted to the board, and negotiations over its wording are continuing. Even if it is approved, any concrete action at the Security Council could face opposition from Russia and China, two of the five permanent veto powers.

Ukrinform to present Victory Commanders at Lviv Book Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:40:00 UTC
10:40:00 KST

Ukrinform to present Victory Commanders at Lviv Book Forum
The presentation will take place as part of the Lviv Book Forum.
The book’s subjects include current Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, Deputy Head of the Office of the President Pavlo Palisa, commander of the “Bakhmut Ghosts” sniper platoon Oleksandr “Ghost,” Head of the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense Oleh Ivashchenko, Commander of the National Guard Oleksandr Pivnenko, and former Commander of the Ukrainian Ground Forces Hennadii Shapovalov.
The book aims to preserve the firsthand accounts of Ukrainian military commanders who are directly involved in the Russo-Ukrainian war, make important decisions on the battlefield, and preserve their stories for future generations.
A distinctive feature of Victory Commanders is that the entire book-production process—from preparing and editing journalistic materials to design, layout, and prepress preparation—was carried out by the Ukrinform team. For the agency, this represents a new direction in working with its own journalistic content and preserving it in book form.
The publication includes original autographs from the project’s subjects, along with handwritten quotations expressing their personal mottos. Another distinctive feature is a bookmark decorated with a spent cartridge case. It was made by Olha Konoval, a volunteer from Ternopil and the wife of fallen Hero of Ukraine Serhii Konoval.
The book is illustrated with unique photographs taken by Ukrinform correspondents, including photographs taken in Donetsk region and on the Zaporizhzhia front. One of the photographs taken by the agency’s photojournalist, Dmytro Smolienko, featuring sunflowers, was included among Time magazine’s 100 best photographs of 2025.
During the presentation, the agency’s team will discuss the book’s creation, from the initial concept and preparation of materials to design and printing. The discussion will also address the role of the media in documenting the Russo-Ukrainian war and preserving the testimonies of those directly involved.
One of the subjects of Victory Commanders, whose name has not yet been disclosed, will also attend the event.
The special guest at the presentation will be Taras Topolya, Honored Artist of Ukraine, serviceman, and frontman of the band Antytila, who will perform an acoustic set.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the agency is publishing Victory Commanders, which brings together more than 20 stories of Ukrainian commanders and their units. The book is based on interviews published by the agency over the course of a year.

Interview: China coach Ma aims to showcase creativity at FIFA U17 Women's World Cup
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:33:43 CST
10:33:43 KST

by sportswriters Yue Wenwan, Yue Dongxing and Hu Jiefei
BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's under-17 women's football team concluded a monthlong training camp on Sunday as coach Ma Xiaoxu prepares her young players for the FIFA U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where they are expected to play with confidence and creativity rather than fear.
"We certainly want to win because results are what count in competitive sports," Ma, 38, told Xinhua. "I also hope the players can show their abilities on the World Cup stage without fear or restraint."
China trained from August 5 to September 6 in preparation for the U17 Women's World Cup.
China is in Group E with the United States, Samoa and Kenya. The top two teams from each group and the four best third-placed teams will advance to the knockout stage.
"At this age, I hope they can show their true abilities from training, show creativity, make their own decisions on the field and enjoy the games," Ma said. "The experience of competing is the most important thing for their development. Meanwhile, we will certainly give everything to fight for the best possible results."
Ma knows firsthand how important a youth World Cup can be. As an 18-year-old player in 2006, she helped China finish runner-up at the FIFA U20 Women's World Cup and won both the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player and the Golden Boot as its top scorer.
That same year, she was named AFC Asian Player of the Year.
Twenty years later, Ma is preparing for a global youth tournament from the other side of the touchline.
"When I first took over this team, I felt like I suddenly went back to their age," Ma said. "Seeing their young energy and vitality was exciting for me and gave me motivation."
Ma, however, said she would not simply reproduce the methods that worked for her as a player.
"Every player has a different path of development, and football is constantly evolving," she said. "I am also continuing to learn. I hope to teach them more advanced ideas and, after filtering out some of the problems I experienced before, give them better things."
"I hope every player can have her own personality. As a coach, I need to think more carefully and treat every player individually. The most important thing is to let them maintain their love for football. I think it is very important that they do not lose that love as they get older."
China earned its World Cup berth by reaching the semifinals of the AFC U17 Women's Asian Cup in May. The team came back from two goals down to level the semifinal against defending champion the Democratic People's Republic of Korea at 2-2 before eventually losing 4-2.
Ma said securing a World Cup place was the team's most basic objective.
"We also came through that age group ourselves. Whether you can participate in a world-class tournament makes a completely different impact on a player's development," she said. "Their future development will also help drive the overall development of Chinese women's football."
The semifinal also highlighted both the progress and the weaknesses Ma wants her players to address. Against the DPRK's high press, China tried to build through passing combinations from the back rather than repeatedly resorting to long balls. But mistakes under pressure gave opponents opportunities to shoot.
"I think we have to make some changes and not blindly play long balls," Ma said. "But that does not mean pursuing buildup from the back for its own sake. The most important thing is to get the ball behind the opponent's defense and into the penalty area to create dangerous attacks."
Ma praised her players' execution but said they needed to improve their ability to adjust during matches.
"The players have strong execution, but they still need to improve their ability to adapt during the game," she said. "Under high pressure, they may not even be able to hear some of the reminders we give from the sideline."
"I hope they can bravely face the challenges of high pressing. Results are certainly important, and we will try to win every game. But for 17-year-old players, I think it is more important in this process to develop the habit and awareness of thinking independently."
Ma noted that 18 to 20 years old is an especially important period for young players to develop, and that playing overseas can expose them to higher-level competition.
"I think those few years from 18 to 20 are when players improve the fastest," she said. "If they can experience higher-level leagues and have teammates with stronger technical and tactical abilities, they will gradually adapt to the pace and intensity of matches, learn how to make decisions more quickly under pressure and make better use of their bodies in physical confrontations."
Ma has also used the past several months to develop as a coach.
After completing the Asian Cup campaign, she briefly joined China women's national team coaching staff as an assistant to head coach Ante Milicic during the team's training camp and matches in central China's Wuhan.
"For me, as a coach who has just started out, being able to work with a high-level foreign coach and see their working methods, their thinking and how they organize training camps has been very helpful," Ma said.
"The national team coaching staff is very open. Whenever I have questions, they are willing to help."
Ma said she and the senior coaching staff share similar views on many aspects of modern football, while adding that young Chinese coaches need more opportunities to learn.
"I think we have a consensus on some of the ideas of modern football," she said. ■

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Host Germany powered past Mali 83-58 to secure second place in Group A and a quarterfinal qualification game against South Korea as the group stage of the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup concluded Monday.
Frieda Buhner scored 21 points in less than 20 minutes, including four 3-pointers, while Luisa Geiselsoder added 17. Germany responded to Mali's opening 2-0 lead with seven unanswered points before pulling clear in the second quarter.

Live: Are you struggling to access basic health care? Have your say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:33:00 UTC
10:33:00 KST

Are you struggling to access basic health care? Australians share their stories — as it happened
Whether you are battling high costs, long distances or stretching waitlists, many Australians have told us that accessing health care is becoming harder than ever.
We heard from readers about their experiences, and heard from the Grattan Institute's Peter Breadon and ABC health reporters Stephanie Dalzell and Lauren Roberts.
Look back on the blog below.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
New: Filters
Choose what information you see below by using filters
Thank you all for sharing
We know health care can be such a personal and sensitive topic to discuss.
Thank you all for sharing with such honesty, and for providing our experts with such interesting questions.
We are wrapping up this blog for today, but here's some further reading on the issues facing Australian healthcare:
Why is it so expensive to see a GP in Canberra?
Why is the GP bulk billing rate so much lower in Canberra than the rest of the country? Until recently we had precisely zero bulk billing GP clinics in the whole city. $100-$110 for a 15 minute consult is typical while the Medicare rebate is $43 - why is the gap so huge, and why can't Canberra GPs make ends meet under the bulk billing incentive while clinics elsewhere can?
- Paul
Hi Paul, as a fellow Canberran I feel your pain. The ACT consistently has the lowest bulk-billing rates in the country and there are a few reasons for this.
Firstly, Canberra has the highest average incomes in Australia, and evidence suggests bulk billing is usually less common in wealthier areas (one argument is that doctors perceive wealthier people have more capacity to pay, so they then don't bulk bill them).
But there are also broader structural issues — Canberra's a small market, and that means it's harder to attract and retain GPs. When there's less supply, there's less incentive to bulk bill as the demand means clinics can still fill appointment slots even when charging higher fees.
Doctors here have also argued that there are high operating costs involved in running a practice in the ACT that mean they need to charge more for consults.
In terms of the gap, that's a broader issue. The rebate has been a long-held gripe of doctors, who argue it doesn't cover the cost of providing care, even with the incentive.
But the Health Minister Mark Butler has said he can't justify increasing rebates without conditions attached, so the incentive is the way the government's currently trying to shift the dial.
Can the National Health Reform Agreement improve public specialist wait times?
I think the national health reform agreement 2012 is partly to blame for long public specialist wait times. This is because oublic hospitals have addressed inefficiency in inoatient care but still struggle at the 55% share of costs- this was meant to be 50% commonwealth/state. The loser is outpatient care where hospitals use outnoded medicare billing vs NHRA funding. State health services are underfunding outpatient care by underreporting activity and this way they avoid the 55% co pay. For context, i am a metropolitan public hospital specialist of 35 years and have never been less busy!
- DR
Peter has answered this one for us, DR!
Yes, the national reform agreement should do a lot more to reduce specialist wait times.
One part you mentioned is how public specialist care is funded. I agree that public specialist care should be funded through hospital funding, not the Medicare Benefit Schedule (MBS). The MBS is the wrong way to pay for this care.
The MBS is too rigid, requiring care by a named medical specialist. But that doctor might not be working when the patient comes in, or the care might be best delivered by a team member who isn't a medical specialist.
The funding model also creates opportunities for cost-shifting between governments, and in some cases there has been inappropriate MBS billing.
Another area where the national reform deal could help is productivity. It's a big problem if the skills of an experienced specialist like you are going to waste!
Our research found a lot of differences in how public clinics work, even in the same city, ranging from what kind of patients they see, to how they schedule care, to the roles that different health workers play. There is a lot of room to spread best practices and improve efficiency
So, while there should be more funding for public specialist care, it should come with more accountability for productivity. That means the prices governments pay should reflect efficient practices, and there should be public reporting on both wait times and how much care each dollar buys.
The new National Health Reform Agreement, which governments struck earlier this year, creates opportunities for some of these changes. It didn't have the big expansion of public specialist care we proposed. But it does commit to a new national reporting framework, and significant funding to spread new models of care.
Both could be used to help improve the productivity of public specialist clinics.
Shortages may disproportionally affect women
The structural barriers to health care may also have a gendered aspect.
In 2023, the National Women's Health Advisory Council conducted the #EndGenderBias survey to ask Australian women about their experiences of barriers and bias in the health system.
Sixty-two per cent of those women who responded found health care unaffordable, and 45 per cent found it inaccessible.
That included long wait times to consult with healthcare professionals, from the GP level to surgery.
These workforce shortages often left women more disadvantaged than men, the survey noted.
One rural woman who responded said it meant she was left with limited specialist options.
"I have no choice if I want to see a [medical specialist] locally. She is only available every six months and one of those appointments will be by telehealth, which is pointless, except for a prescription renewal that the local doctor can't do."
Are long ED waitlists the 'new normal'?
More of a rant than a question! It worries me that really long wait times in the ED is now so common we're accepting it as the "new normal". EDs will always be busy places, but they're not meant to be places where you stay for long periods of time. The whole point is they're a pitstop to be seen rapidly, stabilised, and sent onwards for the right treatment. But people are stuck there with nowhere to go. The part that worries me the most is it's risky. It's not about frustration or entitlement - it's about safety. These are often people who need to be watched closely or need a specific type of care that the ED was never designed to do. It's not good enough and it should worry us a lot more seeing it get worse and worse every year.
- Alex
Yeah, Alex, you're right.
And a lot of this comes back to the need for better preventative healthcare. If people had more community-based support, including better access to GPs and mental health services, they could avoid a trip to the ED altogether.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare keeps track of potentially preventable hospitalisations and as the name suggests, these are conditions where hospitalisation may be avoided altogether with better primary health care and early disease management.
We can see the rate of these types of hospitalisations has been slowly trending upwards, from 24.43 hospitalisations for every 1,000 people in 2020-21, to 27.21 hospitalisations for every 1,000 people in 2024-25.
A 19-year wait for tonsil removal
My friend just got booked in for getting her tonsils out in regional Victoria. She's been on the waitlist for 19 years! The last updated referral on the record for her was 10 years ago. They were so surprised by how bad her situation was that they got her straight in. Does this feel like waitlists are being assessed correctly? Maybe people need to be spoken to rather than just being a number on a list.
- Prue
Gee, 19 years is a long time for your friend to wait, Prue!
We know advocating for your health is so important (or having a loved one do it for you if you're unable to).
Loading
A lack of home care services 'not just a rural' issue
Kelley Wright, who has a physical disability as a result of a workplace injury and is studying to re-enter the workforce, is unable to provide all the care her aging mother needs.
So, she recently moved her family from Gatton, about 90 kilometres east of Brisbane, closer to the city in the hope of securing better home care supports.
She says her 83-year-old mum needs support to travel to appointments and recently had a lengthy hospital stay after surgery as Kelley's been unable to look after her at home.
But since they both relocated to Ipswich, Kelley has rung at least a dozen providers, to no avail.
"There's just not the physical bodies to fill the jobs, even if you get the approval and the financial assistance is there," Kelley said.
"It's a systemic thing; it goes across the board. It's not just a rural or just a city issue."
Kelley would like to see better incentives for people to work in the home care industry, as well as more migration to fill the jobs.
"We need them as much as they need us," she said.
"It seems to be getting worse and worse. I'm hearing all my mum's friends not having support.
"We're OK at the moment, but my husband and I are aging. What happens in a few years?"
How to find services for the elderly people in your life
How do you find out what services are available for elderly people or older people who have poor health and limited money/rely on the pension? It is hard to support family ourselves, and knowing if there are any services available might alleviate some of the burden we are starting to feel having to support family who are getting older and sickly
- Aimee
I know this is an annoying answer Aimee, but it really depends on where you live and what health concerns your family members have.
Let me give you a hypothetical example.
If the person in need lives in WA and has Parkinson's disease, I'd reach out to the local Parkinson's support group in your region and ask for specific advice about what support they might be eligible for. Often the best advocates are people with lived experience, because they know how to navigate the system.
Council on the Ageing, Australia's peak advocacy group for over 50s, may also be able to point out some low-cost options to help make things a little easier as your family gets older.
And be kind to yourself, caring for others can be challenging, so make sure you're getting the support you need as well.
Key Event
Is Trump coming for the PBS?
i’m worried about Trump’s trade practices and how they’ll effect the future of the PBS. i have psoriasis; not the elbow kind, the all over my body kind. i had to jump through four types of chemotherapy to access a biologic drug that costs $5k per dose every twelve weeks. thanks to the PBS it costs me $35. i’d look like one of those “you can’t ask that” episodes if not for the PBS. what will the government do to make sure our prescription structure remains Australian and never American?
- Anthony
Great question Anthony!
Drug pricing schemes like the PBS have certainly been firmly in the sights of US President Donald Trump and US pharmaceutical companies, who argue they undervalue innovation and threaten billions of dollars in lost sales.
The federal government has been adamant that the PBS is "not for sale" nor up for negotiation. But there's a broader issue here which we're seeing play out.
In order for the PBS to be sustainable, the government needs to negotiate lower prices for drugs it's putting on the scheme, otherwise it wouldn't be able to subsidise as many medications as it does.
But big pharmaceutical companies, who have been emboldened by Trump in recent months, have been rejecting those prices in negotiations, threatening to withdraw — or actually withdrawing — medications from the PBS.
Loading
This is now a major challenge the government has to overcome: how does it keep negotiating with pharmaceutical companies in a sustainable way, without them taking their drugs elsewhere?
In the meantime, the medicines industry has been arguing there are some things the government can do to safeguard the PBS.
It says wait times are more of an issue than Trump's potential tariffs, with a major review in 2024 finding it takes a median time of 22 months for a medicine to land on the PBS once it's approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration.
It wants the government to respond to the review's recommendations with greater haste.
How each state compares on subsiding travel for cancer treatment
The Leukaemia Foundation has released new data which shows striking differences between states and territories on subsidies for people who need to travel to access life-saving cancer treatment.
Current subsidies range from $49.50 per night in Victoria to $110 in South Australia.
Leukaemia Foundation CEO Chris Tanti says cancer treatment can involve months and sometimes years of travel, accommodation and time away from work.
"For people in regional, rural and remote communities, travel is not optional. It is often the only way to access specialist cancer care," Chris said.
"Yet assistance across Australia is inconsistent and, in too many places, has failed to keep pace with the real cost of fuel, vehicle use, accommodation and everyday living."
The foundation says 1 in 8 blood cancer patients in Australia are missing, delaying, or cancelling treatment because they can't afford it.
Leukaemia Foundation also compared states on how much of people's car travel is subsidised. You can look at all of data here.
How do we get doctors to stay in regional and rural Australia?
As a non-medical partner to a medical professional, one of the main reasons I see as a barrier to more doctors working rurally is the lack of opportunities for their partners and children - less skilled work is available, less childcare, less education options. There is only so much money alone can do to incentive people to move rurally (often away from family and existing support systems) when it would have massive negative impacts on their partners career and/or family life. I don't think this is considered enough when investigating barriers to increasing the rural workforce.
- Kaitlin
Hey, Kaitlin, appreciate your insights. And you're spot on.
I said this earlier, but I'm based in Darwin and have been here for more than 10 years.
We have a dire shortage of healthcare workers here, and not just in the capital. We need more people right across regional and remote areas.
Often when we talk about incentives to bring more workers to the bush, it's about luring in young healthcare workers, but if we want to retain people in the regions long-term, we need to be able to offer their families — partners, kids — something as well.
I think another part of the puzzle we often miss is the importance of training up people already living in the town, who want to stay by offering more traineeships or targeted programs.
Mental health care IS health care
Seeing people share stories of struggling to access the right (and enough) mental health care is heartbreaking. I can't think of any other health issue where someone needs to wait until their condition is life threatening before they can get specialist health care in the public system. Mental health care IS health care.
- Lex
100% agree with you there, Lex.
Thinking of all of you who are currently struggling with mental health support and access!

Can only rich people afford good mental health?
Mental healthcare is simply inaccessible for low income Australians. Free and low cost options are simply not helpful if you have a complex presentation, and they carry long wait times. The medicare rebate still leaves me with a large gap, and it only covers ten sessions a year. I've been putting off seeing a psychologist for the past year because I'll face significant out of pocket costs that I simply cannot afford. I'm struggling with work and study, but the alternative is to pay the hefty fees and struggle to make ends meet.
- Riley
Hi Riley, you're not alone there, and many experts have argued the system has become increasingly difficult to access for those struggling with cost-of-living pressures.
Various studies have told us cost is a major barrier to mental health care, with people like yourself delaying or avoiding getting help because they simply can't afford to.
The divide between those who have money for care and those who don't means people are seeking help later — when their symptoms are harder to treat —and are more likely to present at emergency departments needing more urgent care.
Experts like prominent psychiatrist Pat McGorry have argued the system spends too little on early intervention. And they argue governments, and crucially people, are paying the price with rising ED presentations which are overall much harder for the patient, and more costly to the system.
For its part, the federal government has argued it has invested heavily in mental health services — like its Medicare Mental Health centres, which provide free services.
But many experts and doctors argue more needs to be done to ensure mental health is equitable.
Mental health costs a key concern for many of you

Mental health the most reported long-term condition in the 2021 Census
Last month's census was only the second time Australians have been asked to report long-term health issues.
The first time was in the 2021 Census, and at that time mental health surpassed all physical health conditions, with one in 11 Australians reporting they had a long-term mental health condition.
Census data helps government and non-government groups decide where to distribute resources.
Steph Schmidt, a psychologist and farmer who lives in South Australia's Mid North, is hoping the census results may help bridge the divide between urban and regional spending on services.
"From what I've seen on the ground, I wouldn't necessarily think that [the prevalence of mental health conditions] is going to have gone down a whole lot in the last couple of years," she said.
"It's an ongoing issue, whether you are rural, whether you are urban."
You can read more on this story by the ABC's Matthew Ward Agius below.
Why is women's health such a low priority?
I had a stage 3 bladder prolapse in May 2025. It took a year to get an appointment to see a Urogynacologist in Townsville. It would have taken longer had I not complained. The consultant diagnosed me as a stage 4 by this time and put me down as a category 2. I had to wait a further three months before I was sent an appointment for pre-admission on 7 August this year. I have been told by the Surgical Bookings office that I will have to wait approximately another 150 days before they can schedule me for an operation because there are 39 other patients in front of me and they only have one Urogynacologist to cover from Mackay all the way up to Cairns. I would like to know why women’s health has to be such a low priority in this day and age. Why are the waiting lists almost 3 years long to have a prolapse surgically fixed? I think it is terrible in this day and age that women have to suffer like this and have their quality of life impacted so dramatically. Is anyone in the government ever going to do anything?
- Linda Stuart
Hi Linda, thank you so much for reaching out. I'm so sorry you've gone through this. It's simply not good enough. Pelvic organ prolapse, where the bladder, uterus and/or bowel protrudes into the vagina, is common in Australia.
And, unfortunately, your experience is not isolated, women are waiting longer for surgical repairs.
Data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare shows the median wait time for anterior and posterior vaginal repairs — one type of surgery to fix pelvic organ prolapse — has been trending upwards.
And the percentage of Australian women waiting more than a year for surgery is also increasing.
As for what's been done about it? A recently announced Senate select committee on women's health will examine issues affecting women's health, including barriers to diagnosis, treatment and support.
Experts are encouraging women, like yourself, to share their stories in the hope that the lived experience of women will spark change.
All the best for your recovery.
To stay or go? The tough choice Queenslanders face for health care
The social connection of living in a small regional town was something Kerry and Kathy MacDonald were desperate to hold on to when Kerry's health began to decline several years ago.
Since 2020, the 80-year-old, who has a heart condition, has made multiple trips from his home in Longreach to see specialists in Brisbane.
It is a 2,400-kilometre round trip, which is no easy task for the couple.
He was offered a spot in a three-year trial in Brisbane for a treatment that could help prolong his life.
"We agonised over it. We'd have to leave and virtually start another life," he said.
Kerry said their eldest son had offered them a place to stay in Brisbane.
In the end, they stayed put.
"It would have created so much upheaval to us that I feel it would have had a more detrimental effect on Kerry's health and probably mine," she said.
Have you also had to choose between staying in your home, or moving to a new place just for better health care?
Let us know in the comments above.
Would there be consequences if the private health insurance rebate was binned?
What if we were to scrap the private health insurance rebate and invest that money into our public hospitals. What would be the consequences, if any?
- Michael
Hi Michael, like many things in the health space the answer depends on who you ask.
Private health insurance has been a contested area of policy for decades, with some experts arguing the billions of dollars spent subsidising private health insurance would be better spent on the public system.
While in the cons column, the private health insurance industry (who of course has a stake in the argument) says reducing the rebate would encourage people to drop or downgrade their cover, pushing demand on to public hospitals already struggling.
There is also a middle ground here with some arguing the subsidies should be reformed rather than binned.
The federal government recently decided to wind back a more generous rebate for those aged 65 and over, which has proved quite controversial, with the Coalition vowing to block it in Parliament and some states demanding the policy be dumped.
So, the reality is a broader move to scrap the rebate entirely is very unlikely. The federal government doesn't want to pick a fight with the industry, and many families with private health insurance rely on the rebate as a cost-of-living measure.
Why are ED wait times so long?
Why do we have so long wait times at the ED, it defeats the purpose of being at ED. I went there with my aged mother, and it took us 10 hours to get some sort of attention.
- Nit
Oh, Nit, that sounds like such a horrible experience, hope your mum is OK.
In 2024–25, one in 10 patients spent more than 11 hours in the ED, which is up from seven hours in 2014-15.
And according to the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine, there's a few reasons why more patients are waiting longer.
One of them is bed-blocking, where there are simply not enough beds for patients.
Another reason is increasing demand, with healthcare workers managing 286,000 additional annual presentations to public EDs over the past five years.
Are you living in a 'pharmacy desert'?
Data recently published by the Australian Journal of Rural Health shows which parts of the country have fewer or even no community pharmacies — and the results might surprise you.
It shows Aboriginal communities in West Arnhem Land and the Tiwi Islands have no community pharmacies at all, as well as rural towns south of the Blue Mountains and the coastal region of Jervis Bay.
But it's not just the bush with fewer community pharmacies, also known as retail pharmacies.
Areas just outside of big city centres, including outer-city Melbourne and outer-city Perth, recorded pharmacy density levels below the national average.
In the graphs below you can see the average number of community pharmacies per 10,000 people in your location.
The study found there was an average of 2.2 community pharmacies for every 10,000 Australians.
This is "well below" the global average of 2.75, according to the study's lead author Michael Leach.
He said overall, community pharmacy density across regional, rural and remote areas was significantly higher than in metropolitan areas.
We know pharmacies might be the first point of contact someone has with the health system when they're unwell, and vital for those who need to regularly take medication.

Hong Kong aviation success today means more than just adding routes

Ken Chu (LLD) is the chairman and CEO of Mission Hills Group, with businesses in hospitality, leisure, entertainment, sports, wellness and education in China. 
When Cathay Pacific Airways announced direct flights to Almaty starting next January, the significance went beyond adding another destination. The service will be Cathay Pacific’s first to Central Asia and the only non-stop passenger connection between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan.
Another announcement pointed to Hong Kong’s growing aviation reach from a different direction. Qatar Airways Cargo relocated its regional office to Hong Kong and agreed with the Airport Authority to increase frequencies and develop new routes through the city. The airline already operates around 56 cargo flights a week via Hong Kong.
Taken together, these developments offer an interesting glimpse of how Hong Kong’s aviation map is evolving.
As Cathay celebrates its 80th anniversary this year, Hong Kong also finds itself entering a new era for its airport. The three-runway system and Skytopia development signal ambitions that extend well beyond aviation. Hong Kong International Airport is no longer being positioned simply as one of the world’s best to arrive at or for transit, but as an integrated destination for tourism, business and entertainment.
In this year’s budget, the government reaffirmed the Airport City development as a strategic economic initiative. Hong Kong’s airport handled some 63 million passengers in the year ended March 31, nearly 15 per cent more than in the previous year, while remaining the world’s busiest cargo airport.
Yet these developments also pose an important question. If Hong Kong’s ambitions for its airport have evolved, has our thinking about what makes a successful aviation hub kept pace?

Hungary: Meta failed to stop anti-LGBTI content on Facebook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

This press release contains information that some readers may find upsetting
Meta failed to address harmful rhetoric on Facebook against the LGBTI community in Hungary by ineffectively applying its own moderation policies, a new Amnesty International briefing shows.
‘It erodes my soul’: Meta’s contribution to anti-LGBTI discourse in Hungary, shows how Meta’s policy decisions, including the weakening of safeguards for high risk groups in January 2025 and the significant reduction in proactive content moderation, have negatively affected the LGBTI community in Hungary.
“Meta contributed to adverse human rights impacts experienced by LGBTI people in Hungary through its policy decisions, and failed to take adequate steps to prevent the resulting harm. Risks to LGBTI people in Hungary were foreseeable and well documented, yet Meta did not adequately act on them,
Daniela Schnidrig, Interim Policy and Advocacy Adviser at Amnesty International’s Big Tech Accountability Team.
One of Meta’s failures was not properly assessing the risks that changes to its global policies posed to the Hungarian LGBTI community. This was despite knowing the hostile political climate and existing legal restrictions on LGBTI-related assemblies, including Pride, and sustained anti-LGBTI rhetoric, including by government and government-aligned actors.
Facebook occupies a uniquely influential position within Hungary’s information environment, reaching over half of the population. LGBTI people interviewed for this research said that sustained exposure to anti-LGBTI content on Facebook caused them anxiety, frustration and feelings of helplessness even in cases where they reported the harmful content.
“Facebook is just another piece in the pile of my anxiety… to them (Meta) users are not people, they are just numbers,” one interviewee told Amnesty International.
Some interviewees temporarily withdrew from the platform and participation in public discussions to protect their mental health. Others self-censored fearing a backlash if they openly expressed their sexual orientation, gender identity, or support for the rights of LGBTI people on the platform. These experiences raise concerns over whether Facebook failed to protect the rights to freedom of expression and non-discrimination, by undermining LGBTI people’s ability to participate in public and civic life on an equal basis with others.
“Over the last decade, members of the Hungarian LGBTI community faced severe smear campaigns and repressive laws from the Orbán government. They also could not express themselves freely on Meta platforms which largely added to their despair” – said Eszter Mihály, LGBTI rights officer at Amnesty Hungary.
Facebook’s central role in debates
As part of the research, Amnesty International also conducted a social listening exercise of public discourse on LGBTI issues across various social media platforms. We found that discussions concerning LGBTI people were characterized by fearmongering, misinformation, and derogatory rhetoric, with Facebook serving as a central forum for these debates.
Representatives of Háttér Society, a Hungarian organization that supports and advocates for the rights of LGBTI people, shared with Amnesty examples of harmful content on Facebook identified between January 2023 and December 2024. They included comments calling for physical violence against LGBTI people, with statements such as “Beat them to death immediately”, “I would shoot this”, “Throw them off the bridge”, and “Death to the extreme genderfluid vermin”.
Other comments used dehumanizing language, referring to LGBTI people as “rats”, “mutants”, “earthworms” or “scum”, while some explicitly advocated the eradication of transgender people. Several other examples pushed narratives portraying LGBTI people as threats to children, public morality, or social order. Some harmful content remained accessible for a period of time after being reported, including content that was still available when checked in March 2026. The continued availability of such content indicates ongoing shortcomings in the consistency and effectiveness of Meta’s enforcement systems.
Interviewees repeatedly encountered anti-LGBTI content despite actively seeking to avoid it by blocking accounts, reporting harmful content, and communicating their disinterest to Facebook.
“Now my feed is really unhealthy. It is not just one or two videos: it’s a series of videos. Now I only can see that. There is rarely any content from friends.
Ádám Kanicsár, an LGBTI activist and journalist, told Amnesty International
Other interviewees also noted that they were shown content they were not interested in.
“Taken together, these findings raise concerns that Facebook’s design may also have increased users’ exposure to harmful anti-LGBTI content. The findings suggest that engagement-driven systems may be contributing to repeated exposure to harmful and divisive content,” said Alia Al Ghussain, the Head of Amnesty International’s Big Tech Accountability Team.
Under the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA), Meta is required to identify and prevent systemic risks related to platform design to ensure that its products are not causing or contributing to human rights abuses. The company must reassess the impact of its January 2025 policy changes in different contexts, and strengthen content moderation and enforcement. This includes an effective complaint mechanism, improve transparency on the enforcements and effectiveness of its policies and the provision of effective remedies to those affected by any harms. The European Commission must robustly enforce the DSA and investigate Meta’s compliance with its obligations. Amnesty International wrote to Meta on 28 July sharing its conclusions. On 11 August, Meta replied stating that, given the scope and detail of the findings presented, it could not share a response within the stipulated timeline.
Background
The research was conducted amid a worsening environment for LGBTI rights in Hungary. Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, the government introduced discriminatory laws and policies with government aligned actors portraying LGBTI people as threats to children, families, and Hungarian values. These trends intensified in 2025 and 2026 with new laws restricting LGBTI related gatherings, including Pride events.

Cambodia Confirms Resumption of Joint Military Exercises With US Next Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:28:00 UTC
10:28:00 KST

Cambodia’s army has confirmed that it will resume joint military exercises with the United States early next year after a decade-long suspension, the latest sign of the improving ties between the two nations.
The Royal Cambodian Army announced on Facebook on Friday that officials from the two nations had concluded an Initial Planning Conference for Exercise Angkor Sentinel 2027, which it said would be held in February of next year.
The exercise has the aim of “strengthening interoperability and disaster-response capabilities, reflecting renewed momentum in Cambodia–U.S. military cooperation and a shared commitment to strengthening defense cooperation.”
The announcement follows several high-level meetings between U.S. and Cambodian officials. These include a meeting last month between Prime Minister Hun Manet and Elbridge A. Colby, undersecretary for policy at the U.S. Department of War, during which the two discussed expanded defense cooperation.
Hun Manet said at the time that he was satisfied with the “positive momentum in Cambodia-U.S. relations” and the ongoing talks about the resumption of Angkor Sentinel, the Associated Press reported. “The joint exercises and training not only build military capability but also serve as a vital bridge to foster close friendship between the armed forces of both countries,” he added.
This was not long after Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, traveled to Phnom Penh for meetings with officials including Gen. Vong Pisen, the commander-in-chief of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces, and Vice Adm. Tea Sokha, the commander of the Royal Cambodian Navy.
The visit “reaffirmed the United States’ long-term commitment to strengthening bilateral relationships and partnerships that advance a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific,” the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement at the time.
Angkor Sentinel was held for the first time in 2010 but was unilaterally canceled by the Cambodian government in early 2017, shortly after Cambodian troops took part for the first time in Golden Dragon, a joint military exercise with the Chinese military. The move reflected the mutually reinforcing deterioration of Phnom Penh’s relations with Washington and its growing proximity to China.
The resumption of the exercise has been anticipated by both sides for some time. It was first publicly discussed in early 2025, just prior to President Trump’s return to the White House, and has been referenced in most high-level diplomatic meetings since then. It reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations since the midpoint of the Biden administration, as Phnom Penh has sought to diversify its foreign relations and the U.S. has worked to pull the country out of China’s orbit.
However, the rapprochement has gained inexorable momentum since the inauguration of the second Trump administration, whose transactional mode of diplomacy has been much more to Phnom Penh’s liking. In particular, President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter USAID and cut off U.S. funding for democracy promotion efforts and media outlets like Radio Free Asia removed a key impediment to improved relations on the Cambodian side. As I noted in 2025, Cambodia’s government finally has what it has always wanted: “a relationship with the U.S. that strengthens, rather than undermines, the CPP’s hold on power.”
Last June, the U.S. government officially removed Cambodia from its arms sale blacklist, a month after an American ship docked for the first time at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. The latter was particularly significant, given the extensive Chinese refurbishment of the base, which U.S. and Western officials feared was intended to host a permanent Chinese military presence. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command, described the port visit as a sign of the “strong upward trajectory” of relations between Phnom Penh and Washington.
These improvements have come even as branches of the U.S. government have come to officially recognize the extent of the Cambodian elite’s involvement in the country’s gigantic online scamming industry. According to U.S. government agencies, online scamming cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

Alleged killers of Australian, US surfers go on trial in Mexico
ENSENADA – The suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hot spot went on trial on Sept 7, two years after their killings in a suspected robbery.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024.
Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing. They bore gunshot wounds to their heads.
Three men are on trial over their killings.
The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings.
Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner Martin Robinson earlier told reporters.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.
The couple did not speak to reporters after the first hearing. Martin told AFP they will do so at the end of the proceedings, which are expected to conclude within a month and a half.
Martin is expected to testify on Sept 8.
‘Good phones’
Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burnt near their bodies.
Three witnesses appeared before the court on Sept 7, including the stepson of one of the defendants, identified as “Ramon”.
Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused – known as “El Kekas” – to the crime scene.
Ramon said he was in the vehicle listening to music when the “commotion” began.
“I heard a lot of noise, got out of the pickup and ran as fast as I could to my uncle’s house, where I hid in the bathroom,” he said.
He said he rejoined the group following the crime, after they called to warn him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos” would happen to him if he said anything.
Ramon described his stepfather as violent and said that he had previously attacked his mother. She confirmed the violence in her testimony.
The girlfriend of the witness’ stepfather was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2025 after admitting she had instigated the robbery in order to steal the pickup’s tyres.
Ary Gisell Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had “good phones and good tyres”.
“El Kekas” previously faced charges for enforced disappearance, but these were eventually dropped.
The other two suspects were initially arrested for possession of methamphetamines. Evidence was later found linking them to the robbery and murder.
The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanised a major search on social media for their bodies.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the United States. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad played professional football in Guatemala and ran a clothing company in San Diego. He was killed a few months before he was set to marry.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.
Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the north-west.
Their bodies were later burnt. AFP

US Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon described the rise in antisemitism in the United States as a "national crisis," pledging that combating antisemitism would remain one of her top priorities at the Justice Department.
Speaking Thursday at a gala for the Israeli-American Council (IAC) in San Diego, Dhillon detailed lawsuits against universities and businesses, criminal proceedings for hate crimes, and settlements totaling nearly half a billion dollars.
"The rise in antisemitism is not a wave of isolated incidents. This is a national crisis that requires national determination," Dhillon said. "Communities are being tested, institutions are being tested, and leaders are being tested."
According to Dhillon, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division is working to ensure that every American, including Israeli-Americans, can "live, learn, pray, and work without fear."
DOJ official details antisemitism enforcement efforts
Dhillon listed a series of institutions that have been the focus of government action.
She cited a lawsuit against Harvard University under civil rights law, claiming that Jewish and Israeli students were harassed and excluded.
Dhillon also mentioned two lawsuits against UCLA following incidents at protest encampments, where, according to her, Jewish students were blocked, assaulted, and sprayed with pepper spray.
She also mentioned agreements with Columbia University, Northwestern University, Cornell University, and Brown University, and added that more than 100 colleges, universities, medical schools, and law schools are under investigation.
Dhillon also noted the use of a law against planning restrictions targeting Orthodox Jewish communities and another law to protect synagogues and religious schools.
According to Dhillon, the Justice Department is simultaneously pursuing indictments in California, New Jersey, New York, and Washington, DC.
"When a Jewish person is attacked because they are Jewish, it's a federal crime," she said.
Oakland café case prompted by community report
Outside university campuses, Dhillon highlighted legal action against an Oakland café accused of refusing service to Jewish customers.
"We are currently pursuing legal action against a café that refused service to Jewish customers – clear antisemitic discrimination in a public place," she said.
Dhillon did not name Jerusalem Café in Oakland, but gave prominent attention to the lawsuit against it.
Jerusalem Café, located on Telegraph Avenue in Oakland and owned by Fathi Abd Al-Rahim Harara and Native Grounds, has closed its doors while facing three lawsuits. The federal case is expected to begin on October 26.
The owners have claimed that the proceedings are part of an effort by "Zionist organizations and the federal government" to use the courts to suppress support for Palestinians, and vowed to continue the "fight for the liberation of Palestine."
The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on June 9, 2025.
According to the lawsuit, Jonathan Hirsch arrived at the café with his five-year-old son. Harara allegedly asked whether he was a Zionist, called the Star of David a "violent hat," demanded that the two leave, and called the police.
In another case, customer Michael Radis was allegedly told, "You're the Jew, you're the Zionist. We don't want you in our café."
Dhillon said a report from the community had prompted the initial investigation.
"In the case of the café, a report from the community led to the opening of our initial investigation," she said.
Dhillon urged Jews and Israeli-Americans to continue documenting incidents and providing testimony, even in the face of fears of retaliation.
"As long as I hold this position, fighting antisemitism will be one of my top priorities," she said.

The canal, which handles 5 percent of global maritime trade, has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 34 starting on September 4.
A further reduction will start on September 15, when the limit will be 32 ships.
Espino, who took over as administrator of the Panama Canal Authority on Monday, told the AFP news agency that restrictions could be tightened again if the drought does not subside.
She said she was not ruling out the possibility that in February or March, the limits “could be reduced to 29 or something similar”.
She said rainfall over the coming months would determine whether further restrictions are needed.
“Depending on how much rain falls in September, October and November – the three critical months – that will determine whether I need to lower any slots further in January, February or March,” she told the Reuters news agency last week.
The restrictions are not expected to become as severe as during the 2023-24 drought, when daily crossings fell as low as 22.
The Panama Canal depends on freshwater to operate the locks that raise and lower vessels travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Water comes mainly from the artificial Gatun and Alajuela lakes, which are replenished by rainfall.
An average transit consumes about 200 million litres (about 53 million gallons) of water.
That dependence makes the 80km (50-mile) canal particularly vulnerable to prolonged dry weather, and levels in both reservoirs have already dropped with the onset of El Niño.
This year’s El Niño – which affects weather patterns and pushes up global temperatures – is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
Apart from reducing the number of vessels transiting the Panama Canal, authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6 metres (50 feet to 48 feet).
Draft is the depth of water a ship needs to float safely. A lower draft limit means vessels may have to carry less cargo to pass through the canal.
The disruption comes at a sensitive time for global shipping.
The Panama Canal’s importance has increased as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East has fallen sharply amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Some vessels have recently paid more than $1m at auction to secure transit slots through the canal.
Panama is betting on a new reservoir at Rio Indio – a river in the country’s centre – as a longer-term solution.
The project is intended to provide water for canal operations and more than half of Panama’s population for the next 50 years, but it is expected to take five to six years to complete.
Espino, the new administrator, told Reuters that the reservoir would “ensure that the canal never again has to resort to lowering the draft or reducing the number of transits”.

Israeli poll shows Yashar party leading Netanyahu’s Likud by 25 seats to 21
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
01:08:33 UTC
10:08:33 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party would emerge as the largest party in Israel’s parliament with 25 seats compared with 21 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud if elections were held today, according to a poll released Monday.
The survey was conducted by the Israeli market research and public opinion polling institute Midgam for Israel’s Channel 12.
Yashar gained one seat compared with the channel’s previous poll, giving it the largest representation in the 120-member Knesset.
Likud, meanwhile, lost two seats.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together party secured 13 seats, dropping by two to its lowest level in the channel’s recent polls.
The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, a former Israeli army deputy chief of staff, remained unchanged at 11 seats, while Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party lost one seat, falling to eight.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, led by Yaakov Asher, received eight seats, while Aryeh Deri’s ultra-Orthodox Shas party secured seven.
An alliance between the right-wing Religious Zionism and Zehut parties, led by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, respectively, was projected to win six seats.
Amcha Yisrael, led by Ofer Winter, received four seats.
Among the Arab parties, the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, secured seven seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List received four.
Several parties failed to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, including Benny Gantz’s Blue and White and Avi Maoz’s Noam Yisrael.
In terms of political blocs, the opposition secured 68 seats, including 57 for Jewish parties and 11 for Arab parties.
Netanyahu’s bloc meanwhile received 52 seats, gaining two after the parties led by Smotrich and Winter crossed the electoral threshold.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
When respondents were asked who they believed was better suited to be prime minister, 42% chose Eisenkot compared with 35% who favored Netanyahu, giving Eisenkot a seven-point advantage.
The poll results come ahead of Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27.
Earlier Monday, Israeli parties submitted their candidate lists for the elections a day before Tuesday’s deadline.
The submissions came amid divisions over electoral alliances, most notably Eisenkot’s decision not to merge his party with Bennett’s.
Winter also decided to contest the elections independently without joining Smotrich’s party.

Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:07:47 BST
10:07:47 KST

Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
- Published
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.
It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.
In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".
Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.
According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".
The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.
Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.
He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.
Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.
In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.
Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.
Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.
Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.
Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.
In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said.
During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption.
Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine.
However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC.

Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 3, injuring 16, as brief truce ends in missile fire
Unknown

Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 3, injuring 19, as brief truce ends in missile fire
Smoke rising following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Sept. 8, 2026. (Eugene Kotenko / AFP via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Key developments so far:
- Russia launched a large-scale drone and missile attack at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on Sept. 8, killing 3 people and injuring 19.
- The strike signals a definitive end to the aerial truce the Kremlin declared while Kyiv hosted U.S. officials for peace talks.
- The attack damaged residential buildings, a school, warehouses, and vehicles.
- Civilian infrastructure in Kyiv Oblast was also targeted, and one civilian injured.
- Air raid alerts sounded throughout the morning as Russian jet-powered drones continued to target the capital.
A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least three people, injured 19 others, and sparked a series of huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged in the attack, signaling a violent end to the brief respite for the capital during a diplomatic visit by U.S. envoys over the weekend.
"It's like The Hunger Games, it's just about survival," Dariia Kolisnyk, a resident of a building damaged by a missile in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, told the Kyiv Independent.
"You just go to bed, wondering whether you'll wake up or not. That's life in Kyiv."
The strike follows Russia and Ukraine's agreement to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for three days. While the precise expiration time of the truce was hazy, there is no doubt about its end.
Liudmyla Akhremenko, also a resident in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, said her home has been damaged for the second time in an attack in the area.
"The blast wave blew out the windows, and stones flew into the house. People’s furniture was damaged," Akhremenko told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Akhremenko, no shelter has yet been built nearby, so she was at home when the attack occurred.
"It was very scary," she said. "I was sleeping and woke up to the explosion. I saw that the windows had opened, the glass had shattered, and the flowers had fallen. Everything jumped up to the ceiling."
Explosions rang out in the capital at around 3:30 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Another loud blast occurred about 10 minutes later.
At around 4:14 a.m. local time, Kyiv Independent journalist Yevgeniya Doluda reported a series of up to six explosions in rapid succession.
"There was a very strong bang," Kolisnyk said. "I opened my eyes and saw the window flying, and big flashes. I ran to the second room, where my child and my husband were sleeping and climbed through the broken door and windows."
"I got the child, thank God, sat him up, everything is fine. My husband was cut a little by the glass. But, thank God, everything is fine," she added.
The blasts followed warnings from Ukraine's Air Force that Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones were bound for Kyiv. Monitoring channels reported that at least 12 ballistic missiles have targeted the city in the span of about an hour.
The Air Force later reported that Russian forces launched 32 cruise missiles, 166 Shahed-type drones of which "more than half" were jet-powered, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles. Two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones were intercepted, it said.
It added that missile and drone strikes were recorded at 29 locations.
At around 12:40 p.m. local time, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the death toll had risen to three.
As of 1 p.m. local time, 19 people had been injured in the attack in Kyiv, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
"The Russians tried to deliberately cause as much harm to life as possible — ballistics, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered 'shaheds,'" President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Speaking to reporters later in the morning, Zelensky described the interception of almost all Russian cruise missiles as "a good result."
"Is it enough? No. We need (interceptor) missiles," he added. "We need a package of ballistic missiles from the Americans. They heard in detail what we need, when we need it."
"I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic. And, God willing, we will get a result."
At least two multistory residential buildings in the capital were damaged by drones, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported. Fires also broke out in warehouses, and garages and vehicles were reported damaged.
Rescuers evacuated two people from a 16-story apartment building that was damaged in the attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Another 10 people were rescued after being trapped in a five-story building during the strike.
A drone attacked the building of the We-Ukraine TV channel, which is part of Ukraine's national telethon, which has been broadcasting since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. The attack occurred during a live broadcast, injuring at least five people, Zelensky said.
"‘Shaheds’ against the media is a new chapter in Russia's degradation, and there must certainly be a response from Europe and the world to this," Zelensky said.
The TV channel reported its newsroom and offices were struck during the attack.
Yevhen Panchenko, one of the residents in the Solomianskyi district whose homes were damaged, said he was initially in his apartment on the ninth floor during the attack but ran down to the first floor as the explosions intensified.
"I already call this street a 'training ground' because these attacks are not happening for the first time," he said.
"These attacks destroy people’s lives and livelihoods. They have nowhere to live or work. It’s horrible."
The State Emergency Service reported fires and damage in several neighborhoods, including Kyiv's Holosiivskyi, Solomianskyi, Darnytskyi, Podilskyi, and Dniprovskyi districts.
The attack comes after sustained Russian drone attacks against Kyiv that, before the weekend's truce, targeted the capital around-the-clock for nine consecutive days.
In an apparent sign of their resumption, air raid sirens sounded throughout the morning with the Air Force reporting several jet-powered drones in the airspace above Kyiv.
read also
The assault also targeted communities in the surrounding region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration. Russia targeted the region from the evening of Sept. 7 into the morning of Sept. 8, targeting residential areas and civilian infrastructure.
One person was injured in a strike in the town of Bila Tserkva, Tkachenko said. Two apartment buildings, a house, a warehouse, and a production facility in the town were also damaged.
Damage to homes, warehouses, businesses, and vehicles occurred in the Kyiv Oblast districts of Brovary, Boryspil, Fastiv, and Obukhiv, Tkachenko said.
Air raid alarms also sounded overnight in other regions of Ukraine, including Rivne Oblast in the northwest and other areas far from the front lines. The Air Force warned less than an hour earlier that Russia had likely launched cruise missiles from its Tu-95 and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Moscow on Sept. 6 announced a three-day pause on attacks against Kyiv while U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the city for peace talks. The Kremlin declared the truce would "begin at midnight today," without specifying if that meant Sept. 5 or 6.
While Witkoff and Kushner's visit passed without an aerial attack against Kyiv, Russia immediately began firing drones at the capital after their departure on Sept. 7.

The conflict escalated after Liang remarried and moved out with his new wife, leaving his daughter in Xu’s care. After 15 years of caregiving, Xu expressed that she could no longer continue due to financial pressures and sought compensation from her son.

EU trade chief to meet CEOs over China strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Maroš Šefčovič speaks to the media as he arrives for a meeting of G7 trade ministers in Évian-les-Bains, France on May 6, 2026. | Pool photo by Benoit Tessier via AFP/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič is expected to meet European CEOs on Sept. 18 to get their feedback on the European Commission’s push to diversify critical supply chains away from China, according to four people familiar with the meeting.
The Commission has floated a “diversification tool” to encourage companies to source critical imports, such as raw materials, from at least three different suppliers where alternatives are available.
But before formally proposing such a measure, the EU executive wants to secure industry buy-in — and understand how far companies are willing to go to reduce their dependence on China, given the costs involved.
Advertisement
The push comes as the Commission has stepped up engagement with Chinese officials over the summer as Brussels seeks to reduce the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with the Asian giant. The meeting will happen two days after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivers her landmark State of the Union speech, in which she is expected to address the EU’s anxiety about the threat China poses to its industrial base.
After technical talks with Beijing, Šefčovič will speak by videoconference with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in mid-September before heading to Beijing in early October.
Should these talks not yield results, national leaders have urged the EU executive to devise new ways to tackle China’s industrial overcapacity in time for their mid-October summit.
The Sept. 18 meeting is expected to bring together CEOs from the machinery, electrical components, automotive and chemical sectors, two people familiar with the event said.
“I’m glad that I hear more often that even the business leaders themselves — many of them — are realizing that the cost of diversification is smaller than the cost of disruption,” Šefčovič told POLITICO last week.
“That’s the logic which I would like to develop further. I’m inviting the key stakeholders for [a] special forum.”
Šefčovič said such discussions help shape the Commission’s thinking on how such a tool should work.
Among the input sought is “what would be the best design of such an instrument, where we can have the buy-in for the economic leadership of our leading companies,” he said.

LONDON — King Charles has invited leading figures from the artificial intelligence industry to an exclusive event set to take place this month, according to two people familiar with the plans who were granted anonymity because it has yet to be publicly announced.

Advertisement
King Charles has also shown an interest in the development and regulation of AI.

He also hosted a banquet at Windsor Castle during President Donald Trump’s state visit to the U.K. last September which was attended by tech industry leaders including Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman.
