Qatar seeks to 'phase out' US-Iran crisis through regional dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:57:43 UTC
09:57:43 KST

Qatar has sought to "phase this crisis out" rather than pursue an immediate end to the US-Iran war, aiming to establish conditions for comprehensive regional dialogue and a sustainable political resolution, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari confirmed.
Speaking to CNN, Al-Ansari stated that Doha believes the conflict cannot simply be frozen, cautioning that an abrupt pause without addressing root causes risks paving the way for another round of confrontation.
"We have to phase this crisis out rather than end it immediately," he said.
"What we need to do is make sure the playing field is in a place where we can have the right negotiations for a sustainable solution."
He stressed that Qatar does not want the region to transition between recurring cycles of intense fighting: "We do not want to go from a high-intensity conflict to a high-intensity conflict. We don't want to freeze this conflict and be back here a couple of months later."
Inclusive dialogue
Al-Ansari outlined Doha's two immediate operational priorities: mitigating economic pressure and preventing military escalation across the Gulf and Iran.
"Right now, what we are doing, we have two main priorities. One is make sure that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that the economic pressure on all of us collectively and the peoples in the region, including the people of Iran, has left us," he stated.
The second priority is to halt further military strikes to foster an environment in which regional stakeholders can pursue inclusive engagement.
"When we get to that point, this is the point we need to have a regional push, all of us collectively, to make sure that dialogue happens and it is a comprehensive dialogue that includes all of us, not just outside," he said.
Identifying political will and technical hurdles as the primary barriers to an agreement, Al-Ansari noted that Qatar is actively preparing proposals to address both challenges.
He observed that sanctions have failed to yield expected diplomatic breakthroughs, underscoring that "this issue will only be resolved through a deal. It will only be resolved at the negotiation table."
He also issued a strong warning against normalising maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, which threaten global energy and food security: "We need to kill this in its infancy. It cannot become the new normal in war for countries to basically just close waterways in this way," urging accountability and respect for international law.

Clock ticks down as parties still scrambling over final slates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:50:23 UTC
09:50:23 KST

The first day of filing has ended, and by 10 p.m. Tuesday — or midnight if the chairman of the Central Elections Committee extends the deadline — the final makeup of the party slates competing in the 2026 election should become clear.
Six major parties have yet to submit their candidate lists. Some are waiting for additional candidates, others are still settling internal disputes, and at least one was forced only Monday to announce the replacement of a senior candidate.
With the deadline approaching, here is where each party stands — and where last-minute surprises could still emerge.
Likud
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party has endured several turbulent days over its candidate list, particularly the slots that the party leader is permitted to fill with handpicked candidates rather than primary winners.
Netanyahu has delayed announcing those candidates despite a deadline imposed by Likud’s internal court and appears intent on withholding his decisions until close to the filing deadline.
A meeting of the Likud Secretariat that was expected to approve the reserved slots and was originally scheduled for 11 a.m. Tuesday was postponed to 2 p.m. — and even that time was not considered final.
Netanyahu has also struggled to recruit candidates for the reserved positions, and it remained unclear whom he would ultimately choose.
High-tech entrepreneur Oren Dobronsky, whom Netanyahu had offered a reserved place in the top 10 of Likud’s slate, announced Monday night that he had decided not to run for the Knesset.
United Torah Judaism
United Torah Judaism, the Ashkenazi Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, alliance made up of the Agudat Yisrael and Degel HaTorah parties, has undergone a dramatic shake-up in recent days, with its new slate expected to look markedly different from the previous one.
Longtime party chairman Moshe Gafni was unexpectedly ousted Sunday, with lawmaker Yaakov Asher named to replace him. Lawmaker Uri Maklev will also not be included on the slate.
On the Agudat Yisrael side of the alliance, veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler will give up his place to Elyakim Stark, a senior figure in the Belz Hasidic movement.
Shas
Shas chairman Arye Deri convened the Sephardic Haredi party’s Council of Torah Sages on Sunday to discuss the composition of its Knesset slate.
Several new names are expected to appear, including Yosef Elnatanov, a representative of Israel’s Bukharan Jewish community, and Lt. Col. (res.) Dror Amos, head of Haifa’s religious council, who left career military service about two years ago.
Some incumbent lawmakers have meanwhile been concerned that they could unexpectedly lose their places. Minister Yoav Ben-Tzur and former deputy minister Moshe Abutbul held discussions with several of the party’s rabbis to clarify their status amid concerns they could be dropped, though that now appears unlikely.
Joint List
The slate for the revived Joint List alliance of the predominantly Arab Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties has yet to be announced.
One candidate who will not be on it is Jaafar Farah, who had been designated for the No. 4 position but withdrew amid allegations of sexual harassment.
Hadash, Farah’s party, said members of its secretariat and central committee would choose his replacement Tuesday. The party appears likely to select a woman for the slot.
Religious Zionist Party
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, which has struggled in polls to cross the electoral threshold, had hoped to unite with former senior military officer Ofer Winter’s Amcha Israel party.
Winter’s party, however, closed the door on an alliance and submitted its slate Monday.
The Religious Zionist Party is instead hoping that a joint run with former lawmaker Moshe Feiglin’s Zehut party will strengthen both factions. The agreement is a technical electoral alliance only, with the parties planning to separate again after the election.
Under the agreement, Feiglin received the No. 2 spot on the joint slate, while Zehut was allocated three places in the top 10.
Blue and White
Another party polling below the electoral threshold is former defense minister Benny Gantz’s Blue and White.
Gantz failed in efforts to forge an alliance with former UN ambassador Gilad Erdan’s Unity party. Erdan has since announced that he is withdrawing from the election entirely.
Reports nevertheless continue of a possible alliance between Blue and White and former lawmaker Yoaz Hendel and his reservists’ movement.
The party has also undergone a last-minute personnel shake-up. Lawmaker Michael Biton informed Gantz that he was leaving the party. Just hours later, former Beit Shemesh Mayor Aliza Bloch announced that she was joining Blue and White.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- U.S. forces on Monday sank a vessel in the eastern Pacific that allegedly served as a floating refueling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations, the U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said.
"Intelligence confirmed the vessel's involvement with the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," SOUTHCOM said in a statement on X.
"Individuals removed from the vessel will be transferred to Ecuadorian authorities," the command said. "After clearing the vessel and disembarking the crew, U.S. forces sank it."
The command said the U.S. military continues to conduct "precise and professional operations to dismantle the logistical networks fueling narco-trafficking in the Western Hemisphere."
The operation was the latest in a series of U.S. maritime interdictions targeting vessels allegedly used as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking networks in the eastern Pacific. ■

Durban Conference, 25 years on. Paul Divakar Namala: “Solidarity and resistance work in the long run”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:31:00 UTC
09:31:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Paul Divakar Namala. I am the Executive Director of The Inclusivity Project and Convenor of the Global Forum of Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent. My work focuses on communities whose social status, occupations and exclusion are inherited across generations through caste, analogous hierarchies and systems rooted in traditional slavery.
I am a Dalit. Dalits were historically treated as “untouchable” and placed at the bottom of, or outside, the caste hierarchy. This can shape every part of life: access to a common water source, where a child sits at school, where a family may live, what work a person is expected to perform and whether others will eat with or even be seen with them. Poverty is widespread in South Asia, but its burden falls disproportionately on Dalits because caste restricts access to land, education, dignified employment, public services and political power.
Inherited hierarchies remain deeply entrenched
Across South Asia, constitutional guarantees and democratic institutions coexist with caste discrimination and practices of untouchability. These persist in villages and cities, and in public institutions, private workplaces and corporations. Dalits may face threats or violence for asserting land rights, entering places of worship, marrying across caste, accessing common resources, seeking education or standing for elected office.
Dalits in South Asia are not alone. Roma communities in Europe and beyond, Burakumin in Japan, Haratine and other communities affected by traditional slavery in the Sahel, Osu communities in Nigeria, Quilombola communities in Brazil and other communities in Latin America experience distinct histories and realities. They should not be collapsed into a single category. Yet many face structurally connected patterns: inherited stigma and social status, endogamy, segregation in housing and education, exclusion from land and decent work, confinement to dangerous or degrading occupations, trafficking and forced labour, and backlash violence when they resist. We describe these peoples, in all their diversity, as Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent, or CDWD.
Reconnecting with my identity
Where I grew up in India, my family faced repeated attacks as we asserted our rights, including rights over public land. When I was 21, a petrol-bomb attack took the life of my mother.
Only as I grew older did I understand how much of what happened to my family was connected to caste. My father taught me that our purpose should not be limited to seeking justice for ourselves; we had to dismantle the structures that allow such abuses to continue. That teaching guided me away from vengeance and towards challenging the social norms and caste structures that treat some human beings as inferior, exploit their vulnerability and assign them a life of servitude.
Together with my spouse, who came from a different caste, I helped build a community of human rights defenders. For too long, Dalits were portrayed only as victims or survivors. We are also organisers, advocates and defenders of human rights. This work began more than four decades ago, when I was in my twenties.
In 1998, together with leaders from across India, we formed the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights. We wanted caste-based discrimination and violence to be documented and discussed nationally and internationally. Looking back, I realise how groundbreaking that effort was, especially with so few resources.
Bringing caste to Durban
When we learned that the United Nations was organising a World Conference Against Racism, our immediate response was: “We have to be there.” We were new to these international processes. We contacted people working on caste discrimination and were invited to a preparatory meeting in Bellagio that helped shape the agenda for Durban.
At Bellagio, many participants supported putting caste on the agenda, including Pierre Sané, then Secretary General of Amnesty International. Civil society succeeded in making caste a major issue in the Durban process, but several Asian governments resisted its explicit inclusion in the final Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, arguing that it would target their countries or interfere in internal matters.
Although the final Declaration did not contain the explicit recognition we sought, what the movement achieved was extraordinary. Durban gave unprecedented international visibility to caste discrimination and helped move Dalit rights from the margins towards the centre of international human rights debate.
Dalit activists were present in large numbers, carrying documentation, testimonies, drums and protest across the conference grounds. People approached us and said, sometimes awkwardly but with genuine solidarity, “You are untouchable? Let me hug you.” Those encounters showed both how unfamiliar the issue was internationally and how quickly human connection could challenge the stigma imposed upon us.
Solidarity, resistance and the unfinished agenda
Over the years, we have connected with communities and advocates in Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya, Niger, Mauritania and Nigeria, with Roma movements across Europe and beyond, and with Quilombola and other communities in Latin America. Their histories are different, but their struggles reveal how inherited status, stigmatised work and exclusion can reinforce one another across generations. Working together makes these structures visible and prevents governments and institutions from excusing them in the name of culture or tradition.
Durban also taught us that affected communities must speak for themselves. They must not be treated merely as victims or sources of testimony, but as human rights defenders and leaders who define the problem and shape the solution. Solidarity does not require us to claim that every oppression is identical. It requires us to respect distinct histories while recognising common structures of dehumanisation and standing together against them.
Amnesty International can make an important contribution by adopting a clear global approach to discrimination based on work and descent; undertaking comparative research across regions; integrating CDWD into its work on racial justice, gender, labour rights, corporate accountability, climate justice and access to justice; and supporting defenders from affected communities to lead this agenda.
The fight is far from over. We are working for stronger international recognition, including comprehensive CERD guidance and, ultimately, a Declaration on the Rights of Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent. Yet the real test is always on the ground. International declarations have meaning only when they change the life of a woman confronting untouchability, a sanitation worker demanding safe and dignified work, a Roma child resisting school segregation, or a Haratine family seeking freedom, land and equality.
This story was originally published by IPS.

Russia’s three-day pause on strikes against Kyiv appeared to unravel before its own stated deadline Monday, as Russian drones were detected over the capital while US-led diplomatic efforts were still underway.
The temporary halt had been tied to visits by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv as Washington sought to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At 8:45 p.m. Monday, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a jet-powered Russian drone over Kyiv, while several others were reported approaching the capital – more than three hours before Moscow’s stated 11:59 p.m. deadline.
The attacks intensified overnight. A series of strong explosions rang out across Kyiv early Tuesday as Russia launched missile and drone strikes on the capital and surrounding region.
The blasts were heard by Kyiv Post reporters across the city at around 3:30 a.m., after authorities declared an air raid alert and warned of a missile attack.
Russian drones also struck the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of Kyiv region. Fires broke out at industrial facilities in Boryspil, seven trucks were destroyed, and a logistics complex was struck twice, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.
Questions over when pause ended
Russian state news agency TASS reported that the three-day suspension ordered by Russian President Vladimir Putin had expired.
However, its precise timing remained disputed. As Kyiv Post reported earlier Monday, Russian accounts said the halt began at midnight between Friday and Saturday, placing its expiration at 11:59 p.m. Monday.
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Kravchenko Resigns Over Corruption Accusations
Russian drone activity was reported well before that deadline. At 8:45 p.m. Monday, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a jet-powered drone over Kyiv, while several others were reported approaching the capital – suggesting Moscow breached even the timeline it had publicly set for the truce.
The pause was limited largely to strikes on Kyiv and Moscow rather than a broader ceasefire.
Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine continued throughout the weekend. On Saturday, explosions were heard near Boryspil during an air raid alert, while strikes in other regions killed and wounded civilians.
‘Better than Patriot’
Putin agreed to the temporary halt as Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend as part of Washington’s latest effort to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The brief pause came only after Kyiv and the surrounding region had endured more than eight consecutive days of Russian drone and missile attacks, repeatedly forcing residents into shelters and putting additional strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
The sudden quiet during the US envoys’ visit prompted Zelensky to joke about their effect on the capital’s security.
“Today, you worked even better than the Patriot systems for our citizens here in the capital,” Zelensky told Witkoff and Kushner, urging them to “come visit more often.”
Witkoff later said the meetings had produced progress and raised the prospect of renewed trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
But Russia’s failure to abide by even a brief three-day truce underscored a familiar reality for Ukrainians: even high-level diplomacy has failed to stop Moscow from bombarding innocent civilians in Ukrainian cities.

Iran conveys its ‘conditions’ to US – source
Iran has conveyed its conditions to the US through intermediaries after Washington recently sent new proposals to Tehran, a political source in the Iranian capital has told RT.
The reported contacts come amid renewed regional efforts to revive diplomacy after last week’s flare-up, when the US carried out several rounds of strikes on Iran and Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on American military facilities in Jordan and Bahrain.
“Following the halt of negotiations resulting from US breaches of commitments and its repeated failures in military engagements, the US has recently conveyed proposals to Tehran through mediators,” the source said.
Given Washington’s “repeated violations” and “constant fluctuations in its positions,” Tehran responded by conveying its own conditions to the intermediaries, the source added.
The source did not disclose the details of either the American proposals or the Iranian conditions, but said mediators “continue to talk to both parties.”
Tehran has been pushing Washington to honor the commitments outlined in the June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), but the US is now reportedly seeking a new, broader agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program, the Financial Times reported last week.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities were themselves the main obstacle to inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), arguing that Washington was responsible for the resulting lack of access while simultaneously using the issue to increase pressure on Tehran.
“The ball has long been in the US court,” Baqaei said, adding that Washington must end its military attacks, economic sanctions and naval blockade if it wants to resolve the confrontation.
“Diplomacy is a dynamic and continuous process,” the spokesman said, noting that delegations from Oman and Pakistan have visited Iran in recent weeks, while Qatari representatives held talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told CNN that Doha had put forward several ideas and was exploring different scenarios aimed at addressing the concerns of both sides.
Tehran and Muscat have meanwhile reported significant progress on a separate arrangement for a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials have stressed, however, that such an agreement would not amount to the full reopening of the strategic waterway, as Washington has claimed.

Palestinian resistance group Hamas has warned that Israel is attempting to conceal evidence of genocide committed against Palestinians in Gaza by removing, crushing, and transporting rubble under which the bodies of thousands of missing people remain trapped.
In an official statement, the group condemned "attempts by the occupation government and its army to conceal evidence of the brutal crimes committed against our people in Gaza through the removal, crushing and transportation of rubble."
It stressed that these actions are occurring despite the presence beneath the debris of "the bodies of thousands of missing people and material evidence of the crimes of genocide committed by the occupation over two years."
Hamas stated that tampering with sites containing human remains and potential legal evidence "constitutes a violation of international law and the International Court of Justice's order to preserve evidence," describing it as "an assault on the dignity of the martyrs and the right of their families to recover and bury the bodies of their loved ones."
Calls for international forensic teams
Hamas welcomed a warning issued by Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the Palestinian territories, who cautioned that Israeli debris clearance risks erasing traces of "atrocity crimes."
Calling upon the UN and the International Criminal Court to safeguard these sites, Hamas urged the dispatch of international forensic investigators into Gaza to oversee body recoveries and document forensic material.
While stressing that clearing rubble and rebuilding remains an "urgent humanitarian and national necessity," Hamas maintained the operation must ensure the recovery of missing persons without permitting Israel to evade accountability.
On August 3, the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor reported that commercial Israeli firms were involved in crushing and clearing debris across military-occupied zones covering roughly 66 percent of the enclave.
The monitor estimated that at least 10 million tonnes of rubble had been displaced or crushed, documenting approximately 100 trucks moving debris out of Gaza daily alongside 400 demolition and crushing machines.
Israel's two-year genocide has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, injured over 174,000, and left over 9,000 missing beneath devastated infrastructure.

Under pressure to explain super policy, Joyce says he is 'not Jesus Christ'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:07:01 UTC
09:07:01 KST

Barnaby Joyce pushes back on need to model impact of One Nation super policy
In short:
Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the economic and financial impact of One Nation's early access superannuation policy.
The policy would allow Australians to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
What's next?
Mr Joyce has pushed back on warnings the scheme would have an inflationary impact by pumping more money into the economy, which may worsen the cost-of-living crisis.
One Nation Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the impact of the party's proposed early superannuation access scheme, saying he is "not Jesus Christ" while being questioned about the policy's financial and economic consequences.
Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or have a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
The money would retain the favourable tax concession Australians already receive on super savings under the plan, which One Nation said would provide "breathing room" for people struggling with the cost of living.
On Tuesday, Mr Joyce sidestepped questions about modelling of the proposal after economists warned it could have an inflationary impact.
"The implications that I have to model you getting your own money, I find a little bit perverse. It is actually your money," he said.
He later said one reason One Nation had not modelled their policy was because Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had not awarded the minor party additional staff and resourcing.
When pushed on the loss of people's retirement savings over time, Mr Joyce insisted he was across the detail of the policy.
"I'm the Treasury spokesman, not Jesus Christ. I mean, you have to actually give me the details of these things, if you got to put them forward to me," he told 7.30 on Monday.
Australians 'not stupid', Joyce says
Mr Joyce argued the money in retirement savings was already circulating in the economy because it was being invested via superannuation companies, and therefore would not be inflationary.
Independent economist Saul Eslake said he found the comments "disturbing" because they showed a lack of understanding from Mr Joyce about how the economy works.
Mr Eslake said money that is invested in superannuation is used to buy shares, government bonds and investments in overseas markets, which means it is not circulating in the Australian economy and adding to demand for goods and services.
"If you instead take money out of superannuation so that there is less invested in financial and real investment assets, and instead it is sitting at least initially in a bank account, which history shows [people] are likely to withdraw to fund to use on additional spending, it will then go into the economy," he said.
He warned pumping more cash into the economy would put upward pressure on inflation, and said the Reserve Bank would likely be forced to increase interest rates.
Mr Joyce also said "anyone with a brain" would be able to effectively use the scheme, which would not be means tested.
"People are not stupid,"
"The presumption by the socialists is that everyone's a total moron and is going to take money from a good return and take it to a bad return if they don't need it.
"If there's extra money in the economy and you put it into your bank account and don't spend it, it has no inflationary aspect."
But Mr Eslake said people, especially those on lower incomes, historically did not save additional salary, but spent it.
"What evidence shows us from a wide range of studies over a long period of time is that people on lower incomes, and younger people, are more likely to spend any additional income they get compared to higher income people,"
Pandemic super withdrawals spent quickly
At the height of the COVID pandemic, many Australians found themselves with less work and struggling to make ends meet.
Because of that, some people jumped at the opportunity presented by the Morrison government to access their super savings early.
In total, 2.6 million Australians withdraw money from their retirement nest egg, which was capped at $20,000.
A study written by economist Steven Hamilton, who now works for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, found a significant portion of the $38 billion accessed by people was spent quickly.
Nearly half the money was spent within eight weeks of it landing in personal accounts, and spending increased by an average of 130 per cent in the first two weeks.
The largest spending category was ATM withdrawals, and the second largest category was gambling expenditure.
Researchers found that overwhelmingly, people who withdrew from their super were not experiencing a reduction in their wage relative to before the pandemic.
The federal opposition's housing spokesman, Andrew Bragg, said the Coalition was looking at ways people could use their superannuation to afford a home.
Senator Bragg said the Coalition was reviewing policy ideas, including letting people use their super to offset their mortgage or as collateral for a loan.
A party spokesperson later denied the options were being considered.
The ideas have previously been discussed as part of Senate committee work Senator Bragg chaired in 2024.
ABC accused of 'socialist' agenda
One Nation announced its policy on Monday, and Mr Joyce has since accused the ABC of being "socialists", pointing to a line of questioning in a number of interviews about the modelling of the proposal.
"I understand the ABC socialist position, that it's not really your money, it's somebody else's money. Therefore, you have to go through a bureaucracy before you get entitled to get your own money," he told ABC Radio Breakfast.
He said it was a "philosophical view" that distorted the reality of the inflationary impacts of the proposal.
"This money is your money," he said.

Durban Conference 25 years on. Adnan Barq: “The very fact of existing is a fight in itself”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:00 UTC
09:01:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Adnan Barq. I’m 25 and I’m a Palestinian from the Old City of Jerusalem. I’m a journalist and also make films.
The Durban Conference was happening when I was one year old. It’s fascinating to see how many people got together back then to try and shape justice in the world but, without being too pessimistic, I see that things are getting worse. This is happening everywhere, not just in Palestine.
Refusing to normalize injustice
I got involved in activism when I was at university, out of a refusal to normalize the occupation. I see how my people survive by being forced to normalize Israeli practices of injustice, apartheid, and colonialism but I just could not do that.
I studied in Bethlehem University, so I always had to cross a checkpoint back and forth to Jerusalem. That was my biggest exposure to the Israeli occupation’s physical system of oppression, even though I also experienced it as a child, when Israeli settlers wanted to take over the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
 
As an adult, I realized that being able to speak English was a privilege and a tool, so I had a responsibility to send a message to the world about Palestine, to expose the occupation. That was in 2020. 
Apartheid, racial profiling and otherness
Israel’s apartheid is sophisticated. The Israeli soldiers on the walls of Jerusalem are trained to racially profile people. Whenever they see a Palestinian, you are dragged from the street out of hundreds of white settlers, and you are taken to the wall and you get fully body inspected while your ID says that your house is in that specific street. 
 
I think the Israeli occupation forces are aiming to create a coercive environment that makes us want to leave because they cannot easily uproot us. But all these practices make us embrace ourselves even more. They reject our existence and this makes us scream louder. 
Systemic racism and resistance
I wish that it was only the government that was the problem so we could fight for change. But the genocide, the call to erase Palestinians is now fully embedded in public discourse.   
 
This is what systemic racism is. It’s coming from everywhere. 
Just the fact of existing is a fight in itself. Me walking from my house to a school, me walking from my house to a café with friends, is in fact resisting the occupation by existing.
I don’t want to accept this but I also don’t want to spend all my life fighting. It’s exhausting.
The power of social media
As Palestinians, we are destined to be like lawyers for our cause.  
 
I felt the need to just show the world how my people are living and social media was a good tool for that. The fact that our cause is universal. The people who are harassing my friends are from Florida, from Norway, London, Germany. The ones who stop me at checkpoints are like some random Spanish Jewish people who just live in Israel.
When the violence escalated in 2021, I had to fully engage in activism. I had the opportunity to travel to Belgium and to other countries and met many parliamentarians to explain what we are going through.
 
I try to keep what I show as real as I can, showing what we are suffering but also that I have a full life. I have family, friends and I also go to parties, we study, we enjoy basic activities and at the same time can talk about why and how we are resisting the occupation. Showing that there are many sides to our lives as Palestinians is very important to me and it is part of the fight.  
Not the end game
It’s difficult to understand the pain that otherness and racial profiling causes unless you experience it. The best thing we can do is unite and keep calling out all these systems that are built to victimize us. We need to organize, meet, plan and seek solutions and not rely on empty slogans that are only good for a sticker. We need more than that.
In this era, we are privileged to have access to each other digitally, but this kind of connection is not enough, we need to turn it into something real. Social media is an important tool, but not the end game.
This story was originally published in ElDiario.es

In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style

In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style
Marina Square’s future revamp typifies the rise of mixed-use developments incorporating retail, office, residential and other components
Last Monday, property developer Singapore Land Group (SingLand) said in a statement that Marina Square, which was completed in 1986, would close on March 31 for a redevelopment that would include features such as luxury residences, serviced apartments and offices with a gross floor area of more than 360,000 sq m.
The revamp, slated for completion in 2031, will have a 304-key hotel that will place guests close to the Marina Bay area, and Marina Square will be refreshed into a four-storey shopping centre offering a wider variety of food and drink options and pet-friendly environments, according to SingLand.
Three new towers will be integrated into the site, including a 49-storey residential tower hosting 204 luxury homes, while offices will occupy eight floors of a new mixed-use tower, providing around 13,000 sq m of lettable space.
Local media reported that the news of Marina Square’s closure came with disappointment from shoppers and tenants alike. Parents lamented the loss of the shopping centre known for its indoor playgrounds and children’s retail outlets, while tenants said they were shocked by the short notice.
Retail experts point out that consumers today are increasingly seeking experiences, community and connection, and this shift is fuelling the growth of mixed-use developments around the world.

Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong, sparking property demand in education sector

Hong Kong’s bid to become a global education hub is likely to transform the sector as a sustainable source of property demand, with the city tipped to see around 200,000 non-local students by 2035, according to CBRE.
The city’s international schools are estimated to require enormous additional real estate to accommodate nearly 30,000 to 40,000 non-local students, as the institutions would need to set up 40 to 50 new school campuses.
This could mean up to an extra 1.11 million square metres (12 million square feet) of gross floor area, a study released by the consultancy on Monday showed.
Moreover, the student accommodation segment would also need more than 70,000 additional beds to provide living space for these students in about a decade.
“Hong Kong’s education sector is undergoing a structural transformation,” said Marcos Chan, executive director and head of research at CBRE Hong Kong.

Iran Threatens to Target U.S. Energy Assets in Gulf If U.S. Strikes Again

Unknown Publisher

09:00:00 KST

Iran warned on Monday that it could target U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf if the U.S. launches any new attacks on its assets.
Responding to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s warning that “if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said: “It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed. American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure.”
“Strike our assets and you get struck,” he added. “We’ve already proven it.”
Ghalibaf’s warning comes as Tehran seeks greater leverage amid Washington’s ongoing economic pressure campaign and stalled efforts to negotiate an end to the war that the U.S. and Israel launched on Feb. 28.
Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, told Iranian state TV on Sunday that Tehran has concluded “new strategies must be adopted in the war, in negotiations, and in confronting the blockade.” Among the measures planned is a new “exclusion zone” in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. The zone would begin at the blockade line, extend through the Strait of Hormuz, and continue into the Persian Gulf, Rezaei said. Vessels entering the zone to transit the Strait would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list.
The latest flare-up began Saturday, when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked U.S. warships in the region. The U.S. responded by striking three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub. The U.S. and Iran have for the past week exchanged a flurry of attacks, ending a brief respite in active hostilities. Oil prices reached near six-week highs on Monday as commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments flowed before the war, has fallen sharply.
Negotiations remain at a standstill
Diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran have stalled. The two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on June 17, agreeing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and engage in technical talks to end the war. But the truce was short-lived.
After a commercial vessel was struck in the Strait in late June, the U.S. attacked Iranian missile storage and radar sites, prompting Iran to retaliate against U.S. military installations in the region. Intermittent attacks continued in July, and fighting resumed in late August after a brief, informal pause.
The Trump Administration has said it is investigating a U.S. strike last week on a family compound in southern Iran where a wedding celebration was underway, killing at least five people and wounding more than 60, according to Iranian state media.
No new formal negotiations have been announced since the MOU’s 60-day deadline expired on Aug. 17. Although some of Iran’s top officials, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, have signaled a willingness to return to the MOU and resume talks with the U.S., the two countries’ positions remain far apart. The U.S. wants to significantly restrict or dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and guarantee unrestricted commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has called for broad sanctions relief, access to frozen assets, an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, and a role in managing the Strait.
Hard-liners in Iran have shown little appetite for compromise on those red lines, and analysts previously told TIME that Iranian leaders may believe time is on their side, with Tehran prepared to absorb further economic and military pressure in hopes that rising energy prices will eventually prove too politically costly to U.S. President Donald Trump.
“The Iranian nation accepts neither threats nor coercion, nor negotiations whose outcome would be the weakening of the country’s rights,” Hossein Taeb, head of the IRGC’s Basij paramilitary force, said on Monday. “Negotiations are for securing the nation’s rights, not surrendering them.”
While Trump faces domestic pressure to rein in gas prices and avoid an open-ended war in the Middle East ahead of the November midterms, he has also appeared determined to secure an outcome he can present as a victory.
“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump posted on Truth Social last week. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable.”
Iran considers new tactics
Iran is planning to establish a new restricted zone to amp up global economic pressure and force an end to the U.S. blockade. At the same time, Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and are in talks on its future administration—an arrangement that could formalize Tehran’s role in managing the waterway against U.S. opposition.
But Ghalibaf acknowledged in parliament on Sunday that Iran is struggling with sharp inflation, a collapsing rial, and high unemployment.
Washington’s economic pressure campaign, which includes the naval blockade, sanctions on Iran, and the threat of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners, has squeezed Tehran. The International Monetary Fund estimates that inflation in Iran is near 70%.
The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran began restricting at the start of the war, has been the country’s most important bargaining chip. But that leverage may be weakening as Gulf states turn to routes that bypass the Strait and the U.S. escorts shipments through the corridor. The conflict has also inflicted mounting costs on Iran’s own economy by trapping tens of millions of barrels of Iranian crude inside the Gulf.

Yang Shuyu added 15 points, five rebounds and four assists in a team-high 33 minutes, while Wang Siyu contributed five points, five rebounds, six assists and two steals.
Matilde Villa led Italy with 15 points on six-of-11 shooting. China led for 39 minutes and 39 seconds, while Han posted a game-high efficiency rating of 24 in just over 30 minutes on court.
China completed the group phase with two wins from three games. Third-placed Italy will meet Australia on Wednesday, and the winner will face Spain in the quarterfinals. ■

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing seven in Yemen prison attack

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing seven in Yemen prison air strike
Houthi media outlet released footage of destruction and rescue efforts after the Saudi air strike on al-Hazm prison.
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in the northern city of al-Hazm, killing seven people, including a child.
The strike on the Central Corrective Facility in al-Jawf province, on the Yemeni side of the border with Saudi Arabia, also wounded at least seven people, including a woman, Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, said on Monday.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV channel aired footage it said showed the aftermath of the alleged attack, including a collapsed building and people searching through the rubble.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the allegations.
Al Masirah TV also released footage it claims shows Houthi forces using ballistic missiles to attack Saudi supply trucks containing military equipment at a border crossing in Yemen’s Hadramout province.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of “committing massacres” in al-Jawf, flying reconnaissance drones and supplying mercenaries with weaponry.
“The ongoing Saudi aggression against Yemen will not go unpunished, and the Saudi enemy must bear the consequences of its crimes against the Yemeni people,” he said.
Saree also claimed that the Houthis had shot down four Saudi reconnaissance drones over the previous 24 hours, including a CH-4 drone that he said was carrying out “hostile missions” in al-Jawf.
“This aircraft is the second of this type that was shot down during the past 12 hours, and the fourth during the past 24 hours,” he added.
Dually, Riyadh has not commented on Saree’s allegations.
The Houthi claims come as fighting between the group and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has flared up in recent weeks. The Yemeni government said it made significant territorial gains against the Houthis, including in the al-Jawf, Bayda, Dahle, and Marib provinces on Sunday.
Over the past days, government-aligned forces conducted counterattacks in Taiz and Hodeidah after the Houthis launched a major offensive in a struggle to control the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait, with hundreds of people reportedly killed over the past 24 hours.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called Monday on the country’s warring parties to halt hostilities and exercise maximum restraint, warning that the latest escalation could spiral into a full-scale war.
Air strikes on prisons have occurred several times during Yemen’s decade-long war. In 2022, the Saudi-led coalition struck a detention facility in Saada province, killing at least 87 prisoners and wounding about 266 others.
In 2019, the coalition struck a Houthi-run detention facility in Dhamar province, killing more than 100 people and wounding dozens.

====================================================================================================

Eiffel Tower shut by staff protest after female workers moved for religious visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:46:44 BST
08:46:44 KST

Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
- Published
An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group.
A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday.
"Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage.
BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.
Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate".
Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable".
An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again".
In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".
"Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said.
Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women".
BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in a Parisian suburb.
In a statement on X, BAPS said the trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".
It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation.
BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.
Politicians in France have condemned Saturday's incident.
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."
French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."
Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

What is celebrated on September 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:45:42 EEST
08:45:42 KST

What is celebrated on September 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 8, the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, Literacy Day, Physical Therapy Day, and the International Day of Journalists’ Solidarity are observed. State holidays are also celebrated.
On September 8, one of the greatest Christian holidays — the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary according to the new church calendar, International Literacy Day under the auspices of UNESCO, World Physical Therapy Day and International Journalists’ Solidarity Day — are observed, UNN writes.
International Literacy Day
An official date under the auspices of UNESCO, established at the 14th session of the General Conference in 1966 on the recommendation of the World Conference of Ministers of Education on the Eradication of Illiteracy. The day is intended to remind the global community that literacy is a fundamental human right, the basis for personal development and a key tool for building resilient societies.
Despite global progress, hundreds of millions of adults worldwide still lack basic reading and writing skills, which is why UNESCO dedicates this day each year to a specific theme — from the digitalization of education to expanding the rights and opportunities of linguistic minorities.
World Physical Therapy Day
A professional holiday established in 1996 by the World Confederation for Physical Therapy (World Physiotherapy) to highlight the important contribution of rehabilitation specialists and physiotherapists to restoring people’s health, mobility and quality of life.
This date symbolizes the solidarity of physical rehabilitation specialists around the world and draws public attention to the importance of the comprehensive adaptation of patients after serious injuries, surgeries and strokes, as well as wounded military personnel.
International Journalists’ Solidarity Day
A commemorative date established in 1958 at the 4th Congress of the International Organization of Journalists in Bucharest in memory of Czech journalist, writer and anti-fascist Julius Fučík, who was executed on September 8, 1943, in Berlin’s Plötzensee prison.
On this day, media workers and human rights organizations around the world express support for colleagues who face persecution, censorship and arrest for their professional activities, and also honor the memory of journalists who died while performing their professional duties in hot spots.
Independence Day of North Macedonia
The country’s main state holiday commemorating the referendum of September 8, 1991, during which more than 95% of citizens voted to leave Yugoslavia and establish a sovereign state.
The day is an official public holiday and is marked by a ceremonial flag-raising, speeches by the country’s leadership, award ceremonies for prominent figures and mass festivities.
Victory Day in Malta (Il-Vitorja)
A national holiday that commemorates three important historical events at once: the end of the Great Siege of Malta by Ottoman forces in 1565, the capitulation of Napoleon’s French garrison in 1800, and the lifting of the naval blockade and Italy’s capitulation in World War II in 1943.
The celebrations include a traditional sailing regatta in Valletta’s Grand Harbour, religious processions and ceremonial wreath-laying.
National Day of Andorra (Our Lady of Meritxell Day)
The principality’s main state and religious holiday, dedicated to the country’s patroness — Our Lady of Meritxell.
The tradition of honoring her dates back to the signing of the Act of the Pareage in 1278, which established joint rule over Andorra, and on September 8, a solemn Mass is held at the Meritxell Sanctuary, along with nationwide cultural festivals.
Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
According to the new calendar, the Orthodox and Greek Catholic churches celebrate the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary — the first of the twelve most important feasts of the new liturgical year. The feast was established in honor of the birth of the Virgin Mary to the righteous Joachim and Anne in Jerusalem, which, according to tradition, came as an answer to their sincere prayers after many years of childlessness.
In folk tradition, the Lesser Feast of the Blessed Virgin was considered a harvest festival, a women’s day and a time to give thanks for the harvested grain, marking the beginning of the wedding season.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy martyrs Adrian and Natalia, who suffered for the Christian faith at the beginning of the fourth century in Nicomedia during the reign of Emperor Maximian. Adrian was a pagan official who, struck by the steadfastness of Christians during their torture, himself came to believe and was executed, while his secretly Christian wife, Natalia, supported her husband until the final moments of his life.
People called this day "Natalia the Oat Woman," as it was then that the mass harvesting and threshing of oats began.

OpenAI top scientist urges ‘extreme caution’ with pace of AI

OpenAI top scientist urges ‘extreme caution’ with pace of AI
- OpenAI's chief scientist warns AI is evolving too fast, urging voluntary slowdowns to ensure safety and better human control.
- AI models now perform complex tasks and soon may self-improve without humans, raising serious concerns about consequences.
- Despite risks, companies and startups invest heavily in advanced AI, including recursive self-improvement, aiming for more human-like intelligence.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI’s top scientist has warned that artificial intelligence is evolving so rapidly that it is becoming increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control, saying he expects AI labs to voluntarily slow development for safety reasons.
In a relatively short space of time, AI models can operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems and carry out research projects, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote in a post on Sept 6.
It will not be long before they can also improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as recursive self-improvement, he said.
“This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” Pachocki wrote in the post.
“I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.”
Developers can either try to steer AI more closely to align with human interests or “slow down future development as needed”, he wrote.
“I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”
Pachocki’s remarks are consistent with broader doomsaying by AI technology executives.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that AI could replace half of all entry-level jobs.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once made a similar prediction but told Bloomberg TV in an interview last week that the AI industry had not done enough to communicate the potential benefits to humanity.
At the same time, companies are pushing ahead with ever-more capable models.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on social media platform X that “AGI (artificial general intelligence) has arrived”, in response to the release of OpenAI’s latest model, a reference to AI that is more capable than humans.
The giddy pace of AI releases has coincided with breakthroughs in cybersecurity capabilities, scientific discoveries and apparent formalisation of longstanding mathematical problems.
OpenAI has said the AI models that attacked the research platform Hugging Face coordinated with each other through message boards without being detected.
The company has opted for a limited release of its latest GPT-6 Astra model, citing its advanced cybersecurity capabilities.
Anthropic has not yet released its cutting-edge Mythos model to the public for similar reasons.
A growing number of start-ups are trying to bring about the very thing Pachocki warns about – self-improving AI.
Investors are flooding into recursive self-improvement, betting that this is the route to AI that is truly human-like, or more impressive.
Inherent, founded by former DeepMind researchers, raised US$50 million (S$63.2 million) earlier in 2026.
Recursive Superintelligence, an AI lab founded by renowned scientist Richard Socher pursuing similar research, also landed US$650 million in financing.
Pachocki’s employer, OpenAI, has said it wants to build a “true automated AI researcher” in less than two years. BLOOMBERG

Qatar calls for phased de-escalation for sustainable solution to Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:41:06 UTC
08:41:06 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Qatar is seeking to “phase this crisis out” rather than pursue an immediate end to the US-Iran war, with the broader goal of creating the conditions for comprehensive regional dialogue and a sustainable political solution, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said Monday.
Speaking to CNN, Al-Ansari said Doha believes the current crisis cannot simply be frozen, warning that a temporary halt in hostilities could pave the way for another escalation.
“We have to phase this crisis out rather than end it immediately,” he said. “What we need to do is make sure the playing field is in a place where we can have the right negotiations for a sustainable solution.”
He said Qatar does not want the region to move from one period of intense conflict to another, stressing that any resolution must address the underlying regional issues.
“We do not want to go from a high-intensity conflict to a high-intensity conflict. We don't want to freeze this conflict and be back here a couple of months later,” he said.
Al-Ansari said Qatar’s immediate priorities are to ease economic pressure and prevent further military escalation across the region, including attacks affecting Gulf states and Iran.
“Right now, what we are doing, we have two main priorities. One is make sure that the Strait (of Hormuz) is open and that the economic pressure on all of us collectively and the peoples in the region, including the people of Iran, has left us.”
The second priority, he said, is preventing further military escalation so that regional actors can eventually push for an inclusive dialogue.
“When we get to that point, this is the point we need to have a regional push, all of us collectively, to make sure that dialogue happens and it is a comprehensive dialogue that includes all of us, not just outside.”
Al-Ansari said political will and technical issues remain the two main obstacles to reaching a settlement, adding that Qatar is developing proposals aimed at addressing both.
He also argued that sanctions have failed to deliver the expected diplomatic results, saying the conflict ultimately can only be resolved through negotiations.
“But at the end, this issue will only be resolved through a deal. It will only be resolved at the negotiation table.”
He also warned against allowing the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz to become normalized, saying the consequences could extend beyond the region through energy, food and economic shocks.
“We need to kill this in its infancy. It cannot become the new normal in war for countries to basically just close waterways in this way.”
He called for accountability and international law to prevail, warning that normalization of such tactics could have consequences far beyond the current conflict.

08:41:03 KST

An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.
Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family’s suburban Chicago home last Tuesday, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.
Prosecutors said Walsh had become “very invested” in Clancy’s nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12.30pm. that day. A neighbor found Barrett less than four hours later.
Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the “devil” and the “antichrist”. Her attorney, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy’s death a tragedy for the entire family.
Police were called to Walsh’s home in Frankfort, about 35 miles south-west of Chicago, shortly before 4pm after a neighbor discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors’ petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.
The neighbor found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.
Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.
The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy’s trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.
Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy’s trial played a role in the killing of Walsh’s son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.
Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will county did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.

ISW assesses Putin's new deadline: At current pace, Russian forces would not capture Donetsk region until 2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:41:00 KST

ISW assesses Putin's new deadline: At current pace, Russian forces would not capture Donetsk region until 2032
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said this in a new assessment, according to Ukrinform.
According to the report, Putin has set no fewer than 15 reported deadlines for the seizure of the Donetsk region since February 2022, and Russian forces have failed to meet every one. Russian forces will not meet Putin's new deadline of seizing all of the Donetsk region by December 31, 2026. Russian forces have been fighting for Kostiantynivka since October 2025 and have not seized it in 11 months. Russian forces have not reached, much less entered or seized, the other Fortress Belt cities of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka, and will not be able to seize all three within the remaining four months of 2026, considering that they have failed to complete the seizure of even one in nearly a year.
"Putin's many deadlines to seize all of Donbas reflect in part his need to provide a significant informational victory to the Russian people. Putin has promised Russians victory in exchange for enduring the burdens of war without bringing Russian society to a full wartime footing," the report said.
According to analysts, Russian forces will not seize the Donetsk region until 2032 at their current rate of advance – if they can seize it at all.
The Russian rate of advance across the theater was 2.91 square kilometers per day in August 2026, a slight increase compared to recent months. The average Russian rate of advance for Russian forces' priority effort in the Donetsk region was lower at only 2.36 square kilometers per day in August. Russian forces would take until October 2, 2032, to seize the remaining 19 percent of the Donetsk region at this rate – over a year after the next State Duma elections, which will likely be held in September 2031.
At the same time, ISW is not prepared to assess that Russian forces will be able to take the rest of the Donetsk region on any timeline, however. Russian forces will have to fight attritional urban battles through the cities of Ukraine's Fortress Belt before attempting to advance across fields – terrain that Russian forces have historically struggled to advance through.
"The Russian rate of advance has slowed significantly across the theater since 2025, when Russia's rate of advance had already begun to slow. Ukraine has proven that it can contest the tactical initiative in several areas of the frontline and hinder Russian logistics in 2026, and Russia has struggled to counter these Ukrainian efforts. Neither the trajectory nor any likely dynamics of the current conflict suggest that Russian forces will be able soon to accelerate their rate of advance dramatically as long as Western support for Ukraine continues at roughly current levels," the analysts wrote.
They attributed Putin's ambitions to capture the Donbas to the fact that the Russian military systematically misinforms him about the state of the front line in part due to the pervasive culture of lying within the Russian armed forces that milbloggers refer to as "beautiful reports." Russian high-ranking military commanders also routinely present exaggerated Russian advances as part of Russia's systematic cognitive warfare effort to portray Russian forces as making sweeping advances and Ukrainian defenses as collapsing. The lies and distortions of Russian military commanders at many levels are likely leading Putin to harden his perception that Russian forces can achieve his intended objectives in Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026 and thus that he need not make any compromises in his aims.
The analysts added that Putin is doubling down on the fictional battlefield situation that he defines as "reality" and insisting that his misrepresentation of the actual state of the war become the basis for any peace negotiations on Ukraine. In particular, on September 6, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said that Putin provided a comprehensive assessment to Witkoff and Kushner of Russian "significant advances" along the frontline – an exaggerated claim that does not match realities on the ground.

"My feeling (is) that Putin needs Trump," he said. "He doesn't want ... to upset him."

"It's not only about missiles," he said. "It's also about LNG (liquefied natural gas) ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation."

"We have this September, October to find any way to speak," he said. "Without dialogue … we will not have (a) result."
"I think that President Trump can find a way to (a) real beginning of the process of negotiating before (the) cold winter," he added.

In a statement, it warned of “attempts by the occupation government and its army to conceal evidence of the brutal crimes committed against our people in the Gaza Strip through the removal, crushing and transportation of rubble.”

100 Palestinian students expelled from Israeli universities for criticizing Gaza war: Rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Serdar Dincel
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Israeli universities have permanently or temporarily expelled 100 Palestinian students for criticizing Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip since October 2023, according to a Palestinian-run rights group based in Israel.
A report by Adalah examined changes in how Israeli higher education institutions have treated Palestinian students since the Gaza war began.
It documented cases in which Israeli universities suspended Palestinian students and launched disciplinary proceedings against them, classifying some of their social media posts as “support for terrorism.”
“In more than 80 cases, institutions imposed temporary suspensions before holding any hearing and before even determining whether the alleged violation had occurred,” it said.
“In 20 cases, students were permanently expelled or suspended from their studies for periods ranging from one to five years."
Adalah said the disciplinary measures targeted a wide range of forms of expression, including criticism of government and military policies and the war on Gaza as well as expressions of solidarity with Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
"Simply liking a post, displaying the Palestinian flag or the word Palestine on a personal account, sharing a news report, or praying for the people of Gaza” was enough to prompt a complaint or disciplinary proceedings in some cases, it added.
The group said students were summoned “to appear before disciplinary committees without being informed of the subject of the complaint,” adding that “in other cases, institutions did not verify when the content had been posted or whether the social media account belonged to the accused student.”
Adalah said that institutions “expanded the scope of their disciplinary powers beyond their legal limits, specifically against Palestinian students.”
By contrast, it said, “institutions in many cases maintained the limits of their authority when dealing with Jewish students and refrained from intervening in expressions unrelated to academic matters, even in the face of calls for the extermination of the Palestinian people and racist and inciting posts.”
The report warned that Israeli academic institutions have adopted a “two-track apartheid system” since Oct. 7, 2023, with Palestinian students facing emergency-based disciplinary measures while Jewish students enjoy greater protections for freedom of expression.
It said the policy "creates an atmosphere of intimidation among Palestinian students" and violates international law principles prohibiting racial discrimination and protecting minority rights.
Arab citizens make up roughly 21% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Since the war on Gaza began, Israel has imposed tight restrictions on social media posts and arrested activists who expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
Since October 2023, Israel, with US support, has been committing genocide in Gaza, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians and injuring over 174,000 others while destroying 90% of the infrastructure.

“In the face of the great rift that opened on Oct 7, and in the face of the immense challenges before the State of Israel, I believe we need a leadership that knows how to rise to the magnitude of the hour, that knows how to unite and bring unity around what we share, and to fundamentally restore the principles of stateliness and Zionism,” Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot also touched on other hot-button issue in the upcoming election, such as the exemptions and benefits granted to ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.
“Will we go on for more years under a government that promotes evasion of duty without shame? A government that hands out billions of shekels to those who neither serve nor work?” he said.
According to a poll by Israel’s public broadcaster Kan published on Sept 6, Yashar is expected to win 23 Knesset seats out of 120, slightly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud at 20.
The anti-Netanyahu bloc is projected to win 51 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud and its coalition partners are polling at 52 in total.
That means that neither bloc would have the 61-seat majority needed to govern, unless it secures support from unaligned parties, including two Arab-majority lists that together account for 13 seats.
Eisenkot appeared confident that his party would be able to draw away votes from Likud, the historic political home of the Israeli right.
“I meet many people who have been voting for the same party for decades. They tell me how hard it is to vote differently,” he said. “I reply: just as you trust me, I trust you to make the courageous and right choice for Israel.” AFP

Von der Leyen touts $200 mn on Greenland PR junket
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said Greenland’s future is for its people and Denmark to decide, pushing back against US President Donald Trump’s threat to annex the Arctic island.
Greenland is an autonomous Danish territory rich in minerals and strategically located close to North America. Denmark, which oversees the island’s foreign and security policy, is a member of both the EU and NATO. Trump has repeatedly argued that the US needs Greenland for national security and its mineral resources, putting Washington at odds with its European allies.
“Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide, no one else,” von der Leyen said in the island’s capital, Nuuk, on Monday, concluding a two-day visit. She cited territorial integrity, sovereignty and the inviolability of borders as fundamental principles of international law.
The EU chief also announced €200 million ($232 million) in investment for this year and next as Brussels seeks to deepen its presence on the island. The package covers areas including internet connectivity, hydropower and critical raw materials.
Greenland’s mineral wealth is of particular interest to the EU. The island holds 25 of the 34 raw materials Brussels classifies as critical, and closer access could help the bloc reduce its dependence on China.
Von der Leyen’s trip came as Trump posted a map on Monday depicting Greenland, Canada and other parts of the Americas under the US flag. The image also included Iceland and was labeled ‘United States of America.’
Washington’s push for control of Greenland has strained relations with Denmark and other European allies. White House officials said earlier this year that military force remained “always an option,” raising the prospect of a confrontation between the two NATO members. Trump has also repeatedly questioned the alliance’s value to the US.
The visit also coincided with the start of Arctic Shield, military drills involving 11 NATO countries and around 400 troops in Greenland. No US personnel are taking part in the exercises, which run from September 7 to 18.
