Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:32:21 UTC
07:32:21 KST

Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Power has been restored to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) after more than two weeks in emergency mode, the CEO of the Russian state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has said.
The main external power line to the plant was cut off in March following what the Ukrainian authorities described as “damage” to transmission towers. It has never been restored, with no explanations from Kiev.
Since then, the ZNPP has had to rely solely on the backup line – until August 20, when it was shut down by automatic control systems following an unspecified “incident” in territory controlled by Ukraine. That forced the power plant to fall back on emergency diesel-powered generators.
On Monday, Likhachev told journalists that the external power supply to the ZNPP had finally been restored, and the facility was now “operating as normal.” The Rosatom chief thanked all the parties involved in establishing a temporary local truce needed for the repair work, including the Russian defense and foreign ministries. He also praised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its “mediation efforts.”
The ZNPP operator also confirmed that external power had been restored. No violations of safety limits were reported, and the radiation situation at the plant and in the surrounding area remained stable and did not exceed natural background levels, it said in a statement. The operator added that the second power supply line has yet to be restored and regular fuel supplies to the station need to be facilitated.
Diesel fuel deliveries to the station were “problematic” because of Ukrainian shelling targeting the roads in the area, ZNPP communications director Evgenia Yashina told Interfax earlier.
Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and the adjacent city of Energodar have been targeted by Ukraine on multiple occasions with artillery and drones since Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In July, a Ukrainian drone hit a ZNPP service vehicle on the edge of the plant’s industrial site, killing its chief engineer, Aleksandr Yakovlev, and his driver. At the time, Likhachev called the strike a “deliberate terrorist act.”
According to the Rosatom CEO, more than a dozen employees of the plant have been killed and many others wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the past three months. Kiev’s actions pose the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting parts of Russia, Ukraine, and the EU, he warned.
Several months ago, the Ukrainian military also started remotely mining the area near the ZNPP and Energodar, where plant employees reside, according to the nuclear chief. In early August, four ZNPP employees were injured by Ukrainian landmines dropped by drones.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the IAEA, which has experts deployed at the ZNPP, for acknowledging the attacks on the facility but stopping short of blaming Ukraine for them.

Israel sees 58% drop in returning citizens amid rising emigration: Knesset panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:27:30 UTC
07:27:30 KST

The number of Israelis returning to the country fell by 58% in 2025 compared with 2009, an Israeli parliamentary committee revealed Monday, amid estimates that nearly 1 million Israelis are living abroad.
The figures were presented during a meeting of the Knesset’s Committee for Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs convened to examine the growing emigration of Israelis, according to the parliament’s official website.
Data from the Knesset Research and Information Center showed that 4,483 Israelis returned to the country in 2025, down from 10,903 in 2009.
Between 2005 and 2024, approximately 141,000 Israelis returned after living abroad, an annual average of roughly 7,000, the center said.
Estimates presented to the committee indicated that around 1 million Israelis currently live outside the country.
- Where are Israelis returning from?
According to the center’s analysis, 45% of returning Israelis came from the US, followed by 6% from the UK, 5% from Canada and 4% from France.
Germany, Russia, Romania and Ukraine each accounted for 3% of returnees, while Australia, Italy and Moldova each accounted for 2%.
More than a quarter of those returning were minors, while 47% were aged between 28 and 60.
Around 70% returned after living abroad for at least five years, the data showed.
- Government accused of inaction
Gilad Kariv, chairman of the Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs Committee, accused the Israeli government of failing to take steps to encourage Israelis living abroad to return.
“Since our last discussion on this issue, additional data have been published indicating a decline in the number of Israelis returning to Israel,” Kariv said.
He said the committee had called on the government to formulate a five-year plan aimed at bringing Israelis living abroad back to the country.
A similar plan was introduced in 2010 but has not been renewed since, he added.
“We presented a wide range of measures that could be taken to encourage Israelis to return to their homeland, but unfortunately, the government chose to ignore our recommendations,” Kariv said.
He added that the government had also failed to establish a roundtable to examine ways to encourage Israelis to return.
“There is no body in Israel responsible for addressing emigration,” he said, accusing the government of refusing to take responsibility for the issue.
The meeting also highlighted a growing exodus of medical professionals.
“We are seeing an increase in the number of doctors leaving Israel and a decline in the number of those choosing to return,” said Itai Ater, a professor at Tel Aviv University.
Highly experienced senior doctors account for around 20% of those leaving, he said, noting that other countries offer incentives to attract medical professionals.
The Israeli daily Haaretz reported Sunday on a study by Tel Aviv University showing that at least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025.
One in five doctors who left during the period was over the age of 45, a trend the study described as “worrying.”
A previous report by the Israeli Finance Ministry found that around 24% of specialist doctors at public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Nearly 25% of doctors currently working have already passed retirement age but remain in their positions because of staff shortages, according to the report.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in early August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country for at least three months between 2023 and 2025, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have attributed the rising emigration to the repercussions of the Gaza war, soaring living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken the judiciary.
A Kantar poll conducted for KAN and published on Aug. 9 found that nearly one-fifth of Israelis had considered emigrating during the previous two years.
Around 12% said the outcome of the upcoming general election could affect their decision to remain in or leave the country.
The Israel Hayom newspaper also reported on Aug. 7, citing an internal Tax Authority document, that the emigration rate among wealthy Israelis doubled between 2019 and 2024.
Annual tax losses resulting from their departure rose from around 500 million shekels ($166 million) to 1.2 billion shekels ($400 million) in 2023 and 2024, according to the document.
The figures come as Israel continues its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, most of them women and children, while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.
They also coincide with Israel’s continuing attacks on Lebanon and its ongoing threats against Iran.

Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map: MEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:23:42 UTC
07:23:42 KST

India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa".MEA said the resolution's purpose is to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses, and it neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names.
"India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation, stressing the underlying principle of promoting equal-area cartographic representation. We also highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries," said Randhir Jaiswal.The resolution received abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against it from US.
The resolution noted that the Mercator projection remains widely used in educational, media, digital and official materials, despite the considerable distortion of landmasses to the North and South, far from the equator.
It expressed concern that this distortion contributed to minimising the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world. India welcomed the intention behind the resolution to promote more accurate and representative cartographic practices.

Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Kravchenko Submits Resignation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:23:40 UTC
07:23:40 KST

Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation on Monday, Sept. 7, calling the move a “political decision” days after anti-corruption investigators searched premises used by him and other senior officials at the Prosecutor General’s Office.
“This is a political decision. And I made it consciously,” Kravchenko said in a statement on Telegram, adding that he did not want the prosecutor general’s post to become an instrument of political confrontation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kravchenko said his position regarding the allegations against him had not changed. He thanked prosecutors working on criminal cases, assisting victims, documenting Russian war crimes and defending Ukraine’s interests, as well as President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Verkhovna Rada, and asked them to accept his resignation.
The announcement marked an abrupt turn from comments Kravchenko made only hours earlier.
Speaking to journalists on Monday, he said he did not intend to resign voluntarily, although he would leave if Zelensky initiated his dismissal or parliament approved such a move.
“I am not clinging to the position,” he said at the time.
Ukrainska Pravda later reported, citing political sources, that Zelensky met with Kravchenko and Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction, on Sept. 7 to discuss whether Kravchenko would remain in office.
Burnham, Trump Agree to Keep Working Toward Ukraine-Russia Ceasefire
Sources told the outlet that a decision on his future was expected following the meeting. Kravchenko announced his resignation later that evening.
The resignation comes amid the fallout from a major investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) into an alleged criminal organization operating within the Prosecutor General’s Office.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, investigators launched an operation targeting a group allegedly involved in protecting fraudulent call centers and laundering illicit proceeds.
On Sept. 5, the Prosecutor General’s Office confirmed that NABU detectives had searched official premises used by Kravchenko, First Deputy Prosecutor General Mariia Vdovychenko and other staff.
The confirmation followed initial denials that Kravchenko’s home or office had been searched.
Kravchenko said Monday that security personnel initially prevented NABU detectives from entering because investigators had not shown which offices they intended to search. He said he later spoke with the heads of NABU and SAPO and ordered that investigators be given access to his office, other rooms and safes.
NABU and SAPO say their Operation Carthage investigation uncovered a criminal organization allegedly headed by an official at the Prosecutor General’s Office. Investigators accuse members of taking bribes in exchange for shielding fraudulent call centers and laundering proceeds from the scheme.
Ukrainska Pravda identified the suspected official as Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the Prosecutor General’s Office’s International Legal Cooperation Department. Kropyva was detained and on Sept. 6 remanded in custody with bail set at Hr.120 million, about $2.7 million.
Kravchenko has denied involvement in protecting illegal call centers.
His submission does not immediately end his tenure. Under Ukraine’s Constitution, the prosecutor general is appointed and dismissed by the president with the consent of the Verkhovna Rada. Ukrainian law states that the prosecutor general’s powers end when the relevant parliamentary resolution takes effect.
Kravchenko has served as prosecutor general since June 21, 2025, after parliament approved his appointment and Zelensky formally appointed him by presidential decree.

Eiffel Tower employees strike after female workers removal

Unknown Publisher

Eiffel Tower employees strike after female staff removed
September 8, 2026
The Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Visitors to the tower on Monday saw a message that says its opening is "delayed for operational reasons."
The staff released a statement in which they condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the religious group's visit.
Around 100 men from the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement were visiting the landmark.
The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited.
Emmanuel Gregoire, Paris' Socialist mayor, called the incident "unacceptable."
"Equality between women and men will never end at the foot of our historic monuments, nor anywhere else in this city," Gregoire said.
Eiffel Tower operator regrets incident
SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake.
"These conditions should not have been accepted," SETE said.
Company head Ariel Weil told the AFP news agency that SETE will "draw the necessary conclusions" from the case. Weil himself is an elected official in Paris.
"No motive of a religious order could justify a distinction based on gender or any other discriminatory consideration in welcoming the public," Weil wrote on his X account.
The Eiffel Tower sees some seven million visitors a year. It was closed all day due to the strike, but will open again on Tuesday, a staff representative said.

North Korea slams joint drills by US, South Korea and Japan, warns of consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:17:57 UTC
07:17:57 KST

North Korea has denounced a five-day military exercise by the US, South Korea, and Japan, warning of consequences from what it called Washington's increasingly provocative military activities on the Korean Peninsula.
The fourth iteration of the Freedom Edge exercise began with an opening ceremony at Yokota Air Base in Japan and will run through Friday, according to the US Pacific Command.
The drills are being conducted in international waters and airspace south of South Korea, as well as at military installations and command posts in Japan.
Freedom Edge focuses on interoperability across air, maritime and cyber domains, along with integrated air and missile defence.
South Korea has described the exercise as defensive and aimed at strengthening deterrence and response capabilities against North Korea's nuclear and missile threats.
'Military provocations'
North Korea, however, condemned the trilateral drills as a threat to itself and other countries in the region.
In a Defence Ministry statement carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), North Korea accused Washington of pursuing "military provocations" and vowed to take "response measures."
North Korean Defence Minister Kim Song-ji issued "a note of warning against the reckless military moves of the US and its satellite countries to create a serious military confrontation and possibility of conflict on the Korean Peninsula" in the statement.
He also "solemnly" warned of "the consequences to be entailed by them," according to KCNA.
The statements said there would be no change in Pyongyang's policy of responding to US hostility with the "toughest stand to the last."
The drills come weeks after US President Donald Trump said that he had instructed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" separate planned bilateral military exercises between the US and South Korea, citing their cost and his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Trump said those exercises sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 8, 2026
Unknown

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 8, 2026
Jakarta airport and four others near Indonesia’s capital reopen after volcanic ash disruption
Indonesia’s main airport and several other air travel hubs reopened early on Sept 8 after days of closure due to ash from a volcanic eruption, the Transport Ministry said.
The ministry wrote on Instagram that the airport serving the capital Jakarta and four others near the city or around the island of Java are now operating again, as the air safety crisis that left hundreds of thousands of travellers stranded subsides.
Mount Anak Krakatau, about 150km from Jakarta, erupted on Sept 5, spewing a fountain of lava and a plume of volcanic ash.
Eight airports halted operations over the weekend after ash was detected in their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded, the Transport Ministry reported on Sept 7.
Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Britain is set to announce wide-ranging economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank as soon as Sept 8, according to seven officials briefed on the measures, in what experts say would be a significant censure of Israeli policy toward Palestinians.
The measures are expected to include a trade ban on goods produced in the settlements, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Three of the officials said the measures could also include sanctions on companies helping to build settlements.
Israel has become increasingly isolated on the world stage in the aftermath of the devastating war in the Gaza Strip, and international attention has focused on Israel’s tightening grip over the West Bank.
Paris probes claim that women were hidden from Hindu delegation at Eiffel Tower
Female employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to step out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation at the weekend, according to union representatives, prompting a staff protest and an investigation by the Paris city authorities.
The monument was closed late on Sept 7 as employees held a meeting over the incident, which has angered staff and drawn criticism from French politicians.
The dispute stems from a private visit on Sept 5 by a delegation of about 100 people linked to BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha), a Hindu group whose representatives were in France for festivities related to the inauguration of a Hindu temple in the Paris suburbs.
Europe’s biggest mobile operators in talks for satellite-to-mobile venture
A group of Europe’s biggest mobile operators are in early talks to create a consortium to bid on satellite spectrum and offer direct-to-mobile service, which would rival Elon Musk’s Starlink service on the continent, people familiar with the matter said.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone Group and Telefonica would jointly bid for a share of airwaves that the European Union has proposed reserving for a local operator, a plan aimed at increasing sovereign satellite capabilities, the people said, asking not to be identified because the plans are private. No final decisions on the consortium or plans to bid have been made, they said.
To comply with the EU’s proposal, any satellite operator would need to be majority controlled by a European business.
Elena Rybakina tops Naomi Osaka, sets US Open quarter-final clash with China’s Zheng Qinwen
World number two Elena Rybakina swept past four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4 on Sept 7 to line up a US Open quarter-final against China’s Zheng Qinwen.
Kazakhstan’s Rybakina, who added the French Open title to her 2022 Wimbledon crown this year, is into the US Open last eight for the first time in her career.
The meeting with 2024 Olympic gold medallist Zheng will carry extra weight. If Rybakina reaches the semi-finals she is assured of supplanting Aryna Sabalenka atop the world rankings, even if the Belarusian wins her third straight US Open title.

SANAA, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others injured in an airstrike on a prison in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen on Monday, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported, attributing the strike to Saudi Arabia.
The strike hit the prison in Al-Hazm, the Houthi-controlled provincial capital, the broadcaster said, adding that the injured had been taken to a nearby hospital.
Al-Masirah cited the provincial civil defense chief Hassan Saboula as saying that 25 inmates remained trapped beneath the rubble.
Footage aired by al-Masirah showed extensive damage to the facility and rescuers searching through debris.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The attack came amid an escalation in Yemen, where government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have been battling Houthi forces on several fronts.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
A UN-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022 expired six months later without a formal extension, but a fragile de facto ceasefire has largely held until the recent escalation.
The Houthi group announced a maritime ban on Saudi shipping in July and has since claimed attacks on Saudi tankers and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia. ■

Sensing the mood of the court, senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi sought to withdraw the petition.The court allowed his plea for the withdrawal but before that, it expressed its concern over the growing number of incidents of doctors being attacked by politicians and said that it cannot be justified.Rohatgi said the group of people responsible for the assault in Palghar was different, but SC said they belonged to the same party. Breast size dissatisfaction does not lower a mother’s confidence in breastfeeding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:00:01 UTC
07:00:01 KST

Many women experience dissatisfaction with their breast size, but these aesthetic concerns do not appear to lower their confidence in their ability to breastfeed. A study of pregnant women in Türkiye found no link between breast size dissatisfaction and prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy. The findings were published in the Journal of Health Psychology.
Breasts are heavily scrutinized under cultural and societal beauty standards. Globally, up to 70 percent of women report wanting a different breast size than the one they have. This widespread dissatisfaction often negatively affects self-esteem and mental well-being. The pressure to conform to an idealized body shape can cause localized appearance anxiety.
Researchers wanted to understand if these appearance anxieties spill over into biological and maternal functions, specifically breastfeeding. Past research in various countries has shown that having a generally positive body image is linked to higher confidence in breastfeeding. A positive view of the body often translates to a stronger belief in the body’s physical capabilities.
However, specific anxieties about breast size are less understood. Misconceptions persist worldwide that smaller breasts cannot produce enough milk or that larger breasts are inherently better for feeding infants. These myths can erode a mother’s confidence before the baby is even born.
In psychological terms, this confidence is known as self-efficacy. Self-efficacy refers to a person’s belief in their own ability to succeed in specific situations or accomplish a task. High prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy is a strong predictor of actual breastfeeding initiation and duration after birth.
To investigate this localized body anxiety, nursing researchers Kıymet Yeşilçiçek Çalık and Ebru Küçük Erdöl at Karadeniz Technical University, along with Hatice İkra Şan at Ankara Etlik City Hospital, evaluated maternal perceptions in Türkiye. In Turkish culture, breastfeeding is highly valued and viewed as a fundamental duty of motherhood. The researchers sought to find out whether a mother’s subjective dissatisfaction with her pre-pregnancy breast size might act as a psychological barrier to her self-efficacy.
The researchers recruited 518 pregnant women from the antenatal clinics of a university hospital. The participants were between 28 and 42 weeks of gestation. The women were experiencing uncomplicated, single-infant pregnancies. The average age of the participants was nearly 31 years old.
During private face-to-face interviews, researchers asked the women to provide demographic information and details about their pregnancy history. Just under half of the participants were experiencing their first pregnancy. The researchers also asked the participants if they believed breast size affects breastfeeding success or milk production.
To measure body dissatisfaction, the researchers used a visual rating tool consisting of 14 computer-generated images of women. These images featured progressively increasing breast sizes but lacked facial features to prevent bias. Participants selected the image that best matched their current size and the image that represented their ideal size. The numerical difference between these two selections represented their level of dissatisfaction.
Next, the researchers measured breastfeeding self-efficacy using a 20-item questionnaire. This tool asked participants to rate how confident they felt about various aspects of breastfeeding on a scale from one to five. A higher total score indicated greater confidence.
The results showed a high level of dissatisfaction among the participants. More than 65 percent of the women were dissatisfied with their breast size. The most common desire was for a smaller size, which accounted for nearly 49 percent of the total group. Only about 17 percent of the women wished for larger breasts.
Despite this widespread dissatisfaction, the women displayed high levels of confidence in their ability to breastfeed. More than 80 percent of the participants stated that they did not believe breast size affects breastfeeding success. Additionally, 86.5 percent did not associate breast size with milk production.
When the researchers analyzed the data, they found that the results were not statistically significant regarding a link between breast size dissatisfaction and breastfeeding self-efficacy. In other words, feeling unhappy with the aesthetic appearance of their breasts did not correspond to lower confidence in their functional ability to nourish a child.
This lack of association remained true even after the researchers adjusted the statistical models to account for women who had previous breastfeeding experience. The data suggest that in certain contexts, women mentally separate their feelings about how their body looks from their belief in what their body can do.
The authors propose that the transition to motherhood might prompt a cognitive shift. In societies where the maternal role is deeply revered, the functional utility of the breast as a feeding organ appears to take priority over its form. Appearance anxieties simply do not translate into a lack of health confidence for these mothers.
The study relied entirely on self-reported questionnaires, which can introduce bias if participants provide answers they feel are socially acceptable. The cross-sectional design of the study also captures only a single moment in time during pregnancy. This prevents researchers from observing how maternal confidence might shift after the baby is born.
The research was conducted at a single hospital in Türkiye, which limits how the findings might apply to other cultural settings. The specific sociocultural environment, where maternal identity is highly salient, likely plays a protective role against aesthetic anxieties.
The participants also reported very high baseline confidence in breastfeeding overall. This high overall self-efficacy might buffer the subtle effects of localized body dissatisfaction. A population with lower baseline confidence might show different results.
Future investigations will need to track women longitudinally from early pregnancy through the postpartum period. Researchers suggest that educational programs focusing on the biological utility of the body, rather than its appearance, could help dismantle lingering myths about breast size and milk production for those who still hold them.
The study, “The Association Between Pre-Pregnancy Breast size dissatisfaction and prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy: A correlational study,” was authored by Kıymet Yeşilçiçek Çalık, Ebru Küçük Erdöl, and Hatice İkra Şan.

Company can be punished for offence carrying imprisonment, term can be replaced by fine: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:58:58 UTC
06:58:58 KST

NEW DELHI: A company having no physical body cannot be imprisoned and having no mind cannot possess mens rea (guilty mind), which is essential for conviction in a criminal case. So can a firm be convicted and punished?SC Monday answered the tricky questions by holding that a company can be convicted even when it cannot have a guilty mind of its own and can also be punished, though the punishment of a jail term can be substituted by a fine.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and Manoj Misra said there is a need to bring a law for corporate criminal liability but said the issue comes within the legislature's prerogative and it cannot be done by a court. It held that a company is not rendered immune to prosecution merely because the offence carries a mandatory sentence of imprisonment. Referring to a constitution bench ruling, the bench said a judicial discretion to impose a fine alone must be read into such provisions when dealing with juristic persons."The position under Indian law is thus clear that a corporation can be prosecuted for an offence notwithstanding that it carries a mandatory sentence of imprisonment or requires proof of mens rea. It appears that a corporation cannot be prosecuted only where the offence is punishable with imprisonment alone, or where the offence, by its nature, requires personal malicious intent, such that it is incapable of commission by a corporation at all," the bench said.
SC passed the order on a plea by Sanofi India Ltd which said a prosecution against a corporation like it, for an offence requiring mens rea, is maintainable only where a natural person has been identified and arraigned as an accused alongside it. It said that corporations alone cannot be convicted and pleaded that proceedings against it should be quashed. Rejecting the plea of the company, the bench said non-identification of the natural person does not, by itself, render the allegations incapable of disclosing the corporation's role in the offence.The case pertains to the supply of pharmaceutical products by Sanofi India to Bhabha Atomic Research Centre. As per CBI, a BARC officer had conspired with the company to procure medicines at inflated prices and in quantities exceeding the requirement. A case was registered against Sanofi, which challenged its prosecution on the ground that none of its employees had been made accused and a company alone cannot be prosecuted.
"... where the surrounding facts and circumstances, taken as a whole, disclose the possibility that the corporation acted with the requisite mens rea, that disclosure is not defeated merely because no particular individual has been identified as its source. Therefore, the ingredient of mens rea can still be disclosed even where no individual has been identified," the bench said while rejecting the plea of the company.

Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:55:27 UTC
06:55:27 KST

Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Adam Rasgon and Aaron Boxerman
LONDON – Britain is set to announce wide-ranging economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank as soon as Sept 8, according to seven officials briefed on the measures, in what experts say would be a significant censure of Israeli policy towards Palestinians.
The measures are expected to include a trade ban on goods produced in the settlements, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Three of the officials said the measures could also include sanctions on companies helping to build settlements.
Israel has become increasingly isolated on the world stage in the aftermath of the devastating war in the Gaza Strip, and international attention has focused on Israel’s tightening grip over the West Bank.
The sanctions come at a time when Israeli extremists have been repeatedly attacking Palestinians, on occasion assailing homes with little intervention by Israeli forces.
Some analysts say Britain’s move could foreshadow decisions by other European countries to impose harder-hitting and broader sanctions.
While the details are still unclear, a British product ban would likely have a limited impact on the US$8 billion (S$10 billion) in annual trade between the countries, given that goods made in Israeli settlements are only a small fraction of that amount. But the measures go well beyond previous British sanctions related to the West Bank, which targeted some extremist Israeli settlers and two far-right ministers.
Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister, said last week that “Israel will act” against any new British sanctions, without elaborating. The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on Sept 7. The British Foreign Office declined to comment.
Britain, a long-time ally of Israel, has long condemned Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which are widely considered illegal under international law, saying they undermined the possibility of a future Palestinian state. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shrugged off international criticism and promoted building more settlements at a breakneck pace.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. About three million Palestinians live in the territory alongside some 500,000 Israelis. Their exports include kosher wine, produce, plastics and other products.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham entered office in July pledging a tougher stance on Israel over the war in Gaza. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Faisal Mahmud
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
China’s foreign minister said Monday that relations between China and Mexico should remain free from third-party influence while urging closer political and economic cooperation with the Latin American country.
Wang Yi made the remarks during talks in Beijing with Mexican Foreign Minister Juan Ramon de la Fuente Velasco, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
“China-Mexico relations do not target any third party, nor should they be affected by any third party,” Wang said.
Velasco is on his first official visit to China since becoming foreign minister in April, according to the ministry.
Wang said Beijing supports Mexico in maintaining independence, sovereignty and security and opposes external interference.
He called for stronger high-level exchanges, greater political trust and deeper cooperation across various sectors.
Velasco reaffirmed Mexico’s adherence to the one-China principle and UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, while pledging to expand practical cooperation with Beijing.
China and Mexico established diplomatic relations on Feb. 14, 1972 and upgraded their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2013.
China is Mexico's second-largest trading partner globally, while Mexico serves as China's second-largest trading partner in Latin America, trailing only Brazil.
Bilateral trade reached $109.38 billion in 2025, including $89.16 billion in Chinese exports to Mexico, according to Chinese customs figures cited by the Foreign Ministry.

Arab committee calls for ‘deterrent’ measures against Israeli attacks in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:42:29 UTC
06:42:29 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi and Lina Altawell
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The Arab Ministerial Committee on Jerusalem called on Monday for "restrictive and deterrent measures" to halt Israeli attacks on holy sites and occupier terrorism.
The committee also welcomed a Qatari initiative to launch a media platform dedicated to monitoring and documenting Israeli violations in the occupied city.
The call came in a statement issued following the 11th meeting of the Arab ministerial committee, which is tasked with international action to confront Israel’s illegal policies and measures in occupied Jerusalem.
Held on the sidelines of the 166th session of the Arab League Council at the ministerial level in Cairo, the meeting was chaired by Jordanian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, with the participation of committee members and Arab League Secretary-General Ahmed Aboul Gheit.
The committee agreed to “strengthen Arab efforts and diplomatic contacts with influential international parties to push for restrictive and deterrent measures to stop attacks on holy sites and occupier terrorism.”
Platform to document violations
The committee welcomed Qatar’s initiative to launch a “sustainable institutional mechanism”—including a media platform—to monitor, document, and expose Israeli violations against holy sites and worshippers while highlighting their consequences.
It tasked the Arab League General Secretariat, in coordination with member states, with implementing the mechanism, defining its operational methods, and identifying funding sources.
Additionally, the committee called for a coordinated Arab and international diplomatic and media campaign to expose Israeli violations in Jerusalem and the broader occupied Palestinian territories, mobilizing international pressure to stop them.
Arab–Islamic action
The committee agreed to intensify efforts within the international community, particularly the UN Security Council, to rally support for requiring Israel to halt its violations against Islamic and Christian holy sites and respect the historical and legal status quo.
It also emphasized the need for continued collaboration with regional and international organizations to document Israeli breaches of international law and international humanitarian law in Jerusalem and at its holy sites.
-Condemnation of the E1 settlement Plan
The committee strongly condemned Israeli authorities for issuing tenders to build 1,234 illegal settlement units under the E1 plan east of occupied Jerusalem.
It warned that the plan would sever geographic continuity between the northern and southern areas of the occupied West Bank, isolate East Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings, and undermine the possibility of establishing an “independent, viable, and geographically contiguous” Palestinian state.
Israeli authorities issued the tenders on August 18 as part of the broader E1 project, which encompasses roughly 3,400 settlement units in the area between East Jerusalem and the Ma’ale Adumim settlement. The plan has drawn widespread international opposition due to its severe impact on West Bank territorial continuity.
Raid on UNRWA center
The committee also condemned the raiding and evacuation of the Qalandia Training Center—affiliated with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees—in occupied Jerusalem by Israeli authorities.
It described the action as a “dangerous escalation and a flagrant breach of international law,” as well as a violation of the immunities and privileges granted to UN organizations. The committee firmly rejected the “systematic Israeli campaign” targeting UNRWA’s presence and operations.
On August 25, Israeli forces raided the facility and removed its staff, with Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir announcing that authorities had initiated the evacuation process. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that the action was carried out to enforce domestic legislation regarding UNRWA.
The Qalandia Training Center is one of the oldest vocational training facilities operated by the agency.
Al-Aqsa Mosque and Hashemite custodianship
Regarding the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, the committee condemned the “unprecedented escalation” of Israeli violations aimed at altering the site's historical and legal status quo.
The committee reiterated that the Al-Aqsa Mosque / Al-Haram Al-Sharif, encompassing its entire 144-dunum area, is “a place of worship exclusively for Muslims.”
It also underlined the significance of the historical Hashemite custodianship over Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem in safeguarding the locations and preserving their identity and historical status.
The Arab Ministerial Committee on Jerusalem was established in May 2021 by a decision of the Arab League Council to engage permanent members of the UN Security Council and other influential nations to counter Israeli policies in occupied Jerusalem.

Westpac forecasts RBA rate hike in November to 4.6%
Westpac has become the last of the big four banks to change its interest rate prediction and is now forecasting a rate hike at the RBA's November meeting.
The bank had previously expected that the RBA's next move would be down, but chief economist Luci Ellis says the data is now telling a different story.
"The likelihood of an additional rate hike has risen enough to make a November rate hike (+25bp to 4.6%) the base case again," she said.
"The main reasons for the shift are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from the spillovers from the data centre boom.
"Although the housing market is looking weaker than our previously published forecasts, its impact on consumer spending is more than offset by the wider boost coming from a globally-driven surge in tech-related spending.
"An unprecedented pipeline of investment in data centres and associated renewable electricity generation and distribution is expected to drive business investment and so GDP growth – but also limit the pace of disinflation."
A former assistant economic governor at the RBA, Ms Ellis added that it was unlikely the central bank would lift rates in September and would instead wait until the November meeting after more data landed.
Westpac however has not changed its forecasted timing for rate cuts, with three cuts of 0.25 percentage points beginning in August 2027.

There's a reason economics is known as the dismal science, Josh.
To paraphrase a quote from the 2001 DreamWorks classic Shrek, the economy is like an onion — it has layers.
An economy contains a lot of moving parts, and those parts change all the time, so naturally the various economic indicators change as well.
It's also worth pointing out that these are just different indicators being put out by the various big banks, so it's not unusual they say slightly different things. Different economists have different opinions and subscribe to different schools of thought, and that's perfectly normal.
That's why we, and the RBA, put more focus on the official economic data the ABS releases.
In between those data points we're looking at other indicators to get a better look at how those economic layers are evolving.
It's complicated for sure — but we're here to try and help make sense of it all.

Key Event
Choosi misled consumers on insurance comparison services, court finds
Insurance comparison provider Choosi misled customers through its insurance comparison services, the Federal Court has ruled.
Last year, corporate regulator ASIC announced it was suing Choosi, alleging it had misled Australians by claiming to compare a range of funeral and life insurers.
ASIC alleged that Choosi only compared policies from insurer Hannover, which had paid Choosi about $61 million in commissions to advertise its products since 2019.
All up, ASIC alleged that 4,225 Hannover funeral insurance policies and 9,478 Hannover life insurance policies were sold through Choosi's website between July 1, 2019 and November 30, 2024.
The Federal Court found Choosi's website conveyed that it compared products from a range of funeral and life insurers.
"Through the Choosi Website, and each of the impugned advertising materials, Choosi falsely gave consumers the impression that its Comparison Service compared policies from a broader range of insurers than it in fact did," the judgment by Justice Anderson said.
ASIC boss Sarah Court said the ruling sent a strong message to businesses that they must be upfront and transparent with Australians.
"Consumers deserve clear and accurate information about how comparison services operate and the products they do, or do not, compare," she said.
"Businesses cannot create the impression that they offer consumers genuine choice from a range of products when that choice does not exist."
A spokesperson for Choosi said the company has already made changes to its website and advertising after ASIC first raised the concerns.
"Having now received the judgment, we will undertake that exercise again to ensure that it addresses any further issues identified by the Court," they said in a statement.
The case will return to court at a later date to determine potential penalties.

NSW Premier Chris Minns has ruled out writing a "blank cheque" for embattled Sydney property developer Bathla Group.

Key Event
NAB warns of 'slowing growth' as business conditions drop
The latest NAB monthly business survey has also been released today, with businesses seeing a drop in both confidence and conditions.
In August, business confidence fell by 2 points to -8 index points — putting it 13 points below its long-run average of +5 index points.
Business conditions fell by 5 points to -1 index points, making it the first time in six years it's been in negative territory and is well below its long-run average of +6 index points.
So what's behind the drop in business confidence? NAB says it's all to do with ongoing global uncertainty, the volatility in oil prices and continued cost pressures.
The fall in business conditions was broad-based across industries, and NAB puts it down to a 10-point fall in profitability and 5-point fall in trading conditions, putting both at new post-COVID lows.
Interestingly, the decline in profitability is at odds with the employment indicator captured in the report.
"The divergence between the employment index and the profitability index is unusual, and unlikely to be sustained," the report said.
"Should the profitability index remain at depressed levels, we would expect weaker employment outcomes to follow."
The report also noted that cost and price growth measures were broadly unchanged last month, but are still higher than their long-run averages.
"Overall, the key signals from this month's survey are slowing growth amid a backdrop of persistence in cost and price pressures."
In other words, it all makes for a pretty grim summary.

Key Event
Sharp fall in consumer sentiment on fuel prices and rate hike fears
The latest Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index for September has just been published, and it's confirmed what a lot of people are feeling — pretty pessimistic.
The index declined sharply by 5.2% to 84.4 points in September, down from 88.9 in August.
"The falls takes sentiment back towards the deeply pessimistic levels seen earlier in the year," notes Matthew Hassan, Westpac's head of Australian Macro-Forecasting.
He said both fuel prices and the prospect of higher interest rates appear to be driving the decline in sentiment.
"Local pump prices have lifted back above $2/litre for the first time since April, reflecting higher global energy prices and the end of the temporary halving in fuel excise tax," he said.
"Meanwhile, a stronger than expected monthly CPI read in July has stoked fears that the RBA will raise interest rates further in coming months. This has weighed on consumer expectations for finances and the economy.
"It has likely also added to unease about the continued weakening in housing markets."
Other key points from the survey include:
- Nearly two-thirds of consumers are now expecting mortgage rates to rise
- Consumers are feeling uneasy about jobs, particularly those working in construction and hospitality
- The housing market downturn is starting to weigh on the sentiment of homeowners
- Homebuyer sentiment has declined too, but expectations on prices are steady
The full report is available here if you fancy a deeper dive.

BERLIN, September 8. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has stated that he does not intend to change his governing coalition’s policy toward Russia or its support for Ukraine, despite the decisive victory of the Alternative for Germany party and growing support for opposition forces in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election.
"I will not retreat one millimeter from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom, including against Russia. I will probably have to explain this much more often and much more intensely," Merz said at a press conference in Berlin. He also pledged to continue supporting Ukraine.
The German chancellor also addressed the recent high-profile incident involving the discovery of a drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Responding to criticism from politicians who considered the public accusations premature, Merz stressed that he had deliberately decided to promptly inform the public about the results of the investigation. "Some may consider this tactically wrong. But I did not want to wait any longer to share this information with the public, along with the conclusions to be drawn from it. I will act in exactly the same way in the future," the German chancellor emphasized.
On September 1, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August and announced the termination of operations at the Russian House, the closure of Moscow’s Consulate General in Bonn and other measures. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev firmly rejected all accusations made by Berlin, calling them unfounded and absurd. The diplomat stated that Russian House employees must leave Germany within seven days.
Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier pointed out that Germany’s new anti-Russian decisions, taken under the pretext of the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, were another grave mistake by the German authorities, running counter to the interests of their people. In his view, these decisions are linked to Germany’s domestic political situation and, in particular, Merz’s difficult position.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election was held on September 6. According to preliminary official results, the Alternative for Germany party won a decisive victory with 43.8% of the vote. The German chancellor’s Christian Democratic Union of Germany came in second, losing more than half of its support compared with 2021. The Christian Democrats received only 17.2% of the vote, their worst result in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany came third with 9.3% of the vote, followed by the Greens with 8.9% and the Left Party with 8.6%. The BSW party of Sahra Wagenknecht also entered the state parliament with 5.3%.

Israel intensifies south Lebanon strikes, killing 13 after weeks-long lull
Israel launched a wave of air strikes across southern Lebanon, killing 13 people, including women and children, Lebanon’s health ministry said on Monday, marking an escalation after weeks of relative calm. Israel said it would continue targeting Iran-backed Hezbollah over alleged ceasefire violations. Hezbollah has not commented on the strikes.
Israel conducted a wave of airstrikes in south Lebanon, killing 13 people including women and children, the Lebanese health ministry said on Monday, in an intensification of violence after a weeks-long lull.
Israel's military vowed to continue targeting Hezbollah, accusing the Iran-backed militants of repeated violations of a ceasefire in place since June.
Hezbollah has not commented on the threat, or on the escalation in strikes seen in recent days.
Israel hit swathes of south Lebanon hard during the Middle East war that erupted with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, and its forces continue to occupy what it calls a "security zone".
One of the overnight strikes hit a building in the town of Kfar Rumman, killing 11 people, including two children and four women.
Another attack in the same town killed a rescuer and wounded another, according to the Lebanese health ministry.
Read moreIsrael warns of 'full-scale war' if Palestinian Authority launches Oct. 7-style attack
A later strike on Rihan, also in the south but further from the border with Israel, killed one person, while a strike on the city of Nabatieh wounded nine including two children and three women.
Israel has been intensifying strikes in the southern Nabatieh area after saying on Thursday that it had seized the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge from Hezbollah, a claim the Iran-backed group has not commented on.
The Israeli military in a statement said it had struck Hezbollah "infrastructure sites" across southern Lebanon after the launch of two explosive drones towards its troops, as well as "several terrorists" it said were transferring weapons.
The army said it "will continue to operate to remove threats while remaining committed to the ceasefire agreement".
In a separate statement, it said it killed a Hezbollah member in the area of the Beaufort fortress who opened fire on its troops from inside a building, and that "during the close-quarters encounter, two IDF soldiers were lightly injured".
School books in the rubble
Fighting in Lebanon, which erupted in March after Hezbollah targeted Israel in support of Iran, had decreased since a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran on the wider Middle East war and an Israel-Lebanon framework agreement later that month.
On Monday, Israel's foreign ministry accused Hezbollah of "repeated drone attacks" and "attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon".
The ministry said Hezbollah had violated the ceasefire agreement between Lebanon and Israel that includes disarmament of the group.
The rescuer who was killed was just 18 years old, according to his civil defence organisation which is affiliated with the Amal movement, a political ally of Hezbollah.
An AFP photographer saw the building that was hit in Kfar Rumman had been destroyed, with school books and remnants of furniture strewn across the rubble.
Rescue teams were searching the debris on Monday morning for other victims.
Villagers had returned home following the June truce after being displaced by the war.
"Since we returned here, we've lived in fear," Fouad Chakaron told AFP.
He insisted the targeted building was inhabited by "peaceful people with no connection to anyone".
Neighbours fled after the strike, which also damaged nearby buildings, AFP's photographer said.
The NNA later reported additional strikes on the Nabatieh area, and controlled detonations of unexploded munitions in at least two parts of the south.

'I couldn't believe it'
Israel issued no warning to Kfar Rumman before the strikes but released an evacuation order ahead of a separate attack in nearby Deir Zahrani.

"They called me at 2am and told me to get out of the house because it is being targeted," resident Abbas Toufeili told AFP, referring to the Israeli army.
"I said that's impossible, why is my house being targeted? There's nothing in it. I couldn't believe it."
He said he took his wife, children and elderly mother outside in their pyjamas and they stood on the street watching their house be destroyed.
On Sunday, Israeli strikes killed seven people. Attacks on Friday killed four.
The Israeli army has said it is responding to Hezbollah's launch of two drones towards its soldiers inside Lebanon, but did not specify whether any of its troops were wounded.
Hezbollah has not claimed any attack since June 20.
Israeli air strikes and a ground invasion of Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March, Beirut says.
Israeli forces are operating inside a self-declared "security zone" around 10 kilometres (six miles) deep inside Lebanon along the border.
On Sunday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun urged Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks.

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Germany's industrial production fell 1.1 percent in July from the previous month, official data showed Monday, marking a setback at the start of the third quarter after output had picked up earlier this year.
The decline was mainly driven by a sharp drop in the automotive industry, where production fell 9.2 percent month-on-month, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Citing the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA), the office said a multi-week production shutdown during the conversion of a plant for electric vehicle manufacturing was among the main reasons for the decline.
More broadly, Germany's auto industry remains under pressure. Passenger car production in the first seven months of the year was still 15 percent below the level recorded in the same period of 2019, according to the VDA.
Germany's economy ministry said on Monday that industrial production had remained relatively resilient in the second quarter despite higher energy prices, but the effects of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East appeared to be increasingly weighing on output.
Restrictions on Rhine shipping due to low water levels since mid-June may also have dampened production during the summer months, the ministry said, adding that key industries such as automotive manufacturing and mechanical engineering remained under growing pressure.
"Overall, the prospects for a broader recovery in industrial activity over the rest of the year remain subdued," it noted.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said in an analysis the latest data underscored the fragility of Germany's cyclical economic rebound.
Brzeski said the government still lacked key elements of the fundamental reforms needed to put Europe's largest economy back on a sustainable growth path, including a clear plan for affordable energy and tax cuts to boost domestic demand and investment. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: Handmade memories at a Ramallah market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:31:04 CST
06:31:04 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhao Weihong
RAMALLAH, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- One summer evening, I went for a stroll down Issa Ziada Street in the old city of Ramallah. The rich aroma of coffee, the herbal scent of handmade soap, and the smell of freshly baked bread filled the air.
Yet it was not those inviting aromas that stopped me, but some crimson and indigo threads -- fine as veins, dense as memory, stitched into cloth by hands that refused to forget.
Ayyam Tamimi, a 50‑year‑old embroiderer from East Jerusalem, picked up a panel of fabric and gently ran her fingers over the stitches.
"This is Tatreez," Tamimi said softly.
Tatreez, the traditional Palestinian art of cross-stitch embroidery, gained international recognition in 2021, when the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization inscribed it on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Tamimi told me that she had spent over 20 years mastering the craft, first as a seamstress, then as a shop owner, and finally as the founder of her own brand.
"This is the heritage passed down from our ancestors," she said, her eyes tracing the patterns as if reading a landscape she could no longer return to.
"We Palestinian women stitched the landscapes of our occupied villages into cloth," she said. "The villages did not survive. The cloth did. We may not be able to inherit our ancestors' land, but every time I see Tatreez, in homes, at weddings, in shops, I remember where our roots lie."
Beyond Tamimi's stall, the street opens onto a parking lot transformed into four rows of booths. They were part of the Harjeh Market, which reopened this summer after a two-year suspension following the outbreak of the latest Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.
The seasonal market, intended to support Palestinian artisans and small businesses, ran on Fridays during summer and usually hosted about 100 stalls. Here, memory lives on -- stitched into cloth, carried by place names and carved into olive wood.
At a nearby booth, Sameh Abdullah bent down to pick up a placard reading "Jaffa" in both Arabic and English. His grandparents had been forced to flee that city to the West Bank city of al-Bireh in 1948.
Beside him, 30-year-old Mohammad Omar politely asked me not to film him, saying he wanted "to avoid unnecessary trouble."
Omar had driven more than four hours from Tulkarm in the northern West Bank, navigating multiple Israeli military checkpoints that turned what would normally be a 40-minute journey into a half-day trip.
"My goods are often detained at Israeli checkpoints," he said quietly.
For the past 10 years, Omar has sold placards bearing Palestinian place names. Whenever he travels to other cities, he sends them ahead with supply trucks.
"They are afraid," he said, lowering his voice. "Afraid that we will remember the name of every occupied city, every hill, every river."
Violence has continued to escalate across the West Bank. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs documented more than 1,300 settler attacks causing casualties or property damage in the first seven months of the year, the highest pace on record.
Thousands of olive trees have been burned, cut down, or otherwise vandalised. For Palestinians, these trees are far more than a crop cultivated for millennia and a vital source of livelihood; they are symbols -- quiet and enduring -- of resistance and of home.
At another booth at the Harjeh Market, Aida Al‑Shawa arranged gleaming refrigerator magnets carved from olive wood in the afternoon sun.
"Israeli soldiers and settlers are cutting down and burning olive trees across the West Bank," she said. "So we hold tightly to every trunk and pour our hearts into our work. We want the world to see that this land belongs to us."
Her words echoed what an elderly Palestinian farmer once told me: bulldozers may split an olive trunk, but as long as the roots remain, the tree will grow again.
In Al-Shawa's hands, those roots were transformed into everyday reminders. She told me that she carves the names of places that she believes are being erased and turns them into objects for daily life.
"That way," she said with a smile, "every morning when people open the fridge to get some milk, they catch a glimpse of the homeland they may never return to." ■

Finland's largest Viking Age silver coin hoard discovered
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:58 CST
06:30:58 KST

HELSINKI, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Finland's largest known Viking Age silver coin hoard has been discovered in the municipality of Sysma, southern Finland, Lahti City Museums said in a press release on Monday.
The hoard dates to the Viking Age, commonly considered to have lasted from 793 to 1066 in European history. It was discovered near the center of Sysma on Sept. 3 by metal-detecting enthusiast Kalle Lappinen, according to the press release.
The site was inspected the following day, and the hoard was recovered under the direction of Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist with Lahti City Museums.
The museum has confirmed it was the largest Viking Age coin hoard discovered in Finland to date.
In addition to silver coins, the hoard contains a fragment of silver used as payment, a silver bracelet, a silver fitting and a silver bead.
The coins and other objects had been placed in two birch-bark containers and buried about 45 centimeters underground between stones. The two containers were about 12 meters apart.
The coins weigh a total of approximately 4.5 kg. As they have yet to be cleaned, separated or counted, their exact weight and number, as well as their more precise dating, will be determined through further research. The museum said the hoard contains thousands of coins.
Previously, Finland's largest known Viking Age coin hoard was one discovered in the municipality of Nousiainen, southwestern Finland, in 1895. It contains about 1,700 coins and other objects weighing a total of approximately 2.2 kg, according to Lahti City Museums.
Lappinen, who has pursued metal detecting for years, told Finnish national broadcaster Yle that the hoard was found at one of his regular search sites, an area that had also been explored by other enthusiasts.
Lappinen said the discovery left him in disbelief, noting that most signals picked up while metal detecting turn out to be rubbish or mineral deposits. He immediately reported the find to the Finnish Heritage Agency, whose experts later excavated the entire hoard.
Lahti City Museums serves as the regional museum authority for the Paijat-Hame region in southern Finland, which includes Sysma. ■

Iran increases gasoline price for its heaviest consumers as economy struggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
Iran increases gasoline price for its heaviest consumers as economy struggles
Iran early Tuesday introduced a higher price for its heaviest users of gasoline, state media reported, in the latest economic pinch caused by months of war. It’s the second such hike since December.
Such gas price increases can be sensitive and contribute to inflation. An increase in 2019 sparked nationwide protests and a crackdown that reportedly killed over 300 people.
Without specifically mentioning the war with the United States, the government’s announcement cited the “current situation,” adding that the extra money from the price increase will be given to households.
Under the new system, people buying more than their quota of 110 liters (29 gallons) of gasoline a month now must pay 100,000 rials (about 7 cents) per liter, or twice as much as they have been paying since December.
Iran still has some of the world’s lowest gasoline prices, but the price increase adds to daily pressures for many of the country’s more than 90 million people. Already, the currency has been dropping to record lows, and purchasing power has weakened. On Monday, the U.S. dollar was trading at 2.22 million rials.
Keramat Veis Karami, the CEO of the state oil distribution company, on Monday said the new gasoline rate would affect 15% of consumers, the official IRNA news agency reported.
The CEO said consumption reached a record high at 145 million liters (38 million gallons) per day in August, while domestic production capacity was 122 million liters per day. The rest of the supply is imported.
Raising prices can help calm high consumption, which experts have blamed on aging cars and spare parts in Iran as well as insufficient public transportation.
But experts also say increases in gasoline prices will lead to higher inflation in a country that's already struggling with an annual inflation rate of about 67%, according to the country’s statistics center, a government agency.
Cheap gasoline has been viewed for generations as a birthright in Iran, sparking mass demonstrations as far back as 1964, when a price increase forced the shah to put military vehicles on the streets to replace those of striking taxi drivers.

Japan must reckon with how it views foreign workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Japan must reckon with how it views foreign workers
As Japan raises fees for residence permits and tightens the requirements for permanent residency, the effect on long-term settlement warrants attention
Japan will substantially raise its fees for residence permits next month. Depending on the period of stay applied for, renewing or changing one’s residency status could cost as much as ¥75,000 (US$480). The application fee for permanent residency will rise to ¥200,000 from ¥10,000.
The government is also tightening the requirements for permanent residency. Applicants are already expected to be able to support themselves. New criteria proposed include an above-average household income, sufficient projected pension benefits, Japanese-language proficiency, and an understanding of Japanese institutions and rules governing daily life. The changes go beyond a simple revision of administrative fees.
Japan is becoming increasingly dependent on foreign labour. Faced with a shrinking, ageing population and labour shortages, successive governments have expanded the channels through which foreigners can enter and work, while refraining from describing Japan as an immigrant society.
Last year, the number of foreign workers hit another record high, reaching 2.57 million at end October. Although they accounted for only about 3 per cent of the labour force, the Bank of Japan estimates that foreign workers represented more than half of the labour force increase between 2023 and 2024.
Official data showed that last year, manufacturing employed 24.7 per cent of foreign workers, followed by the service sector at 15.2 per cent, wholesale and retail at 13.3 per cent, accommodation and food services at 12.4 per cent, and construction at 8 per cent.
The burden of the higher fees may not be evenly distributed. According to Japan’s 2020 population census, male foreign workers were considerably more likely than Japanese men to be in non-regular employment. Among male employees, excluding company executives, the proportion was about 15 per cent for Japanese nationals, compared with about 53 per cent for Brazilians, 45 per cent for Indonesians and around 40 per cent for Vietnamese, Nepalese and Peruvians.

Estonia strengthens protection against Russian cyberattacks — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
Starting in September, emails from Russian servers and the .ru domain will be sent to the quarantine of Estonia’s government institutions. The number of DDoS attacks on the country has increased to 756.
Estonia is strengthening the cybersecurity of the public sector and restricting incoming emails from Russian servers. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), reports UNN.
Details
It is noted that starting in September, emails from Russian servers and addresses with the ".ru" domain will not be delivered directly to Estonia’s government institutions. Such messages will be automatically redirected to quarantine for additional screening.
Estonian Minister of Justice and Digital Technologies Liisa Pakosta explained that this is necessary to protect government institutions from cyberattacks
It is indicated that Estonia’s decision is linked to the rapid increase in the scale of cyber threats. The number of DDoS attacks in the country increased from 484 in 2023 to 580 in 2024 and 756 in 2025. Pakosta noted that a significant portion of these cyberattacks is linked specifically to Russia.

Ukraine restores external power supply to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:23:00 EEST
06:23:00 KST

Ukraine restores external power supply to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Ukrainian power engineers reconnected the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to an external power supply on 7 September.
Source: Ukraine's state-owned nuclear energy company Energoatom; Rafael Grossi, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
Quote from Energoatom: "The auxiliary systems of the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant were supplied with power from the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 overhead line on 7 September at 19:02. The plant's current consumption is 11 MW."
Details: Energoatom said that external power had been restored thanks to Ukrainian power engineers and a local ceasefire, which allowed repair work to be carried out.
The IAEA also said the connection was restored following three days of repairs by Ukrainian engineers under the protection of a ceasefire coordinated by the agency.
Grossi noted that it is "a crucial step to help prevent a nuclear accident".
Restoring the external power supply after an outage lasting almost three weeks means that the ZNPP can once again get power to cool its reactors and spent fuel pools, as well as to support other essential nuclear safety and physical protection functions.
Energoatom noted that the ZNPP had been without external power since 20 August, with all of the plant's critical systems supplied by backup diesel generators during that time. The prolonged loss of external power had placed additional strain on the plant's safety systems.
Background: Energoatom previously said that the actual condition of the temporarily occupied ZNPP pointed to a continued erosion of fundamental nuclear safety principles.

Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:17:52 UTC
06:17:52 KST

Ukraine's new top commander wants the army's combat-tested sergeants to have real careers, real authority, and clear paths to promotion — not just a role training recruits. Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi has met the senior sergeants of the force's branches, corps, and command bodies and set concrete steps to reform the sergeant corps, saying most had come straight from combat zones, Texty reported.
The push targets an old weakness. Ukraine inherited its rank system from the Soviet army in 1991 — a centralized model in which officers decided almost everything and sergeants were little more than senior soldiers, with no authority or career ladder of their own. A 2020 reform law began to change that by aligning the system with NATO standards, making the sergeant an independent figure.
Drapatyi, who became commander-in-chief in July 2026 with a mandate to carry that overhaul forward and a reputation for favoring decentralized command, is now pressing it directly.
Sergeants outgrow the training role
The sergeant's job long ago stopped being only about preparing troops, Drapatyi said. Sergeants now settle new arrivals into combat areas, handle supply and equipment, ready personnel for tasks, and command them directly in battle.
"A sergeant was a soldier yesterday. Today, he is a commander who is closest to the soldier and sees the real state of the unit on the ground best of all," Drapatyi said.
Drapatyi assigns the reform tasks
The meeting worked through the structure of the corps, the split of responsibility between sergeants and officers, training, appointments, and pay. For each, Drapatyi continued, he set specific tasks, defined next steps, and named the people responsible.
"We cannot build a modern, combat-capable sergeant corps on old approaches," Drapatyi said.
He believes that a sergeant's combat experience should turn into authority, professional development, responsibility, and a real say in how troops are trained and led.
