Costa puts EU taxes at heart of his grand budget tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:33:03 UTC
03:33:03 KST

Costa puts EU taxes at heart of his grand budget tour
The European Council president is heading to Berlin, Warsaw and Madrid as EU capitals search for a landing zone on new sources of revenue for the bloc’s next long-term budget.
BRUSSELS — António Costa's EU budget tour is reaching the bigger capitals, with Berlin, Warsaw and Madrid on the agenda for the coming days. The settings may change, but the main question the European Council president is asking remains the same: Can we all agree on new EU taxes to help fund the long-term budget?
Introducing new EU-wide levies is crucial to lay the groundwork for a budget agreement by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations.
Costa — who has been touring EU capitals to assess what each wants from the budget — will bring up the topic of taxes when he meets Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday. The following day, he will meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in Madrid, along with Portugal’s Luís Montenegro in Lisbon. He will finish the week in Finland, meeting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on Sunday.
Advertisement
“Ambition cannot be realized without the right financial instruments,” Costa said on Saturday. “A budget not just about numbers, but as the ultimate political choice, a choice about our future.”
The topic of new taxes — own resources, in EU-speak — was also the focus of a meeting of European ministers in Dublin last week, when the real horse-trading began over the European Commission’s €2 trillion Multiannual Financial Framework proposal for 2028-2034.
Countries that pay more into the EU budget than they receive are resisting higher contributions, while governments across the bloc support increased spending on defense, security and competitiveness. That leaves new EU-level revenue streams as the most plausible way to expand the budget without directly asking national treasuries to pay more.
“We cannot do more with less,” Spanish Secretary of State for Europe, Fernando Sampedro, said in Dublin, summing up the fundamental tension underpinning Costa’s tour.
Search for new money
Costa’s top takeaway from the trip so far? A sense of urgency.
“The awareness of the leaders about the need to reach an agreement by the end of the year, that's very, very widely shared by the leaders,” said an EU official familiar with preparations for the trip and granted anonymity to speak freely.
Advertisement
Yet as the Council chief prepares for stops in the bloc’s heaviest economic hitters, the positions of these capitals seem intractable.
Germany is among the nations that want a smaller budget pot, lower national contributions and a different balance of spending. Poland and Spain are fighting to protect spending on regions, agriculture, and fisheries, while also backing more investment in defense, security, and competitiveness.
But the most important information Costa has gathered so far concerns not simply where governments stand on spending priorities, but how firmly they oppose — or are prepared to consider — proposed new EU taxes.
The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is steering the budget talks. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
The aim is to narrow down the options in October, when EU leaders meet for a summit in Brussels. But governments have already made clear that they dislike different elements of the five Commission and three European Parliament ideas that have been shortlisted, making it difficult to assemble a package large enough to finance the bloc’s ambitions.
The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the budget talks, welcomed “consensus” among governments on new EU-wide levies on foreign carbon imports and electronic waste, but noted strong opposition on other tax proposals, according to a document seen by POLITICO.
In preparation for a meeting on Tuesday, Ireland also asked EU ambassadors to suggest changes to the Commission’s proposals and quantify the desired total revenue from the new own resources.
Advertisement
Establishing how much money the new resources could raise would help set a ceiling for the negotiations and define the contours of a possible deal. Without that, governments remain stuck in an abstract argument between more free-spending countries and frugals, and between new priorities and traditional ones.
Storm clouds over Germany
Berlin will be Costa’s most sensitive stop.
Merz faces mounting pressure after the far-right AfD won a state election in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. The far-right party is calling for a huge reduction in EU spending.
Germany, the bloc’s largest net contributor and responsible for around a quarter of the EU’s long-term budget, is struggling with a weak economy. The country's export-heavy economy is feeling the heat from China and U.S. tariffs, Europe Minister Gunther Krichbaum said on the sidelines of the informal General Affairs Council in Dublin.
“Our national budget at the moment is really under pressure,” Krichbaum said, adding that the Commission’s €2 trillion proposal was “a fantasy.”
But he backed Costa’s target of reaching agreement by the end of this year, given governments need to agree on a framework in time for the new budget to kick in on Jan. 1, 2028.
Advertisement
“The political context is very much in everybody's minds. Not only what's happening in their own countries, because every leader has their own constraints, but also regarding what's happening in other member states,” said the EU official quoted above.
“We are all now in a position to find a compromise,” Krichbaum said. “Next year it will not be easier also to find compromises. We have elections in different states.”
Good humor, sharp divides
There was a striking degree of bonhomie in Dublin between Krichbaum and his Spanish counterpart Sampedro, who took part in a backslapping conversation with a small group of journalists.
Piotr Serafin arrives at a College of Commissioners meeting in Brussels on May 6, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
Sampedro complimented Krichbaum on his tie, asking whether his wife had chosen it. Krichbaum said it had been a gift, though he said he could not remember from whom.
“There might be a gap at the moment, but finally it’s necessary to find a compromise,” Krichbaum said, referring to the duo’s difference in budget positions. “That’s very easy, like always in Europe,” he joked.
The warm exchanges concealed a sharp disagreement over the substance.
Advertisement
Spain wants to preserve the budget’s traditional spending areas and opposes further reductions to the Commission’s proposal, which Sampedro described as “already not enough but a good basis to work on.”
“We need to preserve … the ambition on cohesion, agricultural policy, fisheries also, but certainly on competitiveness too,” Sampedro said. “We are opposing further cutting.”
Sampedro said Germany and other frugal countries opposed increasing their national contributions, but not necessarily increasing the amount of money available for European priorities. That could leave room for a compromise involving own resources, common borrowing and the gradual repayment of NextGenerationEU money, the €575 billion recovery fund financed by EU-level borrowing to boost economies after the coronavirus pandemic.
“My personal reading is that they don’t want to increase their national contributions,” Sampedro said, pointing at his German colleague. “We don’t share that view, but we respect it. We have a way to solve their concerns.”
Poland is taking a similar line, arguing that competitiveness spending should include cohesion and agricultural funding. Poland’s economic success demonstrated that investment in those areas could also strengthen the EU’s competitiveness, said a Polish government official, speaking on condition of anonymity about the sensitive budget negotiations.
EU Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin has warned that competitiveness and security could become the first casualties if governments focus cuts on areas where the Commission has proposed increases.
“If the big cuts are concentrated on those areas that we call competitiveness and security, they would be detrimental not only for the EU, but also for those who are asking for them,” Serafin told POLITICO. But he said he was optimistic that a landing zone could be found.

A checkpoint regime is in effect, and streets are patrolled by foot and vehicle patrols — how security was tightened in Uman during Rosh Hashanah
Kyiv • UNN
In Uman, a checkpoint regime and reinforced patrols are in effect at the entrances to the area where pilgrims stay during the pilgrimage of Hasidic Jews. Ukrainian and Israeli services have been involved in security.
In Uman, the police are operating in an enhanced mode to ensure security during Rosh Hashanah — a checkpoint regime is in place at the entrances to the area where pilgrims are staying, and the streets are patrolled by foot and vehicle patrols, UNN reports, citing the National Police.
Details
Deputy Head of the National Police of Ukraine Oleksandr Fatsevych, together with the Chief of Police of Cherkasy Region Yaroslav Mezhennyi, inspected the organization of law enforcement officers’ work in Uman, where Hasidic pilgrims are staying during the celebration of the Jewish New Year — Rosh Hashanah.
"The police continue to ensure public order and safety during the Hasidic pilgrimage. The main task is to protect public order and prevent criminal and administrative offenses," Oleksandr Fatsevych said.
A consolidated unit is operating in Uman, involving оперативники, investigators, patrol officers, representatives of the Dialogue Police, the special-purpose police battalion, canine units, and bomb-disposal experts. Emergency Service rescuers, servicemen of the National Guard of Ukraine, and representatives of other services are also involved in ensuring security.
According to Oleksandr Fatsevych, cooperation among all the forces involved has been established, and the situation is under the constant control of law enforcement officers.
A checkpoint regime is in place at the entrances to the area where the pilgrims are staying. Police officers are checking citizens and vehicles. The streets are patrolled by foot and vehicle patrols.
"The police are operating in an enhanced mode. Checkpoints with baggage scanners, stationary posts, a visa support point, and checkpoint groups have been organized. The number of investigative and operational groups has also been increased," said Chief of Police of Cherkasy Region Yaroslav Mezhennyi.
As in previous years, representatives of the Israeli police have also arrived in Uman to help their Ukrainian colleagues maintain law and order during the Rosh Hashanah celebrations, said Paul Tymkivskyi, the representative of the Israeli police in Ukraine and the CIS countries.
He thanked Ukrainian law enforcement officers for their high level of preparation and organization of work and noted that Israeli police officers would remain in Uman until the end of the Rosh Hashanah celebrations.

The letter, shared by the Lord Chamberlain on behalf of the King, said that the couple would also not be able to use the titles of His and Her Royal Highness.

"This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected," it continued.
The letter was issued "to help avoid doubt or confusion" over Harry and Meghan's status.
It also addressed the pair's expected return to public appearances as they support their charities.
"The charitable work of the duke and duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter said.
Harry and his family are reported to be living in a home in the affluent Cotswolds area of southwest and south-central England since their return in August, with their children already having been found a new school.
Their move comes amid continuing uncertainty over their security arrangements and whether the state will fund any protection.
Addressing the security issue last month, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was a "private matter" for Harry and Meghan and that the government "wished them well" with their move.
The Royal and VIP Executive Committee decides which public figures and royals get security.
During Harry and Meghan's six years in the US, they gave a tell-all interview to Oprah Winfrey, in which they discussed their decision to head across the pond, with Harry citing scrutiny from the British press and a lack of support as part of their rationale for the move.

New Mexico is currently governed by Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. She has been on the job since January 1, 2019, and was reelected in 2022.
The governor said in a post on X that "New Mexico's name isn't up for debate — it's been ours since before the United States existed."

Majority of Israelis want government to refuse haredi demands on religion-and-state policies - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:23:00 UTC
03:23:00 KST

Almost two-thirds of Israel's Jewish adults support forming a broad coalition after the next election, either without the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties or including them without accepting their demands on state policy based on religion, including policies on the draft, funding for religious institutions, public transportation on Shabbat, and civil marriage, according to Hiddush's annual survey published on Monday.
The survey, conducted by the Smith Polling Institute for Hiddush, an organization advocating for religious freedom and equality in Israel, involved a sample of 800 men and women representing Israel's Jewish population 18 and up.
It found that on every religion-and-state issue tested, the majority position was opposed to the government's current policy, including on the haredi draft.
Some 84% of participants supported conscripting yeshiva students in some form, with 51% believing everyone should be conscripted into full regular service or essential service, and 31% believing there should be an annual quota of exemptions for outstanding students, with everyone else conscripted.
Only 16% of respondents held the position that all yeshiva students should be exempt from army service, down from 25% in 2022.
Majority of participants showed support for High Court over government policy towards draft evasion
Additionally, 66% of the participants support the High Court and Attorney General's decision to expand sanctions against yeshiva students who don't enlist by cutting public subsidies and increasing arrests, according to Hiddush.
Respondents were also largely in favor of cutting State funding for haredi schools that refuse to teach the core curriculum and administer external exams, with 55% believing that funding should be cut entirely and 21% believing it should be cut in half.
About 77% also believe that all ties between educational institutions and political parties should be severed, and when asked about the disparity between government funding of religious Jewish, general Jewish, and Arab schools, 70% of those with an opinion said that all discrimination within education should be eliminated, and that full funding equality should be guaranteed for all students in Israel, regardless of religion or race.
According to Hiddush, the survey's findings "expose the wide gap between the government's repeated claim that it represents the will of the people and the actual positions of the majority of the adult Jewish public."

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Mexico’s president defended the country’s electoral system on Monday after Colombia’s former leader warned about possible manipulation through algorithms, artificial intelligence, and social media.
“It’s the citizens that count the votes,” Claudia Sheinbaum told a morning news conference, defending Mexico’s electoral model.
She said the National Electoral Institute is responsible for organizing elections, with the Electoral Tribunal responsible for certifying the results.
Sheinbaum said Mexican citizens selected to serve on polling station boards count the votes, distinguishing the system from Colombia’s, where former President Gustavo Petro has raised concerns about private companies involved in the counting process.
The Mexican president acknowledged that irregularities have occurred at polling stations.

Sheinbaum said authorities should identify networks financed to spread political propaganda in different countries and urged political parties to fulfill their responsibilities during elections.

He said such tools had played a role in Colombia’s presidential election and urged governments to strengthen political communication to counter such operations.
Petro also raised his concerns with Sheinbaum during a meeting at Mexico’s National Palace last week, according to the Mexican president.
During his visit, Petro claimed that 2 million bots had been used to influence voting in Colombia. He warned that Mexico could face similar risks from digital manipulation.
Colombia’s electoral authorities declared Abelardo de la Espriella president-elect in June. The Organization of American States recognized the result and highlighted the acceptance of the outcome by his main rival, Ivan Cepeda.
Mexico’s next major electoral process will take place amid growing debate over the role of digital platforms, political advertising, and AI in shaping voters’ opinions and influencing democratic processes.

Up to €45 billion in 2026: what conditions Ukraine must meet to receive EU funding
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:16:18 EEST
03:16:18 KST

Up to €45 billion in 2026: what conditions Ukraine must meet to receive EU funding
Kyiv • UNN
The government plans to adopt the necessary decisions by November 1 to enable Ukraine to access the funding. The Ukraine Support Loan package for 2026–2027 totals €90 billion.
The Ukrainian government plans to adopt the necessary decisions by November 1 to fulfill its commitments to the European Union under the Ukraine Plan and the new macro-financial assistance mechanism in order to receive grants. Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhii Koretskyi reported this on September 7, UNN reports.
Ukraine’s access to billions of euros in budget support depends on the timely implementation of reforms, while the EU’s total loan package for 2026–2027 amounts to €90 billion. Separately, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, approximately $15 billion in partner financing depends on 44 government decisions, while another approximately $15 billion is linked to decisions by the Verkhovna Rada.
Details
Head of the Ukrainian government Serhii Koretskyi said that on September 7 he discussed financial support for Ukraine in 2026–2027 with Valdis Dombrovskis, the European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity. According to the head of the Cabinet of Ministers, his subordinates are working to fulfill the commitments stipulated by the Ukraine Plan and the Memorandum of Understanding on macro-financial assistance.
"We expect to make full use of the financial resources provided for by the relevant instruments. We plan to adopt the necessary government decisions by November 1. At the same time, we are working with the Verkhovna Rada to adopt the necessary legislative acts," Koretskyi said.
What sums are involved
One of the key sources of financing for Ukraine over the next two years is the Ukraine Support Loan. The EU has approved a €90 billion loan for Ukraine for 2026–2027. Approximately €60 billion of this amount is to be allocated for military and defense-industrial support, while about €30 billion will go toward general budget assistance.
For 2026, Ukraine has been granted access to financing of up to €45 billion. Of this amount, €28.3 billion is intended to support defense-industrial capabilities, while another €16.7 billion is intended to support the state budget.
The budgetary €16.7 billion, in turn, is divided into two parts: up to €8.35 billion is to be provided as macro-financial assistance, and another up to €8.35 billion through the Ukraine Facility mechanism.
The €8.35 billion in macro-financial assistance is to be paid in three installments: €3.2 billion, €3.7 billion, and €1.45 billion. The first tranche of €3.2 billion was transferred to Ukraine by the European Commission on June 25.
At the same time, these funds do not arrive in Ukraine automatically. Before making subsequent payments, the European Commission assesses the implementation of the agreed reforms and other conditions.
What Ukraine must do to receive the money
The Memorandum of Understanding between Ukraine and the EU sets out a specific list of legislative and government decisions.
In particular, this concerns changes to tax policy. Ukraine has undertaken to regulate the taxation of income received through digital platforms, as well as to abolish the tax exemption for imported parcels, except for goods intended for security and defense needs. The commitments also include bringing corporate taxation closer to EU rules on combating tax evasion.
A separate section concerns reforming the property valuation system, improving VAT administration, and increasing the level of compliance with tax legislation.
In the area of public finances, the government must, among other things, develop a new public investment management system and integrate related information systems with DREAM, Prozorro, the state budget, and the Treasury system.
The Cabinet of Ministers must also approve the Budget Declaration for 2027–2029. It must contain calculations of revenues, expenditures, the deficit, and public debt consistent with the fiscal targets agreed with the IMF. Reviews of public expenditures are also planned, with the aim of identifying opportunities for their optimization.
Other conditions include further reform of the customs system and bringing Ukrainian customs legislation closer to the EU Customs Code, digitizing the State Customs Service, and strengthening the institutions of state financial control.
For the next stage of financing, the Memorandum also provides for the preparation of amendments to the simplified taxation system. The reform should include combating the artificial splitting of businesses, changes to the rules for remaining in the simplified system, and other tax measures. The expected additional fiscal effect is set at at least UAH 70 billion per year.
In addition, Ukraine must prepare long-term estimates of future pension system expenditures, taking into account the planned pension reform.
Anti-corruption reforms — a separate condition
The financing is also directly linked to Ukraine’s adherence to the principles of the rule of law, effective democratic mechanisms, and the fight against corruption.
The Memorandum also provides for no "backsliding" from the anti-corruption measures that Ukraine previously introduced במסגרת EU or International Monetary Fund programs.
What will happen if the conditions are not met
Before each disbursement, the Ukrainian side must provide the European Commission with documents confirming that the relevant conditions have been met. The Commission then conducts an assessment and, if necessary, may request additional evidence. In the event of a negative assessment, the European Commission has the right to delay the corresponding payment. Thus, failure to meet individual conditions does not mean the automatic loss of the entire €90 billion package, but it may result in delays or the failure to receive specific tranches.
At the same time, the Ukraine Facility is in effect — a separate EU mechanism for 2024–2027, with disbursements also linked to the implementation of the reforms provided for in the Ukraine Plan. In July, the EU revised this plan and added new reform steps, particularly in the areas of the rule of law and the fight against corruption. Additional financing through the Ukraine Facility in 2026 amounts to more than €8 billion.
Around $30 billion depends on decisions by the Cabinet of Ministers and Parliament — Zelenskyy
As early as September 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that a significant amount of external financing depended on Ukraine’s fulfillment of its agreements with international partners. According to him, the government needed to adopt 44 decisions that would unlock around $15 billion in partner support.
"One part is the government’s decisions — 44 decisions are needed, and this will be $15 billion. Everything is quite specific; the government will ensure that these decisions are adopted by November 1," the president said.
According to Zelenskyy, another approximately $15 billion depends on the work of the Verkhovna Rada and the adoption of the necessary laws.
At the same time, these approximately $30 billion in partner financing should not be directly equated with the €30 billion budget component of the Ukraine Support Loan. This refers to a broader set of agreements between Ukraine and its international partners, including the EU, the IMF, and other creditors.
Ukraine and the EU will coordinate needs for 2027
During the conversation, Koretskyi and Dombrovskis also agreed to strengthen cooperation between Ukrainian ministries and the European Commission’s directorates-general, as well as coordination with the IMF and other international partners. According to the prime minister, it is important for Ukraine and its partners to develop a coordinated assessment of the country’s budgetary and defense needs for 2026–2027.
Separately, the head of government raised the issue of strengthening sanctions pressure on Russia, monitoring compliance with the restrictions, and countering their circumvention. He also emphasized that Ukraine’s accession to the EU remains an unconditional priority, and that Kyiv expects the remaining negotiating clusters to be opened as soon as possible.
Previously
At the end of July 2026, the Council of the EU approved amendments to the Ukraine Plan, adding €8.3 billion in loans for 2026. The reforms provide for strengthening the rule of law and the fight against corruption.

Xbox controller shapes become furniture in IKEA’s nine-piece YXSTABY collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:10:07 UTC
03:10:07 KST

There is a stool in IKEA and Xbox’s new YXSTABY collection that looks immediately familiar. Its seat is an enormous Xbox thumbstick, developed from the controller’s original 3D files and enlarged until something normally moved with one finger can support a whole person.
IKEA designer David Wahl worked with Xbox’s device team to get the curve and balance right while keeping the original grip texture and the slight movement of the control. ‘It even moves the way a thumbstick does, so it tilts with you while you play,‘ he says.
Wahl is a lifelong gamer, and even queued overnight for the first Xbox console 25 years ago, so he’s familiar with these shapes. They appear throughout YXSTABY at different scales. The controller’s D-pad becomes a cushion, while another version is made from shiny stainless steel and used as a platter. A mirrored display box gives controllers and collectibles a place of their own. Some references are obvious from across the room, but others take a second look.
The collection began with a change IKEA and Xbox had both been watching for some time. At home, gaming can go on wherever there’s a screen and somewhere to sit. This can be anywhere from the sofa to the dining table.
‘How people play at home has shifted, and it is as much about relaxing and connecting with others as it is about performing,‘ says Philip Dilé, Product Design Developer at IKEA of Sweden. Thus, the furniture changes around the player too.
Designers from the two companies visited homes where gaming already shares space with everything else happening around it, paying attention to the small inconveniences that come with moving equipment through a room. One of their answers is a rolling TV stand, the first IKEA has developed, with storage for gaming gear built into the back. The screen can follow the player across the house and move away again afterward. A portable toolbox keeps controllers and cables together, while its closed lid becomes a laptop stand.
IKEA’s first rolling TV stand moves the screen between different spaces in the home
FROM THE SCREEN TO THE FURNITURE AROUND IT
‘At Xbox, we think a lot about what helps players feel immersed in a game,‘ says Carl Ledbetter, Head of Design at Xbox. ‘The hardware is an important part of that, but so is the world you create around it.‘
For YXSTABY, this world extends into fairly ordinary pieces of furniture. A rolling side table gives a controller somewhere to land beside the sofa and hides charging space behind sliding doors. The monitor stand lifts one or two screens and leaves room beneath for equipment.
The collection avoids the aggressive visual language that has long followed gaming furniture. White, black, and beige dominate, with green used around pockets and compartments made for equipment. The objects can sit among furniture people already own without asking the entire room to announce what happens there. Then the thumbstick stool comes along and has a little more fun with it. YXSTABY was recently unveiled at Gamescom and will arrive at IKEA stores and online from October 1st, 2026.

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. This means that satellite data users have formulated a mission brief, which specialists from the relevant space agencies and foreign ministries, acting as coordinators, must now translate into legal, contractual language. In other words, there is a BRICS component in every sphere that has already become part of day-to-day operations," Ryabkov noted.
According to him, "this is routine work in the best sense of the word, but broadly speaking, it guarantees that there is no longer any room for revisionism within BRICS – or for questioning the very purpose of the endeavor; such things are simply impossible."

Likud tribunal gives Netanyahu deadline to reveal reserved slate spots or face secret vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:08:56 UTC
03:08:56 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ignored a 9 p.m. deadline imposed Monday by Likud’s internal tribunal to reveal the candidates he intends to place in reserved positions on the party’s Knesset slate, escalating an internal dispute just hours before Israel’s election filing process enters its final day.
Despite the tribunal’s warning that continued delay could open the way to a secret ballot in Likud’s party secretariat, Netanyahu did not publish the names by the deadline.
Likud sources told ynet that Netanyahu had “no intention of allowing such a vote.”
Instead, Netanyahu, through Likud legal adviser Ilan Bombach, said he intends to release the list of reserved candidates Tuesday morning, arguing that this would still give secretariat members “several sufficient hours” to review the proposal before voting.
The party secretariat meeting, originally scheduled for 11 a.m. Tuesday, has meanwhile been postponed to 2 p.m., and even that time is not considered final. Parties have until 10 p.m. Tuesday to submit their final candidate lists to the Central Elections Committee.
Netanyahu rejects tribunal timetable
The Likud tribunal had ordered Netanyahu to publish his proposed reserved slots by 9 p.m. Monday, warning that releasing the names only shortly before the vote could appear to be an improper last-minute maneuver.
The tribunal said that if Netanyahu failed to comply, Likud’s legal adviser would have to explain why the delay should not be treated as implicit consent to a secret ballot without the usual requirement that 10% of secretariat members first request one.
Such a ballot could allow party officials to reject individual reserved placements.
Bombach sharply criticized the tribunal’s handling of the case.
“Only 115 minutes were allocated to study a petition of dozens of pages and its appendices, receive instructions, clarify the facts, formulate a position and submit a legal response,” he wrote.
He said the timetable was “unreasonable and disproportionate” and argued that it materially impaired Likud’s ability to present its case.
Bombach also objected to the fact that the tribunal issued its decision without first requesting Likud’s response and said the ruling created a new practical consequence concerning the secretariat’s voting procedure.
“This response is therefore being submitted under protest, solely out of caution, without exhausting the respondent’s arguments or waiving any procedural or substantive claim,” he wrote.
Court warned against a last-minute ‘ambush’
Earlier Monday, tribunal member Yitzhak Bam acknowledged that unusual political circumstances could justify deviating from the normal requirement that secretariat members receive 48 hours’ notice before voting on reserved candidates.
But he said the justification for further delay had weakened because some of the parties affecting Netanyahu’s political calculations had already submitted their slates to the Central Elections Committee.
“If the movement chairman intends to use reserved slots, the proposal regarding them should be published promptly,” Bam wrote.
He said the 48-hour period was designed to allow secretariat members to consider the proposed appointments and decide whether to seek a secret ballot.
“Publishing a proposed decision a short time before the vote could be interpreted as an improper ambush,” he wrote.
Netanyahu nevertheless appears determined to wait until close to the last possible moment.
Still searching for a ‘game changer’
The dispute over timing comes as Netanyahu has yet to finalize all the candidates he wants to add to the Likud slate.
He has already held talks with potential recruits, and one prospective candidate has reportedly even filmed campaign material. The video has not been released because Netanyahu has still not made a final decision.
Behind the delay is not only Netanyahu’s longstanding preference for making political decisions at the last moment. Likud officials say he has so far failed to secure a recruit who would be considered a genuine electoral “game changer.”
Senior ministers and members of Netanyahu’s immediate circle, including his wife Sara and son Yair, have been pressing him to choose figures firmly identified with the political right.
One concern repeatedly raised in those discussions is the possibility of the rival blocs ending the election tied, with Netanyahu’s allies seeking assurances that none of his personally selected candidates could later cross political lines and provide the opposing bloc with a decisive 61st Knesset seat.
So far, Netanyahu has announced only a handful of protected placements.
Oren Dobronsky is the only figure brought in from outside the existing political list, while Gideon Sa’ar, Haim Katz and Israel Katz have also been guaranteed places. MK Michel Buskila, a close ally of Sa’ar, is expected to receive another slot under the agreement with New Hope.
Senior Likud officials say attorney David Peter is among the candidates considered most certain to receive a reserved position.
Peter, a lawyer and researcher at the conservative Kohelet Policy Forum, has represented the government in several High Court petitions as well as National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
Netanyahu is also considering Prof. Keren Assayag, although some people around him reportedly oppose the choice, viewing it as a political gamble with limited electoral value.
With the Central Elections Committee deadline approaching Tuesday night, Netanyahu now has only hours to resolve both the identity of his remaining recruits and the growing internal fight over how Likud will approve them.

Israel warns of 'full-scale war' if Palestinian Authority launches Oct. 7-style attack
Israel on Monday threatened a “full-scale war” against the Palestinian Authority if it believed the West Bank-based body was preparing an attack on Israeli forces or settlements resembling Hamas’s October 7, 2023 assault. The warning was denounced by Palestinian authorities as an attempt to fuel the conflict during the Israeli election season.
Israel on Monday threatened a "full-scale war" against the Palestinian Authority if it prepared an attack against Israeli forces or settlements similar to the one launched by Hamas from Gaza on October 7, 2023.
The unusual warning, denounced by Palestinian authorities as an attempt to fuel the conflict during the Israeli election season, comes as violence surges in the occupied territory.
The remarks from Defence Minister Israel Katz followed a stabbing attack that wounded an Israeli settler in the northern West Bank, with the military saying it had shot and killed the Palestinian assailant.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. Recent months have seen soaring attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians, often with little or no legal consequence.
"If... the Palestinian Authority's security mechanisms and related bodies initiate, or we know with certainty that they are about to initiate, a terror attack in the style of October 7 against IDF forces and Jewish settlements – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and I have instructed the IDF to prepare for the opening of a full-scale war," Defence Minister Israel Katz said.

Katz added in a statement from his office that the military campaign would target the "senior leadership and mechanisms" of the Palestinian Authority, which is based in the West Bank city of Ramallah, as well as "all terror infrastructure" in the territory.
He said it would include "targeted killings of senior figures" and the "evacuation of residents from the cities and villages from which terror activity is carried out", with a permanent Israeli military presence in those areas.
Katz said the operation would emulate the so-called "security zones" in which the Israeli military currently operates in Gaza and southern Lebanon.
'Remove threats from Hezbollah'
Israel's military in a separate statement issued on Monday said that it would continue to "remove threats" from Hezbollah following air strikes in south Lebanon overnight, which killed 12 people including two children.
The Israeli military said it had struck Hezbollah "infrastructure sites" across southern Lebanon in response to the launch of two explosive drones towards its troops, as well as "several terrorists" it said were transferring weapons.
In a separate statement, it said it killed a Hezbollah member in the area of the Beaufort fortress who opened fire on its troops from inside a building, and that "during the close-quarters encounter, two IDF soldiers were lightly injured".
The militant was later "eliminated", the military said.

The Palestinian Authority does not officially take part in militant activity and its security forces have worked to crack down on local militancy in the West Bank.
There was no indication that Monday's attack was carried out with the consent or knowledge of the Palestinian Authority.
Soaring violence

Israel's Magen David Adom emergency services said the stabbing victim had been taken to hospital in a moderate to serious condition.
The civil affairs authority identified the Palestinian assailant as 34-year-old Mahmoud Mohammed Arabi Mohsen.
His uncle, Nizar Arabi Mohsen, said he had been "suffering from a mental illness" for around four years.

The Israeli military said troops had been dispatched to the area "following a report of friction" between Palestinians and settlers.
It said Palestinians had thrown stones at soldiers, who "carried out arrest procedures, including firing warning shots into the air, followed by fire toward key instigators".
"Hits were identified," it said, adding that the incident was under review.
Violence in the West Bank has surged since Hamas's October 2023 attack on Israel sparked the war in Gaza.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed at least 1,106 Palestinians in the West Bank, including both militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war.
Israeli figures show at least 48 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

Zelenskyy receives message from Trump's envoys that "Russians are ready to negotiate"
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said after meeting US envoys that he had received a message from them: "the Russians are ready to negotiate".
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with Axios, as reported by European Pravda
Details: On 6 September, Zelenskyy met presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv. They had arrived in the Ukrainian capital after meeting Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Zelenskyy said the message he received from the US envoys was that "the Russians are ready to negotiate".
He remains sceptical, however, as Russia's actions on the battlefield and the recent escalation in attacks do not indicate a readiness for compromise.
However, Zelenskyy said that the US envoys made it known that Putin is "ready to discuss" ideas for moving the negotiation process forward.
The Ukrainian president also noted that the envoys travelled to Moscow and Kyiv primarily to "unblock" the diplomatic process, but also brought several new ideas.
He declined to disclose all the details, but said some of the discussions concerned potential de-escalation steps by Russia and Ukraine ahead of and during the winter.
"There are ideas around energy [facilities] and around grain [shipments], around electricity [facilities] and around oil and gas [exports]. We have different interests, Russia and we," Zelenskyy said.
When asked whether the new US approach involved both resuming negotiations and seeking agreements that would allow Ukraine and Russia to get through the winter without a serious escalation, Zelenskyy said that this interpretation was "very close to the reality of these conversations".
He described the first goal as resuming negotiations and the second as an attempt to make the coming winter different from previous ones. The president added that the aim would be to find measures, either before or during the winter, "which can bring [the] sides closer to the peace".
Zelenskyy said the US also supports a separate "winter package" for Ukraine, which would include assistance in air defence and the energy sector.
"It's not only about missiles. It's also about LNG [liquefied natural gas] ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation," he added.
Background:
- A source at the Élysée Palace has told European Pravda that Putin will be ready to resume peace negotiations on Ukraine after the Russian parliamentary elections on 18-20 September.
- Following the talks in Kyiv with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the national security advisers from France, Germany and the UK – Emmanuel Bonne, Günter Sautter and Jonathan Powell – agreed to draw up, together with their Ukrainian counterparts, the conditions they will put forward in further negotiations with Russia over the coming weeks.

For Palestinian women, Gloria Steinem's feminism is anything but
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:04:00 UTC
03:04:00 KST

Breadcrumb
For Palestinian women, Gloria Steinem's feminism is anything but
Women leaders and cultural icons are held to an impossibly harsh standard, scrutinised for every statement they make, every alliance they’ve ever had, every cause they have embraced, in ways that men are not and never will be. So I am reluctant as I criticise Gloria Steinem, out of concern that what I write might provide fodder for misogynist haters. Nevertheless, I cannot join the crowds that are celebrating her as if she could do, and has done, no wrong.
My criticism of Steinem, whom I have called a “faux feminist” in many of my essays, is grounded in my analysis of her harmful politics. And of course I understand, even assume, that many of us have made mistakes in our youth, and will continue to do so in our old age. I’m also aware that some of my criticism of Steinem dates back to her youth. Nevertheless, recent statements she made before her death suggest she still held the same deeply problematic views.
Faux Feminism, as I explain in Palestine and Feminist Liberation, is a colonial, imperialist ideology that seeks a bigger piece of the pie, without questioning the toxic ingredients of that pie. Genuine feminism wants an altogether different pie, made from healthy ingredients. For decades, I have argued that women knocking down doors or breaking the glass ceiling to enter a violent masculinist space does not qualify as a feminist achievement, and only superficially changes that space. Lipstick on a pig.
Women joining the army do not make it a less murderous force; Hillary Clinton or Kamala Harris becoming president of the world’s uber imperial power would not have stopped hypermilitarism, genocide in Gaza, or the disproportionate incarceration of people of colour in the US.
Feminism must be nuanced: the change we need is not women attaining the “equal right” to do what men do. What we need is to stop the harm racism, misogyny, and heteropatriarchy inflict on the world.
So while I do appreciate some of Steinem’s essays, like ‘If Men Could Menstruate,’ and ‘A Bunny’s Tale,’ her expose of the Playboy Bunny exploitation of young girls, and am immensely grateful for every woman, including Steinem, who demanded that we have bodily control and legal abortion, as well as financial autonomy, I also strongly resent her having worked for the CIA, her ardent Zionism, and her lifelong Orientalist views of Arab and Muslim women.
Let me explain.
Steinem worked for the CIA from 1958 to 1962, heading the “Independent Research Service,” a fully CIA-funded front agency for spying on young activists with Socialist leanings, by sending undercover agents to infiltrate their activities on campuses and at youth festivals. Put bluntly, she was a defender of capitalism, which was her comfort zone.
Indeed, even her fans acknowledge that Steinem’s brand of feminism is deficient in class analysis. Some years later, when asked about her work with the CIA, she did not try to distance herself from it, blaming it on youthful naivete. Instead, she stated that the agency is an “honourable, enlightened, liberal” organisation.
I guess Steinem considers coups, military interventions, political assassinations, human rights violations, and torture to be honourable practices.
Yes, this was in her youth, but bear with me as I trace a pattern.
In 1975, in a major victory for Third World countries who had always understood the reality of Israel, the United Nations overwhelmingly passed General Assembly Resolution 3379, declaring that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination.” Naturally, the resolution met opposition from Israel, the US, and many European countries, and there was a global effort to rescind it, with Gloria Steinem signing a letter decrying it and asserting that “human rights are indivisible.”
"As women committed to the worldwide struggle for human rights and equality," it is "our unanimous conviction that all human rights are indivisible. We are appalled at the ‘racist’ label applied solely to the national self-determination movement of the Jewish people. We decry this implicit denial of Israeli statehood and this incitement to world wide anti-Semitism," her letter reads.
But to assert that human rights are indivisible, while defending Zionism, which dispossesses Palestinians, is to deny the very humanity of the Palestinian people.
Between 1975 and the present, millions of Americans, Jewish and non-Jewish, have renounced the Zionism they had once espoused. They had been Zionists either because they had specifically been brought up with that ideology by their parents, or because it was the dominant discourse they had not yet sufficiently questioned. But as they developed their own critical thinking, they shrugged off Zionism.
Not Steinem. In late 2023, she was the lead signatory of a statement denouncing the alleged “systematic Hamas rapes” of Israeli women and girls on October 7, which opened with: “As women’s rights activists and leaders, we stand for the right of every woman and girl, of every nationality, religion, and community, to live free of all forms of violence, including rape and sexual assault.”
Not only do these allegations remain unsubstantiated to this day, with many of the specific claims having been debunked, but Steinem never said anything about the meticulously detailed reports by Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and B’Tselem, all documenting sexual torture by Israeli security forces of Palestinian men, women, and children.
Palestinians had been documenting and denouncing these abuses for decades, and the Palestinian Feminist Collective recently published A Predatory State, their latest, damning 200-page report on Israel’s longstanding pattern of sexual violence against Palestinians. Yet Orientalism is such that only reports by non-Palestinians are considered reliable.
Amnesty International’s report states: “Palestinian women in Gaza have been subjected to a range of gendered forms of bodily and mental harm, including reproductive and other gender-based violence.” The Human Rights Report, appropriately titled More than a human can bear, states: “There is no escape from the conclusion that Israel has employed sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinians to terrorise them and perpetuate a system of oppression that undermines their right to self-determination.”
B’tselem’s report, Welcome to Hell: the Israeli Prison System as a Network of Torture Camps, similarly details the pervasiveness of sexual violence and rape of Palestinians by Israeli security forces in Israeli prisons.
There was not a peep from Steinem, despite her earlier assertion that human rights are indivisible.
The pattern of Steinem’s outrage at criticism of Israel, and her utter silence about the oppression of Palestinians, reveals both Zionism and its accompanying worldview, Orientalism.
And ultimately, today, where one stands on Zionism is a political litmus test. Ignorance can no longer be used as an excuse when the genocide of the Palestinian people, perpetrated by Zionists, is livestreamed. Whereas for decades, one could be a Zionist by default, simply because that was the dominant discourse, today, with the widespread availability of evidence of Israel’s savagery, one can only be an ideological Zionist, a committed one, not a “default Zionist.”
Steinem was an ideological Zionist. So if we agree that Zionism is racist, and we know that Steinem was a Zionist, what does that make her? A “flawed feminist,” I am told, with the expectation that I should understand, should not “cancel” her just because of that flaw. We can’t be purists; we must build bridges, I am told, to fight the fascists…
But enough. It is not lost on Palestinians that the one “flaw” we are consistently asked to overlook is the powerful ideology that calls for our eradication.
Nada Elia is Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at Western Washington University, and author of Greater than the Sum of Our Parts: Feminism, Inter/Nationalism, and Palestine.

Berlin built a wall around the AfD. Voters just smashed it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:03:53 UTC
03:03:53 KST

Berlin built a wall around the AfD. Voters just smashed it
On the night of September 7, 2026, the results of landmark state elections were finalized in Berlin. Officially, the numbers recorded a crushing defeat for the ruling elites in one of Germany’s smaller states – Saxony-Anhalt, home to just 2.1 million people. Yet many are already interpreting these figures as a complete breakdown of Germany’s postwar political order.
For the first time, the right-wing conservative party Alternative for Germany (AfD), led by Ulrich Siegmund, captured a historic 43.8% of the vote, coming within a single step of an absolute majority in the state parliament. Add to that the result of the left-wing conservatives from the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) at 5.3%, and the historic collapse of the CDU, which plummeted to 17.2%, and the math of Germany’s crisis becomes unforgiving: an overwhelming majority of residents in this eastern state officially voted for a radical break from the policies of the current federal government under German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The long-standing Berlin consensus of the traditional parties – the much-touted political Brandmauer (firewall) designed to isolate Eurosceptics from financial and political power – has now collapsed. In German expert circles, an uncomfortable diagnosis is increasingly being whispered, if not yet spoken aloud: modern Germany is gradually sliding into systemic, ungovernable chaos, which, in terms of its fractured personnel, social fabric, and psychological state, directly evokes the pre-Reich atmosphere of the late 1920s. Attempts by the liberal mainstream in Berlin and Brussels to interpret this resounding explosion simplistically – purely through the lens of the migration crisis – only reveal a deep functional blindness. The ‘Saxon filter’ has sifted out the political chaff, exposing the underlying processes that are inexorably transforming Europe.
The success of the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance and why it matters
Attempts to dismiss the Saxony-Anhalt case as a flare-up of xenophobia or protest voting by marginal societal groups appear unfounded – the significance of 43.8% for the AfD and 5.3% for the BSW extends far beyond migration debates. The primary driver here, in our view, is the dire state of the Mittelstand – the small and medium-sized enterprise sector which forms the backbone of Germany’s national economy.
Looking at the typical AfD voter, one finds men of working age between 35 and 69, workers and the self-employed, along with individuals who soberly rate their current economic situation under the strain of inflation as poor. These are not abstract radicals, but the skilled labor base of Germany, whose industrial and family capital Brussels has cynically sacrificed to geopolitical interests and climate dogma. Remarkably, a massive portion of the party’s electoral surge came from citizens who had previously avoided voting altogether but now turned out to the polls for the physical survival of their real-economy jobs.
In parallel, the ‘Saxon filter' registered another historical fracture that would have been unimaginable on the electoral map of the former GDR before 2026. In this eastern state, the climate ideologues of the Green Party virtually tied in vote share with the traditional standard-bearers of the left flank – the Left Party (Die Linke). However, this was not due to a victory for the green agenda. Rather, industrial collapse and economic chaos meant that the core protest electorate of the old East German socialists was absorbed wholesale by the triumphant AfD and the pragmatic Wagenknecht Alliance. As a result, the Left Party crashed to the brink of survival, where they were overtaken by the Greens, who gathered the frightened urban middle class under their banner.
The importance of this shift is compounded by the result of the Wagenknecht Alliance (5.3%). Contrary to the canonical dogma of incompatibility between the right and left flanks, a consensus is currently forming in East Germany whose goal can be described as saving German industry and the Mittelstand, with these forces now controlling nearly 50% of the state parliament. Wagenknecht’s left-conservatives and Siegmund’s right-wing sovereignists are tightly bound by a shared macroeconomic platform: demanding an immediate end to the sanctions war with Moscow, a halt in funding for Kiev, and a return to hard-nosed national self-interest. Berlin can no longer mathematically ignore this consolidated revolt by the industrial core – the old model of governing Germany has officially been nullified.
Herein lies the most unpleasant aspect for the current federal coalition government: political elites spent years building a wall around alleged fringe groups like the AfD and BSW, yet now, after these elections, they are obligated to engage with them and maintain dialogue within the framework of existing democratic processes.
Moreover, the chief existential nightmare for intelligence services in Berlin and Brussels lies in the inevitable institutional legitimization of these “radicals” through purely state-level coalition agreements. By sitting down at the negotiating table in Magdeburg, representatives of the AfD and the Alliance legally gain direct and legal access to classified state security channels and secret documents – including operational reports from the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (the domestic counterintelligence agency) and infrastructure plans for strategic facilities.
Although legal authority over major energy imports remains exclusively with the federal government, a state government in Saxony-Anhalt formed by pragmatists wields a powerful lever of ultimatum pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A consolidated demand from an entire industrial region for the immediate rescue of the Mittelstand through a return to cheap Russian pipeline gas could split Germany’s economic and political stability from within, paralyzing Berlin’s will.
The root causes: The current state of Germany and its East
The electoral defeat of the ruling CDU in Saxony-Anhalt is a direct result of Friedrich Merz’s economic policies, which prioritized military budget increases while stripping the eastern states of social and industrial support. The special irony is that Berlin’s ambitions to build a powerful independent army in the 21st century are merely an illusion: the Bundeswehr is de facto completely devoid of autonomy and remains under strict, pervasive oversight from Washington and the Pentagon. The attempt to sacrifice Saxony-Anhalt’s real economy to transatlantic military dogma has permanently erased voter trust in the traditional elites.
In examining the broader causes of this crisis, it is necessary to dismantle the myth of a “united Germany,” which has served as Berlin’s polished showcase for thirty-six years. The former GDR never truly became an equal partner within the federation. Instead, it was relegated to a kind of internal protectorate for the western states – a subordinated region systematically drained of its raw materials and skilled personnel.
By 2026, the economic and infrastructural disparities between a prosperous state like Bavaria and the struggling region of Saxony-Anhalt had reached critical thresholds. According to official reports from the Federal Statistical Office of Germany (Destatis), the gap in living standards has widened into a chasm: while Bavaria’s annual GDP per capita stands at nearly €59,000, Saxony-Anhalt firmly anchors the bottom of the federal list at just €36,517. In real terms, a resident of an eastern state generates nearly half the economic output of a southerner. Against this backdrop, the 2.7% decline in real industrial output in Saxony-Anhalt (particularly in manufacturing and chemicals) looks catastrophic, and far worse than the overall German recession.
The industrial base of East Germany, shaped during the Soviet era, was originally designed for deep integration with the Eastern Bloc. Under the guise of “European integration” following reunification, however, these manufacturing hubs were systematically hollowed out or dismantled. The few enterprises that managed to survive – ranging from the massive Leuna chemical complex to Magdeburg’s heavy machinery plants – were left entirely dependent on cheap Russian pipeline gas and placed under the external corporate management of Western conglomerates.
When the previous federal coalition under Olaf Scholz dissolved Germany’s established energy routes with the stroke of a pen, West Germany possessed the deep financial reserves and infrastructural flexibility to partially absorb the shock by pivoting to expensive transatlantic LNG. For East German industry, however, this geopolitical maneuver was a death sentence.
Saxony-Anhalt’s current state is a mirror of the systemic degradation that Brussels cynically labels the “green transition.” The state’s real economy is being decimated by bankruptcies among small and medium-sized businesses. Living standards, human capital, and social guarantees in Magdeburg and Halle are rapidly deteriorating against the backdrop of thriving cities like Frankfurt or Munich.
It is precisely this colonial snobbery from the federal center that has transformed Saxony-Anhalt into a scorching political filter. Voters in the East have come to a stark realization: to the Berlin establishment, their factories, their jobs, and their right to a stable life are nothing more than bargaining chips in a grand geopolitical game. Therefore, the triumph of the AfD and Sahra Wagenknecht’s alliance in Magdeburg should be viewed as a fierce declaration by East Germany that it is abandoning a bogus liberal consensus.
The fate of Europe and prospects for Russia
Saxony-Anhalt has acted as a harsh filter, which may also signal a general rightward shift across Europe. Moreover, the liberal establishment in Brussels does not yet fully grasp the true scale of this process. The fact that the AfD’s triumph has become a central topic on the global agenda is confirmed by the rapid reactions of key figures on the global conservative flank: Elon Musk openly endorsed the results with an overnight statement, and Donald Trump quickly posted the election statistics on his social media platform, TruthSocial. It is clear that this local electoral revolt in East Germany is breaking the entire isolation strategy that Brussels spent years building against Eurosceptics and erecting a powerful geopolitical shield for the sovereign-minded elites of the Visegrad Group.
However, behind this outward euphoria lies a deep structural divide, as not all right-wing forces on the continent welcome this victory. The situation holds a fundamentally different, far more unsettling meaning for Western Europe’s leading right-wing leaders, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and France’s Marine Le Pen. For Meloni, who anchored Rome’s EU strategy on compromises with Brussels and unconditional alignment with the West’s anti-Russian course, the AfD’s triumph is a painful blow to her concept of “respectable conservatism.” Saxony-Anhalt has bluntly demonstrated that European voters demand unyielding economic self-interest, not subservience to the European Commission.
For Marine Le Pen in Paris, who previously demonstratively isolated the AfD in the European Parliament in order to bolster her own mainstream image, the overnight 43.8% in secured in Magdeburg represents an existential challenge. They understand all too well that a resurgent, nationalist Berlin could eventually revive old geopolitical ambitions, completely upending the delicate balance of power within the Paris-Berlin axis for decades to come.
For the political map of Europe in the coming years, the ‘Saxon filter' marks the threshold of an era defined by profound chaos and the irreversible fragmentation of the unified supranational space. Brussels is rapidly losing its monopoly over the pan-European agenda: the left-liberal dictates of the European Commission are being systematically supplanted by the harsh, cynical, and aggressive national egoism of key sovereign players. The centuries-old European strategic tradition, long anchored to the ideal of monolithic unity, continues to crumble as the continent splinters into competing economic and ideological enclaves.
However, for Moscow, rather than promising tactical dividends in the form of revived gas contracts, this rightward turn of the EU’s industrial locomotive introduces existential, long-term challenges. The deep historical programming of any European ultra-nationalism inevitably carries within it a creeping revision of the outcomes of World War II and the systematic dismantling of the historical legacy of the Yalta-Potsdam security architecture.
As these nationalist forces consolidate power, Moscow will inevitably face coordinated attempts to rehabilitate the dark pages of Europe’s past. Within this emerging ideological landscape, the sacredness of victory in the Second World War and the immutability of post-war borders will become the primary targets for ideological assault. In the medium term, the complete paralysis of the EU leadership’s ability to forge consolidated decisions will transform the European architecture into a scorched field of egotistical bargaining – a hostile arena where Russia will be forced to aggressively defend both its core values and its national security.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner attributes the lack of progress on Gaza to upcoming Israeli elections: "Makes them a little irrational"
President Trump's special envoy Jared Kushner directly linked the lack of progress on the rehabilitation of the war-torn Gaza Strip to upcoming Israeli elections.
Israel will hold elections in late October, and polls show it is a tight race between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponents.
"We're working through some political issues in Israel. I think we agree with them on the end state," said Kushner, who was speaking at a conference on Sunday in Kyiv, where he was holding talks to end the Russia-Ukraine war. "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."
Kushner's remarks are a rare and candid criticism of Netanyahu's government by a senior Trump administration official over the conservative Israeli leader's Gaza policy.
U.S. efforts to advance plans to disarm Gaza militant group Hamas and open the way for investment into rebuilding the devastated Palestinian enclave have stalled amid disagreements with Israel and Hamas about the proposed roadmap.
Large parts of Gaza were destroyed during the war sparked by Hamas' attack on Israel nearly three years ago. Many Palestinians are still living in tent encampments a year after Israel and Hamas agreed to a U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
Kushner, who is Mr. Trump's son-in-law, did not elaborate on how the Israeli government is impeding the Gaza peace plan.
"Gaza has not worked for a very, very long time. It was basically built by NGOs and terrorists," he said, adding, "Now we have a plan to go forward."
A U.S. official familiar with the matter told CBS News one of the issues irking Washington is that Israel had not given guarantees needed to set up a new police force in Gaza. That police force is needed to create a security architecture independent of Hamas that could facilitate the entry into the Strip of a new technocratic government backed by Washington. Israel is also not meeting its commitments to allow in materials needed for certain reconstruction projects, the official said.
The Israeli prime minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Nickolay Mladenov, a senior diplomat on the Board of Peace, tasked with advancing the U.S. peace plan, said in remarks to the United Nations in late August that Israel's continued airstrikes in Gaza impede getting Hamas' fighters to give up their weapons.
"It only delays the demilitarization that would happen, and it obstructs the civilian transition that should take place to ensure that remilitarization will not be possible in the future," Mladenov said.
Israel has continued to carry out near-daily airstrikes in Gaza since agreeing to a ceasefire in October. Israel says the strikes are aimed at preventing imminent threats to its soldiers and to foil efforts by Hamas to regroup and rearm. Israel has also continued an operation to kill those who participated in the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas into Israel that sparked the subsequent war.
While Israel retains the right to defend its troops in Gaza, U.S. officials see some of the Israeli airstrikes as going beyond that scope and perpetuating insecurity in the enclave, said the U.S. official familiar with the matter.
The peace plan negotiated by the Board of Peace in August calls for Hamas to gradually disarm while Israel simultaneously gradually withdraws from territory it controls in Gaza. Israel has controlled over half of Gaza's territory since the start of the ceasefire.
Last month, Netanyahu rejected that plan, saying Israel would not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is "genuinely disarmed."
Israeli officials have expressed doubt that Hamas would relinquish all of its weapons unless Israel keeps the whole of its leverage over the group, including its military presence inside Gaza.

Italy faced hottest summer since 1950
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:02:54 UTC

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Summer 2026 was the hottest in Italy since 1950, surpassing the previous record set in 2003, according to an analysis by the Institute for Bioeconomy of Italy's National Research Council, financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore reported Monday.
“The average temperature of 24.3 degrees Celsius (75.7F) recorded in summer 2026 exceeds the previous record of 23.6 degrees Celsius (74.5F) set in 2003,” said Lorenzo Arcidiaco, a researcher at the institute.
The institute analyzed temperature data recorded since 1950 in the ERA5-Land database of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
August was also the hottest on record, with an average temperature of 25.6C (78.1F), surpassing the previous records of 24.6C (76.3F) in 2024 and 24C (75.2F) in 2017, Arcidiaco said.
He said the data suggest 2026 could end as Italy's hottest year since 1950, noting that July and August were the hottest months on record consecutively for the first time.
Spring also saw a record average temperature of 12.1C (53.8F), matching the level seen in 2024, which was the hottest year since 1950.
From January through August, about 70% of Italy's territory saw temperature anomalies of more than 1C (1.8F), while around 40% saw anomalies exceeding 2C (3.6F), according to the institute.
The areas most affected included lowland areas in northwestern Italy and the Apennine regions.
The institute said much of the affected land is cultivated, with higher temperatures and drought in some areas making the agricultural sector particularly vulnerable.
Rome, Florence, and Turin were also hit repeatedly by heat waves in June, July, and August, with maximum temperatures exceeding the 90th percentile for at least six consecutive days.

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of a strike on a prison in northern Yemen, killing 7, including a child
Houthi rebels in Yemen accused Saudi Arabia of striking a prison on Monday in the country's north, killing seven, including a child, as tensions escalate between the group and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.
The strike on the Central Corrective Facility in the strategic city of Hazm in Jawf province also wounded at least seven people, including a woman, said Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry.
The prison’s warden told the Houthi al-Masirah news channel that 35 prisoners and a woman who was visiting her husband were trapped under the rubble.
Yemen plunged into civil war in 2014 when the Houthis descended from their northern stronghold and seized the capital, Sanaa, forcing the internationally recognized government to flee southward, then into exile in Saudi Arabia. A Saudi-led coalition entered the Yemen war the following year in an attempt to restore the government.
Houthis’ al-Masirah satellite news channel aired 46 seconds of footage it says shows the aftermath of Monday's strike: a collapsed building, with structures crumbled into rubble and broken slabs scattered across the ground.
Several people, including what appeared to be rescue teams, were seen moving carefully across the debris, searching through the wreckage.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes and “committing massacres” in Jawf, as well as deploying a reconnaissance drone and supplying mercenaries with various weaponry.
“The ongoing Saudi aggression against Yemen will not go unanswered or unpunished,” he said.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia’s media ministry.
Saree said later Monday that Houthi forces downed a total of four reconnaissance drones belonging to Saudi Arabia over the past 24 hours, including one that was spotted Monday morning in Bayda province.
The Houthi claim came as forces of the internationally recognized government advanced across multiple fronts in Yemen, including in Jawf, Bayda, Dahle, and Marib provinces.
Strikes on prisons haven’t been uncommon during the war.
In 2022, a strike by the Saudi-led coalition hit a detention facility in the northern province of Saada, killing at least 87 prisoners and wounding about 266 others. Another strike in Sep. 2019 hit a Houthi-run detention facility in southwestern Dhamar province, killing over 100 people and wounding dozens.
The civil war in Yemen has killed at least 150,000 people, according to U.N. estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine. A ceasefire that had mostly held since 2022 is now in tatters.

Gadi Eisenkot unveils Yashar’s final candidate list for 2026 election
Eisenkot's list is heavily focused on security, but each member represents a different sector of Israeli society, which may appeal to many in Israel's dissatisfied center-right
With one day left before the deadline, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar submitted its final electoral list. At 40 candidates, the list is one of the longest and is filled with a mix of legacy politicians and new faces.
With Eisenkot being a former chief of staff, the list has a strong focus on candidates with a background in security and defense, ranging from reservists to commanders, but also a significant contingent of educators and cultural figures.
Yoram Cohen is the list's number 2 and a former head of the Shin Bet. Cohen served for over 30 years in the Shin Bet, monitoring and responding to threats in the West Bank, eventually rising to be the agency's director from 2011 to 2016. Cohen was the first religious person to hold the role.
Cohen returned to the political forefront in 2023, leading the campaign against the Likud's judicial reform from the right, arguing that the reform was tainted by Netanyahu's personal interests.
In a surprise merger, Hili Tropper joined Yashar as number 6 only a day after having split from The Reservists party with Yoaz Hendel. Tropper was a member of Gantz's Blue and White until this year, and served as a minister during Blue and White’s time in government.
Tropper said he joined Eisenkot to "grow, repair, build and do everything" to improve the country and heal the "deep fracture" caused by the war. Aner was at the Nova festival with his friend Hersh Goldberg-Polin and was killed after throwing seven grenades back out of a shelter.
Kamil Abu Rokan, number 13, joined Eisenkot's party in July and represents two major constituencies: the IDF General Staff and the Druze community. Abu Rukun also served as head of COGAT from 2018 until 2021, when he retired. The Abu Rukun family also has deep roots in public service, his father was mayor of his hometown Isfiya for over 20 years. The Druze vote will be an important battlefield for Eisenkot as he tries to sway them from their traditional support for the Likud and more recently in Benny Gantz's Blue and White.
Dvora Sharifian-Bachar, the list's number 14, has perhaps the most interesting background of any politician. Sharifian-Bachar was born just after the Islamic Revolution in Iran and was smuggled out of the country at the age of 7 in a covert Mossad operation. She initially served as a counterterrorism field operative for the Shin Bet, fighting as part of the joint Shin Bet–Israel Police Tequila Team.
Sharifian-Bachar then served in the Mossad, where she specialized in data and cyber intelligence before going on to head the intelligence branch of the Mossad Operations Department. She said upon joining Eisenkot's party in July that that she was there to fight for the periphery and wanted to make clear that the state needs to give "every boy and girl in the periphery the tools to lead and excel."
Eisenkot's list is heavily focused on security, but each member represents a different sector of Israeli society, meaning that what initially appears to be a narrow slate is actually considerably broader. The list may appeal to many in Israel's center-right who have become dissatisfied with the Likud under Netanyahu and are now looking for a new vision that does not compromise on security.
