Record fuel price rise sparks honking protests in Portugal amid public anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:07:58 UTC
02:07:58 KST

A slow-drive protest and blaring car horns marked the day fuel prices rose again in Portugal, with fuel costs hitting record highs across Europe.
Portugal woke up to another rise in fuel prices which, in the case of diesel, reached an all-time high. This time, the price increase, which has been occurring throughout the year, was marked by protests on the country's roads.
In the morning, drivers staged a mass horn protest on the 25 de April Bridge, the crossing that links Lisbon to the city of Almada on the south bank of the Tagus river.
At the same time, further south, a go-slow march towards Galp's refinery in Sines, the Portuguese multinational energy corporation, was getting under way. The protest, organised via WhatsApp and social media, was still ongoing after lunchtime and had no scheduled end time.
Images on social media showed cars with Portuguese flags on their bonnets, sounding their horns. According to the Lusa news agency, protesters were also carrying placards reading "Enough of rising fuel prices" and "families cannot take it any more".
The National Republican Guard told the agency that between 60 and 100 vehicles took part in the protest.
Petrol at highest level since Ukraine invasion
According to projections by the Automobile Club of Portugal (ACP), diesel rose on Monday by 15 cents (to 2.169 euros per litre) and petrol increased by 12 cents (to 2.142 euros per litre).
These amounts do not take into account the reduction in the Tax on Petroleum Products (ISP), applied by the government on an exceptional basis, which set the increases at 12 cents for diesel and 9 cents for petrol.
This is the biggest jump in fuel prices in the last four years and the highest diesel price ever, according to calculations by the Portuguese financial outlet Dinheiro Vivo. In the case of petrol, it is the highest level since the energy crisis triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Fuel prices have been rising across Europe throughout the year. In Germany too, the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine explains that fuel prices have hit a record high, with petrol surpassing the previous record of €2.203 per litre, set in March 2022.
However, Portugal is among the countries with the highest fuel prices.
On Monday, Portugal ranked as the third European country with the most expensive petrol. Only France and Denmark had higher prices. As for diesel, Portugal's position improved with the UK, Italy, France and Denmark ahead.
Portuguese energy minister says rises are in line with Europe
The Portuguese Minister for Environment and Energy, Maria da Graça Carvalho, held a press conference on Monday evening. Maria da Graça Carvalho said that the increase in fuel prices is in line with the rest of Europe, drawing a comparison with France and presenting Spain as an exception.
The minister listed the government's measures to soften the rise in fuel prices, namely the reduction of ISP, the extension of the solidarity gas cylinder scheme and support measures for the agricultural and social sectors.
Responding to the secretary-general of the opposing Socialist Party (PS), Maria da Graça Carvalho also said that "the government is not profiting from this fuel crisis".
Previously, the rise in prices had led the minister to request a study from the Energy Services Regulatory Authority (ERSE). But the study, published in mid-August, found "no evidence of operators taking advantage". It also said that no "rockets and feathers" phenomenon was observed, with prices that rise quickly and fall slowly.
"The results therefore do not support the view that price decreases are passed through persistently more slowly or less fully than price increases," the study says.
ERSE also explained the price difference with Spain by pointing to taxation. But it stressed that in Portugal the tax burden has remained constant, "in line with most countries in the European Union and the eurozone".
Hormuz and refining capacity
The rise in fuel prices in Europe has been linked to the conflict in the Middle East and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz, which has had a disruptive effect on trade routes.
But experts also point to limited refining capacity, even when crude is available. This situation mainly affects diesel.
In terms of taxation, an extraordinary tax on oil companies' profits is now on the table.
According to AFP, the ministers of Portugal, Germany, Italy, Austria, Poland and Spain have sent a letter to Ireland's finance minister so that the issue can be discussed at the next meeting of finance ministers.
The meeting is scheduled for 18 and 19 September in Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the European Union.

Haiti gangs shift operations into countryside, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:07:01 UTC
02:07:01 KST

Haiti gangs shift operations into countryside, report says
Sept 7 - Haiti's armed gangs are increasingly expanding from Port-au-Prince into rural areas, adopting hit-and-run tactics including kidnappings, cattle theft and roadblocks while security and political responses remain focused on the capital, a new report said on Monday.
The analysis, published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime's Haiti Observatory, said the shift amounts to more than an extension of urban gang activity into the countryside.
• Gangs are using small, mobile units to carry out rapid raids, harass communities and move between areas serving as sanctuaries and targets, the report said. The approach allows armed groups to project influence and disrupt daily life without permanently occupying territory.
• The report cited the recent attack on Kenscoff, a mountainous community outside Port-au-Prince, as an example of the changing nature of gang violence. The assault killed dozens of people and involved a mass kidnapping, it said.
• It also highlighted worsening insecurity in Artibonite, one of Haiti's main agricultural regions, where gangs have targeted communities, transport routes and farmland.
• The growing violence in rural areas poses a challenge for Haitian security forces, which the report said lack the personnel, equipment and training needed to counter highly mobile armed groups across mountainous and dispersed terrain.
• The report said a security response alone would be insufficient, calling for measures to protect farmers, restore local economies and address long-running land and community disputes, alongside efforts to disarm and reintegrate gang members. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

AfD victory exposes divisions in France’s far-right as National Rally stays silent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:03:48 UTC
02:03:48 KST

France’s far-right responded in markedly different ways to the AfD’s sweeping victory in Germany’s regional elections, with the National Rally (RN) maintaining a conspicuous silence on Monday while Éric Zemmour’s Reconquête openly celebrated the result.
France's National Rally party reacted to the victory of Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party with a noticeable silence on Monday, a move that reflects its complicated ties to the party.
Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella — who are respectively campaigning to be France's next president and prime minister — made no mention of the AfD after the party took 43.8% of votes in Saxony-Anhalt’s elections, racing ahead of Christian Democratic Union, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party, which secured 17.2%.
Meanwhile, the Reconquête party — which is positioned further to the right than the National Rally and sits in the same group as the AfD in the European Parliament — welcomed the victory, reflecting political divergences within France's far-right.
Although the National Rally's leading figures have yet to comment publicly, other MPs from the party have weighed in. Bardella had also addressed the issue before the vote, when reporters at the Ambrosetti Forum — an annual economic and geopolitical conference held in Italy — questioned him about the prospect of the National Rally renewing ties with the AfD on Saturday.
In response, he said that this was not "planned," but underlined that "the electoral pressure exerted by the AfD in Germany has helped shift the political landscape within [Chancellor Friedrich] Merz's government, as Germany reinstated border controls a few months ago."
A campaign to recover the party's image
The silence at the top of the party is not surprising, given that Marine Le Pen has spent over a decade working to normalise the image of the National Rally (formerly known as the National Front), both at home and abroad, as part of a campaign to move away from the overt racism and antisemitism promoted by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, the party’s founder.
At present, her party is leading in the polls, with around 34 to 36% of respondents stating they intend to vote for her in the first round of the presidential elections scheduled for April 2027, according to a poll by IPSOS/BVA published by the French newspaper Le Parisien on Saturday.
National Rally politician and Patriots for Europe (PfE) MEP Pierre-Romain Thionnet told Euronews that the AfD's result "should not come as a surprise to anyone", arguing that its victory was vested in issues which mainstream parties have not worked to solve: "mass immigration, loss of national identity, and social and industrial decline."
According to the MEP, the result reflects "the collapse of the mainstream parties in favour of political forces that truly represent the aspirations of the European people."
Despite this, he ensured that the National Rally's decision to "no longer be an ally of the AfD" in the European Parliament would remain "unchanged."
"Several members of that political party continue to hold positions on historical and remembrance issues that we find unacceptable, and because there are very significant differences on other issues, such as foreign policy," said Thionnet.
The National Rally party and AfD were formerly part of the Identity and Democracy group, along with Italy’s League and Austria’s Freedom Party (FPÖ), among others. However, things came to a head ahead of the 2024 European Parliamentary elections, following a series of controversies involving some of the AfD's senior figures.
This included comments made by Maximilian Krah, the AfD's lead candidate in the Parliamentary elections, who stated that membership of the Nazi SS did not automatically make someone a criminal, during an interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica.
The Identity and Democracy group voted to exclude the AfD in May 2024, just weeks before the European Parliament elections. Following the election, the AfD helped form a new far-right group, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), which was formally established in July 2024.
Echoing these points, another MEP from the Patriots for Europe group told Euronews that "nothing will move before the French election," stating that "no one wants to be associated with the AfD, even though we have some points in common and cooperate on many topics."
Reconquête comes out in support of the AfD
The National Rally party may be keeping quiet, but the Reconquête party, part of the same political group as the AfD in the European Parliament (Europe of Sovereign Nations), came out in support of the election results.
In an X post shared on Sunday evening, MEP Sarah Knafo described the results as "historic," stating that "the European peoples have shown a great deal of patience. Today, they want to take their destiny back into their own hands. An entire continent is rising up."
Meanwhile, Éric Zemmour, the leader of Reconquête, who has said he will wait until December to announce whether he will run in France's 2027 presidential election, qualified the results as "the hour of truth." In the first round of France's 2022 presidential election, Marine Le Pen took 23.15% of the votes, while the hard-right secured 7.07%.
The Reconquête party aligns itself with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on a number of points — notably on the concept of “remigration” — which the National Rally avoids endorsing explicitly, instead presenting its policy as favouring the systematic expulsion of illegal immigrants and foreign criminals.
According to Gilles Ivaldi, researcher and professor of politics at Sciences Po Paris, the political strategy adopted by Reconquête is more similar to the AfD's than the National Rally's.
"The AfD expresses itself in a more radical and openly far-right manner, if I may say so, whereas the National Rally is currently trying to tone down its platform significantly in order to win the presidential election, because they know that to do this, they need to normalise their image," Ivaldi told Euronews.
"Ahead of the last presidential elections in 2022, we saw two different political strategies emerge: Le Pen continued to try to normalise her image and de-demonise her party, whereas Zemmour pursued a much more aggressive strategy of radicalisation and reclaiming certain political themes."
"I think we need to be careful not to treat the National Rally and Reconquête as completely different, because they share many common views on migration, crime, and a whole range of issues concerning Ukraine and France's proximity to Russia."

Finland has fenced itself off from Russia: Helsinki has completed a large-scale 200-kilometer project
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:00:30 EEST
02:00:30 KST

Finland has fenced itself off from Russia: Helsinki has completed a large-scale 200-kilometer project
Kyiv • UNN
Finland has built about 200 kilometers of barriers along its border with Russia at a cost of €356 million. The system includes fences, cameras, and sensors.
Finland has completed the construction of approximately 200 kilometers of barrier structures along its border with russia. UNN reports this, citing Finnish media and government sources.
The project, implemented over several years following a sharp deterioration in the security situation and cases of instrumentalized migration by the russian federation, cost approximately €356 million.
Details
The official project completion ceremony took place on September 7 in the area of the Nuijamaa border crossing near Lappeenranta. It was attended by Finnish Minister of the Interior Mari Rantanen, Border Guard leadership, and representatives of contractor companies.
Finland's total land border with russia is approximately 1,340 km long. The fence covers approximately 200 km, or about 15% of the border. At the same time, this is not a continuous structure but dozens of separate sections in areas that the Finnish authorities consider most vulnerable to illegal or mass border crossings.
About 140 km of barriers were built in the southeast of the country and in the Kymenlaakso region, another 35 km in North Karelia, and approximately 25 km in Kainuu, Koillismaa, and Lapland. The main fence is approximately 4.5 meters high. The system also includes surveillance cameras, lighting, sensors, loudspeakers, patrol roads, and a strip cleared of vegetation along the border. The technical equipment is designed to automatically notify border guards of suspicious activity.
The project began to be prepared in autumn 2022, and construction of the first pilot section near Imatra began in spring 2023. Large-scale work got underway in 2024. According to the latest estimates, the total construction cost was approximately €356 million, about €22 million less than the initially allocated budget. Annual maintenance of the system is estimated at approximately €1.5 million.
One of the main reasons cited by the Finnish authorities for constructing the fence was the threat of so-called instrumentalized migration. In autumn 2023, citizens of third countries began arriving en masse at border crossing points from the russian side without the necessary documents.
According to Reuters, approximately 1,300 asylum seekers crossed the russian-Finnish border between August and December 2023. Helsinki accused moscow of deliberately directing migrants toward the border for the purpose of political pressure. russia denied the accusations. Following this, Finland closed the land border crossing points on its border with the russian federation. They remain closed today. In June 2026, the Finnish government decided to maintain the restrictions indefinitely due to the risk of a recurrence of instrumentalized migration.
In addition, at the beginning of September, the Finnish government proposed extending until the end of 2028 the validity of a special border security law that, under exceptional circumstances, allows the temporary restriction of the acceptance of applications for international protection in certain areas.
Minister of the Interior Mari Rantanen also did not rule out that Finland might build additional sections of fencing in the future and secure funding for them from the European Union.
Recall
A month earlier, Spain introduced border controls at all air and sea crossings with Italy due to a dispute over migrants. Italy had previously suspended the Schengen Agreement, citing an influx of migrants to Ceuta.

US now accesses more than half of Australia’s military bases: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:58:23 UTC
01:58:23 KST

Esra Tekin
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The US military and its defense companies have access to 110 military facilities in Australia, or more than half nationwide, The Guardian reported on Monday, citing data compiled by the Nautilus Institute, a California-based think tank.
The data shows that the US military controls 17 facilities on the Australian mainland and has access to 75 military facilities operated by Australia while American defense companies have access to a further 18 facilities.
The number of military facilities in Australia that are either controlled by or accessible to the US military and American defense companies has reached 110, accounting for more than half of all military facilities in the country.
Richard Tanter, honorary professor of political and social studies at the University of Melbourne, who prepared the study, said this was not a matter of penetration but of pervasiveness, noting that more than half of the defense facilities examined had some level of American access.
Tanter argued that for more than a decade, the US has been developing the capacity to use Australia for intensive military operations in the event of a potential war with China, while Australia has fully “aligned itself with American strategic planning.”
The 92 defense facilities accessible to the US military are reportedly used for intelligence gathering, access to satellite data, interception of communications, training, deployment of military assets, and as logistics hubs storing weapons, ammunition, and fuel.
The joint US-Australian intelligence facility at Pine Gap, north-central Australia, is reported to play a critical role in identifying targets for US military strikes.
It hosts a ground control station for signals intelligence satellites, a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems, and a facility used to intercept foreign satellite communications.
Under a force posture agreement, US forces and contractors are granted unimpeded access to and use of agreed military facilities, provided that Australia’s sovereignty is fully respected.
The US military presence is expected to expand further next year, with as many as 1,200 US personnel set to operate from the HMAS Stirling naval base on Garden Island in Western Australia.
The Australian government, however, says the presence of American troops will constitute a “rotation” rather than a permanent base.
Former Defense Minister Christopher Pyne said the AUKUS security and defense partnership between Australia, the US, and the UK is “much more than submarine procurement.”
He said the partnership effectively creates a new base for US submarines in the Indian Ocean, providing the United States with a “huge strategic advantage.”
Current Defense Minister Richard Marles, meanwhile, said the “US presence is growing” in Australia and stressed that this is important for national security.
He said the American military presence on the continent would increase over the next several years.
 
Australians’ trust in US declines
Separately, Australians’ trust in the US has reportedly declined.
According to a Lowy Institute poll, the proportion of Australians who trust the US to act responsibly in international affairs has fallen to 31%, while only 21% trust US President Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs.
A survey by the Australia Institute found that 59% of Australians believe the country’s interests would be better protected through a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the United States.
Emma Shortis, director of the Australia Institute’s international and security affairs program, argued that Australia’s increasing integration with the US military is progressively weakening the country’s capacity to make independent and sovereign decisions.
Albert Palazzo of the University of New South Wales also argued that the accelerating US military buildup poses a risk to Australia’s security, accusing the government of “waltzing” the country toward a war between the US and China.
Vince Scappatura, the author of a book on the US lobby and Australian defense policy, described US access to bases across Australia as a “second wave of colonization” and said Australia was increasingly becoming a “forward element” for the projection of US military power in the region.

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) head Rafael Grossi has said that giving the UN nuclear agency access to key nuclear facilities in Iran would have "positive repercussions" for Tehran, as a draft resolution reportedly proposes referring Tehran to the UN Security Council.
"The best, shortest way for a positive outcome is for Iran to engage with us," Grossi told a press conference on Monday after opening the quarterly meeting of the IAEA board of governors.
"If Iran engages with us in a serious dialogue, we can start getting access. I can guarantee to you that this will have very, very positive repercussions," he said.
The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day war in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged access.
UNSC resolution
A resolution drafted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany expected to be submitted and voted on this week seeks to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The draft asks Grossi to "submit this resolution to all members of the agency and to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations," AFP reported.
Asked whether such a referral was the right course of action, Grossi said that "my job with Iran continues, irrespective of the resolution".
Before the June 2025 strikes, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent, which is close to the 90 percent needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67 percent limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
In a statement ahead of the meeting, Grossi called the lack of contact with Iran "regrettable".
"These issues are not going to disappear until we address them, until we have the necessary access, until we can return," he said.
Iran's mission to the UN on X called the draft resolution a "new desperate action" that would bring "no benefit".
In June, the board approved a Western resolution demanding that Iran immediately provide information and give access to its uranium stockpile and production facilities.

Ukraine Turns Russian Stronghold Into a Trap, Retakes Rybine Near Huliaipole
Ukrainian forces have retaken the village of Rybine near Huliaipole after a months-long operation that first severed Russian supply routes before troops moved in to clear the settlement, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Regiment reported on September 7.
Russian forces captured Rybine on January 20 and subsequently turned the village into an important defensive position in the Huliaipole sector.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
By summer, however, Ukrainian troops had begun systematically dismantling the Russian position rather than launching an immediate frontal assault.
The first stage focused on logistics. Troops from the regiment’s 2nd Assault Battalion cut a key supply route used by Russian forces to bring ammunition, food and fuel into Rybine.
Once that artery was disrupted, the Russian units inside the village became increasingly isolated. Reinforcing the position and maintaining regular supplies became considerably more difficult, while Ukraine also restricted Russian attempts to move additional troops into the cut-off settlement.
Ukrainian forces then moved to the final stage of the operation, clearing Russian troops from Rybine itself.
On July 30, Ukrainian soldiers raised the national flag over the village, marking its return to Ukrainian control.
The 1st Assault Regiment stressed that Rybine was not retaken in a single assault. Instead, the operation relied on gradually weakening the Russian position by disrupting its logistics, limiting reinforcement routes, and only then moving to clear the settlement.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian forces would need more than six additional years to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the Donetsk region if their current rate of advance continues, putting the potential timeline well beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.

Brother of prominent Egyptian journalist dies in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:56:24 UTC
01:56:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Brother of prominent journalist dies in Egyptian prison amid reported medical neglect
The brother of a prominent Egyptian journalist died after suffering a heart attack in his cell amid harsh conditions, sparking concerns over medical negligence.
The detainee, Mohammed Alaa el-Din Abdel-Azim, brother of Mohammed Nasser, died aged 64 around an hour and a half after suffering a heart attack.
Prison authorities reportedly did not intervene to save him, despite calls for help.
Abdel-Azim was detained in February 2018 on charges including mocking state institutions and insulting a police officer. The prosecution initially ordered his detention for 15 days pending investigation; however, he has remained behind bars since.
Some reports state his arrest was also linked to his brother, who is an exiled critic of President Abdelfattah al-Sisi.
According to Jawar, a platform that monitors and documents detainees’ cases in Egypt, several detainees banged on cell doors to get attention from prison guards when Abdel-Azim was suffering from a heart attack.
The report further added that Abdel-Aziz had been suffering from a severe heart condition but had been kept behind bars since 2018 despite his health problems.
Abdel-Azim was transferred to the Wadi el Gedid prison last year, located in the western desert, a move that reportedly worsened his physical and mental health, with repeated court hearings and dislocation taking a toll on him.
Targeting of dissidents’ families
The Association for Freedom of Thought and Expression said the case was part of a broader trend of targeting family members of dissidents, with Nasser considering his brother's arrest an attempt to pressure him into stopping his criticism of the government.
Egyptian political activist Osama Rushdi told local media that Abdel-Azim’s death was part of a series of retaliatory acts he said the Egyptian government was carrying out against dissidents living abroad, by targeting their family members and relatives.
“Targeting the relatives of Egyptian dissidents abroad has become one of the methods of punishment and revenge used by authorities to pressure those who express their opinions, after failing to silence them or reach them in countries where they reside,” he said.
He said Abdel-Azim’s death following years of detention “reveals the extent to which this revenge can extend, to the point that individuals with no connection to political activity pay the price for the stances of a family member,” he continued.
Rushdi noted that Abdel-Azim’s death should not be viewed as an isolated incident, but as part of a broader pattern of a crackdown on dissidents and their families, giving the example of Mona el-Shazly, a UK-based dissident, who has had five family members detained due to her activism.
“This is beyond traditional political arrest; this is cross-border repression, where the targeting is not limited to the individual dissident, but extends to their family to force them into silence and to curtail their activism,” Rushdi said.
Activists have raised the alarm over the death, accusing authorities of failing to intervene and save Abdel-Azim despite repeated pleas for help.
The death has also garnered attention due to Nasser’s role presenting the popular Egypt Today programme, on the opposition Mekameleen channel, which is based in Turkey. As one of the most prominent media Egyptian voices critical of the regime, authorities have accused him of incitement, spreading false news and sentenced him in absentia.
In December 2015, an Egyptian court sentenced Nasser to life imprisonment in a case where authorities accused him of leading a terrorist group. On another occasion, Egypt’s State Information Service accused Nasser of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
The death has also shed light on the plight of elderly and sick detainees held in Egyptian prisons.
To date, no official information has been published regarding Abdel-Azim’s medical conditions, or prison authorities’ efforts to assist him.
Activists have called for an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death, as well as his medical record and reasons for his continued detention for so many years.

Jerusalem currently hosts embassies of the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and Somalia’s so-called breakaway Somaliland region, which is not internationally recognized.

Israel has been intensifying efforts to repair its foreign relations amid global popular and official anger over its US-backed genocide in the Gaza Strip since Oct. 8, 2023.
In 2017, US President Donald Trump, during his first term, recognized Jerusalem, both its eastern and western parts, as Israel’s claimed capital, the occupying power, and decided to move the US Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.

At least 11 climbers were killed and six others remained missing Monday after a massive avalanche swept through Russia’s Caucasus Mountains, authorities said, in a disaster captured in dramatic videos that spread across social media.
Footage from the Kabardino-Balkaria region shows an enormous mass of snow and ice racing down the mountainside beneath clear skies. Investigators believe the avalanche may have been triggered by the collapse of a hanging glacier, though the cause has not been definitively established.
The avalanche struck the Bezengi Gorge at around 5 p.m. local time Sunday while a group of 33 climbers was in the area.
Eleven were confirmed dead and six were still unaccounted for, while the remaining members of the group managed to descend safely, according to Russian authorities.
A search involving 56 rescue personnel continued Monday, supported by an Mi-8 helicopter.
‘You only see things like this in movies’
One video posted online was filmed by tourists watching the avalanche from a distance.
“Damn! You only see things like this in movies,” one man can be heard saying as the avalanche surges down the slope.
Another asks whether they should leave.
“Yes, let’s go, let’s go,” the first man replies, before adding: “But how can you just walk away from a sight like this?”
The tourists apparently did not know at the time that climbers had been buried by the avalanche.
Bezengi Gorge stretches for about 14 kilometers, or nearly 9 miles, near Russia’s border with Georgia and is surrounded by some of the highest peaks in the central Caucasus, rising from roughly 4,000 to 5,200 meters.
The area is also home to the vast Bezengi Glacier and attracts climbers drawn to its steep, rugged terrain.
A region known for dangerous conditions
The Caucasus Mountains attract thousands of mountaineers, skiers and snowboarders each year but are notorious for rapidly changing weather and hazardous alpine conditions.
Nearby Mount Elbrus, the highest mountain in Europe, records an estimated 15 to 30 deaths each year, many involving climbers who are unprepared for its extreme conditions.
Earlier this year, another enormous avalanche caused alarm in the same Russian region after sweeping through a ski area on the slopes of Elbrus. That incident ended without fatalities.
Sunday’s disaster, however, has left rescue teams racing to locate the six climbers who remain missing as authorities investigate whether collapsing glacier ice set off the deadly cascade.

What is Israel's reported 'grey line' plan for southern Lebanon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:54:18 UTC
01:54:18 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Israel's reported 'grey line' plan for southern Lebanon?
The Israeli military could establish a "grey line" in southern Lebanon that would effectively see it pull back closer to the border while maintaining its freedom of movement to strike.
According to a report by Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan, the security establishment is considering a significant reduction in forces deployed in southern Lebanon and a withdrawal from some forward positions, in exchange for establishing a new security zone extending three to four kilometres inside Lebanese territory from the border.
The plan, which has yet to be finalised and has not received approval from Israel’s political leadership, provides for the establishment of new military positions along the proposed line, where Israeli forces would be stationed. Tel Aviv claims this would be to protect northern communities in Israel from Hezbollah attacks and prevent the militant group from approaching the border again.
But talk of reducing the deployment does not amount to a full withdrawal. Keeping Israeli forces as far as four kilometres inside Lebanese territory would, in practice, mean maintaining a military presence across a strip of land containing towns, neighbourhoods and agricultural areas, while limiting residents’ ability to return to their homes and cultivate their land.
The absence of an official map of the proposed line has raised several key questions, including which towns and villages would fall within it.
Israel invaded southern Lebanon during fighting with Hezbollah at the start of October 2024 and retained five hilltops along the border. Since March this year, when all-out war resumed, Israeli forces have expanded their invasion of the region and now occupy swathes of southern Lebanon.
Earlier this year, the Israeli military established what it called the "yellow line", a security zone along the entire border spanning between eight and ten kilometres inside Lebanese territory. The zone includes dozens of southern towns and villages, many of which have been completely razed or heavily damaged as part of Israel’s scorched-earth policy.
Political analyst Karim Bitar said the terminology surrounding the various zones and lines risked obscuring what he described as a broader Israeli strategy.
"Expressions that are constantly used – buffer zone, security zone, yellow line, blue line, green line, now grey line – are quite problematic because they end up giving the impression that what is happening is merely a security issue, while we are facing a clearly expressed expansionist policy," Bitar said.
"What is striking is that the Israelis and their leading officials – I’m talking about Netanyahu and Katz, not only Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – are saying pretty much out loud what they are going to do," he added, in reference to Israel's premier, defence, national security and finance ministers respectively.
Ali al-Taher
According to Israeli reports, the proposed "grey line" is linked to the completion of operations in the Ali al-Taher ridge and the destruction of alleged Hezbollah infrastructure and tunnels that Israel says it has found beneath the hills.
The Israeli security establishment believes its control of the high ground has allowed it to reassess the scale of its troop deployment and move to a defensive line closer to the border.
Israel recently announced its capture of the highly strategic ridge, which overlooks the city of Nabatiyeh and large swathes of southern Lebanon and parts of northern Israel. Israel says one of Hezbollah’s largest command centres and military complexes lies beneath the ridge and plans to blow it up soon.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said the capture of the ridge had given Israel full control of the security zone, or "yellow line", along the border.
Hezbollah has neither confirmed nor denied Israel’s capture claims, nor has it responded to statements about blowing up the alleged underground fortress.
But shifting from forward positions to sites closer to the border, as proposed with the "grey line", does not resolve the fundamental issue. Even in its most reduced form, the plan would keep Israeli forces inside Lebanese territory, while a full withdrawal remains tied to unresolved security and political conditions, including a widescale deployment of the Lebanese army, the future of Hezbollah's arsenal and the outcome of US-sponsored negotiations.
Under a US-sponsored framework agreement signed in June between Beirut and Tel Aviv, Israel was supposed to start gradually handing over occupied towns and villages to the Lebanese army, which in turn would ensure that all Hezbollah infrastructure and weapons were dismantled and confiscated.
But implementation has made little progress as Israel refuses to withdraw and has escalated its deadly attacks on the south in recent nights, killing and injuring dozens. Israel says it will not pull out of Lebanon until Hezbollah fully disarms.
Hezbollah, for its part, has rejected the June deal and any disarmament efforts without an Israeli withdrawal.
Negotiation tactic?
The leak of the proposed "grey line" may be part of a negotiation process rather than an announcement of a final military plan. Israel could present a reduction in its occupying forces as a concession while effectively maintaining a security zone inside Lebanon, while demanding that Beirut take steps to extend state authority over the south.
Bitar compared the proposal to Israel’s use of territorial divisions during the Oslo Accords process in the occupied West Bank, arguing that such arrangements could allow Israel to delay difficult decisions while continuing to establish facts on the ground.
"What we are seeing in Lebanon is straight out of the Oslo playbook," he said. "At the time, Israel also divided the West Bank into areas A, B and C, and would often use this as a delaying tactic or a negotiation tactic whenever there was intense US pressure."
"They would promise to give more autonomy to one of the regions or to rein in the settlers, but ultimately they continued implementing their policy of establishing facts on the ground that rapidly became irreversible."
"I do not buy this idea that they will pull back closer to the border. Maybe right after the Israeli elections, if Israel needs a rebranding or wants to give the impression that it is negotiating in good faith, it might accept a few gestures of goodwill. But deep down, I think the strategy is to maintain an indefinite occupation of south Lebanon."
It also remains unclear whether areas that could be vacated by Israeli forces under the new "grey line" proposal would be handed directly to the Lebanese army or left devastated, under constant Israeli surveillance and within range of Israeli fire.
Negotiations between Lebanon and Israel have stalled, and a new date for talks this month, set to take place in Rome, is yet to be confirmed.
Bitar said the uncertainty surrounding the talks and the proposed security arrangements should make Lebanon wary of expecting an Israeli withdrawal.
"Many in Lebanon still succumb to wishful thinking by saying that these negotiations and this trilateral framework will end up leading to Israeli concessions," he said. "The time has come to wake up and smell the coffee and realise that what is happening in Lebanon is pretty much what happened 30 years ago with Oslo, when the peace process became a mere process."
"We are witnessing a similar situation in Lebanon, where all the delicate issues are being indefinitely postponed and we are talking of pilot zones, and even in these zones Israel is not showing good faith."
"The Lebanese army is facing an impossible situation, so there are few reasons to be optimistic and to believe these latest Israeli statements that they will pull back closer to the border."
Israel's offensive on Lebanon has killed more than 8,900 people, including 253 children, and injured more than 30,600, since it began in October 2023.

Germany plans “Cyberdome” and mobile anti-drone units after Leipzig airport sabotage attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:53:47 UTC
01:53:47 KST

Germany’s Interior Ministry is preparing a package of measures to protect the country from Russian drone attacks, computer network intrusions, and acts of sabotage, according to a Bild report citing Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt. The measures are being developed following an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, which Berlin has blamed on Russia.
Dobrindt’s plan calls for expanding the federal police mobile anti-drone units. Teams equipped with helicopters and specialized vehicles are expected to be based in Frankfurt, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
They would be tasked with protecting airports, train stations, and other major transport hubs, along with Berlin’s government district. In addition to intercepting drones, the units would be responsible for defusing bombs and other explosive devices.
Operators of critical infrastructure — including water and energy companies, as well as defense plants — would also be given the authority to counter drones on their own. The proposed powers would allow them not only to detect drones but also to actively repel attacks.
Dobrindt told Bild that Russian hybrid attacks had become an everyday reality. He cited the facts of drones carrying explosives, agent activity, network intrusions, and acts of sabotage.
Another part of the plan would expand the use of artificial intelligence, biometric facial recognition, and video surveillance at train stations and other locations. The technologies would be used to identify people preparing attacks or espionage operations and to automatically detect weapons and suspicious behavior.
To counter cyberattacks, the German authorities plan to create a national system called “Cyberdome,” which Bild described as a network of digital sensors designed to detect and repel attempts to break into government and corporate systems.
In early August, Leipzig/Halle Airport temporarily suspended operations after a drone with a detonator was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft. A separate cargo plane was diverted to Hanover due to the closure and struck an unidentified object while still near Leipzig; police found damage to the front of the aircraft after it landed.
Investigators later identified two individuals that it suspects participated in preparations for the attack: a Russian-born man carrying a Latvian passport and a Belarus-born man who holds a Russian passport.
German investigators believe the first man organized logistics and acted as an instructor. The second was identified through traces of DNA found both on the drone and on an antenna near the airport. Three drones, either intact or in pieces, were eventually discovered at the scene.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of organizing the attack, citing the results of its police investigation and intelligence findings. Berlin said that in response to the incident it would close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn effective Sept. 18, terminate an agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin, and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens.
The Russian authorities rejected the accusations, calling the incident a “provocation.”
On Aug. 28, a collection of European countries bordering the Baltic Sea said they planned to create a task force to counter drones and other hybrid threats. At a meeting in Flensburg, Dobrindt said the group was intended to ensure rapid information sharing. The initiative followed a wider rise in drone sightings near European airports, as well as sabotage incidents involving undersea cables and gas pipelines.

Ukraine’s Brave1 says it can down Russia’s Banderol missiles with  cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:53:05 UTC
01:53:05 KST

Ukraine says it has found a way to shoot down Russia's Banderol jet missiles for less than the missiles themselves cost. A system from a developer in the Brave1 defense-tech cluster has already destroyed at least four of them, Brave1 said, releasing video of the intercepts.
The point is the price tag, not the kills. The Banderol is built to be cheap for Russia and expensive for Ukraine to stop, forcing Kyiv to spend scarce, costly air-defense missiles on a low-cost weapon. A counter that costs less than the target flips that math back against Russia.
A cluster developer downs four Banderols
The footage Brave1 shared shows a defender in the cluster hitting at least four Banderol missiles.
"The cost of interception is substantially cheaper than the cost of the drone-missiles themselves," the cluster said.
It added that several products capable of countering the Banderol now exist, and that it is scaling the ones that work.
Kronshtadt built the missile to bleed defenses
The S8000 Banderol is a hybrid of a cruise missile and a jet-powered attack drone, made by the sanctioned Russian firm Kronshtadt, which also builds the Orion reconnaissance drone that launches it. It flies at a cruising speed of 520 to 560 km/h and up to 650 km/h at full throttle, and carries a 114.3-kilogram fragmentation-high-explosive warhead, of which 49.5 kilograms is explosive.
The design is built for cheap mass production: it runs on a Chinese hobby turbojet sold online for about $16,000, and Ukrainian media have put the cost of a single Banderol near $100,000, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Russia has used it to strike Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, and Black Sea ports.
Ukraine keeps finding cheap answers
Brave1's system is the newest in a pattern of low-cost counters. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s. The task now is to turn scattered successes into enough deployed systems to blunt a weapon Russia is firing in growing numbers, which is what Brave1 says it is racing to do.

Asia-Pacific media champion own voice in AI era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:52:59 UTC
01:52:59 KST

In an age when algorithms have the power to both empower and mislead, media leaders from across the Asia-Pacific gathered in a southern Chinese innovation hub, pledging to uphold journalistic responsibility while championing a distinctive narrative for the region.
The Asia-Pacific Media Forum opened on Saturday in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, with the theme of "Building a Path to Shared Prosperity for the Asia-Pacific Community: Media Consensus and Action."
More than 400 representatives from over 40 countries and regions, as well as UN agencies and international organizations, attended the event. At the opening ceremony, 16 founding organizations from China and abroad jointly formed the Organizing Committee of the Asia-Pacific Media Partnership Program.
Participating guests emphasized that development and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region depend on the active participation of media. The media are expected to share stories of openness and integration, provide comprehensive coverage of the region's progress and achievements across various fields, and help foster a favorable public opinion environment for the region's open development.
RESPONSIBILITY, CREDIBILITY AS CORE VALUES IN AI ERA
Artificial intelligence (AI), as an efficient tool for journalists, can also create misinformation and deepfakes on an unprecedented scale, according to Nur-ul Afida Kamaludin, chief executive officer of the Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama).
"Technology must therefore enhance journalism rather than replace its fundamental values," she said at the forum, adding that accuracy, balance, fairness, transparency and human accountability must remain at the heart of media work.
"In recent times there has been a lot of talk about the digital transformation of the media, but at the current stage the debate leads us to ask ourselves how we do this transformation without losing our journalistic responsibility," said Felix Paz Quiroz, general director of the Peruvian news agency Andina.
"Technology has allowed us to multiply our ability to report, but trust continues to depend on values that digital cannot replace," he concluded, highlighting the importance of verification, transparency, neutrality, ethics and responsibility.
U Ye Tint, deputy minister for Information of Myanmar, also cautioned against the spread of fake and false news in the era of AI, stressing that this makes the media even more critical in safeguarding peace, stability and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region, as well as in building a stable, peaceful and harmonious society.
"Through responsible journalism, quality content and greater cooperation, the media can serve as a constructive force in bringing our peoples closer together," he noted.
In July, 29 countries signed an agreement in Shanghai on establishing the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization to cope with opportunities and challenges posed by thinking machines.
REGION'S OWN VOICE
Aminath Namza, chairperson of Public Service Media of Maldives, noted that while much of the narrative about the Global South has centered on its vulnerabilities and crises, it is equally important to highlight its achievements and contributions to the world.
"Because some of the smallest nations can have stories from which the world can learn," she said.
Nur-ul Afida shared a similar opinion. "The Asia-Pacific is more than a collection of crises, disputes and economic statistics. It is home to diverse histories, cultures, aspirations and human stories that deserve to be understood," she said.
To better tell the region's stories, Virgandhi Prayudantoro, chief editor of Indonesia's national news agency LKBN Antara, stressed the importance of cooperation.
"Together, we can deepen media cooperation through joint reporting initiatives, collaborative learning, and regional knowledge-sharing, providing a robust platform for intellectual exchange and support for APEC members," he said.
Under its Asia-Pacific media partnership framework, Xinhua News Agency has launched a training program for 100 Asia-Pacific media professionals this year, offering immersive sessions on China's media integration, AI applications, AIGC content creation and urban dissemination innovation.
Consensus should be translated into practical action through the exchange of news content and professional experience, joint reporting projects, expanded exchange programs for young journalists, regional fact-checking networks, and the ethical use of AI, said U Ye Tint.
China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in November this year, which will mark the country's third hosting of the event following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.
This year marks the APEC "China Year," with the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." Approximately 300 APEC-related meetings and events will take place in multiple Chinese cities throughout the year.
Adjacent to Hong Kong, Shenzhen was one of China's first special economic zones and has since evolved, over four decades, into a global hub for innovation and advanced manufacturing.

Kosovo joins US-led Gaza International Stabilisation Force
Balkan state joins short list of countries agreeing to send peacekeepers to Palestinian enclave.
Kosovo has agreed to join the short list of countries signing up to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) in Gaza.
The small Muslim-majority Balkan nation signed on Monday a formal agreement to join the United Nations-mandated force, according to a social media post by the United States-backed Board of Peace.
“Representatives of the Republic of Kosovo, the Board of Peace & the International Stabilization Force signed the Participating Country Agreement for the inclusion of Kosovo in the ISF,” the post said.
The accord, signed by Kosovo Security Force Commander Lieutenant-General Bashkim Jashari and US ISF Commander Major-General Jasper Jeffers, formally establishes the Kosovo’s inclusion in the planned force.
“The landmark event underscores Kosovo’s commitment to the ISF mission and its continued support for President [Donald] Trump’s 20-point peace plan”, according to a Board of Peace statement.
The plan is a US-Israeli framework agreement introduced one year ago to end the war in Gaza.
Among its provisions, it envisages the creation of a multinational security mission to maintain stability, manage demilitarisation and train a Palestinian police force to oversee security in post-conflict Gaza.
Countries confirmed to be contributing troops include Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania and Uganda.
Turkiye will not participate after Israel vetoed Ankara’s involvement.
Roadblocks
Israel’s government approved key legal measures to allow for the entry of the ISF to Gaza in July, with an official saying the force will operate “in full coordination with” the Israeli military, according to the Times of Israel.
But deployment of the ISF has met roadblocks due to disagreements on the timing of the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the disarmament of Hamas.
On Monday, Nikolay Mladenov, high representative for the Board of Peace, said Israel must implement its commitments under the Gaza peace roadmap for the process to move forward, according to the Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency.
“We are still at the point at which we need to make sure that what has been agreed is going to be implemented and is going to change significantly the lives of the people in Gaza,” he said.
“Unfortunately, we’re not there yet,” he added, saying discussions were continuing with Israel on “the implementation of their part of the commitments” required to move the process forward.
Mladenov told Al Jazeera last month the board had “determined the mechanism for deploying the [ISF] and its deployment locations in the Gaza Strip”.
The force’s “advance elements should arrive in the Gaza Strip soon”, he added.
In August, the Trump administration told Congress it is committing more than $206 million to the ISF.
Reuters reports the funds will go towards equipment, infrastructure, vehicles and operational costs. An additional $6 million would repurpose US armored vehicles to support the force.

Forty-five people were placed in home quarantine in France after being identified as high-risk contacts of a teenager diagnosed with the Andes strain of hantavirus, France Inter reported on Monday.

Russian Su-35 fighter jets collide over Kursk, killing pilot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:51:08 UTC
01:51:08 KST

- Russian military channel Fighterbomber reported that two Su-35S fighter jets collided in Russia's Kursk region, killing one pilot and seriously injuring another.
- The report claims 10 confirmed Su-35S losses since Russia's invasion began, attributed to Ukrainian air defenses, strike drones, and aviation incidents, a figure that could not be independently verified.
Two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided in Russia’s Kursk region, according to Fighterbomber, a Telegram channel with reported ties to the Russian Aerospace Forces. Follow-up reports indicate one pilot was killed in the collision and another was seriously injured, though the full circumstances of the incident are still being determined.
Neither Russia’s Defense Ministry nor Ukrainian officials had confirmed these details independently at the time of this report. Kursk region, which borders Ukraine, has been the site of repeated Russian aircraft losses since Ukrainian forces launched a cross-border incursion there in August 2024, and it remains an active zone for Russian aviation operations.
The Su-35S is a twin-engine, highly maneuverable fourth-generation-plus fighter that Russia has used extensively during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, both for air superiority missions and to escort strike aircraft.
The total number of confirmed Su-35S losses since the war began is 10 aircraft, attributing the losses to a mix of Ukrainian air defense systems, strike drones, and various aviation incidents.
Russian military channels and independent Russian outlets have documented several Su-35S losses over the course of the war that were not caused by Ukrainian action at all. Independent Russian investigative outlet The Insider has reported at least two cases in which Russia’s own air defense systems shot down Su-35S jets by mistake, once near Mariupol and separately near Tokmak in the Zaporizhzhia region, incidents Fighterbomber itself has publicly acknowledged and, in one case, used to warn Russian pilots that their own air defenses posed a greater danger than Ukraine’s. Ukraine’s air force has also claimed several confirmed shootdowns of Su-35S aircraft through more conventional means, including one in Kherson region in May 2023 and another along the Kursk front in June 2025.
That June 2025 engagement, first reported by German outlet Bild, involved a Ukrainian-operated F-16 that shot down a Su-35 near the town of Korenevo in Kursk Oblast, marking the first known aerial kill by an F-16 under Ukrainian command. According to Bild’s reporting, Ukraine’s air force used a Swedish ASC 890 airborne early warning aircraft to detect the Russian jet at a range of 200 to 300 kilometers and relay its position to the F-16 pilot in real time, who then fired an AIM-120 missile that forced the Su-35 pilot to eject.
The Su-35S has drawn scrutiny throughout the war both for its combat losses and for a series of incidents unrelated to enemy fire, including at least one crash attributed to engine failure. Russia has continued flying the aircraft on the front lines despite the losses, reflecting its role as one of the Russian air force’s primary fighters alongside the older Su-30SM and the Su-57 stealth fighter.
The condition of the injured pilot and further details on the collision, including whether either aircraft was destroyed on impact or during an attempted landing, have not been independently confirmed.

A health MOT is just one step towards prevention | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:50:56 UTC
01:50:56 KST

Devi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies. Such measures can help identify health risks earlier. However, I would take issue with her suggestion that a “health MOT” is “precisely what prevention is all about” (Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see, 2 September).
Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.
Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.
In England, people living in the most disadvantaged communities can expect about 19 fewer years of healthy life than those in the least disadvantaged communities. Free testing is welcome, but a genuinely upstream approach would focus not only on identifying risk, but also on tackling the social and economic conditions that make healthy choices possible in the first place.
Dr Louise Lawson
Lecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow
Prof Devi Sridhar is right to emphasise prevention and the importance of identifying cardiovascular risk early. However, screening is only the first step. As a GP in London, I worry that suggesting annual “health MOTs” risks creating expectations that the NHS currently lacks the capacity to meet. Without substantial investment in general practice and community services, what happens after we identify millions more people with pre-diabetes, obesity, mildly raised cholesterol or borderline hypertension?
These patients will understandably seek advice, support and follow-up from their GP. Yet many of these conditions are driven less by a lack of diagnosis than by wider societal factors such as diet, inactivity, housing and poverty. They are not problems that can simply be solved with a prescription, or advice.
Articles advocating routine health checks without this context may also encourage patients to request annual MOTs from their GP when these are not clinically indicated or commissioned. At a time when primary care is already under intense pressure, increasing demand without increasing capacity risks diverting resources from those with established illness and greatest need. Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows.
Dr James Hibberd
Barnet, London
 I always appreciate Devi Sridhar’s articles for their straightforward and sensible approach to health. However, could I humbly suggest that she reconsiders the inclusion of a press-ups test? For far too many of us, particularly those with the musculature of an anaemic grasshopper, nightmares of the school gymnasium spring to mind, with those familiar and ignominious collapses on to a sweat-speckled floor. Never to be forgotten.
Bob Forster
Shipton-under-Wychwood, Oxfordshire
 I agree with Devi Sridhar that annual screening tests offer the prospect of improving the health of the nation, starting with NHS cholesterol testing for 40- to 84-year-olds. Alas, I’ve just had my 85th birthday, so I’m presumably fit only for the knacker’s yard.

AI transcriptions are no time-saving measure for doctors | Letters

I am an out-of-hours GP, and I am glad to see a news report on this issue, which has been causing me increasing concern at work (Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns, 31 August). There are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand and contradict itself, which can lead to dangers for the patient, but I will concentrate on the supposed “time-saving” aspect.
Many of the patients I see will have been assessed by someone else first on the phone, and I am used to reading through a triage assessment before I call in the patient. My heart sinks when I see that AI has been used – the consultation is invariably long, with duplications, and sometimes contradictions. Often, any history I take turns out to be significantly different from what is listed. So I can never trust that it is correct – I can state with certainty that I find meaningful errors far more often in AI consultations than in those typed out by colleagues.
You may blame the original clinician, but anyone who has tried to proofread something they have created, particularly under time pressure, will know how difficult this is. So how can this save time, when the first clinician has to check through a long, repetitive account, and the second clinician can’t trust what is written and has to check it again?
In addition, turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn, as any medical student can tell you. If we do not learn and maintain this skill, we will lose a lot, and so will our patients.
Dr Mary Gibbs
Manchester

A consultant I worked for as a secretary had a week’s trial of voice recognition software. He gave up the idea when “I recommend two weeks on lansoprazole” turned into suggesting a two-week holiday on Lanzarote. A prescription I’m sure the patient would have been more than happy to try.
Debbie Cameron
Formby, Merseyside

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he does not feel a need to step down amid his Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party's loss in Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
"I am thinking non-stop about how we can return to working successfully across party lines. Giving up is not an option for me," Merz said at a news conference in Berlin, fielding questions about his potential resignation in the wake of the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt election. Merz explained that he sees it as his duty, as well as the federal government's, to "open up opportunities for the next generation."
"Our responsibility, including my personal responsibility, is exactly to make sure our children and grandchildren have the same opportunity to live in a country such as Germany in an atmosphere of freedom, peace and prosperity. This is our responsibility. And I do not dodge this responsibility," the German leader said.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election was held on September 6. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive victory with 43.8% of the vote, according to early official results. This was the AfD’s best-ever result in any German state, doubling its share of the vote from the previous state election five years ago. Merz’s CDU came in second, losing more than half of its vote share compared with 2021. The Christian Democrats received just 17.2% of the vote, the CDU’s worst-ever result in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) scored third with 9.3% of the vote. The Greens received 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%. The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance -- Reason and Justice) also cleared the threshold to enter the Landtag with 5.3%.
Experts suggest that CDU's defeat reflects disillusionment that has grown in Germany for Merz's policy course, including toward Russia.

Israel mulls letting in Syrian Druze workers amid labour shortages
Israeli authorities are considering a proposal that would allow members of Syria’s Druze minority to enter the country to work amid ongoing labour shortages, particularly in the agricultural sector, the Israeli news website Ynet has reported.
The proposal would allow Syrian Druze to work on farms but would also give them vocational training in a number of fields, such as agriculture, medicine, and other professions.
Since deadly sectarian violence broke out in Syria’s Druze-majority Suweida province in July 2025, most of the province has been under the control of separatist militias opposed to the Syrian government and sympathetic to Israel.
Israel has tried to position itself as a “protector” of the Syrian Druze community while Druze spiritual leader Hikmat al-Hijri recently said that Suweida province is an “integral part of Israel”.
Ynet reported that the much higher wages in Israel would provide an incentive to Syrian Druze wishing to work in Israel, pointing out that one day’s wages would be equivalent to roughly three months of wages in Syria.
The Israeli outlet also said that the country's military was planning to allow meetings between Druze in Syria and their relatives in Israel, at designated locations near the border on the Syrian side.
After the Assad regime fell in December 2024, Israel seized land in Syria beyond the Golan Heights and has frequently launched attacks and incursions in Syria.
Israel first mooted the idea of bringing in Syrian Druze workers in April 2025, amid shortages of foreign labour caused by the Gaza War.
However the Israeli government reportedly cancelled the plan at the last minute.
The plan intended to establish a “bridge” between Israel and residents of Syrian towns between 5 and 10 kilometres from the Israeli border.
However Israeli security agencies reportedly vetoed it.

Claimed Israeli capture of Lebanese ridge reshapes negotiation dynamics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:42:51 UTC
01:42:51 KST

Claimed Israeli capture of Lebanese ridge reshapes negotiation dynamics
Israel’s continued strikes challenge Lebanon’s push for an elusive peace agreement and stability.
Beirut, Lebanon – On Friday, Israel claimed to have established operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, a development in its fight against Hezbollah that analysts believe could also give Israel greater leverage in negotiations with the Lebanese government planned for later this month.
The Israeli operation to seize the ridge has been ongoing for weeks – and what it says are Hezbollah tunnels underneath – with frequent drone and air strikes by the Israeli military. Analysts told Al Jazeera that the strategically important high ground is significant for the Israelis and Hezbollah because it overlooks a number of nearby regions, including the southern city of Nabatieh.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Nearly 9,000 killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since 2023
- list 2 of 3Israeli air attacks kill at least 12 people in southern Lebanon
- list 3 of 3Israeli air attacks on Lebanon kill at least four
As well as its claims about a network of Hezbollah tunnels, Israel also says the Iranian-backed Lebanese group had underground operations rooms, weapons stores and living quarters for fighters. Despite Israel’s assertion that it has control over the ridge, military operations and attacks are reportedly ongoing.
That is despite the June “ceasefire” Israel agreed with Lebanon, but which is being repeatedly violated.
Political and security analyst, Bassel Doueik, told Al Jazeera that Ali al-Taher is crucial to the outcome of Lebanese-Israeli negotiations.
“Israel has continued to breach the ceasefire daily and the Lebanese government is still trying to negotiate because it doesn’t have any other choice,” Doueik said. “However, if Israel actually occupies the hill, it will give it more of an upper hand in the negotiations because it will be occupying more land.”
Lack of optimism
Israel and Lebanon began engaging in US-mediated direct negotiations in April, despite Hezbollah’s opposition.
The talks come after nearly three years of Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The latest war began on October 8, 2023, when Hezbollah attacked Israel after the beginning of its genocidal war on Gaza. Israel then unilaterally intensified fighting in September 2024, eventually killing more than 4,000 people in Lebanon and assassinating much of Hezbollah’s military leadership, including longtime Secretary-General, Hassan Nasrallah. It also invaded southern Lebanon and began demolishing homes and infrastructure throughout the area.
A ceasefire was agreed in November 2024 but Israel violated the agreement more than 10,000 times. Hezbollah resumed its attacks in response to this year’s US-Israeli war with Iran.
Israel responded by re-invading Lebanon and launching attacks across the country, including killing more than 350 people in what became known as Black Wednesday. In late June, a framework agreement was announced between Tel Aviv and Beirut aimed at ending the fighting in Lebanon, launching so-called “pilot zones” where the Lebanese Army would disarm Hezbollah.
Despite the agreement and ongoing negotiations, Israeli forces never stopped attacking Lebanon. Beirut says it continues talks because it is the only option it has.
Israel now says the framework agreement is failing, even if the Lebanese government doesn’t want to give up on it just yet.
“The Lebanese are pushing for pilot zones in areas where the Israelis are currently operating, so they can pull back their troops, but Israel is more interested in pilot zones in areas it is not operating,” Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera.
He added that few in Lebanon appear optimistic about the pilot zone plan.
Strategic importance
In recent weeks, Israel has focused many of its attacks on the Qantara mountain range and the Ali al-Taher ridge, where Hezbollah fighters are reported to be.
On Sunday, the Israeli military killed seven people in the southern villages of Arab Salim and Nabatieh al-Fawqa. On Monday, 12 people were killed in Israeli attacks in Kfar Rumman.
Analysts said the ridge has geographic importance to both Hezbollah and Israel.
“The location is of strategic importance to Hezbollah,” Blanford said. “It has dominating views looking west over Nabatieh, dominating views over east over Marjayoun and Khiam to Shebaa, and part of [the occupied] Golan Heights in northern Israel looking south, so it is a strategic area and entirely credible that [Hezbollah] has a massive bunker complex within that hill.”
However, Blanford does not expect the Israelis to attempt to hold Ali al-Taher.
“If the Israelis wanted to keep Ali al-Taher, they would have to seize the high ground to the north and northeast because otherwise it would be vulnerable to attacks by Hezbollah,” he said, recalling a similar dynamic during the Israelis’ 18-year occupation of south Lebanon from 1982-2000. “I’m not sure the Israelis would want to extend that deep, so they would likely dynamite it and pull back their forces to more defensible ground.”
Future of negotiations
Hezbollah continues to oppose direct negotiations with Israeli leaders. It has previously said it prefers indirect talks, similar to how the 2024 ceasefire was arranged.
“The negotiations seemed to have reached an impasse because Lebanon and Israel fundamentally disagree on the implementation of the pilot zones scheme,” David Wood, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “Lebanon argues that Israel has not withdrawn from any areas that it directly occupied, while Israel insists that it will not withdraw until Hezbollah disarms.”
The question now is whether the Israeli advance in Ali al-Taher will give them even more leverage over Lebanon in talks set to resume later this month.
Doueik said that talks were unlikely to change the status quo on the ground, with the Israeli government focused on projecting an image of strength ahead of elections next month.
“The most crucial point in the Lebanese-Israeli negotiations is the upcoming October elections,” he said.
