Embrace structured immigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:27 UTC
01:40:27 KST

There is no shortage of discussion surrounding Taiwan’s demographic crisis. The government has rightfully, and fairly, attempted to reverse the trend by offering financial incentives to young people to have children. Yet, Taiwan must confront an uncomfortable truth: Cash handouts are not enough. Taiwanese society must accept that managed, large-scale immigration is no longer just an option — it is a necessity. The demographic shift is so deep that even in the unthinkable scenario that every Taiwanese woman of childbearing age begins having three children by next year, it would not be enough.
If Taiwan is to open its doors, the nation must look closely at the historical mistakes made in Europe. Taiwan’s approach must be free of ideology and be deeply respectful, but also unapologetically interest-driven. Immigration only succeeds when host country’s offer potential migrants a genuine stake in their future. Those Taiwan wants to attract need clear, long-term horizons, whether they choose to stay permanently or eventually return home.
Taiwan must abandon the illusion that it can simply bring in foreign workers for a few years to clean the backsides of its aging population and then expect them to vanish.
When Germany adopted its Gastarbeiter (“guest worker”) policy in the 1970s, it assumed the laborers would eventually leave. Instead, the lack of long-term perspectives and systemic discrimination bred poor integration. The result was the emergence of isolated parallel societies in major German cities — a mistake that continues to exact a heavy societal cost. Exclusion breeds rejection.
To avoid this fate, Taiwan’s legal framework requires a massive overhaul, not just minor, superficial adjustments.
First, the path to permanent residency must be clear and standardized. Anyone who has lived and worked legally in Taiwan for five years, earning an industry-standard average wage — rather than an arbitrary multiplier of the minimum wage — should automatically qualify for a permanent residence permit. Maximum stay limits must be abolished; the longer a migrant contributes to Taiwan’s economy through their own income, the more secure their legal status should become.
Second, Taiwan must dismantle the extreme dependence of domestic caregivers on their host families, a power dynamic that frequently invites substandard conditions. If a caregiver’s employment is terminated, they should be granted a realistic five-month grace period to find a new position. Many caregivers face threats of immediate deportation for perceived “disobedience.”
Taiwan must also broadly accept dual citizenship and grant all graduating foreign students an adequate grace period to secure employment. Having already benefited from and contributed to the Taiwanese system, it makes zero economic sense to discard these educated resources.
Ultimately, Taiwan’s immigration system should pivot around one fundamental question: Does the migrant contribute to society? To prove this, presenting a clean criminal record and a valid employment contract paying an industry-standard average wage should suffice. Meaningful labor does not require a master’s degree or a doctorate. Private enterprises are far better suited than bureaucrats to decide whether an employee brings economic value.
While integration carries upfront costs, they are rapidly offset by the long-term economic returns. Taiwan should provide free Mandarin language courses to lower-income migrant groups. Mastering the local language shields workers from exploitation and accelerates their adaptation into the community.
Taiwan must also stop romanticizing the idea that it can selectively recruit only “socially desirable” or elite migrant groups.
When immigrants are given a real future, they are far more likely to lay down roots and raise families. A migrant’s legal status should be positively influenced by their children, with the ultimate societal goal of helping blue-collar families transition into white-collar professions over a generation.
That shift would require an open, honest national discourse on social adaptation. The path forward lies in a pragmatic middle ground between demanding total cultural assimilation and abandoning Taiwanese identity.
Taiwan need a majority culture that fosters inclusion. To achieve this, major corporate leaders must use their leverage to pressure political parties and candidates who resort to xenophobic rhetoric for cheap electoral gains. Hostile, border-line fascist campaigns — such as the rhetoric targeting Indian migrants — must face harsh financial consequences. Pulling corporate campaign donations would quickly quiet down the political opportunists.
Taiwanese do not need to fear “European conditions” if Taiwan implements a well-managed, steadily growing immigration strategy. Coexistence and mutual economic benefits are already a quiet reality in many sectors of society. Anyone harboring irrational anxieties is ignoring that Taiwan’s future prosperity depends entirely on its ability to integrate new communities.
The facts of Taiwan’s demographic decline are locked in. It is time for the nation to grow up, change its laws and build an immigration system based on mutual respect and mutual interest.
Claudius Petzold is a German attorney-at-law.
Taiwan is home to thousands of foreign residents who build careers, families and lives here. However, what happens when one of those residents loses the ability to prove his identity — not because he has broken Taiwan’s laws, but because his own government refuses to renew his passport? That is the situation my husband, Matteo (not his real name), a Nicaraguan national, has found himself in. After about three years of attempts to renew his passport, our future in Taiwan remains uncertain. It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan
The devastation in Tibet from flooding caused by a glacial collapse in the Himalayas was immediate and profound. Entire communities were left in shock, families were torn apart and countless lives were disrupted. That was followed by deafening silence from the Chinese authorities. No official tally of the missing, no acknowledgment of the dead — only a void filled with rumor, grief and suspicion. Disasters demand transparency. The first responsibility of the state is to inform its citizens of the scale of tragedy. By withholding that information, Beijing reduces Tibetan lives to abstractions, erasing their suffering from public record. The refusal to

For this reason, many were published on this page. Several months ago, this person contacted the Taipei Times and requested that the articles be unpublished. FIFA confirms Infantino to run in next year’s vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:23 UTC
01:40:23 KST

Gianni Infantino is to stand in the FIFA presidential election in March next year, despite the backlash over his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the World Cup, soccer’s global governing body announced on Sunday.
“The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027,” a FIFA spokesperson said. “Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election.”
The 56-year-old Swiss has taken a pummeling since the announcement in late July of his short-lived FIFA Forward Enterprise plan to bring private investment into FIFA events.
Photo: Reuters
However, now for the first time since the plan became public, FIFA has reiterated Infantino’s intention to run for a fourth and final term in next year’s elections.
Should he be re-elected, he would continue to serve as head of world soccer until 2031.
Infantino is in Poland for the FIFA Women’s Under-20 World Cup, but refused to answer queries about his future when questioned by journalists on Saturday.
UEFA has accused Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” over the scheme and was the ringleader of the initial fightback to the announcement, including threatening to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups, if it was not shelved.
However, it has also found solid support from North American body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).
CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani is widely seen as the likeliest challenger to Infantino — UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin has ruled himself out. Montagliani, a FIFA vice-president, had long been regarded as a close ally of Infantino, but there were signs, even before he distanced himself over the now-scrapped plan to allow private investment into World Cups, that he viewed FIFA’s purpose somewhat differently to the Swiss.
However, Infantino is not without friends — 2034 World Cup hosts Saudi Arabia came out in support last month, with the Confederation of African Football and South America’s CONMEBOL also supportive.
As the only declared candidate so far for the election, Infantino would need a simple majority of votes from the 211 federations affiliated to FIFA to extend his term of office, which began in 2016 and was renewed in 2023.
Candidate nominations for next year’s election must be submitted by Nov. 18.

Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz on Sunday posted his most convincing win in his injury return at the US Open, downing Tommy Paul in straight sets to line up a quarter-final clash with Ben Shelton, while all three Taiwanese players played in women’s doubles won.
Hsieh Su-wei and her Latvian partner, Jelena Ostapenko, defeated Spain’s Sara Sorribes and the Czech Republic’s Marie Bouzkova 6-1, 7-6 (7/4).
Wu Fang-hsien and Japan’s Miyu Kato won against Ukrainian sisters Lyudmyla and Nadiia Kichenok 6-2, 4-6, 6-2.
Photo: AP
Another Taiwanese player, Chan Hao-ching and Australian Maya Joint defeated Germany’s Tamara Korpatsch and Argentine Nicole Fossa Huergo 6-0, 6-7 (3/7), 6-4.
Two-time women’s defending champion Aryna Sabalenka also advanced, booking a last-eight date with Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova.
Second-seeded Alcaraz, playing his first tournament since he was sidelined by a right wrist injury in April, looked closer to his brilliant best in a 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 victory over Paul, the 20th-seeded American who posed the Spaniard’s sternest test yet.
“I played my game,” said Alcaraz, who unleashed 33 winners as he moved fluidly around the court, thwarting Paul at every turn in the two-hour 20-minute match.
He is to face red-hot Shelton — a 6-2, 6-3, 6-4 winner over Greece’s Stefanos Tsitsipas — for a place in the semi-finals.
“I tried to play my style,” Alcaraz said. “Tommy is such a talented player. His shots are pretty dangerous and sometimes it’s really difficult to control the ball when it comes to you.”
“I just tried to be ready for a battle and tried to be aggressive all the time,” he said.
Alcaraz grabbed the first break of the contest in the final game of a tight first set.
From there, he was in control. He broke Paul twice in the second set and again early in the third.
He finished it off with a gutsy hold of serve in which he saved a pair of break points, the second with a swinging forehand volley that he followed with a forehand winner to set up the only match point he needed.
“I’m really happy with the performance today,” Alcaraz said.
Shelton, who needed four sets in each of his first three matches, raised his game to dismantle former world No. 3 Tsitsipas in just one hour and 52 minutes.
The American, riding high after a strong August that included a title at the ATP Montreal Masters, blasted a dozen aces and never faced a break point.
“I played a complete match from start to finish,” Shelton said. “I think the level that he’s [Alcaraz] been playing at is really, really impressive. To not play for five months then do what he’s done so far this tournament has been super-human.”
“I think it’s going to be fireworks on Tuesday night,” Shelton said.
Sabalenka kept her bid for a rare US Open three-peat on track with a 6-4, 6-3 victory over the US’ Taylor Townsend.
The Belarusian, whose world No. 1 ranking is on the line in New York, is to face a tough quarter-final against sixth-ranked Czech Noskova, who edged dangerous Ukrainian Marta Kostyuk 7-5, 5-7, 6-4.
Sabalenka needed all her resolve against the multi-faceted Townsend, whose blistering service returns and net prowess flummoxed the Belarusian star in a first set that opened with five breaks of serve.
However, her sustained power and precision proved too much, and after falling behind 3-1 in the second set, she won the last five games to seal the match.
“I was just trying to stay focused on myself and play not only point by point but ball by ball,” Sabalenka said. “I’m happy that I was able to turn around that second set.”
Noskova needed six match points to seal her victory over Kostyuk, failing to convert two in the second set.
“I am more than relieved,” Noskova said. “This match was so tough, emotionally more so than physically.”
The US’ Frances Tiafoe, the 11th seed who has twice reached the semi-finals in Flushing Meadows, booked his quarter-final berth with a 7-6 (7/1), 6-4, 7-6 (8/6) victory over former champion Daniil Medvedev.
“Hell of a match,” Tiafoe said. “I played well when it counted.”
Tiafoe is to face compatriot Alex Michelsen for a place in the semi-finals. Michelsen defeated Argentina’s Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6 (8/6), 6-4, 6-4.
Women’s third seed Jessica Pegula also advanced the US cause. Pegula, one of the players with a chance to supplant Sabalenka atop the rankings in New York, reached the last eight with a 6-3, 6-4 victory over Romanian Sorana Cirstea.
She is to play fellow American Emma Navarro, who defeated Anna Kalinskaya 6-4, 6-2.

EDITORIAL: Trump keeps pressure on Fed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:18 UTC
01:40:18 KST

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to halt trade with countries that have trade surpluses with the US unless the US Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. Trump’s ultimatum came after the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that US employers added 162,000 jobs last month, about triple the number that many economists had expected. In addition, employment data for June and July were revised up, with July rising from a job loss to a gain of 21,000 jobs and June rising to a gain of 31,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the data showed.
Trump’s rationale, according to his Truth Social post, was that the strong jobs report means that the US is in a better credit position “than it was just a short time ago.” That should entitle the US to a lower interest rate or even the lowest in the world, he said. However, from the perspectives of mainstream economics and monetary policy, and based on the reality of international trade, the logic behind Trump’s threat to suspend trade with countries running a trade surplus with the US if the Fed does not cut rates is unreasonable and even self-contradictory.
First, Trump appeared to forcibly align the Fed’s monetary policy with US trade, but the central bank’s mandate is to maintain price stability and maximize employment, not to improve the country’s trade deficit. In his attempt to leverage trade sanctions to force the Fed to cut rates, Trump ignored the economic reality that rate cuts would exacerbate inflation when the economy and job market gain steam.
Second, Trump seems to believe that high rates lead to a stronger US dollar, which would weaken the competitiveness of US goods and result in trade deficits. However, if the Fed cuts rates, lower borrowing costs would likely stimulate domestic consumption and investment demand in the US. That could simultaneously prompt the US to import more foreign goods if domestic industries cannot meet the increased demand, widening trade deficits even further, counter to Trump’s intention.
Third, threatening to halt trade with countries with which the US has trade deficits is too radical. As the US is highly dependent on imports in many key sectors, such as consumer electronics, auto parts and semiconductor materials, his threat, if carried out, would lead to severe shortages of goods in the US. The supply constraints would trigger severe price spikes, cripple the US manufacturing sector and plunge the economy into stagflation. In that scenario, the Fed would be even less likely to cut rates, and instead be forced to raise them to curb inflation.
Trump’s remarks appeared to have no impact on US Treasury yields, Wall Street stock indices or the US dollar, indicating that the market generally ignored the US president’s post, viewing it as emotional venting rather than a credible policy threat.
However, Trump’s renewed pressure on the Fed to cut rates further complicates matters for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who — at his debut at the annual gathering of global central bankers in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, late last month — reaffirmed the central bank’s 2 percent inflation target as non-negotiable and emphasized that restoring price stability remained the central objective of the Fed’s monetary policy.
At Jackson Hole, Warsh offered a clear analysis and constructive assessment of the US economy, but refrained from giving traditional forward guidance as expected. Still, in his speech, Warsh signaled that under his rein, the Fed would be more disciplined, rules-based and inflation-centric. Even though Trump handpicked Warsh to replace Jerome Powell, Warsh’s hawkish tone in Jackson Hole and his commitment to protecting the Fed’s independence during his US Senate confirmation hearing in April, along with encouraging US economic data, indicate that he would likely prioritize combating inflation rather than responding to Trump’s political pressure.
However, the real test would come this week when the US releases the consumer price index for last month, which is the final major inflation gauge before the Fed policymakers meet next week. If the data show no meaningful changes, or even an uptick in inflation, and yet the Fed still stays put, Warsh would have to present a new rationale. Otherwise, the market would again question the Fed’s credibility and capability, while investors would wonder if Warsh is really an inflation fighter or if he just talks tough while yielding to political compromise ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Record MRT funding earmarked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:18 UTC
01:40:18 KST

The government has earmarked a record NT$49.9 billion (US$1.58 billion) in subsidies for local MRT construction next year, more than five times the amount budgeted for this year and the highest annual allocation for local MRT projects to date, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said yesterday.
The ministry hosted a news conference to present statistics after local governments in Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Taichung accused the central government of curtailing the budget for the MRT projects in their localities and sought additional funding.
Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Wu Sheng-yuan (伍勝園) said yesterday the central government determines its subsidies based on the progress of individual projects, taking into account factors such as construction schedules, tender awards and budget execution.
Photo copied by Wang Jung-hsiang, Taipei Times
The central government has provided more than NT$716.1 billion in subsidies for local MRT projects over the years, with Taipei, New Taipei City and Keelung accounting for NT$488.2 billion, or about 68 percent, Wu said.
For subsidies to be allocated for next year, Wu said the amount was determined following a meeting with local governments officials on May 4 on the progress of their MRT lines. Some are still in the planning stage, while others are already under construction, he said. The average subsidy rate for local MRT projects was about 80 percent last year, Wu said.
Approved subsidy funding for the Taipei-Keelung-Taoyuan region for next year is about 80 percent of its overall budget request, while the figure for southern Taiwan is about 70 percent, Wu said, adding the ministry has made similar fiscal arrangements in the same way in the past few years.
New Taipei City has requested an additional NT$5.4 billion after its MRT subsidies were cut in next year’s budget and has formally asked the ministry to prioritize restoring the cut. Taipei said it is short NT$6 billion in central government funding, while Kaohsiung says it has a NT$13.6 billion shortfall. Wu said there is no indiscriminate spending of public funds for MRT projects. The ministry has established review guidelines for subsidies for MRT construction projects, he said. Local governments submit their funding needs, after which the ministry reviews the proposed projects and assesses whether the funding is warranted, he said, adding that projects with unclear plans would not be approved.
All projects are subject to rigorous scrutiny at every stage, including an initial review by the Railway Bureau, a review by the ministry and an assessment by external committee members.
The ministry said that an amendment to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法) last year has reduced the central government’s financial resources available for local infrastructure.

Cinema under the stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:17 UTC
01:40:17 KST

On selected weekends, moviegoers settle into reclining deckchairs on Dream Plaza’s rooftop garden in Taipei’s Xinyi District (信義). Wearing wireless headphones and surrounded by city lights, they watch everything from romantic favorites to independent films and Hollywood hits.
Skyline Film (屋頂電影院 ) has become an established fixture in Taipei’s outdoor entertainment scene. When Joe Chao (趙冠喬) and his collaborators staged their first screening in 2016, however, it was still an experiment inspired by the open-air cinemas he had encountered in London.
IF YOU BUILD IT, THEY WILL COME
Photo: Ben Lee
Back in 2016, this rooftop cinema concept started out as a side project for Chao.
“We wouldn’t call ourselves movie buffs... but we have watched a lot of movies,” Chao said.
The inspiration came when Chao was living in London and attended several open-air cinemas.
“I remember going to a Romeo and Juliet screening in an old, abandoned chapel,” he said. “It was an interesting concept… to watch a movie and see the city from different rooftops over a couple drinks.”
Then in 2016, the first ever rooftop screening became a reality after many months of preparation to secure the location, equipment, screening licenses and other operational hurdles.
The eventual success led Chao to hold regular viewings in 2017.
BEHIND THE SCENES
Movies range from quirky arthouse indies to classics like Casablanca, as well as the latest commercial films.
“Initially, the movie curation process was based primarily on our own personal preference, as it was difficult to know what the audience liked,” Chao said.
Over the years, Chao discovered that romance is the genre that resonates most with audiences, with About Time, La La Land and the Before trilogy among the most popular titles.
But not every pick lands with the audience.
Chao said that he received a lot of negative feedback after a screening of the black comedy Frank.
They’ve also shown blockbuster titles like The Revenant and Dune at one of their Fulong Beach screenings in New Taipei City.
“Watching Dune on the beach with sand right at your feet was a cool experience. The setting created a powerful connection with the film,” Chao said.
THE EXPERIENCE
After checking in, audiences can explore the rooftop garden and check out the views. A concession stand offers snacks and beverages (no outside refreshments allowed).
Each guest receives a pair of noise-cancelling wireless headphones with adjustable volume. One viewer, however, said the headphones did not completely block the noise of a nearby ventilation fan.
The seats are reclined canvas deckchairs, and while they appeal to most, they may be a trade-off for some.
Attendee Lin Hsiao-i (林烋毅) said that they aren’t as supportive as standard theater seating and can be taxing on the back.
For Wang Yu-tzu (王郁慈), however, the setup is just right.
“[Watching] a movie with the sky and cityscapes in the background really makes you feel at ease.”
As the credits roll, a few people hang around for one last look at the night sky and a take few quick snaps before heading for the exits.

When representatives of Taiwan’s Public Television Service (PTS) traveled to Singapore to meet Netflix, they brought two dramas: A Touch of Green (一把青, 2015), a sweeping story of war, displacement and military families, and Wake Up (麻醉風暴, 2015), a tightly constructed medical thriller. They were not simply trying to sell programs. They were trying to change an idea of Taiwan. International perceptions of Taiwanese television, PTS executives recalled in interviews conducted for my joint research with Chairman Hu Yuan-hui (胡元輝), were still strongly associated with the idol dramas that had enjoyed enormous regional popularity

Health ministry moots more vaccines

Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Lin Ching-yi (林靜儀) yesterday said if a batch of 200,000 doses of enhanced influenza vaccines, which are to be introduced for the first time into the publicly funded vaccination program next month, prove to be effective, the ministry would purchase more next year.
The Federation for the Welfare of Taiwan’s Seniors yesterday held a news conference in Taipei to promote flu vaccination and disease prevention among older people, inviting health officials, physicians and lawmakers.
The federation’s chairperson Fang Li-hsiu (方力脩) said Taiwan has been providing publicly funded flu vaccines to older people for almost 30 years, but with changes in population structure, vaccine development and long-term care services, policies for older people should keep up.
Photo: Taipei Times
He said the federation appreciates the government policy of introducing enhanced flu vaccines in the public-funded vaccination program this year, but the amount purchased this year is very limited, and they hope more can be offered to older people next year.
The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) last month announced that among the more than 7 million doses of publicly funded flu vaccines purchased for the new flu season starting in October, 200,000 doses of enhanced flu vaccines are included, which would be prioritized for long-term care facilities.
At the event, CDC Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) yesterday said Taiwan is the first country in Asia to include enhanced flu vaccines in its national vaccination program.
There are two brands of enhanced flu vaccines this year, a vaccine by TTY Biopharm, which would be available from Oct. 1, and a vaccine by Sanofi that would be available later in the same month, he said, adding that residents and workers of 11 types of long-term care facilities would be eligible for the new vaccines.
Flu activity is climbing early this year, with more than 100,000 medical visits for flu-like illnesses already reported in a week, and flu viruses are expected to spread faster with students returning to school. Infection risk for adults and older adults is likely to increase when it enters an epidemic period.
Huang Li-min (黃立民), a professor of National Taiwan University Hospital, said that older people might have a weaker immune response to the traditional flu vaccines, but the enhanced vaccines can improve the defensive performance by about 20 percent.
Lin said Taiwan’s COVID-19 prevention performance received international praise, but disease prevention measures should be practiced every day, and as Taiwan is a super-aged society, it is important that the senior population get correct information about vaccines and get vaccinated.
She said if many people are willing to get the enhanced flu vaccines and they prove effective, then the ministry would try to acquire up to 600,000 doses for the publicly funded vaccination program next year.

NASA’s newest space telescope launches on a quest to explore the hidden universe  NASA最新太空望遠鏡升空 探索宇宙奧祕
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:15 UTC
01:40:15 KST

NASA’s new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on Aug. 10 on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a roughly US$4 billion project, was carried aloft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket through blue skies just after sunrise, embarking on a potentially decade-long observation mission.
The telescope, which will park itself beyond the moon, is designed to investigate cosmic enigmas such as dark energy and dark matter, while also testing gravity at vast scales and searching for exoplanets — planets beyond our solar system.
Photo: AP 照片：美聯社
Roman will travel through space toward an orbital location called Lagrange Point 2, situated about 1.6 million km from Earth. Its mission is planned for five years, though the US space agency said the telescope may have enough fuel for five additional years.
Mission scientists will spend the next 90 days commissioning the spacecraft and preparing the observatory for its science operations. It is expected to beam back its first high-resolution images “before the winter holidays,” Roman telescope project manager Jackie Townsend told reporters.
Roman will build on the capabilities of other orbiting observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, and the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
“It will be as if Hubble and James Webb kind of peered through a keyhole at the universe, while Nancy Grace Roman will kick the door down,” Nicola Fox, chief of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, told reporters on Aug. 29.
“Roman has broadly the same sensitivity and sharpness of vision as Hubble, but we survey the sky much faster,” Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, told reporters at a briefing in July.
McEnery said one month of Roman observations can survey our entire home galaxy.
“One month of observations to survey our Milky Way galaxy would take about a century with Hubble,” McEnery said.
WIDE ANGLE AND ZOOM LENSES
Webb has provided a new understanding of the early history of the universe, finding among other things that primordial galaxies formed sooner and were bigger than previously known. Webb is capable of looking across vast distances and back into deep time, because of the time it takes light to travel.
Roman instead is able to take panoramic views. NASA likens Roman to a camera’s wide-angle lens and Webb to a zoom lens.
Roman will help in the understanding of two mysterious cosmic components — dark energy and dark matter — by creating the most comprehensive 3D map of the universe to date. Its main survey, to take more than a year to complete, will cover more than two billion galaxies.
The Big Bang event roughly 13.8 billion years ago initiated the universe, which has been expanding ever since. Scientists in 1998 disclosed that this expansion was actually accelerating, with an invisible force called dark energy as the hypothesized reason.
The universe’s contents include ordinary matter — stars, planets, gas, dust and all the familiar stuff on Earth — as well as dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary matter represents perhaps 5 percent of the contents. Dark matter, known through its gravitational influences on galaxies and stars, may represent about 27 percent. Dark energy may represent about 68 percent.
Using Roman to gauge dark matter’s pull and dark energy’s push across the universe will bring scientists closer than ever before to solving both mysteries, according to NASA.
Roman also will conduct one of the most comprehensive searches ever for exoplanets. It is expected to discover thousands of new ones and provide the first statistical census of planetary systems similar to our own.
(Reuters)
美國太空總署（NASA）最新一代旗艦級天文觀測器 8月30日於美國佛羅里達州發射升空，其任務是探索天體物理學及宇宙學最大的一些謎團。
這項耗資約40億美元的「南希．格蕾絲．羅曼太空望遠鏡」（Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope）計畫，由SpaceX的「獵鷹重型」（Falcon Heavy）火箭搭載，在當天日出後不久，從NASA甘迺迪太空中心升空進入藍天，展開這項可能長達10年的觀測任務。
羅曼太空望遠鏡將進入比月球更遠的太空，主要研究暗能量與暗物質等宇宙謎團，同時測試大尺度下的重力作用，並搜尋系外行星，也就是太陽系以外的行星。
羅曼望遠鏡將前往稱為「拉格朗日點2」（Lagrange Point 2）的軌道位置，距離地球約160萬公里。任務原定執行5年，但NASA表示，望遠鏡所攜帶的燃料可能足以再延長5年。
科學家將利用接下來90天進行太空船啟用與測試，並為天文觀測任務做準備。羅曼太空望遠鏡計畫經理傑姬．湯森告訴記者，預計望遠鏡將在「冬季假期前」傳回第一批高解析度影像。
羅曼太空望遠鏡將延續其他太空天文台的能力，例如2021年發射的詹姆斯．韋伯太空望遠鏡（James Webb Telescope），以及1990年發射的哈伯太空望遠鏡（Hubble Space Telescope）。
NASA科學任務理事會主管妮可拉．福克斯8月29日對記者表示：「這就好比，哈伯望遠鏡與韋伯望遠鏡只是透過一個鑰匙孔窺探宇宙，而羅曼望遠鏡則會直接把門踹開」。
位於馬里蘭州的NASA戈達德太空飛行中心（Goddard Space Flight Center）羅曼望遠鏡計畫資深科學家茱莉．麥肯納里7月在簡報會中表示：「羅曼望遠鏡的靈敏度與視覺解析度大致與哈伯望遠鏡相當，但羅曼望遠鏡觀測天空的速度要快得多」。
麥肯納里表示，羅曼望遠鏡只需一個月的觀測，就能掃描我們所處的整個銀河系。
她說：「要完成對銀河系的觀測，哈伯望遠鏡需費時約一個世紀；羅曼望遠鏡只需要一個月」。
廣角與變焦鏡頭
韋伯望遠鏡已讓我們對宇宙早期歷史有新的理解，包括發現原始星系形成的時間，比過去所認為的更早，規模也更大。由於光線傳播需要時間，韋伯望遠鏡能夠觀測極其遙遠的距離，也就等於回望宇宙遙遠的過去。
羅曼望遠鏡則能夠拍攝宇宙的全景影像。NASA將羅曼望遠鏡比喻為相機的廣角鏡頭，而韋伯則像是變焦鏡頭。
羅曼望遠鏡將繪製迄今最完整的宇宙三維地圖，以協助科學家了解兩種神秘的宇宙成分——暗能量與暗物質。這項主要巡天觀測任務預計耗時一年以上，將涵蓋超過20億個星系。
約138億年前發生的大爆炸（Big Bang）開啟了宇宙，而宇宙此後便持續膨脹。科學家在1998年公布的研究指出，宇宙膨脹其實正在加速，而假設中的一種無形力量——暗能量——可能就是造成加速膨脹的原因。
宇宙的組成包括普通物質——恆星、行星、氣體、塵埃，以及地球上所有我們熟悉的物質——還有暗物質與暗能量。普通物質可能只占宇宙總成分約5%。暗物質可透過其對星系與恆星產生的重力作用被觀測到，可能約占27%；暗能量則可能約占68%。
NASA表示，利用羅曼望遠鏡測量暗物質在宇宙中的引力，以及暗能量推動宇宙膨脹的力量，將使科學家比過去更可能解開這兩大謎團。
羅曼望遠鏡也將進行有史以來最全面的系外行星搜尋行動之一。預計將新發現數千顆太陽系以外的行星，尋找類似我們太陽系的行星系統，並建立首次統計普查。

AIDC, Bombardier sign 20-year deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:13 UTC
01:40:13 KST

Taiwanese aircraft maker Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC, 漢翔航空) yesterday announced that it has secured a 20-year partnership agreement with Canada-based Bombardier Inc.
The two companies held a ceremony in Taipei yesterday to exchange signed copies of the agreement, launching the 20-year partnership under which AIDC would supply cockpit and forward fuselage structural components for Bombardier’s super-midsize Challenger 3500 business jets, the Taiwanese company said.
The agreement represents a new milestone in cooperation between the two companies, which dates back to 1999, with the Taiwanese supplier having provided rear fuselage structural components for more than 1,000 Challenger 3500 aircraft, it said.
Photo: CNA
The forward fuselage structural components for the Challenger 3500 require a high level of technical expertise, it said, adding that Bombardier in April completed a review of the Taiwanese supplier’s production capabilities.
AIDC said that the agreement represents the most significant development to date for its civil aviation business.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫), who witnessed the exchange, said AIDC’s supply of fuselage structural components to international clients, including Bombardier, demonstrated international confidence in “Made in Taiwan” products.
AIDC has demonstrated its ability to produce fuselage structural components, Kung said, adding that, by expanding its technological capabilities to include forward fuselage structures and securing the long-term agreement with Bombardier, Taiwan has become one of the few countries capable of supplying fuselage structural components for large and medium-sized aircraft.
Amid restructuring of the global aerospace supply chain, many international aircraft makers are seeking partners, and AIDC has demonstrated its capabilities as a resilient supplier, he said.
Given the value of the Bombardier orders, AIDC is expected to enlist other Taiwanese suppliers to help fulfill the orders, he said, adding that the agreement is expected to benefit Taiwan’s aerospace supply chain.
The forward fuselage is the most technically demanding section of the airframe because of its complex shape and the need to meet cabin pressure and airtightness requirements, as well as its integration of the cockpit structure, passenger doors and numerous system interfaces, AIDC said.
Only about five suppliers worldwide have this capability, it said.
The company added that it expects to deliver structural components for at least 500 Challenger 3500 fuselages to Bombardier over 20 years.
Eric Filion, Bombardier’s executive vice president for programs and supply chain, said that AIDC has served as a critical supplier to the Canadian company for many years and that trust is the most important key to the cooperation.
The latest agreement with AIDC reflects the long-standing and stable relationship between the two companies, Filion said, adding that Bombardier will continue to cooperate with qualified suppliers worldwide to meet customer expectations for quality, performance and reliability.

FAA investigating cause of fatal crash in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:12 UTC
01:40:12 KST

US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) investigators yesterday were detailing their plans for determining what caused an Amazon.com Inc cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames.
The aircraft overran the runway at about 2pm on Sunday after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
It was not immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
Photo: AFP
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said.
The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy was to hold a news conference yesterday, the agency said.
Among the factors investigators are likely to consider is whether the plane flew too far before touching down, experts said.
Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914m) of a runway.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the US Department of Transportation, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
It was not raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.
The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. About 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership in the past, including by a Russian company.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a Web site that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320km north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

對話 Dialogue
清清：華華，你覺得你最好的朋友是誰？
Qīngqing: Huáhua, nǐ juéde nǐ zuìhǎo de péngyou shì shéi?
Photo: Unsplash 照片：Unsplash
華華：坦白說，以前我應該會說是你，但現在可能是AI。
Huáhua: Tǎnbái shuō, yǐqián wǒ yīnggāi huì shuō shì nǐ, dàn xiànzài kěnéng shì AI.
清清：謝謝你喔！其實我可以理解啦！你也每天都用AI嗎？
Qīngqing: Xièxie nǐ o! Qíshí wǒ kěyǐ lǐjiě la! Nǐ yě měitiān dōu yòng AI ma?
華華：對啊！我有什麼問題都會問問它的想法和意見，也會請它幫我找資料。
Huáhua: Duì a! Wǒ yǒu shénme wèntí dōu huì wènwen tā de xiǎngfǎ hé yìjiàn, yě huì qǐng tā bāng wǒ zhǎo zīliào.
清清：可是有時候我會想AI畢竟不是真人，怎麼能把它當做真正的朋友呢？
Qīngqing: Kěshì yǒu shíhòu wǒ huì xiǎng AI bìjìng búshì zhēnrén, zěnme néng bǎ tā dàngzuò zhēnzhèng de péngyou ne?
華華：雖然它不是真人，但是它隨時都可以陪我聊天，也不會嫌我煩。你可以嗎？
Huáhua: Suīrán tā búshì zhēnrén, dànshì tā suíshí dōu kěyǐ péi wǒ liáotiān, yě búhuì xián wǒ fán. Nǐ kěyǐ ma?
清清：呃……，我在睡覺或是在忙的時候不行啦！聽起來，AI 好像真的已經變成現代人生活中重要的好朋友了。
Qīngqing: È…… Wǒ zài shuìjiào huòshì zài máng de shíhòu bùxíng la! Tīng qǐlái, AI hǎoxiàng zhēnde yǐjīng biànchéng xiàndàirén shēnghuó zhōng zhòngyào de hǎo péngyǒu le.
華華：是啊！不過我覺得我們還是需要真正的朋友和家人，所以下班以後我們就一起去吃飯吧！
Huáhua: Shì a! Búguò wǒ juéde wǒmen háishi xūyào zhēnzhèng de péngyou hàn jiārén, suǒyǐ xiàbān yǐhòu wǒmen jiù yìqǐ qù chīfàn ba!
翻譯 Translation
Qingqing: Huahua, who do you think your best friend is?
Huahua: Honestly, I probably would’ve said you before, but now it might be AI.
Qingqing: Well, thanks. Actually, I can understand that. Do you use AI every day, too?
Huahua: Yes. Whenever I have a question, I ask for its thoughts and opinions. I also ask it to help me find information.
Qingqing: But sometimes I wonder: AI isn’t a real person, is it? How can we treat it as a real friend?
Huahua: Even though it’s not a real person, it can chat with me anytime, and it never gets annoyed with me. Can you do that?
Qingqing: Uh… not when I’m asleep or busy. It sounds like AI really has become an important friend in modern people’s lives.
Huahua: That’s true. However, I think we still need real friends and family. Let’s go out for dinner together after work.

3. 想法 (xiǎngfǎ) thought; idea
4. 意見 (yìjiàn) opinion
5. 畢竟 (bìjìng) after all
6. 真人 (zhēnrén) real person
7. 隨時 (suíshí) at any time
8. 嫌 (xián) to dislike; to find annoying

Navy fleet needs overhaul: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:11 UTC
01:40:11 KST

Taiwan needs to restructure its naval fleet from focusing on large warships, which are “sitting ducks” for China’s advanced tracking technology, to smaller, stealthy corvettes that are harder to detect but retain sufficient firepower to deter a Chinese invasion, a Taiwanese academic and a former US military commander said in an article published on Friday in the journal Foreign Affairs.
Taiwan does not need a fleet capable of competing with the Chinese navy for traditional control of the Taiwan Strait, but rather “sea denial” capabilities that would prevent China from freely using the waterway, Taiwanese aerospace and security expert Holmes Liao (廖宏祥) and former US Navy admiral Dennis Blair wrote the article, titled “How Taiwan can win the Strait: A nimbler navy can deny China.”
The focus of “sea denial” is “preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion” by deterring its forces with smaller vessels, as well as shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with anti-ship missiles and submarines, they said.
Photo: Taipei Times
“Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet,” they said, adding that Taiwan’s current naval plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large, expensive new ships.
However, China has invested in cutting-edge surveillance, intelligence and reconnaissance, as well as electronic warfare systems, drones and missiles, making Taiwan’s large surface ships “a liability,” they said.
“These same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives” as they would be necessary for an assault on Taiwan, the article said.
Taipei could take advantage of that asymmetry by replacing large destroyers and frigates with numerous small surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial Chinese strike and remain capable of deterring an invasion fleet, the authors said.
The smaller ships could “operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks,” they said.
Liao and Blair, who was commander in chief of the US Pacific Command from 1999 to 2002, said that Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign — which “combined land-based anti-ship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones and external intelligence” — showed that a weaker power could constrain a stronger opponent in contested waters.
Taiwan’s continued commissioning of “lightweight but heavily armed” missile patrol ships are helping the nation restructure its fleet, they wrote.
Sustained production of the ships would lower costs and new weapons, sensors and uncrewed systems could be incorporated into successive batches of the vessels, which cost less than US$200 million, compared with an estimated US$2 billion for a single 7,000 tonne warship, they said.
“The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical,” as large ships are attractive to politicians because they are a highly visible symbols of national defense that bring shipyard contracts and “a sense of national achievement.”
“Rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs,” Liao and Blair wrote.
“The country needs a dispersed, agile and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait,” they said. “Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion.”

Property market cooling continues, 591.com says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:10 UTC
01:40:10 KST

Taiwan’s housing market is showing further signs of cooling, with developers sharply scaling back planned launches for the autumn sales season as tighter credit controls and weakening demand weigh on the sector.
Developers are planning 246 projects nationwide in the upcoming fall sales season, down 21.2 percent from a year earlier, according to online property listing platform 591.com (591新建案) operated by Addcn Technology Co (數字科技).
The total value of planned projects is expected to shrink 23.3 percent to NT$545.2 billion (US$17.28 billion) from NT$710.65 billion last year, the lowest level in six years, the platform said.
Photo: Hsu Yi-ping, Taipei Times
The decline reflects developers’ growing caution, with postponing new projects becoming a key strategy, as financing conditions tighten and buyers remain on the sidelines, it said.
Developers are increasingly focusing on selling existing inventory rather than adding new supply, meaning the market is likely to remain in consolidation next quarter, with owner-occupier demand and selected projects by major developers providing much of the support, it added.
Among major cities, only Hsinchu City and Taipei are expected to see growth in project value, 591.com said.
Hsinchu City is set to record the biggest increase, with project value surging 2.25 times to NT$60.81 billion even as the number of projects remains unchanged. The increase partly reflects a low comparison base and several major developments in affluent districts.
Taipei is also bucking the downturn. Although the number of projects is declining, total project value is expected to rise about 30 percent to NT$149.75 billion, driven by a major development in Nangang District (南港). Excluding that project, launch value would decline, 591.com said.
New Taipei City’s project value is expected to fall about 40 percent to NT$135.47 billion despite major developments in Taishan (泰山), Linkou (林口) and Yonghe (永和) districts, it said.
Taoyuan’s project count and value are expected to drop about 30 percent to NT$103.37 billion, with only one project exceeding NT$10 billion in potential sales, it said.
The slowdown is steeper in central and southern Taiwan, with Taichung’s project value expected to plunge about 50 percent to NT$56.93 billion, falling below NT$100 billion for the first time over the past few years, while new launches are increasingly concentrated in well-established districts, 591.com said.
Tainan’s project count is relatively stable, but potential sales are expected to fall 40 percent to NT$17.78 billion, while Kaohsiung faces the steepest decline, with project value plunging 66.6 percent to NT$21.09 billion, it said.
Kaohsiung’s development hotspots are also shifting, with Nanzih (楠梓) and Zuoying (左營) districts — beneficiaries of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (台積電) plant expansions — giving way to more central areas such as Fongshan District (鳳山), it said.
The shift highlights developers’ move away from investment-driven hotspots toward more stable end-user demand as the housing market enters a prolonged adjustment, it added.

Preparing for educational chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:09 UTC
01:40:09 KST

With primary and junior-high schools reopening across the nation, many schools have been struggling to recruit enough teachers, even after lowering their standards to university graduates who have no teaching experience.
Even where schools have filled vacancies and warded off a pending crisis, they are still likely to face two major problems as the school year begins precisely because many new hires lack training and experience.
First, ineffective teaching and chaotic classroom management would lead to a steady stream of complaints. Education is a specialized field that requires professional knowledge and skills.
In an attempt to fill shortages, schools are resorting to a scattershot approach of hiring anyone with a degree. The results would be entirely predictable: disorderly classrooms and poor student learning outcomes. If the teachers also cannot manage student behavior and resort to harsh language or disciplinary methods, parents would inevitably lodge complaints, leaving schools to deal with endless administrative meetings over teacher conduct.
Second, new teachers, feeling helpless and frustrated, might quit partway through the school year.
Among the new hires, some might have misconceptions about education and believe that managing students would be easy. Coupled with an overestimation of their abilities, feelings of frustration could quickly pile up. Eventually, and often within the first one or two months of the school year, they would walk away.
At that point, schools might have no alternative but to fill the gap with substitute teachers. It could then become commonplace for a class to go through six or seven substitute teachers in a semester. Ultimately, it is the students who suffer.
The Ministry of Education must not turn a blind eye to the difficulties facing schools and frontline teachers. The ministry must confront the problem head-on and take steps to resolve it; it cannot continue to delay taking action. Handled poorly, these challenges could rapidly undermine students’ ability to learn and Taiwan’s future competitiveness.
Lee Chi-fu is a teacher.

Some pesticides can harm cats in particular
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:09 UTC
01:40:09 KST

Insect repellent or pesticides containing pyrethrins or pyrethroids will be required to include a cat warning label, the Ministry of Environment’s Chemicals Administration said yesterday.
Some commercially available insect repellents or pesticides containing pyrethrins — a mixture of natural chemicals extracted from pyrethrum daisy — and artificial pyrethroids are labeled with the statement “low toxicity to mammals,” it said.
However, pyrethrins have a higher toxicity to cats and such statements might mislead pet owners, it said.
Photo: Su Chin-feng, Taipei Times
Pyrethrins are widely used in the control of public health pests, it said, adding that it is less toxic to humans and most other mammals, as they have higher capacity for toxic metabolism than cats, allowing them to rapidly eliminate pyrethrins.
Cats have slower metabolism of pyrethrins than most other mammals due to congenital deficiency in glucuronidation metabolic capacity, it said.
As a result, pyrethrins are more toxic to cats than other mammals, and they are prone to adverse neurological reactions following exposure, it said.
The agency said it has convened a meeting to consult environmental toxicologists and suppliers of products containing pyrethrins.
The meeting established that a cat warning must be added to the product labels of all products containing pyrethrins, it said.
The warning should read, “Harmful to cats. Read label before use,” it said, adding the font size must be at least 5mm with the warning text colored differently.
Pyrethrin-containing products already circulating on the market would not be recalled, it said.
Sales channel operators are advised to add the warning to the retail area of such products, it added.
People should keep cats away from areas where products that contain pyrethrins or pyrethroids are being used until the treated space is dry and well ventilated, it said, adding that areas where cats frequently visit should be cleaned to reduce exposure risk.

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday expressed hope for expanded Taiwan-Japan industrial ties to build safer, more resilient and “non-red” supply chains.
Lai made the remarks while receiving a delegation from the Japan-Taiwan Friendship Association of Kanagawa Prefecture at the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Taiwan and Japan share a deep friendship forged through difficult times, with a relationship that is as close as those between family members, and are also important economic and trade partners, he said.
Photo: CNA
Bilateral trade reached US$84.851 billion last year, up 17.36 percent from the previous year, while exchanges between the two sides have grown increasingly close in industries such as electronics and information and communications technology, as well as machinery and components, he said.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) established a design center in Kanagawa, a major hub for high-tech industries and advanced manufacturing in Japan, while 13 Taiwanese companies, including ASE Technology, have also set up operations in the prefecture, Lai said.
At the same time, 78 Kanagawa-based companies, including Nissan Motor, have invested in Taiwan, he said.
TSMC is the world’s leading company in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, while ASE is a global leader in semiconductor packaging and testing, he said.
That both companies have invested in Kanagawa demonstrates the close ties between Taiwan and the prefecture, he added.
Taiwan has strong capabilities in semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) manufacturing, while Kanagawa has strengths in research and development and precision manufacturing, Lai said.
The president expressed hopes that by expanding cooperation, the two sides can build safer and more resilient supply chains that are less dependent on China.
Association head Kenji Nakanishi said Kanagawa is home to the well-known Hakone hot springs, and expressed hope that the Japanese town and Taipei’s Beitou District (北投), also known for hot springs, could establish a relationship.
The idea received enthusiastic support at a meeting with the Taipei Hot Springs Association and other organizations, he said, adding that he hopes Hakone and Beitou could sign a memorandum of understanding at a celebration marking the association’s 60th anniversary on Nov. 27.
Nakanishi said that Taiwan’s economy has been driven by its AI and semiconductor industries, while TSMC’s investment in Kumamoto Prefecture has helped revitalize the economy on Kyushu and contributed to Japan’s broader economic growth.
Beyond AI and semiconductors, there is room for cooperation in fields such as space and quantum technology, he said, expressing hope that the two sides can further deepen Taiwan-Japan ties.

China security laws spell travel risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:08 UTC
01:40:08 KST

China is set to implement several laws in the coming months that expand the definition of national security, creating greater risks for Taiwanese traveling to or doing business in China, Taiwanese officials said yesterday.
Beijing’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect on July 1, while a draft “Internet Information Service Management Measures” finished its public consultation on Aug. 2, but has yet to be adopted. China’s Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration are to take effect on Tuesday next week, while amendments to its National Defense Mobilization Law and the Ministry of Public Security’s Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security are to take effect on Oct. 1.
An official familiar with cross-strait affairs, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the laws reflect Beijing’s continued expansion of the concept of national security beyond traditional security concerns to information, business, and the movement of people, money and information.
Photo: Reuters
These laws allow authorities to regulate such activities in the name of national security and national interests, the official said.
The measures come as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) prepares to hold its fifth plenum this year and its 21st National Congress next year, the official said, adding that Beijing needs a relatively stable social environment.
Social control and security management are likely to become increasingly stringent, with the laws providing a more systematic framework for such efforts, they said.
Terms such as “national security” and “national interests” are broadly defined, they said.
The Mainland Affairs Council has described such provisions as providing “blanket authorization,” allowing Chinese authorities considerable discretion in determining what constitutes a security or national-interest concern.
This creates uncertainty for Taiwanese traveling to China while providing a legal basis for cross-border repression, the official said.
The measures are not limited to Chinese citizens: Anyone deemed to have harmed China’s national interests or national security could face investigation or punishment under Chinese law, they said.
The laws also decentralize enforcement powers.
Under the new exit and entry regulations, for example, authorities in border counties and cities would have enforcement powers, the official said.
The forthcoming cyberspace security inspection measures would allow county-level public security authorities to investigate individuals and inspect items such as mobile phones and laptops, the official said.
“Law is merely the packaging,” the official said, adding that arrests and searches have already occurred in various forms.
The new laws would directly authorize local government agencies to carry out such actions while warning that certain behavior or speech could result in arrest or harassment, which could encourage self-censorship and create a chilling effect, they said.
The laws also explicitly refer to Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and socialism, reflecting a more closed ideological environment, the official said, adding that they could help lay the legal and ideological groundwork for Xi to secure a fourth term as party leader at the 21st National Congress.
As the CCP has consistently framed cross-strait relations around the “one China” principle, the laws are likely to negatively affect the movement of people, money and information across the Taiwan Strait, the official said.
Taiwan should issue appropriate risk warnings, they said.
One of the most consequential measures is the amended National Defense Mobilization Law, which represents the first comprehensive overhaul of the legislation since it was enacted 16 years ago, another Taiwanese national security official said.
The revised law would allow the Chinese state to seize private property whenever deemed necessary, they said.
It should not be viewed solely as a strategic tool aimed at Taiwan, the official said, but also as a mechanism for comprehensively integrating domestic resources and a reflection of Beijing’s growing security concerns amid intensifying competition with the US.
The current version of the law focuses on the division of responsibilities between military and civilian authorities, particularly how the government could mobilize civilian resources and personnel to support the military during wartime or emergencies, they said.
The latest revision has five notable features, they said.
First, it expands the purpose of the legislation to include protecting China’s “development” interests.
Second, it explicitly establishes the leadership of the CCP and Xi’s military-strengthening doctrine as fundamental political principles governing national defense mobilization.
Third, for the first time, it defines national defense mobilization as activities designed to “ensure a rapid transition between peacetime and wartime,” and convert economic and social strength into national defense capabilities.
Fourth, it changes the legal treatment of civilian resources from “requisition” to “expropriation.” The distinction is significant because expropriation provides less protection for ownership, meaning the state could forcibly acquire private property where deemed necessary.
Fifth, the law expands mobilization to include data and modern technologies, including supply chains and artificial intelligence. It also calls for supply-chain security assessments to address the risk of disruptions.
The amendments seek to comprehensively integrate domestic resources by bringing technology, industry and infrastructure under greater state control, the official said.
They also reflect the CCP’s concerns about the security of its rule, the official said.
Using legislation to bolster state control shows that the authorities increasingly view almost everything as a security issue.
For Taiwanese businesses, the amendments could increase both political and economic risks, they said. Taiwanese companies could have their assets expropriated or have their operations classified as resources related to China’s “development” interests, raising the risk that investments could be “gone for good,” the official said.

Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power. Do not restart nuclear power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:07 UTC
01:40:07 KST

News reports indicate that an underground nuclear shelter has been installed at a facility associated with the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association’s Taipei office, which some have interpreted as a move to prepare for a potential “Taiwan contingency.”
Even without considering the risk of a nuclear attack, following the 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear power plant disaster, Japan revised its nuclear-emergency planning guidelines with a recommendation that people with 30km of a disaster at a nuclear reactor prepare for indoor sheltering or evacuation. During the 2011 disaster, the US advised its citizens within 80km of the plant to evacuate the area.
The Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association’s Taipei office is about 21km from the Guosheng Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei City’s Wanli District (萬里). If the plant were restarted and a major accident were to occur, the association’s office would fall within the evacuation zone.
In the event of a major nuclear accident at the Guosheng plant, employees of the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association have, if the reports are true, an underground nuclear shelter to take refuge in.
However, what about the nearly 6 million people who live within 30km of the plant, or the nearly 9 million within 80km? Where would they take refuge? About 100,000 people are within a 30km radius of the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春) and about 3.5 million are within 80km.
If a nuclear accident were to occur, would it be possible to evacuate and accommodate that many people?
Nuclear accidents can also release radioactive contamination over an extended area for many years. Fifteen years after the Fukushima disaster, radioactive contamination continues.
If a disaster were to occur at the Guosheng plant, employees of the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association could return to Japan, but many Taiwanese would be forced to live under the shadow of radioactive contamination for years to come.
It is not possible for the government to build enormous nuclear shelters capable of accommodating all those who could potentially be affected, but, at the very least, it should properly decommission aging nuclear power plants that have been shut down for years, rather than create further risks of a nuclear disaster.
Tsai Ya-ying is an attorney-at-law.

PieceMakers eyeing design royalties

PieceMakers Technology Inc (補丁科技) expects to begin generating royalty revenue from its intellectual property next year, as volume production of high-bandwidth custom chips for artificial intelligence (AI) applications nears, the chip designer said yesterday.
Revenue contribution from custom chip design services rose to 40 percent in the first half of this year, compared with 34 percent last year and 4 percent in 2024, thanks to the AI boom, PieceMakers said.
DRAM chips made up the remainder of its revenue.
Photo: Vanessa Cho, Taipei Times
The bulk of AI-related revenues was driven by non-recurring engineering fees, reflecting substantial upfront design wins before transitioning into mass production, it said.
Revenue more than tripled to NT$1.09 billion (US$34.5 million) in the first half of this year, compared with NT$313 million a year earlier, company data showed.
As rapidly growing demand for AI computing power is prompting expansion of memory bandwidth, custom memory chips are gaining traction, PieceMakers president Lee Hsiao-wen (李曉雯) told a media gathering in Taipei.
The company’s 3D-stacked memorychip technology delivers the optimal solution for AI inference, she said.
In contrast, the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips from the world’s top three chipmakers are better tailored for heavy training workloads in data centers, she added.
That is reflected in the new AI chip unveiled by Nvidia Corp at the annual GTC conference in San Jose, California, Lee said, adding that the new AI inference chip architecture is built around on-chip SRAM, not HBM.
SRAM offers cost-efficient chips with larger bandwidth, Lee said.
The company is collaborating with DRAM maker Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技), its largest shareholder with a 35 percent share, in production, Lee said.
PieceMakers is scheduled to debut on the Taipei Exchange’s Emerging Stock Board at NT$740 per share on Wednesday next week.
The company’s net profit surged to NT$564 million in the first half of this year, compared with NT$205 million a year ago, with earnings per share increasing to NT$9.35 from NT$0.82. Gross margin climbed to 67 percent, from 54 percent in the same period last year.

A total of 19,695 candidates have registered for 11,051 positions in the nine-in-one local elections set for Nov. 28, including 26 from China who are naturalized Taiwanese nationals, Central Election Commission (CEC) Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said yesterday.
The CEC and local election commissions are scheduled to complete candidate eligibility reviews by Oct. 16 and draw numbers for eligible candidates on Oct. 23, You told a news conference in Taipei.
Candidate registration closed on Friday.
Photo: Taipei Times
Compared with the 2022 local elections, the total number of candidates decreased slightly by 130, while the number of Chinese-born candidates increased by seven, You said.
However, the changes are in line with long-term trends observed since the first nine-in-one local elections in 2014, indicating stable political engagement over the past 12 years, he said.
Of the 26 Chinese-born candidates, two are running for the position of councilor in the six special municipalities, two for county councilor, one for township mayor, two for township councilor and 19 for borough wardens, he said.
In response to questions about a person who registered as a candidate despite having relinquished their Taiwanese household registration and National Health Insurance and having lived in China for an extended period, You said the eligibility of all candidates would be determined based on the law.
Meanwhile, a national referendum on whether the government should abolish its nuclear-free homeland policy would be held alongside the local elections after being approved by the opposition-led legislature. The referendum was approved by the CEC on Aug. 28.
The commission rejected two other referendum proposals approved by the legislature: one seeking to introduce caning as a criminal punishment and another proposing that traffic fines be used to improve road safety.
You previously said that the two proposals did not fall within the scope of matters that can be put to a referendum under Article 2 of the Referendum Act (公民投票法).
