Explainer: 5 key questions about mudslide on China-Nepal border
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:29:13 CST
00:29:13 KST

KATHMANDU, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck areas along the China-Nepal border on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and severe losses on both sides.
The disaster has raised widespread concern and prompted stronger cross-border emergency assistance, meteorological cooperation and broader discussions on climate change.
WHAT TRIGGERED THE DISASTER?
In Nepal, more than 1,350 people have been killed in the disaster, with roughly 5,000 others missing. Chinese and Nepali experts, as well as scientists worldwide, have confirmed that the disaster was triggered by a fractured glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal at an elevation of around 5,200 meters. The glacier collapse generated an ice-rock avalanche that plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring mountain slopes and developing into a massive debris flow.
The United States Geological Survey said that the glacier-related slope failure generated the energy equivalent of a 5.2-magnitude earthquake. The resulting debris flow and flash flood traveled roughly 100 kilometers, according to the agency.
Austin Lord, senior fellow at the U.S. think tank Stimson Center, noted that the architecture for Nepal's monitoring systems, like most, was built around gauge and station networks designed for monsoon flooding and glacial lake outbursts.
"Unfortunately, a sudden catastrophic flow of this speed outruns it; there is simply no time to share an alert," Lord said in a commentary published on Aug. 28.
WHAT EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE HAS BEEN OFFERED?
China has dispatched specialists, including tunnel rescue and DNA identification experts, to support Nepal's post-disaster response.
In addition to emergency cash assistance, Chinese relief supplies were delivered to Nepal in three batches. The supplies included urgently needed items such as drones, DNA testing devices and reagents, water-purification units, lighting gear, tents, blankets, mortuary refrigerators, medical protective suits and satellite communication equipment.
Reshmi, press officer at Nepal's rescue command camp, said that the Chinese rescue experts were among the first international personnel to arrive in Nepal for search-and-rescue operations.
Pushpa Raj Pradhan, editor-in-chief of Nepal's People's Review, highlighted the significance of China's support given that China itself was also affected by the same transboundary disaster.
Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said his country appreciates China's generous assistance at a time of crisis.
WHAT CHALLENGES DO RESCUE OPERATIONS FACE?
Rescue operations in Nepal were hampered by mud, water, blocked roads, limited helicopter capacity and harsh mountain weather conditions.
Roads and bridges leading to the affected region had been severely damaged, leaving some areas completely inaccessible by land, Khanal said.
At a Nepalese rescue command center in Bidur, Xinhua correspondents saw helicopters taking off and landing almost continuously as rescue operations proceeded at an intense pace.
However, helicopter availability remained limited. Nepal's rugged mountainous terrain and volatile weather conditions sharply reduce the time helicopters can safely operate each day.
Furthermore, for safety reasons, each tunnel search mission can last no more than two hours. Despite these obstacles, the rescue teams have continued to move toward areas inaccessible to ordinary rescue vehicles.
HOW DOES CROSS-BORDER COOPERATION SUPPORT THE RESPONSE?
China and Nepal cooperate in meteorology, water conservation, disaster prevention and reduction, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Following the deadly mudslide, China has provided Nepal with daily meteorological, hydrological and glacier data updates through a disaster information notification mechanism.
The two sides held video weather consultations immediately after the event, according to the China Meteorological Administration. The administration has been providing Nepal with a range of meteorological products through MAZU, China's homegrown AI-powered meteorological early warning system, including multi-source satellite data and products from the Fengyun-3 and Fengyun-4 meteorological satellite series.
Khanal said that satellite and monitoring data shared by China supported Nepal's ongoing disaster response and helped authorities identify potential secondary risks. "China has almost provided Nepal with real-time information so that we remain alert for potential future disaster," he said.
WHAT ARE THE CLIMATE-CHANGE TAKEAWAYS?
During a meeting with Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, Khanal said that Nepal and China share the Himalayan ecosystem and are both vulnerable to climate change impacts. He added that Nepal agrees with China that addressing climate change is a shared responsibility of the international community.
Khanal clarified that Nepal has no intention of separately seeking "climate justice compensation" from any specific country, and will seek compensation from the international community under the frameworks of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement.
Dan Shugar, director of the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary in Canada, told PBS News that steep Himalayan mountain landscapes are continually evolving due to climate change. He argued that the global community must step up efforts to mitigate risks and enhance the resilience of people living in disaster-prone areas, stressing that wealthy Western nations are "largely responsible" for climate-linked disasters. ■

Xinhua Headlines: International journalists witness China's rescue efforts in mudslide-ravaged Gyirong
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:29:07 CST
00:29:07 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Even with prior knowledge of the catastrophe, Brazilian journalist Bruno Falci Bitarelli Medeiros was struck by the harsh rescue conditions after a bumpy 12-hour bus ride from Lhasa to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The final stretch wound through rugged mountain roads, unpredictable weather and falling rocks. "It's a very difficult condition for the workers, and I very much admired how they keep searching for people," Medeiros said.
Medeiros was among a group of journalists from international media outlets including CNN, Reuters and NBC who visited the devastated port from Saturday to Sunday.
At a media briefing by the local emergency rescue headquarters, they heard from technical experts and local officials about ongoing efforts on multiple fronts: the search for the missing, victim identification, community assistance and secondary disaster prevention.
The fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port in Xigaze City on the China-Nepal border on Aug. 26. As of 6 p.m. on Sept. 5, 43 people were confirmed dead and 519 remained missing.
SEARCH GOING ON
At the core disaster zone, a 35-meter-high flood mark, roughly the height of a 12-story building, was scored into the cliff above the ruins.
"Everything below the flood mark was originally underwater," said Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters and acting mayor of Xigaze City. "Power was gone. What you see now is what we've restored in the past couple of days."
Land access to the port was restored on the morning of Sept. 2, allowing heavy machinery to move in and clear working areas.
Mud deposits average four meters deep in the hardest-hit zone, with some areas reaching 16 meters. Inside the core area, vehicles and machinery are conducting deep-search operations -- excavating, searching and clearing layer by layer during grid-by-grid sweeps.
Konda Jagan Mohan Varma from the Press Trust of India watched the operation. "The glacier breakdown brought down a lot of slush, mud and huge rocks together," he said. "A large part of infrastructure was damaged on both sides, in China and Nepal."
He noted the scale of the rescue effort unfolding around him -- heavy machinery carving through the debris, teams fanning out across the ruins in methodical searches.
Just an hour after the journalists arrived, the valley turned from sunshine to pounding rain, forcing an emergency evacuation. Rescuers have persisted in such conditions for more than 10 days.
As of 6 p.m. on Sept. 5, China had deployed over 2,500 rescue personnel, more than 500 vehicle trips and over 9,000 sets of search equipment, and air-dropped more than 5 tonnes of supplies. Two people from a nearby village have been rescued, and nearly 1,000 personal items have been recovered.
BEYOND BORDERS
After repeated verification, authorities confirmed that 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries, including Nepal, India, Latvia, the United States and Britain, remain missing.
For identification, each body is numbered, photographed and sampled for DNA and dental records at the scene. The headquarters has set up a dedicated identification team. So far, none of the bodies retrieved are foreign nationals.
Responding to a question about the identification process for the missing, Yang Lahong, deputy director of the foreign affairs office of Xizang, said at the briefing that the names and specific information of missing foreigners have not been made public to protect their privacy, but have been shared with the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels.
A 24-hour hotline for families of missing foreign nationals has received 509 calls, with feedback provided promptly, Yang added.
At Nepal's request, the Chinese government has dispatched tunnel rescue and DNA testing experts to Nepal, along with emergency material assistance. Through a China-Nepal disaster prevention information notification mechanism, daily updates on meteorology, hydrology, glacial lakes and glaciers are shared with Nepal.
After the disaster, many Nepalese border residents were stranded in China due to the port closure. Local authorities have seen to the daily needs of 1,720 Nepalese border residents.
Green channels for foreign personnel entry and exit have been opened. A total of 3,388 foreign nationals originally planning to leave via Gyirong Port have been diverted, and authorities have helped 365 Nepalese border residents cross the border to return home.
WATCHING FOR NEXT DANGER
Preventing secondary disasters remains a priority. More than 170 experts and technicians are now monitoring the area with over 150 sets of equipment, including slope radar and drones.
Along the main rescue route, 58 geological hazard spots have been identified, seven of them high-risk.
Hu Bo, leader of the China Anneng rescue detection team, serves as a "sentinel" for frontline workers. When upstream data showed abnormal movement, he sounded the retreat signal. Whistles echoed through the gorge as personnel and machinery pulled back to safety zones.
Hu said such scenarios can happen several times a night.
Muhammad Asghar from the Associated Press of Pakistan observed the monitoring efforts. "The monitoring for secondary disasters is being done tirelessly, day and night," he said.
On the site, Medeiros spotted civilian drones flying to observe potential risks for a secondary disaster.
"The technology today is being very helpful to rescue operations in this disaster," he said. "Some countries use drones for war, but China uses drones to help people."
Medeiros noted that, as global warming is the root cause of the disaster, more concrete actions from the world are needed to prevent these kinds of disasters from happening again, citing China's push for a green economy as an example.
Asghar agreed. "Climate change is not the issue of only one country. The whole world should put their heads together," he said. ■

UNEP says investing in climate action, air quality to boost economic prosperity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:29:05 CST
00:29:05 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Investments in climate action and air pollution control are key to driving economic prosperity and improving ecosystem and human health, according to a report released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on Monday.
The report, titled "Hidden Assets: The economic and health case for climate and clean air action," was released on the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, which is observed annually on Sept. 7.
Compiled by UNEP and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, the report is the first comprehensive global economic assessment of integrated climate and clean-air action.
The study demonstrates a significant return on investment, showing that every 1 U.S. dollar allocated toward climate and air pollution solutions generates approximately 15 dollars in economic returns, alongside substantial reductions in pollution-linked mortality and medical expenses.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen underscored that carbon neutrality and air quality are foundational to global development, public health, energy and food security, and environmental stability.
Andersen emphasized that strong leadership from both the public and financial sectors, coupled with effective policy frameworks and technological innovation, is critical to curbing climate-warming emissions and improving global air quality.
To operationalize these goals, the report recommends 25 specific interventions that span six sectors: energy and fossil fuel systems, industry, transport, agriculture and food systems, residential cooking and heating, and waste management.
It combines both long-term decarbonisation measures and measures that target super pollutants such as methane, black carbon, and hydrofluorocarbons.
Should the 25 solutions be implemented, annual economic benefits would reach around 2.8 percent of global GDP by 2035, 4.5 percent by 2050 and 11.4 percent by 2100. Market returns exceed implementation costs within 10 years, according to the report.
In addition, the 25 measures could avoid an estimated 0.34 degrees Celsius of global warming by 2050 and 1.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, the report says.
The 25 measures will also avert 144 million air pollution-related premature deaths alongside millions of cases of chronic disease by 2050, according to the report. ■

JAKARTA, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies are playing a leading role in Indonesia's development of waste-to-energy projects, said Fadli Rahman, CEO of PT Daya Energi Bersih Nusantara, a state-owned company that is responsible for running those projects, at a press conference in Jakarta on Monday.
Since late last year, the Indonesian government introduced two rounds of bidding for a number of waste-to-energy projects. There were 21 submissions in the first round for three projects, all of which were from Chinese companies. The second round attracted 68 proposals for eight projects, with Chinese companies accounting for about 60 percent of the submissions, Fadli said.
"The Chinese companies are very active," Fadli said, adding that many Chinese firms were also working with Indonesian companies to form partnerships tailored to the needs of projects in different regions.
Melda Mardalina, director of waste management at the Ministry of Environment, said waste-to-energy was part of a national strategy that includes waste separation at source, organic waste treatment, improved waste collection and processing facilities, and the use of technologies such as refuse-derived fuel, biogas and composting.
According to the ministry, Indonesia currently generates about 144,000 tonnes of waste a day, but only around 25 percent is properly managed, while the government aims to have all waste managed by 2029 and no longer disposed of into the environment.
Indonesia is accelerating the development of waste-to-electricity facilities in 40 cities facing waste emergencies, with completion targeted in stages in 2027-2028, while projects already under construction include those in Bali, Bekasi city and Legok Nangka in West Java. ■

African officials call for stronger protection of critical infrastructure against terrorism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:28:57 CST
00:28:57 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Enhancing the protection of critical infrastructure and public spaces against terrorist threats is central to Africa's goals of peaceful development, inclusivity, and social cohesion, senior African officials said on Monday.
Speaking at the fifth Nairobi Caucus meeting in Kenya, delegates highlighted the increasing vulnerability of the continent's strategic assets, including roads, bridges, airports, ports, and digital infrastructure, as threats from armed groups intensify.
Convened by Kenya's National Counter Terrorism Center and the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism, the two-day forum is being held under the theme "Protecting Critical Infrastructure Systems and Public Spaces from Terrorism."
The event has brought together senior policymakers, security experts, development partners, scholars, and civil society representatives to explore innovative strategies to prevent terrorist attacks on public infrastructure.
Musalia Mudavadi, Kenya's prime cabinet secretary and cabinet secretary for foreign and diaspora affairs, noted that Africa has become the global epicenter of terrorism, with the critical infrastructure that sustains local livelihoods bearing the brunt of attacks.
"In 2026, the continent of Africa has suffered major terrorist attacks, including targeting critical infrastructure," Mudavadi said, noting that six out of 10 countries most impacted by terrorism are in sub-Saharan Africa.
He urged regional governments to strengthen intelligence sharing, adopt global best practices, and implement security reforms to safeguard vital infrastructure, including power facilities, railways, dams, healthcare centers, and sports venues.
Steven Siqueira, deputy director of the United Nations Counter-Terrorism Center, said that preventing terrorist attacks on Africa's critical infrastructure is essential to sustaining economies, connecting communities, and delivering public services.
Siqueira added that the agency has partnered with the African Union, regional governments, and the private sector to intercept potential threats through technological tools, capacity building, heightened public awareness, and multi-stakeholder collaboration.
Kibiego Kigen, director general of Kenya's National Counter Terrorism Center, stated that the forum provides a platform for African nations to develop home-grown innovations to detect and prevent terror attacks on continental infrastructure.
Kigen advocated for integrated early warning systems, intelligence sharing, and predictive vulnerability mapping, alongside enhanced rapid stabilization capacity and resilient infrastructure design.
Launched in 2022, the Nairobi Caucus is an annual consultative forum that brings together regional bodies and international partners to address pressing security challenges and share counter-terrorism best practices across East Africa and the Horn of Africa. ■

Prosecutor General: I have no plans to resign, but I'm not clinging to the post

Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko states that he has no plans to submit a letter of resignation of his own accord, though he assures that he is not clinging to his position.
"I am not clinging to my position, nor will I ever do so... this is a decision of the team, a decision of the president and the Verkhovna Rada [to dismiss the prosecutor general], but as of today, I have not made such a decision [to submit a letter of resignation of my own accord]," he said during a meeting with journalists on Monday, responding to a question from Interfax-Ukraine about whether he considered it appropriate to resign in light of the damage to his reputation following the release of materials related to the Carthage operation.
Kravchenko added that on Tuesday he will attend a meeting of the relevant Verkhovna Rada committee, to which he was invited by Serhiy Ionushas, a member of the Verkhovna Rada from the Servant of the People faction and Ionushas, chairman of the parliamentary committee on law enforcement, and will answer all questions posed to him by parliamentarians.
"If the MPs want me to resign – there is a procedure; the Verkhovna Rada can remove me from office," he said.
The Prosecutor General said "on all issues where there are questions for me, I have answers that are in accordance with the law, and I am ready for any investigations."
"I am ashamed that there are people on our team who are suspected of crimes. I am frankly ashamed. Everyone (in the Office of the Prosecutor General) understood that, for me, the very idea of such a crime was like drugs – the topic was taboo. This isn't negligence or an accidental traffic accident. I understand that I was simply kept in the dark and that my authority was abused," Kravchenko said.
Responding to a question about the existence of materials concerning employees of anti-corruption agencies that may have been seized by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) during a search, the Prosecutor General noted that he had no information on the matter, but added: "According to reports from my staff, there were materials in their offices, as well as documents related to criminal proceedings involving other law enforcement agencies."
Kravchenko expressed surprise that NABU officials did not present search warrants. "State Security did not let them in because they refused to show the warrants," he said.
Speaking about the searches at his home, the Prosecutor General said that no obstacles were raised; on the contrary, he facilitated the process. "I believe the searches are lawful because there is a court order. I respect the court," he added.
Commenting on reports that he was allegedly in the hospital, Kravchenko said he did not know where this rumour came from, since he was at work on Saturday and journalists could have verified this. "Was I in any hospital? No, I wasn't. Was I hiding? No. I wasn't hiding," the prosecutor general said.
"I have no evidence [to speak more specifically about whether this could have been a provocation against him]. I believe this is a provocation," he said.
The Prosecutor General also said that complaints will be filed with the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission for Prosecutors regarding actions taken by a prosecutor [specifically, by Serhiy Kropyva, the deputy head of the PGO Department of International Cooperation and a suspect in the Carthage case] that bring the office of prosecutor into disrepute, and that an internal investigation will also examine the involvement of other employees of the prosecutor's office in unlawful actions.
"Right now, it is important for me to preserve the morale and psychological well-being of the team," Kravchenko said.
As previously reported, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) exposed five members of a criminal organization led by an official from the Prosecutor General's Office, who systematically received illicit benefits for covering up a network of fraudulent call and laundered over UAH 42 million through the purchase of real estate – including apartments in the Carpathians – jewelry, and the deposit of funds into relatives' accounts. For its part, the PGO also stated its intention to assist with the investigation and announced that the suspect had been suspended from his official duties.
On Sunday, September 6, the court ordered Serhiy Kropyva, deputy head of the Department of International Cooperation at the PGO, to be held in pretrial detention until November 2, with the option to post bail in the amount of UAH 120 million.
Kravchenko denied any involvement in receiving or laundering funds from illegal call centers, and regarding his family's financial situation and living expenses, he emphasized that all expenditures and trips were made exclusively within the limits of his declared income.
"From the conversations [made public by the anti-corruption authorities], it is clear that the anti-corruption authorities' previous claim regarding my involvement in receiving funds from illegal call centers and their laundering has no basis whatsoever. Conversations are just conversations, just as a photo of a safe with money is merely a photo of a safe with money that has no connection whatsoever to me or to the prosecutor's office – it is, according to my attorneys, simply a photograph from another criminal proceeding," he said.

US to pull air defences from Iraqi Kurdistan in September exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:26:06 UTC
00:26:06 KST

Breadcrumb
US to pull air defences from Iraqi Kurdistan in September withdrawal
The United States will withdraw all its forces and air defence systems from Iraq by 30 September as planned, Iraqi government security adviser Qasim al-Araji said on Sunday.
Al-Araji said the US withdrawal from Iraq would include air defence systems stationed in the Kurdistan Region, including Patriot and C-RAM systems that have played a key role in intercepting Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks.
Speaking to reporters in Baghdad, Al-Araji said US-led international coalition forces would leave Iraq completely by the end of September, in line with an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington.
"On 30 September, coalition forces will withdraw completely from Iraq, and this is the implementation of the agreement between the previous government and the international coalition," he said.
Baghdad and Washington reached an agreement in September 2024 setting a deadline of the end of September 2026 for concluding the international coalition's mission against the Islamic State group (IS) in Iraq, following months of talks between the two sides.
Al-Araji said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaydi's government was proceeding with the agreement and that the US had expressed its readiness to withdraw by the agreed date.
He said the withdrawal would include all coalition air defence systems deployed in the Kurdistan Region, adding that the phased removal of troops and equipment had already begun.
The systems have served as an important security shield for the Kurdistan Region against repeated Iranian attacks.
A Kurdish official in Erbil separately told The New Arab that coalition forces would withdraw completely along with the air defence systems.
The official said the Kurdistan Regional Government had expressed concern that their removal could leave the region vulnerable to repeated Iranian attacks and potentially result in casualties.
The regional government had sought guarantees from Baghdad that Iranian attacks would not resume following the US withdrawal and that any renewed attacks would be stopped, the official said.
However, the official said neither the federal government nor the Kurdistan Regional Government currently had clear assessments of what the security situation would look like following the withdrawal.
Al-Araji also linked the withdrawal to efforts to bring weapons held by armed factions under state control.
"The issue of regulating weapons will be discussed after the coalition forces withdraw," he said. "A comprehensive mechanism will be agreed to place all weapons under state control."
He pointed to progress in talks between the Iraqi government and armed factions over the issue.
"The talks are going very well, and there is a positive understanding. The committee of the Coordination Framework, under the direct supervision of the prime minister, is continuing its work to resolve this issue," he said.
The comments come as several powerful Iran-aligned Iraqi factions resist government efforts to bring their weapons under state control, with some demanding the withdrawal of foreign forces as a condition for doing so.
Under the timetable agreed by Iraq and the United States, US forces are due to withdraw from their remaining bases and conclude their military mission in Iraq by 30 September 2026.
Despite the reduction in its military presence, the United States has said it will continue cooperating with Iraqi forces on training, intelligence sharing and counter-IS operations through bilateral arrangements that do not require a large-scale military presence.
No official figures have yet been released on how many US troops or other international coalition personnel have already left Iraq.

Sudanese refugees face the effects of humanitarian funding cuts in Chad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:25:09 UTC
00:25:09 KST

In eastern Chad, near the border with Sudan, more than 117,000 refugees live in the Ouré-Cassoni camp. As new families continue to arrive after fleeing the war in Sudan, needs are increasing while humanitarian funding is declining. In this isolated camp, the consequences of reduced aid are being felt directly in people’s daily lives. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) urges for Ouré-Cassoni to be among the priorities of the humanitarian response in Chad.
Sadia knows Ouré-Cassoni from the inside
Sadia arrived in Ouré-Cassoni with her family after fleeing violence in Sudan. Today, she works in the camp as a health promoter with MSF.
“I arrived here as a refugee and today I work with other refugees,” says Sadia. “I know what it means to wonder what tomorrow will bring.”
Ouré-Cassoni is located in a remote region of Ennedi-Est, in north-eastern Chad. Its isolation makes access to services and the delivery of aid more difficult. Since the war in Sudan began in April 2023, the camp has experienced several waves of arrivals.
More than 60,000 people arrived in May 2025 following the fall of Zamzam camp, in North Darfur state. Following the takeover of El-Fasher, more than 21,000 new arrivals were registered between October 2025 and August 2026. MSF teams continue to observe daily arrivals from Sudan.
The camp is therefore growing, but the resources allocated to the humanitarian response do not follow the same trajectory.
When food assistance is reduced
For families in Ouré-Cassoni, the insufficiency of food is very real, it means not having enough to put on the table for their children. Salwa, a mother in the camp, explains.
“There are times when we do not know what we will feed our children the next day,” she says. “When distributions are reduced, we have to make do with very little.”
MSF teams are also seeing an increase in malnutrition among the children screened. Between 2025 and 2026, severe acute malnutrition increased from 2.2 per cent to 3.4 per cent, while moderate acute malnutrition increased from 10 to 13 per cent.
Behind these percentages are children arriving at health facilities in need of nutritional support, and parents trying every day to find ways to feed their families. The reduction in food assistance adds further pressure. This situation forces families to make difficult choices.
“Before, we could at least rely on distributions to help us feed the children,” says Salwa. “Now, we have to do more with what we have. When there is not enough food, the whole family suffers.”
Before, we could at least rely on distributions to help us feed the children. Now, we have to do more with what we have.
Two litres of water a day
Water is another urgent concern. In Ouré-Cassoni, only around two litres of water is available per person per day, far below the 15 to 20 litres generally recommended in emergency situations.
Getting this water to families requires a complex chain: pumping it from the lake, treating it, checking its quality, transporting it, and distributing it across the different areas of the camp. For MSF, this shows what funding makes possible – or no longer makes possible – in concrete terms on the ground. Reduced funding translates into less clean water being provided to people in the camp.
In July, more than 14 per cent of consultations carried out by MSF in the camp concerned cases of non-bloody diarrhoea. Although a lack of clean drinking water is not the only cause, it is certainly among the causing factors.
“When we talk about humanitarian funding, we also need to think about very concrete needs: keeping pumps running, treating water and making sure it reaches families in sufficient quantities and on a regular basis,” says Joshua Ayuba Mpato, MSF project coordinator in Ouré-Cassoni.
“For people living in Ouré-Cassoni, access to safe water in sufficient quantities is not a luxury: it is a basic necessity for their health and dignity,” he says.
A precarious roof and difficult access to healthcare
After food and water, shelter is one of the main needs identified by communities. Thousands of families have to improvise homes using whatever materials they can find, often in conditions that provide limited protection.
These living conditions also have consequences for health. Respiratory infections, particularly those associated with precarious housing conditions, account for more than 30 per cent of MSF consultations across different areas of the camp and among all age groups.
However, Ouré-Cassoni has only one health centre, and specialist healthcare is not directly available within the camp. People requiring specialist care must be referred to other facilities, where only critical cases are supported financially.
Dire living conditions and lack of assistance also translate into increased risks for women and girls, who are forced to leave the camp to collect water and firewood. Between January and July 2026, MSF teams provided care to 91 victims and survivors of sexual violence in Ouré-Cassoni. Although it is not possible to determine how much of this violence took place in Chad after people fled Sudan, going outside the camp exposes women to an increased risk of violence.
A huge camp, a shrinking response
It is against this backdrop that the question of Ouré-Cassoni’s place in the humanitarian response arises. Ouré-Cassoni was not included in the priority areas outlined in the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan for Chad. For MSF, the contrast is concerning. Needs are increasing at the very time that available resources are decreasing.
“Ouré-Cassoni must be a priority for donors,” says Ayuba Mpato. “We are talking about more than 117,000 people, with considerable needs, and new arrivals every day. The situation we are seeing here is not sustainable. Needs are increasing, but resources are not keeping pace. Without an urgent increase in assistance, the gap between people’s needs and the humanitarian response will only continue to widen.”
In Ouré-Cassoni, the consequences of reductions in aid are therefore not abstract. They are felt in the meals families are able to provide, in the amount of water available, in precarious shelters, and in inaccessible healthcare.
For MSF, the scale and urgency of the needs in Ouré-Cassoni fully justify prioritisation of the camp in the humanitarian response in Chad.

Finland completes section of Russia border fence amid security, migration concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:24:52 UTC
00:24:52 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Finland on Monday completed construction of 200 kilometers (124 miles) of fencing along its border with Russia, public broadcaster Yle reported.
The fence covers part of Finland’s 1,340-km (834-mi) border with Russia, the longest border with Russia with any EU or NATO member state.
Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said further sections could be considered in the future and called for EU funding to support border security projects in eastern member states.
Rantanen said the fence was necessary as Europe’s security situation changed following the 2022 start of the Russia-Ukraine war and what she described as various hybrid influencing operations.
Finland closed its border with Russia in late 2023 amid suspicions that Moscow was deliberately directing asylum seekers toward the border as a form of hybrid pressure.
The government also proposed extending its Border Security Act for another two years.
The legislation is aimed at strengthening border security and preparing for serious cases of what authorities call “instrumentalized migration.”
Construction began with a pilot project near the city of Imatra in 2023 after Finnish political parties the previous year reached a cross-party agreement on the need for partial fencing along the border.
The project cost an estimated €380 million ($443 million) and was completed slightly ahead of schedule.
Around 140 km (87 mi) of fencing were built in southeastern Finland, with additional sections in North Karelia, Kainuu, and Finnish Lapland.
The Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939. The Winter War, as it is known, lasted for over three months and despite heavy losses, the USSR won.

Warning signs abound for Republicans as midterm campaign begins final sprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:24:22 UTC

News analysis
Warning signs abound for Republicans as midterm campaign begins final sprint
- President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity is threatening Republican chances in the midterm elections, with Democrats likely to win the House and possibly the Senate.
- Democrats face internal divisions but have higher voter enthusiasm and historical advantage against the president’s party.
- Republicans hold structural advantages via redistricting and strong funding, but ties to Trump and economic dissatisfaction pose risks to their success.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – As the unofficial start of the campaign sprint kicks off on Labour Day on Sept 7, US President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity is imperilling Republican chances of maintaining their narrow majorities in Congress with just two months before November’s midterm elections.
Midterm elections are, above all, a referendum on the occupant of the White House, according to election experts.
That is even more of a truism in the era of Trump, who has spent the better part of a decade as the country’s dominant political figure and could face stiff political headwinds in his final two years in office.
If Democrats win a majority in the US House of Representatives, as appears likely, the party would be able to open damaging investigations into Trump’s administration while forcing the White House to compromise on most legislation.
Party leaders have already vowed to launch probes into what they describe as Trump’s corruption.
The race for US Senate control is much too close to call, according to analysts, but a Democratic majority in that chamber could block many of Trump’s nominees, including any Supreme Court justices in the event of a high court vacancy.
While Democrats face their own challenges, including an ideological divide between their centre and left flank, Trump’s unfavourability has become a political anchor for Republicans.
His approval ratings are mired at an all-time low, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos survey, with broad majorities dissatisfied with the war in Iran and the economy.
His net disapproval is nearly twice what it was at the same point in 2018, when Democrats gained 40 seats in the House.
Democrats express more enthusiasm about voting than Republicans, a finding backed up by robust Democratic turnout in recent special and primary elections. Registered voters say they prefer Democratic candidates to Republican candidates by 5 percentage points.
Democrats also have the weight of history in their favour. The incumbent president’s party has lost House seats in all but two midterm elections since 1938.
“I think that there is just a general sense that the President is not focused on the No. 1 issue with voters, which is affordability,” said Jessica Taylor, a Senate analyst at the Cook Political Report. “If you want to voice your displeasure with the President, the only way you can do that during the midterm elections is by voting against his party.”
That said, Democrats face challenges of their own as insurgent progressive candidates, including democratic socialists, have defeated establishment-backed moderates in a series of intra-party contests, raising questions about the party’s leadership, messaging and unity.
Republicans retain several structural advantages.
In the House, where Republicans currently hold a narrow 218-214 edge, the party could net as many as 10 additional seats based solely on redrawn maps after winning an unprecedented mid-decade redistricting war.
All 435 House of Representatives seats and about a third of the 100 seats in the Senate are on the ballot in the Nov 3 election.
Winning in Trump country
The Senate map, meanwhile, is even more inhospitable for Democrats.
Even if they prevail in tough races in Georgia, Maine, Michigan and North Carolina, Democrats would still need to win at least two of four states where Trump won in 2024 by double digits: Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.
While Democratic candidates nationally have outraised their Republican opponents, Republican national party committees and Republican-aligned super PACs have far outstripped Democratic counterparts. Trump’s own super PAC is sitting on a US$400 million (S$506 million) war chest.
“There is no doubt Democrats will win the national popular vote,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “It’s a question of whether those structural barriers prevent them from winning the majority.”
Republicans, led by Trump, have sought to portray Democrats as socialists and even communists, pointing to candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan.
“This is a ‘Contrast for America’ year,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said, in a nod to Republicans’ “Contract with America” midterm campaign in 1994. “It’s a contrast between common sense and crazy.”
Whether those attacks will land amid widespread frustration over affordability is unclear. In particular, several states with high-profile Senate races may be feeling outsized impacts from some of Trump’s policies.
In Iowa, farmers have been hit by rising energy costs and Trump’s tariffs, while Texas cattle ranchers were angered by his decision to lift import taxes on foreign beef. Michigan and Maine could suffer from Trump’s escalating trade war with neighbouring Canada.
Republicans will hold an unusual midterm convention this week, an event party officials hope will re-energise its base while reminding voters of Trump’s tax cuts and other accomplishments.
But the convention’s focus on Trump, who will speak on both nights, could also backfire by tying vulnerable Republicans to the President.
While affordability and the war are top issues, many campaigns will also focus on healthcare, Israel’s war in Gaza and the debate over data centres.
Election Day is still eight weeks away, an eternity given Trump’s unique ability to change the political conversation from one day to the next. But it may already be too late for Republicans to alter voters’ negative perception of the economy, analysts said.
“Can Republicans get their enthusiasm up some more?” said Kyle Kondik, an elections expert at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics. “The flip side is that there is no recovery, and Trump’s approval decline is terminal. That’s the big question of the election to me.” REUTERS

Weimar Triangle to continue firmly supporting Ukraine
This was said in the Joint Statement by the Weimar Triangle Foreign Ministers – Johann Wadephul of Germany, Jean-Noël Barrot of France and Radosław Sikorski of Poland – marking the 35th anniversary of the format. The declaration was published by the German Federal Foreign Office, according to Ukrinform.
“We are determined to bring about a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace for Ukraine that is in accordance with international law. We are prepared to contribute to robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine, including within the framework of the Coalition of the Willing, and to strengthen Ukraine's capacity for effective deterrence and self-defense,” the Statement says.
The document notes that the three countries will continue supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary, including through military assistance, funding and donations of priority equipment, industrial procurement, research and development cooperation, joint production, strengthening Europe’s defense industry to ensure rapid and long-term supplies, and financial support for Ukrainian defense production.
At the same time, the three countries stressed their readiness to further increase pressure on Russia’s war economy through targeted and effective sanctions.
“We will continue to take action against Russia's revenues from the energy sector, the Russian shadow fleet, the Russian financial sector, and Russia's military-industrial complex,” the ministers said.
They noted that the Weimar Triangle plays an important role in organizing and consolidating sustained support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
“We intend to rigorously pursue the opening of negotiating clusters and the merit-based enlargement process with Ukraine and Moldova,” the Statement emphasizes.
Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has fundamentally changed the security landscape of the continent, the diplomats said, stressing the importance of strengthening their own security. In view of the long-term threat posed by Russia, the Weimar Triangle will continue addressing a broad range of Russian activities, including hybrid warfare.
The Statement says the Weimar Triangle expects a coordinated European response to Russia’s cyberattacks against the EU and the interests of its member states.
“We will continue to develop robust countermeasures to protect and safeguard our citizens, our democratic institutions, and our critical systems from hybrid influence,” the Foreign Ministers said, noting that amid growing security challenges, Germany, France and Poland play a decisive role in strengthening European security.
“We are determined to further strengthen NATO's deterrence and defense posture. Recognizing the immediate threats on NATO's and the EU's eastern flank, we pledge to ensure the defense of all NATO and EU land, air, and sea borders. Europe must become more sovereign, take greater responsibility for its own defense, and be better equipped to act autonomously and in a coordinated manner, based on a 360-degree approach, and to respond to immediate and future challenges and threats,” the Ministers said.
They also stressed their support for developing a more resilient and competitive technological and industrial base for European defense, including through EU programs such as SAFE and EDIP, as well as within the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF).
As previously reported, Johann Wadephul, Jean-Noël Barrot and Radosław Sikorski met in Weimar on September 2–3.

Thousands attend Bosnian Serb war criminal's funeral in Belgrade despite EU warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:19:31 UTC
00:19:31 KST

Serbian ministers attended despite earlier assurances no serving officials would be present, with Mladić's coffin arriving draped in the national flag and his medals on display. The EU said any glorification of convicted war criminals "has no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries".
Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb commander convicted by a UN court of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, was buried in Belgrade on Monday before a crowd of thousands, despite renewed warnings from Brussels against glorifying him — warnings Serbia's government continues to reject.
Prior to the funeral, Mladić's body lay in state since Monday morning at the Serb Orthodox Church of St Luke in Belgrade, where thousands arrived early to honour him, despite being found guilty of the worst bloodbath on European soil since World War II.
His military officer's cap and sabre rested on the coffin, which was flanked by men in fatigues, with his medals also on display.
The crowd gathered included his former soldiers in military garb and young men carrying banners with his image and flags of Serbia and the Bosnian Serb-majority entity of the Republika Srpska, as hundreds of football fans joined the procession to the Košutnjak graveyard.
The crowd clapped as soldiers carried Mladić's coffin, a gun salute rang out and a military orchestra played.
The head of the Serb Orthodox Church Patriarch Porfirije, who led the funeral service, said Mladić's name would "remain deeply etched in the memory and prayers" of Serb Orthodox people who "feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him."
Although it was earlier announced that no serving officials would be in attendance, Serbian justice, culture, defence and public investments ministers came to pay their respects, along with Russian ambassador to Serbia Alexander Botsan-Kharchenko and President Aleksandar Vučić's son Danilo. Political representatives of Bosnian Serbs were also present.
While the funeral arrangements were formally made by Mladić's family, the Serbian government sent a plane last week to bring his remains to Belgrade, accompanied by Justice Minister Nenad Vujić — who initially announced that Serbia would give Mladić "all the military and state honours," a decision Vučić later tempered.
Soldiers carried Mladić's coffin wrapped in the national flag on arrival to an unmarked maroon van, which was then given a police escort down Belgrade’s main motorway.
A military commemoration was held Saturday at an official Serbian army venue, which the government said was organised by an association of retired generals.
Honours or no honours?
Authorities earlier said Mladić would not be buried with military or state honours. There would be no artillery salutes or ceremonial military presence, and he would not be buried in the Alley of the Greats or the Alley of Distinguished Citizens despite requests to that effect.
Yet according to head of research and advocacy at the Youth Initiative for Human Rights (YIHR Serbia) Marko Milosavljević, while Mladić's funeral as such is private and organised by the family, the pomp around it and the involvement of state institutions and representatives amounts to state honours — which Milosavljević points out are contrary to Serbian law.
"After he was found guilty, he lost his rank in the army, and with that he lost the right to any state or military honours," Milosavljević told Euronews. "But as we can see in practice, in Serbia the same rules don’t always apply."
Milosavljević pointed out that one of the organisers of Mladić's funeral is Svetozar Andrić, Mladić's wartime associate suspected of war crimes who is wanted on several criminal indictments, including for ordering the expulsion of Bosniaks from eastern Bosnia in 1992.
"This wave of celebration of Ratko Mladić absolutely encourages people like him who are still at large that they will never be held accountable for war crimes despite existing evidence," he explained.
Milosavljević believes that by de facto honouring Mladić, Belgrade has opened itself to a potential lawsuit for breaching the European Convention on Human Rights — which was successfully litigated elsewhere in the past.
“Survivors and families of victims of crimes Mladić was convicted for could sue Serbia in front of the European Court of Human Rights on non-discrimination grounds, and there are several cases of family members of victims in Vukovar and in Kosovo who sued for reparations in front of domestic courts in Serbia," he said.
'Emotional outpouring'
Serbia, a candidate country for European Union membership, has faced strong criticism for honouring Mladić after his death.
EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled an upcoming visit to Serbia in protest, arguing that "the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built."
"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," a European Commission spokesperson said in a statement on Monday.
"Reconciliation and good neighbourly relations in Western Balkans remain central to building a shared future," the statement added.
Vučić, who did not attend the funeral, described it as an "emotional outpouring" that "has nothing to do with whether Vučić allowed something or not."
Belgrade, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war in the neighbouring country, has remained defiant over its wartime role and has repeatedly accused the West of anti-Serb bias.
"We have been persecuted and harassed for 30, 40 years ... always guilty whatever happens," Vučić said. "People just won't take it any more."
According to YIHR's Milosavljević, the emotional outpouring Vučić described had not happened by accident.
“Over the past decades, especially while he was at large, a myth was forged of Mladić as a great military commander, but also as someone who embodies resistance against the hypocritical West which has also committed its own war crimes," Milosavljević said.
“So Mladić became an exponent against NATO, against the EU … a useful symbol to represent the collective traumas.”
Vigils, murals and flares
The nearly four-year-long war in Bosnia, which broke out in 1992 after the former Yugoslav republic declared independence, left more than 100,000 people dead and some 2 million displaced and seeking refuge before it ended in 1995 in a US-brokered peace agreement.
Mladić was sentenced for orchestrating the genocide of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, and the years-long siege of Sarajevo, where his troops on the surrounding hills conducted a daily campaign of shelling and sniping at the Bosnian capital's residents.
Since the announcement of his death in The Hague on 27 August, his admirers have held vigils, painted fresh murals of him in Belgrade and lit flares in his honour.
On Sunday evening, Red Star Belgrade fans displayed a large image of Mladić and a line referencing the summary execution of thousands in Srebrenica, and chanted his name at a football match in the Serbian capital.
Serbia has refused to recognise that genocide was committed in Srebrenica, calling the summary execution of thousands a "horrific crime" instead.
Last year, Belgrade buried another convicted war criminal, the former army chief of staff Nebojša Pavković, with full military honours at a cemetery for distinguished individuals.
The ICTY sentenced Pavković to 22 years in prison for war crimes and crimes against humanity during the war in Kosovo in 1998-1999.

Small German leftist party emerges as potential far-right kingmaker

Unknown Publisher

Small German leftist party emerges as potential far-right kingmaker
MAGDEBURG, Germany - The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could end up forming its first state government with the help of a small leftist party that shares its hostility both to mass immigration and to the mainstream parties’ efforts to exclude more radical parties from power.
The AfD surged into first place in the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sept 6 but fell just short of an absolute majority, with 39 of 83 seats in the regional legislature.
While mainstream parties, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU conservatives, have long refused to work with the AfD, in a policy known as the “firewall”, the far-left BSW reaffirmed its readiness to play kingmaker after it cleared the 5 per cent threshold to enter Saxony-Anhalt’s state Parliament.
“We’ve made no secret from the beginning that we’ll talk with all parties. The AfD is part of that,” Thomas Schulze, the BSW party’s lead candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, told Reuters on Sept 7.
Schulze said the mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the AfD was “undemocratic”. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has branded the AfD as “extremist”.
Upending Germany’s consensus
As well as their hostility to Germany’s political establishment and their social conservatism, the two parties share a number of priorities, including a hostility to mass migration - which the BSW says harms local workers’ rights - suspicion of the mainstream media and a desire to end financial and military support for Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
“Hopefully, there are now majorities in the Magdeburg state Parliament in favour of a change of course in energy policy, an end to sanctions against Russia, better education and a fundamental reform of public service broadcasting,” party founder Sahra Wagenknecht said in a statement.
“The BSW intends to use these majorities to improve people’s lives.”
The BSW was founded in 2024 by Wagenknecht and nine others who had broken away from Die Linke (the Left), the main far-left party in Germany and heir to the old East German Communist Party.
Despite its ideological hostility, the BSW in late 2024 joined a coalition with Merz’s conservatives and the Social Democrats in the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia.
But the situation there has become complicated after a row over working with the CDU prompted local members to break away from the main party and form their own group. Wagenknecht herself has favoured working instead with the AfD.
The AfD came first in Thuringia’s state election, too, but fell well short of a majority and was unable to persuade other parties there to join it in a coalition government.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s Siegmund said on Sunday evening that the BSW was “not part of the solution but part of the problem”.
For now, however, Schulze remains supportive of the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt.
“The AfD won the election, Mr Siegmund is the winner. It’s his job to form a government,” he said. REUTERS

Museum to return remains of 39 people taken during colonial rule in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:16:16 UTC
00:16:16 KST

Oxford University museum to return remains of 39 people taken during British colonial rule in India
An Oxford University museum has agreed to return the remains of 39 people who were taken during Britain's colonial rule in India.
The university's Pitt Rivers Museum told Agence France-Presse on Monday that it is preparing to repatriate the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community in northeast India. The decision came after the university approved a restitution request by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) and other groups.
The remains "have been away from their homeland for far too long," museum director Laura Van Broekhoven told AFP in a statement.
CBS News reached out to the university for further comment.
"Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land but importantly about memory returning to where it belongs," the FNR and other Naga organizations said in a statement sent to AFP.
According to the museum, the group's request covered 40 sets of human remains; however, the university approved the return of 39 of them in July because one "does not have a clear provenance as Naga."
The museum said it was "working closely" with the Naga community to agree on a date for a handover ceremony, which has not yet been set.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, one of the world's leading institutions for anthropology, ethnology and archaeology, holds over 6,000 Naga artifacts.
Dr. Ellen Konyak Jamir, an FNR member and coordinator for Recover Restore and Decolonise, a research initiative led by two Naga academics, told MorungExpress that recovering the artifacts involves a complex process and is not their current focus.
In the past, the museum has faced charges of racism and cultural insensitivity because it displayed its famous collection of shrunken heads and other human remains. In 2020, it removed the collection as part of a broader effort to "decolonize" its collections.
"Our audience research has shown that visitors often saw the museum's displays of human remains as a testament to other cultures being 'savage', 'primitive' or 'gruesome','' Van Broekhoven said in a statement at the time. "Rather than enabling our visitors to reach a deeper understanding of each other's ways of being, the displays reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's values today.''
The museum ultimately decided to remove 120 human remains, including the tsantsas, Naga trophy heads and an Egyptian mummy of a child.
The agreement between the university and the FNR forms part of a wider international movement to repatriate artifacts and human remains acquired by Western institutions during the colonial era.
Earlier this year, the University of Edinburgh returned the skulls of six people from the Muscogee Nation in the United States. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation, now based in Oklahoma, were the people of the Southeastern territory on the Mississippi River. The nation has about 103,000 people and is the fourth largest federally recognized tribal nation in the U.S.
In 2022, London's Horniman Museum returned 72 artifacts to Nigeria, including 12 Benin bronze artifacts. Meanwhile, Greece has for decades demanded the return from Britain of the Parthenon Marbles, saying they were looted in the early 19th century by Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire.
London insists they were legally acquired and successive British governments have noted that the decision rests with the British Museum, where they are kept.

Assad's Syrian reactor was configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:11:20 UTC
00:11:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Assad-era Syrian reactor was configured for nuclear weapons, IAEA chief says
The Assad-era government in Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Monday.
The “configuration” and the “technical features” of the nuclear reactor under construction in Syria during the leadership of ousted former President Bashar Assad were “very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be directly used for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” IAEA director general Rafael Grossi said.
“Of course, that was never declared, that was always denied, so, and again, intentions cannot be judged, but that was a very serious proliferation concern that we had, and this has been difficult work,” he told reporters on the first day of a regular meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors, in Vienna.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear program under Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province.
Following Assad’s ouster, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.
During a visit to Syria in August, IAEA inspectors confirmed that “the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country.
Inspectors had to ‘tear down walls’ to find hidden material  
Syria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a July 17 letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found.”
The IAEA said in its confidential report circulated to member states last Tuesday and seen by The Associated Press that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding.” The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.”
Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras at the location.
Syria to decide what happens next 
Asked if the nuclear material will remain in Syria or be removed, Grossi said that this is “a matter that the Syrian government will have to decide.” He added: “We are not requesting them to do this or to do that. For us what’s important is that we know all the time where this (material) is until the last gram.”
Logan Mintz, a director for nuclear materials security at the Washington-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said that natural uranium metal is not directly usable for a nuclear weapon but it could be “diverted to a covert weapons program that further processes it into plutonium for a nuclear weapon.”
She said that once deemed safe to move, the material could be “transported in certified containers” to a third country that can “safely and securely disposition it into a more chemically stable and more widely used form” for possible use in nuclear power plants.
“As with any transport of nuclear material, this movement would require robust security from theft or sabotage,” she said.

Ukraine’s 700 km/h BARS Jet Drone Enters Production in Europe With 1,000-km Range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:11:03 UTC
00:11:03 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine’s 700 km/h BARS Jet Drone Enters Production in Europe With 1,000-km Range
A European joint venture has been established to manufacture Ukraine’s BARS jet-powered drone, with production beginning in early September and the first systems expected to reach Ukraine’s Defense Forces starting October 10, the drone’s developer told RBC-Ukraine on September 7.
The move gives the Ukrainian-designed system a production base outside the country as its developers work to scale output and expand the BARS family for missions ranging from frontline operations to long-range strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“With a move to official and transparent exports, we see opportunities only to increase and expand production capacity,” the developer said.
The main obstacle to faster production is no longer the airframe itself but the availability of turbojet engines, with delivery lead times currently limiting how quickly additional BARS drones can be manufactured.
Meanwhile, the platform continues to evolve rapidly.
The newest BARS configuration can reportedly fly up to 1,000 kilometers, or roughly 620 miles, while carrying a warhead weighing as much as 60 kilograms. Earlier versions were rated for approximately 700 kilometers of range with a 22.5-kilogram payload.
The jet-powered drone can exceed 700 kilometers per hour, or about 435 mph.
BARS was designed from the outset as a modular platform rather than a single fixed configuration. Developers can alter the balance between fuel capacity and payload depending on the mission, allowing the same basic architecture to serve at different ranges.
The system is divided into three principal mission categories: DeepStrike, MiddleStrike, and FrontStrike.
A longer-range configuration can dedicate more internal volume to fuel, while shorter-range versions can trade that endurance for a heavier payload.
That flexibility has been refined continuously. According to the developer, BARS has already undergone more than 40 upgrades and design iterations since the original prototype.
Artificial intelligence is also being incorporated throughout the development process, from engineering work to terminal guidance.
“We use the tools that AI technologies provide us today, and we do not shy away from them at any level—from development and solving engineering problems to implementing machine vision in our target-guidance systems,” the developer said.
During the final stage of flight, the operator can choose to retain manual control or hand the engagement over to an optical terminal-guidance system.
Earlier, Ukraine and Germany signed an implementation agreement to jointly produce Ukrainian-designed BARS jet-powered strike drones, with Germany financing the initial production phase and all completed systems destined for Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The agreement was signed on July 8 by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on the sidelines of the NATO Summit in Ankara as part of the “Build with Ukraine ” initiative, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and statements published by Sybiha.

Russia Identifies US Missile Sites in Norway It Would Target in a Military Conflict
Russia has identified US missile deployment sites and their command-and-control centers in Norway as potential targets in the event of a military conflict, following Washington’s reported deployment of a missile system capable of launching Tomahawk cruise missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on September 7, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Moscow would pay “particular attention” to locations associated with the US missile systems, warning that the deployment had further undermined prospects for strategic stability talks between Russia and the United States.
The Russian Foreign Ministry specifically pointed to a US missile system based on Mk-41 launchers deployed in Norway. The launchers can accommodate different types of missiles, including Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Moscow claimed that missiles launched from Norway could reach a significant portion of European Russia, including Moscow. Reuters reported that US media had indicated Washington delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said the deployment sites and command-and-control centers associated with the US systems “would become targets in the event of a military conflict.”
The ministry also argued that the deployment of US ground-based intermediate-range missile systems in Europe had effectively eliminated conditions for renewed discussions with Washington on strategic nuclear stability.
“Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation ‘reset to zero’—to put it mildly—the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues,” the ministry said, according to Reuters.
Moscow linked the Norwegian deployment to the broader breakdown in arms-control dialogue between Russia and the United States. The Russian Foreign Ministry said strategic stability talks had been curtailed under the previous US administration and described the current administration’s plans for multilateral negotiations involving China as “unrealistic.”
Earlier, a pro-Russian hacker group known as Server Killers declared “cyberwar” on Norway and claimed responsibility for DDoS attacks targeting government digital services, saying the campaign was launched in response to Oslo’s military and financial support for Ukraine.
