Emor: Brand preferences vary considerably across the Baltic states, but one favourite unites them all  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:22 UTC
23:54:22 KST

According to Emor’s survey, brand preferences among residents of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania differ in several respects, but YouTube was rated as the most likeable brand by residents of all three Baltic states.
The survey ranked the most likeable brands among consumers. “Although the top-ranked brand is the same in all three Baltic states, the rankings quite clearly reflect the distinctive character of each market,” said Emor’s research expert Katrin Männaste. The top three brands differ considerably between the countries: in Estonia, YouTube is followed by Swedbank and Kalev; in Latvia, by WhatsApp and Apple; and in Lithuania, by Lidl and Google.
“Estonia stands out for having more brands with local roots and brands developed for the local market at the top of the ranking – in addition to Kalev, A. Le Coq, Coop, Selver and Smart-ID are also among the ten most likeable brands,” noted Katrin Männaste. In Latvia, two local food brands ranked highly: meat brand Forevers and Kārums, best known as a curd snack brand and currently in the process of being acquired by an Estonian company. The locally founded DIY and home improvement retail chain DEPO is also among Latvian residents’ favourite brands. Of the three Baltic states, Lithuania has the most international brands at the top of its ranking: among local players, retail chain Maxima and Lithuanian National Radio and Television (LRT) are represented in the top ten.
“Brand preferences across the Baltic states are united primarily by international brands and the strengthening position of digital brands – behind the leader YouTube, brands such as Apple, Google and Samsung are also among the 25 most likeable brands in all three Baltic states,” Männaste commented. Compared with the previous survey conducted across the Baltic states (2021), ChatGPT, Smart-ID and Waze have now also entered the top 25. There is, however, common ground in other sectors as well: Swedbank and the retail chains Lidl and Maxima are among the top 25 in all three countries. “The extent of change varies between countries: compared with 2021, the composition of Lithuania’s top ten has remained relatively unchanged, while the top of the Latvian ranking has changed more noticeably over the past five years,” the research expert added.
To identify the most appealing brands, Emor conducted an online survey in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in May 2026, in which respondents were asked to select up to five brands they found most appealing from a predefined list. The selection included more than 190 brand names and logos in Latvia and Lithuania and more than 160 in Estonia. The list is based on the experience gained by Emor and its Latvian and Lithuanian partners from various brand studies. The survey included 1,236 residents of Estonia, 1,609 residents of Latvia and 1,548 residents of Lithuania aged 16–74. The survey is representative of the population in this age group.

Where Art Connects through Light: Rothko Museum Announces Autumn Exhibition Season  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:17 UTC
23:54:17 KST

At 4 pm on Friday, 11 September, the Rothko Museum opens its autumn exhibition season, bringing together artists of different generations from France, Italy and Latvia. Through sculpture, painting, ceramics, graphic art, textiles and installation, the new season reflects on encounter, understanding and the search for light at a time when shadows grow ever longer.
Light and Shadow: Yves Brayer and Contemporary French Art
Yves Brayer (1907–1990) belonged to a generation of French artists whose creativity was shaped by a pivotal period in Europe’s search for a renewed cultural identity. Informed by extensive travels across the Mediterranean, his works reveal the richness and diversity of European culture through everyday scenes, where Brayer’s concern is never the outward drama of events, but the presence of people within space and time.
A deeply patient and observant gaze became a defining quality of his art, where composition, rhythm and light are as significant as the subject itself. Light and shadow also run through the exhibition’s contemporary section, bringing together seven French artists – Géraldine Guilbaud, Anthony White, Marie Izaac, Marie Paule Benoit-Basset, Zhenyu Wu, Enrico Nagel and Pascal Pignon JAF. In dialogue with Brayer’s work, they reflect on war and peace, human vulnerability, the importance of memory, the fragility of freedom and the pursuit of light in a world marked by tension and uncertainty.
Umberto Mastroianni: Chromatic Abstraction. 1934–1992
The exhibition introduces Umberto Mastroianni (1910–1998), a major presence in 20th-century Italian art, whose practice was a constant and inventive exploration of abstraction across sculpture, painting, graphic art and textiles. From bronze to paper, from cardboard to tapestry, through bold experiments with cuts, folds, engravings and colour, matter in his art becomes a space for movement, rhythm and intense emotion.
At the Rothko Museum, Mastroianni enters into a symbolic dialogue with Mark Rothko – not through a direct relationship, but through a shared artistic aspiration to move beyond representation and explore the emotional and spiritual potential of art.
Laima Eglīte: Before Words
Laima Eglīte’s (1945) artistic language evolved from her experience at the Rīga Pantomime – a form of stage art and a way of thinking where movement and gesture became a language in their own right. Moving from the stage to the canvas, she kept thinking in terms of pantomime. This is why movement in her paintings is not depicted but organically present.
According to the exhibition’s curator Uldis Čamans (Mans’s Gallery), characters in Eglīte’s paintings – mimes, clowns, enigmatic figures and elegant ladies – do not tell stories in the conventional sense. They embody a mix of human vulnerability, self-irony and quiet dignity. Here, a gesture, a turn of the head or the rhythm of the hands can say more than narrative itself. In this world, silence carries meaning.
Iveta Laure: Love and Silk
The exhibition presents Iveta Laure’s (1962) earlier work alongside pieces created specifically for the Rothko Museum. Throughout, her focus is on women’s rights and self-determination, family and inherited roles, the body, sexuality, violence and freedom. Creative impulses emerge from the Latvian poet Aspazija’s defiant “NO” and the suffragists’ struggle, rural life and craft traditions in interbellum Latvia, war and deportation, Latgale’s Catholic cultural code, Eastern beliefs about women and love, and the everyday sexism that still persists today.
Silk weaves these diverse stories into a coherent visual language. Painted, embroidered or folded into spatial objects and installations, it absorbs both deeply intimate experiences and traces of collective history.
Ingūna Liepa: Towards the Invisible
There is no obvious subject or narrative to hold onto in Ingūna Liepa’s (1965) paintings. Forms surface briefly through layers of paint, at times suggesting landscapes, weather, water or dreams, before receding again into abstraction. Colour shapes the emotional resonance. Soft blues, turquoise, violet, muted pinks, warm peach tones and pale greens settle into restrained harmonies, while delicate shifts in tone and transparency allow light to emerge from within the paintings.
The exhibition’s curator Farida Zaletilo points out that Liepa is less concerned with representing the visible world than with translating emotional and sensory experience into paint. Her works invite the viewer into contemplative spaces that continue to unfold the longer one spends in front of them.
Imants Klīdzējs: In Step with the Wind
A continuous dialogue between material, time and human experience runs through Imants Klīdzējs’s (1956) ceramics. For over half a century, he has consistently pushed the boundaries of ceramics, turning clay into a space for thought, where form is not an end in itself but a means of exploring the order of the world.
The artist’s monumental compositions take shape from hundreds, even thousands, of elements. Each stands alone, and yet together they form a whole. The exhibition’s curator Māris Čačka points to their structural similarity to human experience: a life shaped both by great events and countless details that gather and acquire meaning over time.
Pēteris Martinsons: Notes from Kecskemét
Between 1992 and 2003, renowned Latvian ceramicist Pēteris Martinsons (1931–2013) repeatedly travelled to Kecskemét, Hungary, taking part in residencies and symposiums at the city’s international ceramic studio. The porcelain works he created there – stylised architectural forms now held in the studio’s collection – reveal his distinctive sculptural thinking, sensitivity to form and highly individual approach to material.
Presented at the Rothko Museum’s Martinsons House, “Notes from Kecskemét” concludes a year-long programme marking the artist’s 95th anniversary. Developed in partnership with the Latvian Centre for Contemporary Ceramics, it has highlighted significant works by Martinsons from museum collections in Latvia and abroad.
Exhibition Dates and Opening Night
The Rothko Museum’s autumn exhibition season runs from 11 September to 29 November 2026, with the exception of Martinsons’s “Notes from Kecskemét”, which remains on view through 21 February 2027.
Admission to the new exhibitions is free on opening night.
The Rothko Museum’s autumn exhibition season has been developed in partnership with the Yves Brayer Museum in France, Il Cigno GG Edizioni and Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni, the Latvian Centre for Contemporary Ceramics and the International Ceramic Studio in Kecskemét.
The season is supported by the State Culture Capital Foundation of Latvia, the European Union, the Embassy of the Italian Republic in Latvia, Daugavpils City Council and SERDE residency centre.

Terrorism financing case against Kyrgyz citizen postponed in Lithuania  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:54:17 UTC
23:54:17 KST

VILNIUS - Final arguments in the case of Kyrgyz citizen Mukhamad Ali Nurkulov, who is accused of financing or supporting terrorism, were postponed at Vilnius Regional Court on Friday due to unforeseen circumstances.
Judge Nida Vigeliene announced on Friday that proper translations of relevant documents would be submitted at the next hearing, scheduled for October 7.
On the same day, prosecutor Rimas Juodis requested that Nurkulov's detention be extended for the maximum period of three months. His current detention term expires on September 21. According to the prosecutor, the defendant no longer holds a Lithuanian residence permit, and the crime he is charged with carries a mandatory prison sentence. The court will announce its decision on the extension of detention on September 9.
Nurkulov arrived in Lithuania shortly before his temporary residence permit was due to expire. He was detained at the airport, preventing him from renewing the permit and leading to its automatic cancellation. The defendant claims he was unaware that the Al Qassem Brigades, the organisation to which he transferred money, is designated as a terrorist organisation by the European Union.
Nurkulov is accused of providing direct material support to the Al Qassem Brigades, the military wing of the Palestinian Islamist organisation Hamas, while holding a Lithuanian residence permit, with the intention that the funds be used to support terrorist activities.
The defendant maintains he did not know the Al Qassem Brigades were listed as a terrorist group in the European Union and believed the money would be used for food and other humanitarian aid. He previously told the court he deeply regretted his actions and asked for leniency. However, the prosecutor noted that during the pre-trial investigation, Nurkulov had stated he was aware of the organisation's terrorist status.
Under Lithuanian law, such an offence is punishable by three to 10 years in prison.
According to case files, officials also found posts on his accounts calling for Muslims to join a holy war against non-believers and Israel, alongside photos of masked armed individuals.
Nurkulov was detained at the airport after flying to Lithuania from Istanbul. The pre-trial investigation was conducted by the Financial Crime Investigation Service in cooperation with the State Security Department and was led by a prosecutor from the Prosecutor General's Office.

The Kulbergs government's performance over first 100 days has been mixed, but overall direction is positive - political expert  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:16 UTC
23:54:16 KST

RIGA - The performance of Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' (United List) government over its first 100 days has been met with mixed reviews, though the overall direction is positive, political scientist Juris Rozenvalds told LETA.
In assessing the Kulbergs government's first 100 days, Rozenvalds noted that the government's performance has been met with mixed reviews, but he highlighted as a positive the prime minister's distinct communication style compared to that of his predecessor, Evika Silina (New Unity), whose communication, in his view, had been ineffective. The political scientist noted that the prime minister communicates actively, responds promptly, and makes active use of social media. In his view, the public appreciates this, and it may have largely contributed to the rise in the poll numbers of the United List.
Rozenvalds highlighted the government's achievements in the area of security, noting that Latvia has taken a step forward in how the country responds to security challenges. He reminded that one of the reasons that led to the fall of the Silina government was incidents involving drones, whereas now there is a response, as drones are being shot down. Rozenvalds assessed that Defense Minister Raivis Melnis' experience in Ukraine may have played a positive role.
He also noted that cooperation between the National Armed Forces and agencies of the Ministry of the Interior has been successful in resolving the situation at the national border.
Rozenvalds cited the situation surrounding the national airline airBaltic as another positive development. Although there is no complete clarity about its future, in his view, the situation has at least been temporarily stabilized.
At the same time, the political scientist emphasized that the Kulbergs government is a pre-election government, as it was formed three months before the Saeima elections. Consequently, in his view, the government's actions are closely tied to the expected election results. Specifically, the proximity of the elections significantly determines both what this government does and what it does not do.
Speaking about the Kulbergs government's work, Rozenvalds cited the discussions on the plan to restrict immigration as an example. In his view, these discussions contain elements of a political spectacle staged by the National Alliance which was well aware that the Cabinet of Ministers would not approve an uncoordinated document but submitted it anyway.
The political scientist noted that the prime minister had justifiably objected to such behavior, after which the National Alliance responded with criticism and accusations of insufficient concern for national security. In his view, a concrete solution to the issue will most likely be found, but the discussion itself has been largely shaped by the pre-election atmosphere and the political forces' desire to make a name for themselves.
Speaking about the government's shortcomings, Rozenvalds pointed out that the government's action plan contains more than 150 points, and nearly two-thirds of them have a deadline of October 1. Clearly, this indicates that it will be too late to accomplish anything by then, said the political scientist.
As another shortcoming that, according to Rozenvalds, will affect everyone, he cited the lack of clarity regarding the principles for drafting next year's state budget. Although such clarity had been promised earlier, it remains unclear how the government plans to proceed - whether it intends to cut spending, raise taxes, or pursue other solutions.
Summarizing the government's first 100 days in office, he noted that it still has much work to do this month, including on education issues that have caused turmoil within the coalition, as well as in assessing the aftermath of the storm, improving the system, and strengthening cybersecurity.
Overall, in Rozenvalds' assessment, the government's work has seen both achievements and serious shortcomings. Although one cannot say that things are quite good, the overall direction is positive, said the political scientist, adding that there are also serious shortcomings that the government needs to address.
Assessing Kulbergs' prospects of becoming prime minister again after the elections, Rozenvalds noted that current trends in party ratings indicate a strong position for the United List. In polls conducted by both SKDS and Latvijas Fakti, the party currently holds a lead with a noticeable gap over its competitors.
In his view, the United List could take over the role of the largest political force from New Unity after the elections and gain a similar level of voter support as New Unity received in the 2022 Saeima elections. In that case, Kulbergs' chances of becoming prime minister again would be high, the political scientist said.
"Of course, it will depend on how the votes are distributed and what the potential coalition looks like," said Rozenvalds, adding that this will become clear on the morning of October 4.
As previously reported, the Saeima confirmed Kulbergs as prime minister and his government on May 28; thus, September 4 will mark the 100th day since this government took office.
Saeima elections are scheduled for October 3.

TALLINN - The Baltic Cultural Committee will meet in Tallinn on Thursday and Friday, during which representatives of the Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian ministries of culture will sign a cultural cooperation program between the three countries for the years 2027-2030.
"The world has changed a lot compared to 1994, but one thing has remained the same - the cultural cooperation between Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania remains strong," said Merilin Piipuu, Chancellor of the Ministry of Culture. "In the current security situation, this means we must jointly highlight the role of culture and heritage in strengthening society's resilience to crises and reinforcing democracy. Signing the new cooperation program provides a good opportunity to review what we have achieved together and to set goals for the next four years."
The Baltic Cultural Committee is a regular form of cooperation between the Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian ministries of culture, which meets once a year to discuss various practical cooperation topics. This year, the meeting is hosted by Estonia. The close cooperation of the Baltic states on cultural policy issues helps keep cultural topics visible at the European level. In 2027, all of Europe's attention will be on the Baltics: Estonia will organize a Ukraine reconstruction conference in January, the Latvian city of Liepaja will be the European Capital of Culture, and Lithuania will lead the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of the year.
During the meeting in Tallinn, various cultural institutions will be visited, such as the soon-to-be-completed Tallinn Art Hall and the National Library. To conclude the committee's two-day program, participants will also attend the first-ever Baltic Opera Gala on September 4, which will bring together soloists from the Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian opera theaters on one stage.

Tallink Silja Line’s autumn entertainment programme gets off to a flying start in September: the cruise ships will host a two-month-long Spanish Festival at Sea, whilst beloved artists will perform on special cruises on various routes.
While summer may end in August, it is far from over on Tallink Silja Line’s vessels. From September to November, the cruise ships host a Spanish festival, offering a themed atmosphere, Spanish cuisine and drinks, and a specially created show programme.
“We want to give people a reason to come out to sea even when the main festival season is ending, but they’re not quite ready to let go of that summery feeling. The Spanish Festival at Sea extends that lovely summer feeling, turning the entire cruise into one big experience from the moment you step on board. The fiesta atmosphere is created by characteristic colours, authentic flavours, and Spanish artists,” said Kairi Maidla, Head of Entertainment at Tallink Grupp.
At the heart of the festival are four different specially created show programmes. On the Silja Serenade, the internationally renowned choreographer and dancer Marcos Ayala will perform, while on the Silja Symphony and the Baltic Queen, the Spanish entertainment agency Romantic Corporate will bring themed shows to the audience. The performances range from traditional flamenco and street fiestas to contemporary rhythms and the nightlife of Ibiza.
The festival atmosphere also extends to the on-board restaurants, where a range of Spanish-style dishes are served, including authentic Serrano ham, chorizo, Manchego cheese, tortilla española, patatas bravas, seafood paella and much more. The bars offer sangria and special festival cocktails. The children's programme will also have a Spanish theme throughout the festival.
“High-quality entertainment gives the whole cruise its own character and atmosphere, offering travellers of all ages experiences that they simply wouldn’t have on a regular trip. This autumn's selection is particularly varied, as we have both a Spanish festival and a strong line-up of artists on board at the same time," added Maidla.
Another highlight of the autumn is the special cruises featuring star artists on almost every route Tallink Silja Line operates. This year's onboard programmes feature many acclaimed artists, including nublu, 2 Quick Start, Smilers from Estonia, Erika Vikman, Mirella, Pete Parkkonen, YÖ, costee from Finland, and Felicia from Sweden, to name a few.
Tallink Silja Line’s autumn entertainment programme runs throughout September, October and November, offering plenty of reasons to head out to sea even after the summer peak season has ended.

The Riga Central Business District is Riga’s leading centre of business and commercial activity, bringing together Class A offices, financial institutions and the headquarters of international companies. BAKU — An important meeting between Professor Franco Borruto and Professor Islam Magalov in Baku has opened a new chapter in medical cooperation between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Monaco, the Baltic states and the wider region.
Professor Franco Borruto, gynecologist and health-policy consultant from Monaco and President of the Monaco Baltic States Association, met Professor Islam Magalov, one of Azerbaijan’s leading specialists in obstetrics and gynecology, to discuss the development of regional cooperation in gynecologic oncology, cervical cancer prevention and HPV-related diseases.
The meeting also provided an opportunity to discuss a major new initiative: a regional medical congress dedicated to gynecologic oncology, HPV prevention and women’s health, to be held in Tbilisi under the aegis of the Georgian Society of Gynecologic Oncology.
The congress is intended to bring together specialists and experts from the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Baltic region, creating a platform for scientific exchange and cooperation across geographical boundaries.
For Professor Borruto, the initiative is part of a broader vision developed through his longstanding international medical and institutional activities. His work on cervical cancer prevention, HPV vaccination and women’s health has increasingly been combined with efforts to establish international scientific networks.
Tbilisi has been chosen as the host city because Georgia occupies a unique geographical and strategic position between Europe and Asia. The Georgian Society of Gynecologic Oncology will provide the scientific and professional framework for the meeting, while the initiative is expected to involve experts and institutions from several countries.
The meeting in Baku with Professor Magalov was particularly significant in this context. Azerbaijan is an important regional partner, with an expanding medical and scientific community and growing attention to HPV prevention and cervical cancer.
The proposed congress will seek to move beyond traditional national boundaries. Azerbaijan and Georgia would form an important Caucasus axis, while participation from Central Asian countries and the Baltic states would extend the initiative into a wider international network.
Among the subjects expected to be addressed are HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening, HPV genotyping, early diagnosis, management of cervical precancerous lesions, gynecologic oncology and new approaches to prevention.
The initiative also reflects the increasingly important role of medical diplomacy — using scientific and professional cooperation to establish lasting relationships between countries.
For Monaco, the project represents another opportunity to contribute its experience and international connections to a field of global public-health importance. Through the Monaco Baltic States Association, Professor Borruto has developed longstanding relationships in the Baltic region, creating the possibility of connecting Northern European expertise with emerging scientific networks in the Caucasus and Central Asia.
The Baku meeting therefore represents more than an exchange between two distinguished physicians. It marks the beginning of a broader regional initiative, with Tbilisi identified as the venue for the forthcoming congress under the aegis of the Georgian Society of Gynecologic Oncology.
The ambition is clear: to create a permanent scientific bridge linking the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Baltic states and Monaco, with a shared focus on preventing cancer, improving women’s health and strengthening international medical cooperation.
The first step has been taken in Baku. The next meeting will take place in Tbilisi.

She also thanked the participants in the vote on August 21, 1991 - the lawmakers of the Supreme Council. At that time, international recognition was by no means a given. Latvia is safer than ever, and even today the country’s strength lies in its allies and in a shared conviction regarding a free and independent Latvia, Cebotarenoka added.

At the end of her speech, Ülle Madise said: "I watch and listen to our police officers, defense forces members, diplomats, and statesmen with sincere gratitude and civic pride. Thank you to them! I feel respect and reverence, I feel a responsibility towards our people, and a responsibility for Estonia. I am certain that together we can make Estonia greater, happier, and stronger. I am ready to bear the responsibility of the head of state, if you, esteemed members of the Riigikogu, entrust it to me. Thank you!"
At the beginning of the session, the Riigikogu held a minute of silence to commemorate the passing of long-serving members Siim Kallas and Priit Aimla.
The National Electoral Committee registered Madise as a presidential candidate on August 25. She was nominated for the first round of voting in the Riigikogu by 75 of its members.

====================================================================================================

Buying a Car in Latvia: How to Make a Practical and Financially Responsible Choice  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:00 UTC
23:54:00 KST

For many people in Latvia and across the Baltic region, a car is more than a convenient way to travel. It can be essential for commuting to work, taking children to school, reaching medical services, visiting relatives, or managing everyday responsibilities outside major city centres.
Public transport is widely available in larger cities, but mobility options can become more limited in smaller towns and rural areas. In these situations, owning a reliable vehicle can save time, improve access to services, and provide greater independence.
However, purchasing a car is also a major financial commitment. The advertised price is only the beginning. Fuel, insurance, taxes, servicing, repairs, tyres, parking, and financing costs can place considerable pressure on a household budget.
A successful purchase therefore requires more than finding an attractive model at a seemingly good price. Buyers need to understand their actual mobility needs, calculate the full cost of ownership, inspect the vehicle carefully, and choose financing that remains affordable over time.
Start with the way the car will be used
Before comparing brands and models, buyers should define what they expect from the vehicle.
A person who mainly drives short distances in Riga may need a very different car from someone who commutes between towns every day. A family with young children will have different priorities from a driver who usually travels alone. Someone living in a rural area may need greater ground clearance and a durable suspension, while a city resident may value compact dimensions and easy parking.
Useful questions include:
- How many kilometres will the car cover each month?
- Will it mainly be used in a city or on longer routes?
- How many passengers will travel regularly?
- Is space needed for child seats, luggage, pets, or sports equipment?
- Will the car be used on gravel or poorly maintained roads?
- Is towing capacity important?
- Where will the vehicle normally be parked?
- How long does the buyer plan to keep it?
Answering these questions can prevent buyers from paying for size, power, or equipment they do not actually need.
A large sport utility vehicle may appear practical, but it can be expensive to fuel, insure, and maintain. A compact car may be more economical, but it may not provide enough space for a growing family.
The best choice is not necessarily the most impressive vehicle. It is the one that fits the buyer’s normal routine.
Calculate more than the purchase price
One of the most common mistakes is focusing only on the price shown in the advertisement.
The real cost of owning a vehicle includes a wide range of regular and occasional expenses. These may include:
- fuel or electricity;
- compulsory motor insurance;
- optional comprehensive insurance;
- vehicle taxes;
- technical inspections;
- scheduled maintenance;
- unexpected repairs;
- seasonal tyres;
- tyre storage and replacement;
- parking;
- cleaning;
- registration costs;
- financing payments.
Two vehicles with the same purchase price can have very different long-term costs.
An older premium car may be available for the same price as a newer mainstream model. The premium vehicle may offer more comfort and stronger performance, but its parts, repairs, insurance, and tyres may remain expensive.
A lower initial price does not automatically mean better value.
Before purchasing, it is useful to estimate the vehicle’s total annual cost and divide that amount by twelve. This provides a more realistic monthly figure than looking only at a loan payment.
Buyers should also leave room in their budgets for unexpected expenses. A car that consumes every available euro each month is probably too expensive, even if the lender is willing to finance it.
Decide between a new, nearly new, and older vehicle
Each category offers advantages and disadvantages.
A new car generally includes a manufacturer’s warranty, modern safety systems, and predictable servicing requirements. The buyer knows the vehicle’s full history from the beginning.
The main disadvantage is the higher price. New vehicles can also lose value relatively quickly during the first years of ownership.
A nearly new car may provide a useful balance. It may still offer current technology, modern safety equipment, and relatively low mileage, while costing considerably less than a brand-new equivalent.
An older used car can be affordable to purchase, but it usually carries a higher risk of repairs. Its condition depends heavily on how previous owners maintained and used it.
Vehicle age alone should not determine the decision. A properly serviced older car may be more reliable than a newer car that has been neglected or poorly repaired after an accident.
The condition of the specific vehicle matters more than general assumptions about its model year.
Research the market before contacting a seller
Buyers should compare several similar vehicles before arranging an inspection.
The comparison should include cars of the same model with similar engines, ages, mileages, and equipment levels. This helps establish a reasonable market price.
An unusually low price should be treated cautiously. There may be a legitimate explanation, but it could also indicate:
- serious mechanical problems;
- previous accident damage;
- incorrect mileage;
- legal restrictions;
- incomplete documents;
- an urgent need for major servicing;
- expensive worn components.
A good deal should remain good after the cost of repairs and maintenance is included.
Advertisements should also be examined carefully. Buyers should be cautious when descriptions are vague, photographs are limited, or the seller avoids providing the vehicle identification number.
A trustworthy seller should be willing to answer reasonable questions and allow an independent inspection.
Ask detailed questions before viewing the car
A telephone conversation can save time and reveal useful information.
Buyers may ask:
- How long has the seller owned the vehicle?
- Why is it being sold?
- Was it imported from another country?
- Where was it serviced?
- Are service records available?
- Has it been involved in an accident?
- What repairs have been completed recently?
- Are there any known defects?
- How many keys are included?
- Can the car be inspected at a workshop chosen by the buyer?
The seller’s answers should remain consistent during the process.
It is normal for a used car to have signs of wear or minor defects. A seller who openly explains these issues may be more credible than someone who claims that an older vehicle has never required repairs.
Unclear, changing, or evasive answers should encourage the buyer to investigate further.
Check the vehicle identification number and history
The vehicle identification number, or VIN, is one of the most important tools available to a used-car buyer.
The VIN shown in the registration documents must match the number displayed on the vehicle. Buyers should check the locations specified by the manufacturer, including the bodywork and identification plate.
A damaged, altered, or difficult-to-read VIN is a serious warning sign.
Available registers and commercial history services may provide information about:
- recorded mileage;
- technical inspection results;
- previous registration countries;
- ownership changes;
- insurance claims;
- accident records;
- legal restrictions.
Mileage should increase logically over time. If a later record shows fewer kilometres than an earlier one, the buyer should request a clear explanation.
Vehicle-history reports are useful, but they are not complete guarantees. Accidents and repairs performed privately may never appear in a database.
A clean report does not eliminate the need for a professional inspection.
Inspect the car in daylight
A vehicle should ideally be inspected during daylight and in dry conditions.
Rain, darkness, and dirt can hide scratches, corrosion, paint differences, and evidence of repairs.
Buyers should examine:
- gaps between body panels;
- paint consistency;
- signs of overspray;
- welding marks;
- corrosion around wheel arches and sills;
- cracks in windows and lights;
- tyre condition;
- fluid leaks;
- the operation of doors, the bonnet, and the boot.
Uneven gaps between body panels may indicate previous accident repairs. Different production dates on individual windows or lights are not automatically problematic, because parts may have been replaced after minor damage.
However, several inconsistencies together may justify a more detailed examination.
Tyres can also reveal useful information. Uneven wear may indicate alignment problems, suspension wear, or previous structural damage.
Examine the interior carefully
The condition of the interior should be consistent with the stated mileage.
A vehicle advertised with low mileage should not normally have extreme wear on the steering wheel, pedals, gear selector, or driver’s seat.
All electrical equipment should be tested, including:
- electric windows;
- central locking;
- mirrors;
- seat heating;
- air conditioning;
- climate control;
- multimedia equipment;
- parking sensors;
- cameras;
- interior lighting;
- charging ports.
When the ignition is switched on, warning lights should appear on the dashboard and then go out after the engine starts.
If an important warning light never appears, it may have been disabled to hide a fault.
Air conditioning should be tested even during colder months. A seller’s claim that a non-functioning system “only needs gas” should not be accepted without evidence. The real problem may involve a compressor, condenser, sensor, or leak.
Start the engine when it is cold
Whenever possible, buyers should ask to see the car before the engine has been warmed up.
Cold starting can reveal problems that are less noticeable once the engine reaches operating temperature.
The engine should start without excessive delay. Buyers should listen for unusual metallic noises, unstable idling, or persistent vibrations.
Exhaust smoke can also provide clues. Some visible vapour may be normal in cold weather, but persistent blue, black, or heavy white smoke may indicate mechanical problems.
A spotless engine compartment is not always reassuring. In some cases, an engine may have been cleaned immediately before sale to hide oil or coolant leaks.
The fluid levels and general condition should be checked, but a complete assessment still requires professional knowledge.
Never skip the test drive
A test drive is essential, even if the car appears to be in good condition.
The radio should be turned off so that the buyer can listen for unusual noises.
During the drive, the buyer should assess:
- engine response;
- gear changes;
- steering;
- braking;
- suspension;
- vibration;
- road noise;
- visibility;
- seat comfort;
- control layout.
The car should be driven at different speeds and, where possible, on different road surfaces.
Knocking sounds over uneven roads may indicate worn suspension components. Vibrations may be linked to tyres, brakes, driveshafts, wheel bearings, or other mechanical parts.
An automatic transmission should shift smoothly without strong impacts or long delays.
The car should also remain stable during braking. Pulling to one side may indicate a problem with the brakes, tyres, suspension, or alignment.
The test drive is also an opportunity to decide whether the model is genuinely comfortable. A technically sound car can still be unsuitable if the driving position is poor or visibility is limited.
Arrange an independent technical inspection
An independent workshop inspection is one of the most important stages of a used-car purchase.
The workshop should be selected by the buyer rather than the seller.
A professional inspection may cover:
- the engine;
- the transmission;
- the braking system;
- suspension components;
- corrosion;
- electronic fault codes;
- accident-repair evidence;
- tyres;
- safety systems.
The inspection can identify both immediate problems and maintenance that may be required soon.
Minor defects do not always justify rejecting a car. They may instead provide a basis for negotiating a lower price.
However, major engine, gearbox, structural, or corrosion problems can make an apparently affordable vehicle very expensive.
A seller who refuses to allow an independent inspection gives the buyer a strong reason to walk away.
Choose financing carefully
Some buyers prefer not to use all their savings for a vehicle purchase. Others may need financing to obtain a safer or more reliable car.
One possible option for purchasing a used or nearly new vehicle is an car loan. Before signing any agreement, the buyer should evaluate the full cost of the financing and its effect on the household budget.
Important factors include:
- the interest rate;
- the annual percentage rate;
- agreement fees;
- repayment period;
- total amount repayable;
- early repayment conditions;
- late-payment charges;
- insurance requirements;
- other associated costs.
A low monthly payment does not always indicate an inexpensive loan. It may be the result of a longer repayment period, which can increase the total cost.
The repayment term should also be reasonable in relation to the age of the vehicle. A buyer should avoid paying for many years on a car that may already require increasingly expensive repairs.
Financing should make a necessary purchase manageable, not encourage the buyer to choose the most expensive vehicle available.
A sensible monthly payment leaves room for fuel, maintenance, repairs, and other household needs.
Review the documents before making payment
The purchase agreement should contain accurate information about the vehicle and the transaction.
It should include:
- the manufacturer and model;
- the registration number;
- the VIN;
- the recorded mileage;
- the actual purchase price;
- known defects;
- the number of keys and documents;
- the date of the transaction;
- the buyer’s and seller’s details.
Buyers should not agree to record a lower price in the contract than the amount actually paid. This could create problems if a dispute later arises.
Payment should ideally be traceable, such as through a bank transfer.
The buyer should retain:
- the purchase agreement;
- payment confirmation;
- the workshop inspection report;
- a copy of the advertisement;
- written communication with the seller;
- service records.
Before transferring the money, the buyer should confirm that ownership can be changed immediately and that there are no legal restrictions affecting the car.
Plan for maintenance immediately after purchase
Even when the seller says the car was serviced recently, the buyer should request documentary evidence.
If the maintenance history is uncertain, it may be sensible to replace:
- engine oil;
- oil filters;
- air filters;
- cabin filters;
- fuel filters where applicable;
- brake fluid;
- coolant;
- other scheduled components.
The timing belt or timing-chain history should be checked carefully. Failure of timing components can cause severe engine damage.
The battery, brakes, and tyres should also be assessed.
These initial costs should be included in the purchase budget. Completing preventive maintenance gives the new owner a clear starting point for future servicing.
Consider the right type of powertrain
The ideal powertrain depends on how the vehicle will be used.
A petrol car may be suitable for shorter or less frequent journeys. It can be a practical option for city driving and lower annual mileage.
A diesel vehicle may be economical for drivers who regularly cover long distances. However, repeated short journeys may create problems for some diesel emissions systems and lead to expensive repairs.
A hybrid can perform efficiently in urban traffic, where frequent braking and acceleration allow energy recovery systems to operate effectively.
An electric car may be practical for a household with reliable charging at home or work. Buyers should still consider real-world range, charging speed, winter performance, and battery condition.
The most fashionable technology is not automatically the right choice. The powertrain should match the driver’s real routine.
Avoid making a decision under pressure
Car purchases can be emotional. Buyers may be attracted to the design, performance, brand, equipment, or idea of owning a particular model.
The vehicle should be enjoyable, but emotions should not replace a careful assessment.
Sellers may create urgency by saying that another buyer is arriving soon. That should never be a reason to skip checks, avoid a workshop inspection, or sign documents without reading them.
There will always be another car on the market.
Before making the final decision, the buyer should be able to answer these questions:
- Does the vehicle suit my everyday needs?
- Can I afford its full monthly cost?
- Has its history been checked?
- Has it been inspected independently?
- Do I understand the financing terms?
- Will I still have money available for repairs?
- Are all documents complete and accurate?
If any answer remains unclear, the purchase should be delayed.
A good car should support everyday life
The best vehicle is not necessarily the newest, most powerful, or most prestigious one.
It is a car that starts reliably, performs safely, meets the owner’s practical needs, and remains affordable to maintain.
A responsible purchasing process includes defining real mobility requirements, comparing market prices, reviewing the vehicle’s history, carrying out a professional inspection, calculating ownership costs, and selecting financing carefully.
These steps require time, but they can prevent years of financial difficulty and frustration.
A well-chosen car provides more than transportation. It offers independence, saves time, connects people with work and essential services, and makes daily travel more convenient.
The goal should not simply be to buy a vehicle. It should be to choose one that continues to make sense long after the excitement of the purchase has passed.

Serbia's prime minister proposed on Monday dissolving parliament, paving the way for an early election long demanded by the student-led protest movement.
Parliamentary elections were not due until December 2027, but President Aleksandar Vucic announced a vote for late October after nearly two years of anti-government unrest.
The student-led anti-graft movement began after the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station on Nov. 1, 2024, which killed 16 people and was widely blamed on entrenched corruption.

"Serbia has faced protests, blockades, deep divisions, problems in education and heavy pressure on institutions," Macut told ministers.
"For some time, parts of the public have been calling for early parliamentary elections," he said, adding that "a responsible government never ignores such demands."
Vucic, who has been in power since 2012, now has 72 hours to accept the proposal and dissolve parliament.
He had previously signalled he would do so on Sept. 9 or Sept. 10, with the deadline for elections to be held in October.
Students leading university blockades have demanded early elections since May 2025.
Government officials repeatedly said they would call elections, but did not set a date.
Vucic said in late June that he would step down as president before his term expires in April 2027 so that he could participate in the campaign.
His right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) decided at a meeting over the weekend to ask him to head its electoral list and stand as its candidate for prime minister.

The number of homeless people in Brussels is expected to rise by another 25% when the Belgian capital's next homelessness count is carried out in October, with a growing number of families among those experiencing homelessness, according to Bruss'help.
Bruss'help, the coordinating agency for homelessness assistance in Brussels, will conduct its ninth count across the Brussels-Capital Region on the night of Oct. 15-16, alongside similar operations in Flanders and Wallonia, news portal BRUZZ reported on Monday.
The previous count, conducted two years ago, identified 9,777 homeless people in Brussels, representing a 25% increase from the previous count.
Bruss'help said signs from frontline services already point to a further rise in homelessness.
"The signals on the ground are clear: we have to refuse emergency shelter to more and more people," Adele Pierre of Bruss'help said, adding that the number of families seeking assistance is also increasing.
More young people could also be counted among Brussels' homeless population, according to the agency.
Pierre said the planned elimination by the federal government of 1,000 reception places under the Brussels Deal could already be contributing to the situation.
"Those places were indeed filled, but because the responsible minister is providing accommodation to fewer asylum seekers, Brussels is facing more homeless people," Pierre said.
Previous data showed that around one-quarter of people in emergency shelters had been homeless for more than two years, while one in 10 was a single mother with children.
About one-quarter did not have a residence permit.

====================================================================================================

How Three Small Baltic States Ended Up Running Europe's Crypto Plumbing  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:53 UTC
23:53:53 KST

When MiCA came into force, the smart money picked its winners early, and the shortlist always read like a roll call of old money, with Frankfurt, Paris, Dublin, Amsterdam, and Luxembourg turning up in every version of it. Those places have incumbent banks, supervisory headcount and lobbying muscle, so the assumption was fair enough.
The transitional window slammed shut, the raw tallies appear to confirm it. Germany sits at the top of the CASP authorisation table, ahead of France and the Netherlands, out of 322 records across the EEA.
Open that German column, though, and hardly any of the names are crypto companies. It is Commerzbank, DZ BANK, DekaBank and a scattering of regional Volksbanks, a lead built almost entirely on incumbent banks that sit well outside what MiCA was written to govern.
Of the 322 authorisations, 206 went to crypto-native businesses and 116 to traditional institutions adding crypto to an existing book. Only 17 firms on the whole register are licensed to run a live trading platform. Germany’s column is the most bank-heavy of all, which is why its headline lead is misleading.
Counting licences tells you where applications got processed. It reveals close to nothing about where Europe's crypto plumbing is being welded together, and on that question I’d point 1,500 kilometres northeast, to three countries whose combined population would fit inside metropolitan Paris.
Regulators that chose subtraction
Estonia carried 1,234 licensed crypto firms at the end of 2019 and, by 2021, an estimated 55% of the world's registered virtual asset service providers (VASPs) — a widely cited figure that is difficult to independently verify. A licence back then cost only €300 and came with light scrutiny. The country’s Financial Intelligence Unit spent three years dismantling that, and by 1 May 2023 exactly 100 authorisations were left standing.
Lithuania ran the same operation on a slower clock. Around 850 crypto companies sat on its register in late 2022; across 2025 the Bank of Lithuania received 102 MiCA applications from just 55 firms, and had granted three CASP licences by early January 2026.
Latvia never had the volume to lose and has authorised ten CASPs since the regulation took effect (a count that shifts as the register updates), a stablecoin payments firm tenth in July.
Three governments installed a filter, and it did precisely what filters do.
Riga offers consultations — at €2,500
Bank of Latvia does something unusual for a financial supervisor, which is to give its own time away. Prospective applicants get unlimited free consultations (roughly 100 a year, conducted in English) before the company in question legally exists.
Application fees run to €2,500, among the lowest in the EU, with ongoing supervision pegged at 0.6% of gross revenue and a €3,000 floor. Latvia can afford to charge that little because the consultations catch hopeless applications early. If the regulator thinks a structure won't pass, it says so in the meeting, and that's usually the end of it.
Compare this with the jurisdictions where dialogue begins only after you have paid a law firm six figures to guess what the regulator wants. Those markets end up selecting for firms skilled at navigating bureaucracy, which is a different competence from building products people can actually use.
Dual licences are the tell
Four of Latvia's ten licensed CASPs have now paired their MiCA authorisation with a payment or e-money licence from the very same regulator, several of them within weeks of each other.
Stacking MiCA on top of PSD2 is what a company does when its product is a rail. Custody and exchange permissions cover the crypto leg; the payment institution licence covers euros arriving and leaving, along with consumer protections a CASP authorisation by itself does not carry.
Talent compounds where it lands
Vilnius holds the deepest bench in the region. Lithuania's 248 active fintechs employ close to 7,800 people and serve around 40 million customers, and its payment and e-money institutions moved €163 billion last year, up 57% since the end of 2022.
Average team size there climbed from 21 to 31 over five years even as the company count fell from 282 to 248. Fewer firms, bigger firms, more experienced teams.
Tallinn contributes something harder to tabulate, in a country of 1.3 million that has produced ten unicorns and attracted over 130,000 e-residents from 180-odd countries who, between them, registered more than 37,000 Estonian companies. Skype's alumni are still seeding new ventures two decades after the exit.
Riga adds roughly 40,000 ICT specialists, about 4.4% of everyone employed in Latvia, with the country ranking third in Europe for ICT students per million inhabitants. Together, the three produce engineers who can read and handle both regulatory compliance and blockchain infrastructure.
Hiring a compliance officer who has already survived a supervisory review is an ordinary Tuesday in Vilnius. Try that in a city where the crypto industry showed up last year.
The big centres are reading it wrong
Set the compliance bar high enough to screen out the weak and what remains is a smaller, sturdier field. Passporting then carries those survivors across all 27 member states from a single regulator.
With roughly 83% of legacy-registered firms never converting to a full MiCA licence, each early licence looks more valuable by the month. Most of the 322 authorisations Europe is busy counting will never move serious volume, and a Baltic handful will end up moving most of it. Redraw Europe's crypto map around the licences that cover real rails, and its centre of gravity settles a long way north of Frankfurt.

For fintech entrepreneurs and investors, acquiring an existing financial company can provide an alternative route into a regulated market. The right option depends on factors including the business model, target market, jurisdiction and regulatory requirements.

The Gambling Rulebook Is Changing... Here’s What It Means for Digital Gaming  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:50 UTC
23:53:50 KST

Identity checks, spending limits and clearer promotional conditions are now appearing directly inside the digital gaming journey. What once sat mainly in licensing documents or terms and conditions is becoming visible in the product itself. For players, that can mean more prompts, more information and occasionally an extra step before play begins. For developers, it means the rules increasingly influence how a gambling platform is built.
The Rulebook Is Moving Onto the Screen
The European standard EN 18144, published in May 2026, identifies nine behavioural markers that may help operators recognise potentially risky patterns. They include changes in stake frequency, speed of play, deposits, withdrawals, session length, losses and the use of safety tools. It is a voluntary standard rather than legislation, an important distinction. A longer session or a larger deposit is not automatically treated as a problem. Several changes can be considered together instead, placing more emphasis on how behaviour develops over time. That requires more than a warning page hidden in an account menu. The system itself needs to be capable of noticing those changes and deciding when a response may be appropriate.
Mobile Play Has Made the Boundaries Less Obvious
In 2024, mobile devices generated 58% of online gambling revenue, according to figures published by the European Gaming and Betting Association with H2 Gambling Capital. The same dataset put total European gambling revenue at €123.4 billion, with €47.9 billion coming online. That represented 39% of the overall market, compared with 37% a year earlier.
A gambling session now sits beside banking apps, messages, streaming platforms and online shopping. Deposits, verification and account controls have to work within an interface designed for a small screen and quick interactions. Space is limited, so even a short warning or extra confirmation has to compete with menus, balances and game controls. Most mobile products try to remove every unnecessary pause. Regulated gaming sometimes needs to introduce one.
Sometimes the Extra Friction Is Deliberate
A request to confirm an identity or review a spending limit may look like another barrier between the user and the game. In some cases, that barrier is intentional. A short pause can force an active decision where a frictionless interface would normally encourage another tap. Clearer promotional conditions can do something similar by putting information in front of the user before an offer is accepted rather than expecting it to be found later.
Similar design questions already appear elsewhere online. Similar design questions already appear elsewhere online, particularly as age-verification requirements for digital products become more closely tied to how platforms are built rather than relying on simple self-declaration.
What the Licence Changes for the Player
Licensing may sound like background administration, but its effects are often practical. It can influence registration checks, payment information, account controls and the way responsible-gambling tools are presented. For readers comparing those features, a Casino.org guide brings together information on licensing, payments, games and account protections in one place. Casino.org is an independent gambling information and review site that assesses online platforms and publishes guidance on matters including licensing, payment methods, withdrawals and responsible-gambling features. Those details affect the experience from the moment an account is opened, even if the user never thinks of them as part of regulation.
Designers Now Have More Than Usability to Think About
Imagine a routine session. Someone creates an account, verifies their details, deposits money, chooses a game and later adjusts a personal limit. None of those actions looks particularly unusual. Yet each can involve requirements that affect what appears on the screen and when. Under EN 18144, a change in session duration might be considered alongside faster play, larger deposits or different withdrawal behaviour. One action does not produce an automatic judgement, but a digital system may need to recognise patterns across several actions.
The shortest journey is not automatically the best one. A prompt that asks someone to review a setting may serve a purpose precisely because it interrupts the flow. Developers also have to decide where information appears, how easy account controls are to find and which actions should require another confirmation. That includes small decisions such as whether a limit setting sits beside payments or deeper inside the account menu. None of that is as visible as the game graphics or animation, but it affects the experience just as directly. Good app design usually tries to make the machinery disappear. Regulated gaming sometimes needs part of that machinery to stay visible.
What the Player Actually Notices
Most users will never read the standards behind a platform or follow every regulatory update. They will notice the result instead: an extra verification screen, clearer conditions beside an offer, a limit setting that is easier to find or a prompt appearing at a particular point in a session. Those details may look like ordinary interface choices. They are also where the changing gambling rulebook becomes visible.

TALLINN - Estonian Minister of Energy and Environment Andres Sutt hosted the first Nordic-Baltic (NB8) energy ministers' meeting in Tallinn from September 3-4, bringing together energy ministers and senior representatives from the Nordic and Baltic countries.
The meeting, which included a Ukrainian delegation in its initial discussions, focused on supporting Ukraine's energy supply for the upcoming winter, the resilience of critical energy infrastructure, and the development of a competitive Nordic-Baltic energy market.
Sutt stressed that the closely interconnected energy systems of the Nordic-Baltic countries require stronger cooperation than ever. "Energy security in our region today is not just about having enough electricity, but also about whether our infrastructure can withstand potential threats and how quickly we can restore energy supply in the event of disruptions. Our energy systems are increasingly linked, and therefore we must view our preparedness and cooperation from a regional perspective," he said.
Discussions on Ukraine's energy supply centered on the upcoming winter. Russia's ongoing attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure are expected to make the winter extremely difficult, and the ministers explored ways to support the continuity of Ukraine's energy supply and coordinate aid from their respective countries. They also discussed the long-term recovery of Ukraine's energy sector and energy-related preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference, scheduled to be held in Tallinn in January 2027.
"While providing aid to Ukraine, we must not forget its invaluable experience. The ongoing war has taught Ukraine how to protect its energy infrastructure, ensure its operational continuity, and restore energy supply to residents and critical facilities as quickly as possible. We must learn these priceless lessons from the Ukrainians and use them to protect our own countries' infrastructure from potential threats," said Lithuanian Minister of Energy Lukas Savickas.
In addition to regional energy security, the meeting focused on protecting Baltic Sea energy infrastructure and ensuring the resilience of energy systems. The region's energy infrastructure is increasingly interconnected, and recent incidents in the Baltic Sea area have highlighted the need to bolster preparedness against physical, cyber, and hybrid threats. The ministers shared experiences and explored opportunities to enhance the resilience of the region's energy infrastructure and strengthen international cooperation.
"Today's discussion highlighted the importance of Nordic-Baltic cooperation in strengthening regional preparedness and resilience. Together, we form one of Europe's most integrated energy regions," added Finnish Minister of Climate and the Environment Sari Multala.
Regarding the development of a competitive Baltic Sea energy market, discussions centered on investment and financing opportunities and the creation of long-term certainty. The participants also talked about the evolution of electricity demand and production, grid development, and the need to improve the transparency and predictability of the regional energy market.
The meeting reaffirmed the shared commitment of the Nordic-Baltic countries to strengthen energy cooperation and find regional solutions to challenges related to energy security, resilience, and competitiveness. A joint Nordic-Baltic statement on energy cooperation was also issued in conjunction with the meeting.
Estonia holds the presidency of the Nordic-Baltic cooperation in 2026. The NB8 cooperation format brings together Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland.

The prime minister did not specify what kind of assistance had been offered.
Kulbergs said that there is currently a glimmer of hope for finding the Latvian travelers missing after devastating floods in Nepal, but the search is seriously hampered by the rainy season there.
Kulbergs also underlined that the government will do everything it can to help and support the relatives of these travelers. A representative from the Consular Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has now arrived in Nepal to assist the Latvian side on the ground in maintaining contact with the Nepalese authorities. This representative will also assist in the event the remains of a Latvian citizen are found and need to be repatriated to Latvia. Relatives will also be informed about the next steps in such a case.
According to Kulbergs, several foreign tourists are known to have reached Chinese territory during the flood disaster, but Latvia has not yet received a response regarding these people.
For his part, Rinkevics acknowledged that the situation in Nepal is dire, and rescue efforts there are not as straightforward as they might be in Europe or Latvia. Nevertheless, Latvian authorities are working to provide the relatives who remain in Latvia with the maximum possible emotional and informational support.
This week, the State Police reported that it had received information about instances where scammers have attempted to defraud the relatives of Latvians who have gone missing in Nepal.
The president expressed his hope that these scammers will be apprehended and receive the harshest penalties possible, both to send a clear message that such behavior will not be tolerated and to deter others.
Kulbergs acknowledged that scammers exploit any misfortune to line their pockets, and that people must always be vigilant so as not to fall into the traps set by these criminals.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed LETA that a representative of the Consular Department has already started work in Nepal. Meanwhile, the honorary consul continues to maintain active communication with local authorities.
To date, 31 closest relatives of missing Latvians have submitted DNA samples.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs continues to assist and coordinate practical matters that may arise for the relatives of those missing in Nepal, with the aim of providing information on where and what kind of assistance they can receive.
Edite Medne, Director of the Foreign Ministry’s Consular Department, reveals in a video posted on X that the last communication with the guide of the largest Latvian group on the day of the tragedy took place at 8:38 a.m. He spoke with his brother in Kathmandu by phone, and this took place at a border crossing on the Chinese side.
Meanwhile, European Union (EU) authorities report that the information available to them indicates the last communication took place at 8:41 a.m. "In any case, we are talking about a fairly short period of time during which this communication has been lost," Medne said.
As reported, on August 26, a glacier collapsed, triggering a flow of ice debris and resulting in a flood of water and mud from a glacial lake, causing widespread damage in Nepal and China. By the morning of August 31, at least 900 people had been confirmed dead in the natural disaster, while approximately 4,200 were missing.
A large group of Latvian tourists, organized by yoga enthusiasts from the company Yantra, was also near the epicenter of the disaster, while a smaller number of Latvian tourists were in the disaster zone as part of a group organized by the local company Mighty Himalayan Trek. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has information that three Latvian citizens who were in the region at the time were not affected by the flood-induced mudslide in Nepal, but 33 are currently considered missing.

Latvia is taking action in several areas to reduce inflow of Russian and Belarusian goods into market - Braze  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:45 UTC
23:53:45 KST

RIGA - Latvia is taking targeted action in three mutually complementary areas to reduce the inflow of Russian and Belarusian goods into the market and, consequently, economic support for the aggressor states, Foreign Minister Baiba Braze (New Unity) told LETA.
The minister noted that Latvia is already utilizing its national capacity to take action, namely, the law and the government regulations developed on its basis provide for a ban on the import of certain goods originating in Russia and Belarus into Latvia.
She emphasized that the purpose of this regulation is to limit the entry of such goods into the Latvian market. Consequently, responsible local traders are also expected to act in accordance with the nature and purpose of the restrictions, rather than seeking ways to circumvent them by organizing shipments through other countries.
Likewise, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs works on a daily basis to ensure that an increasing number of Russian and Belarusian goods are included in future rounds of European Union (EU) sanctions. At the same time, the adoption of EU sanctions requires the involvement of all member states and can be time-consuming, which is why national restrictions allow countries to act more quickly, the minister said.
Latvia also advocates for a more flexible EU approach, namely, that alongside major rounds of sanctions, more frequent and precisely targeted sanctions are needed. Braze gave the following example: if it is determined that restricting specific goods or components could directly hinder Russia’s military production, such a decision should be implemented as quickly as possible, without waiting for the next major round of sanctions.
At the same time, Braze acknowledged that technology is advancing very rapidly, so frequent and targeted sanctions would be more effective in achieving the goal.
The minister also emphasized that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working to ensure that Latvia’s neighboring countries and other EU partners adopt a similar approach. In her view, the more countries that impose equivalent restrictions, the fewer opportunities there are to circumvent them by rerouting the shipments through another member state.
Commenting on publicly reported information that Latvian traders are using Estonia to circumvent the ban on book imports from Russia, Braze said that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will investigate the reports regarding the use of Estonia to circumvent the ban. If the reports are confirmed, Latvia will ask Estonia to take the necessary measures to put an end to such practices.
At the same time, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will call on the Ministry of Economics to ensure that the circulation of goods in the Latvian market complies with Latvian legislation and established restrictions. She emphasizes that Latvia’s national action thus serves not only as a practical market restriction but also as an impetus for broader and more united action in the region.
As LETA reported, as of September 1, 2026, the import of several industrial goods from Russia and Belarus into Latvia is prohibited, according to regulations drafted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The ban covers printed books, newspapers, and other printed materials; clothing; other finished textile products; footwear; headwear; as well as toys, games, and sports equipment.
According to information provided by the State Revenue Service (VID), the ban applies to printed books, newspapers, pictures, and other printed materials, as well as handwritten documents, typewritten documents, and plans.
The ban also applies to knitted or crocheted clothing and clothing accessories, as well as clothing items and clothing accessories that are not knitted or crocheted, ready-made textile products, sets, used clothing and used textile products, rags, footwear, gaiters, and similar products or parts thereof, headgear and parts thereof, as well as toys, games, and sports equipment, their parts, and accessories.
The ban is in effect until June 30, 2027, according to VID.

Azortum, which specializes in integrating independent technological solutions and selecting the most suitable equipment and technologies for a specific project, emphasizes that such projects are based not only on installing new equipment but also on a comprehensive solution tailored to a company's operational processes and goals.

VILNIUS - President Gitanas Nauseda said on Wednesday that it is realistic to achieve progress in normalising relations with China before Lithuania takes over the European Union Council presidency at the start of next year.
"Efforts are being made (...) to normalize relations or return them to decent tracks (...). In my eyes, this would be simple diplomatic representation, initially perhaps at the level of deputies, and later at the ambassadorial level," the head of state told reporters on Wednesday.
"I think the prime minister has outlined a fairly realistic time horizon for when we can see, if not the final results of improvement, then at least intermediate results showing that our relations are gradually recovering," he said.
The president's comments follow Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius' statement that he expects Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys to make progress in diplomatic relations with China before the European Union presidency.
Nauseda emphasised that he expects Budrys to actively work on this "important page of our foreign policy."
Lithuania will chair the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027.
The ruling coalition has recently spoken more actively about normalising ties with Beijing to a level of diplomatic representation held by other European Union states. Speaker of Parliament Juozas Olekas said in August that he saw progress in the process.
Relations between Lithuania and China soured in 2021 after Lithuania allowed Taiwan to open a Taiwanese Representative Office in the country.
