Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:04:23 UTC
23:04:23 KST

Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month
Germany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.
What happened and why is it significant?
For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.
Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.
Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.
Alice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What might happen next?
The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.
Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.
1:24
'We should have learned more from history': Germans react to AfD win – video
What does the result say about the firewall approach?
The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.
Siegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What does the result mean for the CDU and Friedrich Merz?
Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.
The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.
Friedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA
What about the next two state elections?
Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16 länder, will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.

esoteric’s T-01 turntable lets magnets do the spinning, with no belt in sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:02:12 UTC
23:02:12 KST

Japanese high-end audio manufacturer Esoteric introduces the T-01, its second turntable to employ the company’s patented MagneDrive System after the Grandioso T1 debuted in 2022. Rather than transferring motion through a belt or direct mechanical contact, the system uses magnetic induction to rotate the platter, physically separating it from the motor responsible for making it spin. In a machine devoted to extracting information from microscopic grooves, the logic is almost suspiciously simple: if vibration is the enemy, perhaps the motor should keep its distance.
At the end of the motor sits what Esoteric calls a Magnetic Driver, built around alternating north and south magnetic poles. Close to it, but never touching, a soft-iron induction wheel wraps around the lower edge of the aluminum platter. As the driver rotates, magnetic force sets the wheel –and therefore the platter– into synchronized motion. This contact-free relationship prevents motor vibration and rumble from traveling directly into the record while doing away with belts altogether, combining high torque with the stable rotational speed needed for 33⅓ and 45 rpm playback.
Esoteric T-01 turntable with contact-free platter rotation | image courtesy of Esoteric
A 13-KILOGRAM PLATTER THAT FEELS LIGHTER
The magnetic thinking continues with Esoteric’s Magne-Float platter technology, inherited from the Grandioso T1. The substantial aluminum platter physically weighs 13 kg, but magnetic force reduces its effective load on the spindle bearing to approximately 4 kg. Less pressure means less friction, allowing the platter to rotate more freely while retaining the inertia of its actual mass. An inverted bearing positions the platter’s supporting point closer to the record surface, another decidedly meticulous attempt to keep rotation stable when fractions of movement can become fractions of sound.
Around all this controlled motion, the T-01 uses a triple-layer chassis combining aluminum and wood, with a high-gloss piano-lacquered central section. Esoteric has integrated the MagneDrive motor into the chassis this time, making the architecture easier to install than its flagship predecessor, while enclosing the motor in a vibration-absorbing case. Newly developed isolation feet combine a spike, spike pad and damper into a single component to further suppress external vibration and acoustic feedback. For anyone keeping score, this is quite a lot of engineering devoted to making a rotating object behave as though almost nothing is happening.
13-kilogram aluminum platter engineered for stable playback
ANALOG SOUND, TIMED LIKE A DIGITAL MACHINE
Precision is also handled electronically. The T-01 incorporates Esoteric’s Master Sound Discrete Clock motor driver to regulate platter rotation and can synchronize with an external 10MHz master clock, including the company’s G-01XD and G-05 models. The main turntable and its power supply are housed in separate units, isolating the audio mechanism from the power circuitry, while rotational speed can be fine-tuned in 0.1% increments. The standard T-01 arrives with Esoteric’s static-balanced TA-9S tonearm, while the T-01 AL is offered without one; additional arm bases allow as many as two tonearms to be fitted.
Measuring 539 mm wide with its supplied tonearm and weighing 35 kg for the main unit alone, the T-01 is hardly Esoteric going minimalist. What has been simplified is the relationship between its parts: fewer points of mechanical contact, fewer opportunities for unwanted vibration and a more integrated installation than the Grandioso T1 that introduced the technology four years ago. The turntable begins worldwide shipping at the end of September 2026, continuing the Japanese manufacturer’s curious proposition for contemporary analog listening — that one way to make vinyl sound more physical is to engineer as much physical interference out of the machine as possible.

Esoteric combines analog playback with precise engineering
precision engineering shapes the new turntable
the T-01 combines performance and refined detailing

Higher intelligence might accelerate the development of metacognitive knowledge in mathematics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

A study involving 1,050 German early adolescents found that more intelligent students showed greater increases in metacognitive knowledge (in mathematics) over time. This suggests that higher intelligence accelerates metacognitive knowledge development. Interestingly, math knowledge, motivation, and school class type were not associated with the pace of metacognitive knowledge development. The paper was published in Learning and Individual Differences.
Metacognitive knowledge is a person’s knowledge and beliefs about how their own thinking and learning processes work. It includes knowing what one is good or poor at, which tasks are likely to be difficult, and which strategies may help in a particular situation. For example, a student may know that they remember information better when they summarize it in their own words rather than simply rereading it.
Metacognitive knowledge also includes understanding that different tasks may require different approaches, such as memorizing facts versus solving a complex problem. It is commonly divided into declarative knowledge (knowledge about oneself as a learner, knowledge about tasks, and knowledge about strategies), procedural knowledge (how to apply strategies), and conditional knowledge. Conditional knowledge, which is what this study focused on, involves knowing when and why to use particular strategies depending on the specific situation and task at hand.
This type of knowledge helps people plan how to approach learning or problem solving before they begin. It can also guide decisions about when to change strategies if the current approach is not working. Stronger metacognitive knowledge can therefore support more efficient learning, better problem solving, and greater independence in academic work.
Study author Maria Theobald and her colleagues note that metacognitive knowledge is central to learning and academic success, especially in mathematics. However, the trajectory of metacognitive knowledge development and the role of intelligence in this development remain poorly understood. With this in mind, they conducted a study that examined the development of metacognitive knowledge in the domain of mathematics. They chose this aspect of metacognitive knowledge because it strongly predicts mathematical learning and achievement.
Study authors analyzed data from the project PULSS, which examined the development of academic achievement and motivation in the early secondary school years. Participants of this study were 1,050 5th grade students from seven high-track secondary schools (Gymnasium) in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, federal states in southern Germany. On average, participants were 11 years old at the start of the study. 40% of participating students were girls. 89% had German as their primary language. The primary languages of the other students were most often Russian, English, and Turkish.
Students were tested at the beginning (T1) and the end of grade 5 (T2), the end of grade 6 (T3), and the middle of grade 7 (T4). However, this analysis used only the data from the first three data collection waves (T1-T3), because metacognitive knowledge was not assessed in the T4 data collection wave. Participants completed assessments of conditional metacognitive knowledge in the domain of mathematics (the MAESTRA 5-6 test), intelligence (only at T1, using the Cognitive Ability Test for Grades 4-12), math knowledge (the German Mathematics Test for Grade 5), and math-related motivation (goal orientation, mathematics self-concept, and interest, all assessed at T1 only).
Results showed that students’ metacognitive knowledge in mathematics generally increased over time, but this varied greatly between students. Students with higher intelligence tended to show greater increases in mathematics metacognitive knowledge over time. Study authors indicate that this suggests that higher intelligence accelerates metacognitive knowledge development. Girls showed a greater increase in metacognitive knowledge than boys over time. Math knowledge, motivation, and class-type (regular vs. for gifted students) were not associated with metacognitive knowledge development.
“These findings highlight the variability in metacognitive knowledge development and underscore intelligence as an important predictor of this differential development,” study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on the factors associated with the development of metacognitive knowledge. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any definitive causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper, “The role of intelligence in the development of metacognitive knowledge,” was authored by Maria Theobald, Wolfgang Schneider, and Franzis Preckel.

Israelis should become more selective about where they travel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

It is time for Israelis to rethink their travel plans.
Here is the problem. Since the Hamas-led terrorist attacks on October 7, 2023, Jew-hatred has increased exponentially. Places are simply less receptive to Jews, and especially Israelis. My suggestion is that Israelis travel less, or even better, they become more selective regarding where they travel. Not out of fear, but out of prudence.
This is recognition of the hostility they face, and it is a maximization of pleasure and a reduction of tension.
Zionism was a response to antisemitism.
Early Zionists realized that there was no way to eliminate Jew-hatred. That sage insight into a fear of those who are different – the Jews – has, over the decades, proven to be true. They reasoned that the best way to avoid a harmful, senseless, and destructive bias was to create an independent society that could defend itself.
The Jewish state was created on that foundation.
The model of assimilation and accommodation in host societies adopted by Jews, living in host countries for generations, developed as a survival model. They tried to keep their heads down, keep a low profile, keep to themselves, and be quiet, law-abiding citizens.
The attempt to prove themselves loyal, however, failed. Loyalty alone was not enough. They remained outsiders. They remained unwelcome guests in country after country, decade after decade.
Jewish safety, Jewish life, could not depend on the tolerance of others. Creating a Jewish state was the solution.
Today, as those age-old tensions once again rear their ugly heads, Jews in general, and Israelis in particular, have become moving targets while abroad. Jews – even assimilated Jews, even non-religious Jews, are identifiable. And that means that, for Jews, international travel is not risk-free.
Israelis travel abroad in high numbers
A Pew Research Center study, supported by a Mako survey, reports that 92% of Israelis have traveled abroad at least once in their lives. Some 75% have traveled abroad in the past two years. While those numbers are astonishing in many ways, they are also extremely disturbing.
It is rewarding to know that Israelis, in such large numbers, have the economic capability to travel. It is admirable to know that Israelis have a zest for learning about other cultures, other cuisines, and other climates. With that, of course, comes the realization that Israelis sometimes, oftentimes, just need to get away. From the tensions. From the wars, from the internal conflicts. From October 7 and its after-effects.
Since October 7, Jew-hatred has increased exponentially. It has increased for Jews still living in host countries and it has increased for Israelis living in and passing through those countries. It has been stimulated, in some countries, by the actions and rhetoric of world leaders. It has been carried out by individuals and groups who have been swayed by the vile, vicious, blood libel untruths that a genocide is being perpetrated by the Jewish state.
Not by choice, but out of necessity, Israelis and Jews must change their ways and learn to travel selectively and intelligently. It is time to explore, enjoy, and do business in places where the hosts have proven themselves as countries willing to protect their Jewish guests. It is time to go where Jews are welcome. Passports, hotel reservations, and a cosmopolitan environment do not guarantee a cordial reception.
Modern Zionism’s founding thinkers, such as Leo Pinsker and Theodor Herzl, firmly believed that Jewish safety depended on transforming Jews from guests and minorities who petitioned for their safety, into a power that would and could defend itself in its own home.
It is a colossal mistake to think that Israel and Zionism solved the issue of antisemitism. Rather, it removed Jews from the immediate reach of antisemites and antisemitism. Jew-hatred still exists. Today, an Israeli passport does not magically shield Jews from that hatred. If anything, in certain environments it magnifies the target.
In 2025, the Anti-Defamation League recorded 6,274 attacks against Jews and Jewish institutions in the United States, the country Jews long held to be the “golden country.” While that number was down 33% from 2024, it is still way too high to be considered either acceptable or a statistical anomaly.
The Foreign Ministry recorded 45 Israelis who experienced anti-Jewish incidents between July 2025 and July 2026 while in the United States. That number included fights, spitting, verbal attacks, expulsions from cafés, refusal of service, as well as instances in which Israelis felt threatened. These are by no means all the incidents that occurred; merely those reported or needing diplomatic involvement.
Mathematically, it is highly unlikely that Israeli travelers will be attacked. Until it happens. Until it happens to you. Until you are that Israeli or that Israeli family.
The unfortunate, undeserved message that large swaths of the world have been sending out has been received. A July 2025 survey undertaken by the Israel Democracy Institute reported that 38% of respondents answered that they had changed their travel destinations to accommodate this new state of affairs.
I call that risk-based self-restraint. It is a proactive response; it is not giving the Jew-haters a victory and a reward.
Zionism never promised to eliminate Jew-hatred; it promised that Jews would no longer be defenseless.
Israel exists so that Jews have a place where the state – not a foreign government, and certainly not a hotel manager – is ultimately responsible for the security of Jews.
The writer is a columnist and a social and political commentator. Watch his TV show Thinking Out Loud on the Jewish Broadcasting Syndicate.

FACT CHECK: Was Putin Telling the Truth About Some More Big Russian Victories in Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:58:30 UTC
22:58:30 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Sept. 1 during a conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, said that Russian forces are continually advancing in Ukraine and capturing new towns and villages daily. Specifically, the Russian leader told dignitaries and Krygyz and international media at the event:
“The Sever [North] grouping of forces continues creating a security zone along the Russian-Ukrainian border in the border areas of Sumy region – it is 12 kilometers [7.5 miles] to Sumy, to Sumy’s ring road – and in Kharkiv region. Over the past month, 14 settlements have come under the control of Russian forces, including Kazachya Lopan, and yesterday – the city of Sviatohirsk. In the northeastern part of Kharkiv region, another encirclement of another enemy grouping, numbering up to 2,000 men, has been completed. The area of the resulting pocket is large – 460 square kilometers [178 square miles] – and includes 27 settlements.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A Kremlin-generated transcript of Putin’s comments was posted here.
None of Putin’s claims could be confirmed and most were provably false, Kyiv Post research into the former mid-grade KGB spy’s claims found.
The most compelling recent evidence of the total absence of any Russian forces in Sviatohirsk was recorded on Sept. 5 by Ukrainian Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, during a relaxed walk through town. Biletsky commands the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) 3rd Army Corps, a major combat unit fighting in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region since March 2025. Sviatohirsk is in the center of 3rd Corps’ area of responsibility.Accompanied by a camera operator and two soldiers, an unhelmeted Biletsky is shown talking to a civilian as he walks across the T0521 road bridge across the Siverskyi Donets River to stand in front of the monastery. Aside from a pistol, he is unarmed. He states the town is fully under Ukrainian control, that no Russian soldiers are anywhere near where he is standing, that Ukrainian frontline positions are more than a dozen kilometers to the east, and that in Sviatohirsk: “There are no Russian soldiers anywhere.””Here you need to wear an armored vest, but you can walk around without any problems at all. As you can see, we have a quiet, pretty day here. Cars are driving around freely,” Biletsky said. “I have this to say to the Russian military-political leadership: You should just take off your clown noses and your multi-colored wigs. Stop making fools of yourselves.”
Zelensky Says Putin ‘Needs Trump,’ May Offer De-Escalation Before Winter
Kyiv Post checks of local government agencies showed utilities operational in Sviatohirsk, and small grocery stores, pharmacies, and the town bakery open for business. Biletsky said the main Ukrainian force in the area is the 60th Mechanized Brigade. Sviatohirsk serves primarily as a 3rd Corps rear area support base.
Recent 60th Brigade combat video reviewed by Kyiv Post showed engagements typical of Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) “drone wall” tactics, with kamikaze, bomber drones and mortars seeking out individual Russian soldiers. Directly contradicting Putin’s claim that the city fell on Aug. 31, AFU statements in August described the sector as moderately active with continuing and generally unsuccessful Russian attempts to infiltrate soldiers forward.
2. Putin claimed the Ukrainian Kharkiv region border town Kozacha Lopan (Ukrainian: Козача Лопань) came under full Russian control during August. In reality, Putin was conflating ongoing and mostly unsuccessful light infantry assaults, which really are taking place, with conquest, of which aside from Putin’s words there is no evidence.
Kozacha Lopan is a largely agricultural community a few kilometers from the Russian border – with a pre-war population of 4,000-5,000 inhabitants. Russian forces overran it in Feb. 24, 2022, the first day of the full-scale invasion, and were ejected by Ukrainian forces in September 2022. Since then, civilian life has gone on under intermittent Russian mortar, artillery, and drone attacks.
Relatively recent Russian probes towards Kozacha Lopan date back to June. On Aug. 8, Ukrainian military spokesman Viktor Trehubov stated Russian forces appeared to be attempting to infiltrate infantry into the northern edge of the town, in an attempt to establish footholds.
Reports on the progress of that fighting are split, with the AFU reporting heavy Russian casualties recorded by drone video and the Russian Defense Ministry asserting continuous ground gains, without making evidence public. An Aug. 14 article by the independent Russian analytical magazine Insider reported Russian attempts to capture the town had failed because local commanders ran out of men to send to attack.
A more recent, Sept. 2 report by the overall AFU command headquarters for the sector, 14th Army Corps, stated that “active combat operations” were in progress north of Kozacha Lopan, which, that source said, remained fully under Ukrainian control. Russian forces launched renewed attempts to break into the town in late August. They had lost 178 killed and 210 wounded in the area, that official Ukrainian source said.
A Sept. 2 situation update published by the independent Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concurred that Russian attacks on the Ukraine-held city had been partially successful, with Russian forces possibly having gained footholds in about 13% of the town. The Sept. 5 Ukrainian General Staff situation update said Russian forces had conducted nine attacks toward Kozacha Lopan and surrounding villages, with two attacks still underway.
3. Putin said Russian forces had scored a major victory by encircling 2,000 Ukrainian troops in the northeastern Kharkiv region in a 460-square-kilometer (178-square-mile) pocket. In fact, aside from Kremlin sources, there is no credible evidence that the surrounded pocket of Ukrainian exists or ever existed.On Sept. 3, Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces had, in the vicinity of the claimed encirclement, called by it and other official Russian state media “the Vovchansk Cauldron” captured the Ukrainian villages of Vasylivka, Blahodatne, Dovzhanka, and Slyzneve.
This drew an immediate challenge by the popular and influential Russian milblogger Mikhail Zvinchuk (Handle “Rybar” – 1.5+ million followers), who said that the much more likely situation was that Russian troops were attempting to attack into territory thinly or not even held by Ukrainian ground troops, but densely covered by Ukrainian drones and lethal for Russian forces to attempt to enter. If Putin’s generals attempt to “close the pocket,” the only result will be mass casualties, Zvinchuk predicted.
The Institute for the Study of War’s Sept. 4 assessment called Putin’s encirclement narrative “falsely and baselessly claimed.” Graphics published by the independent Ukraine-based battle information group DeepState, around the purported “cauldron” described by Putin showed stable lines throughout the sector for the past two months at least, and no evidence of even light combat activity.
In a Sept. 3 situation update, the usually dry AFU report on daily combat activities said of Putin’s comments: “The inflating of an information bubble called “Vovchansk Cauldron”…has been going on for the past three months…The enemy media is creating a victorious backdrop…The main thing is to hold fake elections (and manufactured public support to the Russian state) especially in the border areas of the Belgorod region.”
A Sept. 3 statement by Ukraine’s 16th Army Corps explicitly denied the four villages had fallen or that any of its troops had been surrounded. In the territory where Putin claimed a major Russian victory was in progress, in fact, Ukrainian forces had suffered no loss of positions during the preceding six months, that statement said.
In the town of Prykolotne, a town near center of the territory in which Putin claimed thousands of Ukrainian troops were surrounded, on Monday, per Kyiv Post checks, city power and water services were running normally, grocery stores and pharmacies were open for business, and mobile phone coverage was operational. Russian bombs hit the town in March, since then, there has been no significant combat activity. Civilians remain in residence; however, as a border region town, the military controls access and only permits locals to use roads in the area.

‘Not another meal, but a key’: Building a home for lone IDF soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:58:10 UTC
22:58:10 KST

For most Israeli soldiers, being released from base for Rosh Hashanah means going home. For others, the word “home” is precisely where things become complicated.
Some are new immigrants who came to Israel without their families. Others grew up in Israel but, for personal or family reasons, do not have a stable home to return to. And among some young Haredi men who enlist in the IDF, military service can also change their relationship with the family or community in which they were raised.
As soldiers across the country prepare to leave their bases for the Jewish New Year, a new project in Ariel, in the West Bank, is trying to give those without a family support network something that cannot be packed into a military duffel bag: a place that belongs to them.
‘Where are you for the holiday?’
For most soldiers, the question barely requires an answer.
At home. With their parents. With their siblings. Around the same holiday table waiting for them each year.
For Menachem, a pseudonym for a Haredi soldier serving in a combat role, the question is much more complicated.
“In the army, you’re part of a team,” he said. “There are people around you all the time, and you know exactly what your role is. It’s actually when they tell you, ‘Shabbat shalom, enjoy being home,’ that you suddenly realize you don’t have what everyone else has.”
The feeling becomes particularly sharp around holidays, he said.
“You don’t want people to feel sorry for you, and you don’t want to have to look for a family to host you every time. You want to know there’s a place you can simply go to and feel at home.”
It was encounters with soldiers in precisely those moments that led Kfir Traube to a different approach to supporting them.
Through his work helping soldiers, Traube repeatedly saw what happened after the larger moments of military service were over: the equipment came off, friends scattered to their families and a soldier who appeared strong and independent suddenly had to work out where he would sleep that weekend.
Together with the Arzieli Association, Traube is now leading an effort to establish a home in Ariel for lone soldiers, a term commonly used in Israel for service members who lack close family support in the country.
“For a long time, we would go to soldiers and bring food, equipment, treats, anything we could,” Traube said. “But at some point, we realized there was one thing you cannot bring to a military base: a home.”
“You meet a combat soldier who gives everything he has, and then the weekend comes and you realize he doesn’t really have anywhere to return to. For me, that was where the idea was born. Not to give him another meal, but to give him a key.”
Different soldiers, the same need
The planned home is intended for soldiers from a range of backgrounds, including secular, religious and Haredi troops, young people who moved to Israel alone and Israeli-born soldiers who lack a permanent family support system because of personal or family circumstances.
The project is also in contact with IDF officials involved in integrating and supporting Haredi soldiers, reflecting the different needs that may arise among those who use the home.
A soldier who immigrated to Israel alone may need an Israeli family or community to help guide him through everyday life. A Haredi soldier may also need an environment in which he can continue observing his religious lifestyle without having to explain himself.
Others simply need a permanent address.
A place to leave clothes, wash their uniforms, open a refrigerator, sleep and know that the next time they are released from base they will not have to start searching for somewhere to stay all over again.
That is why Traube says the goal is not to create another hostel or temporary accommodation.
The aim is to create a home.
Organizers envision a place where soldiers are known by name, share Shabbat and holiday meals and receive support with personal matters outside military life, providing some of what most of their fellow soldiers receive naturally from their families.
When ‘home’ needs an address
Ahead of Rosh Hashanah, that mission takes on additional significance.
In Israel, the holidays are closely tied to the idea of home: the family table, familiar food, traditional blessings and the people waiting for you to walk through the door.
For soldiers serving without a family support network, none of that can be taken for granted.
The Arzieli Association is now working to complete the house and raise the resources needed to operate it.
For Traube and the organization, however, success is not measured only by how much money is raised.
The test is far simpler.
The next time a commander tells a lone soldier, “You’re released, go home,” they want the word “home” to have an address.

West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari announces crackdown on child marriage after 60,000 underage deliveries

File photo: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari (Picture credit: PTI)
NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday announced a statewide crackdown on child marriage, ordering house-to-house drives to identify underage marriages and pregnancies and warning of arrests, imprisonment and withdrawal of government welfare benefits for those involved.Speaking to the media at Nabanna after a Cabinet meeting, Adhikari said the government would invoke the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the POCSO Act against those marrying minors as well as people who facilitate or solemnise such marriages.
The announcement came after the state health department reported nearly 60,000 institutional deliveries involving underage girls between January 1 and June 30, according to figures cited by the chief minister.
Nearly 60,000 underage deliveries reported in six months
Adhikari said Murshidabad recorded the highest number, with 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls during the six-month period. South 24 Parganas followed with 4,178 cases.He said West Bengal tops the country in child marriages and childbirths involving girls below 18 years of age.The chief minister said every case of pregnancy and childbirth involving a girl below 18 must be reported. The health records would be used by authorities to identify suspected child marriages and initiate action against those responsible.
The proposed house-to-house drives will involve coordination between the police, health and social welfare departments and district administrations, with records of underage pregnancies and institutional deliveries being used to identify vulnerable cases.
Husbands, facilitators face legal action
Adhikari said husbands of women found to have been married while underage would be issued showcause notices and asked to produce valid proof of their wife's age."If they fail to provide valid proof of the age, strict action will be taken," he said.He warned that police would initiate criminal action and make arrests in cases detected during the crackdown."Police action will be initiated, and arrests will be made," Adhikari said.The government will also withdraw welfare and other scheme benefits from people found to be involved in child marriages, he said.The chief minister issued a warning to priests, qazis and others who solemnise or facilitate underage marriages. Those found involved would face imprisonment and fines under the law.The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act provides for imprisonment of up to two years and/or a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh for people involved in promoting, permitting or conducting a child marriage.Adhikari also said the POCSO Act would be strictly applied, pointing out that sexual relations with a girl below 18 constitute an offence irrespective of whether she is married.He said physical relations with a girl below 18 attract provisions of the POCSO Act, with prison terms ranging from 10 years to life imprisonment and, in certain circumstances, the death penalty.Cases involving pregnancy of minors would attract particularly strict scrutiny and action, he said.
Government targets families and those facilitating marriages
The crackdown will target not only families arranging underage marriages but also husbands, facilitators and those conducting the ceremonies, with authorities expected to use health records to identify suspected cases.The issue has particular significance in West Bengal, where 19th-century social reformer Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar led campaigns against child marriage and for women's education.Adhikari also alleged that the previous Trinamool Congress government had failed to share data on child marriages and underage childbirths with the Centre.The chief minister said the administration would treat cases of child marriage as offences requiring police action and prosecution under the applicable laws.

Estonia's new defense minister expected to be named next week
The name of the new defense minister should be known by next week, says Reform Party secretary‑general Kristo Enn Vaga. The Reform Party will also discuss the topic at Wednesday's board meeting.
"The situation is such that the new defense minister cannot take office before the Riigikogu has convened, and the Riigikogu convenes next week. Within the party, different candidates are currently being screened," Vaga said.
"Next week, when the Riigikogu convenes, it should be known," he added.
Vaga said that the first serious discussion on the topic will take place on Wednesday at the party board meeting. "By the end of the week or the beginning of next week, it will be clear who the next defense minister candidate would be," Vaga said.
Search for suitable candidates ongoing

"He has been spoken to, but no official proposal has been made. The screening process is underway, where defense and security policy experts from both inside and outside the party are being considered, in order to restore credibility in the defense field and work to ensure that Estonia is as well protected as possible. Martin Herem is certainly one of Estonia's most reliable defense experts, and I think he would be a very worthy candidate," Vaga commented.
One option is to choose the new defense minister from among the government's existing ministers. However, according to Vaga, they are rather looking for a new person from outside the government. "Everything is possible, but we are not discussing that right now. Rather, we are looking for a new person who would be strong in this field," he said.
Pevkur may not join the defense committee
Riigikogu Reform Party faction leader Õnne Pillak said that Hanno Pevkur, who resigned as defense minister last week, may not join the Riigikogu national defense committee upon returning, but may instead begin working in another committee.
"Considering his previous position — for example, he was justice minister — it could be the constitutional committee or the legal affairs committee. There are different options," Pillak said.
"Yes, his last position was defense minister, but that does not mean he will definitely go to the defense committee because of that. We will discuss these matters next week," Pillak said.
Pevkur said last week that according to the coalition agreement, the chairmanship of the defense committee belongs to Eesti 200.
Defense committee currently without chair
"We will certainly not reopen the coalition agreement because of this change. We'll see. I have not yet discussed this with the faction leadership. But there is time, a wise person does not rush," Pevkur said.
The previous defense committee chair, Kalev Stoicescu, left Eesti 200 at the beginning of August and joined the Parempoolsed party. Therefore, Eesti 200 recalled him from the chairmanship of the defense committee. Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200) moved into the committee as a member instead, but a new chair has not yet been elected.
Hanno Pevkur announced last Wednesday that he is resigning as defense minister. He had served as defense minister since 2022.

The AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right | Cas Mudde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:56:21 UTC
22:56:21 KST

The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) narrowly failed to secure an outright majority in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. But nobody should take comfort from that. The party still won by a landslide. Decades of far-right election gains have made them seem normal to the point where only the biggest victories are deemed newsworthy. But 44% of the vote for a party that is officially classified as “extreme right” is not normal. It is a black day for European democracy, even if it occurs in a small east German state.
While Saxony-Anhalt (and Germany itself) may have dodged the worst outcome because the AfD won’t automatically fulfil its ambition of forming the first far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era, there is no reason to assume it will be so lucky at the next election. Neither will other German states, such as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in two weeks’ time, or other countries, such as France next year. No country is immune from the far right and, perhaps even more worryingly, no far-right party or politician is too extreme for political success (as the US has shown). We must therefore update our analyses and strategies.
Although Saxony-Anhalt, and east Germany in general, is an extreme case, it reflects similar trends in the rest of Europe. Far-right parties are going from strength to strength, with old dominant parties decimated, and party systems fragmented. Consequently, coalition formation is becoming increasingly complicated, particularly if we want to keep the far right out of power. In many countries, provinces and cities, most democratic parties are having to govern together to exclude the far right. This often leads to inefficient and unstable coalitions, in turn feeding yet more political dissatisfaction and far-right support.
Sunday’s results will only intensify an ongoing debate in Germany about the so-called Brandmauer (a firewall maintained by mainstream parties against cooperating with the AfD). Actually, Germany is one of the few EU countries to still have a far-right cordon sanitaire. Throughout Europe, from Italy to Sweden, far-right parties have been normalised and integrated into the political mainstream. In most cases, the (rightwing) parties that collaborate with the far right claim that the latter have moderated and are now “conservative” – a claim that is factually wrong, but increasingly popular with the electorates and members of these parties, and much of the media.
This will remain almost impossible to claim in Germany. The AfD is among the most extreme parties in Europe, and its most successful branches, including the one in Saxony-Anhalt, are among the AfD’s most extreme. This will not prevent some rightwing politicians from claiming that the AfD is less of a problem than the left, and there is even a fear that some parliamentarians from the conservative CDU in Saxony-Anhalt will defect to give the AfD a majority in the state. On the other side of the political spectrum, calls for an AfD ban will become even louder, and while this might be legally possible, it could create a massive popular backlash, going well beyond Saxony-Anhalt.
Both approaches share a too-limited interpretation of the problem. The idea of maintaining the Brandmauer is that the only (or main) problem is outside the system. Yet the system is falling apart as it is. Yes, the AfD (and the far right in general) is a fundamental threat to liberal democracy, but so is the fact that a sizeable and growing part of the population no longer feels represented by its politicians. While many still come out to vote for democracy, they increasingly vote against a party rather than for one.
Even worse, most mainstream politicians have accepted that they are unpopular and try to remain in power by arguing that they are the lesser evil and mobilising people to come out to vote against the far right. Ultimately, this is unsustainable. If democratic parties do not develop inspiring manifestos for what they want to achieve in government, liberal democrats will refuse to come out to vote and the far right will win a majority of votes – even if they represent only a minority of the population.
Developing such manifestos will require realism from politicians, but also from the media and voters. In fragmented party systems with large far-right parties, no party will be able to implement most of its preferred policies. There are no majorities for social democratic, Christian democratic or Green parties and policies. But this should also not be the main concern at this moment. When the far right gets close to governing alone, or dominating coalitions, the main goal should be to strengthen liberal democracy – in terms of institutions and values. This should be something that all liberal democratic parties can agree on.
This does not simply entail strengthening democratic institutions – the judiciary and regulating social media, for example – and promoting inclusion and tolerance. It also means listening to the many concerns and preferences of the majority of voters who do not vote for the far right. In other words, mainstream politicians need to go beyond crime and immigration and focus also on such things as increasing housing provision and public spending, limiting economic and income inequality, fighting the climate crisis and strengthening European integration. And it means accepting that you don’t get everything you want – now or in the near future.
Of course, many countries are not as close to a far-right majority as Saxony-Anhalt is. But we should not forget that in the state’s 2021 election, the AfD had “only” 20% – and the average score of the far right now is roughly 25% across Europe. In other words, there may not be much time left. And, as we can see in countries such as Hungary and the US, the democratic struggle becomes harder and less fair once the far right establishes power.
Democratic politicians must therefore realise that today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power. This requires both fighting the far right and strengthening democracy. Neither the banning nor the normalisation of the far right can achieve this. Democracy neither be strengthened in isolation, nor by the politics of fear. It requires a collective effort from democratic politicians, citizens and journalists, who must show realism, resilience and restraint. And the time for that fight is now.
- 
  Cas Mudde is the author of The Far Right Today, and is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia

South African president weighs court action against electoral commission

South African president weighs court action against electoral commission
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has said his African National Congress (ANC) party is considering Electoral Court action over alleged technical glitches that affected candidate-list submissions ahead of local elections in November.
The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has rejected the ANC’s claims, saying there were no reports of a non-functional system when nominations closed at 5pm on August 28.
Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the ANC’s door-to-door campaign in Tembisa, Ekurhuleni, on Friday, Ramaphosa said the problems were linked to the interface with the Electoral Commission of South Africa’s (IEC) candidate-capture system.
”There were some glitches, glitches with regard to just the interface with the IEC system. The candidates’ list was there for the whole country. They were submitted, and in regard to those areas there were some glitches,” Ramaphosa said.
The ANC has disputed claims that it failed to submit its nominations on time, maintaining that technical problems affected some of its remaining entries. The Commission has also said it will not reopen the system to allow parties or independent candidates to submit nominations after the deadline.
The dispute comes as the IEC processes more than 140,000 candidate nominations for the November elections. The Commission received 142,072 nominations to contest 10,526 council seats, with 504 political parties submitting nominations. Of these, 299 parties submitted through the Online Candidate Nomination System, while 205 submitted nominations manually at IEC offices.
The IEC said 2,274 candidate names were captured on its online system but were not finally submitted by the 5pm deadline on August 28. The names were linked to 45 political parties, with 480 potential proportional representation candidates and 1,794 potential ward candidates among them. The IEC has said these candidates are not in contention because, although their details had been captured, they had not been formally submitted to the Commission by the deadline.
Ramaphosa described the system error as limited, saying its impact was “containable and manageable." He said several political parties had experienced problems, but the ANC was particularly affected because it was submitting a large number of candidates.
”This is not only affecting the ANC. There are a number of other parties, I’m told 34, so there should be a solution to be found, because the technical glitches should not in the end deprive our people from being able to vote for their candidates,” the president noted.
”I’m certain that a solution will be found. The Political Party Liaison Committee, as well as the IEC and the parties themselves, will be able to find a solution,” Ramaphosa said, adding that the ANC was exploring different avenues to resolve the dispute.
The ANC’s candidate-list problems have affected some municipalities in KwaZulu-Natal, the Free State and the Eastern Cape. The party is seeking a resolution to the disputed submissions as the IEC moves towards finalizing the candidate lists. The IEC is expected to publish the final list of candidates on September 16 after completing its compliance checks.

Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
September 7, 2026
A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.
Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative "reset" in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.
Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.
Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.
There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.
More provinces, better governance?
Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.
"Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people," Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.
Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan's four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.
Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.
Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan's growing population.
But there is disagreement over the solution.
"Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level," Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.
He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.
Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.
Altering the political balance
"Pakistan's history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services," Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.
The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.
Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.
New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.
Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.
The political resistance has already begun, with Sindh's provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.
A risky strategy?
Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.
"Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge," he said.
"Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus," he added.
The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.
Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.
He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.
"We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services," Ismail said.
Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.
"In Pakistan's case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions," he said.
For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.
It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions.

More than 400 representatives from over 40 countries and regions, as well as from UN agencies and international organizations, attended the event. Since its establishment more than three decades ago, APEC has propelled the region to the forefront of global development and helped it become the most dynamic region in the global economy.
The representatives pointed out that openness, innovation and cooperation are of great significance for promoting the prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region. They are committed to championing the consensus on openness, safeguarding the multilateral trading system, and reporting and explaining concepts and practices such as the construction of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, regional connectivity, and the stability of industrial and supply chains. They will also facilitate policy alignment and experience sharing, and comprehensively showcase the region's progress across various sectors.
Attendees agreed that digital, intelligent and green transformation presents significant opportunities for the region's development. Committed to interpreting digital development policies and promoting positive narratives on digital technologies, they pledged to expand the application and popularization of artificial intelligence in the media sector and to broaden the media's reach and amplify its influence. This year marks the APEC "China Year," with the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." Approximately 300 APEC-related meetings and events will take place in multiple Chinese cities throughout the year.
Adjacent to Hong Kong, Shenzhen was one of China's first special economic zones and has since evolved, over four decades, into a global hub for innovation and advanced manufacturing.

Based on evidence gathered by counterintelligence and investigators of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), a Russian agent exposed by the SBU in October 2024 for carrying out arson attacks in Odesa region has been sentenced to 10 years in prison with confiscation of property.
"The investigation established that the convicted man is a local unemployed individual recruited by the enemy. He came to the attention of Russian intelligence officers while looking for 'easy' money on Telegram channels. In one such chat, a Russian representative contacted him and offered money for setting fire to administrative buildings and vehicles belonging to Ukrainian soldiers," the SBU press service said.
According to the Prosecutor General's Office, Russian intelligence services instructed the man on how to scout locations and targets, correctly prepare an incendiary mixture, cover his tracks after the arson attacks, and delete correspondence and data.
"The recruit searched for vehicles used by Ukrainian soldiers. In a village in Odesa district, he set fire to a Mitsubishi and filmed it on his phone. He later carried out another arson attack, dousing the entrance door and building of a village community club in Usativ community, Odesa district, with a flammable substance. The video, sent to his handlers, was meant to serve as a news hook for pro-Russian outlets, in order to create a false impression that an 'underground movement' existed in Odesa region," the agency said in a statement on its Telegram channel.
A few weeks later, the enemy published the video of the community center arson on a pro-Russian Telegram channel to create the impression that a "pro-Russian underground" existed in the region.
SBU officers detained the agent shortly after the attack. Searches turned up a mobile phone containing evidence of his subversive activity on behalf of the aggressor state.
Based on materials from the Security Service, the court found the perpetrator guilty under Part 1, Article 114-1 (obstructing the lawful activity of the Armed Forces during a special period), Part 2, Article 194 (intentional destruction or damage of property by arson), and Part 2, Article 258 (an act of terrorism committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy) of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
At the prosecution's request, the convicted man will remain in custody until the verdict takes legal effect.
He did not plead guilty in court.

Lithuania’s State Security Department (VSD) reported on Monday that 22 Belarusian citizens who worked for a technology company in the country had been deemed a threat to national security and expelled. LRT reports, UNN writes.
The State Security Department submitted to the Migration Department its findings regarding the activities of 22 Belarusian citizens in Lithuania. The aim of the project was to develop high-precision satellite navigation receivers capable of using the Galileo High Accuracy Service for agricultural needs, including controlling agricultural machinery and supporting precision farming operations.
The project’s total budget exceeded €1 million, of which more than €745,000 was funded by EUSPA. In fact, the company received €447,272.

Phone subscriptions for internationals: What you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

22:48:53 KST

Partner content
Phone subscriptions for internationals: What you need to know
Whether you’ve just moved here or are looking to change your mobile phone provider, finding a phone subscription in the Netherlands can be a daunting task. So many advertisements! So many choices! So many requirements!
Sometimes, it seems as if you’re stuck in a Catch-22 situation: you need a BSN (Dutch social security number) to get a contract, but you often have to pay for it with a Dutch bank card. But to open a Dutch bank account, you will have to provide most banks with a BSN number (four banks in the Netherlands – ING, bunq, ABN Amro and Revolut – let you open an account without it, but you still have to provide them with a BSN number within 90 days).
To avoid this bureaucratic spiral, mobile service provider Simyo offers contracts without the usual required BSN number, giving you the option of moving beyond the prepaid plans most other companies offer to those without a BSN.
You can also use a foreign bank account to pay for your contract (although you must arrange that with customer service).
What’s the deal?
Simyo has been voted Best in Test by the independent Dutch consumer organization Consumentenbond for the second quarter of this year – its 38th time with that distinction.
Launched by telecom giant KPN some 20 years ago as an online-only mobile service provider, the budget Simyo uses KPN’s reliable 5G network, meaning you get excellent quality for a competitive price. (And if you have KPN internet and TV, you’ll get extra data at no charge.)
“Overall satisfaction with Simyo receives a 9.8 in the second quarter,” writes the Consumentenbond, which rates how satisfied customers are with their provider. Overall, Simyo got a rating of 8.2, “making it the Best in Test in during the second quarter of 2026.”
Specifically, says the Consumentenbond, “Customers report few outages regarding mobile internet and calling. They also experience few issues with slow connections. Administrative problems hardly occur. For example, about 1% reports a non-working SIM card, problems logging into the account, or an unjustified debit.”
Simyo’s mobile abonnement beat out Odido, Lebara and Vodafone/Ziggo, among others, in the consumer organization’s ratings.
À la carte pricing
 Simyo offers both Sim Only and phone subscriptions that bear out its stellar quality to price ratio, with a Sim Only plan costing as little as €6,50 per month for the first year, increasing to €15 per month after 12 months. (And that includes Dutch taxes!)
For those looking for a subscription, plans offering 40 GB of data and 400 min/sms start for just €6,50 monthly (a temporary offer). You choose your plan à la carte, meaning you can decide how many minutes, gigabytes or months you’re looking for and the price will adjust automatically as you build your plan on Simyo’s website.
Buy a data cap
 Don’t forget to take out the data cap for an additional €1 per month to save you from unexpected costs when your bundle runs out; your internet will then stop automatically when it reaches your limit.
Flexibility
 Flexibility is another compelling reason to choose Simyo: monthly subscriptions allow you to adjust or cancel according to your needs and budget, doing away with those one- or two-year set contracts that lock you and your bank account in until they expire. That’s a huge advantage for internationals residing in the Netherlands for just a short period.
Data bundle
 Simyo offers a data bundle for outside the EU that makes calling and internet surfing affordable while travelling.
eSIM cards
 Simyo also offers eSIM (embedded SIM) cards that save you the hassle of inserting plastic chips, as you can download your mobile plan by scanning a code or using an app. You can manage your subscription via the user-friendly Mijn Simyo app.
“I wanted a second mobile number, for distant external contacts, to protect my main number,” wrote user Bert on Trustpilot, who gave Simyo a 5-star rating. “With an e-sim card from Simyo, I fixed that in 15 minutes, and it works fine.”
So if you’re looking for a new mobile phone plan, updating your old one or buying one for your teenage children, Simyo is an easy, affordable and reliable choice.

Netherlands must double water spending, delta commissioner warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:48:09 UTC
22:48:09 KST

Netherlands must double water spending, delta commissioner warns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands must at least double what it spends on keeping the sea out and fresh water in, and even then it will not be able to prevent all the damage from climate change, delta commissioner Co Verdaas said on Monday.
Spending on flood defences, fresh water and climate-proofing currently amounts to about 1% of GDP, or just over €11 billion a year, and needs to rise to at least 2%, broadcaster NOS reported. His statements come ahead of the national budget day next week.
Verdaas gave a six-yearly review of the national delta programme to infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans. Carrying on as before “is not an option”, the infrastructure ministry said in a statement. The review stressed that the country is in “the next chapter of our water tradition.”
“We are world-renowned for our water management,” Verdaas said. “But this summer’s extremes have once again rubbed our noses in the facts. We are not going to make it with technology alone,” Verdaas said.
Pumps and salt
 The review calls for billions of euros in new pumps at IJmuiden and, later, on the Afsluitdijk, so that river water can still be pushed out to sea as levels rise. NOS puts the IJmuiden works alone at around €2 billion. The pumping station protects some 4 million people, as well as Schiphol.
Preparations should also start now on new “Delta Works” to replace the Maeslantkering storm surge barrier near Rotterdam, and the IJsselmeer should be allowed to hold more water so it can keep supplying half the country in dry summers.
But technical fixes will not be enough, Verdaas said. Land use will have to change in the most vulnerable areas, including the bulb-growing Bollenstreek, the sandy soils of the east and south, the Noord-Holland coast and parts of Friesland and Groningen, where salt water is creeping in and farmers may have to change the crops they grow.
Households should expect “wet feet and flooded cellars” more often, the statement says, and hospitals and power installations will need extra protection from cloudbursts.
The findings follow a summer in which the Rhine fell to its lowest level in 80 years and the government formally declared a water shortage. The full Deltaprogramma 2027, with the revised strategy, is published on Prinsjesdag, September 15, alongside the budget.

====================================================================================================

‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:46:42 UTC
22:46:42 KST

‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
Some five million Yemeni children are deprived of essential routine vaccinations amid disputes.
Mirsal Adel, 47, had never struggled to find vaccines for his children. In his hometown of Ibb, in southwestern Yemen, public hospitals and paediatric clinics always provided them free of charge.
But when it came to vaccinating his fifth child, a four-month-old boy, securing a shot was far from straightforward.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Yemeni forces claim strategic Hais district amid Houthi clashes
- list 2 of 3Houthi attacks on Yemen’s Taiz escalate, triggering new displacement wave
- list 3 of 3At least four civilians killed in Houthi missile strike near Yemen’s Taiz
“I visited the hospital more than once, and I was told that UNICEF, which used to provide the vaccines, stopped supplying them, with no word on when they might arrive,” said Adel.
In October 2025, the United Nations children’s agency halted operations in areas controlled by the Houthis following the detention of dozens of UN staff members – including UNICEF workers – and raids on its premises. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government for years, and have periodically cracked down on aid sector workers.
The Health Ministry in Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, confirmed to Al Jazeera that the final vaccine shipment it received arrived on September 4, 2025. In late July 2026, the government’s Ministry of Public Health and Population in Aden warned that nearly five million children in Houthi-controlled areas had been cut off from essential routine immunisations.
One of them was Adel’s newborn.
“Our children’s health is a red line, and we must do everything we can to get them vaccinated,” said Adel, who decided last week to travel with his son to Taiz, a government-held city some 75km (47 miles) away, where vaccines are still available.
He said the trip cost him about $100, a prohibitive expense for many families in impoverished Yemen.
“Vaccination teams used to go door-to-door to vaccinate children, but this year everything changed suddenly, and getting a reliable vaccine now costs a lot,” said Adel, who works as a treasurer at a local company. “Today, not everyone can afford the travel expenses to get their children vaccinated.”
Although he is relieved to have secured the two initial doses of polio and pneumococcal vaccinations, he is already anxious about any upcoming trips. “I hope children’s vaccines will be available locally next time so I won’t have to resort to travelling again,” he said.
Halting UNICEF operations
The war in Yemen broke out in late 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern and western Yemen, including Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries to intervene in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022 significantly reduced fighting, but tensions have escalated since July, with fighting growing fiercer in recent days.
In March this year, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said only 59.3 percent of Yemen’s health facilities remained fully functional, while overall complete vaccination coverage stood at 63 percent.
The figures, however, reflect the conditions before the total exhaustion of vaccine supplies in Houthi-controlled areas by July, meaning current national coverage rates are likely significantly worse.
Anees al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Health Ministry in Sanaa, blamed UNICEF and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, for the collapse of the vaccine supply. He said authorities had informed both agencies early on regarding the impending shortages, yet no action was taken before all nine routine childhood vaccines were entirely exhausted.
“The primary reason for the disappearance of childhood vaccines is the politicisation of humanitarian work,” he said, repeating an accusation made by the Houthis against UN agencies, particularly following last year’s decision to relocate their operations to Aden.
“Since UNICEF halted its operations in Sanaa for political reasons, they stopped supplying us with vaccines,” he added. “Furthermore, because we live under a blockade by Saudi Arabia, we cannot import them ourselves.”
In a statement to Al Jazeera, Gavi said: “Due to operational and security challenges, Gavi and its partners have not been able to deliver vaccines into northern Yemen since late 2025. We remain committed to ensuring children across Yemen have access to essential vaccines and are cautiously optimistic that new solutions can be found that will enable us to break the current impasse.”
When contacted by Al Jazeera, UNICEF Yemen declined to comment on the allegations, saying only that it is doing its best to help every child access vaccines.
Meanwhile, the UN continues to demand the immediate release of dozens of its personnel, alongside staff from international and local humanitarian organisations currently detained by the Houthis. The UN has also called for the return of assets seized during raids on its offices, and the lifting of operational restrictions on aid groups and their personnel.
‘It breaks my heart’
The Health Ministry in Aden said in late July that it had sufficient vaccines for the entire country, including Houthi-controlled areas. However, it accused the Houthis of creating obstacles that prevent the receipt and transport of these supplies from government-controlled areas.
“Vaccines designated for all governorates of the Republic, including those under Houthi control, are available through health sector partners in accordance with approved international supply mechanisms,” it said. “However, the ongoing restrictions and obstacles imposed by the Houthis – which hinder their receipt, transportation and distribution according to technical standards – have prevented them from reaching the targeted children.”
Ali al-Waleedi, the deputy health minister in Aden, said the ministry had planned to carry out two polio vaccination rounds this year but accused the Houthis of not cooperating.
“The Houthis refused to accept vaccines designated for areas under their control and have shown no willingness to resolve the crisis,” al-Waleedi told Al Jazeera. “They rejected the vaccines, even though it had been agreed to allocate more than 65 percent of the total supply to areas under their control.”
Responding to the allegations regarding the rejection of shipments, al-Asbahi said there has been “no coordination” with the ministry in Aden. “We cannot accept shipments arriving by road, as they could be spoiled. UNICEF and Gavi are responsible for this, and they must uphold their responsibility to provide our children with vaccines.”
While the two health ministries present different accounts, parents such as Mohammed Abdulwahed wait for the rival authorities to reach an agreement and restore access to paediatric vaccines.
“There was a shortage of vaccines earlier this year, and we used to struggle to get them, but now we cannot find them at all in Sanaa,” said Abdulwahed. “I know some families are travelling to government-controlled areas, but that costs a lot, and I simply can’t afford it.”
Thikra, a healthcare worker who has served on door-to-door vaccination teams and currently works at a vaccination clinic in a Taiz hospital, said dozens of children from Houthi-controlled areas were arriving at the facility each day to be vaccinated.
“It breaks my heart to see children deprived of essential vaccines while authorities in Sanaa and Aden exchange blame,” she said.
“Political issues should be kept completely separate from children’s health, and both ministries must find a solution so all children can access free vaccines,” she said, stressing that immunisation is a basic right for every child.
“I urge the international community to step in, as the next generation could suffer severe health consequences if an urgent solution is not found to restore vaccine supplies.”
