How far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:45:21 UTC
22:45:21 KST

How far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD) came out well ahead in Sunday’s regional elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the first far-right party to come close to gaining power at the regional level since World War II. The lead candidate of the party in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said Monday that his party had already initiated talks towards building a governing majority.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won Sunday's regional election in Saxony-Anhalt with about 44 percent of the vote, far ahead of the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU). It is the closest a far-right party has come to power at the state level in Germany since the Second World War.
The AfD fell just three seats short of an outright majority. Lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund said Monday that talks were already under way to win over individual MPs from other parties willing to help form a governing majority.
Read moreGermany’s far-right AfD wins big in key state election but falls short of majority
The result strains Germany's "firewall" political consensus against working with the far right and much depends now on the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), a populist left-leaning but immigration-sceptic and pro-Russia party who the AfD could potentially rely on to build a coalition.
FRANCE 24 spoke to Ed Turner, a German politics specialist at Aston University in Birmingham, about what the result means for Saxony-Anhalt and Germany.
FRANCE 24: The AfD didn't just win this election with its usual voters, it gained ground across almost every demographic in Saxony-Anhalt. What does that broader appeal tell us about how the party's support base is evolving in Germany?
Ed Turner: The AfD did particularly well amongst some of the groups which you'd expect. That means working class voters, voters who think their own economic situation isn’t good, voters with a relatively low level of qualification – and those groups are particularly well represented in Saxony-Anhalt.
On top of that, there is something specifically eastern German about some of its support. For example, in eastern Germany, for partly historic and cultural reasons, there is much less support for Germany's backing of Ukraine in its current war with Russia, and there's a sense of being second-class citizens and wanting to give voice to that dissatisfaction.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
But it's also the case that support was by no means confined to the usual suspects in a population. For example, amongst voters of different age groups, the AfD got over 40 percent in every group, apart from the over-70-year-olds, where it got 31 percent. So it did well across the board.
In Germany, people talk about parties with cross-society appeal as being “Volkspartei” [“people’s party”], and in a way, in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD is looking like a Volkspartei.
The AfD came within just a few seats of an absolute majority. Realistically, what are their options now?
I don't see a path to preventing them taking office because it would require not just the CDU to work with the left party – if the numbers had stacked up, then the left party would have tolerated a CDU government – but also the minor party, the BSW, which has said they think it would be undemocratic to see the AfD completely excluded from government.
At some point in the next 30 days, the parliament will assemble to vote on who the minister-president [the state premier] should be in a secret ballot, and there are probably two routes there through for the AfD: one is that they find the BSW abstains, or alternatively, there might be some rebels from the CDU in the secret ballot who either abstain or even vote for their candidates. Either which way, it's really difficult to imagine a scenario where they’re kept out.
What role could the BSW play in the aftermath of this election?
The BSW stands for Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht [Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance]. Wagenknecht was a long-standing left party parliamentarian who got her roots initially in east German communism but over time became associated with what some call a left-wing populism, where she would adopt left-wing economic positions, but at the same time quite conservative, right-wing positions on topics like immigration, and she also was very fiercely critical of Germany's support for Ukraine. That party missed out on seats in the last federal election, but does have a particular appeal in the east.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
They've come up with their own plan for Saxony-Anhalt, which is that there should be a non-political minister-president, and they should govern with whatever majorities – issue by issue – could be found. Nobody regards that as a serious proposition, but what it does do is it means they can say, “Well, we tried a different way, you lot weren't interested in it so we now need to do something else and maybe fall in behind the AfD.”
Their candidates also talked about some areas where they could see policy commonalities with the AfD, so that is a party which potentially could help the AfD.
What could the AfD implement at the local state level in terms of policy in Saxony-Anhalt?
In Germany, states have a very high level of autonomy when it comes to education and the AfD has already said it wants to radically overhaul the school curriculum, particularly on sensitive topics around history – they’ve mentioned doing “more Bismarck and less Hitler”. They’ve also talked about unravelling integration of children with learning disabilities into mainstream education.
They've also mentioned defunding the Protestant Church because they think it takes too active a stance on social questions.
There's also the oversight of the police and the judiciary as well as public service broadcasting, and the AfD has talked about unravelling some agreements to have a common broadcasting framework between three East German states, which would give it a greater voice in public service media.
Read moreGermany: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the ideologist behind the AFD’s plans in Saxony-Anhalt
Germany has long maintained a “firewall” consensus to keep the far right out of government. Does this result suggest that consensus is starting to crack, and what would that mean for German politics more broadly?
The firewall has been pulled down because the far right is very likely to enter the state government in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is considered to be a confirmed right-wing extremist party. It is a much more radical creature than, for example, the French National Rally or Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, and because of that radicalism, because it won't trim its message in order to gain power, I think it's very unlikely to end up in government on a federal level. Instead, its presence and its growing support makes it just much, much harder for mainstream parties to govern.
So what we're seeing is that mainstream German parties are finding it almost impossible to form a government in order to keep the AfD out of power, which has any sort of agreements on the important issues of the day, and so without being anywhere near power, they're causing absolute chaos.

Macron behind failed military mutiny – Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:44:55 UTC
22:44:55 KST

Macron behind failed military mutiny – Niger
Niger has accused French President Emmanuel Macron’s government of inciting and supporting a failed mutiny by soldiers in the capital, Niamey, late last month and threatened possible international legal proceedings.
The Council of Ministers made the allegation following a meeting chaired by Nigerien transitional leader Abdourahamane Tiani on Friday. It described the unrest as an operation with “international ramifications” sustained by a network of collaborators headed by the “French regime.”
The military-led government said “treacherous and renegade elements, promised the moon and the stars, were tasked with carrying out the unfulfilled ambitions of Macron and his cronies” to destabilize the country and undermine its efforts to assert sovereignty over its natural resources. It said “substantial documentation on this aggression has been compiled, and Niger reserves the right to initiate proceedings before international courts.”
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot rejected the accusation on Saturday as “pure fantasy.” He told RFI that Paris has “neither the intention nor the means” to organize such an operation.
Soldiers from the Special Intelligence Battalion launched a mutiny at Air Base 101, located within Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, on the night of August 28. The country’s Defense Ministry said they detained fellow soldiers and opened fire on sensitive sites before advancing on the presidential palace, but were repelled by the Presidential Guard. The authorities said loyalist forces, assisted by Russia’s Africa Corps, suppressed the uprising. Three Presidential Guard soldiers were killed during the clashes, according to an official press release.
In a statement on Friday, the transitional government thanked “friendly countries,” particularly Russia, Algeria and fellow members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) group, for demonstrating solidarity with Niger from the outset of the unrest. Algeria also sent fighter, transport and refueling aircraft to Niamey after the uprising.
Niger and its AES allies Burkina Faso and Mali have repeatedly accused France of seeking to destabilize their countries and supporting armed groups behind a deadly jihadist insurgency in the Sahel. Paris has denied the allegations.
Since 2020, a wave of military coups has reshaped politics across the Sahel region in Africa, toppling civilian governments in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.
France, once the region’s dominant external power, has steadily lost influence amid rising anti-French sentiment and deep frustration over insecurity, economic stagnation, and foreign interference. The former colonial power was forced to withdraw troops from Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in 2023, Niger later that year, and Chad in early 2025.
About 4,500 soldiers had been deployed under Operation Barkhane, France’s largest overseas mission, across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Chad – a campaign that the military governments in Bamako, Niamey, and Ouagadougou have said only permitted Islamist insurgents to expand their activities.
The three West African states have established the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and withdrawn from the International Organization of Francophone Nations (OIF) operating in Francophone countries, many of them former French colonies. The AES has forged new alliances, including with Russia, which its leaders hail as a more reliable economic and security partner.

West Bengal government bans liquor sales on Maha Ashtami, DJ music during Durga Puja
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:44:25 UTC
22:44:25 KST

CM Suvendu Adhikari made the announcements at a coordination meeting at Milan Mela Prangan.
NEW DELHI: West Bengal has announced a series of restrictions for this year’s Durga Puja, including a one-day ban on liquor sales, a complete prohibition on DJ music and curbs on the use of major roads for Puja-related activities.Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari made the announcements on Monday at a coordination meeting with Durga Puja committees at Milan Mela Prangan. The measures are aimed at ensuring that celebrations remain peaceful and orderly.All liquor shops and bars across the state will remain closed on Maha Ashtami, when devotees offer anjali to Goddess Durga.
"On the day when devotees offer anjali (Maha Ashtami) to Maa Durga, all liquor shops in the state will remain closed. There will be no liquor available in bars either," he said.The decision comes despite liquor traditionally seeing strong demand during the Puja period.
DJ music banned, themes to face scrutiny
The government will also prohibit DJ music during the celebrations and immersion processions.Adhikari asked Puja committees to ensure that their idols, pandals and themes do not offend religious sentiments or go against Sanatan traditions. Theme-based Pujas will still be allowed, but organisers have been asked to be more careful while choosing their concepts.
The administration has also placed restrictions on roads being used for Puja activities. National highways cannot be blocked for organising Pujas, while 13 major roads in Kolkata, including Red Road and Cathedral Road, have been identified as areas where such activities will not be allowed.Puja inaugurations will also not be permitted before the start of Devi Paksha.Devi Paksha refers to the bright lunar fortnight in the Hindu month of Ashwin associated with the worship and invocation of Goddess Durga. The previous Trinamool Congress government under Mamata Banerjee had faced allegations over inaugurations being held before Devi Paksha began.
Immersion deadline and special arrangements
Adhikari said organisers would have to complete idol immersions within the stipulated period before Lakshmi Puja."There will be no forcing or threatening anyone to change the immersion date," he said.The state has also planned cultural programmes in six major cities over two days, along with special events at six designated immersion ghats.Special arrangements will be made to help persons with disabilities, residents of old-age homes and people staying in ashrams visit Puja venues.The government will also set up an impartial jury for the Sharad Samman awards. Adhikari said the jury members would be chosen for their knowledge of the traditional, ritual and cultural aspects of Durga Puja. The Sharad Samman awards recognise Durga Puja organisers for creative and artistic excellence.
The announcements come as West Bengal prepares for its first Durga Puja under the BJP government. The administration is seeking to manage the large-scale celebrations while imposing restrictions intended to maintain public order and protect religious and cultural sentiments.

Ukraine now has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones en masse, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He gave the number at a Kyiv press conference alongside US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrinform reported.
Most of those firms are still chasing the problem, and only a few have working systems. The race matters because Russia's jet-powered Geran drones fly too fast for the mobile gun teams that once downed the slower models. Russia has sharply expanded the jets' use over the summer, launching them by day as well as by night and driving air-raid alerts over Kyiv almost hourly.
Prototypes outnumber proven interceptors
"Today, we have about 60 companies in Ukraine already working on intercepting jet-powered drones, and doing so on a mass scale. To be precise, there are 67," Zelenskyy said.
He added that three to five have shown real results, and the next step is mass production.
Zelenskyy calls it all "Plan B"
Zelenskyy framed the entire defensive build-up as a fallback.
"All this defense is 'Plan B,' though right now it is very relevant. 'Plan A' is to accelerate diplomatic possibilities as much as possible, to reduce escalation from Russia," he said.
He spoke as the US envoys pressed a peace push in Kyiv, with no breakthrough announced.
He also called anti-ballistic defense Ukraine's weak point, saying he would raise it in upcoming meetings in Norway and Canada, and that the US plans to increase production of Patriot interceptors next year while Germany expands its own output under existing licenses.
Ukraine needs the interceptors to down Russian ballistic missiles that come several times per week. Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.

Oxford University museum to return remains of 39 people to India's Naga community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:42:59 UTC
22:42:59 KST

The Pitt Rivers Museum said it has been "working closely" with the Naga people on finding a date for a handover ceremony, after which a Naga delegation is set to accompany the remains home.
A museum in the UK has agreed to return a collection of human remains taken during Britain's colonial era to the Naga community in northeast India.
Oxford University's Pitt Rivers Museum, which holds the world's largest collection of Naga material, is set to repatriate the remains of 39 Naga people following years of negotiations.
Many of the Naga artefacts held at the museum were gathered by colonial administrators in the early 20th Century. The museum says it removed all human remains from display in 2020.
It comes after Oxford University received a claim for 40 sets of ancestral remains kept at the museum in February 2026. In July, the university agreed to return 39 of them, saying the remaining set did "not have a clear provenance as Naga."
In a statement to Euronews, the museum's director, Professor Laura Van Broekhoven, the director of the Pitt Rivers Museum, said it had been "humbling" to have been part of the process working towards returning the remains.
"I feel honoured that we walked alongside our partners to find the path to return for these 39 Naga ancestors, who have been away from their homeland for far too long," she added.
The museum said it has been "working closely" with the Naga people on finding a date for a handover ceremony, after which a Naga delegation is set to accompany the remains home.
The deal has been welcomed by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) and other Naga groups.
"Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land but importantly about memory returning to where it belongs," the FNR and other Naga organisations said in a statement sent to the AFP news agency.
According to the Pitt Rivers Museum's website, the museum first received Naga ancestral remains more than 100 years ago from John Henry Hutton, an anthropologist and colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service.
Hutton and a fellow administrator, James Philip Mills, are said to have brought the museum most of the Naga remains in its collection between roughly 1910 and 1940.
"Their 'collecting' was not the neutral, scholarly activity the word implies," the museum says, adding that "remains and objects were frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given."
The Pitt Rivers' Naga collection includes thousands of objects in total.
"Within it, 219 items are listed as Naga human remains: 39 ancestral human remains (primarily skulls) and 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. The current return concerns the 39 ancestors," the museum says.

You paid for Ed Sheeran love songs. You got a Free Palestine rally. Now Jewish fans want their money back - opinion
Unknown

- i24NEWS

- You paid for Ed Sheeran love songs. You got a Free Palestine rally. Now Jewish fans want their money back
You paid for Ed Sheeran love songs. You got a Free Palestine rally. Now Jewish fans want their money back
After Macklemore's MetLife set turned into a political flashpoint, the question isn't whether he had the right to say it. It's whether Jewish concertgoers should be the ones footing the bill
Nobody buys a ticket to see Ed Sheeran expecting a protest song. That's basically the entire argument now blowing up online after Macklemore opened for the famous pop star at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Friday night and turned his set into something a lot of the crowd didn't sign up for.
Before launching into his song "Hind's Hall," a track that accuses Israel of “genocide” and “apartheid,” and criticizes Zionism, Macklemore told the packed stadium he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they hadn't been forgotten, before leading the crowd to join him in a ‘Free Palestine’ chant.
He also went after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, calling it a "terror organization." Then he did it again the next night, at the same venue, in front of another sold-out crowd.
For a chunk of the audience, that was the whole show ruined before Sheeran even walked out.
"It was like a knife in the heart"
Israeli attendees who spoke to Hebrew-language outlets after the Friday show described feeling blindsided. One woman told Channel 12 the set was "very triggering and blatant." Another said she'd brought her kids, and that two Jewish teenagers sitting nearby stormed out in tears.
Two New Jersey residents told Ynet they hadn't even known Macklemore was the opening act, even though it reportedly had been previously announced, and that the moment hit especially hard because friends of theirs had been killed at the Nova festival and in the war. Some in their group left before Sheeran ever took the stage.
That reaction has now spilled well past the stadium and into a much bigger fight online, and it isn't really about Macklemore's opinions anymore. It's about who's supposed to pay for hearing them.
Jordyn Tilchen's post that lit the fuse
Jewish influencer Jordyn Tilchen, who posts as @jtilch, put the argument in the sharpest terms anyone has yet. In a post that's since ricocheted across Jewish social media, she argued that Jewish fans who walked into MetLife expecting Sheeran and walked out having sat through a crowd chanting for what she called the elimination of Israel shouldn't have to treat that as some harmless warm-up act.
She made the point that Jewish people aren't obligated to sit through rhetoric they experience as a threat to Israel's existence just because it's positioned as a prelude to their favorite love songs.
https://x.com/i/web/status/2096392256664080742
This post can't be displayed because social networks cookies have been deactivated. You can activate them by clicking .
Tilchen's stance: if Macklemore wants his own politics to be the point of the show, fine, advertise it that way and let people choose whether to buy a ticket. What he doesn't get to do, in her view, is let people pay hundreds of dollars for a pop concert and then hand them something else entirely without warning, and she was blunt that Jewish fans shouldn't be expected to financially subsidize an experience they see as threatening to their own safety. Her caption left no room for interpretation: "Refunds NOW."
You can read her full statement on her Instagram, @jtilch. She tagged both Macklemore and tour promoter Teddy Spotos directly.
The petition and the pushback
Tilchen's post landed right as a more formal effort was already underway. The Israeli-American Council launched a petition, addressed to Sheeran, tour organizers, and the venues on the rest of the Loop tour dates, demanding Macklemore be pulled from the lineup entirely.
The petition argues this was billed as an Ed Sheeran concert, not a political rally or activist event, and that the real question isn't whether Macklemore is allowed to hold his views. It's where the line sits when an opening act uses a stage that size to push what the petition calls a one-sided agenda, saying: “Freedom of expression does not mean freedom from responsibility. Your show. Your stage. Your responsibility.”So far, Ed Sheeran has not publicly responded.
Suggested articles
Not everyone online is buying it. Plenty of concertgoers pushed back just as hard in the other direction, arguing that music has always been a platform for advocacy, not just an escape, and that Macklemore did nothing wrong by using his own mic time to say what he believes. Some pro-Palestinian voices online have accused critics of trying to silence any mention of Gaza on a public stage, full stop.
So now the conversation has split into two separate arguments that keep getting tangled together.
One is about free speech: does an artist get to say whatever they want during their own set, on a stage they were booked to perform on? Almost everyone agrees the answer there is yes, and Macklemore isn't the first musician to use a concert to make a political statement.
The second argument, the one Tilchen and the IAC are actually making, is different: even if Macklemore had every right to say it, did the people who bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran consent to sitting through it, and if they didn't, who owes them something back? That's a question about consumer expectations and advertising, not censorship, and it's the one nobody quite has an answer for yet.
Macklemore, for what it's worth, isn't backing down. He was announced well in advance as one of Sheeran's official openers alongside Lukas Graham and BIIRD; he's performed "Hind's Hall" at pro-Palestinian events for over a year now, and by all appearances he did the same set again Saturday night, backlash and all.
Neither Sheeran's team nor Macklemore has responded publicly to the refund petition. Whether anyone actually gets their money back is still an open question. Whether they should is apparently one the internet is going to keep arguing about for a while.

China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:42:53 UTC
22:42:53 KST

Shipping documents show how a Chinese state company kept supplying Russia's drone factories with the raw material used in its long-range attack drones, Politico reported. Chinese parts have been recovered from downed Russian drones before. These records are the first to show the raw material shipped straight to the factory—a sanctioned arm of Russia's nuclear giant Rosatom.
Russia's mass-produced attack drones run on parts sourced worldwide that keep slipping past Western export controls, and Ukrainian cities take the hits almost nightly. Kyiv has spent the war naming the foreign suppliers behind that hardware, one component at a time.
What the documents show
The papers trace 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group to Alabuga-Volokno, a Rosatom subsidiary in Tatarstan. The exporter disguised the cargo under a customs code meant for civilian fibers like nylon, said weapons expert David Albright, who studies Russia's drone production. That precursor, polyacrylonitrile, is the raw ingredient for the light carbon fiber in Russia's Shahed-type attack drones.
Drones of that type killed at least 15 people at a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August. Albright estimated the load could yield enough for as many as 1,300 kamikaze drones. The Kyiv-based Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a think tank close to Ukraine's government, gathered the documents and shared them with Western governments. The US House Select Committee on China judged them legitimate, and Ukraine confirmed their authenticity.
Why Beijing can't plead ignorance
Alabuga-Volokno has faced Western sanctions since 2023 from the US, UK, EU, Ukraine, and others. Jilin faces none. Albright said the documents would let the State Department sanction the Chinese supplier. Serhii Kuzan, who heads the Ukrainian center, called China arguably the main and only source of these composite materials.
Former US officials rejected any idea that Beijing was unaware.
"The idea that Chinese state-owned enterprises can hide things from the Chinese government just doesn't wash," said Dennis Wilder, a former CIA deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific.
Denials and a summit
Rosatom claimed it works in full compliance with the law. China's embassy in Washington called the evidence an attempt to "smear and scapegoat China," saying Beijing has never supplied lethal weapons.
The disclosure lands as US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Xi Jinping in Washington this month. In late August, Xi told Vladimir Putin their ties were set to strengthen.

Denmark has completed the procurement process for 16 additional Lockheed Martin F-35A aircraft.
This is according to a report from the U.S. Department of Defense.
The Pentagon’s latest report on F-35 program acquisitions confirms that the Danish government and the Joint Program Management Office finalized the previously announced additional order by April 21 of this year.
Through this contract, the Danish F-35A fleet will grow to 43 aircraft by 2030: the first eight will be delivered in Lot 20, another six in Lot 21, and the remaining two in Lot 22.
This agreement was concluded after an F-35A aircraft intended for the Royal Danish Air Force (RDAF) sustained damage while still on the final assembly line, as noted in the annual report on selected procurements.
Denmark received its first F-35 in 2021, as the country had been participating in the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter development program since 1997, which allowed its specialists to contribute to the fighter’s design and enabled local companies to secure contracts for the production of components.
Subsequently, the Danish Air Force received new fighter jets in batches in 2024 and 2025.
In October 2025, the Danish Ministry of Defense ordered 16 additional F-35A fighters to strengthen the country’s Air Force.
This June, according to a report by the Danish National Audit Office, the total cost of the project exceeded the Ministry of Defense’s initial estimates by nearly €1.91 billion.
At the same time, the U.S. State Department approved a potential sale of AGM-158B/B-2 JASSM-ER cruise missiles to Denmark for use on F-35A fighter jets.

Sweden will purchase the US-made HIMARS rocket artillery system and a large quantity of ammunition in a deal worth more than 7 billion Swedish kronor (nearly $750 million), local media reported on Monday.
The government approved the acquisition after years of preparations, according to Swedish public broadcaster SVT.

Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen described the move as another “milestone” in deepening military cooperation between the two countries, according to the report.

Uttarakhand CM Dhami to launch Yuva Bhavishya Nirman Yojana for free online coaching
DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday will launch the 'Mukhyamantri Yuva Bhavishya Nirman Yojana', a significant initiative aimed at supporting the career and prospects of the state's youth. Under the scheme, young aspirants will receive free online coaching and quality study material to prepare for various competitive examinations.According to the Chief Minister's Office (CMO), the initiative seeks to provide better guidance and essential resources to young people preparing for competitive exams, ensuring that financial constraints do not stand in the way of talented students pursuing their dreams.Under the scheme, students enrolled in universities as well as government and aided colleges across Uttarakhand will be provided online coaching for a range of competitive examinations, including Civil Services (UPSC and State Public Service Commissions), Defence Services (CDS), Banking, Railways and SSC.The programme will also offer guidance for higher education and eligibility examinations such as CAT, MAT, GATE, NET and CSIR-NET.

Exclusive: Trump envoys find Putin still unwilling to compromise on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:37:54 UTC
22:37:54 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin remains committed to escalating his war against Ukraine despite a new U.S. push to revive peace talks, people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent following U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys' visits to Moscow and Kyiv.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner brought revised peace proposals to both capitals, but Moscow appears unwilling to make meaningful concessions, the people said.
The envoys "genuinely want" to make progress toward a ceasefire before winter, one Ukrainian official and one U.S. official said.
"But Putin still hopes to break us this winter and isn't willing to agree to anything," the Ukrainian official added.
The timing of the new peace push was not accidental. Ukrainian and U.S. intelligence increasingly believe Russia is preparing to escalate the war, potentially through a new mobilization drive and another attempt to break Ukraine over the winter.
"Their visit is literally telling (Putin): 'Let's wrap this up; we'll lift the sanctions and move your assets somewhere before this goes any further,'" the official added.
For now, however, the U.S. effort has produced little more than an agreement to resume trilateral negotiations — while Moscow continues to reject the central ideas behind a potential ceasefire.
New push, old demands
Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow on Sept. 5, just a day before making their first official visit to Kyiv in an effort to restart a peace process that has been deadlocked since earlier this year.
The most tangible result of their trip was an agreement between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia to resume trilateral negotiations.
Previous rounds of such talks produced few political results but led to major humanitarian initiatives, including prisoner-of-war exchanges.
People familiar with the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that the U.S. envoys arrived with revised versions of earlier peace proposals. The changes reflected developments since negotiations stalled in February, when the U.S. war with Iran began.
But Moscow's position has changed little.
"The Russian army's successes were noted; confidence was expressed that the set objectives would be achieved; and, of course, the need to eliminate all the root causes of the conflict was emphasized," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the Moscow meeting.
Russia continues to insist that Ukraine withdraw from Donbas, which includes the partially occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, as a key condition for peace.
Moscow is effectively demanding that Kyiv surrender territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
One new proposal involved a potential truce in the air, either focused on energy infrastructure or halting aerial strikes altogether, one person familiar with the talks said.
Russia opposed the idea.
Little to announce
With no major breakthrough on peace, much of the Sept. 6 discussions in Kyiv focused instead on preparing Ukraine for another difficult winter.
Ukrainian officials said the talks brought progress on winter preparedness, with air defense emerging as one of the main issues.
Ukraine faces a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors, particularly PAC-3 missiles, which are among the few weapons capable of effectively intercepting the Russian ballistic missiles Moscow has increasingly used to attack Kyiv.
President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly confirmed that progress had been made.
"If the war continues — and we expect the war will continue — we are counting heavily on the winter aid package... on support for both air defense and the energy sector," Zelensky told reporters during a Sept. 6 press conference.
"The American side will increase the production volumes of anti-ballistic missiles, Patriot systems next year... we are counting on such systems to protect our state."
Still, one Ukrainian official said the U.S. envoys were reluctant to discuss details of the talks publicly at subsequent press conferences, with the official seemingly acknowledging that the visit had produced little in the way of a breakthrough.
By the end of the talks, the official said, all sides had little to announce at the subsequent press conference.
Moscow's message
The two envoys heard little that was new during their visit to Moscow, according to people familiar with the talks. Russia does not appear willing to end the war without achieving its goals in Ukraine.
Russian officials were also unhappy that Witkoff and Kushner planned to travel to Kyiv after visiting Moscow.
Ukrainian airports had been prepared for the envoys to arrive by plane, but Russian aerial attacks, including strikes near the capital's airport, prevented that option.
The trip nevertheless marked Witkoff and Kushner's first visit to Ukraine's capital, despite their previous trips to Moscow, where they met with Putin.
Russian officials advised the envoys against traveling around Kyiv, one Ukrainian official said. The Kremlin "made it clear" that it did not want Ukrainian officials taking the envoys to sites destroyed by Russian attacks, the person added.
Despite that, the Ukrainian president met the two U.S. envoys in the heart of Kyiv, at Sofiiska Square. Most of the photographs from the meeting were taken against the backdrop of a memorial to Ukrainian soldiers killed in the war.
Different roles
Ukrainian officials welcomed Kushner's active involvement in the negotiations, saying he has consistently tried to develop new ideas and present proposals to both sides.
They described Witkoff as less engaged in the process itself.
At the same time, Ukrainian officials said the U.S. administration has a clear understanding of the situation on the ground. U.S. intelligence agencies have provided detailed assessments of developments in the war.
According to the officials, both Witkoff and Kushner understand the potential for further escalation as Putin prepares for a possible new mobilization drive. Ukrainian intelligence has reached a similar assessment.
Yet this understanding has so far failed to produce a breakthrough.
The main obstacle remains Moscow's unwillingness to compromise and Putin's belief that Russia can break Ukraine over the coming winter.
"Russia still has plenty of self-confidence," Zelensky told reporters.
The U.S. side, the officials said, also does not appear to believe that increasing pressure on Russia alone will be enough to change Putin's calculations.
That leaves the new peace process facing the same problem that stalled the previous one: Washington and Kyiv are looking for a way to stop the war, while Putin appears to believe that another winter of fighting could still bring Russia closer to victory.

Thailand's headline inflation quickens to 2.53 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:37:34 CST
22:37:34 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's headline inflation rate accelerated for the first time in four months in August, mainly due to persistently high domestic fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict and the imposition of additional economic sanctions, official data showed on Monday.
The Southeast Asian country's consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.53 percent last month compared to a year earlier, quickening from a 1.95-percent gain in July and registering the strongest reading since May, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Broadly elevated prepared food prices contributed to the upturn, while fresh food costs also increased, partly owing to improved purchasing power on the back of the government's co-payment program, combined with volatile weather conditions that reduced production, the ministry said in a statement.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile fresh food and energy prices, climbed 1.44 percent year on year in August, accelerating from a 1.34-percent rise in the previous month.
For the first eight months of 2026, the headline CPI expanded 1.37 percent compared to the same period last year.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects headline inflation to remain positive in September, primarily supported by rising energy-related, food, and travel costs, while electricity tariffs and personal-care goods prices continue to ease.
The ministry maintained its projection for headline CPI to rise between 1.5 percent and 2.5 percent this year. ■

NANNING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region will become operational on Sept. 16, according to a Monday press conference on the canal's opening.
The 134.2-km canal links the Xijiang River shipping route in the north with the Beibu Gulf in the south. It is China's first major river-to-sea canal project that has been planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949.
Designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal stretches along the country's New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic route linking China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets.
It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, said Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government, in another press conference held in early September.
"The canal not only overcomes Guangxi's longstanding constraints on river-to-sea connectivity, but will also reshape the economic geography between China and ASEAN," said Lu.
Trade between the two sides has seen robust growth in recent years. Data from General Administration of Customs show that bilateral trade between China and ASEAN reached 4.34 trillion yuan (about 640 billion U.S. dollars) in the first half of 2026, up 18.2 percent year on year.
The Beibu Gulf Port, a key hub at the southern end of the canal, has become an important gateway for China's opening up to ASEAN. Its container throughput increased from 2.28 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) in 2017 to 10.06 million TEUs in 2025, and the port has established a comprehensive shipping network that covers major ports across ASEAN. ■

2026-09-07

This undated file photo shows a portrait of Matthias Metz, CEO and chairman of the Board of BSH Home Appliances Group. (Xinhua)
BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- More China-developed products and technologies are reaching global markets, as the country's role in global innovation continues to grow, Matthias Metz, CEO and chairman of the Board of BSH Home Appliances Group, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
"China is not only an important sales market, but also an engine driving global innovation," Metz said at the five-day IFA Berlin, one of the world's largest trade fairs for consumer electronics and home appliances, which opened on Friday.
Metz said China's rapidly evolving consumer market is a key source of that innovative momentum. Chinese consumers are quick to embrace new technologies and increasingly attentive to the benefits they can bring to everyday life, creating strong demand for new products and better user experiences.
Over the past two decades, he has witnessed a profound shift in China's home appliance market. "Consumers have moved beyond a primary focus on basic functionality and are placing greater emphasis on product performance, smart features, space efficiency, design and ease of use."
At the same time, he believed that China's diverse living spaces, kitchen layouts and culinary habits are giving rise to varied and specialized needs. Metz said such changes are pushing companies to respond faster, refine products more quickly and explore new technological solutions.
In response to these evolving needs, BSH has expanded its research capabilities in the country. In 2024, the company upgraded its China R&D center in the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing to a global R&D center. It has since become BSH's largest comprehensive R&D center worldwide, focusing on key product development and emerging technologies.
"As China's R&D capabilities continue to grow, innovations shaped by local consumer needs are gradually finding applications in markets beyond the country," Metz said.
At this year's IFA, BSH showcased two innovative products developed by its China-based R&D teams and now reaching global markets. One example is a drawer-style steam oven. Metz said that Chinese households' demand for efficient use of kitchen space, combined with their preference for steaming as a cooking method, prompted the R&D team to develop a more compact and flexible product format.
"The design concept, rooted in Chinese lifestyles, can address broader demand in other markets for better space utilization, installation flexibility and efficient cooking," he said. "'In China, for China, and for the world' is more than a concept. It is something we put into practice,"
The impact of Chinese innovation on the global home appliance industry is also reflected in increasingly active market competition. Nearly half of the exhibitors at this year's IFA came from China, while Chinese brands have continued to expand their presence in the European market.
Metz said the growing participation of Chinese brands could help accelerate innovation across the industry while also raising the bar for companies themselves. "Competition is always a good source of gaining more power and thinking about where we can do better."
Looking ahead, Metz said BSH will continue to deepen its presence in the Chinese market and seize the innovation opportunities it offers. "By linking insights from Chinese consumers and local market needs with its global R&D resources, BSH aims to bring more innovations developed in China to consumers around the world," he added. ■

Feature: Kung fu stuntmen put Hong Kong cinema on the map
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:36:49 CST
22:36:49 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Suspended from an exhibition ceiling at Tai Kwun in Hong Kong, a prop helicopter brings visitors face to face with the behind-the-scenes secret of Hong Kong action cinema -- the kung fu stuntmen who built an era by putting their lives on the line.
The exhibition, titled Better Together -- Partnering Up for Hong Kong Movies, displays replicas of classic action props to explore the city's enduring cinematic team spirit. Chin Ka-lok, president of the Hong Kong Stuntman Association, helped to curate the exhibition and specifically recommended including these production details.
"Hong Kong action cinema has always been a mix of real and fake. It looks like a deadly risk on screen, but behind the scenes it's all calculated," Chin told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Between the 1960s and 1980s, facing stiff competition from Hollywood, Hong Kong carved out its global reputation through high-risk stunt work. Elite stunt teams led by pioneers like Jackie Chan and Sammo Hung flourished, constantly pushing the limits of physical action.
Chin entered the industry at 15 and spent about a decade training under Hung. He recalled when television crews filmed a dozen scenes a day, yet Chan spent three full days refining a single wire-work shot.
"At the time, that level of dedication was almost unimaginable. That pursuit of perfection stayed with me for life," he said.
The stunt business has an old rule: never say "no" on set. Since Chin began his career, he has said "Yes," "Can do," and "No problem" more than anything else.
"People pay to come to the cinema," Chin said. "If we don't put our lives on the line, we haven't earned their ticket." It was a principle he took to heart in his early days as an extra, and one he has carried with him ever since.
Since taking over as president of the association in 2014, Chin has felt an urgent need to preserve the memory of his peers. Several years ago, when a respected veteran stuntman passed away, Chin tried to compile a memorial booklet for him, only to find no records of when the veteran entered the industry or which films he had worked on. Without documentation, he realized, the names of many who risked their lives would simply fade with time.
A decade ago, Chin saw the skill gap firsthand on set while directing a stunt requiring a jump from the second floor. After repeated calls met only hesitation, a crew member in his 40s finally stepped forward to take the leap. "We must pass our experience to the young," Chin said. "If we don't teach them, who will jump in the future?"
To keep the craft alive, the association organized its first training workshop. Mindful of the local film market's limited capacity to absorb new talent, organizers avoided running it every year. It was not until 2026 that the second edition was launched, marking the first time the program received financial backing from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government's film development fund.
The 12-week training program selected 20 candidates from nearly 100 applicants to train under veteran instructors in wire-work, vehicular stunts, controlled explosions, firearms, and acting. The cohort brought together complete novices and seasoned athletes alike.
Hanging midair during wire-work drills, trainees quickly realized their lives depended entirely on the peers holding their safety ropes below. That mutual reliance captures the true essence of "partnering up" -- watching each other's backs and facing danger side by side.
Amid the rise of artificial intelligence, the trainees remain convinced that the raw emotion and physical reactions captured on camera cannot be replaced.
"We aren't actually brawling in the street, but we have to make the audience believe it," Chin said. "It has to look stylish, yet feel like real combat. That takes real skill."
Back in the gallery, the prop helicopter still hangs overhead. Having witnessed decades of grit on film sets, it now looks down on a new generation ready to step before the camera. ■

Israeli army says West Bank settlement expansion putting its forces under strain
The Israeli military has warned Israel's political leadership that it will struggle to protect new illegal settlements and settler outposts in the occupied West Bank amid rapid settlement expansion and rising settler violence.
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Monday that military officials had raised concerns over the proliferation of new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, many of which lack basic infrastructure needed to protect them.
The military reportedly described the establishment of some of the new sites as a "reckless" move driven by political considerations rather than security needs.
Roads leading to some of the settlements pass through Palestinian villages and areas with poor mobile phone coverage, potentially making it difficult for settlers to call for assistance in an emergency.
Many also lack adequate surveillance systems and have limited access routes, forcing the military to develop additional security infrastructure and commit more troops to protecting increasingly dispersed settlements.
Israeli forces often protect or assist settlers in ways that facilitate attacks on Palestinians, including forcible displacement, land seizures or other abuses.
The number of Israeli battalions serving under Central Command, which oversees the occupied West Bank, is expected to rise to 26 this week - the highest level since the start of the war.
At least 103 settlement outposts and agricultural farms have been approved under the current Israeli government in areas under Central Command and the Jordan Valley, according to Haaretz, with around 80 located deep inside the West Bank.
An Israeli military official said in July that unauthorised outposts had become one of the army's "biggest challenges", with the spread of settlements increasing the burden on forces attempting to maintain control across the territory.
The warning comes amid an unprecedented expansion of Israeli settlements under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government.
Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now said in July that the government had approved 104 new settlements since taking office in late 2022.
Of those, 38 are entirely new settlements, 50 are unauthorised outposts being retroactively recognised as settlements, while 16 were previously designated as neighbourhoods of existing settlements and have now been granted independent status.
Peace Now separately recorded 248 new settler outposts established under the current government by the beginning of August, including 65 during 2026 alone.
All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
Pressure over settler violence
The military warning follows Netanyahu's reported decision on Sunday to order the dismantling of unauthorised settlement outposts amid pressure from Washington over escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
Two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters that Netanyahu had ordered the removals in response to US pressure.
Israeli media reported that around 100 outposts could be affected, although it remains unclear when the operation will begin.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a leading advocate of settlement expansion, confirmed that Netanyahu had issued instructions to remove sites established in Areas A and B of the West Bank.
Smotrich said he opposed the decision while highlighting the government's extensive expansion of settlements in Area C, which remains under full Israeli military and administrative control.
The move came after US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described violent settlers as "terrorists" and called for severe consequences following a visit to the Palestinian town of Turmus Ayya.
Separately on Sunday, Israel's High Court of Justice ordered Israeli authorities to allow three Palestinian families driven from their homes by settlers in the village of Jalud to return within 14 days and to provide security for them.
The families were expelled in July after extremist settlers established an unauthorised outpost near their homes and subjected the residents to attacks and intimidation.
The court sharply criticised the Israeli military, police and Defence Minister Israel Katz for failing to prevent the attacks and subsequent expulsion, as well as for failing to adequately pursue those responsible.
It ordered the military and police to ensure the families could safely return and bring equipment and materials needed to repair damage to their homes and utilities.
The judges described settler violence as "completely unacceptable" and demanded detailed answers from Israeli security authorities about what action had been taken to identify and prosecute those responsible.
The developments come amid a sharp escalation in settler attacks and the displacement of Palestinian communities across the West Bank.
Human Rights Watch said last month that settler violence had fully or partially displaced 107 Palestinian communities, comprising around 5,900 people, since January 2023.
All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are considered illegal under international law, which prohibits an occupying power from transferring parts of its civilian population into occupied territory. Israel disputes this interpretation.

China Focus: China's top court sets rules for AI deepfakes and other disputes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:36:42 CST
22:36:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- A familiar face on a video call may not be what it seems, as artificial intelligence (AI) can now replicate people's faces and voices with startling realism, creating new challenges for the law. On Monday, China's top court issued guidelines spelling out when such AI-generated content can lead to legal liability.
The guidelines, released by the Supreme People's Court (SPC), address a range of emerging disputes, including AI deepfakes and voice cloning, algorithmic price discrimination and AI-generated false information.
They make clear that people cannot use AI to create or distribute recognizable digital replicas of others without their consent, including cloned faces and voices. Such use constitutes an infringement of individuals' rights, while using AI-generated faces or voices to spread false claims or damage someone's reputation can also result in legal liability.
China has already addressed such issues in court. In April 2024, the Beijing Internet Court ruled in the country's first AI-generated voice infringement case that using AI to recreate a person's identifiable voice without their consent can infringe upon their rights.
China is a global leader in AI development. The size of the country's AI industry was estimated to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up 40 percent year on year.
Also, China was home to more than 6,600 AI companies as of June 2026, representing 15 percent of the global total. The country has developed a complete industrial system spanning foundational infrastructure, models and frameworks, and sector-specific applications.
The new rules come as AI-generated impersonation becomes increasingly easy to create and difficult to distinguish from authentic content. A handful of photographs or a short voice recording can provide enough material to produce a convincing digital replica.
The guidelines also address algorithmic discrimination against consumers. Businesses that use algorithms to offer different prices or other transaction terms for the same goods or services without reasonable justification may be held liable if the practice causes harm to consumers.
"We cannot expect every consumer to become an expert at spotting deception. The law must step in promptly to protect consumers' legitimate rights and interests," said Zhou Jiahai, head of the research office of the SPC.
Another challenge is that generative AI systems can produce false or inaccurate information, commonly known as "AI hallucinations."
AI service providers can be held liable if they are notified that their systems have generated content that infringes a person's rights but fail to take timely action.
Users, too, can be held responsible for how they use AI. Anyone who deliberately uses prompts or other methods to induce an AI system to generate infringing content that harms others can be held liable.
The guidelines also provide a way for people to seek swift protection when AI-generated content threatens to cause serious and irreversible harm. For example, someone whose face has been digitally altered and used to spread false and defamatory sexual claims may ask a court for an injunction if waiting to act could cause harm that would be difficult to repair later.
China is advancing its "AI Plus" initiative to promote the extensive and in-depth integration of AI into various sectors and fields of the economy and society.
As AI advances, governments worldwide are grappling with the challenge of encouraging innovation while also protecting people from potential harm.
China has taken a series of steps to address the challenges posed by AI. In September 2025, it put into effect measures governing the labeling of AI-generated and synthesized content. The SPC's latest guidelines set out how courts should handle AI-related disputes, adding to China's evolving legal framework for AI.
During the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in July, China stressed the need for adhering to the principles of openness and win-win and boosting innovation-driven development, strengthening risk awareness and ensuring that AI is secure and controllable, encouraging inclusiveness and promoting mutual learning between civilizations, and advocating solidarity and improving global governance.
At the event, an action plan on international AI ethics governance was released.
It calls on countries to take action in light of their national conditions in areas including ethical governance throughout the AI lifecycle, categorized and tiered risk prevention and control, the development of agile governance mechanisms, the cultivation of a collaborative ecosystem across industrial chains, and the fostering of a favorable social environment.
As part of the efforts of China to implement the plan, stakeholders across industrial chains will be encouraged to clarify the boundaries of their rights and responsibilities. ■

====================================================================================================

The economic risks of a Gulf tanker war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:36:22 UTC
22:36:22 KST

Breadcrumb
As Gulf crisis morphs to tanker war, what are the economic implications?
The escalating conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is beginning to pose a much bigger question for Gulf economies: how long can their enormous financial reserves shield them from a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important energy routes?
For now, countries including the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait have formidable financial defences. But analysts warn that even those buffers have limits if the crisis stretches into 2027.
Fitch Ratings has warned that “rating risks for some issuers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries could increase under a hypothetical scenario in which passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted through most of 2027”.
The agency said the “extremely large sovereign financial buffers in Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar have been a key factor in limiting the conflict’s impact on credit ratings”. But the longer the disruption continues, the more those reserves risk being drawn down to compensate for falling exports, higher shipping and insurance costs, and wider economic damage.
Firas Shaabo, professor of financial management at Istanbul’s Başakşehir University, says the immediate problem is not whether Gulf states have enough money. It is the accumulating “cost of the shock”.
Sovereign wealth funds give governments considerable room to absorb the impact, he says, but that protection is temporary rather than unlimited.
The warning comes as the confrontation at sea has sharply intensified. US Central Command announced that it had targeted three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles towards two US warships.
The IRGC subsequently said it had targeted three tankers which, according to its account, were travelling along unauthorised routes through Hormuz, as well as three vessels linked to the United States.
The result is a rapidly deteriorating environment for shipping, insurance and trade finance - and Gulf economies are among the most exposed. Two large tankers carrying Saudi crude were attacked almost simultaneously as they left the Strait of Hormuz on 31 August.
The Saudi tanker Sadr and the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity were each carrying about two million barrels of crude. Saudi Arabia's National Shipping Company, Bahri, later said two Filipino crew members aboard the Sadr had been killed.
By 2 September, the International Maritime Organization had recorded 72 confirmed incidents targeting international shipping in the region, with 21 seafarers killed.
Shipping slows to a trickle
The scale of the disruption can already be seen in vessel movements. Kpler data showed only five commercial ships passing through Hormuz last Saturday. None were recorded crossing on Sunday.
That compared with 31 vessels during the previous weekend. Traffic remained in single digits at the beginning of September, as large oil and gas carriers increasingly avoided the strait.
For Gulf exporters, that matters because Hormuz is not simply a shipping route. For several states, it is the principal outlet through which their energy exports reach international markets.
Saudi Arabia has some ability to bypass it through infrastructure connecting its oil industry to the Red Sea. Other Gulf states have far fewer alternatives.
Fitch said financial reserves would continue to provide substantial protection under a prolonged-conflict scenario, but warned that extended disruption could eventually damage the credit profiles of states without alternative export routes such as pipelines bypassing Hormuz.
The effect is being amplified by extraordinary increases in insurance costs. War-risk premiums for crude tankers have risen from about 0.25% of a vessel's value before the confrontation to between 7.5% and 12.5% in August.
For shipowners, that can make voyages commercially unattractive. Operators must either absorb enormous additional costs, pass them on through higher freight rates or avoid the region altogether.
When large reserves are not enough
The Gulf states are often portrayed as possessing almost inexhaustible financial resources because of the size of their sovereign wealth funds. But Shaabo says that can be misleading.
Those funds are not vast pools of cash that governments can immediately deploy. Their holdings range from relatively small amounts of liquid reserves, to investments that can be sold quickly but potentially at a loss during turbulent markets, and large portfolios of long-term assets that cannot easily be converted into cash.
The important question, therefore, is not simply how large a country's sovereign wealth fund is. It is how much immediately accessible liquidity it has - and how long that liquidity can sustain government spending and economic support if the disruption continues.
That distinction becomes increasingly important if the Hormuz crisis moves from a temporary shock to a persistent economic problem. A prolonged disruption could weaken growth and government revenues at the same time as states face higher spending requirements.
Eventually, Shaabo warns, that combination could begin affecting sovereign creditworthiness.
Higher oil prices offer only partial protection. They may increase the value of every barrel Gulf producers are able to export, helping compensate for some losses.
But higher prices matter much less if exporters cannot physically move the same quantities of crude. Restricted export routes mean lower volumes, while transport, insurance and import costs rise sharply.
The result could be weaker economic activity even as headline oil prices remain high.
Iran has added to that uncertainty by expanding the number of vessels on its blacklist in the strait to 56 on 2 September. The list includes oil tankers and carriers of liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas.
Iran has threatened listed vessels with fines, seizure or detention, and warned that action could also be taken against ships conducting ship-to-ship cargo transfers with them, according to Reuters.
A crisis extending beyond oil
The risks are also spreading into the financial and legal machinery underpinning international trade. The continuing turmoil has exposed weaknesses in insurance contracts used by lenders and charterers to finance shipments.
Some war-risk clauses may not have been designed for a crisis developing at the current pace. That creates uncertainty over who carries the financial risk when vessels are prevented from sailing or when routes suddenly become too dangerous.
Ship charter agreements can also limit an owner's ability to avoid areas formally designated as war-risk zones. According to Lloyd's List, the result could be prolonged contractual disputes, higher litigation costs and reduced availability of trade finance.
That means the impact of the Hormuz confrontation does not stop with oil tankers. It can gradually spread through banks, insurers, shipping companies, importers and government finances.
Three possible paths
Shaabo sees three broad scenarios. The first - and in his view currently the least likely - is a relatively rapid settlement followed by the gradual resumption of shipping.
Under that scenario, Gulf governments could rely on reserves, additional borrowing and adjustments to spending without putting their sovereign ratings under serious pressure.
The second is considerably more damaging. If disruption lasts several months, what begins as a shipping and logistics crisis could develop into a wider financial and economic problem.
Growth could slow as inflation and government spending rise. Capital could leave the region, bank profits could decline and major investments in transport, logistics, tourism and property could be delayed.
Governments would then face an increasingly difficult choice between maintaining spending and subsidies, depleting financial assets or taking on substantially more debt.
The third scenario is the most severe. Shaabo estimates a 20% to 25% probability of sustained physical damage to infrastructure including oil facilities, ports, refineries, pipelines and power stations.
At that point, the nature of the crisis changes. It would no longer simply be a question of temporarily preventing Gulf states from exporting what they produce.
Their ability to produce energy itself could be reduced. Sovereign wealth funds are far less effective against that kind of shock because the problem becomes a loss of future income rather than a temporary shortage of cash.
That could lead directly to negative reviews of sovereign credit ratings.
Not all Gulf states face the same risk
The impact would also be highly uneven. Economic expert and financial adviser Ali Ahmed Darwish says the Fitch warning should be treated with particular seriousness because the crisis highlights significant differences between Gulf economies.
Saudi Arabia has the advantage of alternative export infrastructure towards the Red Sea. For states whose geography leaves them overwhelmingly dependent on Hormuz, the options are much narrower.
Those countries may eventually have to undertake far-reaching changes to their supply and export networks. But alternative routes can be extremely expensive, technically difficult or simply impractical.
Darwish argues that governments will therefore also need to make greater use of partnerships with the private sector, particularly banks. Banks could work with insurers and reinsurers to maintain trade credit and contain the rapidly rising cost of maritime insurance.
That could reduce the pressure on governments to continually draw on sovereign funds or seek additional external financing. But there is a limit to how long these measures can compensate for a fundamental disruption to trade.
If the war and interruption to shipping continue into 2027, Darwish says Gulf states could face a genuine challenge in meeting financial obligations and preserving monetary stability.
Kareem Ramadan is a Muscat-based correspondent for The New Arab's Arabic edition, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.

Ukraine’s Ground Robots Complete 112,000 Logistics and Evacuation Missions in 2026
The number of missions carried out by Ukrainian unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) has increased 3.3-fold since the beginning of 2026, with the systems completing more than 25,000 logistics and evacuation missions on the front line in August alone.
This was reported by Ukrainian Ministry of Defense on September 7, citing data from Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As of early September, DELTA had recorded approximately 112,000 logistics and evacuation missions involving ground robotic systems since the beginning of the year.
The number of missions has grown steadily each month, rising from 7,511 in January to 7,960 in February and 9,072 in March. The figure increased further to 11,028 in April, 14,059 in May, 16,664 in June, and 19,940 in July, before reaching 25,143 in August.
As a result, the number of logistics and evacuation missions recorded in August was 3.3 times higher than in January.
The growing use of UGVs extends beyond logistics and evacuation missions, with Ukrainian forces also deploying armed platforms in combat operations. Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 UGV, for instance, withstood five FPV drone strikes while carrying out a combat mission before a sixth hit disabled the platform, DevDroid said in a press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
The system was deployed by the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion during a remotely operated mission targeting a concentration of Russian troops.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained operational and continued its mission.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is continuing to expand its fleet of unmanned ground systems as their role on the battlefield grows. The country plans to manufacture at least 50,000 combat and logistics UGVs this year to support infantry units and address personnel shortages along the front line.

Region Producing 40% of Russia’s Oil Prepares for Ukrainian Drone Strikes for First Time
Authorities in Russia’s Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, a sprawling oil-producing region responsible for roughly 40% of the country’s crude output, are preparing for the possibility of Ukrainian drone strikes despite the region being about 2,200 kilometers, or 1,370 miles, from the Ukrainian border.
The regional social development department has proposed formally adding drone attacks to the list of circumstances classified as “extreme life situations,” independent Russian outlet Verstka reported on September 7 after reviewing proposed amendments to local legislation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The designation applies to emergencies in which residents “urgently require immediate assistance of various kinds” and cannot cope with the situation even after “using all available opportunities and resources.”
Natural disasters, industrial explosions and the loss of basic means of subsistence are already covered by the category.
If the amendments are approved, residents affected by future drone strikes would become eligible for emergency government assistance, including hot meals, monthly food packages, clothing, footwear and other support.
The preparations are notable because neither cities nor industrial facilities in Khanty-Mansi have yet been directly hit by Ukrainian drones.
Warning signs, however, have begun appearing.
The region declared a missile alert for the first time on May 5, while drone-threat warnings have been issued repeatedly since late June.
The closest major facility to Khanty-Mansi known to have been targeted by Ukrainian forces is the Tyumen oil refinery, located roughly 200 kilometers, or 125 miles, from the regional boundary. The refinery was struck by a drone on July 25.
Khanty-Mansi itself remains far deeper inside Russia, but Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign has steadily pushed the perceived threat farther from the border.
The region’s importance to Russia makes that particularly significant. Khanty-Mansi is the center of the country’s oil-producing industry and supplies an enormous share of the crude underpinning Russia’s energy exports and state revenues.
The region has already felt the indirect effects of Ukrainian strikes.
Previously, a fuel crisis triggered in part by repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries has reached Khanty-Mansi despite its own enormous crude production, highlighting the distinction between extracting oil and having sufficient refinery capacity to turn it into gasoline and other fuels.

Putin’s 2026 Donetsk Goal Is Six Years Away at Russia’s Current Pace, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:34:33 UTC
22:34:33 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin’s 2026 Donetsk Goal Is Six Years Away at Russia’s Current Pace, ISW Says
Russian forces would need more than six additional years to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the Donetsk region if their current rate of advance continues, putting the potential timeline well beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) on September 6, Russian forces advanced in the Donetsk region at an average rate of 2.36 square kilometers per day in August. At that pace, Russia would not capture the remaining 19% of the region until October 2, 2032.
ISW stressed that the calculation is an extrapolation rather than a prediction that Russia will ultimately succeed. “Russian forces will not seize Donetsk Oblast until 2032 at their current rate of advance — if they can seize it at all,” ISW wrote.
Across the entire frontline, Russian forces advanced at an average rate of 2.91 square kilometers per day in August, slightly faster than in recent months. The pace in the Donetsk region, which remains a priority for Moscow, was slower.
The institute said Russia would also have to fight through Ukraine’s remaining major fortified cities in the region, including Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka. Russian forces have been fighting for Kostyantynivka since October 2025 but have not captured the city after nearly a year of operations.
ISW said Russian leader Vladimir Putin nevertheless appears to believe that Russian forces can seize the remainder of the Donetsk region by the end of 2026.
The assessment cited a person close to the Kremlin who said ahead of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s September 5 visit to Moscow that Putin was confident Russian forces could capture the entire region before the end of the year.
Following Putin’s meeting with the US delegation, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the Russian leader had presented an assessment of Russia’s “significant advances” along the frontline. ISW said that characterization did not correspond with the situation on the ground.
The institute linked the gap between Moscow’s expectations and battlefield developments partly to what it described as systematic misreporting within the Russian military. According to ISW, Russian commanders have repeatedly exaggerated territorial gains and presented claims of advances that have not been confirmed independently.
“The lies and distortions of Russian military commanders at many levels are likely leading Putin to harden his perception that Russian forces can achieve his intended objectives in Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026 and thus that he need not make any compromises in his aims,” ISW wrote.
Putin has reportedly established at least 15 deadlines for capturing the entire Donetsk region since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to ISW. Russian forces have failed to meet each of those deadlines.
The institute also cautioned that simply extending Russia’s current rate of advance into the future does not account for the difficulty of future operations. Russian troops would have to conduct attritional urban battles through Ukraine’s fortified eastern cities before attempting further advances across terrain where Russian forces have historically struggled.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces advanced in parts of the Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Dnipropetrovsk regions, while Russian troops failed to make confirmed gains across several other frontline sectors.
