World Alzheimer’s Month: early dementia diagnosis matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:45:11 UTC
20:45:11 KST

World Alzheimer’s Month: early dementia diagnosis matters
TEHRAN – September, observed as World Alzheimer’s Month, provides an important opportunity to raise awareness among the public and healthcare professionals about Alzheimer’s disease, dementia, their various aspects, and the challenges they present.
Dementia is a condition caused by brain diseases and affects memory, thinking, and the ability to function. More than 57 million people live with dementia worldwide, and nearly 10 million people get newly diagnosed every year. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia and is estimated to account for 60–70 percent of cases.
Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive condition that gradually damages memory and cognitive abilities and, over time, impairs a person’s ability to perform even the simplest everyday tasks. In most cases, symptoms emerge later in life. Beyond its profound impact on patients, the disease also places a significant social and economic burden on families, caregivers, and society as a whole.
Dementia affects an individual’s ability to live independently, work and function, while placing substantial burdens on families and carers. It carries a major economic loss, costing the global economy an estimated US$ 1.3 trillion annually. About half of this cost is driven by unpaid care provided by families and friends. Understanding risk factors and taking action to prevent dementia can improve health and quality of life, helping people live longer, healthier and more independent lives.
Each year, the month is celebrated under a specific theme. This September, it seeks to tackle the persistent stigma and discrimination surrounding dementia by shining a spotlight on the timely and important issue of early diagnosis under the theme: The Earlier You Know, The More You Can Do: A Dementia Diagnosis Matters.
It has been more than a century since Alzheimer’s disease was first identified. However, many individuals and even institutions have no or insufficient knowledge of the disease; many are unaware of their disease in the early stage.
In recent years, global themes and initiatives regarding Alzheimer’s disease have followed a logical, evolutionary path: over the past five years, the trajectory began with raising awareness and understanding the disease, proceeded to underscore the importance of prevention and the management of risk factors, particularly physical inactivity, and ultimately culminated in a focus on action and advocacy.
With the increase in elderly population, dementia and Alzheimer’s disease have become key areas of focus for health policymakers and decision-makers. Delay in diagnosis is a major challenge. Many patients are diagnosed when the treatments have a low efficacy.
That’s why the theme underlines the decisive role of early diagnosis. Timely interventions provide opportunities for better treatment and management of the disease, yielding positive health outcomes.
This year’s theme highlights the importance of early diagnosis as the key to unlocking a whole raft of treatment, care and support options, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological. The month seeks to raise awareness of the benefits that a diagnosis can provide to those living with the condition, alongside carers and the wider society.
Unfortunately, Alzheimer’s disease doesn’t just affect the individuals diagnosed with the disease; it has a profound impact on their families and caregivers as well.
With the passage of time, over 80 percent of home caregivers, who often provide around-the-clock support, suffer from frustration, physical and mental health issues, including backache, sleep disorders, and depression. World Alzheimer’s Day takes place during World Alzheimer’s Month and is on 21 September every year.

Do birds enjoy flying? Scientists asked cockatoos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:30:30 UTC
20:30:30 KST

As a kid, Jorg Massen would watch birds swoop and swirl overhead and wonder whether they were doing it for enjoyment. Massen is now a behavioral biologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, and thanks to a special setup at a nearby bird park, he was finally able to put that question to the test.
For several months each year the birds at Avifauna Bird Park are free to leave their aviaries at certain times every day. When the gates open, each bird decides for itself: fly out into the open sky or stay home. They get no penalty or reward either way.
Among these birds at the time of Massen’s study were 17 pink-and-gray Galah Cockatoos that, in the wild, fly long distances to find seeds. The Galahs chose to fly for almost every 20-minute period offered, Massen and his colleagues reported in a paper published in Behaviour.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Their consistent choice to fly is “in line with the notion that the birds found flight rewarding,” says Michael Mendl, an animal behavior researcher at the University of Bristol in England, who was not involved in the study. The only exception was a pair of birds that skipped flying once, on a day when they had just been given new nest boxes, Massen says: “they had other activities to attend to”—such as courtship and mating—“which are also considered joyful.”
After flight sessions, the Galahs foraged, scratched and raised their crests more—behaviors the researchers interpreted as signs of “positive excitement resulting from free flight.” And in a test designed to measure optimism, the Galahs grew more hopeful of finding their favorite treat (a walnut) when they’d had several days of free flight and more pessimistic about their walnut prospects after several days of being grounded.
The birds’ hormones did not change after flight as predicted, however; an expected dip in the stress hormone cortisol might have been masked by a rise caused by physical exertion, Massen says.
We can’t be certain about whether wanting to fly and liking the experience add up to feeling happy, Mendl notes. Animal-cognition scientists have typically been extremely hesitant to ascribe feelings or desires based on animals’ behavior, but researchers have become increasingly open to attributing such conscious experiences to animals when the data support it. If birds are capable of conscious experience, Mendl says, “the findings would indeed suggest that the birds enjoyed flying.”
For Galahs, Massen says, flight appears to be “an ethological need”: a behavior they’re naturally driven to perform. Massen sees his study as part of a broader shift in animal-welfare science away from simply preventing suffering and toward designing environments that let animals express the natural behaviors that seem to make them feel good.

Bosses are using AI to spy on employees' productivity—does it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:30:06 UTC
20:30:06 KST

Ready for a Whopper with a side of Orwell? Earlier this year, Burger King announced the rollout of Patty, an AI chatbot imbedded in headsets that tracks if cashiers neglect to say please and thank you and chimes in when a soda fountain is running low.
Advances in AI, cameras, sensors and tracking software have given employers unprecedented power to monitor employees. They now observe the physical location of workers, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, and even the tone and pitch of conversations with customers.
Now, as companies search for new ways to watch their workforce, researchers are taking a close look at the consequences of constant surveillance.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Employee monitoring has become standard practice in multiple industries and workplaces. Drivers delivering packages or pizzas are increasingly being watched by AI-powered surveillance systems. Many employees in Amazon warehouses are continuously tracked through handheld scanners, badge swipes and workstation software.
Technologies that keep tabs on employees hold a strong appeal for corporate leadership, says Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany. Leaders may believe that close surveillance can help identify top performers, increase efficiency or improve safety, he says.
In practice, though, such benefits are elusive. When König reviewed studies on employee monitoring in the 2025 issue of the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, he found little to suggest that electronic surveillance improved performance. “My general take is that [monitoring] isn’t going to matter as much as employers assume,” he says.
Despite the lack of evidence, the global market for employee-monitoring technology is expected to exceed $4 billion in 2026, largely due to major companies in North America. A New York Times investigation in 2022 found that eight out of the 10 largest private US employers, including United Parcel Service, Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, tracked productivity metrics of individual workers, often in real time.
US postal workers are also closely watched. Delivering mail “feels less like public service and more like working inside a quiet surveillance state,” said a Reddit user in 2025. “We’re tracked down to the second. Every scan. Every step. Every stop. They monitor our GPS in real time. They can pull up on us unannounced. We get questioned for things as human as needing the restroom or checking a package twice.”
Any employer of any size can get into the monitoring business. Amazon Web Services sells thousands and thousands of software programs for employee monitoring, says Michele Molè, an employment law researcher at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. Adding a monitoring app to the workplace can be as easy as downloading Spotify, he says. But instead of music, employers get a stream of data about how each employee is behaving every minute of their day.
Companies that hope to increase their workforce’s performance through monitoring face a basic obstacle in human nature, König says. Workers might briefly up their game, but they tend to revert to their normal routines. “They become habituated,” he says. In his review, he pointed to growing evidence that even body cameras worn by police — an especially high-profile, high-stakes example of surveillance — don’t significantly change the behavior of either the police or the public over the long term.
When workers do respond to monitoring, there can be unintended consequences. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers were less likely to exceed daily limits for driving hours, but they also were more likely to crash.
König is far from the only skeptic. “There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance,” says Daniel Ravid, a management researcher at the University of New Mexico.
Ravid conducted a 2022 meta-analysis that combined the results of studies involving more than 23,000 subjects in laboratory experiments and workplace settings, including workers in call centers and offices and police on patrol. Taken together, the studies found no correlation between levels of monitoring and employee performance.
That’s partly because some employees find workarounds to monitoring, even if that means tapping their keyboard periodically while they’re reading a book at lunch. “People are incredibly creative and adaptable, and they’ll find ways to reassert their freedom when it’s threatened or taken away,” Ravid says.
Ravid’s meta-analysis found that any type of monitoring — subtle or obvious, incidental or invasive — tended to increase workplace stress. “I think anything that undermines a sense of dignity is also going to undermine employee attitudes,” he says.
A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada underscored the potential downsides of monitoring: Employees who perceived that they were being surveilled on the job reported that they felt more pressure and stress and less autonomy and privacy at work.
In an age of “datafication,” it’s not surprising that companies would look for new metrics to evaluate employees, says Kirstie Ball, a management researcher at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “The systematic gathering of data about people and what they’re doing is part and parcel of modernity,” she says. “Surveillance becomes a means of getting things done.”
But not every company knows how to make good use of all those data points, Ball says. “There are many pitfalls along the way. Are you measuring what you think you’re measuring? Are you interpreting the data correctly according to the purpose that you gathered it, or are you looking at it just because you can?”
Employee surveillance without any coherent plan to use the data has become a commonplace scenario in modern companies, König says. Many workplaces end up collecting data simply because they have the technology, not because surveillance supports the company’s overall business strategy. “They end up with terabytes of data on a drive somewhere but don’t know what to do with it.”
“There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance.” —Daniel Ravid, University of New Mexico
Modern surveillance is an inherently electronic exercise, but companies can’t just install an app and expect results, Ravid says. “If managers think that they have a perfect way to measure performance because they have advanced technologies, they’re wrong,” he says. “They still need human insight and conversations to contextualize that data.”
Laws protecting employees from overly invasive surveillance generally haven’t kept pace with technology, says Molè, who wrote the 2026 book Monitored at Work. While the European Union has strong employee privacy laws, with additional legal protections in nations like Italy, Spain, France and Germany, workers in the US have far fewer safeguards and are more likely to be placed under a microscope.
In 2023, three current or former Amazon delivery drivers in Colorado filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon claiming that they were under excessive AI-assisted surveillance and that delivery quotas made it difficult to take necessary breaks. “The drivers were forced to pee in bottles,” Molè says. “This is not happening in Europe.” Amazon called for arbitration, noting that drivers work directly for outside delivery service providers who have contracts with the multitrillion-dollar company, not Amazon itself. The case is ongoing.
Other legal issues can lurk in the fine print that comes with monitoring software. Bosses who download monitoring apps they can’t customize are essentially letting outside companies take control of their employees’ data with little oversight or knowledge of how the data could be used. “We need more labor laws that target providers of technologies,” Molè says. Surveillance companies should be required to work directly with companies and their employees to clearly explain the technologies and tailor each product to meet specific needs and reach specific goals, he says.
Theoretically, monitoring could be a part of a healthy company culture that encourages success, Molè says. “People under monitoring should have a sense of being valued, and the monitoring should be truly meaningful for improving everyone’s working conditions and methods,” he says. “Good monitoring is based on mutual trust.” Companies that thoughtfully build their own system for tracking employee outputs instead of superimposing some “creepy and odd” tool found online are more likely to see actual benefits, he adds.
Success is certainly possible. Headbands that track brainwaves may seem invasive, but an Australian mining company found that such technology helped reduce fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. A 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork found that the productivity of top-performing workers dropped nearly 20 percent after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software without explanation, suggesting that the software had some benefits.
But productivity didn’t fall when that high-performing group was told they had the opportunity to go without supervision because of their impressive output, underscoring the importance of good management — leading the researchers to conclude that spending money on good managers could yield better results than spending it on monitoring software.
Transparency can go a long way to improving workplace culture, Ravid says. His meta-analysis found that, compared with workers who are surveilled without much explanation or consent, workers who have a clear understanding of how they are being monitored and how the data will be used also have a greater sense of fairness and job satisfaction.
New technologies will continue to join the ranks of Burger King’s Patty and other monitoring devices in the modern workforce. But if companies don’t change their basic approach, the results will likely be the be the same: suspicion and confusion for employees and few tangible benefits for employers.
This article originally appeared in Knowable Magazine, an independent journalistic endeavor from Annual Reviews. Sign up for the newsletter.

Putin spends nearly 25 million euros an hour on war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:28:35 KST

Russia’s federal budget spending on the war in Ukraine reached a historic high between January and June 2026. The aggressor state spent 10.687 trillion rubles (106.28 billion euros) on military needs and weapons production, Dialog.ua reports.
The figures were published by Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, following a review of data from the Russian Ministry of Finance.
Compared with the first half of 2025, Russia’s military spending increased by 30%, with an additional 2.46 trillion rubles (24.5 billion euros) spent.
Compared with January–June 2024, expenditure increased by 65%, or 4.211 trillion rubles (42.1 billion euros). Compared with 2023, the increase amounted to 145%, while spending was 285% higher than in the first year of the full-scale war.
Compared with the pre-war year of 2021, Russia’s military spending has increased more than fivefold. On average, Russia’s military machine cost the state budget 1.78 trillion rubles (17.7 billion euros) per month.
That amounts to approximately 59 billion rubles (587 million euros) per day,
or around 2.5 billion rubles (24.9 million euros) per hour.
Almost half of all Russian state budget expenditure is now devoted to military needs. During the first six months of the year, 43.8% of all budget expenditure was spent on the military and weapons production, marking a new all-time high.
Most of Russia’s current military spending is hidden from the public. Around two-thirds of the military budget is classified. In the first six months of 2026, Russia spent 3.546 trillion rubles (35.25 billion euros) on publicly disclosed defence items, while another 7.141 trillion rubles (71 billion euros) was spent under classified budget items.
Classified expenditure is growing particularly rapidly. Compared with last year, such spending has increased by 42% and is now more than seven times higher than before the war.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian authorities have allocated 57.144 trillion rubles (567.6 billion euros) to military spending and weapons procurement.

Harry and Meghan, who returned to the UK from the US two weeks ago, had insufficient time to clarify any points before details were issued to the media, it is understood.
The letter, the first official public clarification of the couple’s status since their return, was issued by Buckingham Palace’s most senior officer, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon.
It was revealed to the media at 3.06pm on Monday. It is understood the contents were shared with Harry and Meghan’s team almost an hour before at 1.59pm, who sent a response back to Buckingham Palace at 2.19pm asking whether the guidance had already gone out, in the hope of letting the couple know before the media, and for the team to have the chance to clarify one or two points.
Harry was in a meeting and could not be contacted until 3.09pm. The Sussexes’ team received confirmation at 3.11pm it had already been sent to the media.
The letter was revealed before a reported meeting this week of the executive committee for the protection of royalty and public figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security.
Harry is waiting to hear the conclusion of the risk management board’s threat assessment and Ravec is expected to decide at the meeting whether the Sussexes are entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK. The Home Office does not comment on such decision making and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.
Lord Benyon’s letter reiterates the couple’s “current” status as non-working royals. “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.
“Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used.
It says their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity”.
“In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
The letter says questions from official and state organisations about the courtesies extended to the couple, “and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required”, should be directed to Buckingham Palace, adding: “Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities.”
The couple’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are expected to be starting school in the UK near to the family’s reported countryside retreat.

Mamdani Expected to Announce Release of 9/11-Related Documents
Unknown

2026-09-08
11:26:35 UTC
20:26:35 KST

As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York City approaches, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has directed the public release of a trove of documents related to the tragedy.
Mamdani is reportedly set to address the release of the pages on Tuesday. The documents look into the city's investigation into air quality in Lower Manhattan following the attacks on the World Trade Center. In June, the mayor allocated $34.2 million of the city’s $126-billion budget for the 2027 fiscal year to create a public portal of these documents.
“So many of these New Yorkers are ones who made the decision to run towards Ground Zero,” Mamdani told CBS News last week. “And for that, they have suffered medically, and the city should be there for them.”
The New York Times, which had early access to the documents and also reported that the first batch will be released Tuesday, said the trove includes “air quality reports, contamination records, and correspondence among city officials.” Some of the pages were among the documents reportedly found in 68 boxes stashed in a city office, which advocates argue had been kept away from the public for years.
While the Times said that the documents offer only a smattering of reports taken around ground zero and many are “presumably absent,” the so-called Harding memo from 2001, which reportedly displayed city leaders preparing for potential liability to thousands of residents over their claims of toxic air, is believed to be among the pages.
A spokesperson for the mayor told NY1 in July that the portal is expected to host millions of documents, and the mayor’s office has said that additional documents will be added on a rolling basis.
TIME has reached out to Mayor Mamdani’s office for comment.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed on 9/11, but more people are believed to have been killed by diseases related to the attack. The World Trade Center Health Program, which provides no-cost monitoring and treatment for covered 9/11-related health conditions, said thousands continue to be diagnosed with ailments resulting from their exposure to dust, smoke, debris, and the traumatic events.
The city’s Fire Department released a report on Sept. 1 detailing the lasting effects of the 9/11 tragedy on first responders. More than 12,000 FDNY members have been diagnosed and certified with at least one related physical or mental health condition, including cancers, according to the report.
What do we know about the content of the documents?
The documents the Times obtained reportedly included records related to 15 John Street, near the collapsed World Trade Center, which purportedly detected asbestos—at times exceeding acceptable limits—about a year after the attack.
Among the pages was also an audit from November 2001, submitted to the federal Environmental Protection Agency, which reportedly showed high concentrations of benzene, a cancer-causing substance, in the air near the towers.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said that exposure to these contaminants increases the risk of developing health conditions, such as illnesses concerning the airways and digestive systems. The CDC added that after the attacks, around 400,000 people were exposed to these contaminants and other factors that increased their risk for such conditions.
Why Mamdani is under pressure
The release of the documents coincides with Mamdani drawing calls from families of victims of the tragedy and some Republican politicians not to attend the 9/11 remembrance event in New York City on Friday.
In July, 9/11 widower Giovanni Galante began a petition against Mamdani’s attendance, citing concerns over “Mamdani's public positions, associations, and responses to rhetoric that many perceive as hostile.” The petition cites Mamdani’s refusal to condemn those who say “globalize the intifada” as one of the issues. The petition also references Mamdani’s appointment of Ramzi Kassem, who worked for the Biden Administration, as chief counsel to the mayor. Kassem served as legal counsel for Ahmed al-Darbi, who plead guilty to charges stemming from a 2002 al-Qaeda tanker bombing plot and who is the brother-in-law of one of the hijackers in the plane that crashed into the Pentagon.
Former New York Gov. George Pataki told a local CBS affiliate on Thursday that Mamdani should first reject Hasan Piker, who previously earned public ire over a comment that the U.S. “deserved” the attack. Mamdani has already denounced Piker’s comment.
Rudy Giuliani, who was the mayor of New York in 2001, told right-leaning news organization Newsmax that Mamdani should skip the event. “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he's coming,” Giuliani said. The former mayor also attacked Mamdani’s religion, Islam, and baselessly suggested the mayor was supportive of Muslim extremist ideology.
Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor who was nine years old when the attack happened, has long faced Islamophobic comments. Speaking to the Times last year, Mamdani lamented how the 2001 attacks had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim-Americans, claiming: “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other.’”
Before Giuliani’s comments, Mamdani signed city executive orders designating Sept. 11 a New York-wide "Day of Remembrance and Service" and updating emergency preparedness procedures. But the signing caught the ire of some critics after Mamdani handed the 9/11 ceremonial pen to Kassem.
Despite the pushback, Mamdani still plans to attend the commemoration on Friday.
“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city,” Mamdani said. “I love this city. I love this country. And what I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers.”

Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:25:11 UTC
20:25:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of heat, rain and endless displacement
Displaced Palestinian people in the war-torn coastal enclave of the Gaza Strip are find it exceedingly hard to afford new tents or maintain their old ones after nearly three years of an Israeli genocide.
Thousands of displaced families remain in tents and makeshift shelters, many of which were intended to provide temporary refuge but have become their only homes.
When Israel's genocidal war began in 2023, Hanaa al-Soltan, 44, left northern Gaza carrying clothes, documents and a few belongings for her children, believing the family would return home within days or weeks. Nearly three years later, she remains displaced in a tent in central Gaza.
"At first, we said it would only be a few days or weeks. Then the first winter came, followed by summer, then another winter, and we're still here," she told The New Arab.
The summer heat is particularly difficult for the family. Under direct sunlight, the tarpaulin heats rapidly, turning the tent into an oven, while limited ventilation offers little relief.
"At midday, the children can't stay inside. We go out looking for shade and return when the sun becomes weaker. Sometimes I feel like we're living in an oven," she said.
But when summer ends, the damage it leaves behind becomes a threat. Months of exposure to heat and wind weaken the tarpaulin, leaving holes and cracks through which rainwater and cold air enter.
"When it rains, we put pots and pans under the holes and lift the mattresses off the ground. We sleep watching the water instead of sleeping," she said.
Unable to afford a new shelter, Hanaa buys used plastic sheets and attaches them to the damaged sections.
"We're no longer looking for a house. We just want a tarpaulin that will last us," she added.
Little protection
Hanaa's experience is shared by thousands of displaced families who have spent years moving from one location to another in search of safety, only to find themselves trapped in increasingly fragile shelters.
Mahmoud al-Arja, 39, moved several times with his wife and six children before settling in a tent in the al-Mawasi area in Khan Younis City in southern Gaza. Since the beginning of the war, he has bought three tents and repaired each of them repeatedly.
"The tarpaulin traps the heat. We open the sides and lift the cover, but the sun comes in from everywhere. The children sweat all the time and can't sleep," he told TNA.
The prolonged exposure to sunlight has weakened the material.
"The sun eats away at the tent. You buy one thinking it will protect you, but after a while, you discover its edges are starting to tear," he said.
When winter arrives, those damaged sections become entry points for rain and wind. Al-Arja uses plastic sheets, blankets and old clothes to seal the gaps before storms arrive.
"In winter, we fear the rain and wind. When water gets into the tent, there's nowhere else to take the children," he said.
The cost of keeping the shelter standing has also become a burden. Families need poles, ropes, plastic sheets and other materials, many of which have become increasingly expensive.
"We're not buying a tent; we're buying extra time," al-Arja added. "Work has stopped, income has stopped, but the expenses for the tent haven't."
Three years of trying to stay dry
Rasha Salama, a 36-year-old mother of three from Gaza City, could not afford a new tent for her four children, so she bought one that had been used by another family.
"I wasn't looking for a nice or new tent. I just wanted anything to give us a roof over our heads," she said.
During the summer, her children sleep drenched in sweat. Opening the tent from both sides provides some ventilation but exposes the family to dust, insects and direct sunlight.
"Some nights, the children want to sleep outside because it's too hot inside," she said.
Winter, however, brings greater anxiety.
"When it rains, the sand under the tent turns to mud, and water seeps in from several places. We lift the mattresses and pile things on top of each other, then wait for the rain to stop," she said.
Rasha keeps scraps of plastic and old fabric inside the tent for emergencies.
"Every piece has a purpose. This one's for patching a hole, this one's for under the mattresses, and this one's for when it rains," she said.
"We've been living like this for three years. The summer suffocates us, the winter terrifies us, and in between, we just try to keep the tent standing," she added.
Market built around survival
The prolonged displacement has created persistent demand for tarpaulins, ropes, wood and other shelter materials. But as families' incomes have collapsed, many can afford only the cheapest or second-hand options.
Abu Salah, a Gaza-based shelter-supplies vendor, told TNA that the market has changed dramatically during the war.
"At first, people would buy complete tents. Now, many just want a tarpaulin because they can't afford a whole set," he said.
Used tarpaulins have become increasingly common, while poles, wood and ropes are salvaged from damaged or abandoned shelters.
"There are families who ask for the cheapest thing available. Even if the tent has a hole, they say they will repair it themselves," he added.
Political analyst Akram Atallah believes the continued reliance on tents nearly three years into the war cannot be separated from the broader political and reconstruction crisis.
"The transformation of the tent from a temporary solution into a dwelling for years reflects the absence of any real prospect for reconstruction and places residents before a new form of daily depletion," Atallah told TNA.
Restrictions on building materials and shelter supplies, he said, delay reconstruction while leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians vulnerable to weather, poverty and disease.
"The continuation of these conditions deepens the disintegration of life," he added.

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:24:45 CEST
20:24:45 KST

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Nearly three-quarters of Poles (73 percent) use social media networks, driven by a 95 percent adoption rate among young adults, though older generations are far more likely to trust online information and share personal content, a new survey has shown.
The study by the Market and Social Research Institute (IBRiS), commissioned by PAP, found that Facebook remains Poland's most popular service (53 percent), followed by Instagram (31 percent), TikTok (25 percent), and X at 18 percent.
Despite younger generations dominating overall numbers, IBRiS report author Marcin Duma told PAP that older users are far more likely to share their daily lives online and believe the information they find there, whereas younger users exhibit a strong "digital detachment".
Social media adoption stands at 95 percent among adults aged 18–29 but drops to 39 percent for those over 70. Generation Z heavily distrusts online content, viewing it as commercial self-promotion. They form a "silent majority" that rarely posts and strongly guards privacy, Duma said. Older users willingly share personal everyday updates, making them more vulnerable to scams by mistaking commercial content for credible news.
Furthermore, digital confidence shapes threat perceptions. While 85 percent of all Poles have encountered online scams, only 65 percent of young adults view artificial intelligence (AI) fraud as "very dangerous", compared to around 89 percent of older users.
Social media usage also varies sharply by political electorate. Left-wing Razem voters (88 percent) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) supporters (85 percent) boast the highest presence. The high digital presence of Grzegorz Braun's party is surprising because his voters are mostly lower-income, less-educated, and live in rural areas - groups that usually use the internet less. However, Braun's exclusion from mainstream media forced highly effective, targeted online campaigns.
Supporters of the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) and centre-right Development Plus sit at the bottom with just 56 percent usage due to older voter profiles. Meanwhile, the ruling Civic Coalition (KO) maintains high usage despite an older demographic, driven by higher education and urban residency.
A sweeping 81 percent of all respondents demand stricter state cybersecurity regulations, viewing it as a priority or vital issue. Only 4 percent believe current laws are sufficient. This legislative push is highest among Development Plus (97 percent) and KO (94 percent) loyalists, while far-right Confederation voters remain the most sceptical of state intervention (62 percent).
The data is based on an IBRiS survey conducted between August 29 and 30, 2026, across a representative sample of over 1,000 adult Polish residents. (PAP)

Polish presidential couple join National Reading campaign
Poland's President Karol Nawrocki and First Lady Marta Nawrocka joined this year's National Reading, an initiative promoting Polish literature, held at the Adam Mickiewicz monument on Krakowskie Przedmiescie Street, in Warsaw, at noon on Saturday.
This year's chosen text is Forefathers' Eve (Dziady), a landmark work by Mickiewicz, considered Poland's national poet and a leading figure of European Romanticism whose work transformed Polish literary language.
Inaugurating the annual event, Nawrocki said that literature possesses the power to preserve and transmit Polish national identity across generations, to carry it despite the 19th-century partitions or the 20th-century occupations.
"Literature has the power to carry Polishness across the borders of all Europe and the entire world," Nawrocki stated.
Referring to the importance of this year's chosen text, Nawrocki said that there is no Polish literature without Adam Mickiewicz's legacy.
"He remains a fundamental, pivotal figure for understanding the Polish soul and Polish national identity," Nawrocki said.
He also announced that Joseph Conrad's novel Lord Jim had been selected as next year's National Reading featured text.
Forefathers' Eve is a four-part dramatic work composed between 1820 and 1832. The drama's title refers to an ancient Slavic and Lithuanian ritual commemorating the dead. This is a major work of Polish literature, and it is one that elevates Mickiewicz to a position among the "great Europeans" such as Dante and Goethe.
The National Reading campaign was launched in 2012 with a joint reading of Pan Tadeusz by Mickiewicz. Past editions featured pieces by other major Polish writers, including Nobel laureate Henryk Sienkiewicz, novelist Boleslaw Prus and playwright Stanislaw Wyspianski. (PAP)

China’s highest court sets out new AI red lines with rules on deepfakes and privacy
New guidelines provide a broader legal framework for everything from privacy breaches and sexual content to fraud and consumer protection
Although Beijing has yet to pass a dedicated AI law, the guidelines expand the country’s legal framework governing the technology.
The Supreme People’s Court’s 24-article opinion, released on Monday, instead provides guidance for handling AI-related disputes under existing laws, including the Civil Code, Cybersecurity Law, Copyright Law and Personal Information Protection Law.

The court said this could infringe legal protections covering aspects of a person’s identity and elements such as their image, voice and reputation.

EU court rules in favor of Ikea against Belgian far-right party

A far-right attempt at political parody was dismantled by a European court like an old Billy bookcase.
Flemish party Vlaams Belang’s anti-immigration campaign spoofing Ikea’s assembly instructions “may cause significant detriment” to the furniture-maker’s reputation, the Court of Justice of the European Union said in a ruling Tuesday.
In 2022, Vlaams Belang presented its “IKEA-Plan”, standing for “Immigratie Kan Echt Anders” or “Immigration can really be different.” Proposals to reform Belgium’s immigration policy were illustrated with the Swedish giant’s blue-and-yellow logo and the smiley characters found in its instruction sheets. “We do not wish our brand to be used to suggest that we support certain positions when we do not,” an Ikea spokesperson said at the time.
Advertisement
The firm sued Vlaams Belang in Belgium in November 2022, alleging trademark law infringement. The Belgian business court then asked the CJEU for its advice on how to strike the balance between freedom of expression and the right of a business to defend its trademark.
“It does not appear that the use of the Ikea trade marks for the sole purpose of taking advantage of their reputation to reinforce a political message … takes precedence over the rights and interests” of the Swedish brand, the CJEU said in its press release about the verdict.
The fact that Vlaams Belang’s campaign was completely unrelated to Ikea’s business — and that people may have believed that the company had endorsed it — weighed into the ruling, said Elena Izyumenko, assistant professor in intellectual property law at Amsterdam’s Institute for Information Law.
“What the court suggests is that a private company can suppress controversial political expression if it can create any impression of a link between the company and the opinion expressed in the parody,” Izyumenko said.
The case will now return to the Belgian court, which will rely on the CJEU’s interpretation of the law to issue its ruling. Looking at the CJEU’s ruling, “It’s almost obvious that it will rule against Vlaams Belang,” Izyumenko said.
“The non-profit organization Vrijheidsfonds of Vlaams Belang takes note of the ruling of the European Court of Justice and will thoroughly examine its scope in the context of further legal proceedings,” a spokesperson for the party said.
Ikea did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

US seeks more access to Venezuela's mineral wealth after tapping its oil, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:12:22 UTC
20:12:22 KST

US seeks more access to Venezuela's mineral wealth after tapping its oil, sources say
Sept 8 - The Trump administration is seeking greater U.S. access to Venezuela's minerals, including gold, as it expands its push to gain control and influence over the South American country's vast natural resources beyond oil, according to three sources familiar with the discussions.
The effort could open the Venezuelan mining sector to U.S. investment and give U.S. companies access to not only oil, but supplies of minerals crucial for national security, the sources said on condition of anonymity.
It also would expand President Donald Trump's push to more closely align Venezuela's resources with Washington's strategic and economic interests in the wake of the U.S. military's ouster of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in a raid in January.
The Trump administration is considering a range of steps to increase U.S. involvement in Venezuela's mining sector, including a possible executive order focused on critical minerals, the sources said. The order is still being drafted and the administration's strategy to secure minerals in Venezuela could yet change, they added.
U.S. officials have also held meetings with companies to gauge interest in investing in or otherwise participating in Venezuela's mining sector, the sources said.
"We are all watching the oil situation closely and recognize there could be a parallel track with critical minerals," said one of the sources, an executive from a critical minerals firm who met with the administration about Venezuela.
Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said the U.S. and Venezuela are "benefiting from renewed cooperation between our governments and new investments by Western companies in Venezuela’s key industries."
A White House official told Reuters that there is no current need for an executive order, adding the administration believes current laws provide a solid framework for investment.
The effort fits into Trump's broader strategy of reasserting U.S. influence across Latin America and pushing back against China's expanding economic footprint in the region.
Maduro, a socialist who is being held in a federal jail in New York City on charges of drug trafficking, which he denies, had developed strong economic and diplomatic ties with China. Maduro's vice president and ally, Delcy Rodriguez, has pivoted and increased cooperation with the U.S. since becoming Venezuela's interim president after his ouster.
With its enormous oil reserves and potentially significant deposits of gold and other minerals, Venezuela offers the Trump administration an opportunity to tie resource access to its national security and economic agenda.
The administration has already taken steps to open Venezuela's minerals sector to U.S. business.
In March, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control authorized certain transactions involving Venezuelan-origin gold, including activities tied to state-owned gold miner Minerven. Later that month, Treasury broadened the authorization to cover Venezuelan-origin minerals, including gold, while allowing some mining-related services and negotiations of potential investment contracts.
The moves have created a framework for U.S. companies to pursue opportunities in Venezuela's mining sector as the administration seeks to revive investment while expanding U.S. sway over the country's oil industry.
Trump already has moved aggressively to reshape Venezuela's oil industry. Last week, he announced a deal under which the U.S. would take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves, although the precise legal structure of that arrangement has not been disclosed.
There are, however, fears within Venezuela that Trump is turning the country into a modern-day colony.
FURTHER STUDY OF MINERAL RESOURCES NEEDED
Venezuela's mineral potential remains difficult to assess because much of its geological data is outdated and illegal groups control gold deposits in the Orinoco Mining Arc, a vast area near the country's borders with Guyana and Brazil.
While Venezuela has produced gold, iron ore, bauxite and nickel, mining companies and investors are likely to seek updated geological studies before making significant new investments, analysts have said, given the uncertainty surrounding its mineral estimates, weak infrastructure and pervasive illegal mining.
In 2012, Venezuelan officials declined to renew Anglo American's mining concession for the Loma de Niquel nickel mine, which at the time was estimated to hold reserves of more than 4 million metric tons of the metal. The Venezuelan government took control of the assets and has been trying to resume operations ever since.
A 2018 Venezuelan government report estimated the country's resources at 644 metric tons of gold, 14.68 billion metric tons of iron ore, 321.5 million metric tons of bauxite and 407,885 metric tons of nickel. But the report used terms such as "reserve" and "resource" interchangeably, making it difficult to determine how much could be economically extracted.
A 2021 Venezuelan government map, based on data compiled in 2009, identified deposits of numerous other minerals, including copper, nickel, coltan, uranium and tungsten, but did not provide volumes.
The country does not appear to have sizeable reserves of rare earths, which are used in magnets and other advanced technologies.
Venezuelan lawmakers in April unanimously approved a mining law aimed at spurring new investment. It dictated that mineral deposits remain the property of the government and set a royalty tax of up to 13% of the gross production value of a mineral. REUTERS

Four new categories of claims have been launched in Diia for the international Register of Damage

Ukrainians can submit claims through Diia concerning the loss of access to healthcare and education, as well as other international and economic losses.
An application to the International Register of Damage through "Diia" can now be submitted under four more categories related to access to healthcare and economic losses. This was reported by the State Enterprise "Diia," writes UNN.
We are launching four categories of applications to the international Register of Damage on the "Diia" portal. Ukrainians can now document losses related to access to healthcare and education, other violations of international law, and economic losses
Which categories are available:
-  A4.1 “Loss of access to medical care,” for example, if it was impossible to receive necessary treatment or undergo surgery for an extended period due to the destruction of a hospital, the absence of medical personnel, or the inability to reach a
medical facility; 
-  A4.2 “Loss of access to education” – due to damage to an educational institution,
occupation, danger to life, or the lack of an opportunity to study remotely; 
-  A2.10 “Other violations of international law” – for cases that are not
covered by other categories. For example, restrictions on access to humanitarian
aid, water, heating, or electricity, coercion to obtain Russian citizenship, the use of civilians as “human shields,” and others; 
-  A3.7 “Other economic losses” for economic losses that do not fall
under other categories of the Register. In particular, the loss of financial support due to the death or disappearance of a close relative, expenses for medical treatment or burial, the loss of valuable movable property or the assets of an individual entrepreneur, and others. 
To submit an application, you need to log in to the "Diia" portal, select the relevant category, complete the application, and attach the available evidence. After signing it, the application can be sent to the Register of Damage.

Britain’s government on Sept. 8 announced sanctions on trade from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, a minister has indicated, sparking an angry backlash from Israel and the United States.
The move would signal a toughening of the U.K.’s stance on Israel under new Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who entered Downing Street in July after Keir Starmer stepped down.
But it immediately caused friction with allies the U.S. and Israel, with America’s ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee calling the decision “irrational” and Israel threatening retaliatory action.
Huckabee told BBC , “I think without a doubt there will be” a reaction, including at the level of individual states in the U.S.
This could have a “huge economic impact on British businesses,” he said, explaining some could be banned from doing business in certain states.
The move follows weeks of increasing attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the illegally occupied territory that some western governments fear threatens the two-state solution.
Government minister Pat McFadden said Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband would make a statement to parliament laying out “measures specifically targeted at the expansion of these settlements, which are illegal under international law in the West Bank.”
He told Sky News that the changes, on which he provided no further detail, would be motivated by “the idea of keeping alive this possibility of seeing a Palestinian state alongside Israel.”
“I think it’s also important to say that Israel is an important trading partner for the U.K. This isn’t intended to be a boycott of all Israeli goods,” McFadden added.
U.K. government ministers have suggested recently that goods coming out of the illegal settlements could be subject to trade restrictions as part of the changes.
Trade between the U.K. and the Occupied Palestinian Territories was around only $51 million in 2025, according to the government, implying the move could be largely symbolic.
Critics have also said it could be difficult to distinguish goods from the West Bank from those from the rest of Israel.
Miliband, son of Jewish refugees to Britain, vowed last week to announce a “comprehensive” reset of policy towards Israel.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who leads a far-right party that advocates the annexation of the entire West Bank, called for the expulsion of Britain’s ambassador to Israel.
And Israeli President Isaac Herzog said the sanctions would “fall on the wrong side of history.”

Nicaragua accuses Germany at UN court of enabling Gaza genocide through arms sales to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:09:39 UTC
20:09:39 KST

Nicaragua accused Germany at the United Nations’ top court Tuesday of helping enable what it described as genocide in Gaza by continuing to supply weapons and other military support to Israel, AP reported.
The case before the International Court of Justice in The Hague argues that Berlin breached its obligations under the Genocide Convention by facilitating Israeli military operations in Gaza. Germany has rejected the allegations and asked the court to dismiss the case.
Nicaragua’s lead lawyer, Carlos José Argüello Gómez, argued that Germany’s close political, commercial and military ties with Israel meant it knew, or should have known, of what Managua says was a serious risk that genocide was being committed.
“It is impossible that with the type of political, commercial and military relations of Germany with Israel, they could not be aware, or normally should have been aware, of the serious risk that acts that could amount to genocide were being committed by Israel,” he told the judges.
Israel is not a party to the proceedings and strongly denies that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. The war began after Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
Germany has long been one of Israel’s strongest international supporters and is its second-largest arms supplier after the United States.
The current hearings are focused on whether the ICJ has jurisdiction to consider Nicaragua’s case. Germany told the court Monday that Managua had not properly attempted to resolve the dispute before bringing the matter before the judges.
“Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court,” Germany’s lead lawyer, Julia Monar, said.
Nicaragua rejected that argument, pointing to communications sent to the German Foreign Ministry and public statements it says demonstrated that a dispute already existed.
The case is one of several international legal proceedings tied to the Gaza war. South Africa separately brought a genocide case against Israel at the ICJ in 2023.
A ruling on jurisdiction is expected later this year. If the court allows Nicaragua’s case against Germany to proceed, a final judgment could take years.

Cambodia records 163 rare vultures in 2025 census, 10-year high: official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:03:17 CST
20:03:17 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's critically endangered vulture population has reached a 10-year high, with 163 individuals recorded in the latest 2025 census, an environment official said on Tuesday.
"The figures represent a 22 percent increase from the 2024 count, marking the highest annual population recorded since 2016," Khvay Atitya, an undersecretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Environment, told Xinhua.
Cambodia is home to three vulture species: the red-headed (Sarcogyps calvus), white-rumped (Gyps bengalensis), and slender-billed (Gyps tenuirostris) vulture. All three are listed as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
Atitya said that the population rebound reflects successful collaboration between government agencies and NGO partners to protect habitats and implement targeted conservation policies.
He said that to support the population, conservationists routinely protect vulture nests and run "vulture restaurants," periodically feeding the birds with dead domestic cattle. ■

Fourteen men go on trial in Paris over deadliest small-boat Channel crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:02:31 UTC
20:02:31 KST

Fourteen men will go on trial in Paris on Tuesday over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record.
The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.
Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.
The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead also included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.
A team on a French fishing boat near British waters off Calais had raised the alarm when they saw several lifeless bodies floating in the water.
According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes – between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England – began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.
Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived the tragedy.
Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.
Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia.
Among the defendants are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched.
Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.
Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators.
The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as people who were seeking to make the journey themselves.
However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain.
For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by the French fishing vessel.
A separate investigation is ongoing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel – who have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.
The UK’s Cranston inquiry, in its report released in February, found that systemic failings, missed opportunities and inadequate resourcing undermined the UK’s maritime search and rescue response on the night of the disaster. HM Coastguard was placed in an “intolerable position”, it said, with chronic staff shortages and limited operational capacity contributing directly to the failure to rescue people in the water.
It found the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard.
Families of some of the victims will travel from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said.
“Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” the lawyers, Matthieu Chirez, Thomas Ricard and Camille Renouard, said in a statement.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

EU to approve Ukraine's Patriot funding request on Sept. 11, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:02:04 UTC
20:02:04 KST

European Commission to approve Ukraine's Patriot funding request on Sept. 11, officials say
Editor's note: This article was updated to include information provided by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a social media post.
The European Commission is set to greenlight the final 28.3-billion-euro ($33-billion) tranche of this year's defense loans for Ukraine, including an approval for the purchase of U.S.-made Patriot missiles, on Sept. 11, EU and national diplomats confirmed to the Kyiv Independent.
The purchase concerns PAC-3 interceptors, a key tool for defending Ukraine's skies against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
The EU was expected to greenlight the request on Sept. 7, and Ukrainian public media Suspilne reported on that day that the decision had been made.
However, while member states have backed the request, one step remains before formal EU approval can be granted, the Kyiv Independent has learned after speaking with EU and national diplomats.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the agreement between EU countries in a social media post, later on Sept. 8.
"The next disbursement of 3.2 billion euros will enable Ukraine to better protect its skies from Russia’s indiscriminate attacks," von der Leyen said.
"We will continue to work hand in hand to support Ukraine and to strengthen Europe's defense posture."
The Commission still needs to write up the agreement and publish a communication for the approval to be final, which is expected on Sept. 11.
EU approval is required because the terms of the bloc's 90 billion-euro ($104-billion) support loan, from which the 28.3-billion-euro tranche is drawn, impose restrictions on purchasing products from outside the EU, Ukraine, or Norway.
The terms specify that the loan must be spent on materiel that sources 65% of its components from the countries listed above. Products that do not fit this criterion must be granted an exception.
The EU has already approved one such exception for Chinese drone components in April 2026.
The request for a derogation to buy U.S. Patriot missiles was submitted by then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov just before he was fired by President Volodymyr Zelensky on July 15.
However, an approval to buy Patriot missiles is not the same thing as Ukraine actually having new interceptors. There is a global shortage of such missiles, and the Freyja interceptor system, which Ukraine and its European partners are developing, is expected to begin live tests only in mid-2027.
The European Commission's approval of the request to buy Patriots is also expected to greenlight roughly 6 billion euros ($7 billion) in Ukrainian defense spending plans.
That would mean the full 28.3 billion euros of planned spending has been approved.
However, Ukraine has received only about 8.4 billion euros ($9.8 billion) of the total because of delays in providing the specific invoices and receipts for the purchases, which the EU must cross-check to ensure the money is spent as planned.
Von der Leyen's social media post mentions that the next disbursement of 3.2 billion euros ($3.7 billion) is set to be delivered.

Ukrposhta has already begun preparing its clearance system for the new U.S. requirements, according to the company's statement.

"Our main task is to make sure that any changes to international rules go unnoticed by Ukrainian sellers. 200,000 parcels sent to the U.S. under the new rules shows the resilience of our business, the effective work of the Ukrposhta team, and support for the country's economy during the war," Ukrposhta CEO Igor Smelyansky said, according to the release.
Delivery to the U.S. takes from seven days, with the PRIME tariff for international shipments starting at $6, the company said.
Smelyansky had earlier said on Telegram that Ukrainians made 50,000 shipments through Ukrposhta under new EU customs rules that took effect July 1, with the largest number sent to Germany, France and Poland.
The national postal operator had not seen a drop in parcel shipment volumes from Ukraine following the EU's new rules introduced in July, which impose a EUR 3 duty on parcels worth up to EUR 150, Smelyansky told Interfax-Ukraine at the time.
That measure is temporary and will remain in effect until July 1, 2028, pending the launch of the EU Customs Data Hub and the introduction of permanent tariff rates, it was noted at the time.

155 Russian Firms Supply Electronics for Iskander-M and Zircon Missiles, Half Still Escape Sanctions

- Category

155 Russian Firms Supply Electronics for Iskander-M and Zircon Missiles, Half Still Escape Sanctions
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has identified 155 Russian enterprises linked to the production of electronic components and technologies used across Russia’s weapons systems, including Iskander-M ballistic and Zircon hypersonic missiles.
HUR published information on the companies through its War & Sanctions portal, according to the agency on September 8. The enterprises are either part of or managed by Ruselectronics, a holding company within Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ruselectronics brings together industrial enterprises and research organizations specializing in electronic components and technologies, communications equipment, automated control systems, robotics, microwave electronics, computing systems, and telecommunications equipment.
According to HUR, products manufactured by companies within the holding are used across a wide range of Russian weapons, including ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, electronic warfare systems, military vehicles, radar and communications equipment, as well as systems used by tactical, operational, and strategic aviation.
Several Ruselectronics enterprises are directly involved in the production chain for Russia’s 9M723 ballistic missile used by the Iskander-M system and the 3M22 Zircon missile, HUR said.
Among them is the Girikond Research Institute, which produces precision potentiometers for Zircon missiles. NITSEVT supplies flight information processing units for Iskander ballistic missiles, while NPP Integral-V manufactures pulse and heating transformers used in 9M723 missiles.
HUR noted that NPP Integral-V remains outside the sanctions lists of all countries participating in the sanctions coalition. Nearly half of the 155 enterprises disclosed by Ukrainian intelligence are also not currently subject to sanctions.
At the same time, HUR said sanctions already imposed on other companies within the holding have had limited impact on the overall production volumes of the missiles. According to the agency, this does not indicate that sanctions are ineffective, but rather highlights the need to strengthen enforcement mechanisms and increase accountability for sanctions violations.
The disclosure comes as Russia continues to maintain substantial missile stockpiles while producing more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles per month, according to data provided by HUR to Ukrainska Pravda on August 20.
As of August 5, Russia had approximately 130 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system assigned to its military grouping. Its broader arsenal remains considerably larger, with HUR estimating stockpiles of more than 600 Oniks missiles, over 450 Kalibr cruise missiles, more than 120 Zircon hypersonic missiles, and up to 100 Kh-101 cruise missiles.

Russian-occupied nuclear plant ran on diesel for almost three weeks. Ukraine ended that, and the UN’s nuclear watchdog calls it a crucial step against an accident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:01:23 UTC
20:01:23 KST

Ukrainian power engineers restored the Ferosplavna-1 line and put the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) back on external electricity after almost three weeks, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom reported. The repairs took three days and were carried out during a local ceasefire brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN's nuclear watchdog.
The line is back, and the plant is drawing 11 MW
The plant's own needs were energized from the 330-kV Ferosplavna-1 overhead line on 7 September, Energoatom said. Consumption stood at 11 MW.
The work of Ukrainian power engineers and the agreed local ceasefire made the restoration possible, the company said. Ukrainian specialists reconnected the plant to Ukraine's unified power system under constant security risks and what the company called the unpredictable actions of Russian forces, according to Energoatom. It was the seventh local truce IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi has negotiated in this war, the IAEA said.
The plant can now power the pumps cooling its reactors and spent fuel again, along with its other safety systems, the IAEA said.
Almost three weeks on emergency generators
The ZNPP had been without external power since 20 August, Energoatom said. Its critically important systems ran on diesel generators throughout, a mode that created additional risks to nuclear and radiation safety at Europe's largest nuclear plant, the company said.
The plant lost Ferosplavna-1, its sole remaining power line, to military activity north of the Dnipro on 20 August, the IAEA said. The plant had been facing a possible station blackout as the diesel reserves for those generators diminished. The site had cut its running generators to two and begun cycling its cooling pumps to save fuel.

Sweden Adds HIMARS to NATO’s Northern Flank—and Wants Its Ammunition Made at Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:01:21 UTC
20:01:21 KST

- Category
- World
Sweden Adds HIMARS to NATO’s Northern Flank—and Wants Its Ammunition Made at Home
Sweden will acquire US-made HIMARS rocket artillery in a deal worth roughly $729 million, while simultaneously deepening cooperation with Finland and exploring domestic production of the long-range Precision Strike Missile, or PrSM.
The Swedish government announced the procurement on September 7, with the first Lockheed Martin-built systems expected to arrive in 2027.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The purchase will be financed through the Swedish Armed Forces’ investment plan and the country’s 2025-2030 defense program.
Swedish officials say HIMARS will give the army a long-range precision-strike capability it currently lacks, complementing its Archer self-propelled artillery and mortar systems while increasing interoperability with other NATO forces.
According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, the package covers slightly more than 10 HIMARS launchers along with a large quantity of GMLRS guided rockets. The government did not publicly disclose the exact number of launchers.
The acquisition also comes with a new Swedish-Finnish cooperation agreement covering rocket artillery.
Finland already operates the tracked M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System, which uses many of the same munitions and components as HIMARS. The two countries plan to cooperate on training, capability development, maintenance, production and security of supply.
For Sweden, that means access to expertise Finland has spent years developing around rocket artillery rather than having to build the entire operating concept from scratch.
Sweden’s HIMARS deal could also grow into something considerably bigger than an import program.
Saab and Lockheed Martin have signed a letter of intent covering potential integration of Saab’s Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb, or GLSDB, and expanded cooperation on ammunition production in Sweden.
SVT reported that the companies are also exploring Swedish production of PrSM, Lockheed Martin’s newest long-range precision-strike missile.
PrSM is being introduced as the successor to ATACMS and is designed for launch from both HIMARS and the tracked M270 system. Current versions can strike targets at roughly 500 kilometers, or about 310 miles, with future variants expected to extend that reach further.
A HIMARS launcher can carry two PrSM missiles at once, compared with one ATACMS, or alternatively carry a pod containing six GMLRS rockets.
Domestic PrSM production would therefore give Sweden not only a new long-range weapon but also greater control over the supply of some of the most sought-after precision munitions in NATO.
That issue has become increasingly important amid global shortages of rocket-artillery ammunition.
The Swedish government separately said Saab and Lockheed Martin are exploring broader ammunition production for HIMARS and other weapons systems, including Patriot air defense.
Sweden has not yet specified exactly which additional missile types could eventually be manufactured domestically.
Previously, reports emerged that American defense company Lockheed Martin and Germany’s Rheinmetall have agreed to establish the first production facility for ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles outside the United States, with manufacturing set to take place at Rheinmetall’s plant in Unterlüß, Germany.

Finnish pupils' Pisa results nosedive, but still above OECD average
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:53:58 EEST
19:53:58 KST

Finnish teenagers' performance has declined once again in the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) study. Scores fell in all three subjects measured: reading, mathematics and science.
Even so, Finnish students still performed above the OECD average from 91 countries in the results published on Tuesday.
Science was the main focus of this round of the Pisa study, and Finnish teenagers still performed above the OECD average in the subject.
The drop in Finnish teens' performances was found to be especially sharp in reading, with Finland ranking 17th in the latest standings. Things were much different at the turn of the millennium, when Finland ranked first in the world for reading in the initial PISA study.
The reasons behind the decline include less reading of printed books as well as dwindling perseverance.
Only 41 percent of Finnish pupils now say they try harder when a task feels difficult.
"This was the smallest share among the different countries," said Arto K. Ahonen, Finland’s national research director for the Pisa study.
School no longer the great equalizer
A new development evident from the Pisa results is that teens from wealthier families are now seeing the biggest decline. In the past, they performed the best.
This trend is not limited to Finland. Performance has also declined in other countries, with Asian countries being the exception.
"We used to think that perhaps a stronger family background supported pupils' skills so well that they would not decline. This time, that was no longer the case," Ahonen explained.
Differences in performance between schools in Finland remained small compared with the OECD average and were largely unchanged from the previous assessment. At the same time, the gap between students within individual schools has widened and is now considerably larger than the OECD average.
Girls perform better in reading and science, while boys and girls are fairly evenly matched in math.
While Finland's score did not fall by a statistically significant amount compared with the previous results from three years ago, a longer-term decline in performance is clear.
After reviewing the Pisa test results of thousands of 15-year-olds, Ahonen hopes the findings will finally draw attention to differences in pupils' skill levels.
"From an education policy perspective, the most important thing is to stop the gap between students' skills from widening," he said.
Pupils in Finland had an average science score of 504 points, well above the OECD average of 482.
The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is a triennial international study conducted by the OECD that evaluates the skills and knowledge of 15-year-old students. The 15-year-old students took part in the Pisa tests in spring 2025.
