Princess’s story: the case that highlights scourge of illegal care provision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:00:54 UTC
18:00:54 KST

Princess had a hard start in life. Her father drank too much, and referrals were made to social services. As she got older, she started going missing, telling police officers she was being physically abused by her parents, who in turn claimed they could not manage her behaviour. She was eventually taken into care amid concerns about self-harm, aggression and exploitation outside the home.
Even though social workers described her as a lovely child, they struggled to find her a permanent home capable of keeping her safe in England’s dysfunctional, largely outsourced residential care system.
Her social workers were left with no lawful options. Instead, they placed her in hastily cobbled-together illegal provision. Princess was sent to live in a series of unregulated placements, including 11 different Airbnbs or hotel rooms and two “barren and inhospitable” houses, for the best part of a year.
A safeguarding review last year found that the illegal homes could not meet her needs. She continued to self-harm and hurt staff. She sometimes lived in empty rooms, with as many as nine carers dressed in protective clothing. One police officer said: “If she lived with her parents and I came into this house, I’d be removing her for serious neglect.”
Shocking though Princess’s situation was, similar scenarios play out hundreds of times a year in children’s services departments throughout the country. According to the children’s commissioner for England, Rachel de Souza, these children are being endangered by the continued use of illegal care homes, which, an investigation by the Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) has found, have been paid £250m over the last two years by councils in England.
De Souza said: “My previous research has uncovered [Princess’s] story is far from an isolated case. This investigation continues to raise serious questions about the millions spent by local authorities on placements when they cannot guarantee that vulnerable children are receiving the safeguarding and quality of care they need.”
Councils are increasingly turning to illegal provision because the mainstream, profit-driven care market is failing to accommodate rising numbers of vulnerable teenagers, with registered homes often too far away or incapable of meeting their needs. This has generated a growing shadow market for unlawful care, where huge sums are paid for unregulated placements.
The safeguarding review into Princess’s case concluded she was harmed by the council’s failure to find a suitable placement for her. She told the review she hated her time in care and it made her issues worse.
A Guardian and TBIJ investigation has established that the companies staffing the illegal homes where Princess lived for almost a year were paid more than £1m by Peterborough city council. The companies were not named in the review.
Thornbury Nursing Services, which is based in Bristol, was paid £61,000 for staffing her unregistered placements. The company is ultimately owned by the Canadian private equity firm Onex via Acacium Group. Onex announced it had $275m available to distribute to shareholders in 2026.
Council payment records obtained as part of the investigation show Thornbury Nursing Services also received £3.8m from four councils for staffing five other illegal placements during 2024 and 2025.
Thornbury said it complied with all relevant laws. It said it supplied healthcare staff when there were limited options but did not operate children’s homes, adding: “Responsibility for accommodation and placement decisions sits with the relevant local authorities.”
Another agency, CAMHS Professionals, was paid more than £500m pounds for staffing Princess’s unregistered placements. It said it supplied a large team of qualified nurses at short notice to a home commissioned by Peterborough council. “CAMHS Professionals did not provide the home for this young person,” it said.
Peterborough council said it secured the properties but commissioned the companies to provide care and support for Princess. It said unregistered placements were only used when there were no regulated alternatives and were subject to monitoring visits.

I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren Edwards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
09:00:54 UTC
18:00:54 KST

I was elected to Westminster two years ago, when the country was crying out for change and looking to parliament to tackle the big issues that had been forgotten for too long. When that change didn’t come fast enough, trust in politics once again started to ebb away. We have one last chance to prove we can deliver on people’s priorities.
Assisted dying didn’t feature in the manifesto I was elected on. Nor should it have done. Matters of conscience such as this are rightly left to individual MPs to decide upon. There will always be a range of views within all political parties. But this issue has been supported by a substantial majority in the country for a very long time. Reputable independent polling has shown support for assisted dying consistently at about 75%. The latest British social attitudes survey from the National Centre for Social Research found that “it is clear we are observing a continued high level of public support for legal change to allow assisted dying in some circumstances”.
Having examined the issue with great care, MPs decided in the last session to support the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill. On the Labour benches there was a clear majority in favour, as there was on the Lib Dems’. The Greens supported it unanimously. It is the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper.
On Friday, I will be asking MPs to send the bill back to the Lords. There they can amend the bill if they choose, just like any legislation, and if the Commons agrees, that’s fine. But they should not be allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time.
I am not reopening divisions in the Labour party or in parliament, as some have claimed. Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions.
The voters put us here to tackle the big issues they care about, not to constantly kick them down the road. After a shaky start, this parliament has the chance to show that it can deliver; that we won’t shirk our responsibilities and will start to restore the public’s faith in our democratic system.
Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial. It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.
- 
  Lauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood and has reintroduced the terminally ill adults bill in parliament

The law on mandatory shelters has entered into force in Ukraine — what has changed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

18:00:50 KST

The law on mandatory shelters has entered into force in Ukraine — what has changed
Kyiv • UNN
Law No. 4778-IX strengthens civil protection and requires shelters to be planned for new facilities. Centers and classes for safety are also being established.
On Tuesday, September 8, a Law entered into force in Ukraine that strengthens civil protection requirements and provides for the mandatory construction of shelters in new residential, public, and infrastructure facilities. This was reported by UNN.
Details
Law No. 4778-IX was adopted back on February 10 of this year. It concerns amendments to certain legislative acts of Ukraine on preventing emergencies and eliminating their consequences, establishing a fund of civil protection protective structures, and creating safety classes and centers.
This regulatory legal act enshrines in law the concepts of "safety center," "safety class," and "protected space."
From now on, local self-government bodies will be able to establish safety centers for a comprehensive response to hazardous events. One such facility may simultaneously house a fire and rescue unit, an emergency medical care base, and a police station.
Special safety classes may also be established in educational institutions, where children will be taught fire safety and civil protection rules, as well as how to behave during emergencies, including those involving explosive objects.
In addition, the planning of civil protection protective structures and dual-purpose structures is now mandatory in urban planning documentation.
The law separately addresses the certification of emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services. It is conducted to verify their readiness to carry out emergency rescue and other urgent operations, extinguish fires, and obtain authorization to perform such work.
A specific feature of the certification of emergency and rescue services staffed with divers equipped with special gear for underwater operations is the preliminary certification of the diving units of those services to determine the list of underwater operations they are capable of performing. Emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services are subject to certification. Periodic certification of emergency and rescue services and rescuers is conducted at least once every five years. The certification of emergency and rescue services, rescuers, and Ukrainian citizens being hired by emergency and rescue services is conducted by an interagency certification commission established by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine. The regulations governing the interagency certification commission are approved by the central executive body responsible for formulating state policy in the field of civil protection

'Tirana teeth': Albania hopes to be the new Turkey for dental work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
10:00:28 BST
18:00:28 KST

'Tirana teeth': Albania hopes to be the new Turkey for dental work
- Published
Anthony Hook is sitting in a dentist's chair, grinning toothily into a handheld mirror. He has been asked to pose for photos showing off his new smile – and he is only too happy to oblige.
The 58-year-old window cleaner from Bolton, in Greater Manchester, is the proud owner of a sparkling new set of "Tirana teeth".
That is not a brand name – at least, not yet. But it would be a fitting slogan as Albania moves decisively into the medical tourism business.
Tirana, its capital city, is the focus of operations. And once you spot the first tooth, you start seeing them everywhere. They seem to be all over the city centre.
Rest assured, these are not the physical remains from a night out that ended in a punch up. Rather, they are the kind of larger than life-size illuminated molar that – in these parts at least – advertise that a dental clinic is not too far away.
In Tirana's metropolitan area alone, there are almost four hundred dental clinics – and most of them are in the city centre. That's more than enough for a population of around 600,000 people.
So, it is not surprising that dozens of dentists are now targeting customers from further afield. They have set up websites and signage in English and Italian, as well as Albanian.
Dental implants in Albania are typically around €600 ($700; £516) per tooth, similar in price to what is charged in Turkey, which has long been the main overseas destination for people in western Europe who are seeking much cheaper dental work than they can get at home.
The same treatment in the UK, France or German can easily cost four times as much.
For Hook the appeal was irresistible. He made his first visit to Tirana to watch England's footballers play Albania last year – but then found himself intrigued by all the signs for dentists. That nudged him into doing something about his missing teeth.
He thought he's give Albania rather than Turkey, because he was concerned by media coverage of dental or hair transplant work in Turkey that had gone wrong.
In fact, even the UK Foreign Office warns that it is "aware of seven British nationals having died in Turkey in 2025 following medical procedures"., external It adds that "some British nationals have also experienced complications [after surgery in Turkey], and needed further treatment or surgery following their procedure."
Hook says he wouldn't go to Turkey "because I have heard so many bad things", adding that he investigated thoroughly before taking the plunge in Tirana.
"I went onto the internet and looked into it properly. It took me two days to research it because I'm not one for jumping into anything."
Several return trips later, Anthony now has a mouthful of impressive implants – and, unsurprisingly, he is all smiles. "I'd come here once a month for a holiday if I could," he chuckles.
Elite Dental is one of the biggest clinics in Tirana. It is fully licensed by the Albanian health authorities – and so are all of its 15 resident dentists.
The man who runs the place, Ardtur Dema, says he is "not in favour of damaging proper teeth for aesthetics". Instead he says the priority is "changing people's lives" through restoring their ability to chew, and indeed – to smile.
Dema believes that as long as Albania remains outside the EU, prices for treatment are likely to remain low. At the same time, low-cost airlines have greatly expanded their flight network to and from Tirana, meaning that he is as likely to see a patient from Turin as he is from Tirana.
But Dema is concerned that the explosion of tourism could lead to less scrupulous operators ruining the business for everyone. He is a member of the newly-established Albanian Medical Tourism Association – but many others are not, at least not yet.
Albania's Prime Minister, Edi Rama, tells the BBC that the government is playing catch-up after five years that have seen overall international arrivals to Albania more than double. Some sort of official seal of approval for medical tourism facilities is a possibility – but the government has yet to sort out the details.
"It's a new industry that is within the tourism industry umbrella that is showing a big potential and where there are very good people," says Rama.
He adds that the government wants to help all the reputable providers "survive", and to guard against any informal "bad competition".
Along with dental treatments, some visitors to Albania are starting to think "hairline" as well as "coastline".
Some transplant clinics are employing Turkish specialists – others are actually branches of businesses based in Turkey.
Vatanmed, in Tirana, is one of the latter. Sales specialist and health consultant Ayşe Mina Kasemi describes the business as a "global brand", with 15 clinics across a number of countries. That scale, she suggests, makes it "a safe place to trust" for the international patients arriving for treatment.
Besides that, Ayşe notes, Albania has its own appeal.
"When people decide to have a hair transplant operation here in Albania, they also want to have a holiday here, because Albania is a very beautiful place," she says, while adding a note of caution for hair transplant patients. "For the first two or three days, they have to be careful – they are not allowed to be exposed to the sun."
That is not a factor that concerns Anthony Hook. He happily sports a shaven head – and has no intention of following his dental treatment with a radical rug rethink. So enjoying Albania's beaches and scenery was very much part of the attraction of getting his teeth fixed here.
"There's a lot to do in Tirana… there's a lot to do along the coast there, it's absolutely stunning," he says. "I want to do it now before it gets too popular and it's ruined like everywhere else."
With his new teeth, enjoying Albania's cuisine will doubtless also be part of Anthony's programme. Apart from anything else, that smile is going to dazzle in the holiday snaps.

From the airport to a new life: ynet Global Aliyah Summit answers biggest questions facing new olim | Live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:45:28 UTC
17:45:28 KST

The decision to make aliyah can take years. But once the ticket is booked and the suitcases are packed, questions about identity and belonging quickly give way to much more practical ones.
What do you do when you land? Which documents do you need? How do you choose a health fund, open a bank account, transfer money, find work or rent a home? And if something happens in the middle of the night, who do you call?
Today, September 8, ynet Global is holding its Global Aliyah Live Summit, a day of broadcasts devoted to answering those questions and helping prospective and newly arrived immigrants understand what life in Israel actually looks like after the plane lands.
Follow the live broadcasts and continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
The summit brings together senior public officials, Aliyah and absorption organizations, specialists in healthcare, banking, employment and housing, and new immigrants who are experiencing the process firsthand.
Broadcasts will be held in Russian, English and French, with coverage also appearing across ynet and ynet Global.
Today’s broadcast schedule, Israel time
13:00-14:00 — Live broadcast in Russian, in cooperation with Vesti
14:00-17:00 — Live broadcast in English on ynet Global and ynet
17:00-18:00 — Live broadcast in French on ynet Global
You landed in Israel. What happens next?
One of the summit’s central discussions focuses on the first 24 hours after aliyah, when months or years of planning suddenly become reality.
After the flight, the welcome and the first photo in Israel comes a new challenge: navigating a bureaucracy and public-service system that can be unfamiliar even to people who prepared extensively before arriving.
Which documents do new immigrants receive? What must be done immediately and what can wait? When should they register with a health fund, open a bank account or begin dealing with government offices? What benefits are available and how are they accessed?
Today’s summit brings those steps together, giving new immigrants a practical guide to the first days of building a life in Israel.
What should be done before the flight?
Some of the most important preparations begin before an oleh ever reaches Ben Gurion Airport.
The summit will address which documents should be brought to Israel, what arrangements should be made with banks overseas, what to do with savings and other assets abroad and when to begin looking for work.
New immigrants will also discuss the less technical side of leaving: saying goodbye to family and friends, leaving a job, packing a home and confronting the uncertainty of having to build a new routine in another country.
Money, banking and buying a home
Opening an Israeli bank account can raise questions that go far beyond simply choosing a branch.
A financial panel featuring experts and representatives including Bank Leumi and mortgage advisers will examine how newcomers should navigate the Israeli financial system.
Among the issues: transferring money from abroad, handling overseas income and assets, understanding Israel’s credit system, foreign currency and international transfer fees.
The summit will also look ahead to one of the largest financial decisions many olim eventually face: buying a home in Israel.
Mortgage advisers will discuss what new immigrants should know before entering the Israeli property market and what needs to be checked before taking out a mortgage.
Bringing your career to Israel
For many new immigrants, moving countries also means confronting the possibility of starting again professionally.
A doctor, engineer, teacher, executive, entrepreneur or tech professional may arrive with a decade or more of experience only to discover that the Israeli job market does not automatically recognize the career they built overseas.
Employment specialists taking part in the summit will discuss when to start searching for work, how to adapt a résumé for Israel, how to build a local professional network and which professions require Israeli licensing.
The sessions will also address entrepreneurship, retraining and starting a business.
The goal is not simply to help olim find their first Israeli job, but to help them preserve and use the skills and experience they already have.
Healthcare and the number every newcomer should know
Israel’s healthcare system can also require an adjustment for immigrants arriving from countries with very different models of medical care.
Representatives from Clalit Health Services will explain how to join a health fund, choose a doctor, make appointments and begin using the services available to new immigrants.
The summit will also cover medical emergencies.
A dedicated segment will explain what happens when someone calls Magen David Adom at **101**, what information dispatchers need and what newcomers should expect from Israel’s emergency medical system.
Among the many new numbers an oleh needs to learn, 101 is one worth knowing from the first day.
Hearing from olim themselves
The summit is not only about officials and experts.
New immigrants at different stages of the aliyah process will discuss what surprised them after arriving, what proved more difficult than expected, where bureaucracy caused problems and what they wish they had known before boarding the plane.
They will also talk about finding jobs and apartments, building communities and adjusting to everyday Israeli life.
That firsthand perspective is central to today’s event. Sometimes the most useful advice for someone preparing to make aliyah comes from someone who made the same move only weeks or months earlier.
The organizations behind aliyah
The Global Aliyah Live Summit features representatives from many of the major organizations involved in bringing immigrants to Israel and helping them integrate, including the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Hayesod, Ofek Israeli, Nefesh B’Nefesh, Clalit Health Services, Bank Leumi, the Jerusalem Municipality, Masa Israel Journey and Magen David Adom.
Participants also include the minister of Aliyah and Integration and the chairman of the Jewish Agency, who will address the broader questions surrounding immigration to Israel: Who is making Aliyah today? What has changed in recent waves? What barriers remain? And what does Israel need to do not only to bring new immigrants to the country, but to help them build successful lives once they arrive?
Aliyah does not end at the airport
ynet Global’s Global Aliyah project has followed prospective and new immigrants throughout the year with guides, personal stories and practical information about life in Israel.
Today, that conversation goes live.
The summit is designed for those who have already booked their flights, those planning Aliyah in the coming months and those still sitting in Paris, London, New York, Toronto, Moscow or elsewhere wondering whether the time has come.
Throughout the day, the broadcasts will address the large and small questions behind starting a new life: work, money, healthcare, housing, bureaucracy, community and belonging.
Watch the Global Aliyah Live Summit and follow continuing coverage on this page throughout the day.
Because aliyah does not end when you land at Ben Gurion Airport.
That is where it really begins.

The European commute: Which EU country spends the most time getting to work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:44:56 UTC
17:44:56 KST

Just how long do Europeans spend getting to work? Across the continent, the daily average commute sits at 48 minutes, but that hides a massive divide.
For millions of workers across the continent, the daily journey to the office is an unavoidable ritual. But just how long do Europeans actually spend getting to work?
According to new research from talent management company SD Worx, the daily average commute across Europe sits at 48 minutes. However, that continental average masks how differently nations experience geography, traffic, and worker mindsets.
While the European average hovers around three-quarters of an hour, individual countries experience vastly different realities on their roads and rail lines.
Countries such as Italy and Slovenia manage to keep daily travel times relatively brief, hovering around 35 minutes.
At the opposite end, countries push much closer to the hour mark. Sweden and Ireland report hefty averages of 57 and 56 minutes, respectively.
Taking the top spot overall, Belgium officially crosses the one-hour mark at 61 minutes a day. This is driven by the fact that 13% of its workforce are "super-commuters", according to SD Worx, spending two hours or more on the road—the highest rate in Europe—with 14% travelling over 120 kilometres daily.
Distance vs. congestion: The Netherlands and Romania
The data also reveals fascinating differences in why commutes take as long as they do. For instance, the Netherlands and Romania both average 53 minutes for a daily commute, but the underlying dynamics are entirely polar opposite:
Workers in the Netherlands cover 63 kilometres on average, leaning on efficient infrastructure to handle long-distance travel.
In Romania, workers spend that same 53-minute window covering much shorter geographic distances, where heavy traffic and urban congestion eat away at the clock.
The commuting paradox
Perhaps the most intriguing takeaway from the research is how workers psychologically handle their travel times.
Even in Belgium—where the average commute surpasses the 57-minute limit that people generally consider "acceptable"—only 34% of workers view that time as wasted.
Despite enduring some of the longest transit times on the continent, demand for more remote work among Belgian employees sits at just 32%, staying right below the international average.
Across Europe, the daily commute remains a patchwork of infrastructure challenges and personal routines, proving that the time we spend getting to work is about much more than just kilometres on a map.

MSF response not needed in Nepal following flash floods

Read the policies, reports, and plans on how we address issues like racism and reduce our carbon footprint, ensuring our actions align with the highest ethical standards.
In more than 70 countries, Médecins Sans Frontières provides medical humanitarian assistance to save lives and ease the suffering of people in crisis situations.
MSF Access pushes for access to, and the development of, life-saving and life-prolonging medicines, diagnostic tests and vaccines for people in our programmes and beyond.
Based in Paris, CRASH conducts and directs studies and analysis of MSF actions. They participate in internal training sessions and assessment missions in the field.
Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action.
Based in Brussels, MSF Analysis intends to stimulate reflection and debate on humanitarian topics organised around the themes of migration, refugees, aid access, health policy and the environment in which aid operates.
This logistical and supply centre in Brussels provides storage of and delivers medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions.
This supply and logistics centre in Bordeaux, France, provides warehousing and delivery of medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions.
This logistical centre in Amsterdam purchases, tests, and stores equipment including vehicles, communications material, power supplies, water-processing facilities and nutritional supplements.
BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals.
Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care.
Evaluation Units have been established in Vienna, Stockholm, and Paris, assessing the potential and limitations of medical humanitarian action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of our medical humanitarian work.
MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population.
The Luxembourg Operational Research (LuxOR) unit coordinates field research projects and operational research training, and provides support for documentation activities and routine data collection.
The MSF Paediatric Days is an event for paediatric field staff, policy makers and academia to exchange ideas, align efforts, inspire and share frontline research to advance urgent paediatric issues of direct concern for the humanitarian field.
The MSF Foundation aims to create a fertile arena for logistics and medical knowledge-sharing to meet the needs of MSF and the humanitarian sector as a whole.
A collaborative, patients’ needs-driven, non-profit drug research and development organisation that is developing new treatments for neglected diseases, founded in 2003 by seven organisations from around the world.
Noma is a preventable and treatable neglected disease, but 90 per cent of people will die within the first two weeks of infection if they do not receive treatment.
The GeoMSF platform is a dynamic one-stop-shop website for all of MSF's GIS related services and products. Access maps and applications through the catalogue, request geographical support, or produce a map on GeoMSF.
As communities in Nepal turn to recovery, immediate needs do not require MSF response
Share
Project Update8 September 2026
The human cost of the flash floods in Nepal of 26 August is devastating. Thousands of people have been killed, with many still missing, and many thousands more have lost their homes and livelihoods.
After arriving in Nepal on 27 August, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams have carried out assessments in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, the parts of Nepal worst affected by the flash floods. Our teams spoke with people affected, visited health facilities and relief centres, and spoke with municipal, district and disaster management authorities coordinating the response to this tragedy.
People have repeatedly told us that their biggest needs now are for recovery – for roads and markets to reopen, for schools, homes and infrastructure to be rebuilt. It is clear that continued, significant, relief efforts and funding for people in affected communities is required now and in the weeks and months to come.
As an emergency humanitarian medical organisation, MSF’s expertise is in providing humanitarian assistance in the most acute phases of emergencies. Our teams have assessed that the humanitarian response is well mobilised and managed. The government-led response, in coordination with local communities, United Nations agencies, and other humanitarian organisations, has succeeded in meeting people’s immediate humanitarian needs.
MSF has therefore decided not to launch a humanitarian response, as our expertise does not lie in the recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction activities that people in Nepal now need. We extend our admiration and respect to local communities, the Nepali authorities and all those responding tirelessly under difficult conditions, helping people recover from this disaster.
We send our heartfelt sympathies to the people of Nepal and all those who have lost loved ones in this tragedy.

United Russia’s ratings are falling, so why is the Kremlin demanding better election results? Putin joined the campaign.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:42:51 UTC
17:42:51 KST

United Russia’s ratings are falling, so why is the Kremlin demanding better election results? Putin joined the campaign.
Warning: this text contains profanity. If that is unacceptable to you, please do not read it.
Russia’s Presidential Administration has raised the KPI targets set for regional officials based on how the ruling party, United Russia, performs. In regions that are neither prone to protest nor overly loyal — where the party’s ratings run average — the new target is 47%.
Back in July, Meduza reported that the Kremlin’s political bloc had lowered the targets for these regions from 50% to 45%. The Russian business daily Vedomosti wrote in June that United Russia’s nationwide KPI had been cut from 55% to 50%. Sources told Meduza the reduction reflected falling ratings for the party and the president, driven by a gasoline shortage, rising prices, and public fatigue with the war.
Two deputy governors overseeing domestic policy, a political strategist who works with regional authorities, and a source close to the Presidential Administration told Meduza about the sudden increase in the targets.
In regions with average support for the authorities, the KPI rose from 45% to 47%, while in regions with a “higher degree of mobilization,” it rose from 50% to 52-53%. Nationwide, United Russia is now expected to score “more than 50%.”
“Things are heating up,” the political strategist who works with regional authorities complained to Meduza. He had welcomed the earlier cut in his region’s KPI with relief, since United Russia’s ratings were falling and the targets no longer matched reality, but the increase now worries him.
The deputy governors Meduza spoke with share this concern.
“When the KPI depends on reality at least to some extent, that’s reasonable. It’s clear that the results [of the election] and real ratings are different things. But when the rating is falling, and your KPI gets raised, the situation isn’t normal. Normally there’s a direct correlation, not an inverse one,” one of the deputy governors said.
The official said he’ll need to step up “administrative-industrial mobilization” to hit the new targets. Efforts by state-funded organizations and state corporations to get Russians to vote — often through coercion — are typically known as “corporate mobilization.” But in private directives, officials have recently begun calling this tool something new.
“We’re already squeezing out [what we can]. Many people are used to it: they’re understanding about it, so to speak. Those who really don’t want to vote usually weren’t pressured much. Well, now we’ll have to,” the same source suggested.
Meduza has previously reported that authorities tightened corporate mobilization efforts. At large workplaces, employees have been designated “mobilization foremen,” responsible for tracking turnout among a group of colleagues ranging from 10 to several dozen people.
A deputy governor and a political strategist who works with regional authorities say the higher KPI means factoring in a larger share of outright fraud, which Meduza’s sources modestly call “correction.”
“It’s mockery! When they announced the increase, they also talked about legitimacy, about making the results look believable. But those are mutually exclusive things!” the regional official said. “When you’re meeting the targets, you demand that your subordinates bring more people out to vote. If there’s room for correction at some polling station, you give it a higher percentage.”
According to him, officials often exceed the Kremlin’s KPI out of excess caution, but “no one has ever been punished for that.”
He and other sources — another deputy governor and a political strategist working in the regions — say officials have started facing pressure at conference calls with presidential envoy offices to deliver strong election results. “Otherwise, we’re fucked,” one regional official summed up.
At one presidential envoy’s office, officials tied the high target directly to Vladimir Putin’s involvement in the party’s campaign: “the president has put his shoulder to the wheel, we’re working for him.” A source close to the Presidential Administration also links the higher KPI to Putin’s active role in the campaign.
Putin has been actively touring regions beyond the reach of Ukrainian drones and has already met with the top five candidates on United Russia’s list. During his remarks at the second stage of the United Russia congress on August 22, he spoke of “the unity of the front and the rear,” and said he was confident the election results “will confirm the stability of the state, the maturity of the political system, and its ability to withstand any external threats, blackmail, and aggression.”
“He’s lending his personal rating, plus he personally spoke about voting at the [party] congress. There’s no turning back now,” says the source close to the Presidential Administration.
Even so, he calls raising the KPI under current conditions “illogical and wrong.” A political strategist close to the Presidential Administration had earlier not ruled out a further cut in the KPI, but that forecast came before Putin became actively involved in the campaign.
“From a political-technology standpoint, lowering the targets is still the right move,” the political strategist said. “But now the work is aimed at making sure the president is satisfied: he supported the party, it got impressive numbers, and we’ve once again proven something to the West.”

Defence Intelligence reveals 155 Russian companies producing components for Russian weapons
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 155 companies belonging to the Russian Ruselectronics holding company that manufacture components for Russian weapons, including ballistic missiles, aircraft, UAVs and electronic warfare systems. Some of these companies are not subject to any sanctions imposed by Ukraine's partner countries.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Quote: "DIU has released data on 155 companies that are part of or managed by the Ruselectronics holding company, fully owned by Russia's state-owned corporation Rostec, in the Aggressor's Military-Industrial Complex section of the War&Sanctions portal."
Details: DIU noted that the holding company brings together companies and research organisations specialising in the development and production of radio and electronic components and technologies, communications equipment and systems, automated control systems, robotic systems, microwave electronics, computing equipment and telecommunications equipment.
Ruselectronics products are used in almost all types of Russian weapons, including ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, electronic warfare systems, military equipment and radar and communications systems for tactical, operational and strategic aviation, among others.
The holding company includes, in particular, companies involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M tactical missile system and 3M22 Zircon missiles:
- Girikond Research Institute JSC, a manufacturer of precision potentiometers for Zircon missiles
- NICEVT JSC, which supplies flight data processing units for Iskander missiles
- NPP Integral-V JSC, a manufacturer of pulse and heating transformers used in Iskander missiles.
The latter company is currently not subject to sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition, as is the case with almost half of all the holding company's businesses identified by DIU.
"However, the inclusion of Girikond and NICEVT on the sanctions lists of most partner countries has had little impact on the overall production volumes of these missiles. This does not mean that sanctions are ineffective, but rather demonstrates the need to improve mechanisms for monitoring compliance with them and strengthen accountability for violations," DIU noted.
DIU also stressed that components, equipment, software and critical raw materials must not fall into the hands of intermediaries and buyers who cannot confirm that the end recipient is a company with no links to Russia's military-industrial complex.

The Foundation for Science, Innovation and Development (FSID) at IISc has adopted a new governance and leadership model.
Bengaluru: The Foundation for Science, Innovation and Development (FSID) at IISc has adopted a new governance and leadership model, appointing Omprakash Subbarao as its CEO and bringing an industry professional to the helm for the first time.The change marks a new phase for FSID, which said it is seeking to build a self-sustaining Section 8 company anchored around two pillars: innovation and incubation. Historically, the organisation has been led by faculty members of IISc.Under the new structure, Subbarao will be a full-time CEO reporting to the FSID Board, with full operational autonomy and responsibility for the organisation’s day-to-day management, external engagement and execution of activities. Prof Suryasarthy Bose will serve as Professor-in-Charge, providing institutional oversight and acting as the principal interface between FSID and IISc.Subbarao, an IISc alumnus, brings experience across technology, industry, public digital infrastructure and innovation. Before his appointment, he was CEO of CORE Labs at FSID, where he led research and innovation collaborations with large corporations.
“As the world of research, innovation and technology translation evolves rapidly, so too are the expectations of industry, govt and other external stakeholders,” Subbarao said. To respond to these changing requirements “with greater agility, professionalism and scale”, he said, FSID was strengthening its governance and leadership structure.“For the first time, we’re having an industry leader as the CEO to drive this transformation,” he added. FSID has set a target of undertaking 1,000 industry projects and building a portfolio of 300 deep-tech startups by 2030.“With a vision of ‘Built on Science, Scaled for the World’, we are building FSID around two strong pillars: Innovation and Incubation,” Subbarao said. The organisation wants to deepen engagement with multinational corporations, Indian corporates and MSMEs while creating stronger pathways for science and research to translate into real-world impact, he said.
Over the past year, FSID has expanded industry engagement through Innovation Hub, or iHUB, its innovation and research facility that brings corporates and startups closer to IISc’s scientific ecosystem.The facility provides R&D laboratories for corporate partners and infrastructure for incubated startups. BEML, Toyo Ink and Schaeffler are among companies that have established research labs and workspaces there. FSID serves as IISc’s single-window interface for its deep science and deep-tech capabilities, supporting collaborative research, incubation, product development, consulting and industry-funded research.

Russia attacked Kyiv overnight into 8 September with ballistic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles and jet-powered drones, killing two people and injuring ten, Ukrainian local authorities and the Air Force reported. Ukraine's foreign minister says Moscow launched it the moment the US peace envoys left the capital, and the country's president says the weapons were combined deliberately to cause the greatest possible harm to life. Strikes the same night reached six other regions.
The strike came as the pause expired
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first visit to Kyiv on 6 September. Ukraine halted strikes on Moscow for three days around the trip, while the Kremlin said its pause on Kyiv ran only to Monday. Nothing else stopped, and Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites while the delegation was in Moscow.
Russia launched another massive attack on Kyiv the moment the envoys left, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
"[Russian President Putin's] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy. Strike after strike on residential buildings brings him no closer to winning this war—it is nothing but senseless terror," the minister wrote.
Russian forces resumed strikes on the capital after a three-day break tied to the American visit, RFE/RL's Belarus service reported.
What Russia launched
The attack ran from 18:00 on 7 September through the night, the Ukrainian Air Force reported, without giving the total number of launched ballistics.
Russia fired Oniks anti-ship missiles, ballistic Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 missiles, and 32 Kh-101 cruise missiles from four of its regions and occupied Crimea, along with 166 Shahed-type drones, more than half of them jet-powered, and decoys launched from two Russian regions and occupied territory. Air defense downed or suppressed 175 targets by 08:30: two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones. Kyiv Oblast and Odesa Oblast were the main axes.
"It was a hard attack, which the Russians deliberately tried to calculate for the greatest possible harm to life," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine put its own peace proposals on the table as two US envoys reached Kyiv for the first time
Results against cruise missiles were very good, he said, while ballistics remain especially hard, and Ukraine proves that need for interceptors to its partners every day. He said he had already discussed it with the Americans and Europeans and would meet states and companies the same day about supplies and about Ukraine's FREYJA anti-ballistic system.
Ukraine has 67 companies working on interceptors, three to five with real results.
Two dead and 13 rescued in the capital
First explosions in Kyiv came at 03:30. Fires and damage reached at least 16 locations in five districts, the Kyiv Military Administration reported. Warehouses, garages, and cars burned, fire spread from a garage to a business center, and a strike on a 26-story non-residential building wrecked structures at the 23rd floor, the State Emergency Service said. Ten people were freed from a blocked five-story block, the service said, and rescuers saved 13 in all, according to Zelenskyy. Morning drone attacks added a warehouse fire, the city said, and the night's damage forced it to reroute a series of bus, tram, and trolleybus lines.
Beyond Kyiv
Two Russian drones hit the locomotive of the Kyiv–Sumy train in the morning, which a monitoring team had stopped in time to evacuate passengers and crew without casualties, Ukrainian Railways board chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said.
Outside Odesa the strike damaged pavilions at the 7th Kilometer market, the country's largest wholesale market for non-food goods, and hospitalized its 58-year-old guard, oblast head Oleh Kiper said.
In Kharkiv two people were injured, one of them a 17-year-old, and Russian forces most often target energy sites, according to oblast head Oleh Syniehubov, who said they struck settlements across the oblast almost 800 times last week alone.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv Oblast's critical infrastructure, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were also hit.

The company’s 2026 semiconductor talent report found that the three biggest hiring areas were manufacturing and quality control, technical and maintenance work, and research, per Anue. The industry is also seeking more interdisciplinary talent. Companies are placing greater emphasis on knowledge spanning electronics, optics, and materials, as well as collaboration across disciplines.

Overseas hiring is also expanding, with US and Canadian job openings reaching a recent-year high. Asia excluding China, Hong Kong, and Macau remains the largest market for overseas assignments, per Tai Sounds.

Tartu drops plan to subsidize new early Riga bus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

Tartu drops plan to subsidize new early Riga bus
Tartu has dropped plans to subsidize an early-morning bus service to Riga, while passenger train operator Elron plans to introduce a morning rail connection in the first half of next year.
The first bus from Tartu toward Riga currently leaves the university city at 11:10 a.m. Late last year, the City of Tartu said it was prepared to temporarily use taxpayer money to subsidize an early-morning bus service from Tartu toward Riga. The subsidy was estimated at around €30,000 a year.
The plan was to hold an open tender to find an operator under de minimis state aid rules. However, a decision has now been made not to introduce such a measure, Tartu City Secretary Jüri Mölder said.
"This has been prompted by changes in the economic environment around us, which force us to look at the situation more broadly. It has also been prompted by lower-than-expected city budget revenues, meaning we need to assess more carefully what we use the city's money for," Mölder said.
As of December, two companies had expressed interest in operating such a subsidized service: A-buss and Lux Express. The latter has previously offered an early-morning departure from Tartu toward Riga on a commercial basis.
Lux Express currently runs between Tartu and Riga twice a day. CEO Ingmar Roos said Lux Express will not introduce an early-morning commercial service from Tartu to Latvia this season either because there are too few passengers traveling between Tartu and Riga.
"On the existing services between Tartu and Riga, from January through May the better-performing departures carried an average of 20 passengers, while the weaker ones carried fewer than 10. It is true that from June through August, during the tourist season, the number of passengers approached 30 a day, but with the start of September, it has fallen again," Roos said.
"Twenty passengers between Tartu and Riga is still around 30 percent below the threshold at which a bus company operating solely on ticket revenue could provide the service."
Roos added that the existing departures from Tartu toward Riga are made more viable by the fact that the services have been extended to Narva.
"The key is the additional passengers from Narva and Tartu who are traveling to Riga. In that combination, the service is viable. As for the question of how to create a morning connection from Tartu, naturally it would not be feasible to structure the Narva and Riga legs around departures in the middle of the night in order to have a bus leave Tartu at 8 a.m.," the bus company executive explained.
Elron, however, plans to add a morning train in the first half of next year alongside its current evening Tartu-Riga departure. Elron will be able to introduce a morning Tallinn-Tartu-Riga train once its new Škoda electric trains begin operating between Tallinn and Tartu, the company's communications manager Kristo Mäe said.
"We currently have information from infrastructure owner Estonian Railways that we will be able to start serving the Tallinn-Tartu route with Škoda electric trains in January. After that, we will be able to provide the exact dates. It certainly won't happen on January 1," Mäe said.
Elron currently runs one train a day from Tartu to Riga in the evening, with the return service in the morning. Statistics for the first eight months show that more than 29,000 train journeys have been made with Elron to Latvia or Lithuania or from those countries to Estonia, including nearly 12,000 passenger journeys on the direct train.

Aid cuts force mass clinic closures across Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:19:17 UTC
17:19:17 KST

- As war is driving people's health needs in Sudan, humanitarian aid funding cuts are leaving people without lifesaving care.
- As more clinics close, people are forced to take longer, more dangerous journeys to reach care.
- Governments and institutional donors must protect funding for essential health services, and provide flexible transitional financing where facilities are at risk of closure.
Amidst a brutal ongoing war and a catastrophic humanitarian crisis, people in Sudan face reduced access to healthcare as facilities across the country close their doors. The impact of broad and historic international aid funding cuts by governments has begun to take hold. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that this withdrawal of support from an already chronically underfunded crisis is cutting off lifesaving care and pushing the few remaining hospitals to breaking point.
As world leaders gather at the UN General Assembly, governments and institutional donors must protect funding for essential health services in Sudan and provide flexible transitional financing where facilities are at risk of closure.
With aid organisations pulling out, local clinics are left without the funds or medicines needed to function. For patients, this means enduring long, dangerous journeys just to receive treatment. As they seek help wherever they can, the few hospitals still operational are absorbing the overflow: between January and April 2026, admissions in MSF supported facilities in Zalingei and Rokero, in Central Darfur state, jumped by 22.5 per cent compared to the same time last year. The situation has deteriorated even further as in May alone 45 general healthcare centres in Central Darfur stopped receiving support as the organisation that had been providing resources lacked funding.
“War is driving Sudan’s needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response,” says Muhammad Ibrahim, MSF head of mission in Sudan. “MSF’s work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours.”
But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours.
“Donors must protect essential health services and provide sustained, flexible funding to organisations that depend on it,” says Ibrahim.
In Tanedba camp, in Gedaref state, home to 18,400 refugees, the sudden departure of a humanitarian organisation in June resulted in the camp’s maternity and surgical wards closing. Pregnant women who need caesarean sections now face three-hour journeys to the nearest city. MSF has stepped in to run the emergency room there through the end of 2026.
In 2021, around 35 aid organisations were working in and around Um Rakuba camp in Al-Gedaref state. Today, fewer than 10 remain. The camp now hosts around 17,000 refugees, mostly women and children.
“Our hospital in Um Rakuba is now the only lifeline left for both refugees and the local Sudanese community,” says Fabrizio Locuratolo, MSF humanitarian affairs manager. “But the cuts here go well beyond healthcare. Food rations are shrinking and protection programmes are being dismantled, pulling away the last safety nets and leaving refugees completely exposed.”
After the United States (US) government announced the closure of USAID1 in 2025, the grants to many organisations funded to work in Sudan ended in June this year. Although the US government continues to be the largest donor to Sudan, providing funding to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and other organisations, many of the existing healthcare providers have been unable to find alternative funding to continue providing services, with health facilities closing in Sudan as a result.
Just as health providers faced the impending removal of US support, many European governments also reduced their assistance to people in Sudan. European and multilateral aid budgets are also shrinking globally. OECD2 preliminary data show that aid from EU institutions fell by 13.8 per cent in 2025, while several major European donors also reduced their overall aid spending.
Globally, humanitarian aid fell by 35.8 per cent. These figures do not represent equivalent cuts to Sudan, where some European donors have maintained or increased their support. But they point to a sharply contracting international funding environment. In Sudan, that wider squeeze is compounding an already severe health crisis, as specific funding withdrawals and programme closures reduce access to healthcare.
“Closing a clinic does not remove a single patient. It just sends them to the next facility,” says Sebastián Traficante, MSF emergency coordinator in Darfur. “After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full. MSF can reinforce some services, but we cannot absorb every closure.”
In Central Darfur’s Hamidiya displacement camp, a health centre that previously provided maternity, paediatric, and mental health care is now operating at sharply reduced capacity after an international aid organisation ended its support. Daily patient visits have dropped from 200 to barely 40, and vaccinations have stopped. The fall was not a sign that people had become healthier. They had stopped making the journey to a centre that could no longer treat them. A labourer in Darfur earns roughly US$13, a day. The US$2 transport fare to reach a working clinic therefore costs about two days’ wages, leaving residents to choose between healthcare and food. 
“That money could buy food instead,” a patient told MSF. “If there is no food, there can be no health.”
That money could buy food instead. If there is no food, there can be no health.
Despite the presence of around 50 NGOs in Tawila, critical gaps persist for up to 600,000 displaced people. MSF runs the only 200-bed hospital in the area and is the only organisation capable of mounting a large-scale epidemic response. Malaria and malnutrition cases are already rising despite limited rainfall, ahead of the peak of the rainy season — and we expect numbers to increase as the rain intensifies. In August, our teams admitted 191 children under five with severe malnutrition to our inpatient feeding centre, and nearly 22 per cent also tested positive for malaria.
These closures are happening during a large-scale, severely underfunded humanitarian crisis. The UN reports that 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition and 19.5 million people faced crisis-level hunger earlier this year, meaning families either do not have enough food to eat or can only meet basic food needs by resorting to measures such as selling the assets they depend on to survive. Yet the UN’s $2.87 billion response plan is barely 41 per cent funded, and 37 per cent of Sudan’s health facilities are estimated to be completely out of service.4

Bengaluru start up gets US patent for its satellite imaging tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:19:01 UTC
17:19:01 KST

Bengaluru-based space technology startup GalaxEye has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system.
BENGALURU: Bengaluru-based space technology startup GalaxEye has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, with the company claiming that it is the first Indian startup to receive a US patent for satellite imaging technology.The patent covers the architecture and system developed by GalaxEye to align and synchronise optical and microwave sensors for simultaneous acquisition of spatially and temporally matched data. The same foundational technology has already been patented in India.“The development strengthens GalaxEye’s intellectual-property position as it prepares to build a planned constellation of 30 satellites over the next five years. The company expects the network to support defence, govt and commercial applications across national security, agriculture, infrastructure, insurance, maritime intelligence and disaster management,” a statement issued Monday, read.At the heart of the technology is a challenge in Earth observation. Optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors operate on different physical principles and have traditionally been deployed independently or combined through post-processing.
Even when both types of imagery are available for the same location, they can be captured at different times, from different viewing geometries and by different platforms, creating temporal gaps and spatial misalignment.GalaxEye said its patented system addresses this challenge at the sensing architecture level. The technology forms the basis of the company’s OptoSAR approach, combining the visual and spectral information of optical imaging with SAR’s ability to operate in all weather conditions, day and night.
Former Isro chairman S Somanath described the patent as an example of innovation emerging from India’s private space ecosystem. He said the technology’s “uniqueness lies in synchronising optical and SAR sensors at the system level” to deliver spatially and temporally matched Earth observation data, adding that it had commercial potential across applications requiring more actionable intelligence.GalaxEye founder and CEO Suyash Singh said: “This is not just a patent for us. This is an invention, an invention that came out of India,” he said, adding that the US protection was validation of what Indian deep-tech companies could create.The company took the technology to orbit through Mission Drishti, its first satellite, launched on May 3, 2026. However, the satellite was later declared as a failure.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

PISA report: one in three Flemish 15-year-olds fails to reach the basic level in reading, fewer high achievers in Flanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:18:53 UTC
17:18:53 KST

Three in ten Flemish 15-year-olds fail to reach the basic level in reading. In vocational education, this figure rises to as many as three-quarters of the pupils. The figures are contained in a new international PISA study involving nearly 4,000 Flemish pupils. Flanders still scores above the European average in reading, maths and science, but has fewer and fewer high achievers and an increasing number of pupils who perform poorly.
PISA report: one in three Flemish 15-year-olds fails to reach the basic level in reading, fewer high achievers in Flanders
Many Flemish pupils are at a complete loss when it comes to basic skills. In science, one-fifth (22.6 per cent) fail to reach the basic level; in maths, one-quarter (25.6 per cent); and in reading, 29.4 per cent fail to reach the basic level.
At the same time, the group of top performers in the classroom is getting smaller and smaller. Whereas in 2003 one in three Flemish pupils could call themselves a maths top performer, that figure is now just one in nine.
For science and reading, this group is even smaller: 8.2 per cent and 5.6 per cent of Flemish pupils, respectively, are in the top group. Flanders continues to score above the EU average in all three subjects, the scores are continuing to fall systematically over the years.
Political initiative
Flemish Education Minister Zuhal Demir (Flemish nationalist N-VA) intends to get in touch with the relevant European Commissioner and her European colleagues: “You cannot build a strong society without people with sufficient knowledge. We used to be among the best in the world and must now take the lead to get back to that level.”
Another striking finding when compared with the OECD average is that, when Flemish pupils are surveyed, they appear to be less curious and show less perseverance.
They are also less likely than average to say they receive support from their families when it comes to schoolwork. It is striking that, whilst the teacher shortage does cause problems, these problems are perceived as more serious in other countries than they are in Flanders.

Low turnout threatens Commons vote on assisted dying, say MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:16:30 UTC
17:16:30 KST

MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about turnout affecting the vote on Friday, when the bill returns to the Commons for its second attempt to become law.
Those who back the change in the law in England and Wales have been emphasising the “undemocratic” nature of the bill’s rejection by the House of Lords after it was talked out by a handful of peers after passing the House of Commons. The bill fell despite multiple days of debate from peers because of the number of amendments tabled in the Lords.
Several former cabinet ministers and ministers say they intend to speak out on the bill now they are freer to express their views, especially on the conduct of the Lords.
The private member’s bill – originally sponsored by Kim Leadbeater – has been revived by the Labour MP Lauren Edwards. It had passed last year by a majority of 23 in the Commons.
In an article for the Guardian, Edwards said the bill was “the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by former Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper”. She said the Lords should not be “allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time”.
Edwards said she rejected some accusations from Labour MPs that she was reopening divisions in the party at a moment when there was a chance to reunite it now that Andy Burnham had replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister.
“Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions,” Edwards said.
“Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial.
“It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.”
Backers of the bill have stressed that MPs should see the vote as a moment to assert the Commons’ decision-making power, rather than rerun the arguments.
Two former cabinet ministers told the Guardian they now wanted to speak out on their reasons for supporting the bill.
The former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn said he was motivated by the death of his first wife to want to relieve suffering of a loved one. “All of us who have experienced the loss of a loved one to a terminal illness – 47 years ago my first wife, Rosalind, died of adrenal cancer – know how hard it is.
“If someone who has only months to live is facing the prospect of unbearable pain – despite the best efforts of palliative care – how can we look them in the eye and say that we will not help them to bring their lives to an end in a way of their choosing surrounded by those they love and who love them?” he said.
He said that the House of Lords would have “huge responsibility to listen and to vote on the bill rather than repeat the procedural obstruction we saw last time. Those suffering at the end of their lives deserve nothing less.”
Jo Stevens, a former Welsh secretary, said: “I’ve always supported the principle of assisted dying. I have constituents and friends who desperately wanted one and a constituent who I helped after they were arrested for escorting someone who chose an assisted death at Dignitas.
“I and many other MPs, including MPs who didn’t support the bill, are furious at the outrageous behaviour of a small number of unelected peers who went against the will of the Commons. Many of these are former MPs who should know better, especially former ministers who were rejected by the electorate.”
However, several MPs said they believed it was the pro-side that was finding it hardest to convince MPs to stay and vote on Friday. “No one has changed sides, but the numbers are going to be tighter because people are absent,” one MP said.
Two MPs who voted in favour of the bill are no longer in parliament: Starmer, who quit as an MP last week and is yet to be replaced; and the former Makerfield MP Josh Simons, who was replaced by Burnham, who has said he will abstain.
Other high-profile supporters of the bill, including the cabinet minister Louise Haigh, minister Ian Murray and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, have written to constituents previously saying they were uneasy about using the Parliament Act to pass the law. The act would come into force, within certain conditions, if the Lordswere to reject the bill a second time.

Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
08:15:19 UTC
17:15:19 KST

Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch flying car maker PAL-V has been given the go-ahead to start building something that could be in the skies in 2028.
The European aviation safety agency EASA gave the company, based in Noord-Brabant, a production licence, meaning it now has every permit it needs to begin building. It first began designing flying cars 20 years ago.
“Now that EASA approval is in, we will really start producing the first cars soon,” chief executive Robert Dingemanse told broadcaster NOS. “We then have to test them again to show once more that we meet all the guidelines. That takes about a year and a half.”
PAL-V’s models have faced repeated promises and delays in the past – its first car was cleared in 2020 and it said its first commercial model would follow in 2021, which was then postponed to 2025 and then 2026.
The Liberty, which folds its rotor blades away to drive on the road, costs between €299,000 and €499,000. The first 250 are already sold, NOS reported, and the company has stopped taking orders because it can only build 100 per year.
Around half the buyers are fire brigades, police forces and the military, Dingemanse said. The rest are specialists who need to get somewhere fast, plus a handful of wealthy private owners. Apart from the Dutch fire brigade, almost all of them are foreign.
Don’t expect one over your street
 The bad news for anyone dreaming of skipping national traffic jams is that the flying car is likely going nowhere in the Netherlands for regular people, no matter how rich you are.
It has to follow the same rules as any aircraft, and can only take off and land at around 20 small airstrips nationwide. “You can’t just fly anywhere,” Delft University aviation professor Jacco Hoekstra told NOS. “And Dutch airspace is pretty full.”
Aviation expert Joris Melkert said the Netherlands has a perfectly good road network, and that unlike a country like Norway, where getting across a fjord in a hurry can be impossible, “a flying car is not crucial here.”

The last 48 hours in Yemen have seen movement and clashes on numerous frontlines as the Yemen government seeks to push the Houthis back and weaken the Iranian-backed group. Meanwhile, the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has backed the Yemen government for more than a decade in its struggle against the Houthis. After years of fighting, there has been a kind of ceasefire since 2022. However, tensions have recently flared up again.
According to the Major General Turki Al-Maliki, the official spokesman for the "Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen" forces, the Houthis have escalated their attacks. They made a number of attempts to “target Saudi Arabia, its national assets, its citizens, and residents on its territory is a dangerous escalation,” reports said.
The Saudi Press Agency noted that Maliki had said that “the reckless terrorist attacks by the Houthi militias, the latest of which targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of (Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran), resulted in the injury of (73) civilians, including women and children.”
It is clear that Riyadh will respond. This "constitutes a blatant violation of the Kingdom's sovereignty and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents on its territory,” Maliki said.
Yemeni forces advance backed by Saudi Arabia
Over the last day, there have been numerous reports about advances in Yemen by government forces. Backed by Saudi Arabia, they want to try to liberate areas from the Houthis. Over the years, some other members of the coalition have sought to shift their policies.
