Bridge between Russia and North Korea opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:35:43 UTC
15:35:43 KST

The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea has opened across the Tumen River, allowing for easier movement of goods and passengers between the two countries, but Ukraine has warned that it is being built as a corridor for military purposes, writes the BBC.
North Korean state media has announced that the bridge will be used for personnel exchanges, tourism and trade. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian human rights group Truth Hounds has indicated that the bridge is intended primarily for the creation of a secret military logistics corridor.
Relations between Russia and North Korea have become closer since the start of a full-scale war in Ukraine, and Russian dictator Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un have previously spoken of their determination to help each other if either country is attacked by military aggression.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin described the bridge as a new symbol of friendship, while North Korean Prime Minister Pak Thae Song said the opening of the bridge was a historic event. Russian state media
TASS reported that up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people can cross the bridge each day.
The BBC reported in May that satellite images showed the kilometre-long bridge with several new access roads, a border checkpoint, surrounding infrastructure and parking lots.
There are air links between Russia and North Korea, as well as a railway, but the only land route until now has been planks placed on the railway tracks, allowing cars to cross. Reuters reported that the Russian government had planned to use the bridge for freight transport only for now, with passenger traffic to be opened later.
Mishustin said the bridge would allow for further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation. The most immediate impact is likely to be increased arms exports from North Korea to Russia. Researchers at South Korea’s spy agency estimate that North Korea has already shipped 7 billion to 14 billion dollars worth of missiles and artillery shells to Russia by sea. It is believed that around 11,000 North Koreans are currently actively fighting in Ukraine.
Truth Hounds recently reported that, under a cooperation agreement signed in 2024,
the bridge could be used to transport North Korean soldiers, construction workers and high-ranking military personnel
to Russia, while Russia would be able to more quickly transport technology and resources to North Korea.
Construction of the bridge began in 2025 and took 495 days to complete.
Since it was authorized in 2024, Russian tourists have been flocking to North Korea. They are welcomed in the capital Pyongyang and the beach resorts of Wonsan-Kalma, while tourists from other countries are not allowed to visit the communist country.
The bridge will allow for the expansion of the flow of North Korean workers into Russia. South Korea estimates that around 10,000 North Koreans work on Russian construction sites and in logging. Although the UN prohibits countries from using North Korean labor, many North Koreans come to Russia on student visas.

EU foreign policy chief Kallas dismisses Washington’s Ukraine peace effort

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday she hoped US negotiators who visited Kyiv over the weekend had seen for themselves that Russia is not genuinely interested in ending its war against Ukraine.
“I’m happy to see that for the first time the special envoys have also visited Kyiv,” Kallas told reporters in Vilnius. “What it meant for the Ukrainians was three days without bombing of civilians. I think that’s the positive side of this visit.”
“I hope that they also heard what the situation on the ground is and Ukrainians also showed them that Russia is not really interested in peace – the opposite,” she said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the weekend in a renewed effort to end the fighting.
Moscow and Kyiv agreed to suspend strikes while the negotiations were taking place.
Witkoff on Monday praised the weekend discussions in Moscow and Kyiv and suggested they could lead to a schedule for new three-way peace talks. The Kremlin also said Monday that it had not ruled out three-way negotiations involving the United States and Ukraine.
The talks remain complicated by disagreements over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, parts of which Russia does not control but which Moscow has demanded as part of a potential peace settlement.
Kallas said Europe cannot serve as a neutral mediator between Russia and Ukraine because it is directly affected by the conflict.
“In the end, when there is going to be a peace agreement, there are also a lot of asks for Europe to be very clear that these are not some things that we are giving without getting anything in return,” she said.
Kallas warns of growing Russian threat
During her visit to Vilnius, Kallas also warned that political parties in Europe that downplay the threat posed by Russia are gaining support.
Her comments followed an election victory by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, in a state election Sunday.
Following a meeting with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, Kallas said sabotage and other security threats were moving closer to Europe.
“At the same time, the parties that are sort of blind to this threat and say that we should not do anything with this because it’s not our concern, are gaining ground,” she said.
“I’m just afraid that we might wake up in a situation where we haven’t done enough to be able to deter the threats and defend ourselves,” Kallas added. “But of course it’s up to the German people, as a democratic country, to make their choices.”
Sinkevičius said victories by far-right parties should serve as a warning to mainstream political forces that they are failing to meet voters’ expectations adequately.
“I would hope that such cases do not recur and that this does not become a new trend across European countries,” he said.
But he said the AfD’s victory in one German state would not affect relations between Germany and Lithuania.
“Germany has remained and will remain Lithuania’s most important strategic partner,” Sinkevičius said.

One campaign, two realities: Adidas features former Israeli soldier as Gaza amputees struggle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:31:54 UTC
15:31:54 KST

For Palestinian amputees in Gaza, an Adidas campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier who lost a leg has come to embody two starkly different realities.
Former Israeli soldier Shalev Biton appeared in a local campaign promoting Adidas’ “Single Shoe” service, designed for amputees and others who need only one shoe.
In Gaza, meanwhile, thousands of Palestinians who lost limbs in brutal Israeli attacks continue to struggle to obtain basic prosthetics, replacement parts and rehabilitation.
The contrast has angered amputees in the enclave, who question why a former Israeli soldier was chosen for such a campaign while their own needs remain largely unmet due to the Israeli blockade despite a ceasefire deal.
‘How can Adidas do this?
Omar Haliwa, 14, lost his leg in an Israeli strike while on his way to collect water. Several relatives who were with him were also killed.
“How can Adidas bring an Israeli soldier and put him in an advertisement while we, the wounded of the war in Gaza, are suffering so much?” Haliwa says.
He said losing his leg changed his life completely, while attempts to obtain a suitable prosthetic repeatedly ran into shortages of raw materials at Gaza’s prosthetics centres.
For Haliwa, seeing a former Israeli soldier receive services tailored to amputees while Palestinians struggle to obtain basic prosthetic limbs was painful.
He urged Adidas to pay attention to Palestinian children and young people who have lost limbs in Israeli attacks.
‘We have nothing’
Kifah al Fakhouri, who lost her leg in an Israeli strike on a seaside cafe in Gaza City, said she was shocked by the campaign.
“I would have liked Adidas to pay attention to the needs of the people of Gaza and Palestine, because we have thousands of amputees,” she says.
“This soldier lost his leg in 2021 and now has a prosthetic limb and resources. We in Gaza have nothing — no treatment, no equipment, no supplies.”
Fakhouri said prosthetic limbs available in Gaza often fail to meet patients’ needs, with some too heavy or unsuitable for everyday use.
Amputees need modern joints, replacement parts and better prosthetics to regain mobility, she said, adding that losing her leg affected her work, movement and virtually every aspect of daily life.
Ahmed Jawadi al Balawi, another Palestinian who lost a leg during the war, said his prosthetic had already worn out and needed maintenance and replacement parts.
“Look at us with mercy,” he said.
“They do not need help the way we do. They have resources. We have nothing. We make something out of nothing.”
Balawi said many amputees in Gaza are forced to use old or poorly fitting prosthetics and struggle to find shoes and accessories compatible with them.
Nabil Abdullah Mahmoud Ibrahim lost his leg when an Israeli drone struck him while he was playing football with other children at a school sheltering displaced Palestinians in northern Gaza.
“Shouldn’t Adidas support Gaza, when so many people here have lost limbs?” he asked.
He said Palestinians with amputations should receive the same support and opportunities available to others living with similar injuries.
More than 8,000 amputees in Gaza
Munir al Barsh, director-general of the health ministry in Gaza, said estimates indicate that more than 8,000 Palestinians have lost limbs during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, including more than 3,000 children.
He said Gaza has trained specialists capable of producing and fitting prosthetic limbs, but restrictions on the entry of raw materials and medical supplies have prevented many patients from receiving suitable prosthetics.
“The priority should be the Palestinian child who has lost a leg or an arm and needs rehabilitation,” Barsh said.
He urged international organisations and global companies to support Palestinian amputees and help provide prosthetics and rehabilitation equipment.
Boycott calls
The controversy intensified after images from the campaign spread widely online, with pro-Palestinian users contrasting Biton’s access to prosthetics and specialised services with the conditions facing thousands of amputees in Gaza.
Israel’s Channel 15 said posts about the campaign drew millions of views, while calls to boycott Adidas spread across social media.
Amid the backlash, Adidas Arabia, the sportswear company’s regional Middle East social media account, issued an apology over the campaign, saying an image used in a recent local activation had raised “concerns and strong reactions.”
“It was never our intent to cause offence, and we apologise for anyone affected,” the statement said, stressing that the promotion was a local initiative rather than part of a global campaign.
Adidas Arabia also said the company would continue to “listen, learn and work” to ensure its actions reflected its stated inclusive values.
For Gaza’s amputees, however, the controversy exposed a gulf that went far beyond a single advertisement.
One campaign had put an amputee in the spotlight. Thousands of others in Gaza were still waiting for the chance to walk again.
Israeli occupation forces have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza that has destroyed or damaged much of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure since October 2023.

Germany news: Gas reserves historically low ahead of winter
Published September 8, 2026last updated September 8, 2026
What you need to know
- 
	German lobby group says gas reserves are at historically low levels and could run out in the event of a cold winter
- 
	The wars in Russia and Iran have significantly lowered profit margins, thus dampening economic incentive to fill reserves
- 
	Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he has no plans of stepping down after the AfD hammered his CDU in Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday
- 
	Several thousand protesters turned out across the country to voice opposition to the far-right party, which nearly half of Germans say should not be allowed to form a state government
Here are the latest headlines from across Germany on Tuesday, September 8:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Budget battle: Long-term investment plan? Or ruinous debt trap?
German parliamentarians began debate on the country's 2027 budget on Tuesday, with Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD defending what he called "painful compromises" as opposition parties railed against new debt.
"My vision is a Germany of the future that is sovereign and resilient in times of crisis. A strong country that is innovative and also socially just," said Klingbeil.
Since taking office in mid-2025, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has ratcheted expenditures to record levels in an effort to revive a flagging economy and rearm Germany's military. 
 
The draft 2027 budget provides for spending of €555.4 billion ($645 billion), up slightly from 2026. 
Total new borrowing is set to exceed €200 billion.
The government has earmarked €118 billion for investments in AI, data centers, research and development, rail, bridges and tunnels, as well as hospitals and schools.
 
Opposition parties universally criticized the new spending, a clear departure from years of tight budgets that hewed to the sacrosanct "black zero," meaning zero debt.
Now, the Merz government is on track to rack up roughly €1 trillion in debt by the end of its term, something the Left Party's Dietmar Bartsch called "madness."
The Greens and the AfD also accused Klingbeil of using "unconstitutional accounting tricks" to get around debt rules.
Klingbeil argued the country had no other choice but to incur debt if it planned on defending itself, noting that infrastructure in the country had also been sorely under-financed over the years as well.
The budget will come up for a vote in November and many changes are expected over the next several weeks.
READ: Police arrest suspect in power grid sabotage case
Protester shot in face with airgun at anti-AfD rally
A protester was shot in the face with an airgun at an anti-AfD rally in the eastern German city of Halle late Monday according to a police statement issued on Tuesday morning.
The incident occurred at the end of a march attended by roughly 850 people and authorities say the 25-year-old was not seriously injured.
Police secured evidence at the scene and searched two nearby apartment buildings, though a perpetrator has yet to be identified.
An investigation into the incident has been opened.
German pop singer Xavier Naidoo to be tried for incitement
Xavier Naidoo, a German pop singer, will face trial for incitement in an incident involving public antisemitic insults directed at a member of the Amadeu Antonio Foundation — which bills itself as an independent NGO dedicated to strengthening democratic civil society and combating neo-Nazism, right-wing extremism, antisemitism, racism and other forms of bigotry and hate in Germany.
On Monday, a state court in the city of Mannheim, where the musician was born, announced that it would allow state prosecutors to take their case against Naidoo to trial.
Prosecutors sought to bring charges against the celebrity in separate cases in 2023 and 2024, which the court previously rejected for lack of evidence. Prosecutors have lodged a complaint with the Higher Regional Court in Karlsruhe to force the lower court to hear their case on further points.
Monday's decision regards one charge brought in 2023. No trial date has been set.
A popular figure in Germany in the 2000s, Naidoo later made headlines for espousing conspiracy theories, railing against Coronavirus safety measures and hurling antisemitic insults.
In 2021, Germany's top court ruled that Naidoo could be referred to as an antisemite for his song texts.
In 2022, he released a video statement apologizing for the "many mistakes" he had made over the years, including for "troubling statements," saying he regretted having ever made them.
Germany´s exports lose momentum
Germany's exports were down for the first time in months, the German Federal Statistical Office has confirmed.
For the first time since January,German exports fell by 0.8% due to lower demand from Europe and China.
Germany's shipments to China dropped by 9.5%, while exports to the Eurozone declined by 2.8%. Meanwhile, exports to the United States increased by 19%, continuing a slow recovery following President Donald Trump's tariffs.
Industrial production also declined in July, adding to growing concerns aboutfuel supplies in the country.
German students post dismal scores in latest PISA academic assessment
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released its 2025 PISA study in Paris on Tuesday and the results are shocking.
According to the study, overall proficiency in reading, math and science has fallen significantly among 15-year-old pupils in 90 countries, with German pupils faring particularly poorly — posting their worst scores ever in the OECD's Program for International Student Assessment, which has tracked the academic performance since 2000.
"We are seeing historically low levels of proficiency," said Samuel Greiff of the Technical University of Munich.
Released every three years, the 2025 assessment documented a major drop in German students' reading proficiency as well as significant dips in math and science skills since 2022.
"We aren't dramatically behind," said Greiff. "But we are not living up to our own standards as an education nation. We are not among the top performers."
Among the factors contributing to Germany's poor scores were the education system's failings regarding early childhood education, teaching staffing, and digitalization.
Social media use was cited as a particular problem, leading Germany's Federal Commissioner for Drug Issues and Addiction Hendrik Streeck to ask, "How much scientific evidence do we need before we do something? Studies show that early, problematic social media consumption measurably impacts scholastic performance."
Roughly one-third of German students also told pollsters they considered school a "waste of time."
AfD victory prompts protests, opposition to party cooperation
Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide electoral victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday has sparked impromptu protests across the country, with several thousand people turning out in various cities.
The largest of these took place in Berlin, where regional elections will take place on September 20, drawing an estimated 5,000 participants who exclaimed "fascism is not an alternative."
In a survey conducted by the polling outfit YouGov on Monday, September 7, nearly half of respondents spoke out against political parties working with the AfD to form a state government.
Of the 1,862 people aged 18 and over polled by YouGov, 47% opposed cooperation with AfD, whereas 38% looked favorably upon the proposition.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch — which won nearly 44% of Sunday's vote but failed to secure a ruling majority — as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
Storage association warns Germany's gas reserves are dangerously low
Germany's gas and hydrogen storage association INES (Initiative for Energy Storage) on Tuesday said the country's gas storage facilities are at historically low levels as summer heat fades and winter approaches.
In a paper presented in Berlin, INES said reserves were at 53% of capacity as of early September, the lowest they have been at this point in time over the past 15 years.
The lobby group said levels could be brought up to 77% by November but only if input is dramatically increased.
INES said 77% capacity would be enough to cover consumer and industry needs if winter temperatures remain normal but added, "77% capacity will not be enough in the event of extremely cold temperatures."
With profit margins minimized by the wars in Russia and Iran, traders have little financial incentive to store natural gas according to INES. Storage facility operators are therefore calling on the German government to lower storage fees.
The Federal Ministry of Economy on the other hand, sees no reason for panic, adding that new LNG terminals off the German coast and pipeline deliveries from Norway can easily cover any potential shortages.

Source: European Pravda, citing the UK government
Details: As part of the new package, the UK will provide air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery shells and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks this winter.
The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, under which Ukraine's allies purchase US weapons for its needs.
The Patriot missiles and other air defence equipment will be delivered to Ukraine before winter sets in, helping it protect critical national infrastructure, civilians and its armed forces from Russian attacks.
The aid announcement follows visits to Kyiv by the UK prime minister and defence secretary, who heard from the Ukrainian president about the importance of additional support ahead of winter.

We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said.

‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:30:29 UTC
15:30:29 KST

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Expand Hong Kong’s MPF investment choices, lure mainland pension funds: financial council
Official think tank urges broader retirement-fund investments, more mainland institutional capital and reforms to boost listings, bonds and corporate restructuring
Hong Kong should consider allowing the Mandatory Provident Fund to invest in more asset classes, and lure more long-term patient mainland capital, such as pension funds, to invest globally through the city, the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC) said in a report on Tuesday.
The MPF, the city’s compulsory retirement scheme, now has total assets of HK$1.67 trillion (US$213 billion) and invests in stocks, bonds and deposits. The FSDC suggests allowing a portion of the funds to be invested in alternatives and infrastructure.
FSDC executive director Rocky Tung Yat-ngok said mainland patient capital, including insurance companies and pension funds, had strong interest in investing overseas to diversify risk and achieve higher returns.
“There is an appetite for this patient capital to invest via Hong Kong in different currencies, including the yuan,” Tung said during a media briefing on Tuesday. “It would be important for Hong Kong to develop more long-term fixed-income products and other investment choices to meet the demand of the insurance and pension funds.”
The council also urged the city to implement further reforms to reduce the time and costs associated with new listings and other fundraising activities, and to introduce a corporate rescue plan to help troubled companies restructure.

Silvia Urgas: Monoculture is dead, long live the monoculture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Silvia Urgas: Monoculture is dead, long live the monoculture
The death of monoculture is not entirely bad, but the number of cultural references understood across groups and age brackets is shrinking, Silvia Urgas says in a culture column.
This summer's theme in the music world seems to be the final death of monoculture. When looking for a global summer hit, there are two undeniably strong candidates. The duet "Rein Me In" by English singers Sam Fender and Olivia Dean has topped the United Kingdom singles chart for twenty‑three weeks. That breaks a record set in 1953, when Frankie Laine's "I Believe" managed to stay in first place for eighteen weeks.
This week, the English duo lost the top spot in the UK chart to Ella Langley, a country singer from Alabama whose song "Choosin' Texas" has been at the top of the U.S. Billboard chart for twenty weeks. Three more weeks and it will break the record held by Mariah Carey's Christmas song "All I Want for Christmas Is You."
A person who claims they have never heard Mariah's Christmas song is likely mistaken or lying, yet both "Rein Me In" and "Choosin' Texas" are unfamiliar tracks to many music listeners. People say they first heard about "Rein Me In" only when reading about its historic chart achievement. It seems unbelievable that something can be so popular and yet so unknown at the same time.
What should we conclude from this? That charts lie? Probably not, but it is becoming increasingly clear that culture no longer reaches people through the same TV and radio channels, or even the same playlists. Some songs are still a bit more popular than others and break through several social bubbles, but creating a summer hit that unites the public or a cross‑generational favorite is becoming harder. Maybe the search for a summer hit should be retired for good. Everyone has their own summer hit, whether someone generated theirs with AI or another listens to songs from the 1970s regardless of their birth year.
Looking at Estonia's Spotify chart, it is still dominated by Nublu and Sadu, with a bit of Säm and Triibupasta in between. The Estonian‑language pop music world is simply so small that artists known to everyone from preschoolers to retirees are still possible. Nublu's "Kesselaid" got an excellent jump start on the path to becoming Estonia's summer hit thanks to the Eesti Laul program. Eesti Laul and Eurovision seem to be the last breaths of monoculture in this region, but it is already clear that Eurovision can no longer unite an entire continent the way it once did.
It is possible that the only major cultural event that truly unites the world is the soccer World Cup. Only young men from selected countries make it onto the field, but the audience and fans are much broader. Music charts hint at this through the continued presence of Shakira and Burna Boy's song "Dai Dai," made for the tournament. Still, "Dai Dai" is only a pale shadow of Shakira's 2010 World Cup song "Waka Waka," and it is doubtful that anyone will remember "Dai Dai" sixteen years from now, unlike the latter. In Estonia, Villemdrillem and Triibupasta jumped quite successfully onto this year's soccer excitement train with their song "Mr. Atškoo."
The death of monoculture is not entirely bad, but the number of cultural references understood across groups and age brackets is shrinking. People who do not share a common cultural space are easier to pit against one another and easier to manipulate into distrusting those who are different. An annoyingly popular pop hit is silly and simple, but it is an effective way to create the feeling that we are all similar people under the same sky.
--
Editor: Kaspar Viilup, Argo Ideon

attention-seeking AI robot becomes a mobile vase for a single orchid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:23 UTC
15:15:23 KST

Batten and Kamp’s AI Robot Becomes a Mobile Vase for an Orchid
Batten and Kamp’s Beauty Seeker Seeker is an embodied AI vase that uses robotic movement to direct human attention toward a single orchid. Combining a decorative object with an autonomous robotic system, the project examines the attention economy, weaponized cuteness, and the relationship between technology and the natural world. The project considers attention as a resource shared by both living and technological systems. Flowers can be understood as biological mechanisms for attracting insects, while domesticated animals and digital technologies have developed systems that encourage human engagement. Building on this idea, Beauty Seeker Seeker uses an artificial object to examine how attention is sought and directed within domestic environments.
The work develops Batten and Kamp’s 2023 project Comfort Seeker Seeker, which paired an Eames LCW chair with a Boston Dynamics Spot robot as an animated concept. Beauty Seeker Seeker translates this earlier exploration into a functioning physical object, using an existing embodied AI hexapod robot combined with a custom vase designed to hold a single orchid. The vase is made from 3D printedaluminum and glass, while the flower itself is presented as a human-engineered object shaped through cultivation and selection.
The Robot Uses Movement to Direct Attention Toward the Orchid
The designers deliberately reduce the robot’s technological capabilities by removing its onboard camera and other functions. This approach shifts the focus away from technological performance and toward the behavior of the object within a domestic setting. By limiting the robot to a specific purpose, the project transforms an advanced robotic platform into a mobile vessel while retaining its physical presence as an unfamiliar technological object within the home. ‘We wanted to dumb the robot down, underutilize it, to focus on the core question of what it means to have these things coexisting with us in the domestic realm,’ shares the duo. ‘There is an obvious absurdity to a high-tech robot becoming a simple vessel.’ By severely restricting its functions, the designers dull the sense of threat usually associated with robots while introducing that same threat directly into the home.
The robot uses LiDAR to map its surroundings and track nearby people. Its primary behavior is to follow and maneuver around humans in an attempt to direct their gaze toward the orchid. The resulting interaction gives the vase a behavioral dimension, positioning the flower as the object of attention and the robot as a mechanism for soliciting it. Short videos document the current behavior of Beauty Seeker Seeker, combining automated and remote-controlled movements. The designers plan to present the project physically as a fully automated version in 2027. Beauty Seeker Seeker hacks an advanced Hexapod robot to hold a single flower
A Flower and a Robot Reconsider the Value of Human Attention
The project continues Batten and Kamp’s exploration of relationships between technology and the natural world, placing an advanced robotic system in direct contrast with a delicate flower. By making the flower the central focus of the robotic object, the work redirects attention toward an element of nature that might otherwise become part of the domestic background.
The resulting object operates as a speculative design study of attention, examining how algorithms, smart devices, and other technologies compete for human focus. Its behavior parallels the strategies used by natural organisms to attract attention, while its combination of robotics, domestic furniture, and horticulture raises questions about what is considered alive, what carries value, and what deserves attention.

Eyal Golan’s ‘Science Fiction’ is Israel’s most played song of the year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:20 UTC
15:15:20 KST

Eyal Golan’s “Mada Bidyoni” (“Science Fiction”) was the most-played song on Israeli radio during the Hebrew year 5786, according to ACUM, the Israeli organization that protects composers’, lyricists’, and publishers’ rights.
The organization, which is marking its 90th anniversary this year, released its annual survey of the songs, songwriters, composers, arrangers, and performers heard most frequently on Israeli radio on Monday.
ACUM’s annual rankings are based on its AcumOnAir monitoring system, which tracks broadcasts on 34 licensed national and regional radio stations in Israel.
Sexual harassment allegations won't deter Golan's fan base
“Mada Bidyoni,” performed by Golan, was written by Avi Ohayon, who composed it with Idan Shneor and Matan Dror. Dror also arranged the track. Its popularity showed that the new allegations of sexual harassment against Golan have not influenced his fan base.
In second place was Peer Tasi’s “Of Muzar” (“Strange Bird”), while “Michelle,” performed by Noam Bettan, who finished second at Eurovision 2026 with this song, was third. Last year’s most-played song, Tasi’s “Ma Yihye Machar” (“What Will Be Tomorrow”), dropped to fourth place.
Rounding out the top 10 were Osher Cohen’s “Kulam Ganavim” (“Everyone’s a Thief”) in fifth place; Odeya Azoulay’s “Rocky” in sixth; Omer Adam’s “Malkat Hador” (“Queen of the Generation”) in seventh; Hanan Ben Ari and Tasi’s “Halevai” (“If Only”) in eighth; Tasi’s “Hee Lo Yoda’at Lama” (“She Doesn’t Know Why”) in ninth; and Ben Zur’s “Kol Akeva Letova” (“Every Delay is for the Best”) in 10th.
The full top 20 also includes a new version of Naomi Shemer’s “Od Lo Ahavti Dai” (“I Haven’t Loved Enough”) performed by Yehoram Gaon and Subliminal, Hatikva 6’s “Israeli Complet” (“Total Israeli”) and “Vayehi Or” (“Let There Be Light”), Noa Kirel’s “Bridezilla,” and Idan Amedi’s “Lo Nishbar” (“Not Broken”).
Eight years of Ohayon
Avi Ohayon tops songwriters for eighth consecutive year
Ohayon was once again the most-played songwriter and composer on Israeli radio, taking the top spot for the eighth consecutive year.
Tslil Klifi was the year’s most-played female songwriter. She was among the writers of “Michelle,” together with Nadav Aharoni and Yuval Raphael, Israel’s 2025 Eurovision contestant, who, like Bettan, came in second.
Among female performers, Sarit Hadad held onto first place, followed by Eden Ben Zaken, Odeya Azoulay, Agam Buhbut, Yehudit Ravitz, and Noa Kirel.
Golan topped the overall list of male performers. Omer Adam was second, followed by the late Arik Einstein, who came in third, although he died nearly 13 years ago. Veteran singer Shlomo Artzi and Peer Tasi were next in the top five.
The rankings underline the continuing dominance of contemporary Mediterranean and mainstream Israeli pop on radio, but the lists also feature veteran performers and songwriters. Besides Einstein and Artzi, these included Hadad, Ravitz, Gali Atari, Rita, Chava Alberstein, and Ilanit. The late Ofra Haza was the ninth-most-played female performer.
ACUM CEO Assaf Nahum said the past Hebrew year had again been a productive one for Israeli music and said the organization would continue supporting the country’s songwriters and composers.
“I wish our creators a new and fruitful year of creativity, activity, and good music that will continue to bring joy and emotion to all the people of Israel,” he said.
ACUM chairman Yoav Ginai noted that the organization has spent nine decades protecting creators’ rights and strengthening the Israeli music industry.
He wished Israel’s songwriters, composers, publishers, and poets a good year, adding, “May it be a year of peace at home and abroad.”

Secret 1993 Peres-Hussein meeting helped pave way for Israel-Jordan peace, revealed documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:15:07 UTC
15:15:07 KST

Newly revealed documents from a secret November 1993 meeting between then-foreign minister Shimon Peres and Jordan's King Hussein show how the two leaders helped lay some of the early groundwork for the Israel-Jordan peace treaty, the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation revealed on Tuesday, marking the 10th anniversary of Peres's death.
The documents were released on the day of the state memorial ceremony for Peres and the naming of the Jerusalem International Convention Center in his honor. They include excerpts from the minutes of the meeting, which was held at the king's palace in Amman under strict secrecy.
According to the records, Peres's appearance was even altered to prevent identification.
The Peres Center now describes the exchange as a kind of "testament for peace" by two leaders who sought to change the region. During the meeting, Hussein spoke candidly about the urgency he felt and his desire to use the time he believed he had left to advance an agreement.
"Perhaps I have only a year or two left; I will put everything on the line," the king said.
According to the documents, the Jordanian royal palace received a message on October 26, 1993, saying that King Hussein wished to meet with then-foreign minister Shimon Peres. According to the record, Hussein viewed Peres as a creative thinker and was willing to hold a secret meeting as part of the preliminary contacts that ultimately led to the peace agreement signed in 1994.
The meeting did not emerge in a vacuum. It followed years of secret contacts and ties between Israel and King Hussein, including Peres's attempt to advance an agreement with Jordan under the 1987 London Agreement.
Hussein, Peres shared commitment to security, peace
About a week after the message was received, the secret meeting took place. The documents state that "he was assured that the visit would be conducted in secrecy and that the necessary measures would be taken to prevent the foreign minister from being identified."
"My assurance that the partnership between us remains intact in no way expresses complacency; on the contrary, it is a dynamic partnership, open to creative proposals, which, from my experience, I know characterize your approach," Hussein told Peres during the meeting.
Peres, for his part, presented his vision of regional economic cooperation that could serve as the basis for a future agreement, including shared infrastructure, ports, aviation, roads, and regional projects.
"We have many dreams and hopes for the future... I share the commitment that there will be change and that the younger generations will have the opportunity to live with a sense of security, which is peace," King Hussein said during the conversation.
The minutes show that Peres proposed preparing an unofficial document, an "informal non-paper," summarizing the subjects discussed and the understandings reached, so that he could discuss them with prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.
The document states that Peres stressed that he was "working hand in hand with the prime minister," that the two "see eye to eye," and that both felt their time was short and that they were "trying to pull the wagon of peace together."
"Our generation must make difficult decisions before we disappear, and all of this for our children. We must ensure the children's future, so we must not lose momentum. There is a contradiction between the little time available to us and the size of the opportunity before us," Hussein said, emphasizing the sense of urgency.
"History is like a galloping horse. Either you get on it, or you get off, and the horse will continue galloping without you. We do not have much time, and our 'life expectancy' for making peace is limited."
"Your Majesty, there is now tremendous public support for the peace agreement. Young people are fed up with wars, poverty and the absence of freedom," Peres responded.
One of the most personal moments in the meeting came when Hussein referred to the 1951 assassination of his grandfather, King Abdullah I.
"I want to make my position clear. In 1951 there was a tragic event, the murder of my father. I want to bequeath to the future, to my brother Hassan and to the entire government, the best possible legacy. Perhaps I have only a year or two left; I will put everything on the line."
He later said: "When the gaps narrow, the fears will fade, hopes will grow for all the children of Abraham, and the time has come for that to happen."
From secret meeting to peace treaty
According to the Peres Center, King Hussein and foreign minister Peres initialed a memorandum of understanding that night. Less than a year later, in October 1994, Israel and Jordan signed their peace treaty in the Arava.
Prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, with Peres as his foreign minister, led the diplomatic process on Israel's behalf. The Peres Center stressed that the treaty became one of the foundations of Israel's regional relations for more than three decades, including during periods of crisis and tension.
"It is hard not to be moved when reading the documents from that historic meeting between Peres and the king of Jordan.
The secret meeting reflected Peres's worldview, a man of vision who believed in our ability to change reality," Chemi Peres, chairman of the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation, said following the release of the documents.
The Peres Center also noted that throughout his life, Peres sought to strengthen Israel's security and international standing, and that alongside his work to advance peace agreements, he helped establish Israel's defense industries and develop the country's strategic capabilities.
"It is a great privilege and a moral obligation to listen to the testament for peace of two great leaders, Shimon Peres and King Hussein. In the meeting, King Hussein says that his days are numbered and that peace is the most important thing they can leave to future generations," Efrat Duvdevani, director-general of the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation, said.
"The words spoken and written during the secret meeting were part of a process toward the peace agreement between Israel and Jordan, led by prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and Mossad chief Ephraim Halevy."

‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:13:28 UTC
15:13:28 KST

Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway station, talking over the dramatic events of the previous evening and the surge by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland to a historically high vote in the Saxony-Anhalt elections.
“Don’t laugh at me,” she said, “but I wish we could go back to the days of Angela Merkel, when things were OK in Germany”.
The teenagers, from nearby Wolmirstedt, said they were shocked by the AfD’s landslide win. But they felt powerless to do much about it and felt afraid about where it might take their home state.
“We talk about it all the time,” said Maryam, whose name has been changed. “It’s on my mind constantly. My dad came to Germany from Syria in 2015. My mum and I joined him two years later.”
The first clause of the anti-immigrant AfD’s 100-day programme says that – “from the first moment” of being in power – the party will deport people it deems “irregular migrants”. Maryam believes her family could well face deportation.
“We have to renew our residency permits every three years as it is. We’ve always lived in a state of uncertainty. Now after these election results we face going back to Syria which we don’t think is safe, and I can’t even read or write Arabic.”
The AfD won almost 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election, more than even it had hoped for. Doreen, 54, did not immediately admit to having supported the party, but said later in an interview she had put her faith in what she termed “the blues” “out of a sense of desperation”.
When challenged about the human impact the party’s policies could have, for example on immigrant families, she shrugged: “It is what it is.”
“If they [refugees] hadn’t turned up here in such large numbers in the first place, they wouldn’t have to go through such heart-breaking situations now,” she said.
Doreen, a cleaner, said she hoped the pro-Russia AfD would be able to take power and act on promises to end refugee status for Ukrainians (as well as aid to Kyiv). “The winners will hopefully straighten up a few things right away,” she said. “They [Ukrainians] come here in their fancy cars, pretending they’re escaping devastation, but most of them have far more resources and designer clothes than I do.”
Doreen is speaking close to a stolperstein, or stumbling stone – a brass plaque embedded in the concrete – commemorating Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer. Born in 1877, he lived on the spot where a glass-fronted fitness club now stands until he was “humiliated, disenfranchised … (and) took flight in death” (a euphemism for suicide).
But she angrily rejected any parallel between the AfD’s rise in popularity and the Weimar era rise of the Nazis. “Don’t tar me with that brush,” she said. “We are in a different age, with different problems.”
Returning from their daily stroll to the Elbe river, 88-year-olds Ernst and Judith, a retired boiler maker and a design engineer who have been married for 64 years, said they did not want to talk about the election result. But it soon became clear that they were shattered by the news. Voting data has shown a stark drop-off in support for the far-right party among the over-70s.
“It’s not like we didn’t see it coming,” said Judith. “But we don’t quite know what to do with the information. The reality of it hasn’t quite kicked in.”
The couple said they had voted for the far-left Die Linke. Judith said she was “devastated that a party that has so little regard for refugees” had won, and by such a large margin.
Her own life story – she was forced to flee her home in Silesia in 1945 and spent years in temporary accommodation before settling in Magdeburg – has greatly sensitised her to the plight of refugees, she said.
“I see the look in their eyes, it doesn’t matter where they come from, who they are, and I am so empathetic to their situation,” she said. “It breaks my heart to think that almost half of the population has voted for a party that is so anti-immigrant, particularly after all Germany has gone through as a nation in the last century.”
Sitting on a heart-shaped rainbow-coloured bench in front of Magdeburg’s gothic cathedral, Christiane and Franz Josef Jäker, 67 and 71, on holiday from North Rhine-Westphalia, were also digesting the news.
“The populists are ruining everything,” said Franz Josef. “Everything that Germany has built up again after world war two. They promise a lot that they can’t deliver, and they also suppress a lot – such as what is going on in Ukraine – so that they can argue for the resumption of Russian gas imports to Germany.”
Eric, a paramedic cheerily drumming up funds for a hospice, said he was kicking himself for not having voted. The 21-year-old son of a German mother and a Guinean father who spent 10 years applying for a German passport, said: “I try not to think about what the installation of the AfD in government might mean for me as a dark-skinned man.”
Most of all he is worried about “the constitutional changes they might make, and the domino effect that might have across Germany”.
Luisa, a bank teller who says she voted for Die Linke, fears for the image of her state.
“It’s really bad for the reputation of Saxony-Anhalt. A lot of people have said that foreigners here will now choose to leave, but I know enough low-paid foreign workers who won’t be able to afford to do so, and will just have to put up with being badly treated.
“I saw some interviews with Holocaust survivors and they drew parallels with the mood around what’s happening now and the rise of the Nazis. We have to pay attention to this similar sense they say they have – they’re not making it up.”

The transformative roadmap also includes the allocation of state aid to the production of critical components for developing competitive manufacturing in priority sectors through domestic capabilities. The aid will be tightly regulated to prioritize companies demonstrating tangible increases in energy efficiency, job creation, and export volume.
The overarching investment incentive system will transition to a project-oriented framework to target specific regional development needs.
Ankara will also encourage agricultural investments to convert farming byproducts into profitable goods to strengthen the ties between rural agriculture and urban industry.
The local development initiative program will provide funding for private-sector projects addressing regional challenges with technological upgrades and localized job creation.
Türkiye’s future roadmap also includes other efforts to subsidize branding, certification, and e-commerce infrastructure to commercialize local products for global export markets.

Chinese scientists propose turning abandoned coal mines into underground farms
Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, mining tunnels could offer agricultural advantages amid climate change, scientists say
2-MIN READ2-MIN
3
 Listen
Dannie Pengin Beijing
Chinese scientists have proposed developing “underground agriculture” in abandoned coal mine tunnels as part of a push to create a green, circular economy for the country’s massive mining industry.
A team of researchers from Shanxi, a major coal-producing province in central China, described the idea late last month in the journal China Mining Magazine.
An estimated 15,000 abandoned mines in China are expected to close by 2030. Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, these subterranean spaces offer unique advantages.
The researchers, based at the Shanxi Province Coal-based Resources Green and High-efficiency Development Engineering Centre, suggested that existing tunnels, power grids, ventilation systems and groundwater at these mines could be repurposed to support agriculture.
“With climate change intensifying globally, the stability and sustainability of traditional land agricultural systems are facing severe challenges,” they wrote, adding that there was a lot of practical value in developing “closed-environment farming”.
The paper assesses whether critical factors – including light, temperature and water – could support these farming operations.

Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry: economic development is essential for defence and the provision of public services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
06:07:59 UTC
15:07:59 KST

Latvia’s largest business organisation, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LTRK), points out that, under the current circumstances, every instrument that helps generate economic activity and growth is important for Latvia’s development and security, ultimately creating the financial base needed to provide public services. This also applies to immigration policy as one of the components supporting Latvia’s development.
LTRK recognises the importance of national security, social stability and the preservation of national culture as essential factors in shaping immigration policy. At the same time, we believe that achieving these objectives should be based on effective and proportionate monitoring and control mechanisms, maintaining a balance between security and attracting the workforce needed by the labour market. LTRK advocates a well-considered immigration policy that ensures fast and straightforward access to workers from third countries to meet the needs of Latvian businesses, while at the same time managing security risks.
Immigration policy should be pragmatic and rational, clearly distinguishing illegal immigration and violations of regulations from those who come to Latvia to work and help create added value. This also applies to international students, who make a significant contribution to Latvia’s economy while studying and, after graduation, represent a potentially qualified and well-integrated workforce in Latvia.
LTRK President Aigars Rostovskis says: “Latvia cannot simultaneously pursue export and investment objectives while making it more difficult for the people who help achieve these objectives by creating added value and bringing additional funds into the local economy to remain in the country. No policy can be built on blanket restrictions and the assumption that everyone acts in bad faith and abuses the system. LTRK therefore supports a well-considered immigration policy capable of striking a balance between different interests.”
It should also be remembered that, by adopting the new Immigration Law in July 2026, the Saeima has already significantly strengthened both control and accountability. At the same time, compromises have been reached on several complex challenges affecting both national security and economic growth. Therefore, at this stage, during the pre-election period, there is no need to create renewed uncertainty either for the business environment or for society as a whole.

United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrives in Colombia on Tuesday, the first stop on a Latin American tour designed to bolster pro-US leaders and cement influence over the continent.

Since then, Colombia has stepped up air assaults and authorised joint military operations with the United States.

Washington is openly asserting its desire for hegemony over the South American continent in the name of the "Donroe Doctrine".
That is a blend of Trump's first name with that of James Monroe, the fifth US president, who more than two centuries ago declared Latin America the United States' exclusive sphere of influence.

Australia proposes hefty fines for big tech over duty to protect young users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:57:10 UTC
14:57:10 KST

Social media giants face US$78 million fines if they fail to protect young users from harmful content, Australia's prime minister said on Tuesday as he unveiled draft laws reining in big tech.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese released draft laws that would place a "duty of care" on the firms behind popular platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram.
Social media companies would be held responsible for protecting under-18s from pornography, online bullying, content that glorified crime, and content that encouraged eating disorders.
"We took action because the community said 'enough is enough'," Albanese told reporters.
"We would no longer let Australian kids be treated as commodities instead of children."
Social media firms face mounting scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to extreme content to keep them scrolling.
The draft laws build on Australia's world-first social media ban for under-16s, which came into effect late last year.
Companies found to be flouting their "duty of care" could be fined up to Aus$109 million ($78 million), Albanese said.
The legislation includes a requirement that platforms allow users to "opt out" of powerful algorithms that determine what comes up on social media feeds.
"This will give Australians greater choice over their platforms and what they see," Albanese said.
It would require firms like Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said big tech was facing a "reckoning".
"Their platforms and tools have infiltrated our daily lives in ways that we could never have imagined," she told reporters on Tuesday.
"Some good, but some with terrible consequences."
Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social media apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
The draft laws would be introduced to parliament later this year after consultation with social media companies, industry bodies and civil society groups.

The ballet tells the epic story of the famous gladiator Spartacus and his struggle for freedom against the Roman Empire.

With its dramatic structure, powerful choreography and grand stage scenes, “Spartacus” will bring the 33rd International Aspendos Opera and Ballet Festival to a spectacular close.

The monastery was built during the Middle Ages. (AA Photo)
The rock-cut Çukurayva Monastery in the eastern province of Kars’ Kağızman district bridges the Middle Ages and the modern era through its remarkably preserved architecture.
Located near Çukurayva village, about 1.5 kilometers west of the village, the monastery draws attention with its main church, chapels and living spaces carved directly into the rock.
The monastery, dated to the 10th century based on its plan, architectural features and decoration, centers on a cross-shaped church.
The main church and two chapels accessible from its northern section are covered by domes supported by squinches. The structure also stands out for its cross motifs painted with red ochre.
Kafkas University academic Associate Professor Muhammet Arslan told state-run Anadolu Agency that the monastery was built during the Middle Ages.
Arslan said the exact construction date of the monastery is unknown, adding that it is dated to the 10th century based on its plan, architectural features and decoration.
Pointing to motifs made with ochre inside the monastery, Arslan said: ”The main structure of the monastery is a church, and we should emphasize that it is a rock-cut church. It was built in a cross-shaped plan and covered with a dome supported by squinches. One of the elements that makes this place special is the cross motif painted with red ochre at the center of the dome.”
”There are also two chapels accessed from the northern arm of the cross-shaped plan. The chapels were built on a square plan and are each covered with a dome supported by squinches.
As in the dome of the main church, we can also see similar cross motifs painted with ochre at the center of the chapels’ domes,” he added.
Call for archaeological work around monastery
Harun Ağdaş, head of the Kağızman Mountaineering and Outdoor Sports Club, said the monastery is highly important for the region and that they occasionally organize hikes to the site.
Ağdaş called for archaeological work to be carried out around the monastery.
Visitor Sergül Keskin also highlighted the monastery’s importance for regional tourism. ”It is a cave worth seeing. We invite all nature lovers and visitors interested in history to come here,” she said.

Türkiye’s museums, heritage sites draw nearly 66 million visitors in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:54:01 UTC
14:54:01 KST

Türkiye’s museums and archaeological sites attracted nearly 66 million visitors in 2025, according to the latest cultural heritage statistics released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
The number of museum and archaeological site visits rose 6.8 percent year-on-year to 65.86 million. More than half of all visitors, 52.9 percent, visited museums and sites operated by the Culture and Tourism Ministry, while private museums accounted for 21.9 million visits, up 10.8 percent from the previous year.
The country had 664 museums in 2025. Of these, 220 were operated by the ministry, 426 were private museums and 18 were managed by the Presidency of National Palaces. Türkiye also had 148 archaeological and historical sites open to visitors.
Among provinces, Istanbul remained by far the country’s leading museum destination, recording 18.3 million visits. İzmir followed with 4.65 million and Ankara with 4.64 million.
The figures underline the continued popularity of some of Türkiye’s best-known cultural attractions. Istanbul’s Topkapı Palace, Hagia Sophia, Galata Tower and Dolmabahçe Palace, as well as major archaeological destinations such as Ephesus in İzmir and Hierapolis-Pamukkale in Denizli, have consistently ranked among the country’s most visited heritage attractions in recent years.
The country’s museums housed more than 4 million artifacts in 2025, with coins making up the largest category.
Interest in museums was also reflected in the sale of 6.8 million Museum Cards, which provide access to participating museums and archaeological sites.
Beyond museums, Türkiye recorded 130,632 registered immovable cultural heritage assets. Istanbul had the highest number, with 34,558 registered assets, followed by İzmir and Muğla.
The statistics also point to the scale of Türkiye’s protected natural heritage. The number of national parks increased to 50, covering nearly 942,300 hectares, while the number of nature parks reached 274. The country also had 32 nature conservation areas and 111 natural monuments.

The Finnish Border Guard marked the completion of the barrier at the Nuijamaa border crossing in southeastern Finland on Monday, capping a project conceived after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine reshaped the Nordic country’s security policy.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The state’s most important duty is to see to the safety of its nationals,” Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said at the event.
“The eastern border fence is a necessary part of an effective border surveillance system in these unpredictable times,” she added.
The fence covers selected sections of Finland’s 1,340-kilometer frontier with Russia – the longest border Russia shares with any EU or NATO member.
Rantanen said Finland could eventually extend the barrier and called for additional EU funding to help eastern member states strengthen their borders.
The 200-kilometer barrier consists of dozens of separate sections concentrated in areas deemed most vulnerable.
The system includes a 4.5-meter-high fence, technical surveillance equipment, patrol roads and a 25-meter-wide cleared strip along the frontier. The project cost €356 million.
What to Make of Witkoff and Kushner’s Return to Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
                                                                                                                                                                         
From non-alignment to NATO
Finnish political parties agreed in October 2022 on the need to build a partial fence along the Russian frontier, months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Pilot sections were built in 2023, with large-scale construction beginning in 2024.
The decision came amid a historic shift in Finland’s security policy. The country joined NATO in April 2023, ending decades of military non-alignment in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The fence took on added importance after Helsinki accused Russia of facilitating the movement of migrants toward its border in late 2023 as a form of hybrid pressure.
Around 1,000 asylum seekers from third countries arrived at the frontier from Russia that autumn, prompting Helsinki to progressively shut its eastern border crossings before closing them all in December.
Russia denied orchestrating the influx.
Border crossings to remain shut
Rantanen said on Monday the crossings would remain closed, citing the continuing war in Ukraine and concerns over Moscow’s hybrid operations.
“The border crossings with Russia will not be opened because the security situation related to the military attack on Ukraine and hybrid operations has not changed,” she said.
The fence is part of a broader push by Finland to bolster its preparedness amid heightened security concerns over Russia.
Last week, more than 2,000 people took part in a two-day drill in the central city of Kuopio, billed as Europe’s largest civil defense exercise since the end of World War II.
The drill tested how authorities and civilians would respond to cyberattacks, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and the threat of missile strikes from Russia.

Turning crisis into an opportunity to work better
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:52:29 UTC
14:52:29 KST

By Signe Bāliņa, President of the Latvian Information and Communications Technology Association (LIKTA).
We have become accustomed to using the e-services provided by the state and municipalities in our everyday lives. They are practical and convenient, which is why we become frustrated when one of them is temporarily unavailable or when a long-promised digital service takes too long to implement. The governance crisis that has emerged in Latvia’s public information and communication technology (ICT) sector provides a timely opportunity to improve cooperation between the public and private sectors on ICT projects that matter to society, modernise governance in the sector, and strengthen project management.
There is no doubt that Latvia’s ICT sector is a source of national pride. Its annual turnover amounts to €5.8 billion, and it is the country’s fourth-largest taxpayer. Public-sector procurement accounts for only 5% of the industry’s total turnover, yet the consequences of shortcomings in public ICT projects are felt across society. In the view of the Latvian Information and Communications Technology Association (LIKTA), efforts should currently focus on three areas: strengthening the competence of contracting authorities, reinforcing a unified national digital architecture, and modernising the public procurement system and its requirements.
When working on public-sector projects, LIKTA members regularly encounter weak ICT project management on the contracting authority’s side. This means that organisational leaders often struggle to maintain control over projects and remove obstacles that arise during implementation. ICT projects are also frequently implemented in isolation from other organisational processes and from the broader needs of Latvia’s e-government ecosystem.
In our view, Latvia should adopt best practices from other EU Member States and organise public-sector ICT projects in the same way as the private sector does. An ICT project should address the needs of the organisation as a whole, including change management. The objectives of the ICT system should be defined in advance, together with its total cost of ownership (TCO) and the expected efficiency gains. Each project should have a clearly designated business owner with the authority to make decisions, remove obstacles and take responsibility for measurable results. Finally, before launching a procurement procedure, a feasibility assessment should be carried out. This should include dialogue between the contracting authority and the industry, examining comparable examples, assessing similar systems already available on the market, and evaluating whether developing a new system is justified.
Second, all stakeholders should focus on developing public e-services as part of a unified digital platform. This is not currently the case: approximately 1,000 different state information systems are used across Latvia’s public sector. Those responsible for individual systems often do not see how their system fits into the country’s broader ICT architecture.
LIKTA therefore proposes considering the establishment of an empowered and competent national ICT council capable of prioritising projects and assessing their compliance with the overall national ICT architecture. This would help ensure interoperability between systems and prevent inefficient use of resources. At the same time, knowledge and expertise should be concentrated in competence centres to ensure professional project management and consistency of ICT architecture across the public sector.
An excellent example of such knowledge consolidation is the ICT Governance Leaders’ Forum organised by the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development (VARAM). Good examples from other sectors include the services provided by State Real Estate (VAS “Valsts nekustamie īpašumi”) in organising construction procurement and managing projects, as well as the technical specification standards for road construction and maintenance maintained by Latvian State Roads (VAS “Latvijas Valsts ceļi”).
Together, these measures would move us closer to a situation in which every solution forms part of a centrally managed ICT portfolio, with clear accountability, measurable KPIs and regular reporting throughout its entire lifecycle.
Third, Latvia should significantly modernise its approach to public-sector procurement. LIKTA has prepared a range of proposals covering various aspects of procurement, including the assessment of bidders’ qualifications. Most importantly, high-quality tender evaluation criteria should ensure that contracts are awarded to bidders capable of providing higher-quality services and delivering the outcomes intended by the contracting authority.
For example, the State Revenue Service already includes a practical assignment in its procurement documentation, where the level of detail demonstrated in completing the task and the assessment of the required workload form part of the evaluation of the most economically advantageous tender. LIKTA proposes making such assignments a binding reference standard throughout the entire duration of the contract.
In LIKTA’s view, procurement requirements should also include bidders’ financial indicators, such as liquidity ratios, turnover generated from relevant development projects, and mandatory state social insurance contributions. This would provide greater confidence that a company will be able to maintain the necessary team of specialists throughout the contract period and that it does not face significant insolvency risks. In other words, the risk of awarding contracts to bidders with insufficient in-house capacity that rely on a difficult-to-manage network of subcontractors should be reduced.
For smaller ICT system development and maintenance contracts, LIKTA believes that competition could be strengthened by transforming the existing Electronic Procurement System (EIS) e-catalogues into dynamic purchasing systems. Here too, regularly updated information about team capacity and available work assignments would be important. This would promote stronger competition than procurement based on narrowly specified lists of projects.
High-quality procurement of ICT services requires appropriate quality assessment, a proportionate allocation of risks between the contracting authority and the supplier, and clear, objectively verifiable acceptance criteria. Nobody remembers the e-service procurements that worked well, but everyone feels the consequences when information systems fail or provide an inadequate user experience.

EU condemns glorification at Mladic funeral in Serbia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:52:22 UTC
14:52:22 KST

Serbian national military servicemen fire a three-volley salute during the funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide and other atrocities during the war in Bosnia, at the Topcider Cemetery, in Belgrade, Serbia, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP Photo)
The European Union has condemned the public glorification of Ratko Mladic after thousands attended the convicted war criminal’s funeral in Belgrade, which featured military honors and was joined by several Serbian government ministers.
The EU’s diplomatic service said Mladic’s crimes were among “the most heinous crimes known to humankind.”
“Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values,” it said, adding that such acts had no place in the bloc or its candidate countries.
Serbia has been an EU candidate since 2012.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos earlier canceled a planned visit to the country over what she described as the glorification surrounding Mladic’s death.
The former Bosnian Serb military commander died on Aug. 27 at the age of 84 in a U.N. detention facility in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence.
Mourners began gathering early on Sept. 7 at Belgrade’s Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Luke, where Mladic’s coffin was placed on public display.
His military cap and saber rested on the coffin as uniformed soldiers and war veterans stood nearby.
Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije led the service, while large screens were installed outside the church for crowds unable to enter.
Although the ceremony was not formally designated a state funeral, the Serbian government had sent an aircraft to return Mladic’s body from the Netherlands, and soldiers carried his flag-draped coffin.
Defense Minister Bratislav Gasic and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic attended the funeral. President Aleksandar Vucic was absent, but his son Danilo was among the mourners.
Following the service, the coffin, draped in the flags of Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb entity Republika Srpska, was taken in procession to Topcider Cemetery.
Some supporters carried banners describing Mladic as a hero and chanted his name.
He was buried with military honors, including a three-volley rifle salute, beside his daughter Ana, who died in 1994.
The U.N. International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted Mladic in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. His life sentence was upheld on appeal in 2021.
The convictions included his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed, and the siege of Sarajevo.

Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that it condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the visit by the delegation.
"Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation," the staff said in their statement, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.

The Eiffel Tower's website said the landmark was closed on Monday due to "exceptional circumstances."
It advised visitors with tickets to check their emails and apologised for the inconvenience.
