Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel
Czech ammunition manufacturer STV Group told Delfi that Indian company Datasel, with which Estonia signed a contract, is a textbook example of a fraudulent company. STV Group has also been defrauded by Datasel and left without the goods it ordered.
STV Group representative Dominik Drda acknowledged that he is closely following the scandal in Estonia because Datasel advertises STV's products on its website and because STV itself has been defrauded by the same Indian company.
"They lie all the time and use every opportunity, however small, to avoid fulfilling their contractual obligations," Drda told Delfi.
In 2024, STV ordered ammunition from Indian company Datasel, but later discovered that it was an intermediary posing as a manufacturer. Datasel managed to deliver only 10 percent of the goods agreed upon and failed to return an advance payment worth millions of euros to STV. To resolve the situation and recover the money it is owed, STV Group is preparing to take Datasel to court. As the Czech government is procuring weapons for Ukraine as part of an international initiative, STV warned the government that Datasel was unreliable.
"We advised them not to let Datasel defraud them and not to enter into any contracts with the company. Fortunately, they listened to us," the STV Group representative said.
Estonia sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to the Indian company, which had never previously sold a single shell. Instead of complete military materiel, however, Estonia received a succession of new promises, and the dispute is now in court.
In August 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed its first sales contract with Datasel and transferred the first €15 million. The money did not come from Estonia's state budget, however, but from the European Peace Facility.
RKIK's current director general, Elmar Vaher, said he would not have signed the contract and that the decision was made by a very small group of people. He said, for example, that RKIK's head of procurement at the time knew nothing about it.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK at the time, disputed this account. He acknowledged that purchasing ammunition from third countries carries risks, but said no major decisions were made without the approval of ministry leaders.

Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:31:26 UTC
14:31:26 KST

A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.
In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.
The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.
While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.
Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.
Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb.
An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect.
“We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe.
“We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.”
The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.
Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.
“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.
A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.
Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

Landmark study exposes scale of brain injury crisis in rugby league
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:16 UTC
14:30:16 KST

Study on degenerative brain disease finds CTE in 31 former rugby league players
In short:
Of 51 brains of former rugby league players examined, 31 were found to have CTE.
The disease was found in players in their 20s, 30s and 40s, from amateur to professional levels.
The findings were presented at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
A landmark study has found that 31 rugby league players have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
Rugby league players in their 20s, 30s and 40s have been found to have had the degenerative brain disease, which can only be diagnosed after death.
Among them were decorated league footballer and NRL coach Paul Green, 49, as well as Manly Sea Eagles player Keith Titmuss, who was just 20 when he died.
The ABC has obtained the latest statistics, which are based on the first 150 brain examinations of people who played contact sports completed at the Australian Sports Brain Bank.
Of the 51 rugby league players' brains donated to the brain bank, 31 were found to have CTE. They played at various levels of the game, from amateur to professional.
The paper was presented by molecular biologist and data scientist Jennifer Cropley at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
CTE's sole cause is repetitive hits to the head and body. Symptoms can include memory loss, impulsivity, anxiety and anger.
The disease has been found in several athletes who have died by suicide, but experts say more research needs to be done to establish a "causal" link.
'I feel a massive responsibility'
Former league star Paul Green's widow Amanda Green is calling on all collision sports to do more for the next generation of players.
Experts have repeatedly called for football codes to ban contact until the age of 14.
Loading...
Ms Green has appealed for more people to donate their brains to understand the disease and wants more awareness around the issue.
"Now that we know what we do about this disease I feel a massive responsibility, as we all should, to protect the brain health of the next generation of young athletes," Ms Green said.
"I owe it to my kids and their sports-loving mates. We need to ensure they don't make the same mistakes as our generation did. The key here is to pledge our brains and support the incredible and potentially lifesaving work of the Australian Sports Brain Bank."
Ms Green said she had "no idea" about what CTE was until after her husband died.
"I had been involved in the highest level of professional sport in this country and did not understand this disease we now know as CTE," she said.
"That was not OK. I didn't know what CTE was, and since Paul's diagnosis, I have constantly called for more education on the issue. People needed to understand this disease so no-one else suffered in silence."
Green died by suicide in 2022.
Ms Green said that since learning about the disease, she could see her husband was showing CTE signs prior to his death.
"On receiving Paul's diagnosis from [sports brain bank director] Professor Michael Buckland, he had mentioned that Paul had one of the most severe cases of CTE that he had seen, but due to Paul's intelligence, there was a possibility that he had masked a number of his symptoms, but the symptoms I had seen were symptoms such as anxiety, impatience, he was impulsive in his decision-making, he definitely had lower levels of tolerance and quite elevated emotions," she said.
"These were changes that I had seen over time that I put down to the stress of his job."
Swinburne University professor Alan Pearce, who is an author on the paper which reveals the latest rugby league statistics, said more needed to be done to protect players.
"Given rugby league is a collision-based sport, it is not surprising that we found over 60 per cent of rugby league donors had CTE, but this tells us we need to start implementing modifications," he said.
"Introducing contact limits in rugby league is a good start, but rugby league and all contact and collision-based sports must also start modifying to non-contact versions for children to the age of 14 years of age.
"Keith Titmuss's result, having stage two CTE at 20, tells us that this is not an old person's disease.
"Keith passed in 2020, and his brain results typify that exposure risk for CTE starts at junior sport level.
"Keith played junior rugby league from the age of five years old, then schoolboy rugby union, and his brain results show the effect of that."
Titmuss played as a schoolboy at Newington College in Sydney and had had substantial exposure to repeated head impacts throughout his 15 years playing junior contact sport.
Titmuss died of exertional heat stroke after a 2020 Manly Sea Eagles training session.
His CTE diagnosis was revealed in 2024 and sparked warnings that the major football codes were not doing enough to protect young athletes. His parents Lafo and Paul donated his brain for research.
The latest rugby league statistics follow a Four Corners report in June, which revealed 33 Australian Rules footballers have been diagnosed with CTE and exposed the scale of the AFL's brain trauma crisis.
The Four Corners report triggered enquiries by WorkSafe Victoria and WorkSafe WA into incidents related to footballer safety.
Last month, a Boston University study revealed at least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have CTE.
The NRL has been contacted for comment.

City Governments Transform Industrial Buildings into Circular Construction Hubs in New York, London, and Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

During the last week of August, the New York City government announced a new project for the MADE Bush Terminal in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. It involves the transformation of the old industrial building into a center for the recovery, storage, sorting, and redistribution of construction materials during a one-year pilot program. The initiative echoes a wave of similar circular construction hubs recently launched or announced across Europe: a converted warehouse in Brussels, an industrial site adaptation in East London's Royal Docks, and a cross-border network supported by CirCoFin spanning Munich, Copenhagen, Lisbon, and Scotland, each repurposing industrial buildings and infrastructure to support the reuse of construction materials.
Brooklyn's MADE Bush Terminal (Manufacturers, Artisans, Designers, and Entrepreneurs) is a private urban redevelopment project transforming a historic 20-acre industrial property into a mixed-use hub for local producers, fabricators, and creatives. Century-old warehouses are being adapted to preserve the area's rich industrial heritage and to extend the useful life of existing materials on site. The new circular construction hub pilot program will be operated on site by a Brooklyn-based, certified M/WBE ecological landscaping firm that focuses on habitat restoration, low-waste landscape design and operations, and material reuse initiatives: Our Temenos. The partnership between NYCEDC and Our Temenos arose from an "Ideas for Impact" Request for Expressions of Interest (RFEI) submission, an open solicitation inviting nonprofits, startups, academic institutions, community organizations, and other mission-aligned entities to propose partnership opportunities that advance NYCEDC's economic development priorities.
The main purpose of the new circular construction hub in New York is to reduce waste, extend material lifecycles, and generate real-world data on the feasibility of reuse-oriented construction supply chains within New York City. According to DSNY Commissioner Gregory Anderson, "construction and demolition accounts for a massive share of New York City's waste stream." Testing new large-scale recycling projects therefore contributes to the institution's sustainability goals, as described in its Green Economy Action Plan and the operational guide Clean and Circular: Design & Construction Guidelines, dating from 2024. During the testing year, Our Temenos will act as hub operator, testing material intake, handling, and resale activities, while NYCEDC will evaluate the long-term operational model and economic viability through data collection. The collaboration aims to understand the infrastructure investments needed to scale interim material storage, handling, and reprocessing within New York City.
Related Article
A Second Life for Waste: 7 Ways to Recycle Building Materials
The initiative adds to other similar announcements in Europe, where past industrial heritage is being repurposed to serve sustainable development goals. In Brussels, city authorities announced plans to transform a disused warehouse in Ganshoren into a regional hub dedicated to the reuse of construction materials, in a project called "ReUse Park." With financial support from the 2021–2027 European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the project will convert an old, empty warehouse on the citydev.brussels Darwin site into a 6,000-square-meter regional logistics hub, where used building and deconstruction materials can be collected, sorted, and prepared, and where educational and training programs can be hosted for workers and companies in the construction sector. The project was launched in February 2026, and the official operator contract is expected to be announced in early 2027, following a public competition.
Another similar initiative is taking place on a site in East London's Royal Docks, owned by the Greater London Authority and earmarked for later development as part of Silvertown, an area currently undergoing regeneration led by public authorities. The industrial building's adaptation is being carried out by Tipping Point East, a circular construction hub founded in 2025 and organized into three operational areas run by its founding organizations: Material Cultures architecture and research practice, RESOLVE interdisciplinary design collective, and Yes Make, a design and build collective specializing in circular practice. Within the 8,000+ m² industrial site, they bring together material reuse, low-carbon construction, training, and cultural activities related to circular economies. Over five years, the hub is slated to divert just over 1,000 tons from landfill, a small share of the more than five million tons of construction, demolition, and excavation waste the U.K. sends to landfills each year.
In other European cities, such as Munich, Copenhagen, Lisbon, and across Scotland, CirCoFin – Circular Construction Finance is supporting the development of circular construction hubs that combine a physical material bank with a digital marketplace, enabling material traceability and efficient logistics. CirCoFin is a Horizon Europe project designed to accelerate the circular transformation of the region's construction sector by helping European cities create the infrastructure and financial mechanisms needed to support the reuse of building materials. It is a cross-border organization that provides administrative support to local governments and regional initiatives, offering a common, step-by-step approach to developing circular construction hubs that works across different contexts. It understands these hubs as local ecosystems that facilitate the circular reuse of secondary building materials through integrated services such as material logistics, storage facilities, digital marketplaces, and advisory support.
The reuse of construction materials is becoming increasingly commonplace in public and private buildings. In Sweden, construction is advancing on Gothenburg Grand Central, a new station building and prominent western entrance designed by Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter that incorporates material reuse as part of its architectural expression. At the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale, the Türkiye Pavilion will explore this concept in "Spolia Futures," examining the reuse of architectural elements as an evolving architectural method rather than solely a historical practice. Earlier this year, the AJ and The Architectural Review named architect Barbara Buser as the winner of the 2026 Jane Drew Prize, recognized as an innovator in the field of recycling and reuse and an expert in circular construction for pioneering repurposing practices in Switzerland.

Israeli officials do not currently expect a significant expansion of Britain’s restrictions on arms exports to be a central part of Tuesday’s announcement. Their assessment is that London will not substantially broaden those restrictions at this stage, in part because the remaining British military equipment supplied to Israel is considered limited but important.
The move comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between the two countries. For years, Britain largely confined its opposition to settlement expansion to diplomatic condemnations and guidance urging British companies to avoid economic activity in the settlements. Tuesday’s expected announcement would move that policy into direct economic action.
Jerusalem is preparing a forceful response and is expected to accuse the British government of intervening in Israeli politics at a sensitive point in the election campaign. Israeli officials are also waiting to see whether London announces personal sanctions in addition to the trade ban.

A Paris appeals court has shortened Le Pen’s electoral ban, allowing her to run despite upholding her conviction for misusing European Parliament funds. She has appealed to France’s highest court, which is expected to rule before the election, Reuters reported.
The latest Elabe polling places Le Pen at roughly 35% in the first round. Her nearest rival, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, remains below 21%. In a runoff, she narrowly leads Philippe and defeats every other tested opponent by a wider margin.
What a Le Pen presidency can mean for Ukraine
For Ukraine, the election is not an abstract contest between French parties.
France is a nuclear power, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and one of the EU’s two indispensable political heavyweights. The president is commander-in-chief, represents France internationally, and negotiates treaties. Parliament controls budgets and most domestic legislation, but the Elysee has exceptional influence over defense and foreign policy.
Macron has moved France well beyond general declarations of solidarity. Paris supports weapons deliveries, sanctions, Ukraine’s EU accession, and postwar security guarantees. France and Britain are also leading preparations for a multinational force that could deploy after a ceasefire, according to the Coalition of the Willing declaration.
Russia Appears to Break Its Own Three-Day Kyiv Truce Before Deadline
That makes the 2027 election central to two of Kyiv’s most important strategic objectives: maintaining military support and keeping its EU membership path open.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, France’s political position could be decisive for any attempt to move Ukraine toward membership in 2027. An accession treaty would ultimately require unanimous approval from every EU member state.
A French president would not need to abandon Ukraine publicly to damage its position. It would suffice to restrict how French weapons may be used, opposing a postwar force, weakening sanctions, or slowing EU decisions would be enough.
That is why Le Pen’s shift on Ukraine since 2022 matters, but so do the limits of that shift.
Le Pen changed her language, not her policy
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Le Pen openly promoted closer relations with Moscow. She treated Ukraine as part of Russia’s sphere of influence, refused to describe the annexation of Crimea as illegal, and argued that Europe should eventually build a strategic partnership with Russia.
Her party borrowed €9 million ($10.5 million) from a Russian bank in 2014. Le Pen met Putin at the Kremlin shortly before the 2017 French election. Her 2022 campaign printed 1.2 million leaflets featuring a photograph of that meeting. Russia’s invasion turned the image from proof of international stature into an electoral liability.
In a 2022 Kyiv Post interview, European policy expert Georgina Wright said Le Pen’s messaging about her closeness to Putin “died overnight.” Le Pen condemned the invasion, supported accepting Ukrainian refugees, and publicly backed Ukraine’s sovereignty and its right to political, financial, and military support.
The change was real – but it wasn’t complete either.
Le Pen still opposes sending French military personnel to Ukraine. She has said Kyiv should not be allowed to use French long-range weapons against targets inside Russia. In 2024, she said a National Rally government would block such strikes, a position that would reverse Macron’s policy.
She has also warned against sanctions that impose high costs on French households and presents negotiations, rather than Ukrainian military leverage, as the principal route to ending the war. In May 2026, she reiterated that France should leave NATO’s integrated military command while remaining a member of the alliance, Reuters reported.
Her rhetoric has occasionally moved further in Ukraine’s favor. When the Trump administration suspended US military assistance in March 2025, Le Pen called the decision “very cruel” for Ukrainian soldiers and emphasized the importance of American intelligence and technical support.
Where the other candidates stand on Ukraine
Edouard Philippe is the most electorally competitive pro-Ukraine candidate. During a May 2026 visit to Kyiv, he supported Ukraine’s accession to both the EU and NATO and backed deploying European forces after the fighting ends to deter another Russian attack. He would broadly preserve France’s current alignment with Kyiv.
Gabriel Attal offers even clearer continuity with Macron. As prime minister, he defended French deliveries of ammunition, air defenses, and long-range weapons. His presidential platform supports allowing Ukraine to use supplied weapons against military targets inside Russia. He has also advocated using frozen Russian state assets for Ukraine.
Raphael Glucksmann offers the strongest pro-Ukraine position on the left. He supports continued military aid, a harder European approach to Russia, and greater European defense capacity. His difficulty is electoral: he must unite moderate left-wing voters while attracting centrists without alienating supporters of Jean-Luc Melenchon.
Melenchon is the principal exception. He condemned the full-scale invasion but previously defended Russia’s annexation of Crimea and repeated Kremlin-aligned claims about Ukraine. He now prioritizes negotiations and French non-alignment while resisting a more NATO-centered European defense policy. His record, which Kyiv Post examined after France’s 2024 parliamentary election, makes him difficult for many pro-Ukraine Socialists, Greens, and centrists to support.
Bruno Retailleau, the candidate of the traditional conservative Republicans, has also backed Ukraine and chose Kyiv for his first foreign campaign trip. Green leader Marine Tondelier supports continued military assistance and stronger European security guarantees.
The result is a strategic imbalance. Le Pen has one consolidated party and a dominant position. The candidates most firmly committed to Ukraine are divided across the center, center-left, Greens, and traditional right.
Russian-linked disinformation networks have already targeted Glucksmann, Philippe, and Attal with fabricated stories and imitation news reports. France’s Viginum foreign-interference agency identified several operations, while Attal accused Moscow of trying to weaken Le Pen’s opponents because of the National Rally’s history of support for Russia, Le Monde reported. That political conclusion has not been independently established.
Le Pen is already through the first gate
France’s presidential election has two rounds. A committed base can secure a place in the runoff, but victory there requires a broader coalition.
Le Pen appears to have solved the first problem.
She received about 18% in 2012, 21% in 2017, and 23% in 2022. She then took more than 41% against Macron in the 2022 runoff.
She now polls at roughly 35% in the first round, close to twice the support of the best-placed alternative. A major legal, political, or personal shock would probably be required to keep her out of the runoff.
The second-round barrier has weakened as well. Macron defeated her by more than 10 million votes in 2017. Five years later, his margin fell to about 5.5 million. Current polling places Le Pen narrowly ahead even of Philippe, the opponent who performs best against her.
The 2022 gap was about 5.5 million votes. Le Pen could close it through a combination of new supporters and anti-Le Pen voters staying home.
The Le Pen name no longer produces the same reaction
Marine Le Pen’s father, the late Jean-Marie Le Pen, showed how France’s two-round system could produce a political earthquake and then contain it.
In 2002, the left split across multiple candidates. Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin missed the runoff by fewer than 200,000 votes, allowing Jean-Marie Le Pen to face incumbent President Jacques Chirac.
France mobilized against him. More than 3 million additional voters participated in the second round, and Chirac won more than four out of every five valid votes, according to the official results.
That response became known as the front republicain, or republican front: mainstream voters supporting almost any democratic opponent to block the far right.
Marine Le Pen has spent years weakening it. She expelled her father from the party, changed its name from the National Front to the National Rally, and shifted its public emphasis from its extremist origins toward purchasing power, public services, migration, and opposition to Macron.
The firewall still exists, but it is no longer automatic.
Macron received two-thirds of the runoff vote against her in 2017. In 2022, his share fell below three-fifths. Current polling suggests that no prospective opponent can count on the overwhelming cross-party support that carried Chirac or even Macron to victory.
France has already seen this erosion in parliamentary politics. After the 2022 legislative election, Kyiv Post noted that gains by both Le Pen and Melenchon would make French policy more difficult and unpredictable for Ukraine. The presidential race has now concentrated that same problem around control of the Elysee.
The electoral map has moved in her favor
Le Pen’s original strongholds were concentrated in the deindustrialized north and northeast and along the Mediterranean coast. Those regions remain important, but the National Rally is no longer confined to them.
In 2022, Le Pen finished first in more than 20,000 communes, compared with fewer than 12,000 for Macron, according to a commune-level analysis. By the 2024 European Parliament election, the National Rally led in more than nine out of every 10 French municipalities, according to Reuters.
Its support has spread through rural France and small and medium-sized towns, particularly in areas with lower incomes, less formal education, higher unemployment, and longer journeys to work.
Melenchon dominates a different France: major cities, working-class suburbs around Paris, parts of the southwest, and overseas territories. Glucksmann draws more support from educated, urban, and strongly pro-European voters. Philippe can compete across the center and traditional right.
Le Pen, however, has built the broadest geographical base of any opposition candidate. Her rivals remain stronger within narrower social and regional blocs.
Turnout could decide the election
France’s 2022 runoff showed how much of the electorate remained available but unconvinced. More than 13.6 million registered voters stayed home. Another 3 million cast blank or invalid ballots.
Those voters were not evenly distributed. In the first round, almost half of voters aged 25 to 34 abstained. Among people in their sixties, only about one in eight did, according to Ipsos.
Le Pen performed strongly among workers, employees, and voters who described themselves as disadvantaged. Macron dominated among managers, affluent voters, and people over 70, according to the Ipsos runoff study.
This creates both a weakness and an opportunity for Le Pen. Parts of her working-class and younger electorate are less reliable at the polls. But many voters who oppose her are also becoming less willing to support whichever candidate faces her.
In 2022, roughly four out of every 10 Melenchon voters did not cast a valid ballot for either runoff candidate. Current polling suggests that transfers between the left and center could be even weaker in 2027.
Le Pen therefore does not need France to become uniformly far right. She needs her opponents to remain divided into groups that increasingly refuse to vote for one another.
Melenchon, Glucksmann, and the search for another Macron
Melenchon came much closer to the 2022 runoff than is commonly remembered. He finished only 421,308 votes behind Le Pen, a gap small enough that a modest shift in urban turnout or support from other left-wing candidates could have produced a Macron-Melenchon runoff.
He remains capable of reaching the second round because the left is divided. But reaching it and winning it are separate questions. His strength among younger voters, major cities, and overseas France is offset by intense opposition from centrists, moderate social democrats, and the traditional right. Elabe’s current runoff test gives Le Pen roughly two votes for every one cast for Melenchon.
Glucksmann is more acceptable to pro-European centrists and moderate left-wing voters, but he does not yet have Macron’s 2017 opening.
Macron entered a race in which the Socialist Party had collapsed and the center-right candidate Francois Fillon was damaged by allegations that members of his family had received public money for parliamentary work. Macron occupied the vacant center, reached the runoff, and then benefited from a much stronger republican front.
No comparable lane exists today. Melenchon retains a large left-wing base. Philippe leads the center. Attal is competing for Macron’s former electorate. Tondelier represents the Greens, while other candidates draw smaller but potentially decisive shares of the vote.
Philippe is currently the strongest challenger because he can attract centrists, moderate conservatives, and some Macron voters. But Attal divides that constituency.
Glucksmann can unite parts of the center-left but must first overtake Melenchon without losing the voters he would need in a runoff.
Le Pen has already assembled the coalition she needs to reach the final round. Her rivals are still fighting over which one of them will be allowed to face her.
Just how likely is she to win?
Le Pen is more likely to become president than at any previous point in her career.
Her first-round position is dominant. Her legal path to the ballot has reopened. The National Rally’s vote is geographically broader, and the coalition prepared to stop her is weaker than it was in 2002, 2017, or even 2022.
Yet, she is still not inevitable. An eight-month campaign can erase a narrow runoff lead. Her electorate includes voters whose participation has historically been less reliable. A single mainstream challenger could still consolidate the center, moderate right, and parts of the left. Her appeal before France’s highest court also remains unresolved.
The difficulty is producing that challenger before the first round eliminates everyone else.
The most important figure is not Le Pen’s roughly 35% but the much smaller share currently divided among Philippe, Attal, Glucksmann, Melenchon, Retailleau, Tondelier, and the rest.
If that fragmentation survives until April, France’s republican firewall may not be defeated by a majority embracing Le Pen but by everyone opposing her separately.

Second-hand smoke: 2.7 billion exposed, 767 million of them children, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:09:42 UTC
14:09:42 KST

Second-hand smoke causes serious health harm, including heart disease, respiratory illness and cancer, and remains a leading cause of preventable death worldwide.
A third of the world’s population is exposed each year to second-hand smoke — also known as passive smoking — which continues to be a major source of illness and mortality among non-smokers.
An estimated 2.71 billion people around the world were exposed to second-hand smoke— a combination of two types of smoke inhaled by non-smokers — in 2023, contributing to 1.66 million deaths. This includes 767 million children under 15, who are especially vulnerable, along with 1.49 billion women.
These new findings come from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 study, published in The Lancet Public Health, which estimated second-hand smoke exposure and health impacts across 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Need for stronger regulation
Despite the scale of exposure, the study found that approximately 70% of the world’s population is not protected by comprehensive smoke-free laws.
As of 2024, only 79 countries, approximately 70% of them in the Americas, have achieved the highest protection standards of the World Health Organization framework — with all public places completely smoke-free or at least 90% of the population covered by legislation.
The proportion of the global population covered by comprehensive smoke-free legislation has increased from 3% in 2007 to 33% in 2024, now covering 2.6 billion people.
However, the authors noted that while smoke-free policies directly reduce smoke exposure, there is a need for extra measures such as tobacco taxation, marketing bans, plain packaging and cessation programmes.
Regional patterns
The researchers found that the number of people impacted by second-hand smoke exposure remained broadly the same globally, but rose sharply in sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa and the Middle East, which they attributed to population growth.
The exposure prevalence in the Central Europe, Eastern Europe and Central Asia region was 37.7% — higher than the global average of 33.9% — affecting 146 million people.
Most of the countries in Western Europe were included in the “high-income super region,” which showed some of the most significant progress in reducing passive smoking.
Denmark and Norway achieved some of the world's largest reductions since 1990, at -48,8% and -44,3%, respectively.
Broad health impacts
Beyond how many people are exposed, the report found that second-hand smoke accounted for the loss of 44.8 million years of healthy life and continues to be a major contributor to disability and premature death.
While a smoker inhales "mainstream smoke" through the cigarette's filter, non-smokers primarily breathe in sidestream smoke. This is unfiltered and contains higher per-unit concentrations of toxic and carcinogenic compounds than the smoke inhaled by the smoker.
The researchers estimated that second-hand smoke remains a substantial driver of global health loss, particularly through cardiovascular and paediatric respiratory diseases.
Exposure to tobacco smoke was associated with several health conditions, including stroke, lower respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, type 2 diabetes and cancers of the trachea, lung and breast.

At least 73 people were injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Tuesday, as it vowed a firm response to the latest escalation in hostilities.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen and the country’s most populous areas, launched attacks on targets in the Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, according to the coalition.
Coalition spokesman Col. Turki al-Malki described the escalation as “dangerous,” saying the Houthis had targeted civilian and economic sites in Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter and the de facto leader of OPEC.
“The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confront its hostile approach,” Malki said in a statement posted on X.
The attacks come amid renewed tensions between the Houthis and Riyadh. The group has been launching attacks toward Saudi Arabia since announcing a naval blockade against the kingdom in July, including strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.
The Financial Times reported Monday that facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Jazan had been struck in the latest attacks and that the extent of the damage was being assessed. Reuters said it was unable to independently verify the report, while Aramco had not commented.
The latest exchange marks a renewed escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis after years of conflict in Yemen, with the coalition now warning that further attacks on the kingdom will draw a military response.

Singapore ministers set for pay rise with entry-level pay up to US$1.4 million
First pay update since 2012 aims to ensure political salaries do not ‘fall further behind’ market rates, the prime minister says
The entry-level ministerial salary benchmark will rise to S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) from S$1.1 million, while the prime minister’s pay benchmark will increase to S$3.6 million from S$2.2 million, in line with recommendations made by an independent committee.
Wong said during a ministerial statement in parliament on Tuesday that he would donate the increase in his salary to “suitable good causes” but did not expect other political office holders to follow suit.
“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue. The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely and why many feel strongly about the matter,” he said.
Wong said as the prime minister he held “ultimate responsibility” for the salary framework. “So I want to be clear about how I will personally handle the increase and why I am taking these changes forward, because I believe they are in Singapore’s interests.”
The review was conducted by an eight-member committee formed in January, after a deferment amid geopolitical uncertainty arising from the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. The review, which is held once every five years, was initially set for 2023.

From Bulgari to Hilton: New hotels set to open across Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Planning a Turkish getaway? Here are some of the upcoming hotel openings to know about in Bodrum, Istanbul and Cappadocia.
Türkiye’s historic cities, turquoise coastal waters, and bustling cultural scene have long offered travellers a destination that combines weekend breaks with beach escapes, delicious food as well as a rich heritage.
With its tourism offerings evolving all the time, a new wave of hotels and resorts are set to give visitors even more reason to return – or, like me, board a flight for the first time to visit.
Whether you’re looking for an ultra-luxurious stay or sleek new properties, here are some of the upcoming hotels in Türkiye to have on your radar.
Bulgari Resort & Mansions, Bodrum
Travellers will have to wait a while as this new luxury Bulgari property will not be opening until 2028. It will be located in Bodrum, in the heart of the picturesque Türkbükü coast, where yachts and marinas are a common sight.
A short distance away from Bodrum’s bustling boutiques and entertainment centres, the Bulgari Resort & Mansions will feature 43 rooms and suites, alongside 40 standalone villas. Guests will be spoilt for choice of culinary concepts, including Bulgari’s La Spiaggia restaurant, Il Ristorante – Niko Romito, as well as Hoseki Japanese restaurant where dishes are served with a side of sweeping views as standard.
For those looking to get on the property ladder at an exclusive residential address, 101 Bulgari mansions will also feature as part of this development. With a choice of four mansion types offering between three and six bedrooms, the outdoor landscapes will include an infinity pool, as well as a garden that extends to a private beach.
NG Sign Hotel, Bodrum
This villa hotel is set to open in 2027, offering accommodation options ranging from two- and six-bedroom stays with plenty of glass surfaces – letting in the sun all throughout the day.
The Sign Villa can house up to 14 people across six bedrooms. Guests can also enjoy views from the large 300 square-metre private garden area. Whatever the season, the infinity pool is set to have both heating and cooling facilities.
Meanwhile, for smaller travel parties, NG Sign’s one-bedroom suites can accommodate two people and will feature ceramic flooring and wall tiles, as well as terraces for an ideal spot for viewing Bodrum’s horizon.
The hotel is set to have fitness, yoga and meditation areas alongside the Aliva Spa, where guests will be able to take full advantage of open-air massages alongside sea views, hammam treatments.
There will also be no shortage of dining spots, either. Guests will be able to have breakfast, brunch and lunch dishes at Egio Restaurant, seafood dinners at Ilios Restoran, pan-Asian cuisine at Signio, and sweet treats at Rosetta Patisserie.
Gist Istanbul, Tapestry Collection by Hilton
Slated to open in 2027, Hilton will be bringing 46 new keys to bustling Istanbul.
According to the hotelier, the Gist Istanbul, Tapestry Collection will be a stone’s throw away from the Bosphorus Strait, a 32-kilometre-long waterway connecting Europe and Asia, as well as Galataport, where visitors can enjoy waterfront dining, shopping and explore cultural hubs.
The hotel will also feature a restaurant and rooftop bar, and a fitness space for guests to use throughout their stay.
Also set to open next year is the brand’s Hilton Garden Inn Kocaeli Dilovasi in the country’s north west. It will feature 104 contemporary guest rooms, an in-house restaurant as well as wellness facilities, including an indoor pool, gym and Turkish hammam.
Les Temps Istanbul Karakoy, Curio Collection by Hilton
If 2027 and 2028 are too long of a wait, Les Temps Istanbul Karakoy, Curio Collection by Hilton opened its doors to guests this summer. On offer are a selection of 93 guestrooms and suites within the 1909-built Generali Han – a historic building on what was once Istanbul’s most important commercial hub, Bankalar Street.
Now restored and close by to destinations such as Taksim City Centre and the Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque, the property pays homage to its heritage with the Generali Han Suite accommodating up to three guests.
For rest and relaxation, the hotel’s La Calme Wellness area offers an array of treatments and therapies, including a steam room, sauna and cold plunge area. Meanwhile, the state-of-the-art gym is open 24 hours a day.
After working up an appetite, guests can either order room service or head to the Levantin Restaurant where breakfast, lunch and dinner is served. For lighter options, opt for Café du Temps, where Turkish sherbet, coffees and artisanal pastries can be enjoyed beneath the same ceiling that once hosted Istanbul’s bankers and merchants of old.
Fortuna of Cappadocia, Autograph Collection by Marriott Bonvoy
Nestled in the hillside village of Uçhisar, Marriott Bonvoy's Fortuna of Cappadocia, Autograph Collection hotel also opened in 2026.
Overlooking Cappadocia's extraordinary landscapes, the property includes 125 guest rooms and suites. It also features 28 private villas, with all stays designed to blend seamlessly with the surroundings, including its fairy chimneys.
The hotel’s Fortuna Table offers all-day dining inspired by the flavours of Cappadocia, while the Fortuna Terrace welcomes guests from the afternoon through to the evening, with Mediterranean offerings against a rooftop view.
Elika Cave Suites Cappadocia, Curio Collection by Hilton
Cappadocia is also the location of Hilton’s first cave hotel.
Elika Cave Suites Cappadocia, Curio Collection by Hilton features 36 keys, each with their own individual design, shaped by the original cave structure. Guests can choose between rooms with private pools, whirlpool baths, terraces and hot tubs, while the Elika Villa comes with a Turkish bath and sauna.
The hotel also boasts a gorgeous spa, with two treatment rooms, a hammam, steam room, sauna and rain shower as well as an outdoor pool.
On the food front, guests can try a mix of Cappadocian and Anatolian cuisine at Colastre.

The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

You might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?
For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.
This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.
A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.
Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.
Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.
Leaflets saying only the Greens, or only Labour, can win here are arriving through letterboxes – and it’s true, no one else is likely to. That Polanski is seeking the nomination boosts the Greens. Tot up issues where they challenge Labour, and many resonate with the student population. They oppose nuclear weapons and seem divided over increased defence spending. They back rent controls that Burnham has rejected. They oppose Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea oil and gas drilling, which may both be approved any day now. They want rapid nationalisation of utilities, where Labour hesitates. Locally they campaign on crime, mobile phone thefts and housing.
But it’s Gaza that may shift votes from Labour to Green: in the 2024 election, Starmer’s vote share was slashed and a pro-Palestinian, independent candidate came second with 18.9% of the vote. Arresting thousands for terrorism for silently holding placards supporting Palestine Action is another gift to the Greens. Labour instead points to impossible promises in the party’s £160bn tax, spend and borrowing pledges.
The Green campaign asks: “Why elect just another Labour MP, when a Green MP in parliament will challenge the government?” But this week Labour looks set to select not just “another Labour MP” but Sagal Abdi-Wali, Camden council’s leader and community organiser, popular with her party and a well-known dynamic force locally. Green criticism of Labour over Gaza comes up against a hijab-wearing Muslim woman who has spent years calming racial and religions tensions, and building relationships with many Jewish voters here, too. “If Greens stir up community antagonisms over Gaza,” she says to me, “that would be disgraceful”.
Reform has no foothold here but its attacks on her from afar may galvanise Labour people to come out and vote. Its poisonous home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spits out Reform’s usual ethno-nativist bile, pointing out on X that Abdi-Wali “was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” Georgia Gould MP, former Camden council leader, ripostes on X that she “has dedicated her life to public service” and is “the elected leader of Camden council, a community where she grew up and has lived for 35 years” who “embodies the best of our values … an outstanding example of British success”. Telegraph headlines similarly define her primarily as a “Somali refugee”. All this will remind Labour voters that fighting off the racist right is Labour’s great cause.
On the doorstep with Abdi-Wali, in a social housing estate, I saw how she is known and liked for her community work. She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism. But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will “never vote Labour again”. Not for Abdi-Wali? It’s all about Palestine.
Nonetheless, Polanski takes a big risk here after sliding in the polls. For Labour, the challenge is to show how Burnham’s raft of positive policies can ward off hopeless wishes and still reach the left with his hopefulness.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

UK retailers to create 100,000 placements for young people out of work

2026-09-08
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

UK retailers plan to create up to 100,000 short-term placements for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years to give them a first step on the ladder to paid work.
In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home, Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The move comes after the former health secretary Alan Milburn warned in a recent report that the 1 million Neets in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervened.
Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, welcomed the retailers’ initiative, saying too many young people were stuck in a vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities.
He said: “Six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. Unless we can increase work opportunities, Britain’s Neet crisis will get worse not better.”
Other employers signed up to the scheme include Tesco, New Look, Wickes, Currys and Greggs.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.”
The scheme, known as Opening Shift, follows the appointment earlier this year of the former M&S chief executive, Marc Bolland, to head a taskforce to tackle the growing youth unemployment crisis.
Bolland, who led the retail chain from 2010 to 2016, has secured the support of retailers for the work placement scheme amid warnings that the country risks a “lost generation” without urgent intervention.
Participants will continue to receive universal credit throughout their placement, mainly because of the logistical barriers claimants face when accepting short-term jobs that mean quitting and then rejoining the welfare programme.
The programme was developed with retailers through the British Retail Consortium and the DWP and has 11,305 placements already pledged.
Bolland, who is also a senior non-executive director at the DWP, is understood to have been chosen for the role thanks to his involvement with the charity Movement to Work, which had already helped more than 200,000 unemployed young people find jobs.
He said: “My work as founder and chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what’s possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people.
“Today’s announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain’s biggest industries and I’d encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.”
Each participant will be guaranteed an interview at the end of their placement, which will vary from 16 to 35 hours each week. Retailers will offer each recruit a “buddy” to help them navigate the new role, with the aim of moving as many recruits as possible into a job should one be available, Bolland added.
The DWP said it would use jobcentres to allow Neets to access the scheme.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the Neets crisis, given the industry’s scale and reach touching every corner of the country.
“Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the Neet crisis.”

José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

One of my favourite summer memories is making collares de moras as a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces. We’d always eat some too, of course, as well as wearing them, and we’d always come home with stained hands and big smiles. At the time, I never imagined that one day I’d be cooking sardines and pairing them with those same wild berries, but that’s the magic of food. The ingredients that filled my childhood with such simple joy have become part of the dishes I love creating today. Every time I make this recipe, it takes me straight back to those carefree summer days.
Grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
Prep 10 min
Cook 25 min
Marinate 1 hr+
 Serves 4
3 tbsp olive oil
  2 banana shallots, peeled and finely sliced
1 red or orange bell pepper, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely sliced
4-5 fresh thyme sprigs 
  2 tsp coriander seeds
  1 tsp black peppercorns
  1 small pinch chilli flakes (optional)
200ml white-wine vinegar, or cider vinegar
200ml white wine
  150g blackberries, washed
  Sea salt and black pepper
  8 good-sized fresh sardines, butterflied (ask the fishmonger to do this for you, if need be)
Heat a tablespoon of the oil, then gently fry the shallots and bell pepper for six or seven minutes, until lovely and tender. Add the thyme and spices, fry for a minute more, then add the vinegar, wine and 100ml water, bring to a simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced by about half. Stir in the blackberries, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.
Meanwhile, put the rest of the oil in a large nonstick frying pan on a high heat. Season the butterflied sardines inside and out, then fry them skin-side down for three or four minutes, until golden and crisp. Flip over and fry for just a minute longer on the flesh side.
Arrange the cooked sardines skin-side up and side by side in a suitable deep-sided dish, pour the warm escabeche all over the top, then leave to marinate and cool down for at least an hour. Serve at once, or cover and chill in the fridge until you’re ready to eat.

From crowns to pirates: Israel’s fringe parties turn election filing day into a spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:42:59 UTC
13:42:59 KST

Every Israeli election brings them back: the tiny parties with little expectation of entering parliament but every intention of making their appearance at the Central Elections Committee memorable. They were back Monday as candidate slates were formally submitted for the upcoming Knesset election, alongside the larger parties fighting to cross the electoral threshold and, in some cases, lead the next government.
This year’s breakout character was “Sharshar,” the stage name of Eitan Shvili, who arrived at the Knesset wearing a blue cape and crown to submit the slate of his party, “Sharshar for Love and Unity of the People.” 
The party requested the Hebrew ballot letters “Tzedek” (צדק), meaning “justice.” Even Central Elections Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg joined in, asking him: “Where is the queen?” Shvili said his slate included 12 candidates and described his mission as giving a voice to hundreds of thousands of Israelis suffering from post-traumatic stress and combat trauma. “I go everywhere and donate to soldiers. I want to unite the people. I will be Israel’s next prime minister,” he said.
The “queen,” he explained, is Tami, a travel agent who holds the No. 2 spot on the slate. “With God’s help, I’ll make sure she gets a position,” he promised. Shvili said Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana had already assured him he could walk through parliament wearing his cape and crown. “It’s a unique treatment method for post-trauma,” he said. Speaking to ynet later, this time without the cape but holding a large number of U.S. dollar bills, he added: “Netanyahu will be foreign minister in my government. The people are hungry for money, and I’m coming to put things in order. I’m 100% post-traumatic, and proudly post-traumatic.”
Immediately after Sharshar came the Pirates. Israel’s Pirate Party, which requested the Hebrew ballot letters “Tzaf” (צף), has contested elections since 2013 but has never crossed the threshold. This time, however, it arrived with a high-profile recruit: behavioral economist Prof. Dan Ariely, author of Predictably Irrational, who was placed third on the slate. Wearing a pirate hat, Ariely also found himself in an unusual exchange with Sohlberg, who jokingly asked whether the number he had received was “rational.”
“The party was founded at a time when there was internet piracy, in order to rethink intellectual property,” Ariely said. “After that, we added questions about what democracy is. People come once every four years and give up responsibility, and we think modern democracy needs more transparency.” He added: “We want to appeal to people who feel they don’t have a place. Those who haven’t found a political home should join us.”
Another slate registered Monday was “Gan Eden,” or “Garden of Eden,” which requested the Hebrew ballot letters ה or יה, both associated with the name of God. Its chairman, Yeshua Ben David, is described on the party’s website as its candidate for both prime minister and finance minister. Wearing a breastplate-style badge evoking the biblical High Priest, he said he would like to serve as a priest in the future Temple. “If I can’t, we’ll start with the Knesset. It’s a Sanhedrin,” he said.
The party platform calls for a partially religious-law-based state, sweeping debt forgiveness including the cancellation of mortgages, changes to the judicial system and the closure of the Welfare Ministry. Asked why he was running despite the party’s remote chances of crossing the electoral threshold, Ben David said: “I think that if we break through in the media, it will allow the people of Israel, who are getting a lot of judgments imposed on them here, to choose new parties.”
Who pays?
According to a report in the Israeli financial newspaper Calcalist, new parties competing in the election, including Naftali Bennett’s Beyachad and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, receive election financing according to the number of lawmakers they eventually bring into the Knesset, plus one financing unit worth 1.835 million shekels. Because Bennett is running on a joint slate with Yesh Atid, an existing parliamentary party, the two parties will receive public campaign funding separately and under different formulas.
When candidate lists are filed with the Central Elections Committee, parties are eligible for campaign-finance advances based on their existing number of Knesset members. New parties can obtain an advance of about 10 million shekels by providing a bank guarantee, protecting the state if they fail to cross the electoral threshold. A new party that wins at least 1% of valid ballots but does not enter the Knesset is entitled to one financing unit worth 1.835 million shekels; if it is left with unpaid debt, the guarantee can be collected.
After the new Knesset is inaugurated, parliamentary factions can also take out 54-month loans to cover campaign expenses and debts. Repayment is deducted from part of the monthly public funding each faction receives, currently about 98,000 shekels per lawmaker, while each faction also receives a fixed monthly payment of the same amount regardless of its size. Parties running together on joint slates receive that fixed payment separately even when they contest the election under one combined list.

Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:38:29 UTC
13:38:29 KST

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.
Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.
Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.
Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.
New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.
They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.
The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.
“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.
Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.
The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.
“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.
“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”
The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.
“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”
The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.
The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.
“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.
“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.
“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”
A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.
“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.
“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”
Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.
“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”
Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.
“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”
Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.

Letters Targeting Kashmiri Pandits Surface on Social Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:12:00 UTC
13:12:00 KST

Letters threatening Kashmiri Pandits that surfaced on social media in August have set off a wave of panic among members of the community living in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). They have revived memories of the “hit lists” and assassinations that forced around 350,000 Pandits to flee the Kashmir valley over 36 years ago.
Three letters, all issued in the name of the United Liberation Council (ULC), said to be a front organization of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, have surfaced on social media so far. The most recent letter, dated August 27, was explicitly linked to the Indian government reopening investigations into the massacre of Pandits by Islamist militants at the height of the anti-India militancy in the 1990s.
“If the SIA [State Investigation Agency of J&K] or any other agency is so eager to reopen closed cases involving migrant Pandits, they should also investigate cases like Bijebehara, Gawkadal, Sopore, Handwara, etc., where the so-called Indian mercenary security forces deliberately opened fire on innocent Kashmiris,” the letter said. “We will slaughter all those involved in these crimes no matter how much security they have.”
The first letter, dated August 7, named six Pandits working in the J&K government’s revenue department and included their cell phone numbers. It called on them to “change their ways.” The second letter, dated August 23, named six more Pandits and provided their residential addresses, including house numbers and street names. It described them as “white collar terrorists” and “traitors,” working for their “masters” in Delhi.
The letter’s contents were ominous. “Wherever you are and wherever you go, we are watching your every move,” it said. While the August 7 letter named Pandits working in the valley, the August 23 post listed Pandits in Jammu.
Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus and indigenous to the Muslim-dominated Kashmir valley. At the start of the militancy in 1989-1990, several Pandits, including Tika Lal Taploo, Neelkanth Ganjoo, Sarwanand Koul Premi and Virender Koul were assassinated. Sarla Bhat, a nurse, was abducted, raped and killed. Although militants claimed they were killed for their links to the Indian state – Taploo was a politician and Ganjoo was a high court judge—amid the rising tide of Islamism in Kashmir, it caused immense fear among the Pandits.
In an article I wrote for The Diplomat in 2020, I recounted what Ashok Dhar, a Pandit previously living in Baramulla in the valley, told me about what happened in 1989-90. “It was evident that Kashmiri Muslims wanted us to leave the Valley,” he recalled. Militant groups like the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front and the Hizbul Mujahideen brought out “hit lists” with names of Pandits to be eliminated. People shouted anti-Pandit slogans in mosques and at rallies. “They wanted sharia rule in Kashmir,” Dhar said, adding that Pandits were given a choice to convert to Islam or leave the valley.
Around 70,000 Pandit families comprising over 350,000 women, men, and children fled the valley in 1990. Dhar and his family were among them.
Most of the Pandits who left the Kashmir valley were subsequently housed in migrant camps in Jammu and Delhi. Many settled in other Indian cities. Most of them have never returned home. A few hundred families remained in the valley.
In its letters, the JLC has distinguished between those who remained in the valley and those who left. It is the latter that it is targeting now, the letters say.
While for most part, Pandits in the valley were left unharmed over the decades, Islamist militants have targeted the community periodically. The Lashkar-e-Taiba and the Hizbul Mujahideen massacred 23 Pandits, including four children, at Wandhama in 1997 and another 24 Pandits, including two children, at Nadimarg in 2003.
Memories of the terror they experienced remain deeply etched in the memory of Pandits.
Soon after the second letter emerged, Dhar, who now lives in Bengaluru, spoke to The Diplomat. The JLC’s lists providing names and other identifying details of Pandits “are no different from the hit lists of 1990,” he said.
Since 2008, when former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh announced a rehabilitation package, New Delhi has promised government jobs, cash doles, accommodation and security to Pandits returning to the valley. Yet this has not been enough to convince them to return in large numbers.
Continuing attacks on Pandits in the valley – in October 2021, for example, a pharmacist who stayed back in Srinagar, J&K’s capital, in 1990, was shot dead – have kept the community on tenterhooks. The government may have provided returning Pandits with tight security but since they live in clusters, they fear they are sitting ducks for Islamist militants.
In recent months, New Delhi has reopened investigations into several high-profile murders and massacres by militant groups in Kashmir. Among the cases that have been reopened are the rape and murder of Sarla Bhat, and the massacre at Wandhama.
These investigations could serve to meet the demands of Kashmiri Pandit organizations that have been demanding justice. But also, they will reopen old wounds.
Meanwhile, this is sure to prompt Kashmiri Muslims to demand justice in incidents of mass killings by the Indian security forces. The ULC referred to this in its third letter. “It appears to be positioning itself as a guardian of Kashmiri Muslim interests. But Kashmiris, “even the Muslims, are unlikely to be impressed as they have suffered for decades, even as the militant groups operated from the safety of camps in Pakistan,” Dhar said.
When two non-Kashmiri Indian laborers working at a brick kiln in Kulgam district in the valley were shot dead on July 31, analysts pointed out that militants were hitting “soft targets” as they were not strong enough to take on India’s security forces. The targeting of Pandit civilians is yet another example of militants seeking to assert their presence by intimidating unarmed people.
Should the letters prompt Pandits to leave again, it will deal a blow to New Delhi’s efforts to normalize the situation in J&K.

Breaking: Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment to Big Bash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:08:01 UTC
13:08:01 KST

Cricket Australia (CA) has agreed to invite private investment into the Big Bash Leagues, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades franchise.
The success of that process will determine whether CA considers taking other franchises to market.
What's next?
CA says it intends to have the Renegades playing under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.
Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.
The Cricket Australia (CA) board made the announcement on Tuesday, with the sale process of the Renegades to be the first venture into bringing private investment into the franchise T20 league.
CA is hoping the Renegades will play under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.
Depending on the success of the Renegades sale, CA said in a statement on Tuesday that it would "consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each State member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community".
CA chair Mike Baird said the decision was a major moment for cricket in Australia.
"Beginning the sales process for the Renegades allows us to take the first step in a self-determination model for our members and represents a defining moment for the game," he said.
"Importantly, CA and its members will maintain control over the most significant aspects of Australian Cricket operations, including international scheduling, player availability, the Big Bash Leagues' salary caps, branding proposals as well as the reserve price for a licence to operate that must be achieved, and approval of investors."
The move to bring private investment into the Big Bash Leagues has been debated for months.
CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said in May that private investment was "inevitable", and privatisation was thrust into the spotlight when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Renegades in June.
Baird said inviting private investment would allow cricket to grow at every level of the game.
"Cricket Australia and its state members are united in our commitment to investing in and growing the BBL and WBBL, and to advancing the interests of cricket at every level," he said.
"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash Leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level.
"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."
