Canada’s retaliatory tariffs take effect as US trade talks stall
- Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on US goods worth US$20 billion, with duties from 15 per cent to 50 per cent, escalating the 18-month trade war after failed negotiations in August.
- US tariffs target Canadian sectors like wine, furniture, and dairy, affecting 5 per cent of Canadian exports and causing uncertainty over the USMCA trade agreement's future.
- Despite rising tensions, Canada aims to keep trade talks open, with public support for Prime Minister Carney possibly declining as trade war impacts grow.
AI generated
OTTAWA – Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect just after midnight on Sept 8 as Prime Minister Mark Carney increased economic pressure on his country’s biggest trading partner after negotiations collapsed in August, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war.
The counter-tariffs cover US$20 billion (S$25 billion) of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 per cent to 50 per cent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics.
The dollar-for-dollar retaliation marks an escalation in the dispute between the neighbouring countries, and US and Canadian officials have traded blame for scuttling a deal that seemed close to fruition two weeks ago.
The rising tensions create uncertainty about the broader US-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) free trade agreement, which is up for annual review after US President Donald Trump declined to extend it for another decade.
“What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations.
“But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage,” Harvey said.
US tariffs hit Canadian wine, furniture and dairy
Trump’s tariffs implemented in August hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering US$20 billion, or 5 per cent, of Canadian exports to the US.
According to Canadian and US government data, Canada has shipped almost 68 per cent of total exports to the US in 2026, out of which roughly 80 per cent moved duty-free due to exemptions under the USMCA pact. Protections under the agreement have provided the domestic economy some resilience.
The new tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era US law, do not allow Ottawa to exercise USMCA exemptions.
Concerns about the USMCA’s future have fuelled uncertainty about investment and growth, as Canada wages a trade war against an economy 13 times its size.
Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.
Just 20 per cent of Americans approved of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefits both countries.
Trump threatened in August to raise US tariffs on all cars, trucks and automotive parts from Canada to 50 per cent starting Jan 1, and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
A government source said there are currently no talks between the two sides among ministers or government officials.
“The Canadian government needs to keep channels open to the United States and not go overboard in terms of rhetoric and reacting to the rhetoric from the American side, while waiting for the American decision-making process to come back to economics,” Harvey said. REUTERS

Ukrainian drones ignite blaze at Russia's Saratov Oil Refinery, locals report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:05:14 UTC
13:05:14 KST

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Saratov Oil Refinery in Russia overnight on Sept. 8, according to footage shared by locals on social media and analyzed by monitoring groups.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Residents of Saratov reported explosions and a fire at the refinery overnight, posting photos and videos of the attack. Independent Russian outlet Astra analyzed the footage and concluded based on geolocation that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and was burning.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin later said that 10 people, including three children, were injured in the attack. Six were hospitalized, though none were in life-threatening condition, according to the governor. Busargin did not specify the target of the strike.
Residents of the Saratov Oblast town of Engels also reported air defense activity near the Engels-2 military airfield, home of Russia's strategic bombers. It is not yet clear whether the base was hit.
Russian regional authorities also reported casualties and damage elsewhere.
In Belgorod Oblast, attacks over the past day killed one person and injured four others, while regional authorities claimed that 130 drones had been downed or suppressed.
In neighboring Kursk Oblast, three settlements lost power after a drone struck a power line in the Belovsky district, according to the Russian Telegram channel Pepel Kursk. The channel also reported damage to homes and a shop, as well as a separate drone strike on an energy facility in the Khomutovsky district.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 384 Ukrainian drones were intercepted and destroyed overnight over multiple Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports at the time of publication.
The Rosneft-owned Saratov refinery is a major oil-processing facility that has been targeted by Ukrainian forces in multiple previous strikes. The plant has an annual processing capacity of about 4.8 million tons and produces over 20 types of petroleum products, including gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen.
According to Ukraine's General Staff, the Saratov Oil Refinery helps supply the Russian military.
The General Staff confirmed a successful strike on the facility on Aug. 2. A month before, a July 8 strike forced the plant to halt processing after its only crude distillation unit was reportedly damaged.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone campaign, contributing to fuel shortages and pushing Russian refinery output down sharply over the summer.
The reported Saratov strike came as Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones overnight, bringing the respite afforded by a brief diplomatic pause in attacks on the capital to an abrupt end.

Houthi attacks injure 73 civilians in southern Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
04:03:23 UTC
13:03:23 KST

At least 73 civilians were injured following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group targeting cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said Tuesday.
At least 73 civilians were injured in Houthi attacks targeting cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, Saudi authorities said Tuesday, as Riyadh warned against continued attacks on civilians and commercial shipping.
In a statement, the Saudi Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on civilian and economic facilities in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, saying they injured 73 civilians, including women and children.
The ministry also denounced the group’s continued targeting of commercial vessels in the Red Sea, saying the attacks threaten freedom of international maritime navigation.
It reiterated Saudi Arabia’s rejection of what it called the Houthis’ “hostile approach and criminal behavior,” saying they threaten the security and stability of Yemen and its Arab and Islamic surroundings and undermine peace efforts.
The ministry affirmed the kingdom’s right to take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty and national capabilities and protect the security and safety of its citizens and residents.
It also warned against the Houthis’ continued targeting of civilians and civilian facilities and called for an immediate halt to all forms of escalation and continuing threats to maritime security.
Riyadh called on the international community to shoulder its responsibilities and implement relevant UN Security Council resolutions, particularly resolutions 2216 of 2015 and 2722 of 2024.
In a separate statement, the Saudi Energy Ministry said fires broke out at energy facilities and installations following attacks in the country’s southern region.
The attacks caused a temporary halt to some operations at the targeted sites, the ministry said, adding that specialized teams had begun containing the fires and securing the facilities.
Separately, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of launching “senseless attacks” against civilian and commercial sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran.
Al-Maliki characterized the strikes as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty.
He accused the group of deliberate “extremist and criminal behavior” that undermines peace and stability in Yemen and neighboring Arab states.
Al-Maliki affirmed that the Joint Forces Command of the coalition would deploy “all necessary operational measures” to deter the attacks and protect Saudi citizens.
The coalition also vowed to take all necessary measures to neutralize the sources of the threat.
In a concurrent statement, the Yemeni army declared its “complete readiness” to stand “steadfastly” alongside Saudi Arabia.
The military leadership backed Riyadh’s “absolute right to take whatever measures it deems appropriate” to defend its security, stability and sovereignty, expressing preparedness to coordinate to “eliminate the sources of threat and chaos.”
The attacks came as Yemeni government forces reported significant battlefield gains on Monday across four separate fronts.
According to Yemen’s official Saba news agency, the military advances took place in the Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda, Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates, following a vow by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi to sustain operations until state authority is fully restored.
The recent fighting has raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict, disrupting a relative lull observed since April 2022.
Yemen has suffered nearly 12 years of war since the Iranian-backed Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.
The Houthis have also targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea, while Saudi Arabia, the principal external actor backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government, announced a mission in July to form an international maritime alliance.
Fires broke out at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia following attacks targeting the sites, the Saudi Energy Ministry said Tuesday.
The ministry added in a statement that the attacks caused a temporary halt to some operations at the targeted facilities.
“Specialized teams have begun containing the fires and securing the affected sites,” it said.
The statement came after Saudi authorities said early Tuesday that attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group targeted civilian and economic facilities in the southern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi-led coalition called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and vowed to take necessary operational measures to neutralize the sources of threats.
Two children were killed and 15 people injured in Houthi shelling targeting a gathering of displaced people in Yemen’s central Marib province, local authorities said Tuesday.
The government-run local authority said in a statement that the Houthis fired several projectiles at a gathering of displaced people in the Raghwan district in northern Marib on Monday evening.
The attack killed two children and injured 15 people, including eight children, it said.
The shelling also caused extensive damage to the homes and property of displaced families.
According to the statement, around 16 shelters and their contents were destroyed, leaving 23 families without accommodation and basic belongings, while three vehicles were also damaged.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthi group on the statement.
Yemen’s Houthi group on Tuesday confirmed carrying out large-scale missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and vowed to continue operations deep inside the kingdom amid a sharp escalation between the two sides.
In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group carried out a “large-scale” military operation using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
He said the attacks targeted Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as Khamis Mushait Air Base.
Saree claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and caused extensive damage to the targeted facilities.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was in response to Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, claiming that Saudi Arabia had carried out 121 strikes over the past three days in Marib, Al-Bayda, Al-Hudaydah, Taiz and Al-Jawf provinces.
He also accused Saudi Arabia of striking the Central Prison in Al-Hazm, Al-Jawf, causing casualties among inmates and visitors, including women and children.
“We will continue our operations deep inside Saudi territory, target its military buildups, and consolidate the equation of ‘blockade for blockade’ until the aggression stops and the blockade on our dear country is lifted,” Saree said.
The statement came after Saudi authorities said earlier Tuesday that Houthi attacks on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran injured at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi Energy Ministry also reported fires at energy facilities in the kingdom’s southern region and said some operations at the targeted sites were temporarily halted.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and said the coalition would take all necessary operational measures to deter the Houthis and neutralize sources of threats.
The Yemeni army said Tuesday that it had recaptured the Al-Yatmah area in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen from the Houthi group.
“Our armed forces managed to liberate the Al-Yatmah area in Khabb wa Al-Shaaf district in Al-Jawf from the grip of the Houthi militias,” the army said in a statement.
It said the development came amid continued field advances against the Houthis, without providing further details.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthi group.
Al-Yatmah is one of the key areas in the strategic Al-Jawf province, which is located near the Saudi border. It shares border with the oil-rich Marib province, one of the most important strongholds of the internationally recognized government.
For days, military confrontations have escalated between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda provinces, alongside airstrikes on the group’s positions.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday condemned fresh attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group targeting cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia.
"I condemn in the strongest terms, the cowardly attack by Houthis targeting civilian and energy facilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which have left many people injured," Sharif said in a post on the US social media company X.
Pakistan, he said, stands in "unwavering" solidarity with the Saudi leadership and its people.
"Such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the Kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all those injured," Sharif added.

Canada's counter-tariffs take effect on several US goods as trade war reignites
Canada's counter-tariffs on billions of dollars in US products took effect Tuesday, as a trade war between the two countries heated up. Ottawa's pushback comes weeks after US President Donald Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products, over what Washington deemed as "discriminatory treatment" against US alcohol, automobile and dairy industries.
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars in US products took effect Tuesday, as a trade war between the North American neighbours heats up.
The announced duties of 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent apply to $27.6 billion (US$20 billion) in imports from the United States, covering steel and aluminum products as well as dairy goods like cheese. But Canada removed some seafood products from the initial list.
Ottawa's pushback comes weeks after US President Donald Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products, over what Washington deemed as "discriminatory treatment" against US alcohol, automobile and dairy industries.
The US tariffs hit items like hockey sticks and cement, impacting about 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States.
On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales of Canada's Bombardier Aviation in the United States, unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
"No more selling Bombardier in the United States!" Trump posted in all caps on his Truth Social platform, though he did not specify how he would achieve a sales halt.
Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines' domestic fleets.
In a statement Monday, the aerospace company touted its creation of "tens of thousands of jobs across the United States", with "direct employment" in more than 20 states, including Kansas, Texas, Arizona and California.
The company also noted that it spends over $2.5 billion annually with suppliers, and said its supply chain is "made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states".
"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," the company's statement said.
US tariffs pose a modestly negative risk to Canada's overall economy, but analysts note that they have a sharper impact on Central Canada's manufacturing sector.
Negotiations between both sides broke down August 21 after days of meetings in Washington, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney saying he decided to suspend the trade talks.
Read moreTrump threatens to ban Canadian Bombardier jets from US market
At the time, Carney said the Trump administration's terms were ultimately unacceptable, adding that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the eleventh hour.
US officials also made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture", he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.
But Trump's top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted that the US government is aware that French language protections are sensitive and important.
"This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line," he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month.
War of words
Ottawa and Washington have not resumed negotiations since, and have continued trading barbs.
Asked if both sides were in a trade war, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week (Aug 31) that he did not think one could be in a tit-for-tat fight with a country that is 13 times larger.
"We're not at war with Canada," Bessent said on the sidelines of a G20 finance leaders' meeting. "How are we going to be at war with Canada? They're going to take their two set submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us?"
He was referring to a former attraction at a shopping center in the Alberta province.
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth separately appeared to mock the physical appearance of a Canadian soldier on social media.
Read moreHow the French language became a sticking point in the US-Canada trade war
Carney said a day later that the remarks were "beneath their office", adding that this was "not constructive".
He said both sides can have discussions "when the Americans stop doing memes" and start being serious.
Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as "Lake America".
This has sparked anger in Canada, amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by Trump's hostility.
At the start of his second presidency, Trump also ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America. He has made claims that Canada should become the 51st US state as well.
Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbour. Nearly 60 percent of Canada's imports come from the United States and about 70 percent of its exports go to the US market.
To help businesses and workers, Canada's government has unveiled an aid package of $7.5 billion (US$5.4 billion).

China says imports and exports surged in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
03:59:25 UTC
12:59:25 KST

The country's imports and exports saw robust growth in August, official data showed on Tuesday, helped by a global AI buildout that has fuelled demand for Chinese tech.
In US-dollar terms, exports spiked 25 percent year-on-year while imports jumped 28.2 percent, the General Administration of Customs (GAC) said.
Shipments to the United States climbed 34.4 percent year-on-year last month, compared with the 17 percent increase seen in July.
The 28.2 percent rise in imports last month was faster than the 27.5 percent year-on-year increase in July.
Both exports and imports registered double-digit growth for a fourth straight month, and import growth exceeded that of exports for a sixth successive month. 
Meanwhile, the country's trade surplus came in at US$119.09 billion in August, up from US$112.5 billion the previous month.
After achieving an historic trade surplus in 2025, China's trade has continued to boom this year, due largely to heightened overseas demand for semiconductors, computing hardware, electric vehicles, and products linked to the artificial intelligence boom.
In January through August, the value of China's exports of computers and related parts surged 49.4 percent, the GAC data showed.
“China is very competitive in its tech goods exports,” said Chi Lo, a senior market strategist for Asia Pacific at BNP Paribas Asset Management. 
“China has moved aggressively up the value chain and has become a major player in AI infrastructure and industrial automation,” he said.
The boom in exports contrasts with the weaknesses in domestic consumption, investment and the property market. 
While the AI wave has lifted the profits of advanced manufacturers, industries relying on the domestic market have been grappling with producer price inflation and soft demand.
Premier Li Qiang in August called for efforts to stabilise external demand and expand international trade cooperation while acknowledging insufficient domestic demand, hardships facing industries and companies as well as rising uncertainties in the international environment.
A trade truce between Beijing and Washington, reached late last year, has held despite on-and-off frictions. 
The two countries are now exploring reciprocal tariff cuts on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side as they prepare for another summit between President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump in Washington DC later this month. (Xinhua/Agencies)

Zelensky said the US envoys – who held separate talks with the Ukrainian and Russian leaders – told him that “the Russians are ready to negotiate”.
“Russia really thinks that this winter can help them to break us,” he told Axios.
But the administration of US President Donald Trump could pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to de-escalate, he added, and Putin “doesn’t want” to “upset” his US counterpart.
Zelensky said the weekend talks included US proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
The Ukrainian leader said the US approach aimed to resume negotiations between the warring countries and ensure the coming winter was different from previous ones.
The goal was to make progress before or during winter in order to “bring (the) sides closer to the peace,” Zelensky said. AFP

LGBTQ dating app faces hefty payout over HIV data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
03:52:09 UTC
12:52:09 KST

LGBTQ dating app faces hefty payout over HIV data
US-based LGBTQ dating app Grindr has agreed to a multi million-pound settlement in a UK lawsuit alleging it shared users’ private information, including their HIV status, with advertising companies without consent.
The £26 million ($35 million) settlement covers claims brought by around 12,000 users over the company’s handling of personal information before early 2020. Grindr disputes the allegations.
“The settlement includes no findings or admission of liability,” Grindr said in a US regulatory filing submitted late last week. It nevertheless acknowledged the “distress and loss of trust” expressed by some users.
The legal action was launched in April 2024 by law firm Austen Hays at the High Court of England and Wales. Information allegedly disclosed also included HIV test dates and whether users took medication to prevent infection, according to the firm. Anonymity orders were granted to protect those bringing the case.
Under the settlement, reached on September 2, Grindr will pay £13 million by the end of this year and another £13 million by March 31, 2027. Individual awards have not been specified, and legal and insurance costs will be deducted under the terms published by Austen Hays.
Founded in 2009, Grindr was owned by Chinese gaming group Beijing Kunlun Tech during the period covered by the UK claims. It was sold in 2020 after the US authorities raised concerns that American users’ personal information could be accessed by China’s government. The company said it had since overhauled its privacy program.
In 2018, Norwegian researchers found that Grindr had shared users’ HIV status with two analytics providers. Grindr subsequently announced that it would stop the practice.
In a separate case, Norway’s data protection authority fined Grindr 65 million Norwegian krone ($7 million) in 2021 for sharing personal information for advertising without valid consent. An appeals court upheld the penalty in October 2025.
The court also found that Grindr’s assurance that it did not sell users’ personal information to third parties for advertising was misleading, according to the Norwegian Consumer Council.

COLOMBO, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka is developing a national strategy to standardize, test and commercialize drone technology as its use expands across agriculture, industry and other sectors, the Ministry of Science and Technology said in a statement on Monday.

====================================================================================================

How the Nepal-Tibet disaster became the latest victim of China’s ‘Clean Internet’ campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
03:14:43 UTC
12:14:43 KST

Tsering Phuntsok watched news of the Nepal-Tibet flood unfold from thousands of miles away in southern India. The 46-year-old Tibetan in exile has missing family members on both sides of the border; those in Nepal are named in official government lists, but in Tibet he has received no information.
“I have started praying for the lost ones now. I have to accept they will not return [because] … I’m not getting any information.”
The flooding disaster is an example of the increasing use by Chinese authorities of “Clean Internet 2026”, the latest version of a long-running campaign by the Ministry of Public Security that criminalises anything officials regard as false information, which includes unofficial accounts of the floods.
It follows a well-established playbook in which authorities promote official narratives, suppress independent accounts, discourage efforts to look back at the causes of a disaster and punish those who post claims that differ from the government-approved narrative.
While earlier versions of the campaign focused on cybercrime and hacking, it is increasingly being used to target what the authorities call “rumours” which include unofficial information about the disaster.
“The campaign serves a dual purpose. Tackling genuine problems like fraud and misinformation while tightening control over public narratives,” says Tencho Gyatso from the International Campaign for Tibet, a US based Tibetan advocacy group. “That dual purpose is what makes it more nuanced and challenging to criticise.”
In the hours after the floods, researchers say they saw a huge surge in interest across Chinese social media. The topic was trending, but then fell away as comments were removed in real time.
Screenshots seen by the Guardian show the Chinese app WeChat restricting posts about the floods. In one case, a user was notified by WeChat that a post about the flooding had been reported and then deleted for containing “politically sensitive content”. Another was stopped from being shared. It was said to be “unavailable due to policy violation” and that it contained “prohibited content”.
“[The trend] was constantly shifting and being manipulated because there was real interest,” says David Bandurski, director of the China Media Project, a research group that monitors Chinese media. “A ‘crackdown’ is not the right word, because they don’t crack down. It’s a consistent, persistent, everyday application of a policy of public-opinion guidance.”
On 30 August, four days after the disaster, police in Tibet reported 10 cases under the Clean Internet 2026 campaign relating to “rumours” about the disaster. In the majority of cases there were claims that more than 1,000 people had been swept away in the floods. So far, Chinese authorities have released a death toll of 43. Human rights and Tibetan advocacy groups have accused the Chinese government of concealing the true scale of the death toll.
The police notice said that spreading of “rumours” “misleads the public and disrupts online order” and it intended to “ensure that disaster relief work proceeds smoothly”.
A user from Jiangxi, a province 3,000km away from the disaster, posted on a video platform claiming “the number of missing people had risen to 826”. According to the police report the user faced “administrative punishment” without specifying what that involved.
‘Proving that the state is working hard’
One former Chinese state media journalist, who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, says control in times of crisis also works through simple omission of information as much as suppression: “Official news coverage devotes enormous space to proving that the state is working hard, but gives very little information answering the most basic questions: who is missing? Where were they last seen? Which buildings have been searched?
“Controls have become much stricter, especially regarding the internet, though there are nuances, as there are still ways to bypass restrictions. For instance, by posting quickly or using veiled language to get content through,” they say.
But allowing some reporting can serve the interests of central authorities, says one former CGTN editor who worked at the broadcaster during the Covid pandemic and who also asked not to be named for fear of reprisals.
“The government needs journalists to uncover uncomfortable truths because it needs accurate information in order to govern effectively,” they say. “But if journalists are given completely free rein to uncover and publish those truths, they may expose things that are politically uncomfortable or challenge the interests of the state.”
Bandurski says: “The [Communist] party sees itself in a global public-opinion struggle. It is wrestling with the world fighting to get its view out. This is how China sees information globally, in a very, very oppositional framework.”
Phuntsok hopes his family on the Nepal side could still be alive. His grandfather, Wangyal, uncle Janngchup, aunt Sumchok and their young child Yeshi Dorjee are still missing.
On the Tibet side he is unwilling to share the names of his missing relatives with the Guardian for security reasons.
Kalsang Jigme, a Tibetan journalist based in New Delhi, says: “Normally, when there’s some disaster, people are very active, praying and support, and they send goods to the affected area. But this time they’re completely silenced.”
Additional research by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

CANBERRA, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The total value of Australia's residential dwellings fell 0.3 percent in the June quarter of 2026, marking the first quarterly decline since September 2022, official data showed on Tuesday.
Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed the total value of residential dwellings fell by 34.1 billion Australian dollars (24.6 billion U.S. dollars) to 12.7 trillion AUD (9.1 trillion USD) in the June quarter.
"The value of dwelling stock fell for the first time since the September quarter 2022," said Mish Tan, ABS head of finance statistics.

In value terms, residential dwelling stock fell 2.0 percent in New South Wales, 1.6 percent in Victoria and 0.7 percent in the Australian Capital Territory during the quarter.
Despite the quarterly decline, the total value of Australia's dwelling stock remained 8.5 percent higher than a year earlier.
The number of residential dwellings increased by 54,400 during the quarter to 11.53 million. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Japan posted a current account surplus of 2.99 trillion yen (about 19.2 billion U.S. dollars) in July, returning to the black for the first time in two months, government data showed Tuesday.
The surplus increased 15.6 percent from a year earlier as the services deficit narrowed on improvements in travel and other businesses, while the primary income surplus rose on increased dividend receipts from overseas subsidiaries, data released by the Finance Ministry showed.
Primary income, which reflects earnings from Japan's overseas investments, rose 5.8 percent to 4.29 trillion yen.
Among other key components, the goods trade balance registered a deficit of 399.9 billion yen. Breaking it down, exports grew 24.1 percent to 11.26 trillion yen, while imports climbed 25.9 percent to 11.66 trillion yen.
The current account balance is one of the widest gauges of international trade. ■

S. Korea's revised real GDP grows 0.6 pct quarter on quarter in Q2
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:14:27 CST
12:14:27 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's revised real gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, grew 0.6 percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter, as exports and consumption held up, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The second-quarter growth was unchanged from the preliminary figure released on July 23, stabilizing at a healthy level after sharply rebounding 1.8 percent in the first quarter. Real GDP retreated 0.1 percent in the final quarter of last year, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Exports, a key driver of the export-driven economy, climbed 1.3 percent quarter-on-quarter in the April-June quarter thanks to strong demand for semiconductors, machinery and equipment, while imports rose 0.7 percent, led by automotive and industrial equipment purchases.
Private consumption added 0.4 percent, propelled by gains in both goods and services, while fiscal spending inched up 0.1 percent on higher outlays for healthcare insurance benefits.
Intellectual property investment advanced 3.4 percent on growth in research and development (R&D) and software development.
Facility investment ticked up 0.2 percent owing to an expansion in machinery, notably semiconductor manufacturing equipment, but construction investment slipped 0.1 percent due to sluggish civil engineering projects.
Nominal GDP increased 9.2 percent in the second quarter compared to the previous quarter.
On a year-on-year basis, nominal GDP soared 26.4 percent in the second quarter, marking the highest growth rate in 47 years since the third quarter of 1979.
Nominal gross national income, which measures the combined income earned at home and abroad by people and businesses, expanded 8.8 percent in the April-June quarter from three months earlier.
The GDP deflator, or the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP that gauges changes in prices of all goods and services produced in the country, jumped 21.9 percent year-on-year in the second quarter. ■

Accused killers of American and Australian surfers go on trial in Mexico
Three men accused of killing two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot went on trial Monday, two years after their killings in a suspected robbery.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico's Pacific coast in April 2024 when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies.
They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing, and they bore gunshot wounds to their heads.
The Robinsons' parents traveled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings.
Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.
"It's about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here," her partner, Martin Robinson, had earlier told reporters.
"We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why," he said.
The surfers were reported missing on April 27, 2024, while camping in Ensenada. The assailants "intentionally surprised the surfers and shot them with firearms, taking their lives on Sunday, April 28," according to the prosecution. Their bodies were found on May 3, 2024.
Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent.
Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the "commotion" began.
"I heard a lot of noise," he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him.
He said they warned him that "the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him" if he said anything.
Ary Gisell Silva, the girlfriend of the witness's stepfather, was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery in order to steal the pickup's tires.
According to evidence presented by the prosecution, Silva was the first to make contact with the tourists and noticed they had valuables. Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had "good phones and good tires."
The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, where the surfers' friends and families galvanized a major search on social media for their bodies.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the U.S. His brother Jake Robinson was pursuing a career in medicine. He had traveled to the U.S. to visit his brother and was about to start a job as a doctor upon his return to Australia, CBS News' partner network BBC News has reported.
Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry. His fiancée had told the court, "He was my safety in the world. My life is now a nightmare," the BBC reported.
Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.
Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico's Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Dedicated Freight Corridor to become fully operational as PM Modi set to inaugurate final three sections of Western DFC, linking JNPT Port to Dadri. (Representative Image)
NEW DELHI: Nearly 20 years after the Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) project was approved, India’s freight rail network linking eastern, northern and western regions will become fully operational Tuesday, when PM Narendra Modi inaugurates three remaining sections of Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) today.WDFC connects Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Mumbai with Dadri in UP, where it intersects with Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor (EDFC), completing the country’s dedicated freight rail backbone.
On the eastern side, the DFC from Sonnangar in West Bengal to Ludhiana in Punjab is fully operational. Though EDFC was originally planned from Dankuni in West Bengal, a 538-km section from Dankuni to Sonnagar was de-scoped from the DFC project and multi-tracking of this part is now being carried out by railways.After its inauguration, the 2,843 km of WDFC and EDFC will become operational.In a statement, PMO said three sections — New Sanand-New Makarpura, New Umbergaon-New Saphale and New Saphale-New JNPT sections — that Modi will dedicate to the nation covers 326 route km and has been built with a more than Rs 20,700 crore investment.
Direct connectivity of Jawahar Lal Nehru Port will facilitate faster movement of export-import cargo, strengthen connectivity between industrial centres and ports, reduce logistics costs and help decongest Mumbai’s railway network, it said.
Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that before 2014, no physical work had been completed on the project. NDA govt took this forward by addressing long-pending challenges and resolving issues across different sections.According to railways, as of Aug, the already operational DFC stretches had handled approximately 5.2 lakh freight train trips, averaging around 435 trains per day. The dedicated freight network has generated around 658 billion gross tonne km (GTKM) and 360 billion net tonne km (NTKM).

Argentina says it will file criminal charges against energy company in Falklands row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:29:59 UTC
11:29:59 KST

Argentina’s government said on Monday it will file criminal charges against the Israeli energy company Navitas Petroleum and its executives for operating in the Falkland Islands.
The move follows remarks on Friday by the Argentina president, Javier Milei, who vowed to sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory as he stepped up the South American nation’s sovereignty claims.
According to a statement from the presidency, foreign minister Pablo Quirno will file the criminal complaint against several Navitas subsidiaries and partners operating in the territory, along with their corporate directors.
Navitas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
The government alleges the firms violated Argentinian law by holding hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation licenses issued by the UK in the North Falkland Basin.
Milei last week singled out the Sea Lion offshore oil project as he announced measures targeting companies involved in Falklands oil and gas activities, with penalties potentially extending to shareholders, directors and suppliers.
The Sea Lion field is operated by Tel Aviv-listed Navitas Petroleum, which holds a 65% stake.
Gideon Tadmor, a prominent figure in Israel’s energy sector and the company’s chair, holds about 9% of its shares, according to LSEG data.
Last week Milei said in a televised address that “winds of change” favourable to Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands are blowing around the world, after Donald Trump had earlier suggested he was reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the South Atlantic islands.
Officially, the US takes a neutral position on who has rightful sovereignty over the islands, which Britain first claimed in the late 17th century and has held almost continually since 1833. In practice, Washington recognises British administration over the territory, which was the subject of an Argentinian invasion and subsequent military conflict with Britain in 1982.
In response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the Falklands, Trump last week said: “I always review every position – that’s just one of many”.
Milei portrayed Trump’s response as a “threat” that was “not innocuous”.
“The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina is a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said. He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK immediately condemned Milei’s comments, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.
Speculation about a US switch of allegiance over the islands has been swirling for months.
In April, a leaked Pentagon email suggested reviewing Britain’s claim in response to its lack of support for Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. Trump is also unhappy with what he says is the small amount spent on defence by Nato alliance countries.
A switch of US position would represent a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands.
After Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, the decision by Margaret Thatcher’s government to dispatch a naval taskforce that eventually resulted in their recovery was bolstered by staunch diplomatic support from Ronald Reagan, who came down on Britain’s side, even though Washington was also an ally of the Argentinian ruling military junta.
Additional reporting by Robert Tait and Tiago Rogero

Russia to strip contract soldiers of one-off payment if laws violated at home
- Russia plans to reclaim part of the one-off payment from contract soldiers found guilty of criminal offences at home to encourage legal compliance.
- Soldiers receive a minimum of 400,000 roubles for signing one-year contracts to fight in Ukraine, with payouts sometimes reaching millions depending on the region.
- Domestic violence cases involving soldiers have increased, prompting the defence ministry's proposal amid reports of hundreds of such incidents since the 2022 invasion.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia’s defence ministry wants to claim back part of a one-off payout from contract service personnel found guilty of criminal offences at home, a document showed, amid increasing cases of domestic violence among those fighting Russia’s war on Ukraine.
Russia provides a minimum one-off payment of 400,000 roubles (S$5,900) for soldiers signing at least a one-year contract to fight in the war with Ukraine that Moscow calls “a special military operation”. Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
In practice, one-off payouts may reach a few million roubles per soldier, depending on the region, in addition to a monthly salary. Russia is also reducing sentences for those serving time in prison in exchange for signing up for the war, among other benefits, as it seeks to bolster army numbers.
Russia has seen a rise in domestic violence as fighters return home for leave, and the defence ministry wants to claim part of the one-off payments “in order to increase the motivation of military personnel to comply with the law”, in case of a criminal offence, a draft law published on Sept 7 showed.
If active contract service members are found guilty of a criminal offence which does not imply a prison sentence, they should pay back a portion of the one-off payout based on the months of the service left, the document showed.
Russia does not disclose official statistics on domestic violence committed by its service personnel but independent media, citing military courts data, reported hundreds of such cases, including murders, since the start of the 2022 invasion. REUTERS

By the time she died last week at the age of 92, Gloria Steinem had become almost synonymous with the modern feminist movement in the US.
The arc of Steinem’s life – and activism – was a long one. From going undercover as a Playboy bunny to becoming a radical publisher bringing feminism into the mainstream. She was a fearless reproductive rights campaigner. In Ms Magazine she wrote about having an abortion – and encouraged other famous women, and readers, to do the same to break the stigma around it.
Stateside host Carter Sherman tells Annie Kelly that Steinem’s legacy as an icon is secure – but that, at the time she died, many of the rights she fought so hard for are under attack. “Obviously, Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022. Nearly half of US states have some sort of abortion ban in effect at this time, and Gloria Steinem talked about feeling really angry that this was still a fight that was going on in her later years.”

Merz has no good answers as the far right targets his downfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — Germany’s far right is moving to turn its landslide election victory into a knockout blow against Friedrich Merz and his beleaguered conservatives — and the chancellor appears at a loss over how to respond.
Merz seemed to have no clear plan for saving himself and his party as his government confronted its biggest political crisis yet, beyond ambiguous promises to become a better, more empathetic politician 16 months into his chancellorship.
“We are all deeply shocked,” Merz said Monday, after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) reached a new high in Saxony-Anhalt’s weekend election while support for his Christian Democratic Union fell by more than half. “This is the worst election defeat the CDU has suffered in years — or even decades,” the chancellor added. “Of course, there will have to be consequences.”
Advertisement
But what those consequences will be remains uncertain. Merz’s dismal approval ratings and the AfD’s convincing win have fueled speculation that his conservatives could seek a Kanzlertausch, or “chancellor swap,” to revive their political fortunes. But Merz said Monday that he would remain in office and stay the course on economic reforms he argues are long overdue and will, with time, solve the country’s economic problems.
The AfD has made little secret of its intent to turn the election loss into a still greater debacle for Merz. The far-right party is openly courting conservative lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt to defect and join its ranks — a strategy aimed not only at securing the three additional seats it needs to govern alone, but also at fracturing the conservatives and breaking Merz’s control of his party.
“The conservative bloc will never again be able to win a federal election, that is a fact,” AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel said in Berlin on Monday. “The gap between us and them is already at 10 percent, and my stated goal is to significantly widen that gap in the shortest possible time.”
Merz on Monday acknowledged that he is part of the problem. Only 9 percent of people voting in Saxony-Anhalt approved of his performance as chancellor, according to one exit poll for German public television.
“I know that my persona, too, has been a recurring topic in this election campaign,” Merz said. Germans are anxious about their economic wellbeing and security in turbulent times, he went on, adding: “We must try — myself included — to connect more deeply with people, including their full range of emotions.”
Under pressure
The pressure on Merz is likely only to build in the next weeks, particularly as elections loom in two eastern regions on Sept. 20. Merz’s CDU is headed for clear defeat in the state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where the AfD is ahead of all other parties. In Berlin, where the CDU is currently governing, the party is likely to fall out of power to a coalition of left-wing parties.
Advertisement
With four more state elections set for next year, conservatives face a clear choice: continue confronting the rising far right under a deeply unpopular chancellor, or fundamentally change course with a new leader at the helm.
Merz appeared to acknowledge the dilemma his party is facing. “This election result is causing major upheaval, not only in our country, but also within my party,” he said Monday. “I take this extremely seriously, and I intend to do my best over the coming days and weeks to personally address the gravity of the situation.”
While most of the talk of replacing Merz is taking place in private, signs of conservative dissatisfaction with Merz’s leadership are beginning to spill out into the open.
Alice Weidel speaks to the media in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
“Anyone who wants to regain trust and credibility must, in the wake of such a result, question everything,” CDU lawmaker Sepp Müller wrote in a social media post.
“After a result like this, we cannot simply carry on as usual,” Gordon Schnieder, the CDU state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate, wrote on X. “If the democratic center wants to regain trust, we must start with ourselves. It is not up to the people to better understand our politics. We must deliver what people expect from politics: less conflict, clear decisions, and concrete results.”
‘Matter of compassion’
The AfD is attacking the chancellor on multiple policy fronts — hitting him on migration, blaming his energy policies for the country’s industrial malaise and pushing for the restoration of cheap energy flows from Russia.
Advertisement
But many of the AfD’s most effective attacks are merely tactical.
Even as the AfD seeks to win power in Saxony-Anhalt by attempting to peel off conservative defectors, the party is presenting itself as willing to work with the CDU, knowing full well that Merz would not sanction a collapse of the “firewall” that keeps centrist parties from cooperating with the far right.
This allows the AfD to simultaneously attack Merz as ignoring the will of the people in the face of the party’s surging popularity, while also depicting conservatives as leftists in disguise for preferring to work with an array of left-wing parties.
The election in Saxony-Anhalt illustrates the strategic dilemma the CDU faces — and one the AfD is benefiting from. To avoid governing with the AfD, the CDU would theoretically have to work with every other party in state parliament, all of them on the political left, including the far left. As conservatives buckle under the strain of governing alongside ideological opposites, the AfD hopes that growing divisions over the firewall will ultimately bring about Merz’s downfall.
“People have lost confidence in the party,” the AfD’s Weidel said Monday. “Before elections, they always promise one thing. And after the elections, they do the exact opposite. And that’s how every party loses the acceptance and trust of its voters. No chancellor before has been as unpopular as Friedrich Merz, who has become a major obstacle to Germany’s prosperous development.”
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national leader, said that if the CDU does not abandon the firewall, it would mark the party’s end. If the party “continue down this path,” he said, “then in the short term there will no longer be a CDU in eastern Germany.”
Advertisement
While these AfD’s attack lines are proving highly effective, Merz offered no clear plan on Monday for countering them — other than, in effect, becoming a better politician.
“This isn’t just a matter of rational political understanding — it’s also a matter of compassion, empathy, and emotions,” a somber-sounding Merz told reporters in Berlin. “I’m not the type to wear my emotions on my sleeve every day, but the public wants to see different answers.”
He acknowledged he had failed to connect with voters — but suggested there was still time for him to learn.
“It’s certainly true that I have this problem — and you can see it in the polls — that many people don’t follow me in my thinking and in how I assess things,” Merz said. “That’s my responsibility, and I accept it. I’ll try to do things differently — to do better — in the coming weeks and months.”
The question is whether his party will be that patient.

Nigel Farage exploring Ukraine visit, Reform officials say

LONDON — Nigel Farage’s critics have long accused him of having a weakness on Vladimir Putin. Now Reform UK wants to tee up a visit to Ukraine.
Two party officials told POLITICO on Monday that discussions have been held between the party and Ukrainian contacts about the prospect of a trip for the Reform leader.
Farage’s opponents often hurl at him comments he made back in 2014 that he “admired” the Russian president as an “operator.” Then, a decade later, he triggered a mid-general election backlash by claiming it was the West that “provoked” Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Polling carried out by More in Common last year suggests that while every voting group in Britain overwhelmingly backs Ukraine, only 26 percent believe that Farage feels the same. Some 21 percent reckon he sympathizes more with Russia.
But Reform hopes it could go some way to dispelling that perception by arranging for Farage to visit Ukraine.
“I know it’s been discussed,” said a first official, whose comment was backed up by a second official. Both were granted anonymity to discuss plans yet to be finalized.
Neither could say at what level the talks have been held. Reform declined to comment, as did the Ukrainian Embassy.
The first official said they believe a visit could go some way to dispelling the impression Farage has any sympathy for Putin — but warned a visit could “piss off a lot of our members.”
Advertisement
Separate research by Opinium last year suggests that Reform voters are significantly more skeptical about continued British support for Ukraine than backers of other parties.
Should the visit go ahead, it would mark the latest attempt from Farage to distance himself from his past statements. In October, he called Putin “a very bad dude” and said the U.K. should shoot down Moscow’s jets that enter British airspace.
The most maximalist ambition for a visit to Kyiv would be a meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself, though officials declined to comment on whether that prospect had been discussed.
Guidance from the Foreign Office, which isn’t facilitating parliamentarian travel to Ukraine, warns against any travel to most of Ukraine because of the assessed risk to British nationals. A Whitehall official pointed out this advice applies to MPs as well as regular Brits.
It would not be unheard of for opposition leaders to visit the Ukrainian president: Keir Starmer did it while Rishi Sunak was prime minister in 2023.
Reform has been arranging a series of visits, due to take place later this year, with international allies, including Marine Le Pen, the president of France’s far-right National Rally party.
Advertisement
Le Pen would be French president if she wins next year’s elections. Jordan Bardella, who played a big role in Reform’s party conference in Birmingham last weekend, would be her pick for prime minister.

The least free place on earth: Occupied Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

People play chess in a park in front of a sculpture reading "Russian Spring" in the Russian-occupied Crimean city of Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
No political rights. No freedom of expression. No protection from secret detention without access to family, an attorney or a physician. No protection from deportation.
Welcome to Russia-occupied Ukraine.
For the second year running, U.S.-based democracy tracker Freedom House has listed Ukraine’s occupied eastern and southern territories as the most unfree places in the world — outranking South Sudan, North Korea and the Gaza Strip.
Advertisement
Inhabitants here are subject to repressive Russian legislation, including forcibly imposed citizenship and the use of antiterrorism laws against political dissidents and religious minority groups, Freedom House says. And it is this system of surveillance, repression, indoctrination and statetheft that pushes occupied Ukraine to the top of the list.
Discriminatory policies publicly encoded in Russian law permeate every aspect of residents’ lives — measures that appear to be changing the region’s demographics. Russia is “deliberately changing the ethnic composition so as to destroy a culture or tip the political balance in favor of another group,” the report notes.
International humanitarian law forbids any occupying power from introducing permanent changes to territories it occupies, particularly in demographic, social and economic domains. But Moscow claims these areas are not occupied — they are simply a part of Russia, and therefore subject to Russian law.
“This occupation is one of the most well-documented systems of repression, oppression and human rights violations because so much is put on the public record,” said Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission to Ukraine. “This is a systemic approach to restricting people’s rights and fundamental freedoms.”
The regime has “all the signs of cultural genocide,” said journalist Andrii Dikhtiarenko, a native of now-occupied eastern Ukraine.
Advertisement
From passportization to deportation
Starting from 2014, Russia has occupied about 20 percent of Ukraine in the country’s south and east — land Moscow calls “new historical territories.” And one of the processes aiding the Russification of these areas is passportization.
By officially designating Ukrainians living in Russia-occupied territories as “foreigners,” occupation authorities compel them to obtain Russian citizenship — which they can do through simplified procedures — in order to access essential rights, such as health care, social services, employment or property ownership.
For Liudmila Chub, it all began with her job. Speaking to POLITICO, Chub said that in 2023, she was told by her employer in Melitopol — located in the occupied Kherson region — that she had to obtain a Russian passport to keep working in his shop, or he would be fined. Chub went to the passport office, where she recorded an angry video about being forced to get a “chicken passport” — a dig at the two-headed Russian eagle emblem. The office’s security guard marched her straight to the occupation police.
A man waits for documentation to apply for a new Russian passport at a center in Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region in August 2022. | AFP via Getty Images
Chub spent the next eight months in detention in Kherson, with the courts regularly extending her arrest, alleging she was breaking military curfew. She was eventually given a statement to read out on camera, saying she did not want to live in Russia, then was allowed 15 minutes to collect items from her apartment and transported under armed guard to Russia’s border with Georgia.
Deported from the home she lived in her whole life, Chub still considers herself fortunate. She said others she encountered in prison had gone through the process of obtaining Russian citizenship only to be charged with spying or treason under Russian law, which carries huge sentences.
“They tie this passport to you, and then with it, they make you traitors to their country,” she said. “Everything in me was opposed to getting that passport, and it’s lucky I didn’t get it. That saved me.”
Advertisement
HRMMU has so far documented over 400 such detentions involving treason- and espionage-related charges in Russia-occupied territories, but it’s impossible to track numbers for incommunicado detention.
That is what happened to 59-year-old IT specialist Serhii Gryshchenkov from Sevastopol in occupied Crimea. After Russian security forces took him from his home in May 2025, Gryshchenkov’s family was unable to find out where he was, his daughter Darina told POLITICO. Her father, who did not hide his pro-Ukraine position, was held incommunicado and tortured for a year before eventually being charged with treason in June 2026, she said. The family does not know the details of the charges.
According to Darina, when her father reappeared in pretrial prison, he spoke of fellow prisoners who were still being secretly held after three or four years. “Their relatives don’t even know whether they are alive.”
One strategy encouraging demographic change in Ukraine’s occupied territories is the official confiscation of homes belonging to residents who fled the war, ensuring they cannot return.
Ukrainians who try to comply with this new rule and travel back home have fallen afoul of Russian “filtration,” faced with arrests and entry bans at Moscow’s Sheremetevo airport — the only possible entry point to get to occupied territories, as land borders are closed to them.
Journalist Olena — who was granted anonymity over security concerns regarding her relatives living under occupation — told POLITICO she had fled occupied Donetsk with her family in 2014. Helped by a sympathetic condominium manager, she had paid the utility bills for her own and her parents’ apartments for the next 12 years, hoping one day they could come home.
Later, Olena found out via occupation media that she had been publicly blacklisted as an “enemy.” Meanwhile, an acquaintance of hers was served a 50-year entry ban at Sheremetevo when trying to get back to her home in occupied Ukraine.
People dance at an outdoor bar in Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
With this new law, “nothing can help us,” said Olena.
According to HRMMU monitoring, more than 60,000 private properties in occupied Ukraine have been identified as “ownerless” as of July this year. At least 6,500 of those properties have been expropriated, often given to veterans of Russia’s “special military operation” or sold to immigrants from Russia under preferential terms.
The effect of this has heavily impacted education in the region, with the introduction of a militarized Russian curriculum in schools. New textbooks teach the Kremlin’s official narrative that the occupied regions never supported Ukrainian independence and were always Russian. Parents who refuse to enroll their children in these schools, or enroll them in online Ukrainian education, are fined and threatened with losing parental rights.
These educational institutions can sometimes funnel students straight into the Russian armed forces. Once an individual holds a Russian passport — which the enforced system makes almost impossible to survive without — they can be drafted to fight against Ukraine. A practice that, like deportation, is explicitly prohibited by the Geneva Conventions.
The cumulative effect of all these measures has been the eradication of visible expressions of Ukrainian identity and wider dissent, said journalist Dikhtiarenko. “People who want to survive have to accept the rules of the game.”
Over at HRMMU, Bell’s worst fear is that the world will stop hearing about or noticing these violations. “When the climate becomes that coercive and that restrictive, and people are that silenced, that’s when we stop seeing the reports because people stop daring to speak out,” she said.
As more time passes, some inhabitants wonder whether there will be anything Ukrainian left, even if their home ever comes back under Kyiv’s control. However, despite their enforced Russian citizenship, Dikhtiarenko said the majority of residents still hold on to their Ukrainian passports, hiding them under floorboards or buried in the garden.

====================================================================================================

Ceuta crisis forces Europe’s migrant-rights groups to rethink their playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Spanish national police officers stand as migrants wait during a distribution of food by volunteers at an industrial site in Ceuta on Sept. 2, 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The political reaction to the surge of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta laid bare how sharply Europe’s migration debate has shifted, and how it’s forcing migrant-rights groups to rethink the way they make their case.
Where previous migration crises often divided European leaders between calls for solidarity and demands for tougher controls, the response to Ceuta — where more than 100 people died last month as they tried to enter — was strikingly uniform.
From the far right to the center left, political leaders overwhelmingly called for stronger borders and more effective deterrence.
Advertisement
“The conversation around migration and the language used to refer to migrants has changed in many EU countries, even center-left member states,” said Michele LeVoy, director of the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a network of organizations that advocate for unauthorized migrants across Europe.
In response, migrant-rights groups are changing tactics. As humanitarian appeals lose political traction, they are turning more heavily to the courts, building broader alliances and experimenting with new ways to talk about migration.
“We’re trying to be stronger together by working with organizations from across civil society, working with lawyers to challenge litigation, and really showing that these policies are bad for everyone, not just migrants,” LeVoy added.
From rescue to deterrence
In 2013, the death of hundreds of migrants in a shipwreck off the Italian island of Lampedusa shocked the continent.
Top EU officials, including then-Commission President José Manuel Barroso, traveled to the site to declare that “the European Union cannot accept that thousands of people die at its borders.”
The bloc’s then-Home Affairs Commissioner Cecilia Malmström called for a “change of approach towards migration,” adding that “this restrictive approach is not sustainable and that it is now time to move towards more openness and solidarity.”
Advertisement
The 2015 refugee crisis initially generated a similarly humanitarian reaction, with German Chancellor Angela Merkel calling on Europeans to welcome more than 1 million people fleeing war in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The European Commission sought to manage the crisis through measures including the redistribution of asylum seekers among EU countries.
But that approach ran into resistance from figures like then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Poland’s Law and Justice party.
Florian Trauner, an expert on EU migration at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the College of Europe, said a handful of right-wing politicians succeeded in establishing an “institutional deadlock” that halted EU efforts to integrate migrants and allowed for a “wider shift to a more restrictive, control-oriented approach to migration.”
José Manuel Barroso attends a press conference at Lampedusa Airport on Oct. 9, 2013. | Tullio M. Puglia/Getty Images
That evolution is visible in the EU’s response to Ceuta. Center-left figures like Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen echoed right-wing Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s call for a more robust defense of the bloc’s external borders, and twenty-two EU leaders signed onto a letter demanding a coordinated effort to “deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen likewise stressed that “control of our European borders matters.” Without mentioning the rising death toll, she instead celebrated the fact that “not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU.”
The far-right factor
The bloc’s shift on migration has been accelerated by the rise of far-right parties and a scramble by centrist rivals to neutralize them by embracing parts of their agenda.
Advertisement
“The buffer zone that once separated the democratic right from the far right has effectively disappeared,” said Estrella Galán, a European Parliament lawmaker with the far-left Left group who is the shadow rapporteur on the EU’s return regulation.
As hard-line positions have gone mainstream, the far-right has started to push for further measures, including “remigration” — the removal of immigrants from Europe.
“As their policies have become widely accepted, the far-right groups have moved further and further right on other issues,” said Trauner.
Hungarian border police officiers patrol the Hungarian-Serbian border on Dec. 15, 2022. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration’s approach to migration — including large-scale deportations — “has given legitimacy to European actors who have been able to reject criticism by pointing out that the world’s major international power is embracing the exact same position,” Trauner said.
Helena Maleno, spokesperson for Caminando Fronteras, an NGO that defends migrants’ rights along the western Euro-African border, said her group was increasingly being targeted by the far right.
“There is a total dehumanization of migrants, especially if they’re Muslims,” she said. “We have had to reinforce protection and security — from digital attacks, but also from threats to our physical safety.”
Advertisement
The far right, however, argues that migrant-rights groups have not lost influence — and still have too much of it.
“I wish we could speak of the failure of pro-immigration NGOs, but what happened in Ceuta proves they have not failed,” said Jorge Buxadé, a European Parliament lawmaker from Spain’s Vox party.
He accused migrants’ rights groups of being “21st-century pirates” who use “hybrid warfare” to undermine Spain’s territorial integrity.
A Polish border guard stands at the Polish-Belarusian border on July 21, 2025. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
“Billions of euros every year go toward funding the structure and influence of organizations whose sole interest is ensuring that immigration to Europe remains massive and uncontrolled,” he said.
Change in tactics
In the new climate, the humanitarian argument traditionally used by rights groups — that migrants are human beings in need of protection — no longer carries the same political weight, said LeVoy.
Increasingly, NGOs have found themselves on the defensive, fighting criminal sanctions and restrictions on their activities rather than shaping the broader debate.
Advertisement
That pressure is pushing migrant-rights groups to rethink where — and how — they fight.
One response is to take the battle into the courts, investing resources in legal challenges to restrictive legislation, including EU rules governing returns and the criminalization of assistance to undocumented migrants.
Migrant-rights groups are also seeking to broaden their alliances. In Spain, the recent push to grant legal status to hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants was backed by support from the country’s conservative employers’ association and the Catholic Church.
Migrants from various detention centers across Italy are escorted by police upon arrival in Shëngjin, Albania on April 11, 2025. | Adnan Beci/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s more important than ever to be in strong coalitions,” LeVoy said. Her group is also reaching out to local authorities, health professionals and housing organizations.
LeVoy advocated for shifting the narrative on migration by focusing less on dangerous sea crossings or dramatic border surges. Instead, she argued, rights groups should highlight the much larger population of unauthorized migrants already living alongside Europeans.
She likened the strategy to that of successful campaigns for marriage equality, which sought to change public perceptions by presenting LGBTQ+ people not as an abstract political constituency but as friends, colleagues and neighbors.
Advertisement
“Borders are really a very small part of this issue, because the overwhelming majority [of Europe’s unauthorized migrants] come in regularly,” LeVoy said.
Caminando Fronteras has likewise reinforced its legal work and security measures and built transnational networks with other rights groups.
But Maleno said her NGO was also staying true to its long-standing commitment to amplify the voices of families whose relatives have died or disappeared at Europe’s borders.
“We will continue to work to make the public administrations listen,” she said. “Europe will one day have to account for all those deaths and disappearances.”
